Mark Brinkley declined to tell Air & Space Forces Magazine exactly how many FQ-42s are rolling off the company’s production line right now, but did confirm production is underway. “Some of those aircraft will become company aircraft,” he said, meaning that not all are for its Air Force customer.
Brinkley said the company’s potential production expansion could be used to answer international demand for its Gambit series of autonomous drones, which are closely related to the FQ-42.
General Atomics also said in its statement that it is self-funding FQ-42 production today as it awaits Congressional fiscal 2027 appropriations. The new fiscal year launches Oct. 1, but lawmakers failed to pass a budget for fiscal ’27, and instead passed a continuing resolution that would hold current year funding steady, but provides no new funding. The measure ensures funding through Dec. 11, 2026.
GA’s self-funding will help support the government’s procurement plans and prevent delivery delays, the company said, and building aircraft for its own fleet will help it invest in new technologies that reduce risk and increase capabilities.
The Air Force plans to use CCAs as a complement to crewed fighters in a bid to add combat capacity at a lower cost than convention fighter jets. CCAs are designed to be flown semi-autonomously, at times alongside piloted fighters like the F-22 and F-35 Lightning II, and could eventually carry out a variety of missions including air-to-air or air-to-ground strikes; intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance; or electronic warfare operations. The concept is still comparatively early in its development.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 that USAF is aiming to field at least 500 CCAs by 2032. The Anduril and General Atomics CCAs were selected following a competition in April 2024, andboth companies won initial production contracts in June 2026.
General Atomics said a new FQ-42 was delivered to Creech Air Force Base, Nev., on Sept. 18, for test and evaluation. Creech is home to the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit, which has been experimenting with CCAs to develop approaches to how they might be employed in real-life operations.
Jason Levin, Anduril’s senior vice president for air dominance and strike, said Sept. 14 that his firm delivered an FQ-44 to the EOU in August. Prior to that, the YFQ-44A prototype took part in two exercises with the EOU, the first in April and the second in July.
The July exercise at Creech, Levin said, demonstrated that CCA had advanced enough for a single Air Force operator to launch and recover an aircraft on his own after just a few hours of training.
“The Air Force was operating mission autonomy by themselves, which was a first,” Levin said. “They were flying multiple times a day, operating mission autonomy without Anduril personnel—they were on-site kind of helping, but it was really the Air Force operating that.”
Levin said that during the July exercise, Fury flew in the same airspace as crewed fighters and other drones using mission autonomy, helping build Airmen’s trust that CCAs can operate in congested airspace.
The production model of the FQ-44 that will start to roll off the line next year at Arsenal-1 will be able to carry four air-to-air weapons, such as the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, under its wings.
The FQ-42, General Atomics said, has flown in formation with piloted F-35 Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle jets to prepare for future test flights, when fighter pilots will actually command the drones. The FQ-42 represents fifth-generation stealth and operates with an internal weapons bay.
General Atomics previously conducted flights of its MQ-20 Avenger drone, operating as a CCA surrogate, to demonstrate how collaborative control flights might work. The company said its aircraft, including the Vengeance, Avenger, and XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station, have flown both semi-autonomously and autonomously using AI pilots and under the collaborative control of human pilots flying in the F-22 Raptor and F-35.
“The CCA program’s rate of progress has been incredible,” said Mike Atwood, vice president of advanced programs at General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, in a company statement. “Every week, the Air Force is pushing forward with new and more impressive accomplishments using Vengeance. It’s amazing to think of how far this program has come in such a short amount of time.”

New Zealand says China is its most persistent state-backed cyber threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:38:40 UTC
06:38:40 KST

New Zealand's cyber security agency said China was the country's most persistent and capable state-backed cyber threat, as foreign actors targeted government agencies and organizations in sectors including health, education and information technology.
The National Cyber Security Center (NCSC), part of the New Zealand intelligence community, said it had identified activity suspected to originate from foreign state actors that put sensitive New Zealand information at risk.
It linked suspected state-sponsored cyber activity to actors from China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, according to its annual Cyber Threat Report released on Thursday.
"Of these nations, the People's Republic of China is the most persistent and capable state actor undertaking cyber activity in New Zealand," the report said.
The assessment is the latest warning from a Western-aligned intelligence agency over alleged Chinese cyber espionage, which Beijing has routinely denied. It follows a report from New Zealand’s security agency in August that said that China was the only country New Zealand had detected conducting espionage "at scale."
Chinese state-backed actors accounted for 86 nationally significant cyber attacks
The Cyber Security report said 86 of 369 cyber incidents deemed to be of potential national significance in the year to June 2026 had suspected links to state-sponsored actors. The incidents included activity targeting government agencies, health and education organizations, and IT managed-service providers.
The agency warned that geopolitical competition was increasingly playing out in the South Pacific, where it was aware of state-backed cyber espionage targeting governments and infrastructure.
New Zealand has close family, cultural, political and economic ties across the Pacific, and such activity could affect citizens, businesses and civic institutions, it said.
State-backed actors were likely to target organizations that operate infrastructure or networks, provide essential public services, or hold information that could offer a strategic advantage, the NCSC said.
It warned that cyber espionage can be difficult to detect, with actors conducting reconnaissance and positioning access in systems over months or years before using it for intelligence gathering or disruption.
Long-running intrusions could lead to the compromise of operational technology and the loss of corporate and personal data, it said.

Turkey’s Bashiqa base handover marks a new chapter for post-ISIS Iraq - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:38:13 UTC
06:38:13 KST

Iraq and Turkey have agreed to a framework that will involve Turkish forces handing over a key Turkish military base in Iraq. “Within the framework of the progress achieved by Iraq through security steps, the Turkish forces will gradually hand over the Baashiqa - Zeliqan camp to the Iraqi Federal Government, in accordance with the agreed mechanism and timetable,” Iraq’s Prime Minister’s Office said on September 23.
This is an important step and comes amid many developments in Iraq. Iraq is also trying to rein in Iranian-backed militias. It says this will happen by June of 2027. In addition, the Yazidi YBS armed group has agreed to disarm. The Kurdish Peshmerga also announced a unification of forces this week. As such, Iraq is moving to consolidate federal control over many areas. This will essentially change the landscape of Iraq.
Many of these bases and issues are remnants of the ISIS war. When ISIS invaded Iraq, the Iraqi state collapsed in many parts of Iraq. This was especially true in Sunni areas, as well as in the Nineveh Plains and Sinjar. ISIS carried out a genocide against Yazidis. As a result, the Iranian-backed militias were empowered to fight ISIS. The Kurdish Peshmerga also stepped forward to take up hundreds of miles of the front line. Turkey expanded its role in Iraq.
Turkey claimed to be expanding its role because it was fighting the PKK
Turkey claimed to be expanding its role because it was fighting the PKK. However, the Bashiqa Turkish base was something else. It helped support the Peshmerga from the heights overlooking the town of Bashiqa. It was also working with some Sunni Arab forces. Turkey was also keen to monitor what was happening in Sinjar. Ankara feared that PKK-linked groups in Syria and Sinjar might exploit the vacuum in power. It was also wary of PKK-linked elements at Makhmour camp, a Kurdish displaced persons’ camp near Makhmour.
According to the Iraqi prime minister’s office, “the Prime Minister of the Republic of Iraq, Mr. Ali Falih Al-Zaidi, and the President of the Republic of Turkey, Mr. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, met in New York on 23 September 2026.” The report says that “the two sides agreed to deepen cooperation in the security field, during negotiations in which the Iraqi and Turkish authorities discussed the strategic relations between the two countries from all aspects; and in this context, they agreed to extend the full authority of the Iraqi state in Sinjar, and to end the presence of prohibited foreign armed elements.”
The result is also a deal for the Bashiqa camp. This camp had several positions near it. The Jerusalem Post covered this frontline near Bashiqa in 2015-2016. The Turkish forces provided fire support against ISIS. The camp was modern and well maintained. “The two sides also agreed to expand the volume of bilateral trade and investment, the immediate implementation of the signed agreements, and the acceleration of joint strategic projects, especially the Development Road project,” the report says.
The meeting will lead to more Iraqi authority in Sinjar. This is a result of YBS saying it will hand over its weapons and integrate with the Iraqi state. Turkey will be pleased. Turkey is involved in a peace process with the PKK. It wants to see all the PKK-linked groups disarmed as part of this process.
This will be important for the Kurdistan Region
Turkey also has numerous bases in the mountains of the Kurdistan region. Bashiqa camp is not in the mountains. It is on land between Erbil and Dohuk, overlooking the Nineveh Plains. Ankara has numerous posts in the mountains near the border, above the city of Dohuk. This is where Turkey was fighting the PKK for several decades.
Rudaw also reported on the handover. This will be important for the Kurdistan Region. The Turkish forces were controversial in several ways. Iranian-backed militias opposed them and conditioned their disarmament on the Turkish forces leaving. Rudaw says “Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan stressed their mutual commitment to pull back Turkish troops from a base in northeast Mosul established in 2015, a joint statement shared by Zaidi’s office said Wednesday, citing the fulfillment of ‘security measures’ that include ending the presence of proscribed ‘foreign armed elements.’”
The deal also comes as US forces of the anti-ISIS coalition are leaving Iraq. As such, many changes are afoot. Iraq is re-asserting its authority.

V'landys steps down as Racing NSW boss to secure firmer grip on NRL
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:32:17 UTC
06:32:17 KST

Peter V'landys has resigned as NSW Racing chief executive after 22 years at the helm.
The move is set to free V'landys up to become the NRL's executive chairman.
What's next?
An announcement about his appointment could be made as early as today.
Peter V'landys' appointment as NRL executive chairman is set to be made official after the veteran administrator stepped down as Racing NSW chief executive.
V'landys confirmed this morning that he was ending his 22-year stint at the helm of Racing NSW, following a period of long-service leave that ends in November.
His resignation looms as the final step in a process of moving into the NRL full time and taking on the most powerful role in rugby league since the Super League war.
Since taking over as ARL Commission chairman in 2019, V'landys has become an increasingly dominant figure in rugby league.
But this move will see his role grow even further, effectively replacing former NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo in his old position while remaining at the head of the commission.
When Abdo announced his resignation in May, V'landys had said only "Superman and Jesus added together" could replace him.
At the time, V'landys refused to speculate whether that figure could be him, but signalled he would take leave from Racing NSW in July to be able to dedicate time to the NRL.
In the months since, the 64-year-old has garnered the support required from both the clubs and the states to allow him to take on the role.
Fellow commissioners have also approved the move, with the appointment now expected to be made official as early as today.
Since the creation of the independent ARL Commission in 2012, no person has held the role of chairman and executive on a full-time basis.
V'landys had been chief executive of Racing NSW since early 2004, after previously spending 17 years as boss of NSW Harness Racing.
He led the racing industry through the equine influenza outbreak, with the creation of The Everest in 2017 among his other key legacies.
"Naturally, this is a very sad day for me. I have put my heart and soul into racing for 22 years. I have been fortunate to work with outstanding, loyal and hardworking boards of directors and staff," V'landys said.
"As a team, we went from a struggling jurisdiction to a world-leading jurisdiction. I take this opportunity to thank everyone who has been in our team. I will miss them greatly, and I wish the industry every success."
In a statement, Racing NSW said V'landys's "many initiatives" had procured $3.5 billion in new funding.
Racing NSW chair Saranne Cooke said his contribution to racing was without parallel.
"Peter V'landys has been, without doubt, the most effective and successful administrator in the history of Australian sport," Dr Cooke said.
"His contribution cannot simply be measured by the extraordinary growth of racing in NSW during his tenure.
"Peter has fundamentally changed the trajectory of racing in this country and made NSW one of the world's leading racing jurisdictions."
Waterhouse says right time to move on
Horse racing legend Gai Waterhouse said it was the right time for V'landys to move on.
Waterhouse came up against V'Landys amidst his failed attempt to sell Rosehill Racecourse in Sydney to the State Government to build residential housing.
The battle saw the two prominent industry figures disagree about the sport's future, with Waterhouse successfully campaigning among Australian Turf Club members not to sell the track, despite Premier Chris Minns and V'Landys pushing to sell the site.
"A lot of money has gone into buying properties that should have been funded back into development of the race tracks and stands," Waterhouse said.
"If we're going to be able to attract people back to the races, they have to be comfortable."
Waterhouse was especially concerned about the state of regional racetracks.
"They've been shockingly neglected over the tenure of Mr V'landys, and they need to have money spent on them," she said.
Waterhouse said his expected move to rugby league from horse racing had come at the right time.
"He's a very strong and very powerful person, but it's time for him to move and he has moved on. So let's move on now," she said.

Moscow’s Ceasefire Bingo Card – What Might the Kremlin Say to Ukraine’s Unconditional Ceasefire?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:31:00 UTC
06:31:00 KST

Ukraine unveiled an unconditional ceasefire proposal on Wednesday, Sept. 23, backed by 50 countries in a joint statement.
Now the key question – how will Russia respond? Russia’s Foreign Minister Lavrov has already ruled out a ceasefire during peace talks – but how will Moscow react to an unconditional ceasefire as a whole?
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Instead of guessing what Moscow will say, here’s a bingo card of what it might say, based on past statements on similar proposals.
Or it could be a combination of different points; who knows.
“Ukraine already violated it”
Russia has in the past moved the starting date earlier, then blamed Ukraine for violating a ceasefire before it was agreed.
The more recent example came in the form of US President Donald Trump’s energy truce, when he claimed both Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to it when, in fact, they had not. Before Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov snubbed it as a “very good idea” a day later, he also accused Ukraine of attacking Russian energy facilities.
But there was never an energy truce, not to mention that Russia had also hit two gas stations in Kyiv the same morning.
Similar patterns were observed in most ceasefire agreements, with both Kyiv and Moscow accusing one another of violations, including the so-called energy truce in March 2025, when Moscow said Ukraine had violated it by moving the starting date, or during Moscow’s May 9 parade, when no one really understood what ceasefire meant on the front.
Russia Must Answer for Crimes in Crimea, Zelensky Says
That’s why the “unconditional” part of the latest proposal matters.
“Good idea. But…”
Here comes the Putin classic – saying yes and meaning no.
One such case happened in March 2025, when Trump pushed for a 30-day ceasefire after his return to office.
In response to that proposal, Putin said the 30-day ceasefire proposal is “good and we absolutely support it but there are issues that we need to discuss” before questioning the effectiveness of the proposal, naming a number of “conditions that need to be studied,” such as the enforcement of the ceasefire along the front.
The result was the 30-day energy truce – see how it worked out in the previous section.
“How about we try something else?”
Remember the Istanbul talks?
A short recap – in the summer of 2025, the EU issued an ultimatum to Putin to move toward an unconditional 30-day ceasefire or face massive sanctions. Putin countered with a plan to resume what he called the Istanbul format, based on early negotiations in 2022 during the first days of the full-scale invasion.
Putin was a no-show and sent a historian in his place who reportedly threatened the Ukrainian delegation. The format, including multiple negotiations, resulted in prisoner swaps but not the ceasefire envisioned.
And good for Putin – without the promised massive sanctions either.
Another example would be August 2025’s Alaska summit, when Trump threatened Putin with massive secondary tariffs, with the two ultimately agreeing to a summit in Alaska instead that earned Putin first-class treatment on US soil after being ostracized since 2022.
Again, no sanctions and tariffs as promised. A win-win for Putin.
“Ukraine doesn’t really want it”
Sometimes it’s as easy as blaming Ukraine for impeding the process without saying how.
“Representatives of the Kyiv regime, the leadership in Kyiv, speak of peace and propose resuming so-called negotiations, but themselves commit such crimes, doing everything to ensure that there is no peace and no negotiations,” Putin told Russia’s Military-Industrial Commission on Sept. 18.
Which raises the question – what exactly should Ukraine do then?
Bonus: Setting out unmeetable conditions
Russia also has a habit of highballing other parties in negotiations, setting conditions that some might consider outrageous.
If the opponents relent and cave in – that’s a win. If they don’t? Blame them for failing to meet the conditions.
A recurring example would be asking Zelensky to come to Moscow for a Putin meeting to settle things once and for all. Another would be to tell Kyiv to withdraw from territories it still controls – that Moscow failed to win for 12 years – as a precondition for peace talks.
Again, this is why the “unconditional” part of the new proposal matters.
“Sure, let’s stop”
If only we had heard this, then perhaps thousands, if not millions, of Ukrainians and Russians would still be alive today.

Ravi Kant is an author, columnist and analyst whose work focuses on technology, economics, international politics and geopolitics. 
A country’s diaspora can be a symbol of its pride and power. A nation’s diaspora can help it build international value through success stories, promote its soft power through culture and contribute to its economic progress through remittances, investments and transfers of expertise.
India and China have among the world’s largest diasporas. They also offer two very different models of how countries can leverage their diasporas.
In India, before the 1991 reforms, people mostly saw those who left as a “brain drain”. But post-liberalisation, people started to see the Indian diaspora as an economic bridge to capital, technology and global markets. In 2004, India set up a ministry to oversee the affairs of Indians abroad, merging it with the Ministry of External Affairs in 2016.

Pupils to be offered vocational GCSEs in radical shake-up of system in England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:30:01 UTC
06:30:01 KST

Teenagers are to be offered a range of new vocational GCSEs under a radical shake-up of the school system in England designed to tackle a crisis that has left nearly a million young people out of work or training.
From 2029, pupils will be able to supplement compulsory GCSE subjects such as English, maths and sciences with courses such as construction, creative media production and child development, marking the biggest changes to the qualification for more than a decade.
The Department for Education (DfE) said the new GCSEs would be two-year courses taken in year 10 and 11, “with nationally set content, grading and assessment” and regulated by Ofqual, England’s qualifications watchdog, to the same standards as academic GCSEs.
The courses are part of an effort by Andy Burnham to fulfil his pledge of “an education system that offers a path for everybody, academic and technical, in equal balance”, made the day after his election as MP for Makerfield.
Announcing the new courses, the prime minister said: “We’ve all heard someone say ‘school wasn’t really for me’ because they were not given the chance to study vocational courses as well as traditional subjects.
“That one-size-fits-all approach isn’t working, so we’re building an education system that values both academic and technical paths. I want to give all young people across Britain the hope that their future will be brighter, whether it starts at university or not.”
Whitehall sources said the courses were expected to be offered from September 2029 but that the education secretary, Lucy Powell, wanted to move more quickly if possible, with schools given the option to add vocational GCSEs to their existing subjects.
Powell said: “Time and again young people, parents and employers tell me they want schools to do more to help them understand and prepare for the jobs of the future. Our new vocational GCSEs will give young people a stronger connection to the careers and industries shaping our economy, helping them discover and develop their talents while maintaining high standards across our education system.
“This is not about creating different routes for different children. It is about ensuring every child has access to a rich and ambitious education that opens doors, creates opportunity and prepares them for life beyond the classroom.”
The change is part of a range of measures that Burnham has announced since coming to power to tackle the Neets crisis, with a call to “value the hard hat as much as the graduation cap”. It follows plans to give local businesses a role in setting curriculums in their areas.
In a review published in May, Alan Milburn said that without significant change the number of young people not in work or education could grow by 25% by the early 2030s, opening up a “generational fault line” between the young and old.
Critics, however, say the focus on technical education risks widening the gap between richer and poorer children. Sam Freedman, a policy adviser to Michael Gove when he was education secretary, wrote last month: “The more we ration a full set of academic GCSEs to children from better-off families, the more we will bake in existing inequalities.”
The shadow education secretary, Laura Trott, said the courses would mean lowered expectations for disadvantaged children who had benefited most from high standards.
“Labour are sabotaging young people’s futures,” she said. “Just weeks after the latest Pisa results showed England’s pupils climbing into the world’s top 10 for reading, maths and science, they want to rip up the system and review existing GCSEs.
“Soaring up international league tables didn’t happen by accident. It followed years of evidence-led reform built around knowledge, rigour and high expectations. Labour risks throwing that progress away and if English, maths and science become merely a ‘common entitlement’, not a requirement for new qualifications, we risk repeating the mistakes of the past.”
The DfE said the subjects offered could include management and finance, creative media production, digital technology and building and construction, and would be designed to lead into further study including A-levels.
The new GCSEs will replace the level-two vocational and technical awards offered by some schools in England, with travel and tourism and health and care courses among the most popular. About 350,000 technical awards and certificates were issued this year, compared with more than 5m GCSEs.
School leaders said the success of the new courses would depend on having the resources and staffing to teach specialist subjects.
The general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, Pepe Di’Iasio, said: “Reshaping and rebadging vocational and technical qualifications is well intentioned but will not in itself address the barriers to more young people taking these subjects. Reform needs to be accompanied by a strategy to ensure that schools have the staffing and resources to deliver them, and a campaign to raise public awareness of vocational and technical routes.”
The general secretary of the National Education Union, Daniel Kebede, agreed. “These proposed changes will fall at the first hurdle unless there is sufficient investment in schools and the workforce,” he said.
The general secretary of the NAHT school leaders’ union, Paul Whiteman, said: “In recent years, the content behind too many GCSEs became unwieldy and the over-reliance on final exams did not play to the strengths of all students.
“It will be crucial these pitfalls are avoided in developing these qualifications and that the government works closely with educators, local leaders and employers to ensure they offer high-quality learning which sets young people up for future training, education or employment.”
The government has also said it will launch a “national mission” by calling on employers to provide an additional 200,000 work experience placements to give young people exposure to the workplace by age 16. No 10 North will offer work experience for students aged 14 to 16 this academic year.

Tories target universal credit claimants in plan condemned as ‘fast track to poverty’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:30:01 UTC
06:30:01 KST

People claiming universal credit (UC) would have their payments cut by a third if they have not paid enough national insurance, under a Conservative plan condemned by one charity as “a fast track to increased poverty”.
Under the proposals, those who receive this “subsistence allowance” would have it paid into a dedicated debit card that would prevent from them buying alcohol or tobacco, based on an Australian system that was scrapped after trials found limited evidence it changed behaviour.
While the proposals are billed by the Conservatives as a way to push people into work, the poverty charity Trussell said trimming incomes so that people struggled with rent and transport was likely to make it even harder for them to find and keep a job.
Under the plan, UC claimants would receive the full amount to which they are entitled for six months, but after this point the sum would be tied to how long they have worked at a level that triggers national insurance payments.
This would have to happen for at least twice as long as the claimant period, meaning someone who has amassed two years of NI payments would qualify for another 12 months of full UC, before falling to the lower rate.
Set at 70% of the standard amount, this would leave a single claimant aged under 25 living on £237 a month, or just over £7.50 a day. For a couple aged 25 or over, under the plan they would lose £200 a month, falling to £466 in total.
Anyone placed on the reduced level would have their UC payments put on to a “back to work card”, which would block purchases of alcohol, tobacco and gambling, or cash withdrawals.
The plan would exclude those already in work – about a third of UC claimants have jobs – and those who are assessed as having what is called limited capability for work and work-related activity, because of a health condition or disability. Separate payments connected to housing or dependant children would be unaffected.
The Conservatives said the plan would affect about 350,000 people in England, Scotland and Wales and save £538m a year.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the aim was to be “tough on those who exploit the system”, adding: “Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can’t be bothered.”
The party argues that in some countries such as Germany and the Netherlands, unemployment payments are contingent on sufficient contributions having been made and can be time-limited.
Those payments, however, are notably more generous and can be between 60% and 70% of someone’s previous monthly wage. There is also separate support for those who have not paid in sufficiently, with single people in Germany receiving about £480 a month.
Sara Ogilvie, the director of policy at Child Poverty Action Group, said: “The reality is that families are still paying the price of austerity cuts to our social security safety net. With living costs continuing to rise, these proposals are a fast track to increased poverty and are the last thing people need as they try to get back on their feet.”
Helen Barnard, the head of policy at Trussell, called the idea “deeply misguided”, saying UC already had strong conditions to ensure people seek work.
She said: “If you’re struggling to afford food and rent, childcare or the bus fare to an interview, then finding and keeping a job becomes harder not easier. Cutting support would only make things worse.”

Lula, Bolsonaro and a divided Brazil: A tight race with stakes beyond its borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:28:59 UTC
06:28:59 KST

Washington, DC — A string of right-wing victories across Latin America, from Argentina and Peru to Ecuador and Colombia, has put Brazil’s election under sharper scrutiny. Now the region’s largest country heads to the polls with its own political direction at stake.
The October 4 vote pits President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, nearing the end of his third term, against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former right-wing president Jair Bolsonaro. The contest brings two familiar names and competing visions of Brazil’s future to the ballot.
The divide runs deeper than policy. It cuts through a country where the Lula and Bolsonaro names have become rallying cries on either side of a bitter political struggle.
Recent polls suggest little separates the two candidates, placing them in a statistical tie in simulated runoffs.
Lula is campaigning on a progressive legacy that helped lift millions out of poverty in the 2000s. Bolsonaro carries the conservative banner, seeking to bring Latin America’s rightward shift to its biggest political stage.
Voters are concerned about many issues, yet what makes this election stand out from other regional ones are two things: a corruption case affecting both leading candidates, and the future of the critical Amazon rainforest.
Future of the Amazon rainforest
Although an environmental issue, the concern is being used as a political tool, raising consequential questions in Brazil's presidential race — and testing whether the country can reconcile its economic ambitions with its role as guardian of the world's largest rainforest.
According to government figures, Amazon deforestation fell to its lowest level in a decade in the first half of 2026.
In July of this year, President Lula da Silva laid out a plan to reach zero deforestation by 2030.
Bolsonaro's campaign offers a different approach, describing the environment as a "strategic asset" and proposing expanded payments for environmental services, bioeconomy development, and economic incentives for people who preserve native vegetation.
"It shouldn't go unmissed that in the latest meeting between (President Donald) Trump and Lula in May, critical minerals were absolutely on the agenda, and the future of the Amazon ecosystem," Elizabeth Dickinson, interim deputy director for Latin America at the International Crisis Group, tells TRT World.
The future of critical-mineral extraction in the same areas is central to this election, and whoever wins may well determine the course Brazil sets.
"Whether it's greater acceptance of extractive industries in this critical ecosystem, or whether it is really a focus on those key climate and ecological commitments that have been a pinnacle of Brazilian foreign policy for some time," Dickinson adds.
Election clouded by corruption
The Banco Master corruption scandal casts a shadow over the election.
At its centre is the Central Bank’s extrajudicial liquidation of the lender in November 2025, with missing funds reportedly totalling $2.2 billion.
The fallout has reached both Lula’s and Bolsonaro’s campaigns, deepening voter disillusionment with the choices on the ballot.
"Polling has really sort of been a toss-up throughout this race, and particularly as the corruption scandal has continued to embroil a growing number of officials," Dickinson says.
"These are individuals from the legislature, the courts, the central bank, and so forth."
Former finance minister Fernando Haddad called the scandal potentially the biggest bank fraud in the country's history, and ongoing investigations implicated numerous high-profile political figures across the spectrum.
Potential complete regional shift
Across Brazil, as elsewhere in the region, the campaign is being shaped by concerns that reach beyond party loyalties.
Violence and everyday safety lead voters’ worries, with the economy and corruption also competing for attention. How candidates answer those concerns could prove central to the campaign.
Another question carries weight beyond Brazil’s borders: how closely should the country align with Washington?
The region’s rightward shift has given the US willing partners in Argentina, Peru, Ecuador and Colombia, including support for Washington’s regional security agenda.
Brazil and Mexico have resisted elements of that agenda. Lula has rejected an outside role in tackling Brazil’s organised crime, insisting that international cooperation must respect national sovereignty.
That stance puts him at odds with the Trump administration’s revival of the Monroe Doctrine, the 19th-century policy asserting US primacy in the Americas, as Washington presses to extend its regional influence.
Brazil is one of the few countries with the size, clout, economic power, and foreign policy apparatus to offer a different narrative.
"This election will certainly determine whether that is the case or whether there is really a shift across the region to a more consistent and full-fledged alignment between Latin American leaders and the United States," Dickinson says.
"All politics is local, and that's certainly reflected in the polling."

French court confirms rape trial for PSG and Morocco star Hakimi
A French court on Wednesday upheld a decision to send Paris Saint-Germain and Morocco footballer Achraf Hakimi to trial on rape charges, a judicial source told AFP.
An appeals court confirmed on June 19, during the World Cup, that Hakimi would stand trial in criminal court over the alleged rape of a woman in 2023, an accusation he has repeatedly denied.
Hakimi, 27, had appealed that decision to the Court of Cassation, the highest court in the French judicial system for civil and criminal matters.
The appeal was Hakimi's final legal recourse. In February, he was ordered to stand trial before the criminal court in the Hauts-de-Seine department on the rape charge.
Hakimi challenged that initial order and then appealed to the Court of Cassation after the Versailles appeals court upheld the decision in June.
"The allegations against Achraf Hakimi, which he has firmly contested from day one, have not been examined by the Court of Cassation," the player's lawyer, Fanny Colin, told AFP.
"They will be during the trial, at which all the evidence in Achraf Hakimi's defence will be presented publicly," the lawyer continued.
She added her client, "who has nothing to hide", had fully cooperated with police and judicial authorities throughout the investigation and would continue to do so during the forthcoming trial.
A lawyer for the plaintiff said the decision to send the case to trial reflected the "strength and rigour of the court of appeal's reasoning".
"After three and a half years of legal battles, after being slandered and dragged through the mud by Achraf Hakimi's defence, my client is determined to obtain justice; she will fight to the very end," the woman's lawyer, Rachel-Flore Pardo, said in a statement sent to AFP.
In February 2023, a woman then aged 24 told police in the Val-de-Marne region southeast of Paris that Hakimi had raped her.
The plaintiff said she met Hakimi in January 2023 on Instagram and went to his home in a taxi ordered by the player, a police source said at the time.
She claimed the player kissed her, touched her without her consent and then raped her.
She said she managed to push him away and text a friend, who came to pick her up.
Hakimi was charged with rape a few days later.
PSG said Hakimi "has always firmly denied the allegations against him" and continued to benefit from the presumption of innocence.
"The club is committed to ensuring a calm and respectful working environment for its player, in accordance with the fundamental principles of the rule of law," PSG said in a statement to AFP.
The French champions also reiterated "their constant and unequivocal commitment to combating all forms of violence, particularly sexual violence."

Why rising bond interest rates put downward pressure on share prices
Reader Bond Fan asked earlier this week why rising bond yields, or interest rates, tend to push share prices lower.
This was my answer, in case people are wondering the same thing today.
Fundamentally, it comes down to the way analysts and fund managers value shares in the present based on their discounted future cash flows.
Meghan Shue, the chief investment strategist at US financial services firm Wilmington Trust, explained it well in this note written in 2019.
"First, the current price of a stock is simply the present value of the sum of all future cash flows (earnings plus buybacks plus dividends)," she wrote.
"Interest rates are directly linked to the cost of capital, or the rate used to discount those future cash flows (earnings plus buybacks plus dividends) of a stock or index.
"The lower that discount rate (in the denominator), all else being equal, the higher the present value of any future payouts (those payouts are in the numerator) and the higher the stock price."
Relatedly, lower interest rates also reduce the "opportunity cost" of owning more speculative stocks that don't currently generate an income stream.
"Second, as interest rates move lower, the relative appeal of other income-generating assets — including stocks — increases, even if they carry extra risk over a traditional bond," she explains.
"As interest rates fall, it lowers the 'income opportunity cost' of investing in stocks over bonds."
Meghan Shue goes on to note that, historically, rising interest rates have generally coincided with rising share prices.
Why?
"Most of the time rising rates are good for stocks because the increase in earnings growth expectations — which typically goes along with that increase in rates — tends to overwhelm the higher discount rate (with one exception being a stagflationary scenario of rising inflation and slowing growth)."
Unfortunately, the latter is the scenario many economists are concerned about for Australia and many other advanced economies.
Obviously, part of the rise in bond yields on Wednesday in the US was good economic news, so that probably minimised some of the fallout on the share market.

It was the worst day in nearly 18 months for US government bonds, as the 10-year yield’s rise saw its sharpest one-day jump since April 9, 2025, a week after Trump’s liberation day tariffs.
NAB's Head of FX Strategy Ray Attrill calls this movement a "fresh bond market riot".
"Bond markets are back centre stage with sharp sell-offs across the US and European yield spectrums, the strength of US S&P Global PMIs a key catalyst and later compounded by a poorly received US Treasury 5-year note auction, which saw yields up through 5% for the first time since 2007," he says.
"Unhelpful to the cause has been a recovery in oil prices on renewed pessimism toward a US-Iran deal to re-open the Strait of Hormuz, and reports the US is preparing to ban diesel exports for 90 days.
"Risk sentiment has been sourced by the bond market riot, while the US dollar is stronger across the board as markets become more convinced about additional Fed rate hikes, with October now seen more likely than not for the next one."
Key Event
Half of young Australian adults now living with parents
With this latest data, one would hope young Aussies are getting on with their parents, as 50% of those aged 18 to 29 were still living at home in 2024.
That's up from 39% in 2001.
The data comes from this year's Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) annual survey, the largest longitudinal study of its kind in Australia, which follows the same 17,000 people each year to understand how our lives are changing.
It also found that, as a nation, we are more stressed about housing and money, tired, worried about our cognitive health, and half of us have jobs we're over-qualified for.
But the positive takeaways include high employment, more women holding university degrees, and our long-term relationships being in pretty good health.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Wednesday remarked that it expected Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla to take an "expeditious" decision on a plea seeking the disqualification of 20 rebel TMC MPs who have joined Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI).A bench comprising CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said it was aware that it could not issue a direction to the Lok Sabha Speaker, "but we just want to remind him about an expeditious resolution".Senior advocate Kalyan Banerjee, representing TMC MP Abhishek Banerjee, submitted that the rebel parliamentarians had not filed a response despite notices being issued and had sought further extension.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Speaker, told SC that Birla had issued notices on the disqualification petitions. "He knows the seriousness of the matter," Mehta said.The CJI remarked, "We will expect anything which is required to be decided expeditiously, the very nature... demands early adjudication."
Mehta responded, "Can a constitutional functionary remind another constitutional functionary of his constitutional duty?" He said the court should not prescribe a time limit for the Speaker.
Justice Bagchi said, "...We may not give imperative directions, but keeping in mind the decision in the Keisham Meghachandra Singh case... have resolution of this issue expeditiously."In the 2020 case, SC had ruled that the speaker must decide defection cases within a reasonable time, preferably three months.Justice Bagchi asked Mehta to submit a timeline for the Speaker's decision. Mehta, however, said he could not give SC a commitment. "This court's monitoring may not be justified. I would urge not to fix the Speaker's schedule," he said.The top court recorded the submission of the rebel MPs that they would file a reply within four weeks and adjourned the matter.

Is NAZA Zionism's worst nightmare or normalisation propaganda?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:25:36 UTC
06:25:36 KST

Breadcrumb
Is NAZA Zionism's worst nightmare or normalisation propaganda?
The documentary film NAZA (an acronym for Nezek Agavi; “collateral damage” in Hebrew), written and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, has created a firestorm of controversy. Though few have actually seen the film, it reportedly contains interviews with 24 anonymous Israeli military and intelligence members who attest to the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and automated surveillance into military targeting systems used by Israeli forces during the ongoing Gaza genocide.
They also allege government approval of operations in which thousands of Palestinian civilians were killed as “collateral damage.”
Since its premiere at Venice, where Abraham and Szor received a record 25-minute standing ovation, the filmmakers have faced an escalating campaign of official condemnation and deadly threats. Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar called for their citizenship to be revoked, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced plans for legislation targeting those who “defame” Israeli soldiers, and Israel Defence Force (IDF) Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir said the military would use “every tool at our disposal” against the film.
Far-right activists have gone further, with calls for the filmmakers to be hunted and hanged, with more threats directed at their families.
On the surface, however, it is not clear why the film and its creators have become such a target of hatred and condemnation within Israel and the broader Zionist movement. Documentation of Israel’s genocidal criminality has been readily accessible for years, mostly from Palestinian journalists on the ground in Gaza, and the use of AI in targeting civilians has been detailed by Abraham himself in April 2024.
Furthermore, Israeli soldiers have documented themselves shamelessly committing an array of war crimes. So why the thuggish wrath by Israeli leaders, then dutifully echoed by their fascist supporters? This response is akin to Pavlov blowing his whistle at his trained dogs: the whistle sounds, and the conditioned response follows.
What distinguishes NAZA is that it brings allegations of Israeli genocide from the Palestinian “out-group” and its allies into the Israeli “in-group,” opening a potential space for Israeli voices to confront and challenge its normalisation, potentially leading to accountability.
The intensity of the reaction becomes more intelligible when examined through the mechanisms of escalation and normalisation described by the Wired to Steal (W2S) model, a neurobehavioral framework for understanding colonial expansion.
Normalisation of genocide
Since the events of 7 October, in which Hamas led a military operation resulting in the murder and kidnapping of hundreds of Israeli security forces and civilians, Israel retaliated indiscriminately, obliterating the Gaza Strip and even targeting its own people. The genocide, as international experts and organisations have termed it, is but a recent development in an ongoing Zionist genocidal-colonial cycle, in which Israel has expanded oppression and dispossession in response to acts of resistance by Indigenous Palestinians.
Crucially, Zionism is not exceptional. In its foundations and operation, Israel manifests other white European settler-colonial projects in which extraction and greed by a ruling class drive a cycle of manufactured identity, segregation, fear, dehumanisation and rewards for aggression. This sustains a self-reinforcing system of dispossession of designated out-groups, while escalation and normalisation reproduce it.
In contrast to Zionist narratives which decontextualise the events of 7 October to portray Israel’s subsequent actions as defensive rather than offensive, Palestinian resistance can be understood as being instrumentalised as an essential, albeit tragic, trigger for renewed and expanded aggression. It nourishes the ongoing Zionist settler colonial project which predates the establishment of the state of Israel in 1948.
According to the W2S model, resistance is also used to justify theft under the guise of “defence”. Settler society then normalises this through media institutions, social norms, incentives, and everyday conditioned behaviour, rendering the resulting construct a perceived reality.
In this way, normalisation expands the moral boundaries of what is considered acceptable, and who is considered human, thereby increasing the resources available for theft. This is clear to see in the deliberate and cynical blurring of civilian and militant categories, and the designation of Palestinian children as “future terrorists” by Israeli military and political leaders in recent years.
Furthermore, normalisation constructs a façade of so-called “open debate” among “varying opinions” and, consequently, a plurality of tolerated voices within settler society, while shifting attention from the conduct itself to the boundaries of permissible debate and the legitimacy of individual critics. Without it, the tawdry fabric of settler society is threatened.
Abraham and Szor as collateral damage
Zionist propaganda, also known as Hasbara, is one of the most sophisticated forms of state propaganda greasing expansion and theft. As an essential branch of hasbara, normalisation has evolved into an intricate web of deception, particularly utilised in the tropes of liberal Zionism, which presents the Zionist project and Israel as reformable and compatible with human rights. It includes a right-to-left political spectrum, democratic and progressive values, and a desire for peace and justice.
The fallout from NAZA reflects a conditioned reaction casting Abraham and Szor as traitors to the Zionist narrative, with a distinct propagandistic function.
In contrast to Palestinian journalists, who could be racialised and scapegoated as clear members of the out-group and subsequently targeted for elimination as “terrorists,” Abraham and Szor represent a new kind of threat to Israeli society - a threat from within. They have been singled out as in-group targets to be made an example of, using tactics typically reserved for out-group members (though still mild, for now), with the effect of discouraging other potential in-group whistleblowers from coming forward. Fearmongering and social rewards for their harassment are utilised, while simultaneously clarifying the internal boundaries of Zionist identity.
Thus, rather than approaching the film as new evidence for Israeli criminality, the firestorm around NAZA can be understood as an internal struggle within the Zionist movement over how to respond to evidence of genocide without challenging the underlying Zionist project.
Some liberal Zionists have embraced NAZA as a vehicle for bringing criticism of Israeli conduct in Gaza into Israeli public discourse and encouraging greater scrutiny of existing policies. Establishment Zionists have pushed back against such claims, in part reflecting concerns that their wider acceptance could contribute to a broader crisis of Israeli social cohesion.
In this sense, the debate in its present form serves to normalise Israel’s actions since 7 October: genocide is recast as something “debatable,” maintaining Israel's impunity for the worst crimes against humanity and war crimes, with the identities of those responsible remaining obscured.
Will the Zionist regime permit the film to screen in Israel? The full extent of NAZA's impact is yet to be determined. Already, its reaction should encourage all to adopt the nonviolent Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel for its oppression of freedom of speech and the targeting of the filmmakers.
Clearly, for it to have lasting moral impact, NAZA and its creators must give other whistleblowers the courage to step forward. Abraham, Szor and their colleagues can do more than hail the 24 Israeli military personnel featured in the film as courageous. They should urge them to come forward publicly from anonymity, which currently gives opponents an easy basis for dismissing the allegations without addressing their substance. Otherwise, NAZA risks becoming a discredited, normalising propaganda tool at the hands of the very forces it set out to hold accountable, and Abraham and Szor may also be swept into the gruesome machinations of Israel's genocide of Palestinian people as mere collateral damage.

US pledges $267 million more to fight Ebola in central Africa
NEW YORK, Sept 23 - The US State Department on Wednesday pledged an additional $267 million toward fighting the Ebola outbreak in central Africa, as health authorities battle to get the deadly virus under control.
Senior State Department officials announced the funding on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, where they hoped other countries would pledge new funds toward a target of $2 billion to deal with the disease, mainly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The outbreak was detected in May and is already the second most lethal on record, behind one in West Africa from 2014 to 2016.
The pledge brings the Trump administration's commitment to tackling the outbreak to $886 million, including $107 million from the Department of Health and Human Services in addition to State Department funding.
The assistance would help countries contain the outbreak at its source, one of the officials said, such as for building treatment facilities, providing diagnostics and medical countermeasures for health workers in the field. REUTERS

US 'totally rejects’ any attempt to control ‘superintelligence'
Unknown

2026-09-23

Efe Özkan
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
The US “totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme of control of superintelligence,” a White House official told the UN Security Council on Wednesday.
“International dialogue in this forum and in others cannot be allowed to drift towards global governance,” Michael Kratsios, who heads the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, said at a meeting on artificial intelligence and international security. Superintelligence is a term US President Donald Trump used to refer to artificial intelligence in his UN address Tuesday.
“As the leader in frontier superintelligence, the US has taken actions to ensure we are able to keep the frontier moving safely and responsibly” which, he added, meant that there was “not a reason to pause its further development or to constrain it with new global governance structures.”
He encouraged country-by-country regulation instead of a global framework.
“The American people's representatives will legislate and regulate on the American people's behalf. You should do the same for your people. Only through an open, cooperative ecosystem built on sovereign infrastructure and domestic capacity can the world realize this technology's potential,” he said.
Earlier in the meeting, the heads of OpenAI and Anthropic told the Security Council that no single actor should dominate artificial intelligence, as they urged international cooperation to manage the technology’s risks as it advances.

OpenAI and Anthropic chiefs warn UN Security Council against single-actor AI dominance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:19:36 UTC
06:19:36 KST

The heads of leading artificial intelligence firms OpenAI and Anthropic have told the United Nations Security Council that no single actor should be permitted to dominate AI, urging coordinated international cooperation to manage catastrophic risks as the technology accelerates.
Addressing a dedicated Security Council session on artificial intelligence and international security, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman framed the era as a historic crossroads: "We have a choice in front of us. AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray."
Altman argued that AI "should be built for people, not simply to turn the crank of the machines faster for their own sake", dismissing hyper-dystopian industry pronouncements as sounding "like the plot of bad science fiction movies."
He insisted that "no one person or company or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their worldview on everyone else", stressing that governance decisions "cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone" and must be shaped through democratic, accountable institutions.
Bioterrorism hazards
Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei warned of two acute hazards: rogue misuse by bad actors—including "bioterrorists to create biological weapons"— and the structural danger of "model capabilities accelerating beyond developers' ability to control them".
Amodei cautioned that "if managed poorly", the technology "could be a risk to humanity as a whole".
While pledging Anthropic will "slow down as much as necessary" to verify system safety, he stressed oversight requires "an industry-wide and global scale", demanding common worldwide standards for testing loss-of-control scenarios.
However, Yoshua Bengio, co-chair of the UN International Independent Panel on AI, rejected corporate narratives framing rapid deployment as an unavoidable competitive race.
"Citizens and governments should not accept the companies’ claim that they are trapped in a race," Bengio told delegates, concluding that "the race is not a law of nature; it is the product of choices, choices made by the companies themselves" and poses a threat to every nation.

The United States Federal Bureau of Investigation says it is investigating a breach of its jobs website by a hacking group that claims to have obtained sensitive data on thousands of employees.
“The FBI is aware of a cybercriminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the fbijobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information,” the agency said in a statement on Wednesday.

“While the point of breach is still undetermined — whether a third -party or the FBI’s enterprise — we are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support fbijobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk.”
Several news outlets, including Reuters news agency, reported they had seen parts of the data, claimed to be part of a larger trove between two and three terabytes by ShinyHunters, a hacking group claiming responsibility for the breach. ShinyHunters said on Tuesday that it had breached the FBI and stolen data on a huge number of current and former FBI employees. It said it is holding the data hostage until the bureau rescinds an unflattering statement about the group issued in May. On Wednesday, the group said it was trying to keep the personnel information from circulating widely in the meantime.
An FBI statement in May characterised ShinyHunters as “threat actors” who often harass or threaten victims, using “their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims”.
The group “may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist,” the FBI said.
The FBI has been a common hacking target.
In March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Also that month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account of FBI Director Kash Patel and posted online what appear to be years-old photographs of him, along with a work resume and other personal documents dating back more than a decade.
The jobs portal was still offline Wednesday afternoon.

OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:15:27 UTC
06:15:27 KST

Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety.
“We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards.
Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”.
“If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said.
The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry.
Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”.
Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models.
While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety.
“If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”.
AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI, Google and Elon Musk.
Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

Three charged with assault after anti-migration protests in Hampshire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:07:55 UTC
06:07:55 KST

Three people have been charged in connection with anti-migrant protests that drew hundreds of demonstrators to a marina in Hampshire on Tuesday night.
Six people were arrested by police, as anti-migrant activists who mistakenly believed a small boat was due to arrive at Gosport gathered in an attempt to disrupt the arrival of any asylum seekers.
Those charged are Shannon Dodds, 32, of Leonard Road in Gosport, who has been charged with two counts of assault by beating of an emergency worker, Sally Pearson, 31, of Forton Road in Gosport, who has been charged with assault by beating of an emergency worker and a racially aggravated public order offence, and Toby Matthews, 33, of Forton Road in Gosport, who has been charged with common assault of an emergency worker.
Dodds and Pearson have been remanded in custody and will appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on Thursday 24 September.
Matthews was bailed but must appear at Portsmouth magistrates court on 9 November.
Hampshire police said in addition to these charges, a 19-year-old man and a 36-year-old man from Salisbury who were arrested on suspicion of aggravated trespass had been bailed with conditions until 22 December while inquiries continued.
They added: “A 67-year-old man from Gosport was also given a fixed-penalty notice for driving without due care and attention. He was also arrested on suspicion of assaulting an emergency worker and has been bailed with conditions until 22 December while enquiries continue.”
The protests in Gosport followed a social media push by far-right activist Daniel Thomas, who styles himself Danny Tommo, who called for action to disrupt the potential arrival of asylum seekers as he livestreamed efforts to apprehend small boats crossing the channel to more than 100,000 followers on Tuesday afternoon.
He is also now facing a police inquiry after he used a knife to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard.
His livestream showed him approaching an empty dinghy which had contained about 50 migrants who had reportedly left from a beach in Normandy. They had been picked up by two RNLI lifeboats once they had reached the UK search and rescue area, but a French official then got on to the craft.
The footage showed Thomas taking out a knife and slashing at the vessel in the channel, shouting at the French rescue worker: “Right, you are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more.”
“Traitor,” Thomas shouted as his boat motored away.
The protesters in Gosport, many of whom wore black clothing and face coverings, chanted “send them back”, wrongly assuming the boat would arrive on the Hampshire coast.
Instead of heading for Gosport, the RNLI transferred the asylum seekers to a Border Force vessel which landed in Dover early on Wednesday.
Hampshire police said they had deployed officers to the town on Tuesday evening “to help facilitate peaceful protest, ensure the safety of the local community and support partners in the event of any emergency at sea”.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “We have been clear that groups creating fear and intimidating communities cannot be allowed to operate with impunity.
“Police should make full use of the powers available to them to deal robustly with criminality and ensure communities, staff and those in their care are protected.”
Campaign group Stand Up To Racism described the incident as “disgusting” in a post on X, and said Thomas’s supporters in Gosport had blocked ambulances during the protests.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, was forced to order an urgent security review after the failure by the Border Force to intercept two other migrant boats in two days before they reached the Kentish coast this week.
She said on Wednesday: “This was not acceptable. Our improved monitoring has led to uncontrolled crossings becoming incredibly rare. But even one is one too many.
“The new tactics adopted by the smugglers, like launches from much further west in France, are a reminder of two things. Firstly, these gangs have no regard for human life. They are putting people on increasingly long and dangerous crossings.
“Secondly, our efforts are having an impact. We are making it much harder for gangs to launch vessels, forcing them to change their approach, and as a result we are significantly reducing the numbers coming here by small boat.”
The total number of migrants who have crossed the Channel by boat so far this year is 17,784, according to the government – a figure 45% lower than at the same point last year.
The shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, said Tuesday’s “chaos” showed the UK was seeing “illegal immigrants crossing at will over ever larger distances and in ever larger boats”.
“This latest fiasco shows that the French are not even trying to stop the illegal immigrants’ boats,” he added.

Burnham backs lifting restrictions on alcohol at English football matches
- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham supports trialling the lifting of four-decade-old alcohol bans for fans at English men's football matches, calling the restrictions outdated and unfair.
- The ban, in place since 1985 due to football-related violence, has been challenged by a safe trial in women’s football and comparisons to other sports like rugby and cricket.
- The UK Football Policing Unit warns alcohol contributes to violence, urging caution and thorough review before any legal changes to allow alcohol at matches.
AI generated
NEW YORK – British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering allowing fans to drink alcohol while watching men's football live in England on a trial basis, arguing that the four-decade-old restrictions are outdated and unfairly discriminate against fans of the sport.
The consumption of alcohol in the stands of the top five tiers of English men's football has been banned since 1985, when fighting between rival fans at matches was common. Fans are allowed to drink alcohol when they are away from the pitch.
“I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different,” Burnham, a lifelong football fan, told reporters travelling with him to New York for this week’s United Nations General Assembly.
“I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis.”
Burnham took over the premiership in July from Keir Starmer, vowing to boost the popularity of the ruling Labour Party in the face of a challenge from Nigel Farage's anti-immigration Reform UK, which is popular among blue-collar voters.
In response to Burnham’s remarks, a spokesperson for the UK Football Policing Unit said alcohol plays a significant role in football-related violence and it would be “irresponsible to fuel this” by allowing alcohol consumption during matches.
Limits are a legacy of 1980s football violence
The introduction of all-seat stadiums, tougher policing and CCTV surveillance, alongside football’s commercial transformation, has helped reduce violence at matches since 1985, when 39 people died after fighting broke out before the European Cup final between Liverpool and Juventus at the Heysel Stadium in Belgium.
English clubs were banned from European competitions for five years as a result.
A trial allowing fans to drink alcohol in view of the pitch was held in the English Women’s Super League during the 2025-26 season. A survey of supporters found that 90 per cent said matches remained safe and family friendly.
Allowing fans to drink in the stands on a permanent basis would involve changes to the Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol etc.) Act 1985 that would require a parliamentary majority.
Burnham, a long-time Everton fan who took Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to a game last week, referred to other sports, such as rugby and cricket, where fans can generally consume alcohol while watching a match live.
“I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently,” he said.
The spokesperson for the UK Football Policing Unit said football experiences levels of violence not seen in other sports, and it would be “incredibly rash” to make any fundamental changes without a thorough review of the evidence and talks with the police.
Across Europe, there are different approaches to allowing fans to drink alcohol at football matches.
While German fans can buy and drink beer in the stands during games, Spain and France are among countries that maintain restrictions on alcohol sales at stadiums. REUTERS

US aviation sanctions disrupt Iran flights, push travellers overland
