US aviation sanctions disrupt Iran flights, push travellers overland
Travel disruptions intensify as Iranian airlines lose access to airspace, pushing civilians towards costly land routes.
Tehran, Iran – Travel is becoming increasingly difficult for Iranian civilians as United States sanctions shut domestic airlines out of much of the world’s airspace and international carriers continue to avoid the country.
The US Department of the Treasury designated 27 airlines on September 8, covering the remaining Iranian carriers that had not previously been sanctioned by Washington. Major names like Iran Air and Mahan are among those already heavily sanctioned, but have continued limited operations.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Milei says UN ‘looking the other way’ on Falkland Islands dispute
- list 2 of 3As major powers act unilaterally, experts say UN faces crisis in New York
- list 3 of 3US judge leaves White House media ban in place for now
Recent designations have also targeted individuals and entities linked to aviation support and procurement in the United Arab Emirates, Turkiye, China, India, the United Kingdom, Malaysia and elsewhere.
Airports and companies that provide Iranian-operated aeroplanes with fuel, landing services, or ticket sales risk secondary US sanctions that could cut them off from the US financial system, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday. It is the latest attempt to squeeze Iran and force it to make concessions amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
Wednesday marked the expiry of a short wind-down period allowing countries to stop servicing Iranian carriers, leading to the cancellation of all but a handful of Iranian flights to Turkiye, UAE and China.
Aviation authorities in several neighbouring countries that had continued to allow Iranian airlines to use their airspace and airport services would no longer be providing them, including Oman, Azerbaijan, and Georgia. In Iraq, Baghdad Airport was declared off-limits to Iranian carriers, but flights to Najaf Airport were still operating on Wednesday.
Many flights between Iran and major transit hubs in Turkiye and the UAE had already been suspended because of the war and sanctions. International airlines have also largely stopped flying to Iran, with Turkish Airlines suspending flights until at least March 2027, and Qatar Airways, Emirates, and Lufthansa’s operations also suspended.
‘A new level’ of sanctions
Iran-based aviation and transit expert Mohammadreza Ebrahimpour said years of US sanctions had already forced Iranian airlines to rely on third countries and work with smaller firms to get fuel or services. Obtaining spare parts needed to keep Iran’s ageing aircraft flying has also become increasingly difficult.
But the decision by aviation authorities in neighbouring countries to formally refuse services to Iranian airlines constituted “a new level of sanctions in action” that could have longer-lasting consequences, he told Al Jazeera.
Ebrahimpour said the US had also effectively prohibited international airlines from flying through Iranian airspace by suspending authorisations for some US-origin aircraft to fly to Iran and limiting US-linked overflight payments.
“This is a big blow because payments for overflights were one of the most lucrative parts of [Iran’s] aviation industry, which could act as a support for developing infrastructure and the overall industry,” Ebrahimpour said, adding that Iran earned more than $300m a year from this.
Beyond the effect on civilian passengers and the import of some goods, the measures could put tens of thousands of jobs at risk across the aviation sector and related industries, including tourism and hospitality.
Ebrahimpour pointed out that the International Civil Aviation Agency and other organisations have failed to offer any tangible protection to Iran’s aviation industry during years of sanctions. Iranian authorities, he said, would likely consider China and Russia among the few countries potentially able to provide assistance.
The two countries have rejected US sanctions against Iran, although some of their more globally connected financial networks and companies have, at times, distanced themselves from Iran to avoid secondary sanctions.
Under pressure from all fronts
The flight cancellations have pushed thousands of travellers towards land crossings, particularly those with Turkiye and Armenia, where onward international flights remain available for Iranians. Heavy congestion has been reported in recent days at the Bazargan and Razi border crossings with Turkiye and along land routes to the Armenian capital Yerevan.
But everyday passenger travel overland into Azerbaijan remains restricted, with Azerbaijan’s government citing internal security and COVID-19 restrictions. As a result, Iranians cannot cross overland into Azerbaijan to catch a flight there.
The Shalamcheh and Chazabeh border crossings with Iraq were also temporarily closed earlier this month, leaving travellers stranded, before reopening to passengers on September 13.
For thousands of Iranians attempting to travel, the flight suspensions mean significantly longer journeys. Some members of the Iranian diaspora have expressed concern online that the lingering effects of war and sanctions could potentially prevent them from visiting parents and other family members in Iran.
Bus tickets from Iran to Turkiye have reportedly sold for quadruple their normal price on the black market amid surging demand.
Some of the people making the journey are young Iranians who are attempting to take international language tests that are not allowed to be administered inside Iran due to sanctions. The tests are often a prerequisite for anyone planning to study, work, or settle abroad.
Iranian academics have also expressed concern about growing isolation from the international academic community. Numerous universities across the globe, including in Norway, Australia, Singapore, Estonia and elsewhere, have in recent weeks rejected postgraduate and research applications from Iranians as a result of US education sanctions.
At the same time, many of Iran’s roughly 90 million people are currently unable to afford international travel – or even domestic flights – as the country’s economic conditions worsen.
The Trump administration has portrayed the war and sanctions as measures directed at the Iranian authorities.
The US Treasury has said its aviation restrictions are intended to disrupt the use of Iranian commercial aviation for weapons procurement and transportation, including activities linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). But the designation of entire airlines under “Operation Economic Outcast”, after nearly seven months of war, has also had sweeping consequences for affected civilians.
Iran’s international aviation network was already badly damaged prior to the latest package of sanctions. Aviation analytics company Cirium reported that international capacity in August 2026 was 49 percent lower than in August 2025, despite a modest recovery from July.
The latest flight cancellations are also expected to further disrupt imports by air at a time when the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in the Strait of Hormuz has constrained maritime trade routes, while war and sanctions have caused disruptions and delays to road and rail cargo routes.
Some of Iran’s medical imports enter the country by air, raising concerns that the latest aviation restrictions could place more pressure on an already struggling healthcare sector. A domestic pharmaceutical company executive told Al Jazeera earlier this month that the cost of some imported supplies, some of which arrived by air, had risen as much as 10-fold as a result of sanctions, wider economic pressure, and war damage.
Addressing the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accused the Trump administration of “bullying”.
“They have tested Iran’s resilience, and now they know full well that Iran cannot be forced to surrender through war,” Pezeshkian said.

Judges appointing judges is a myth, says Justice Datta, points to way in which govt clears collegium picks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:05:19 UTC
06:05:19 KST

Judges appointing judges is a myth, says Justice Datta
NEW DELHI: Holding that the collegium system remains the most viable option for safeguarding judicial independence despite its "opacity and imperfections", Justice Dipankar Datta Wednesday said its deficiencies could not justify ushering in executive participation in collegium deliberations. He said judiciary had been relegated to playing second fiddle to the executive in appointments because of the way collegium recommendations were cleared by govt.Referring to govt's argument that the judiciary had an exclusive say in judges' appointments, Datta said "judiciary cannot always be at the receiving end" and devoted six pages to the issue, saying "relevant observations in response need to be made, lest the silence be misunderstood as a tacit acceptance by the court of such unworthy criticism in circulation".Datta said the executive wielded decisive control and held the reins over appointments at every level. He said it had become fashionable to blame the collegium for every infelicitous choice, conveniently forgetting that aberrations were exceptions and not the norm, and that no system could guarantee infallibility of human choice.The other judge on the bench, Justice S C Sharma said SG Tushar Mehta's submission was "not a criticism of the collegium system or regarding the role of executive in the appointment of judges".
"It was a submission to the effect that if the constitution bench has held the presence of outsiders in collegium as violative of doctrine of separation of powers, a similar independence should be read in executive and rules framed under Art 324 be not declared void on the ground that it does not have an outsider in the selection committee or the executive predominates in it," he said.Sharma said the SG had based his argument on the judgment in the National Judicial Appointments Commission case, where a constitution bench held that the presence of even the law minister in the collegium for appointment of SC and HC judges would violate separation of powers. "Building upon the constitutional principle, the submission of the SG was that a corresponding degree of constitutional independence must be recognised for the executive as well as legislature. He submitted that the committee constituted under rules framed under Art 324 deserves to be declared legal though dominated by members of executive," Sharma said.Datta said, "The oft-repeated phrase that 'judges appoint judges' is a myth, which people have been fed by vested interests through motivated narratives. A sweeping generalisation that collegium acts as a law unto itself overlooks the consultative process envisaged under the Constitution, and the intrinsic role of executive - both at Centre and in the states."He added, "It is undeniable that collegium system has occasionally faltered and its functioning has not been free from aberrations. However, vociferous criticism, by itself, does not offer an alternative.
While absence of an outsider may invite scrutiny, executive supremacy cannot be the cure. The constitutional quest is not to transfer primacy from one organ to another, but to preserve independence through checks and balances."What is worrying is that the sanctity of a collegium resolution is lost each time the executive implements it selectively, approving majority of those recommended while withholding one. Undeterred by piecemeal approvals and fate of those not cleared by the executive, collegium chooses to proceed, to avoid a head-on conflict with the executive, left with a Hobson's choice to keep the institution running. What it averts is a constitutional crisis; but the larger question is: how long can this state of affairs continue, if selective implementation is allowed to acquire the character of an accepted practice?"

====================================================================================================

Monumental ancient ritual baths unearthed at foot of Temple Mount in Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:05:06 UTC
06:05:06 KST

'Three times a year all your men must appear before the Lord your God at the place he will choose' - Deuteronomy 16:16
Pilgrimages to Jerusalem go back a way. The divine spirit is presumably ubiquitous but the Bible commanded Israelite men to attend the divine sanctuary, which would become the Temple in Jerusalem, three times a year: at Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot. Like all good guests, they should not arrive empty-handed, the scripture adds.
Having arrived in Jerusalem from around the land, before entering the sacred sanctuary, the pilgrims would purify their bodies in ritual baths. Maybe they also soaked their aching feet and washed their travel-stained clothes ahead of the final approach. Only once cleansed were they supposed to climb the monumental staircase to the Temple at the top of the hill.
Now archaeologists have revealed a previously unknown complex in the Ophel, the slope descending from the Temple Mount south toward the City of David, that is where the pilgrims would apparently immerse. The monumental complex includes three mikvaot (ritual baths) plus a strange rectangular pool that was evidently not a ritual bath. Prof. Uzi Leibner and Prof. Orit Peleg-Barkat are responsible for this exciting find. Nearby, the team also found two other installations that appear to have been plastered vats.
The discovery was announced following five seasons of excavation in the Ophel by the team, who are from the Institute of Archaeology at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in cooperation with the Armstrong Institute of Biblical Archaeology (formerly known as Ambassador College).
What is the research question underlying the project? The archaeology of pilgrimage in the Second Temple period. There are historical references aplenty, but actual solid evidence is somewhat rarer.
The ground around the ritual complex is still littered with ruins from the Byzantine neighborhood (roughly 4-7th centuries) and also from a monumental government structure from the Umayyad period (7th-8th centuries). The Umayyad structure repurposed precious columns taken from Byzantine churches, and stone blocks from the Second Temple period. Jerusalem archaeology can require monumental deciphering skills.
Preparing body and mind
To be clear, the Ophel and its environs have been undergoing archaeological investigation for over 150 years. In the modern State of Israel, fresh work there began in 1968 by the archaeologist Benjamin Mazar (1906-1995) and continued under his granddaughter Eilat Mazar (1956-2021). More work continued under Ronny Reich with Yuval Baruch, and most recently under Peleg-Barkat with Leibner and most recently by archaeologist Yossi Garfinkel.
In all the century and a half of digging around the Ophel, the ritual bathing complex hadn't been found before – other obstacles aside, first some Byzantine and Umayyad ruins had to be removed.
Actually, Eilat Mazar had observed the ashlar outer wall of the newly reported purification complex, and noticed two wide openings, but she never did discover that these led into ritual baths. The odd rectangular pool just south of the three mikvehs had been noticed half a century ago but was never properly excavated or published, Peleg-Barkat elaborates.
This pool featured steps on all four sides, so one would descend to the bottom like in a ritual bath. But it didn't have a roof. There aren't even pits in the bedrock that could have supported poles that could have held up a fabric covering.
Ritual immersion is supposed to be done in the nude, but this pool had no walls or roof to protect the worshipers' modesty. So it probably wasn't a typical mikveh, Peleg-Barkat explains, although it may have been used to purify objects.
Additionally, in the vicinity of the mikveh complex were the installations that look like plastered vats, that hadn't been discovered before either, Peleg-Barkat tells Haaretz. They could theoretically have been used for washing clothes, she suggests.
While there is no specific indication to support this hypothesis, she wonders if this grand ritual complex could have provided Second Temple pilgrims a sort of full service, enabling them to wash their garb, soak their feet in the open pool while waiting for their turn to go into the mikveh. Then fresh and clean with white clothes they were ready to go up to the Temple."
Up, it would be. That's key to an ancient Jewish pilgrimage: one ascends to the light of enlightenment; and Peleg-Barkat points out that the only approach to the Temple Mount that isn't a descent is from the south. The purification complex is immediately south of the holy precinct. Specifically, it lies at the foot of the stone staircase leading from the so-called "City of David" up toward Temple Mount.
The ritual baths have been securely dated to the late Second Temple period, meaning this complex operated between the early first century C.E. until the year 70, when the Romans crushing the First Jewish Revolt destroyed Jerusalem and looted the Temple. Possibly the rectangular pool lasted longer – it seems to have had three construction phases, one after 70 C.E. Note that the team also found coins minted by the Jewish rebels in the debris.
Fresh water, anyone?
The entire complex is exceptionally well-preserved, with some of the plaster that water-proofed the walls still in place. One of the baths actually survived to its full height, 4.20 meters, beneath the debris and dirt of Jerusalem's wars. That bath even kept its vaulted stone ceiling and the shaft through which the water arrived, and is thus an all-too rare example in Jerusalem of a Second Temple–period structure still mostly intact.
The three structures that are definitely mikvehs feature something that most ancient mikvehs didn't: a drainage system, and an elaborate one at that.
Mikvehs are supposed to contain mayim haim ("living water") from the rain or rivers or streams, not to be filled by hand or, heaven forfend, using vessels. They are also supposed to maintain a minimal level of said mayim haim.
Therefore, most ancient ritual baths had no drainage systems but relied on water being removed carefully by hand when necessary, lest the bath level fall below the sacred. Rarely, ancient baths did have drains that would be plugged when the baths were in use, and these ones now found in the Ophel featured drains.
That makes sense for a purification bath serving dozens, hundreds, or possibly even thousands of people climbing up to the Temple on a holiday. One would wish to change the water now and then.
The mikvehs don't seem exactly enormous, given what one might expect of a ritual bath serving the public, but the archaeologists refer to the complex as monumental. Why?
"First of all, two of the three mikvehs are big. Not enormous, but larger than most domestic examples," Peleg-Barkat says. "Second, and most importantly, the two of three were nicely built with ashlar staircases. Normally, because plaster covers the installation, there is no need to invest in nice stairs. Third, the building's façade is made of finely dressed ashlar blocks, fronted by a wide porch with large stone pavers. But what really makes this complex unique is its crazy drainage system!"
No question, the drainage system was monumental. Crawling through it would have provided welcome relief from the late-summer sun cooking Jerusalem, but one didn't need to crawl: the drain carved out of the bedrock was only about as wide as a reporter's body, but its walls were more than two meters high.
Although it can't be proved some 2,000 years after the event, the scale of the structure and the implications of its drainage system suggest the ritual complex had a constant flow of mayim haim, likely from a branch off the Low Aqueduct that supplied the Temple itself, Leibner tells Haaretz.
"We know a channel that runs under the Triple Gate," he adds - that Triple Gate is blocked up now, but then its three enormous openings loomed over the top of the monumental stairs.
Altogether, the complex of baths, vats and open pool covers approximately 280 square meters.
"The complex goes to the heart of our research into the archaeology of Second Temple-period pilgrimage: how the area immediately south of the Temple Mount was designed to accommodate the many pilgrims who came to Jerusalem to visit the Temple," said Leibner and Peleg-Barkat in a statement.
They also discovered that this grand complex was not the first public facility at the site. Below it, the Hebrew University expedition uncovered remains of an earlier ashlar-built public complex that also had a large ritual bath, probably dating to the first century B.C.E. That suggests the history of public ritual purification below the Temple Mount started in this area already under King Herod, or perhaps under the Hasmoneans.
When it began, we do not know. We know when it ended, in 70 C.E., when Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans, who gloated in the devastation and in looting the Temple. Evidence of this destruction includes dozens of coins dating to the First Revolt against Rome, discovered on the floors of the complex and within the destruction debris.
What next? Shall they continue the project in Jerusalem? Maybe, or maybe they will pursue other options. Digging in Jerusalem is the dream for any archaeologist until one encounters the monumental red tape.

A US-China AI Hotline Won't Be Ready For a While
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

As US president Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping prepare to meet in Washington for a state dinner at the White House on Thursday, AI has become a top priority. Tech executives from OpenAI and Nvidia have confirmed their attendance at the dinner, as a number of key agenda items are on the table.
Chief among them is a US proposal to establish an AI notification system with China, akin to the Cold War hotline with Moscow, which would allow each country to alert the other about national security issues related to AI. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent first announced the notification system on Sunday with Chinese vice premier He Lifeng.
But for all the high-level progress, Trump administration officials tell Inner Loop they expect it to still take a number of weeks to finalize an agreement, even if they are optimistic that the hotline could be in place before the year’s end.
There are several parts that need to be formalized in more detail, including establishing benchmarks on what kind of incident rises to the level of a national security issue, which remains unclear, as well as explicit sign-on from China, which has been noncommittal.
Trump officials tell Inner Loop they are essentially targeting a framework for the system to be functional—and, crucially, agreed to by Trump—by the time Bessent next meets with Lifeng in follow-up talks in two months' time in Shenzhen, China.
The discussions around such a mechanism underscore the growing concern around the rapidly developing capabilities of frontier AI models as the US and China race to become the dominant power in the industry.
Trump officials have internally discussed putting together a framework that lays out criteria for when each country is obligated to alert the other and enforcement measures to ensure it doesn't only become the US alerting the Chinese.
But with the US expected to extend a trade truce and Trump reluctant to stop exports of cutting-edge Nvidia chips to China, developing a framework that has enforcement measures with teeth could take time to get White House approval, sources say.
The administration has granted a limited number of licenses this year for Nvidia to sell its H200 chip to China, a critical component for AI labs to increase compute power to train their models. Nvidia’s supporters have argued that not selling the chips incentivizes Chinese companies like Huawei to develop their own chip technology, though according to recent reports, the company has already achieved that milestone with its commercially available AI chips.
Some Trump officials have also suggested the notification system may also be delayed while Trump decides on who to appoint as his next "AI czar” to lead a so-called "AI Force," which is being envisioned as a role in charge of interagency coordination.
Bessent has been one of the names floated as the AI czar, but it is not clear if he’s the standout. Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House AI officials Michael Kratsios and Sean Cairncross are also in the mix, two sources tell Inner Loop.
It remains unclear if Trump will choose someone who will be wearing two hats or is departing their current role to take the position. The previous AI czar, David Sacks, was in the position as a special government employee. Sacks is not considered to be in the mix to return, the sources say.
The push for Bessent has come in part because the AI notification system is seen as something akin to the US-China dialogue between former Treasury secretary Hank Paulson and former Chinese vice premier of finance Wang Qishan. During the 2008 financial crisis, Paulson credited the hotline as helping to stave off China from dumping a large portion of US government sponsored debt issued by Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae.
Meanwhile, while some Trump officials have chafed at the idea of giving more AI power to Lutnick, he remains in contention insofar as he oversees the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, which successfully navigated crises with frontier AI model companies this summer.

Andy Burnham signals he may lift ban on alcohol in football stands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Andy Burnham has signalled he may lift the ban on drinking alcohol in the stands at football matches, suggesting it is “unfair” for fans to be singled out when it is permitted for other sports.
The prime minister, a committed Everton fan who still attends matches, said there was a case for trialling an end to the ban to bring football in line with rugby and cricket.
The move was welcomed by the Football Supporters’ Association and the English Football League, but police warned it would be “incredibly rash” to make changes without considering their impact on safety.
Burnham has long opposed the ban, saying it is discriminatory and out of date, harking back to an era when football violence was fuelled by drinking within view of the pitch.
Asked by reporters on the plane to New York about lifting a ban, Burnham said: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination.
“There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis. But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently.”
The Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol etc) Act 1985 prohibits drinking in sight of the pitch in England and Wales.
The fan-led review of football governance in 2021 called for the ban to be re-examined and suggested piloting the sale of alcohol within sight of the pitch in lower-tier English football.
A spokesperson for the UK Football Policing Unit, which coordinates football policing policy in England and Wales, said: “The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.
“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.
“Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor report [of 1990 into the causes of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster] for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster. It would be incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area.”
A spokesperson for the English Football League said it would be “receptive” to a review of legislation that “was introduced more than 40 years ago and has not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding”.
Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters’ Association, said: “The FSA has always argued that it’s unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We welcome the prime minister’s comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed. We look forward to being part of that consultation.”
Supporters at Women’s Super League and WSL2 matches have been permitted to drink alcohol in view of the pitch since the start of this season, after a successful 18-month trial period led to a change to the WSL’s regulations this summer, allowing clubs – but not obliging them – to give fans that option.
Since that rule change, 25 of the 26 clubs across the two divisions of English women’s football have decided to take up the option at all of their home games. The only exception is Brighton & Hove Albion’s home matches at Crawley’s Broadfield Stadium, but Brighton have permitted fans to drink in view of the pitch when the team play their home matches at the Amex Stadium, such as last Sunday when they hosted Aston Villa. Women’s matches have typically seen fewer incidents of crowd trouble.

The defence jobs initiative comes before the publication of former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn’s final report on Neets.
Milburn has underlined the importance of work experience in preparing young people for a job, and opening their eyes to potential careers. He said the defence pledge “shows what is possible when employers step up.”
“Defence is one of our great industries – it has both the scale and the opportunity to give young people the experience, skills and confidence they need to build a career,” he added.
Labour is already rolling out a Jobs Guarantee scheme for 18- to 24-year-olds who have been out of work for at least 18 months – with the promise of a taxpayer-funded work placement.

Over 400 ships pass through Bab el-Mandeb in 10 days, Houthis say

TUNIS, September 23. /TASS/. The number of commercial vessels passing through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait reached 408 after the Ansar Allah rebel movement (the Houthis) took control of adjacent areas of Yemen, the Ministry of Transport and Public Works in the Houthi-formed government said.
According to the ministry, 408 vessels passed through the strait from September 11 to 21 "following the liberation of the western coastal areas," compared with 393 from September 1 to 10. This means that more than 40 commercial vessels are now passing through Bab el-Mandeb every day. "Navigation through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is proceeding smoothly and safely for international commercial vessels, with the exception of Saudi Arabian ships," the statement said.
Yemen has been locked in a confrontation between Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis since August 2014. Tensions escalated sharply in early September after Ansar Allah launched an offensive in the country's southwest. At the same time, the Houthis began rocket and drone strikes on Red Sea coastal areas and the outskirts of Taiz, seeking to cut routes to Mokha and advance toward the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait. On September 12, Ansar Allah Political Bureau member Hizam al-Assad told TASS that the Houthis had completed an operation to establish control over areas in western Yemen with access to the strait.

synesthesia translated into light across audrey wright’s musical body at the MET
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:59:30 UTC
05:59:30 KST

At The Metropolitan Museum of Art, violinist Audrey Wright wears a field of electronics across her body while her husband and creative partner Geoff Robertson stands nearby with a tablet. As Wright plays, Robertson moves through visual programs that send light across the wearable display.
The setup comes from Luminous Being, the project the pair began performing in 2024, but the presentation soon shifts toward something still being built. Together with composer Stephanie Ann Boyd, they are developing PRISMBODY, a new work that takes Boyd’s synesthetic experience of music as its starting point and asks how some part of that personal perception might become visible to everyone else.
designboom spoke with Robertson ahead of the performance, when he described the idea through a surprisingly familiar comparison. ‘It’s like subtitles along with audio on a screen,’ he tells us. The lights are meant to communicate information paired with the music, drawing from Boyd’s own associations between sound and color.
Speaking at the Met, he goes on: ‘Audrey is the audio, and the garment has to be the color version of the subtitles.‘ What begins inside Boyd’s perception passes through a violinist’s body before arriving in front of an audience as light.
Robertson built the first Garment himself, teaching himself electrical engineering and programming along the way. Its 46 display panels sit across Wright’s front and back, with more than 3,000 LEDs distributed across the wearable system.
The Garment carries 47 batteries and generates its own Wi-Fi network, allowing Robertson to connect through a tablet and trigger different visual programs during a performance. An onboard microphone also listens to Wright’s playing and feeds audio values into some of those effects. The whole thing runs at roughly 30 frames per second.
Wright calls the wearable ‘a sensory musical instrument itself,’ and Robertson sees his own role in similar terms. ‘There is a bit of that where I’m actually playing the instrument, kind of in tandem with Audrey,‘ he tells us. His tablet sits at the edge of the performance, yet his timing becomes part of what the audience sees. Wright plays the violin while Robertson plays the visual system around her.
image courtesy Audrey Wright, Geoff Robertson
from multisensory to multimodal
PRISMBODY begins with Boyd’s synesthesia. During the Met presentation, the composer recalls realizing in graduate school that color had always been inseparable from the way she understood music. ‘The color was there all the time, like omnipresent,‘ she says. ‘I couldn’t take them apart.‘
For the new work, she has begun turning those associations into a compositional structure, describing PRISMBODY as ‘a codifying of my synesthesia.’ Different passages move through color fields tied to her own perception, while Wright builds layers of violin through loop pedals.
image courtesy Audrey Wright, Geoff Robertson
For Robertson, this changes what the wearable needs to do. The original Garment has five fixed LED colors on each display panel, which leaves little room for the subtle hues Boyd associates with particular sounds. Garment 2.0 introduces RGB LEDs capable of producing a far broader range.
‘The garment transitions from something that is multisensory to something that is more multimodal,‘ Robertson explains at the Met. His subtitle analogy returns here. The goal is to communicate related information through sound and image at the same time, with enough chromatic precision for Boyd to recognize something of her own perception in what appears on Wright’s body.
image courtesy Audrey Wright, Geoff Robertson
a screen that wraps around the body
The second Garment also expands physically. Robertson is developing transparent display panels that will wrap fully around Wright, replacing the clearer front-and-back orientation of the first version with a continuous visual surface. Each panel will contain individually controlled white LEDs alongside an RGB layer, while additional lights cast color inward across Wright as she plays. The external spotlights are evolving too, becoming sculptural extensions of the wearable display and moving the image farther into the room.
That 360-degree view has been on Robertson’s mind since the first Garment. ‘You have a 360 kind of viewing experience,‘ he tells us, recalling the project’s beginnings during the COVID era, when he imagined performances taking place beyond conventional stages. PRISMBODY takes that idea further.
Boyd’s color associations enter the score, then Wright and Robertson move that material into sound and light. The audience receives an interpretation shaped through each person along the way. At the Met, the work was still visibly in progress. That made its central question easier to see: how do you turn somebody else’s way of perceiving music into an image a room full of people can experience?
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership withSolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

naïve my love: ukrainian folk art of the 20th century brings together paintings, textiles, decorative objects, and other works gathered through years of research across ukraine.

LoP's presence in panel to pick CEC, ECs 'ornamental': SC judge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:57:44 UTC
05:57:44 KST

It would not be a fallacious metaphor if it is said that since the umpire is picked by the captain of one side ... and his team wins, even if the decisions taken by such umpire are correct, it has the patina of suspicion: Justice Dipankar Datta
NEW DELHI: Deliberating on the validity of the law on appointment of chief election commissioner and election commissioners by a panel of the PM, a cabinet minister and the leader of opposition, Justice Dipankar Datta on Wednesday pointed out drawbacks and said it gave "overwhelming" power to the executive and made the presence of the LoP "ornamental", undermining the appearance of independence in the selection process. He also noted that since independence, govts had tried to control the poll body."Over seven decades, every dispensation wresting office found it convenient to keep institutions which the Constitution envisioned to be independent under their control. To enact a law on the lines empowered by Article 324(2) would have meant freeing the ECI from exclusive executive control and inviting trouble for the ruling regime. To the mind of this court, this has not been the failing of any one party or one period. A consistent trait of political power, discernible over the decades, has been to preserve leverage over the very body that is meant to judge its claim to power," Justice Datta said.He said if free and fair elections were to be ensured, it was axiomatic that the EC must not only be an independent body but also be seen to act independently and it was "painful to note that not a single party in power, entrusted by the people of India to govern this great nation", took the initiative of enacting a law of the nature which Article 324(2) left to the supreme law-making body, ie Parliament, to legislate.
"Placing its own electoral fortunes in the hands of a truly independent arbiter was not favoured by any political party, for obvious reasons. To remain in power, the consistent pursuit through executive action has indeed been simple - influence the composition of the EC, control the process of appointment of CEC and ECs and, thereby, temper adverse electoral outcomes," Justice Datta said.
Summarising the contentions raised against the law, he added, "The bottom line of the argument runs thus: it would not be a fallacious metaphor if it is said that since the umpire is picked by the captain of one side in a cricket match and his team wins, even if the decisions taken by such umpire are correct, it has the patina of suspicion, for, at the end of the day, the umpire has effectively been chosen by the winning captain."Justice Datta further said, "There can be no gainsaying that free and fair elections, to a large extent, depend on a truly independent EC. It is not enough for the EC to be independent, it must also appear to be independent. The minister nominated by the prime minister, to function as the third member on the selection committee chaired by the prime minister, cannot be expected to defy his own nominator. In such a circumstance, the inclusion of a minister in the selection committee fails to provide the independent counterweight that a neutral selector could and he would merely echo the voice of his leader; and, consequently, the presence of the leader of opposition in the selection committee becomes largely ornamental, without furthering the purpose of his inclusion."

Live: Albanese says OpenAI took three months to report Medicare breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:57:20 UTC
05:57:20 KST

live
Federal politics live: OpenAI took three months to report Medicare breach, PM says
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says an OpenAI agent accessed public and private data after hacking into a Medicare data portal in June.
Mr Albanese said the company took three months to admit the breach.
Follow all the updates in our live blog.
Submit a comment or question
Live updates
New: Filters
Choose what information you see below by using filters
Key Event
Senior OpenAI figure attended conference in Canberra after company notified govt of breach
So how has OpenAI dealt with this whole controversy, and how open has it been with the Australian government?
It’s worth closely scrutinising the timeline here.
The Prime Minister said this morning that the first time Australia was alerted to the breach was on September 10 – when the company sent an email to an open mailbox maintained by Services Australia.
Apparently Services Australia only twigged to that email a few days later, on Tuesday September 15, when it alerted the Australian Signals Directorate.
But it’s worth noting that OpenAI's VP of global policy Ann O’Leary was in Canberra the day before that – on Monday September 14 – when she attended an Australian Strategic Policy Institute event on AI and met with senior Australian officials.
That’s four days after the company sent its email, and one day before Australian officials started to realise what had happened.
And yet it seems – at least if we go by the Prime Minister’s account – that Ann O’Leary didn’t alert anyone in the Australian government to the breach.
That doesn’t necessarily mean she made a conscious decision not to pass on the information. It might be that she was simply unaware of the activity.
But either way, officials in Canberra are unlikely to be impressed.
And what was the Australian government’s main message to the AI sector and Australian businesses from this conference?
The need for an “early warning system” to help deal with the AI cyber threats.
David Pocock asks why big tech companies aren't being held accountable
Independent senator David Pocock says the incident has raised questions about how we police tech companies for data breaches.
He asks why they aren't being held accountable:
"If it was an Australian who hacked the system they'd likely be heading for jail.
"Yet there's no accountability for AI companies developing this technology."
Expert says OpenAI could have accessed data that wasn't cleared for public release
Olivia Shen, who directs the Strategic Technologies Program with the United States Studies Centre at the University of Sydney, is speaking to ABC News Breakfast about the breach.
She was asked to unpick the difference between the terminology of a "breach of systems" and a "hack".
Ms Shen says it's important to note that, based on what we know, OpenAI's agents were trying to conduct research to improve their models.
"They were given a task and tried very hard to execute the task but, in doing so, went beyond the bounds of what OpenAI had instructed them to do.
"What is very reassuring is that it seems, at this stage, no patient data was lost.
"But they seem to have accessed other statistics and filenames.
"Often what happens is that there is a very intensive clearance process before statistics are released to the public ... and it may have been the case that, on this occasion, OpenAI's agents accessed data and statistics that were not cleared yet for release."
Key Event
Public sector union wants stronger AI guardrails
The Community and Public Sector Union's national secretary, Rebecca Fawcett, says better protections are needed to ensure the safe and responsible use of artificial intelligence in the public service.
"The government needs to be a model employer on AI and ensure stronger protections and safeguards are in place for public sector workers," she says.
"Without clear and mandatory safeguards, we run the risk of systems having the potential to negatively affect the community."
Vulnerabilities need to be rectified, says shadow defence minister
The opposition's defence spokesperson James Paterson says the breach of the Medicare services portal shows Australia's cyber defences aren't "fit for an age of AI".
Speaking to News24, he says our government and critical infrastructure networks have holes that can just as easily be exploited by malicious actors for criminal purposes or to advance national interests.
"It's not appropriate in the era that we're living in to have unpatched legacy systems that are internet-facing, that contain non-public information. That should not be occurring," he says.
"Those vulnerabilities need to be identified, and they need to be rectified."
Senator Paterson, who previously held the shadow cybersecurity portfolio, says Australia's intelligence services need to be bolstered.
"I think we absolutely should be reviewing on an almost daily basis whether agencies like the Australian Signals Directorate have the resources they need to defend our networks, not just our government networks but our critical infrastructure networks, because AI can be exploited for ill and it can be guaranteed that there are potential adversaries of Australia who are looking at how to do so right now."
Key Event
Taylor calls for 'leading players' to help plug Australia's security weaknesses
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says Australia needs to get access to "the absolute leading capability" to strengthen cybersecurity:
"That does mean we've got to have relationships with companies in the US and the US government that gives us access to those systems," Mr Taylor says.
"They have to have arrangements in place where we get access to the leading edge capability.
"They have to put that in place across these vulnerable systems."
He goes on to call for the government to use "frontier systems" to help plug cybersecurity gaps:
"If you use them to find the vulnerabilities as your friend, you can fix the vulnerabilities.
"But if you allow them to attack your systems... then you're going to be exposed.
"You've got to get this right and you have to do it quickly and you have to do it in collaboration with the leading edge players."
Key Event
NSW Health also conducting review into whether systems were breached
In NSW, the state's health minister, Ryan Park, says the incident is "very concerning".
"NSW Health on hearing this news is conducting its own review just to make sure that we are going through everything we can to ensure there hasn’t been anything compromised on our end," he told 702 ABC Sydney.
"[There is] certainly nothing to date, but this is a significant concern."
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles said earlier a NSW government website was among four sites accessed by the AI agent.
Mr Park says the state has "pretty robust systems in place" to protect against breaches.
"The team in charge of eHealth in NSW are constantly literally working around the clock to make sure that our systems and our data is as safe as possible," he says.
"Technology is fantastic, AI is fantastic, but from time to time things can go wrong in relation to this and people can also do the wrong thing."
Taylor calls for PM to focus on cyber defence
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says the breach is a "serious warning" about the security of government systems in the age of AI.
Speaking to ABC Brisbane, he says Prime Minister Anthony Albanese needs to focus on cybersecurity, criticising him for not addressing it when he delivered a speech about AI in July at the University of Sydney.
"He didn't talk about cyber defence," he says.
"I would have thought that cyber defence is the number one issue when it comes to AI.
"It's not the only issue, but it's got to be top of the list, and it hasn't been the focus of the government.
"It should be, it must be."
One of the first instances of an AI agent attacking government infrastructure
Michael Noetel, an associate professor of AI Governance at the University of Queensland, said the breach shows government infrastructure isn't "strong enough" to protect against current AI models.
"The last six months we have seen an increasing number of AI models trying to solve problems and hacking other websites, breaking the law in the process, and so starting to attack government infrastructure is showing how fragile our safeguards are," he told ABC News Breakfast.
"This is the first time I have seen an AI model attack government infrastructure."
The AI hack on Australian government sites was in June but wasn't reported until recently.
"It shows that we are relying on the AI companies, their goodwill and disclosure, not laws that require them to disclose incidents.
"Whereas if you look at more established industries like aviation, if there's a crash, there's a requirement we investigate it and report it, and that isn't just that we get like Boeing to decide whether or not they do that," he said.
Mr Noetel highlighted the need for laws around the use of AI and oversight of the rapidly growing industry.
"It's almost like there is a bus heading towards a cliff; we can’t just talk about seatbelts, we need the government to stop the bus."
Angus Taylor questions timing of AI hack announcement
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says the OpenAI hack is a "serious warning" about the security of government systems in a world of artificial intelligence.
He says the government needs to be transparent about the breach.
“When it first became aware of the breach, exactly what information was accessed, what vulnerability was exploited, how they’re closing it."
Mr Taylor says Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is not across the issue, accusing him of "failing to pre-empt" the incident.
He also questioned the timing of the prime minister's announcement.
“Why is he talking about it now when he’s over in the US? I mean this happened some time back. We’ve not heard him talking about these issues,” he said.
Has OpenAI broken any Australian laws? Marles is unsure
"That's a good question," Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles says.
Marles told ABC Radio National Breakfast the government has yet to determine whether OpenAI broke the law for the Medicare portal hack.
"That's one that we are working through here, and so we will look at what is the legal situation in respect of this, and what it means to have gained an unauthorised access, albeit in an unintended way. So that is one of the questions that we're continuing to investigate through the task force," he says.
Marles says that taskforce will look at why the breach had to be reported by OpenAI rather than Australia's security agencies.
But he stressed the data accessed by OpenAI on the portal was on the "lower end of sensitivity" and guarded by a digital "fence".
"I mean, we're not talking about the very highly sensitive information that we have in respect of national security," he says, arguing such data is kept behind a what he described as a "fortress".
Anthropic and OpenAI warned UN of artificial intelligence security risks
Yesterday, the United Nations Security Council was warned of the risks artificial intelligence poses to humanity by leading global AI companies.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei told the 15-member council he believed "AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole", appealing for governments to work together to manage the increasingly powerful technology.
Meanwhile, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said international cooperation was needed.
"If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people they serve," he told the UNSC.
The council was meeting as Prime Minister Anthony Albanese held a press conference in New York, revealing an OpenAI agent had infiltrated the Medicare services portal in June, accessing public and non-public files.
Key Event
Marles doesn't think there was 'a lot of data' involved in hack
Richard Marles is downplaying concerns about the size and scale of the Medicare portal hack.
The acting prime minister told ABC's Radio National Breakfast the impact was "relatively minor", but the government is taking the issue very seriously.
"I don't think we're talking about a lot of data in the sense that it was essentially asking a question and seeking specific answers. But to be clear, we are still investigating all of that and we are working with OpenAI in relation to it," he says.
Key Event
Full statement from OpenAI
We've just got our hands on a full statement from OpenAI regarding the Medicare portal hack.
Here's what a spokesperson for the company had to say:
"As we've shared publicly, OpenAI is conducting an extensive review of misaligned model activity during training and evaluation and notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems.
"During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation. In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.
"Our review found no evidence of patient records being accessed. The information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names. We notified the organisations and are providing technical information to support their investigations and help address potential security vulnerabilities. Our overall review is ongoing, and we remain committed to transparency about these issues and to sharing what we learn as that work continues."
What was Open AI trying to do?
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles has been asked on Radio National Breakfast what led to the incident and whether the government had been told what happened.
He says OpenAI was working on developing "more sophisticated" artificial intelligence models.
In that context, an AI model was given a task to research health and medical statistics and, as a result, approached four Australian government websites.
One was the Victorian Department of Health, another was a New South Wales government website, and then there was the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.
In those cases, it just looked through information that was available to the public.
But Mr Marles said that was not the case with the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal.
"It sought information, information was not given, and then it effectively hacked into that medical portal and got that information anyway," he said.
"And that's the unauthorised access, which we are very concerned about.
"The information is benign in a sense and as I say, the impact is relatively minor, but the incident is very serious."
Key Event
OpenAI says no evidence patient records accessed
News agency Reuters is reporting a statement from OpenAI about the Australian Medicare cyber hack.
The company says its AI agent improperly accessed files involving "several Australian government websites and services", but there is no evidence patient records were accessed.
"We weren't aware of agent activity in Australia until August during an ongoing review of OpenAI misaligned model activity," the statement from the company says.
OpenAI says it notified Services Australia — which administers the Medicare statistics service portal — about the incident on September 10.
'Lots of questions' to answer on cybersecurity, shadow health minister says
Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston says she will be requesting a full government briefing on the extent of the impact on health services.
"We need to understand what our government systems are capable of defending, and we need to have a key audit of those government systems," the senator told ABC Radio National.
"The fact that this happened is serious enough, but the fact that we had to wait for OpenAi to notify the government is even more concerning."
Senator Ruston says it's concerning that it took three months for the hack to be identified.
"There are a lot of questions the government needs to answer."
Indo-Pacific not a 'chessboard', Albanese to say in key speech at UNGA
After signing the security pact with Ukraine, the prime minister will deliver a major foreign policy speech warning the US and China that the Indo-Pacific is not a "chessboard" for global superpowers.
The strategic competition between the two countries is the most "consequential factor" shaping our region, he will say.
"The Indo-Pacific is not a chessboard on which superpowers move the pieces," Mr Albanese will say (according to excerpts from his speech).
"How Washington and Beijing manage their relationship matters profoundly."
You can read more on this from our national affairs correspondent Jane Norman, who's in New York, in the story below.
Key Event
PM signs new security pact with Netherlands on sidelines of UNGA
Reporting by pool reporter Katina Curtis
Anthony Albanese and Netherlands Prime Minister Rob Jetten have signed a new strategic partnership covering cooperation on security and defence, economics and trade, climate, Ukraine, justice for the MH17 victims, and creative industries.
The two leaders met in the GAB-1 bilateral booth just outside the UN General Assembly chamber.
They signed the agreement documents after their talks.
"Australia and the Netherlands recognise the need to continue investing in our close cooperation to meet current and future challenges," the strategic partnership states.
Albanese, wearing his navy and cream "origami rabbit" tie, pointed to the Australian coat of arms on the front of his folder and told Jetten: "A little fun fact about Australia: our coat of arms, these two animals, can't go backwards. They can only go forward."
Jetten replied that that was the "spirit of the agreement".
The Netherlands coat of arms on Jetten’s folder depicted two lions.
Key Event
Timeline of who knew what and when
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles has described the AI hack as a "very serious incident" and "completely unacceptable".
While the hack occurred in June, Mr Marles said the Australian government wasn't notified until months later.
"We became aware of this as government a couple of weeks ago," he told News Breakfast.
"Ministers were informed at the end of last week and over the weekend, and over the last few days we have been assuring ourselves of what the impact has been in relation to data and the portal itself and for what that's worth, that's relatively minor."
Mr Marles says a taskforce has now been established to investigate the incident.
"That will be led by the Prime Minister and Cabinet department, which will also work with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute, to examine everything that's occurred here and to understand what the AI agent did and how this incursion occurred and what the impact of it has been," he said.

Zelensky at UN General Assembly: Putin pays with 248 lives for every kilometer seized in Ukraine

Zelensky at UN General Assembly: Putin pays with 248 lives for every kilometer seized in Ukraine
President Volodymyr Zelensky made this statement during his address to the UN General Assembly, according to a Ukrinform correspondent. Ukrinform broadcast the event.
Speaking from the podium of the UN General Assembly, Zelensky quoted a recent social media post by U.S. President Donald Trump regarding the Russian economy and its inability to supply the country with fuel, specifically his words: “This senseless and endless war against Ukraine must end.”
“I don’t know of a single world leader who would say otherwise. I don’t know of anyone who openly supports this war, except for one person,” the President of Ukraine emphasized.
He reported that in the first eight months of this year, the Russian army has lost more than 248,000 soldiers killed or seriously wounded.
“There are 21 countries in the world with populations smaller than the number of Russian servicemen lost in just these eight months. We have video evidence of each of these losses. And these aren’t just statistics. We’re talking about people. We have an archive of drone footage. Videos showing thousands upon thousands of Russians dying in combat zones. This is madness. But they keep going there to die, because that’s exactly what Putin wants,” the President stated.
He noted that despite such enormous losses, Russia has managed to capture only slightly more than 1,000 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory this year. “And we have already liberated a significant portion of that territory. So, for the sake of another thousand square kilometers, Putin is paying 248 lives per kilometer. Does anyone still think he’s sensible and moderate?” the Head of State remarked.
According to Zelensky, it is also known that the Russian dictator has already, for the “17th or 18th time,” ordered the capture of the Donbas within a few months and promised this to the U.S.
“He said he just needs a few more months. This is probably the 17th or 18th time in five years that he has made such a promise. It’s always the same thing—just a few more months. And then the deadline is pushed back again. This time, Putin will also fail,” Zelensky said.
He called on world leaders to do everything in their power to help end this senseless war.
As reported by Ukrinform, today more than 50 UN member states issued a joint statement calling on Russia to agree to a complete, immediate, and unconditional ceasefire and to begin substantive peace negotiations.

First Nations workers in Australia paid 16pc less per hour, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:54:39 UTC
05:54:39 KST

Landmark reports finds First Nations workers in Australia paid 16pc less per hour
In short:
An Indigenous-led report has found First Nations workers earn 16 per cent less per hour than all Australian workers on average.
After examining factors including age, experience, qualifications and hours worked, the pay gap remained largely unexplained, with the authors pointing to structural racism.
What next:
The report recommends the Racial Discrimination Act be amended to place a positive duty on employers to prevent racial discrimination, in the same way they must prevent sex discrimination.
A landmark report into the First Nations pay gap has revealed Indigenous workers are on average paid 16 per cent less per hour than the average Australian worker.
The report by the University of Technology Sydney's Centre for Indigenous People and Work (CIPW) and Indigenous Business Australia (IBA) found Indigenous workers earned 84 cents to every dollar earned by Australian workers on average.
CIPW director Professor Nareen Young said the size of the pay shortfall was equivalent to losing a lifetime of superannuation payments or working nearly two months every year for free.
"Nobody would accept that in a contract and no one should have to accept this gap," she said.
Australia's gender pay gap is smaller, with women on average earning 11.2 per cent less than men.
"Obviously we still have a problem but [the gender pay gap] is getting much better because of policy interventions," she said.
"But this research shows that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are on average getting paid a lot less for doing the same jobs."
Indigenous women had the greatest pay disparity, earning an average of $41 an hour compared to $52 for all Australian men.
Pay disparities across range of professions
The report found that across all eight major occupation groups, from managers to labourers, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander workers earned on average less per hour.
The largest hourly pay gap was recorded amongst professionals at 19.5 per cent.
IBA chief economist Dr Siddharth Shirodkar said it showed higher-paid or highly skilled occupations were not immune from pay inequality.
"If you've got a post-grad qualification … and you're First Nations, you've got a higher employment rate than non-Indigenous people, but the average annual income for Indigenous people with those qualifications is generally lower."
Dr Shirodkar said the pay gap existed across almost every age category as well.
"That points to systemic issues, structural issues and indeed bias and discrimination," he said.
The report analysed data from 227 occupations and found in three quarters of occupational groups, Indigenous workers earned less per hour than all workers in the same role.
The size of that gap varied, from 34 per cent for environmental scientists to 6 per cent for truck drivers.
"The dominant pattern is persistent underpayment, not isolated anomalies," the report said.
Teachers and machinery operators/drivers stood out as exceptions, earning close to pay parity on hourly wages or even slightly reversed hourly pay gaps.
Dr Shirodkar estimated the pay gap would amount to $170 billion in lost income by 2050, which would have broader impacts on the Australian economy.
"That's not taking into consideration the compounding effect of lower superannuation, lower savings, lower rates of wealth creation as well," he said.
Pay gap attributed to structural racism
The study examined the factors typically given as reasons for pay gaps — such as hours worked, occupation, age and education — and found these could not fully explain the pay gap.
The study found differences in the numbers of hours worked by Indigenous people could only explain about 2 per cent of the gap.
And while Indigenous workers were somewhat more likely to work in lower-paying occupations, the authors said this could only explain 27.5 per cent of the total gap.
Professor Young said that left 70 per cent of the Indigenous pay gap "unexplained".
"We've been told for years that this is about education, about experience, about the sorts of jobs our mob end up in, and we've tested every one of those explanations," she said.
"So what is left is structural racism in the way work is valued and paid.
"What we need to have as an Australian community is a big discussion about the value of Indigenous work."
The report said the gap likely reflected factors such as the legacy of historically discriminatory wage setting, racial bias in recruitment, and limited power for First Nations workers to negotiate salaries and pay increases.
These factors were not directly measured in the report but were identified as potential contributors.
While the report measured pay gaps using average hourly earnings, the authors found strong correlations when examining median pay gaps across occupations as well.
The authors said this meant their findings were unlikely to be skewed by a small number of unusually high or low-income earners but reflected broader differences across occupations.
They said their estimates of hourly earnings were economy-wide figures and should not be interpreted as "like-for-like comparisons of otherwise identical workers".
Employers urged to prevent racial discrimination
The report made several key recommendations aimed at creating fairer pay and employment structures.
The most significant was to place a positive duty on employers to prevent racial discrimination, in the same way they must prevent sex discrimination.
Other recommendations included improving Indigenous employment data collection, and for cultural skills to be valued properly when wages are set.

Fact-checking Trump’s speech at the United Nations General Assembly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:54:26 UTC
05:54:26 KST

Fact-checking Trump’s speech at the United Nations General Assembly
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
Donald Trump’s UN address was packed with claims that are misleading, false or exaggerated. He said the US has more munitions than it could ever use, despite reports of depleting stocks. He claimed the US and Venezuela hold 60% of the world’s oil, despite the numbers not adding up, and he said he had ended the war in Gaza despite ongoing Israeli strikes and deaths since last year's ceasefire. Vedika Bahl fact-checks the speech in Truth or Fake.
Claim: “We have more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using, and we’re building them at levels that we have never done before.”
Trump dismissed suggestions that US weapons stocks are running low, calling those who make such claims “cowards and traitors”.He insisted the US has “more munitions than we could ever possibly even think of using” and is producing them at unprecedented levels. That claim is misleading.
Published analyses and reporting point to significant pressure on US weapons inventories as the Iran war continues. A May analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies found that replenishing some of the most heavily used weapons, including Tomahawk missiles and Patriot and THAAD interceptors, could take years.
In July, NBC News, citing senior US officials, reported that US forces were allowing some Iranian attacks through their defences in an effort to preserve dwindling interceptor stocks.
And last month, a US defence and NATO official told the Associated Press that US military stocks in Europe faced a “beyond critical” shortage, largely because of the Iran war.
Claim: “When you add the United States and Venezuela together, we have more than 60 percent of the oil in the world.”
Trump also made a striking claim about US and Venezuelan oil, saying that combined, the two countries have “more than 60%” of global oil share. But the numbers do not add up.
Based on proven reserves - oil considered recoverable under current economic and operating conditions - the US and Venezuela together account for roughly 21.9% of the global total.
Based on current production, the combined figure is around 23.2%.
Both figures are far below the 60% Trump cited. Venezuela’s damaged oil infrastructure also means that significantly increasing production would take time.
Claim: “A few weeks later, we ended the war in Gaza, saving untold thousands of lives.”
Trump also claimed he had “ended the war in Gaza, saving untold thousands of lives.”
While Trump played a role in brokering the ceasefire announced last October, the claim that the war has ended is disputed by events on the ground.
Israeli military operations and strikes have continued in Gaza, with near-daily reports of further deaths since the ceasefire. Hamas-run health authorities in Gaza also claim that over 1,000 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire.
Meanwhile, the implementation of the US-backed peace plan remains uncertain. The Board of Peace proposed a $2.45 billion reconstruction blueprint Wednesday, but its implementation is uncertain, almost a year on from the ceasefire.
Claim: “The very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming...These are the same people that are now saying that AI is going to kill us all.”
Trump also dismissed warnings about the potential dangers of artificial intelligence as a “hoax”.
He argued that the people now warning about AI are the same people who previously made predictions about the dangers of climate change.
But concerns about AI risks are not limited to climate activists or critics of the technology, more recently the warnings have come directly from within the AI industry.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently called for the industry to slow down its development of increasingly powerful AI systems, which was backed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
Researchers at Anthropic have separately warned that advanced AI could pose an existential risk to humanity.
Trump’s suggestion that warnings about AI are simply coming from anti-AI voices leaves out the fact that the loudest warnings of late are coming from within the sector.

Turkey and Iraq agree Turkey will turn over military camp in northern Iraq
CAIRO, Sept 23 - Turkey and Iraq agreed on Wednesday for Turkish forces to hand over a military camp in northern Iraq to the Iraqi government gradually, they said after talks in New York, adding they also agreed to end the presence of "outlawed armed elements" in northern Iraq.
After Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan met on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, the sides said in a joint statement they had agreed to deepen security cooperation.
"Within this framework, they reached an agreement on fully establishing state authority in Sinjar and ending the presence of outlawed foreign armed elements," they said, referring to Kurdish militants, some of whom are based in the mountainous Sinjar area of northern Iraq.
Turkey is continuing a peace process that it hopes will result in the disarmament of those militants from the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) and end a decades-old conflict.
The statement on Wednesday added that "in accordance with the agreed-upon mechanism and timeline" and security measures taken by Iraq, Turkish forces would gradually hand over the Bashiqa-Zelikan base, a military installation in northern Iraq near Mosul, to the Iraqi government.
An Iraqi military commander familiar with the talks said the phased withdrawal of Turkish troops from the Bashiqa camp and another small base near Mosul was expected to be completed by the end of this year. There was no immediate comment from Turkey on the timeline.
Ankara deployed troops near Mosul in 2015, saying they were there to train and protect Iraqi forces and local Sunni Arab, Turkmen and Kurdish fighters preparing to fight Islamic State, which seized Mosul in 2014.
The deployment sparked a dispute with Baghdad, which demanded the troops’ withdrawal, while Ankara said they were supporting the anti-Islamic State training mission. Turkey still has several bases in the region, which it says are there to protect Turkey's national security.
Tom Barrack, US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, welcomed the move, saying "Iraqi sovereignty and Turkish security, both (were) served" by it.
The joint statement said the two leaders also discussed bilateral ties and trade, stressing the need to urgently implement previously signed agreements and speed up "strategic projects." REUTERS

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Welcoming the latest 550,000 liters of fuel allowed into Gaza, UN humanitarians said on Wednesday that their partners warn the overall volume imported remains short of the bare minimum necessary.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said the fuel allowed in on Tuesday will help keep basic services running but is far from sufficient.
OCHA said last Thursday's allocation of 2 million U.S. dollars from the OCHA-managed humanitarian fund for the occupied Palestinian territory, along with a recent Qatari donation, were stop-gap measures to fund fuel for Gaza's medical facilities.
"Additional funding is urgently needed to sustain the availability of fuel and prevent a dangerous slowdown of health care, water provision, rescue operations, debris removal and other critical services," OCHA said.
The office said its partners report that the current extensive use of backup generators is unsustainable. Approvals for engine oil, spare parts, solar panels, the entry of commercial fuel and the resumption of operations at the Gaza Power Plant are critical.
OCHA said that ahead of the rainy season, its partners working on site management reported that 989 of 1,764 sites for displaced people assessed across Gaza are in areas at medium to high risk of flooding. The sites shelter about 1 million people.
"Many displaced families have remained in deteriorating shelters since last winter, with limited protection, inadequate drainage and shortages of mattresses, blankets and other essential household items," OCHA said. "Partners warn that about 400,000 people may need to relocate once heavy rains begin."
The office said that until then, its partners are improving drainage, reinforcing shelters, delivering essential materials and equipment, and trying to help people already choosing to relocate. Still, resources are limited and very little land remains available. ■

Houthis say over 400 ships crossed Bab al-Mandab Strait in 10 days despite nearby fighting

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:47:38 CST
05:47:38 KST

SANAA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Wednesday that more than 400 commercial vessels had crossed the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait between Sept. 11 and Sept. 21, as fighting continued near the key waterway.
In a statement aired by Houthi-run al-Masirah TV, the group said 408 commercial vessels transited the strait over this period, with 196 heading north toward the Red Sea and 212 south toward the Gulf of Aden.
It said daily traffic averaged more than 40 commercial vessels, including container ships, and claimed that international shipping was proceeding normally and safely, except for Saudi vessels, which it said are subject to a maritime ban.
The group added that the latest figure exceeded the 393 commercial vessels recorded between Sept. 1 and Sept. 10, when 199 traveled north and 194 south.
The numbers could not be independently verified. Separate ship-tracking data have shown fluctuations in traffic through Bab al-Mandab since the latest escalation, including periods of sharply reduced daily crossings.
The statement comes amid heightened international attention on the waterway following the Houthis' rapid territorial gains along Yemen's southwestern Red Sea coast. Houthi forces seized the strategic port city of Mocha on Sept. 10 and Mayyun Island in the heart of the strait the following day.
Bab al-Mandab Strait connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and forms part of a major maritime corridor linking Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal, making developments around the strait closely watched by global shipping.
Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. Renewed fighting in recent weeks has again brought the conflict closer to the Bab al-Mandab Strait. ■
