Milei accuses UN of looking away from Falklands dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:44:32 UTC
05:44:32 KST

Fatma Zehra Solmaz
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Argentine President Javier Milei accused the UN of looking the other way over the sovereignty dispute surrounding the Falkland Islands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, saying unilateral actions continue despite international calls to resolve the issue through negotiations.
“The Falkland Islands are a national cause for us. I repeat, they are a national cause for us,” Milei said.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly, Milei described the Falkland Islands as a “national cause” and said the dispute demonstrates the gap between international institutions and the reality they seek to address.
He referred to UN General Assembly Resolution 31/49, adopted in 1976, which calls on Argentina and the UK to expedite negotiations over the sovereignty dispute and refrain from decisions that would introduce unilateral changes while the dispute remains unresolved.
Milei said that nearly 50 years after the resolution was adopted, the sovereignty dispute remains unresolved while unilateral actions continue.
He specifically cited the Sea Lion oil project, which involves plans to develop oil resources in the North Falkland Basin.
According to Milei, the project is advancing oil extraction on Argentina’s continental shelf through licenses issued by British authorities, which Buenos Aires rejects as illegal and illegitimate.
The Falkland Islands have been under British administration since 1833, while Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim over the archipelago and surrounding maritime areas.
The dispute led to a 74-day war between Argentina and the UK in 1982 after Argentine forces occupied the islands. Britain retained control following the conflict.
Resolution 31/49 specifically urges both parties to refrain from unilateral decisions that could alter the situation while the dispute remains subject to the negotiation process recommended by the General Assembly.
Milei’s remarks come amid renewed tensions over oil exploration around the islands, with Argentina continuing to reject British-authorized hydrocarbon activities in waters it considers part of its sovereign territory.

Erdogan made the remarks at a high-level climate meeting convened by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.
“Last year, you will remember, I stated here that Türkiye was bidding to host COP31. This year, we will hold COP31 in Antalya from November 9-20, 2026,” Erdogan said.

He also said it was unrealistic to expect all countries to move at the same pace while inequalities persist in access to financing and technology.
“As inequalities in access to financing and technology persist, it is not realistic to expect all countries to progress at the same speed,” Erdogan said.
The president emphasised the relationship between climate action, development and prosperity.
“To the extent that we can establish a strong link between climate targets and development and prosperity, we can also make a just transition permanent,” he said.
Guterres convened the high-level meeting to focus on accelerating a just and orderly transition to renewable energy, mobilising affordable financing and investment for developing countries, and strengthening adaptation and resilience amid rising climate risks.

OpenAI, Anthropic chiefs tell UN Security Council no single nation, company should control AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:41:50 UTC
05:41:50 KST

Merve Gül Aydoğan Ağlarcı
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
The heads of OpenAI and Anthropic on Wednesday told the UN Security Council that no single actor should dominate artificial intelligence, calling for international cooperation to manage the technology’s risks as it advances.
Addressing a Security Council session on AI and international security, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said: “We have a choice in front of us. AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.”
He said AI “should be built for people, not simply to turn the crank of the machines faster for their own sake,” adding that some statements from people working on the technology “are so dystopian that they sound like the plot of bad science fiction movies.”
Altman warned that “no one person or company or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their worldview on everyone else,” arguing that decisions about AI “cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone” and must instead be “shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei identified two central risks: misuse of AI models, including by “bioterrorists to create biological weapons,” and the danger of “model capabilities accelerating beyond developers’ ability to control them.”
He stressed that “if managed poorly,” artificial intelligence “could be a risk to humanity as a whole.”
Amodei said his company would “slow down as much as necessary” to ensure each new AI system it releases is safe, but stressed that managing the risks is “bigger than any one company” and has “an industry-wide and global scale.”
He called for “common global standards for testing AI models for loss of control risks and misuse risks,” describing the issue as “the most important global security issue facing the world today.”
Yoshua Bengio, co-chair of the UN International Independent Panel on AI, pushed back against industry framing of AI development as an unavoidable competition.
“Citizens and governments should not accept the companies’ claim that they are trapped in a race,” he said, adding that “the race is not a law of nature; it is the product of choices, choices made by the companies themselves.”
Bengio told Security Council members that despite fragile trust among nations, “the race threatens every nation.”

Breaking: OpenAI agent hacked Medicare portal, PM says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:31:06 UTC
05:31:06 KST

OpenAI hacked Medicare portal, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says
In short:
The prime minister has had a "frank" discussion with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman after an AI agent breached an Australian government website.
The company did not notify Services Australia of the incident until three months after the fact, via email.
What's next?
The prime minister has announced a taskforce to investigate further.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has revealed an AI agent hacked into an Australian Medicare data portal earlier this year.
Speaking in New York, Mr Albanese said the OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia on June 18.
The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files, but Mr Albanese said it did not appear anyone's personal Medicare details were accessed.
Mr Albanese said he had a "frank" discussion with OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman, saying the company took three months to notify the government of the breach and, when it did, the notification was in an email sent to the Services Australia public inbox.
"Today I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident," he said.
"And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred."
He said the "nature" of the notification was also "unacceptable".
"The notification was an email sent just to the public mailbox," Mr Albanese said.
What do we know so far?
OpenAI accessed non-public aggregate health statistics and internal files from an old Australian government website that carried Medicare statistics.
It is understood an AI crawler, which is an automated program that scans websites and collects information from them, was able to find a security workaround to access the data.
Often deployed as a tool by AI agents, crawlers collect data that usually trains AI models, builds datasets or retrieves information for AI systems.
The prime minister said OpenAI was conducting research into public medical spending when it found a way to break through privacy protections.
"The AI agent found a way around those blocks, didn't accept 'no' for an answer, if you like," Mr Albanese said.
The prime minister said Services Australia was not notified until September 10.
On September 15, Services Australia reported it to the Australian Signals Directorate's cybersecurity centre.
Last week, Services Australia got in touch with Katy Gallagher, the minister for the public service. Mr Albanese's office was notified over the weekend.
He said there was no evidence any individual personal information had been accessed, but an investigation aided by the Australian Signals Directorate was now underway.
"[The] evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable," Mr Albanese said.
The prime minister said three other websites may have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Victorian Department of Health.
"It's the same incident. The question is, when it [the AI agent] was trying to harvest data, did it go into these other sites? So we're not confirming that occurred," Mr Albanese said.
He said the premiers of NSW and Victoria had been notified and would get a full cybersecurity briefing today.
The incident was a "significant concern" and NSW Health would conduct its own review, state Health Minister Ryan Park told the ABC.
"Just to make sure that we are going through everything we can to ensure there hasn’t been anything compromised on our end," he said.
Mr Albanese announced a taskforce would be set up to provide an "urgent and immediate review" of the incident.
The investigation will be led by the prime minister's department and will work with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute.
OpenAI says 'several' Australian government websites involved
The prime minister was asked if Mr Altman apologised.
"Yes, he clearly … we can get into word games, but he clearly accepted that the company had not done good enough," Mr Albanese said.
In a statement, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was "conducting an extensive review of misaligned model activity" during training, and notifying third parties when there was a potential impact on their systems.
"During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation," they said.
"In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.
"Our review found no evidence of patient records being accessed. The information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names."
The company said the information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names.
"We notified the organisations and are providing technical information to support their investigations and help address potential security vulnerabilities," the statement said.
They said Open AI's overall review was ongoing and it remained "committed to transparency".
Back in Australia, Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles said the fact a non-human AI agent gained unauthorised access represented "a very serious incident", but the impact on the system was minor.
"For what that's worth, that's relatively minor, and so it's important to assure people of that. No personal information has been accessed here. There's no impact on the system."
Mr Albanese said the incident was complex and unprecedented.
"It was a shock that it occurred because it was real and serious," he said.
"But it also, I think, was something that had been predicted, including by the AI companies themselves."

See the Taurids light up the fall sky with brilliant shooting stars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:28:21 UTC
05:28:21 KST

Annual meteor showers are always high points of the year, but in fall, we are treated to a two-for-one deal that runs for months. Called the Taurids, these showers dazzle the night sky throughout the season and bring an elevated chance of extrabright meteors—fireballs—to help chase the darkening days away.
The first leg of this epic meteor show is the Southern Taurid shower, which began on September 20 and is expected to last through November 20. Peak fireball activity is predicted to occur around the night of November 4 to 5—just after Halloween.
Meteors, also known as shooting stars, are the visible remnants of bits of debris falling from an asteroid or comet. These pieces burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, creating a brilliant streak of light. The source of dust and debris that makes up the Southern Taurids is Comet 2P/Encke, a relatively small comet that measures about 2.98 miles (4.8 kilometers) wide, according to NASA.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
This year just 22 percent of the moon will be lit on November 4 to 5, providing “generally favorable” viewing conditions for the Southern Taurids’ peak, according to the American Meteor Society (AMS).
The Southern Taurids’ sister shower, the Northern Taurids, will begin on October 20, overlap with the Southern Taurids for a few weeks and peak on the night of November 11 to 12, according to the AMS.
You can catch the Taurids without any fancy equipment. Go outside and find a safe location with minimal light pollution and a clear view of the sky. Give your eyes about 30 minutes to adjust to the darkness and look up. The showers are named after the constellation Taurus, but the shooting stars can show up near other constellations, too.
“The best time to look for Taurids is after midnight, when Taurus is high in the sky,” according to NASA, “and when the sky is dark and clear, with no moonlight to mask the fainter meteors.”

Federal Judge Weighs Limits of U.S. Reach in Trial of Accused Kingpin Sebastián Marset
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:28:00 UTC
05:28:00 KST

Reported by
A federal judge will decide by Nov. 6 whether to dismiss criminal charges against Sebastián Marset, the self-proclaimed South American drug lord whose defense attorney conceded in court on Wednesday that while his client is a drug trafficker, his illicit empire fell entirely outside United States jurisdiction.
During a detailed two-hour evidentiary hearing in federal district court in Alexandria, Judge Rossie D. Alston Jr. weighed a number of defense motions seeking to dismantle the federal indictment against Marset, ranging from jurisdictional challenges to allegations of improper interrogations and vindictive prosecution.
The allegation of vindication prosecution didn’t sit well with Alston, who called it a “very serious” allegation and noted he personally had presided over cases involving the prosecutors, for whom he had high regard.
Defense attorney Robert Feitel quickly interjected that he wasn’t referencing individuals but the process by which Marset was captured in Bolivia, sent to the United States and interrogated without lawyers present. He sought to discredit Michael Greisen, one of the lead agents for the Drug Enforcement Administration in its efforts to capture Marset.
Prosecutors maintain that Marset, a Uruguayan national who operated in the southern cone of South America, laundered tens of millions of dollars through European banks and their U.S. subsidiaries with the help of financial operatives like Federico Santoro, a Uruguayan broker sentenced to 15 years in prison in 2025.
Marset was initially charged with money laundering counts but was later indicted on drug trafficking and narco terror charges.
In court Wednesday, Feitel indicated his client doesn’t dispute being a drug trafficker but noted he “studiously avoided” drug activities that involved the United States and accused the government of trying to “shoehorn this case into narco terrorism charges” by retroactively connecting Marset to regional syndicates - Colombia’s Clan del Golfo and Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital - whose official U.S. terrorist designations took effect after the events under investigation.
“Those designations are based on the groups’ historic conduct,” said Anthony T. Aminoff, the lead prosecutor, while also pushing back against defense claims that key evidence was seized in Colombian territorial waters rather than international seas.
Marset’s lawyers argued that the initial charge of money laundering is invalid because it involved a single wire transfer that did not involve the servers of a U.S. bank. They called as a witness former Treasury official Kristofer Doucette, a specialist in financial intelligence.
Lawyers, with the help of Doucette, tried to argue that the wire transfer was between two non-U.S. banks and not routed on a U.S. computer server. As part of international rules, it was routed to a server in Virginia and vetted by Bank of America’s compliance officials, who did not halt the transaction. The movement never touched U.S. banks thus was not a U.S. violation, they maintained.
Prosecutors countered they would show at trial that Bank of America servers were involved and key to the movement.
One of the most contentious issues is the claim by Marset’s defense that confessions were improperly obtained, a legal doctrine called “fruit from a poisonous tree.” They allege while Marset was read his rights to remain silent, prosecutors lagged in allowing him to contact his lawyer until they tried to entice him into pleading guilty.
On the stand, the DEA agent, Greisen, acknowledged recording interviews with Marset while on flights from arrest in Bolivia in March 2025 to Lima, Peru, and then on to Virginia. But Greisen admitted that he used discretion in not recording Marset when detained in Virginia in hopes that he could convince the drug lord to become a cooperating witness.
That could prove important. Greisen suggested he did so for the benefit of Marset, since recording those conversations would have produced an evidentiary record that could endanger him if he became a witness.
Judge Alston ordered both sides to submit brief summary filings by Oct. 12 before he issues a ruling. Marset's trial is currently scheduled for early 2027.

Turkish Airlines finalizes deal for up to 150 Boeing 737 MAX jets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:26:15 UTC
05:26:15 KST

Esra Tekin
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Turkish Airlines on Wednesday finalized an agreement with Boeing covering the purchase of up to 150 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft, marking the carrier’s largest single-aisle aircraft order from Boeing to date.
The agreement, reached following negotiations that began in 2025, is part of Turkish Airlines’ long-term growth strategy and is intended to strengthen the airline’s short- and medium-haul network while supporting the expansion of its fleet.
The deal was finalized in the presence of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Under the agreement, Turkish Airlines will place a firm order for 100 Boeing 737-8 aircraft while retaining options for an additional 50 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft.
The agreement also provides the airline with the flexibility to switch to the Boeing 737-10, the largest member of the 737 MAX family.
This flexibility will allow Turkish Airlines to adjust fleet capacity according to passenger demand and operational requirements across its network.
“This agreement represents an important step in line with our strategy to expand our fleet,” said Murat Seker, chairman of the Board and Executive Committee of Turkish Airlines.
“The new Boeing 737 MAX aircraft will bring greater efficiency and flexibility to our operations and support the extensive flight network we serve from our Istanbul hub.”
Stephanie Pope, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said the order reflected the “mutual trust and shared vision” that have shaped the companies’ longstanding partnership.
“We are proud to continue supporting Turkish Airlines as it expands its Istanbul-based network, connecting more people to more destinations around the world, while also supporting Türkiye’s aviation ecosystem,” Pope said. 
Fuel efficiency and network expansion
The new aircraft are expected to strengthen Turkish Airlines’ short- and medium-haul operations, particularly on high-demand domestic and international routes.
According to the airline, the Boeing 737-8 offers advantages in terms of range and payload capacity, while providing a 20% reduction in fuel consumption and emissions compared with the aircraft it replaces. Turkish Airlines said these characteristics will help it respond to changing operational requirements as it expands its fleet and network.
Turkish Airlines and its subsidiary AJet currently operate more than 200 Boeing aircraft, including 737 MAX, 737 Next-Generation, 787 Dreamliner, and 777 Freighter models.
The latest agreement follows Turkish Airlines’ order for 75 Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft in 2025, further expanding the long-standing relationship between the airline and Boeing. 
Broader industrial cooperation
Beyond aircraft purchases, Turkish Airlines and Boeing are also pursuing long-term cooperation aimed at strengthening Türkiye’s aviation industry.
The two companies signed a strategic memorandum of understanding (MoU) on industrial participation this year, establishing a framework focused on three areas - capability development, value creation and business opportunities.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Wednesday that Putin had been invited to travel to the summit in December, saying that he hopes the Russian leader will take the opportunity to meet with global leaders.

Kyiv Faces Internet Disruptions as Russian Strikes Hit Data Centers and Communications Infrastructure
Around 100,000 households across Kyiv and the surrounding region are experiencing internet connectivity issues following a Russian attack.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation confirmed this on September 23.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Emergency response teams and specialists are currently assessing the extent of the damage across the local network.
Crews are actively working on repairs to restore regular service and bring stable connectivity back to the impacted areas as quickly as possible.
The Ministry of Digital Transformation has not provided a specific timeline for when full service will be restored to the capital and the neighboring region amid ongoing recovery efforts following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
At least three internet service providers in Kyiv—Pavutyna, UTELS, and Crazy Network—reported service disruptions following a attack by Russian forces. Data centers belonging to Pavutyna and UTELS sustained damage, causing network interruptions.
The attack on a traffic exchange point in Kyiv also led to internet connectivity issues for Crazy Network users in Vinnytsia and the Khmelnytskyi region.
The Russian Ministry of Defense has officially claimed to be deliberately targeting internet communication infrastructure in Ukraine, stating that recent strikes against Kyiv-based internet service providers were aimed at "striking facilities supporting the Armed Forces of Ukraine," according to Ukrainian political analyst, Andrii Smolii.
Russian forces are actively targeting Ukrainian data centers in an effort to disrupt early warning systems and leave civilians without critical safety information, according to Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
By striking data infrastructure, Moscow aims to cut off access to life-saving air raid notifications, compromising the nation's civil defense network and putting more civilian lives at risk during ongoing aerial attacks.
The latest strikes followed another daytime Russian attack on Kyiv on September 22, when Russian forces deployed jet-powered Shahed drones.
One of the drones directly struck fuel storage tanks in the capital’s northern Obolonskyi district, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
That attack injured eight people across the city. Three were hospitalized, while five others received medical assistance at the scene or were treated on an outpatient basis.

Vote counting begins in Morocco's parliamentary elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:22:09 UTC
05:22:09 KST

Khalid Mejdoub, Mohammad Sio
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Vote counting began across Morocco on Wednesday after polls closed in parliamentary elections that will determine the composition of the country's 395-seat House of Representatives.
Polling stations opened at 8 am GMT and closed at 7 pm, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
Morocco's Interior Ministry said voter turnout had reached 28.05% nationwide by 5 pm GMT, adding that voting took place under "normal conditions."
Final turnout in the previous parliamentary election, held on Sept. 8, 2021, was 50.18%.
A total of 3,206 observers, including 200 foreign monitors, oversaw Wednesday's vote.
Official figures show that 15,801,162 people were registered to vote. Twenty-eight political parties competed through 1,850 candidate lists comprising 7,288 candidates, including 2,658 women, for the 395 seats in the House of Representatives.
The Interior Ministry is expected to announce preliminary results in the early hours of Thursday.  
Under Article 47 of Morocco's Constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the political party that finishes first in the House of Representatives election. Cabinet members are appointed by the king on the recommendation of the head of government.
A parliamentary majority requires at least 198 seats, making coalition talks likely if no party secures an outright majority.
The next government will face political, economic and social challenges, as well as major projects linked to Morocco's preparations to co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup.
In the 2021 election, the National Rally of Independents (RNI) finished first with 102 seats, followed by the Authenticity and Modernity Party with 86 and the Istiqlal Party with 81.
The current government is headed by RNI leader Aziz Akhannouch in coalition with the Authenticity and Modernity Party and Istiqlal.

Netanyahu heads to UN for brief visit with few high-level meetings, protests expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:19:52 UTC
05:19:52 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to arrive in the New York area Thursday for an unusually brief visit to address the United Nations General Assembly, with few meetings with foreign leaders and no scheduled meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump as Israel faces intense international criticism.
Netanyahu is expected to spend only several hours in the United States, delivering his speech, holding a small number of diplomatic meetings and returning to Israel without staying overnight. The abbreviated schedule marks a departure from previous General Assembly visits, when Netanyahu used the annual gathering to meet numerous world leaders on the sidelines.
Israeli officials have made efforts to arrange meetings with leaders of countries considered friendly toward Israel, particularly in South America. Netanyahu is expected to meet Argentine President Javier Milei and Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša during the visit.
A meeting with Trump, however, is not scheduled. A senior U.S. official said the two leaders' schedules do not overlap, with Netanyahu expected to arrive after Trump has already left New York.
Netanyahu is traveling primarily to deliver his General Assembly address before quickly returning to Israel.
A hostile reception at the UN
The United Nations has long been a venue for sharp criticism of Israeli policy, but Israeli officials are preparing for a particularly contentious reception this year.
Officials expect some diplomats could walk out during Netanyahu's address, while others may stage protests inside the chamber, including by displaying signs accusing Israel of genocide. Israel rejects accusations that its actions in Gaza constitute genocide.
An Israeli official said images involving National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and incidents of Jewish extremist violence in the West Bank have further damaged Israel's standing internationally. The official said there was a perception abroad that Netanyahu had failed to restrain far-right members of his government.
Outside the UN, several demonstrations are planned around Netanyahu's appearance, involving Israeli anti-government activists, left-wing Jewish organizations and pro-Palestinian and anti-Zionist groups. Major Jewish organizations, meanwhile, organized a rally against antisemitism near the UN on Wednesday, a day before Netanyahu's address.
The demonstrations come amid Netanyahu's escalating public confrontation with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has accused the Israeli prime minister of war crimes and genocide, allegations Netanyahu rejects. Mamdani previously said he would seek Netanyahu's arrest based on an International Criminal Court warrant but later acknowledged that he lacks the authority to do so.
Netanyahu said this week that he intends to use his UN address to “tell the truth” about Israel and its military and respond to Mamdani's accusations.
Netanyahu expected to focus on Iran
Iran is expected to feature prominently in Netanyahu's speech.
In recent days, Israeli officials have held intensive discussions over whether classified intelligence related to Iran could be cleared for public release for use in the address. Netanyahu is expected to present aerial imagery concerning Iranian reconstruction efforts and Tehran's nuclear and missile programs.
He is also expected to refer to a series of recent attacks against Israelis, including the latest attack in which IDF reservist Neriya Leiter, the son of Israeli Ambassador to the United States Yechiel Leiter, was seriously wounded.
The speech comes just over a month before Israel's Oct. 27 election, giving Netanyahu one of the world's most prominent diplomatic stages at a critical point in the campaign.
Netanyahu has portrayed the appearance as an opportunity to defend Israel before an international audience that he says has accepted false claims about the country and its conduct. His critics, however, argue that the speech is aimed at least as much at Israeli voters as at the diplomats in the General Assembly hall.
No Trump meeting, no overnight stay
Netanyahu's official aircraft is expected to land Thursday morning at a military airfield in New Jersey rather than John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York.
Reports about the change have cited a combination of security, logistical and protest concerns. Netanyahu is then expected to travel in a secured motorcade directly to the United Nations.
His wife, Sara, and son Yair are expected to accompany him.
Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, has worked to arrange diplomatic meetings around the compressed visit.
Netanyahu had sought a meeting with Trump, according to Israeli sources, but none was arranged. U.S. officials have publicly attributed the absence of a meeting to scheduling, saying Netanyahu will arrive after Trump leaves New York.
Israeli officials also believe there is frustration within the Trump administration over Netanyahu's handling of Gaza, though U.S. officials have not publicly cited that as the reason the two leaders will not meet.
Netanyahu had also sought a meeting with Elon Musk in Texas, but the stop was canceled after security and logistical difficulties arose. The planned Texas visit would also have required an additional U.S. landing for refueling. Reports this week confirmed that the Texas stop was dropped from Netanyahu's itinerary.
The prime minister ultimately decided on a lightning visit that will not include an overnight stay at his usual Manhattan hotel, the Loews Regency.
Israel had already reserved three floors at the hotel, however, potentially leaving the government with a substantial bill despite Netanyahu not staying there. Finance Ministry officials are expected to negotiate with the hotel in an effort to secure credit toward a future stay.
The visit comes as Netanyahu faces protests not only from pro-Palestinian and anti-Zionist activists but also from Israelis opposed to his government. The Israeli expat group UnXeptable, which emerged as a prominent organizer during the 2023 protests against Netanyahu's judicial overhaul, is among those planning demonstrations Thursday.
For Netanyahu, the visit will therefore be markedly different from many of his previous appearances at the annual gathering: hours rather than days in New York, a limited diplomatic schedule, no meeting with the U.S. president and an address delivered amid demonstrations both inside and outside the United Nations.

WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump is expected to press Chinese leader Xi Jinping to free two US citizens held by China, but it is not clear whether other human-rights issues will get similar attention during this week’s summit.
In a preview of Xi’s visit on Sept 18, a US official said Trump is likely to bring up cases of people wrongfully detained in China with Xi.
However, the White House has not said whether Trump will directly raise broader rights issues related to Tibet, the Uighur Muslim minority group, and the country’s new “ethnic unity” law.
Trump has made winning freedom for Americans held overseas a priority, including in China, advocates say.
But the Republican leader has largely avoided talking about China’s rights record, and has not publicly brought up rights issues when meeting other world leaders like Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Trump will ask Xi to free Youlin Chen, a Chinese-born expert on North Korean nuclear tests who has been imprisoned since late 2024, and Min Zin, a scholar arrested in June, according to Chen’s wife, Yufang Rong. Both are US citizens.
Trump raised Chen’s case when he met Xi in Beijing in May but nothing has happened since then, she said.
“We hope to see Dr Chen and Zin come home after this meeting,” said Elizabeth Richards, research director of the James Foley Foundation, a hostage advocacy group.
Human rights groups and Democratic lawmakers say Trump must also press Xi on China’s treatment of Tibetans and Uighurs and speak up for Hong Kong pro-democracy protesters.
Democrats in Congress say Trump is soft-pedalling human rights concerns and taking a transactional approach to international affairs.
“We cannot abandon human rights in our foreign policy,” Democratic Representative Jim McGovern of Massachusetts said on Sept 23. “China’s record is beyond debate and it is atrocious.”
Beijing has signalled that the topic will be off limits. The country’s ambassador to the US warned on Sept 23 that democracy and human rights are “red lines” that cannot be crossed.
Human rights groups say China has detained Uighurs on the pretext of countering extremism and confined them in re-education camps. US secretaries of state from both parties have labelled the treatment of Uighurs as genocide.
“Xi’s visit to Washington is a strategic moment to move beyond words of condemnation on the Uighur genocide,” World Uighur Congress president Turgunjan Alawdun said.

Rights groups and exiles also routinely describe China’s rule in Tibet as “oppressive,” an accusation that Beijing rejects. China has exerted greater control over the region since Xi became chief of the Communist Party in 2012.
Beijing says Washington should stop using “Tibet-related issues to interfere in China’s internal affairs.”
The International Campaign for Tibet called on Trump to ask Xi “to resume substantive dialogue without preconditions” with the Dalai Lama, the spiritual head of Tibetan Buddhists and a Nobel Peace Prize laureate.
The State Department reiterated calls for such dialogue when a Tibetan American died after setting himself on fire in July.
China passed a law this year to create a shared national identity among the country’s 55 ethnic minority groups, which includes penalties for people outside the country for “inciting ethnic separatism.”

Wired for War: The empire’s propaganda wing honors Palantir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:17:01 UTC
05:17:01 KST

Wired for War: The empire’s propaganda wing honors Palantir
Germany’s Axel Springer media monolith is about to award its highest honor to Palantir founder Peter Thiel, in a ceremony illustrating the incestuous relationship between the mainstream media, the defense tech industry, and the US-Israeli order.
Thiel will receive the ‘2026 Axel Springer Award’ at a ceremony in Berlin on Thursday. According to Axel Springer CEO Mathias Dopfner, Thiel “is one of the rare entrepreneurs who does not merely found or finance companies but helps determine the direction of technological development.”
“He reminds us that progress requires courage and nonconformism,” Dopfner added.
Previous recipients of the Axel Springer Award include Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky. None of these laureates have proven as controversial as Thiel, however.
According to Status News, employees at Politico and Business Insider – both of which are owned by Axel Springer – have pushed back against the decision. In a letter to management on Tuesday, 120 staffers argued that Thiel, who funded the lawsuit that destroyed Gawker, should not be honored by a company which, in the words of Dopfner, “stands for freedom of speech and a culture of open discussions.”
They’re missing the point. Palantir and Axel Springer are cogs in the same machine. They share an almost identical world view, marked by a devotion to US-Israeli hegemony, a belief that private companies must serve the interests of this hegemony, and a common parent: the CIA.
The CIA connection
During the Cold War, the US saw strategic control of media outlets as key to preventing the rise of socialism and communism in Western Europe. Axel Springer, the anti-communist press baron who gave his name to the company, was a natural ally in this fight. Springer received $7 million in funding from the CIA in 1957, two former agents told The Nation in 1982. Adjusted for inflation, the donation would be equivalent to more than $80 million today.
Although the agents claimed that Springer ended his relationship with the agency in the mid-1970s, declassified documents show that he was still in contact with the United States Information Agency (USIA) – which funded pro-American news outlets – in the early 1980s. In 1982, Springer was introduced to CIA Director William Casey as “a strong supporter of the United States” who “is doing all he can to strengthen the ties between the United States and Europe.”
Thiel, who co-founded PayPal, launched Palantir in 2003 with the stated goal of taking “the approaches that PayPal had used to fight fraud…into other contexts, like fighting terrorism.” The CIA took notice, and invested $2 million in the company in 2005 via its in-house venture capital firm, In-Q-Tel.
“I wish I had Palantir when I was director,” former CIA chief George Tenet – who set up In-Q-Tel – told Forbes magazine in 2013. “I wish we had the tool of its power.”
The Axel Springer investment pays off
In both cases, the CIA’s investments paid off. Axel Springer is now Europe’s largest publisher, and owns Politico, Business Insider, Bild, Die Welt, The Telegraph, and nearly a dozen other outlets. The American deep state continues to finance its operations, with the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the State Department’s National Endowment for Democracy (NED) pumping just under $34 million into Politico between 2016 and 2025.
In return, Axel Springer has openly pledged fealty to American neoliberalism. Whereas Springer himself described his first newspaper, the Hamburger Abendblatt, as “geared to the underdog and the little man,” staff at Axel Springer publications are today required to adhere to the following code of conduct:
- “We stand up for freedom, free speech, the rule of law, and democracy”
- “We support the right of existence of the State of Israel and oppose all forms of anti-Semitism”
- “We advocate the alliance between the United States of America and Europe”
- “We uphold the principles of a free market economy”
- “We reject political and religious extremism and all forms of discrimination”
In practice, this means that Axel Springer publications will feature lively debate over ‘red versus blue’ politics in the US and Europe, but will never question key tenets of US foreign policy, including America’s alliance with Israel, its dominance over Europe through NATO, and the legitimacy of its proxy war with Russia in Ukraine.
The world according to Palantir
More than two decades after taking CIA money, Palantir is now the largest of the Silicon Valley defense kingpins, and a synonym for the burgeoning surveillance- and military-tech sector as a whole. Palantir is valued at around $427 billion, a figure bolstered by lucrative contracts with the US’ defense and intelligence agencies, including all six branches of the US military, the CIA, FBI, NSA, and DIA.
Palantir’s flagship product is an operating system called ‘Gotham’, which is essentially a data analytics platform for military, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies. Gotham pulls together and analyses existing data that may otherwise take days to sift through. For example, if US Central Command is planning a missile strike in a foreign country, Gotham can combine maps and satellite footage from that country, data from other agencies, including human intelligence from the CIA and signals intelligence from the NSA, and local surveillance data to present CENTCOM with potential targets for military strikes.
Palantir’s international customers include the British, Israeli and Ukrainian militaries, NATO, domestic intelligence agencies in France and Germany, and police departments in Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, and the UK, among others.
However, Palantir is not a mercenary company selling its products to anyone with money. According to CEO Alex Karp, Palantir is inseparable from the US deep state, and “was founded to strengthen US national security, to protect Americans and their freedom.”
Because we get asked a lot.
The Technological Republic, in brief.
1. Silicon Valley owes a moral debt to the country that made its rise possible. The engineering elite of Silicon Valley has an affirmative obligation to participate in the defense of the nation.
2. We must rebel…
Earlier this year, Karp set out Palantir’s world view in a manifesto, which RT already covered in depth in our ‘Wired for War’ series. In the 22-point bulletin, Karp argued that “the engineering elite of Silicon Valley has an affirmative obligation to participate in the defense of the nation,” that “free and democratic societies” must pursue AI superweapons to preserve the hegemony of the US, which “has advanced progressive values” more than “any other nation on the planet.”
In separate comments, Karp has described pro-Palestinian protesters as a “cancerous” influence on American politics, while Palantir describes its work with the Israeli state as “in line with our global support of US allies and liberal democracies.”
Critics called Karp’s manifesto “technofascist,” but it differs little in substance from Axel Springer’s code of conduct. Karp’s remaining points wade into US-centric culture war territory, but the core argument of both documents is the same: the US and Israel are a benevolent force and the private sector has a duty to aid their foreign policy goals; by argument, in the case of Axel Springer, and by force, in the case of Palantir.
The incestuous security state
Back in Berlin, the guest speakers at Thursday’s ceremony further illustrate the incestuous relationship between Axel Springer, Palantir, and the US-Israeli order. Before Dopfner hands him his award, Thiel will be lauded by CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss, a self-described “Zionist fanatic” who was appointed head of the network following its acquisition last year by billionaire and pro-Israel megadonor David Ellison, whose family has donated more than $26 million to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since 2014.

Inside NATO’s online propaganda machine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:11:23 UTC
05:11:23 KST

Inside NATO’s online propaganda machine
NATO has spent years researching online influence techniques involving fake profiles, targeted advertising and purchased social media engagement. RT’s America Now has examined the bloc’s experiments and what they could reveal about efforts to shape online narratives.
Host Ben Swann and investigative journalist Elizabeth Lane reviewed NATO promotional material, published research and reports on experiments involving social media manipulation.
One example is a 2024 NATO promotional video featuring predominantly white European women as the alliance’s “future” in a potential conflict, apparently with Russia. Swann and Lane argue that the unusually non-diverse casting could be intended to prepare European audiences for women taking a greater role in a possible confrontation as Ukraine struggles with manpower shortages.
They also examined two 2019 experiments by NATO strategic communications researchers. In one, researchers created fake Facebook pages and profiles, collected publicly available information on military personnel and used targeted advertising to reach them. They reportedly identified around 150 soldiers, tracked troop movements and even induced some personnel to act against orders. The experiment cost roughly $60.
In another test, researchers spent €300 on artificial engagement, buying more than 3,500 comments, 25,000 likes, 20,000 views and 5,000 followers. They identified over 18,000 accounts involved in providing fake engagement. Four weeks later, roughly 80% of the purchased activity remained online, highlighting weaknesses in platforms’ ability to detect manipulation.
NATO described the experiments as defensive research aimed at identifying online threats. Swann and Lane, however, questioned why a military alliance was developing practical expertise in techniques that could also be used to influence public opinion. They also pointed to NATO researchers’ cooperation with Ukrainian social media analytics company Singularex.
The episode also revisited false stories that had circulated during the early stages of the Ukraine conflict, including the “Ghost of Kiev” fighter pilot and initial claims about the “defenders of Snake Island.” Lane argued that journalists who repeat compelling wartime stories without verifying them can amplify false narratives.
Lane also said independent journalists covering Russia and Ukraine regularly face bot attacks, abuse and threats. She said she had received such messages herself, including one stating, “Zelensky sends his love,” which she suggested could point to coordinated activity.

Turkish president says UN climate summit in Antalya to focus on turning climate decisions into action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:09:50 UTC
05:09:50 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
23 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Türkiye will host the UN Climate Change Conference, or COP31, in Antalya from Nov. 9-20, with efforts underway to make the summit an event where decisions on climate change are translated into action, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Wednesday.
 
Erdogan made the remarks at a high-level climate meeting convened by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.
 
“Last year, you will remember, I stated here that Türkiye was bidding to host COP31. This year, we will hold COP31 in Antalya from Nov. 9-20, 2026,” he said.
 
He said Türkiye is working to ensure that the gathering focuses on implementing decisions taken on climate change.
 
Erdogan also pointed to planned meetings in the Pacific, saying the Pre-COP meeting in Fiji and the leaders’ gathering in Tuvalu would help ensure that the voices of Pacific island countries are heard.
 
“The last 11 years have been the hottest period on record,” Erdogan said, adding that floods in Nepal had demonstrated “in the most painful way” that there is no time to lose.
 
Erdogan said the first 10 years of the Paris Agreement were focused on establishing common targets, while important decisions were taken in the Brazilian city of Belem last year for the success of the agreement’s second decade.
 
“We must achieve much more in Antalya,” he said. “We must bring ambition and capability, and targets and implementation, closer together.”
 
Erdogan stressed that climate policies must take into account countries' social and economic circumstances.
 
“Any proposal that we cannot reconcile with our climate targets and social and economic realities will be doomed to failure,” he said.
 
He also said it was unrealistic to expect all countries to move at the same pace while inequalities persist in access to financing and technology.
 
“As inequalities in access to financing and technology persist, it is not realistic to expect all countries to progress at the same speed,” he said.
 
The president emphasized the relationship between climate action, development and prosperity.
 
“To the extent that we can establish a strong link between climate targets and development and prosperity, we can also make a just transition permanent,” he said.
 
Guterres convened the high-level meeting to focus on accelerating a just and orderly transition to renewable energy, mobilizing affordable financing and investment for developing countries, and strengthening adaptation and resilience amid rising climate risks.

Ontario Jewish community saddened, but not shocked, by synagogue shooting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:08:40 UTC
05:08:40 KST

Doug Warren, 56, was attending Kol Nidre services at the Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, on the eve of Yom Kippur on Sunday. Prayers were just about to begin when he heard the gunshots.
“The rabbi had just started to call us into the sanctuary. We were stepping inside, and we heard this loud bang, and we all stopped,” Warren, a member of the congregation, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency. “It sounded like someone was banging the window or the door.”
It was a 29-year-old former Canadian soldier exchanging gunfire with a police officer stationed outside the synagogue. The shooter, Sean Ward, 29, of Quinte West, Ontario, died from his wounds on Tuesday. The officer, Const. Jeff Smith, a 13-year veteran of the force, remains in the hospital in critical condition.
Little is known of Ward, who served in the Canadian military from 2017 to 2022, and was never deployed.
“We knew this was going to happen,” Warren, a member of Sons of Jacob and a resident of Belleville. told JTA. “We’ve been saying as Jews that we’re very concerned with the rise of antisemitism. What did you think was going to happen? People weren’t taking it seriously.”
Congregation extremely grateful to 'hero,' police officer Smith
As the gunfire continued, congregants scrambled to find safety. “Some people suggested we should go to the basement, others said we should go out the back door,” he recalls. “At the same time, you’re just frozen because you don’t know what’s going on or what to do. Eventually the shots stopped.”
Warren said the congregation is extremely grateful to Smith, who was stationed outside the synagogue in an unmarked vehicle. “This guy’s a hero. I can tell you the gunman was coming for us inside, and he was trying to take out our armed protection first,” he said. “We’re praying for [Smith’s] recovery.”
Once police arrived at Sons of Jacob, they instructed everyone to wait inside until the area was clear. Congregants were then taken to the Belleville police station, where they were offered donuts and coffee, which Warren said they politely declined on account of fasting for Yom Kippur.
Richard Marceau, General Counsel and Senior Vice President of The Center for Israel and Jewish Affairs, echoed Warren’s concerns. “I wish I could say that I was surprised or shocked, but I was not,” says Marceau. “Unfortunately, in 2026 in Canada, we’ve come to expect this type of thing. It just tells us that the promise of Canada has been broken.”
The Belleville shooting came two days after the arrest of 19-year-old Alexander Parfitt after posting online threats to shoot up a synagogue in Southern Ontario.
Marceau said that Canadian politicians have not sufficiently addressed the threat of antisemitism. “There has been an all-level failure in the political sector and in law enforcement,” he said. “It is a failure to understand the threats that Jews are facing.”
Rising antisemitic discourse endangers Canadian Jews
According to Marceau, anti-Israel and anti-Zionist discourse have also contributed to rising antisemitism and endangered Canadian Jews. “Anti-Zionism is driving violence against Canadians, and the double standard against Israel is playing a role,” Marceau said. “Politicians need a clear plan, not just to talk about extremist ideologies, organizations and foreign state actors. There needs to be a meeting of all levels of government to ensure that the extremist networks are disrupted.”
Anti-Israel sentiment was a point of contention Sunday evening. Canadian Jewish politician and leader of the New Democratic Party (NDP) Avi Lewis posted on X shortly after 8 p.m. that on Yom Kippur he was “reflecting on the fact that we have not done our part to stop an ongoing genocide being committed in our name.”
About an hour earlier, Ward opened fire outside Sons of Jacob. It was not clear whether Lewis knew the shooting had occurred when he had posted. He did not respond to a request for comment.
Canadian Member of Parliament Anthony Housefather responded to Lewis’ post, stating that “holding Canadian Jews and Jews across the world collectively responsible for events over which they have no control is despicable.”
Lewis said in a post the following day that the attack “is yet another reminder of the work that remains to create a Canada that is truly safe for people of all faiths, including Jewish people – to worship, to come together, to live without fear.” In a press conference, he rejected claims that he was collectively blaming Jews for Israel’s actions.
Despite the events Warren witnessed on Sunday evening, he remains assured in the resilience of his local Jewish community. Unable to access their synagogue, Warren says the Sons of Jacob congregation gathered at a Best Western hotel on Monday evening for services.
“We want to keep going, but we know it’s not going to be easy. We might get emotional when we first get back inside the synagogue, and we’ll just have to work through that,” he says. “This will not stop us.”

Russian diplomat sees alarming trends of crisis nature within IAEA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:04:59 UTC
05:04:59 KST

GENEVA, September 23. /TASS/. The General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) was unable to agree on key technical resolutions for the second consecutive year, which points to alarming trends indicative of a crisis, Russian Permanent Representative to International Organizations in Vienna Mikhail Ulyanov said.
"During sessions of the IAEA General Conference general debates are held, and regularly updated core resolutions are being approved. They cover the agency primary areas of activity: nuclear and radiation safety, technical cooperation, the agency’s activities regarding nuclear science, technologies and use, and IAEA safeguards. During the last two sessions - last year and this year - a breakdown occurred. It was impossible to reach an agreement on updating and adopting these resolutions by consensus," he said. "Perhaps this is not yet a full-blown crisis, but we are witnessing very alarming trends of a crisis nature."
The Russian diplomat added that there were serious reasons to believe that no consensus will be reached in the coming year as well. At the same time, the majority of the countries chose not to support proposals explicitly aimed at launching efforts to overcome existing differences within the open-ended working group, in order to approach the next session of the General Conference with agreed-upon resolutions. This fact speaks for itself, the diplomat continued.
"As a result, it turns out that the supreme body of the IAEA adopts non-consensus, political and non-core resolutions regarding North Korea, Ukraine and the Middle East time and time again, but proves incapable of making products related to the very core of the IAEA mandate," Ulyanov said. "If this dangerous trend is not halted, the agency could suffer the fate of other international organizations, which have noticeably lost their standing in global affairs amid the current turbulence in the international relations."
Russia will do everything it can to prevent events this scenario, Ulyanov said.

Space Force Weighs Options to Boost Supply Chain Amid Production Surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:01:55 UTC
05:01:55 KST

As the Space Force eyes a possible fivefold increase in the number of satellites it operates on orbit, defense officials are looking for ways to shore up the industrial base to support that growth, which is expected over the next three to five years.
USSF officials have been telling space companies in recent months to invest in new infrastructure and production capacity to prepare for an increase in demand for satellites and other space systems. In April, the head of Space Systems Command, Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, said a significant portion of the Space Force’s historic $19 billion procurement budget for fiscal 2027 would go toward contracts for new satellite lines and an expansion of existing constellations.
“If a company is nominally making 10, we want you to be prepared to make 40,” he said at the time. “We want industry to make the investments in capitalization and facilitization, and in return you’re going to get these large production contracts.”
Garrant and others, including Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, have said the service is weighing multiyear procurement deals for satellites as well as production framework agreements, similar to the massive munitions deals the Pentagon has signed in the past year. The munitions agreements, which weren’t initially backed by funding, are meant to send a demand signal to industry so they can confidently spend their own capital to increase production capacity and be ready to deliver when the contract awards come.
Leadership’s push comes amid a broad increase in private investment in the space industry; according to a new report from British investment firm Seraphim and Relm Insurance, global investment has doubled in the last year, hitting $23 billion in June. However, that funding hasn’t necessarily been directed at manufacturing capacity. A March report from the Aerospace Industries Association and Price Waterhouse Coopers noted hesitance among manufacturers to fund new facilities, workforce, and tooling without guarantees of long-term demand.
“Space programs often lack the volume predictability and multiyear commitments required to support large capital investments, reinforcing a conservative approach among suppliers,” the report states. “While this strategy can accelerate asset degradation and limit productivity gains, federal budget volatility (accounting for more than 20 percent of total space economy), program delays, and shifting priorities all increase the perceived risk that capacity built today may be underutilized tomorrow.”
The Space Force’s new space acquisition executive, Erich Hernandez-Baquero, told reporters Sept. 16 the service is considering how it might be able to help, possibly using similar framework deals and multiyear procurement assurances as tools to drive more stability into the space industrial base—particularly for components and subsystems that have proven difficult to produce at scale.
“What we’re seeing is we need to scale our production capability around satellites in general,” Hernandez-Baquero told reporters at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. “There are lower, subtier elements of that supply chain that cross cut different mission areas that we may want to look at, because those are bottlenecks.”
For example, the Space Development Agency—founded in 2019 as a disruptor for military space with ambitions to launch the Pentagon’s first proliferated satellite constellation—has faced setbacks due in part to challenges producing the laser-based communication systems known as optical inter-satellite links that enable the rapid transmission of data.
SDA Director Gurpartap Sandhoo told reporters Sept. 15 that production of these optical terminals is still a bottleneck for the agency, as are some other components like focal plane arrays.
“I think it’s been very well reported that optical inter-satellite link components are bottlenecks for our systems, so that would be one that I would look to as an example,” Sandhoo said. “What do we need to do to help facilitate that? Anywhere where we have that bottleneck that keeps us from going at speed in support of the mission is something that would be subject to review.”
Hernandez-Baquero said that may be an area where multiyear procurement assurances could provide more support for suppliers.
While those chokepoints have plagued nearly every SDA prime, some, like L3Harris, have seen their early investment in facility expansion and supply chain pay off. The company, to date, has been tapped to deliver 70 satellites for SDA’s missile tracking layer, including an award in July to deliver 18 spacecraft in support of the Pentagon’s Golden Dome missile defense shield.
Rob Mitrevski, the firm’s president of Golden Dome strategy and integration, said the company links some of its success to early decisions to use internal research and development funds to expand production and shore up its supply chain before it had a single contract in hand. That decision, he said, required L3Harris to change the way it perceives demand signal from the government.
“The demand signal in the past, maybe, has been award of contracts. The demand signal today is prioritization of capabilities,” he told reporters Sept. 16 on the sidelines of the conference. “The defense industrial base has to adapt, I think, to how the demand signal is seen. And some of us have taken chances, risks, and are willing to invest.”

All consumers to pay for EV chargers under power monopoly 'waiver'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:01:07 UTC
05:01:07 KST

Energy watchdog backs plan to slug all consumers for EV chargers
In short:
The Australian Energy Market Commission has given preliminary approval to a plan to allow poles-and-wires companies to install EV chargers.
It follows a proposal by the federal government, which wants to fast-track the rollout of charging points partly by recovering the costs from all consumers.
What's next?
Consultation on the proposal will be carried out over the next six weeks, with a final determination due by the end of the year.
Poles-and-wires companies will be able to charge all households for the cost of electric vehicle chargers under a federal government proposal backed by an energy regulator.
The Australian Energy Market Commission has given preliminary approval to a plan that would allow electricity networks to spread the cost of public EV charging infrastructure across all customers.
In a draft ruling, the commission said the benefits of fast-tracking the rollout of chargers would outweigh the costs to consumers, who would have to pay regardless of whether they own an EV.
The determination would affect customers across the national electricity market, which spans Australia's eastern seaboard.
The conditional support comes amid an increasingly fraught battle over who should be able to install public charging infrastructure across the country — and who should pay for it.
On one side are EV charging companies who argue Australia's fledgling market is highly competitive, privately provided and serving motorists well.
On the other are poles-and-wires firms who say their help will accelerate the adoption of EVs by providing much-needed charging infrastructure.
Australians are buying EVs in record numbers, with sales of electric models exceeding those of petrol cars for the first time in August.
However, Australia currently has one of the lower ratios of EVs to public sites in the developed world, with fewer than 4,000 across the country.
Each site, like a petrol station, typically has multiple charging points.
Fixing 'market failures'
Under its draft decision, the AEMC said network companies would be required to help EV charging providers that wanted to install hardware in "high density" inner city areas.
But where the private companies "didn't take up identified sites", the commission said poles-and-wires firms would be able to act as suppliers of last resort.
AEMC chair Anna Collyer said similar provisions would also apply in regional "charging blackspots".
Ms Collyer said the ruling would help unlock $40 million of federal funding that would pay for about 30 per cent of 14,000 chargers "where they are most needed".
She said networks would recover the rest from consumers, adding about $1 a year to a typical customer's electricity bill.
More than offsetting this cost, she said, would be the emissions reduction benefits, which "would accrue to everyone".
"It's looking at areas of potential market failure," Ms Collyer said.
"We're starting to see an emerging market for commercial charge point operators, as they've been called.
"But given the uptake that we've seen in EVs from the fuel crisis … the Commonwealth wants to make sure the charging infrastructure is keeping up with that and to remove barriers for people who may be considering an EV."
According to Ms Collyer, a lack of off-street parking in inner-city areas was an obstacle to many potential EV buyers, while the patchy nature of regional charging infrastructure was fuelling "range anxiety" more broadly.
She insisted the decision would be limited in its scope and targeted in its design.
For example, she said it would only apply to infrastructure delivered under a specific Commonwealth program that would run for five years from mid-2029.
"The Commonwealth's program is a targeted measure to help close the gap between the rising EV uptake and EV charging infrastructure," she said.
"The two will positively reinforce one another as the public continues to consider the transition to non-combustion vehicles."
Change favours 'monopolies'
Although a draft, the ruling sparked a furious response from critics.
Ross De Rango, director of Vehicle Charging Solutions Australia, said the decision was a poor one that would ultimately hurt consumers.
Mr De Rango said there was no market failure when it came to charging infrastructure in Australia, where private firms were risking their own money to compete for business.
Poles-and-wires companies, by contrast, were regulated monopolies whose revenues — and profits — were guaranteed regardless of how much value consumers received.
"The public-facing EV charging infrastructure in this country is virtually entirely competitively owned," Mr De Rango said.
"There is no need for public charging infrastructure to be owned by monopolies where it can be owned by competitive interests instead.
"Allowing competitive ownership fosters innovation, fosters competition, drives outcomes that are better for the populace."
For Mr De Rango, the risk in the commission's decision was that network providers would be empowered to slowly take over the market while delivering poor services.
Whereas private companies lived or died by their performance and the efficient use of charging infrastructure, he said networks were under no such pressure.
As a result, he said there was little incentive for them to ensure their chargers were installed in the most suitable places and used most efficiently.
"Our country is going to need something on the order of $20 billion worth of public EV charging equipment installed over the coming decades," he said.
"And that equipment will all need to be installed, maintained and replaced as and when it fails and requires upgrades.
"The energy networks, being monopolies, would like to change the rules of the game so that in addition to owning the poles and wires, they can also own the charging equipment."
Stewart Joyce, chief executive of the National Electrical and Communications Association, was seething, saying the AEMC had effectively sided with network monopolies at the expense of consumers.
"Putting up electricity bills to pay for EV chargers shows staggering contempt for consumers battling in the midst of a cost-of-living crisis," Mr Joyce said.

New study highlights key differences in how relationship dynamics relate to sexual desire in men and women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:00:29 UTC
05:00:29 KST

The assumption that men’s interest in sex is purely physical and always switched on is a common cultural stereotype, but recent evidence indicates that men’s sexual desire is actually quite complex. A new study published in Psychology & Sexuality suggests that when men feel a sense of fairness and emotional satisfaction in their intimate relationships, their interest in solitary sexual activities tends to decrease, even though their desire for sex with a partner remains unaffected. The findings point toward a more nuanced understanding of how modern relationship dynamics influence male sexuality.
Historically, the scientific and medical communities have treated male sexuality as a straightforward biological mechanism. For example, a 2019 review noted that researchers have traditionally viewed men’s sexual desire as a simple, mostly physical reflex, focusing heavily on bodily functions like erectile response or testosterone levels. This approach leaves little room for understanding how a man’s emotions, relationship quality, or social environment might shape his interest in sex.
“Essentially, we felt there was a need to explore male desire as there is an assumption that men ‘must always’ want to have sex,” Simone Buzwell, a senior lecturer in the Department of Psychological Sciences at Swinburne University of Technology, told PsyPost. “However, we know from our work with male clients this is not the case, and many men struggle with lower levels of desire than they, or their partners, are happy with. We thought it was time to destigmatize something (low male desire) that many men struggle with.”
To address similar gaps in understanding women’s sexuality, a 2018 framework proposed that sexual desire is deeply tied to emotional and relational experiences rather than just biology. This relational perspective splits sexual desire into two distinct categories. The first is dyadic desire, which is the motivation to engage in sexual acts with a partner. The second is solitary desire, which represents the interest in sexual behavior by oneself, such as masturbation.
Applying this two-part definition to relationships yields interesting patterns. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2022 showed that women in fairer relationships reported higher relationship satisfaction, which in turn predicted a stronger desire for sex with their partners. Relationship fairness, or balance, refers to how equally couples share power, household chores, and emotional support.
The current research aimed to see if these same relational dynamics apply to men. “We were motivated to do this study as I had been exploring female sexual desire and I wanted to find out if factors that impacted female sexual desire also impacted men,” Buzwell explained. “While understanding the factors themselves are helpful for knowing what to target for educational strategies and therapy, if the factors differed between man and women, this could impact sexual communication and relationship harmony.”
To investigate this, the researchers collected data from an online survey of 118 cisgender men living in Australia. The participants ranged in age from 18 to 39, with an average age of 28. Most of the men identified as heterosexual, were currently in a relationship, and did not have children.
The survey asked participants to report their levels of both dyadic and solitary sexual desire over the past month. For dyadic desire, this included rating the frequency of sexual thoughts involving a partner. For solitary desire, the men rated the strength of their desire to engage in sexual behavior by themselves.
The men also answered questions about how power and responsibilities were divided in their relationships, allowing the researchers to categorize them into two groups. Out of the 118 men, 101 reported an equal balance of power, while 17 reported an unequal balance where either they or their partner held more control. The participants then completed a measure of relationship satisfaction, rating things like emotional intimacy and communication.
Finally, the participants filled out a questionnaire assessing their adherence to traditional masculinity norms. This measured how strongly they agreed with social expectations that men should be self-reliant, restrict their emotions, possess mechanical skills, and prioritize sexual dominance.
When the researchers analyzed the data, they found that relationship fairness did not appear to impact a man’s desire for partnered sex. There was no direct or indirect link between relationship balance, relationship satisfaction, and dyadic sexual desire. This is a distinct departure from previous findings in women, where relationship fairness boosted partnered desire.
“What people can take away from the study is relationship factors do not impact on men’s sexual desire in the same way as female sexual desire,” Buzwell said. “This suggests, for men, their dyadic desire may rely more on physiological needs rather than emotional ones. Generally for men, the state of the relationship did not change how sexy they found their partner.”
Instead, the primary factor associated with dyadic desire in this sample was masculinity. Men who scored higher on traditional masculine beliefs reported a stronger desire for sex with a partner. The researchers suggest that social scripts surrounding masculinity might encourage men to focus outward on sexual initiation and partner-seeking behaviors as a way to fulfill expected gender roles.
“We also found that men in more unequal relationships (where one partner had more relationship power than the other) reported higher masculinity,” Buzwell pointed out. “Further, high masculinity led to greater dyadic desire, i.e. desire for sex with a partner, but had no impact on solo desire. So feeling masculine only seems ‘sexy’ when with another and is wasted when alone.”
However, relationship dynamics did play a role in men’s solitary desire. The men who reported equal relationship balance also reported much higher relationship satisfaction. This increased satisfaction, in turn, predicted lower levels of solitary sexual desire. In other words, when men felt happy and equal in their partnerships, their interest in solitary sexual activities decreased.
“When men were satisfied with their relationship and felt their relationship was equitable, their solo desire decreased, so they felt less need to self-satisfy,” Buzwell explained. “This also implies that when men are unhappy in their relationship they turn their focus inwards onto their own sexual needs, rather than try to find sexual satisfaction with their partner.”
The study also highlighted a few other interesting patterns. Heterosexual men reported higher dyadic desire, while non-heterosexual men reported higher solitary desire. Additionally, having children was linked to higher relationship satisfaction for the men in the sample, and it did not negatively impact their sexual desire. This contrasts with past research indicating that childcare responsibilities often decrease relationship satisfaction and sexual desire for women, who historically shoulder a heavier portion of caregiving duties.
The researchers suspect social expectations play a role in these differences. “It seems that men demonstrating sexual interest in a presumably female other can be used to ‘prove’ their heterosexuality, while too much interest in self-gratification may be viewed as indicating homosexual preferences,” Buzwell noted. “We also found it interesting that, unlike our female sample, having children had no impact on men’s desire, or relationship satisfaction, perhaps indicating men’s lower involvement in child rearing.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on a relatively small convenience sample of mostly educated men, and a large majority of them reported being in equal relationships. This small number of men in unequal relationships makes it difficult to draw broad conclusions about how severe power imbalances affect sexual desire.
The use of self-report questionnaires also introduces the possibility of social desirability bias. Some participants might have downplayed their traditional masculine beliefs or overstated their relationship equality because those are socially favored traits. Others might have exaggerated their desire for partnered sex to align with cultural expectations of what it means to be a man.
The survey also captured data at a single point in time, meaning the researchers cannot assume that relationship satisfaction directly causes a drop in solitary desire. It is possible that the association works in the opposite direction, or that other unmeasured factors are influencing both variables. The study also did not account for biological or medical factors that can shape male sexual functioning.
Future studies could build on these findings by recruiting larger, more diverse groups of men, including a wider range of sexual orientations and relationship types. Getting input from both members of a couple could also provide a more accurate picture of relationship balance than relying on one partner’s perspective.
“In terms of the practical significance of the effects, the findings are a reminder that what impacts male and female sexual desire differ,” Buzwell said. “What may be good for the goose may not be good for the gander! I also think the findings show male desire is more complex than people may expect and that men’s desire for another is impacted by non-physical factors, especially their feelings of masculinity.”
“I thought the men’s results would be different to what we found with women, but I thought there may have been more similarities in what we found,” she reflected. “Our long-term goals in this area is to assist people to achieve the level of sexual desire they want given we know this contributes to both personal and relationship well-being. Satisfied people are happier people!”
The study, “Sharing the love: Examining the impact of masculinity, relationship balance, and relationship satisfaction on men’s sexual desire,” was authored by Isobel K. Wilson, Eva Johansen, and Simone Buzwell.
