Reacting to the Central Bank of Ireland’s confirmation that on the expiry of the Israel Bonds’ prospectus their sale in Europe has ended Stephen Cockburn, Amnesty International’s Europe Director, said:
“This outcome is a testament to the indefatigable campaigners who protested outside the Central Bank for more than a year, supported by the Parliamentarians who kept pushing for Ireland’s compliance with international law in the halls of power, and all those who spoke out against these Bonds’ sale in Europe.
Today’s confirmation of the end of Israel Bonds’ sale in Europe shows just what this solidarity can achieve
Steve Cockburn, Europe Director at Amnesty International
“States have a clear obligation to act to end Israel’s violations against Palestinians. Rejecting any involvement in Israel’s genocide, apartheid and other international crimes, requires courage and conviction as states in Europe continue to crackdown on this vital activism.
“Today’s confirmation of the end of Israel Bonds’ sale in Europe shows just what this solidarity can achieve. We must continue talking about Palestinians lives and rejecting complacency and complicity.”
Background
To be sold in the European Economic Area (EEA), the prospectus for Israel Bonds needs to be approved by a competent authority in an EU member state. Since 2021 Ireland has been the ‘home member state’ for Israel Bonds. Due to the public pressure in response to Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in the occupied Gaza Strip, in 2025 the Central Bank of Ireland transferred the prospectus to Luxembourg whose competent financial authority approved it. This prospectus expired on 31 August 2026.
In July, Luxembourg’s financial regulator rejected to approve the prospectus for another year. The decision came after increasing pressure from civil society and legal experts. They mobilized and published research to support their call to the authorities to stop the bonds.
Amnesty International has been calling on Ireland, Luxembourg and other EU states not to allow the sale of Israel Bonds in Europe.

PM set to warn China and US the Indo-Pacific not their 'chessboard'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

Albanese to tell China and US the Indo-Pacific not a 'chessboard' for superpowers
In short:
In a major foreign policy speech, Anthony Albanese will declare the post-1945 world order "is no longer fit for purpose", while issuing a warning to China and the US.
The prime minister has signed a decade-long security agreement with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, committing $60 million to help the country defend itself against Russia.
The new agreement provides a "framework" for defence and security cooperation, including military training, rebuilding Ukrainian military facilities and exploring joint manufacturing of missiles and drones.
Anthony Albanese will declare the post-1945 world order "is no longer fit for purpose" and warn China and the United States that the Indo-Pacific is not a "chessboard" for global superpowers.
In a major foreign policy speech to be delivered in New York, the prime minister will say Australia needs to help shape the new global order by building new relationships, standing up for the rules governing how countries interact with each other and rejecting the notion that might is right.
Underscoring the stark warning, Mr Albanese signed a decade-long security agreement with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Wednesday, local time, and announced another $60 million in funding to help the country defend itself against Russia.
The two leaders shared a hug, and Mr Albanese was on the verge of tears when describing his admiration for the "extraordinary" leadership of his "friend" Mr Zelenskyy.
"I think Russia thought it could just steamroll through in a matter of weeks, and what we have found is the people of Ukraine were underestimated," Mr Albanese said during the meeting.
Indo-Pacific not a 'chessboard'
Mr Albanese's comments about the rules-based order echo similar warnings from like-minded leaders, including Canada's Mark Carney, who has said middle powers must unite because "if we're not at the table, we're on the menu".
Mr Albanese will identify the strategic competition between China and the US as the most consequential factor shaping the region.
"The Indo-Pacific is not a chessboard on which superpowers move the pieces," he will say.
"How Washington and Beijing manage their relationship matters profoundly. But it cannot be the only lens through which we see the region.
"Its countries are not spectators. They are shaping its future and writing their own script."
PM named 'global citizen'
Mr Albanese will deliver the speech at a ceremony tonight where he will be awarded the Atlantic Council Global Citizen Award, alongside Finland's President Alexander Stubb, Broadway star and actor Cynthia Erivo and Formula 1 boss Stefano Domenicalli.
It comes a day after US President Donald Trump stood on the floor of the United Nations and threatened to "annihilate" Iran, if the country failed to agree to a deal to end the war, and warned Cuba, a "failed state", would fall.
In a wideranging speech, Mr Trump very publicly slapped down a push from a coalition of middle powers, including Australia, for global regulations to ensure humans remained in control of AI, declaring the US had no plans to rein in the powerful technology.
As Australia launches its bid for a two-year term on the UN Security Council, Mr Albanese will argue global institutions need to be modernised and strengthened.
"The post-1945 world order is no longer fit for purpose," Mr Albanese will say according to draft excerpts of his speech.
"Universal institutions that remain necessary are now not always sufficient for the challenges we face.
"Australia's response to this is to actively seek to shape and build the order that replaces the old."
Rules essential to Australia
Australia has long been caught between two competing forces — relying on China as its biggest trading partner and on the US as its most important security ally.
But with Mr Trump up-ending the global order, and a more assertive Chinese president in power, Mr Albanese will say the imperative for countries to agree and abide by rules remains.
"Australia depends on a region where ships and aircraft move freely, where trade reaches markets unimpeded, and where the sovereignty of small states is respected as fully as that of large ones," he will say.
"The rules that connect our nations remain essential — and they matter to Australia, to the Indo-Pacific and globally."
Australia's bilateral relationship with Ukraine has deepened substantially since Russia's invasion in 2022. Canberra has committed more than $1.9 billion in assistance to the country, including Bushmasters, armoured tanks and other military equipment.
The new agreement provides a "framework" for defence and security cooperation, including stepping up military training, rebuilding Ukrainian military facilities and exploring the joint manufacturing of missiles and drones.

China-US dialogue takes centre stage in Washington
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:58:38 EEST
04:58:38 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping begins a state visit to the United States on 23 September, returning to Washington for the first time in a decade as Beijing and Washington seek firmer channels for managing trade, technology and security disputes. President Donald Trump will receive Xi at the White House on 24 September for talks on trade and technology.
The visit runs from 23 to 25 September at Trump’s invitation. The programme includes an arrival ceremony, formal meetings and a state dinner, giving the two presidents another opportunity to build on months of direct contact between Beijing and Washington.
The meeting gives both governments another chance to put their framework for constructive strategic stability into practice. The approach centres on cooperation where interests overlap, and controlled competition.
That effort carries weight outside the two countries because the scale of their economic relationship reaches through global supply chains, commodity markets and manufacturing networks. US goods exports to China reached $65.2 billion from January through July 2026, while imports from China reached $156.4 billion. Two-way goods trade over those seven months stood at about $221.6 billion.
The direction of US-China policy affects sourcing, investment decisions and prices for companies trading across Asia, North America and Europe. A steadier relationship gives companies more information when planning production, contracts and long-term investment.
Trade is expected to take a large share of the Washington talks. Negotiators have discussed a Board of Trade and reciprocal tariff reductions covering up to $30 billion of goods in each direction.
The product list under discussion includes consumer goods, farm products, energy products and medical devices. Chinese officials want the reductions implemented at an early date, while the final scope will depend on the outcome of negotiations.
Previous talks produced commitments across agriculture, aviation and market access. China agreed to purchase at least $17 billion a year in US agricultural products in addition to an earlier soybean commitment.
Agriculture remains one of the most direct links between political decisions and businesses in both countries. China is an important market for US soybeans and other farm products, while American farmers depend on access to large export markets.
Questions remain over beef, poultry, dairy and seafood access, while technical issues continue to affect some shipments. Further movement in Washington would give both sides a way to show that earlier commitments are turning into commercial activity.
Boeing sales form another part of the unfinished agenda. China agreed earlier this year to purchase 200 aircraft, though the orders had not been completed by September.
Boeing chief executive Kelly Ortberg said this month that the process was progressing and that Chinese airlines would announce orders on their own schedules. The issue links diplomacy with jobs, manufacturing and airline demand in both countries.
Artificial intelligence has also moved higher on the agenda. Washington and Beijing compete over chips, models and global standards, but officials in both capitals face similar questions about safety, cyber risks and crisis management.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said Washington proposed a notification mechanism for AI incidents with national security implications.
Such a mechanism would create a direct point of contact if an AI-related incident threatened national security or produced wider risks. It would not settle disputes over chips or export controls, but it would give both governments another channel for managing unexpected events.
An AI channel represents one area where rivalry and risk management meet. American technology executives and policy specialists have supported some form of US-China contact on AI safety even while Washington keeps export controls on advanced chips and Beijing objects to US technology restrictions.
Chinese officials have also called for dialogue on AI governance. A regular communication mechanism would offer both sides a practical starting point without requiring agreement on every part of technology policy.
The immediate purpose of the summit is to keep high-level contact in place and reduce the risk that disputes spill into a wider breakdown in relations.
Republican Senator Steve Daines, who has worked with the Trump administration on China policy, has stressed the importance of meetings between the two leaders alongside any agreements reached.
The White House visit follows months of contact between the two administrations. Xi and Trump have spoken by phone, exchanged letters and met face to face since late 2025.
During Trump’s earlier trip to Beijing, the two presidents discussed trade, investment, technology and security. Their governments also restored communication channels intended to support negotiations between senior officials.
Business groups in both countries have placed predictability near the top of their expectations for Washington.
Sean Stein, president of the US-China Business Council, has said leader-level meetings help build trust and make work on other issues easier.
Chinese and US business representatives have also called for clearer policy signals on tariffs, investment rules and market access.
Bilateral goods trade grew 13.7 per cent year on year in the second quarter of 2026, while US companies had established more than 84,000 enterprises in China by July.
Those figures show the depth of commercial ties after a period marked by tariffs, export restrictions and political disputes.
The international impact of steadier interaction extends beyond bilateral trade.
The relationship between China and the United States reaches far beyond government meetings.
People-to-people ties form another part of the visit. More than 50,000 young Americans from all 50 states have travelled to China in just over two and a half years under an exchange initiative announced by Xi in San Francisco in 2023.
The programme has taken students to factories, rural communities, schools and cultural sites.
Such exchanges give students and communities direct contact at a time when political disputes often dominate public discussion.
Universities, tourism groups, business organisations and cultural bodies continue to operate alongside the government relationship. Direct contact between citizens offers another layer of communication when official relations face pressure.
The Washington programme also includes cultural events.
First Lady Melania Trump and Peng Liyuan are due to visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art.
The two presidential couples are also scheduled to visit the National Archives to view records linked to the history of US-China relations before the state visit ends.
Expectations for the summit remain focused on incremental progress rather than a single agreement that settles the larger disputes.
Work on a trade board, tariff reductions, agricultural purchases, aircraft sales and an AI incident channel gives officials several areas where movement is possible.
Investment talks face greater obstacles because both governments continue to apply national security tests to Chinese investment in the United States and US technology exposure to China.
The trade proposals give officials one of the clearest routes towards an agreement during the visit.
Reciprocal tariff reductions would follow months of negotiations and provide a visible sign that the two sides remain willing to turn summit commitments into policy.
Agriculture gives negotiators another area with defined targets.
China remains an important market for US farm products, while producers in the United States want stable access to Chinese buyers. Progress on technical barriers and purchase commitments would support trade in both directions.
Tariffs influence trade flows and consumer prices. Export controls influence technology supply chains. US-China demand affects agriculture, aircraft manufacturing, energy and shipping. AI policy increasingly reaches firms and regulators across several regions.
The talks therefore carry consequences well beyond Washington and Beijing.
A period of steadier communication between the two largest economies gives businesses more certainty, creates space for diplomatic negotiation and gives officials more routes for dealing with crises.
The formal programme will continue through Friday. Trump and Xi are due to hold meetings during the state visit, while the two first couples will attend a state dinner and later travel to the National Archives.
The visit gives both governments an opportunity to move practical negotiations forward while keeping channels open on the disputes that continue to divide them.

Owing to a cycle of retrials, appeals and judicial proceedings, Weinstein has remained incarcerated since his 2018 arrest and is now serving time in a prison medical ward.
Weinstein, first publicly accused of wrongdoing in 2017, was detained a year later. As major powers act unilaterally, experts say UN faces crisis in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:54:24 UTC
04:54:24 KST

As major powers act unilaterally, experts say UN faces crisis in New York
Experts warn the UN faces crises of funding, relevance, and Security Council gridlock.
As world leaders gather in New York for the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), experts say the institution is battling an existential crisis of funding, relevance and Security Council gridlock.
Major conflicts appear intractable, and powers like the United States and Russia can bend the UN’s Security Council to their will; member states are looking for new mechanisms to bring accountability to the venue and for a new secretary-general to voice their concerns. The body has been accused of failing to stop what its own experts have said is a genocide in Gaza.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Geopolitical divides fueling Security Council inaction, UN chief warns
- list 2 of 3State of world getting worse as UN Security Council paralysed: Guterres
- list 3 of 3UN launches hunt for next chief amid rising challenges
World leaders are not under any illusion that the UNGA is in good health, said Daniel Forti, head of UN Affairs at the International Crisis Group. Yet many still understand the venue’s power.
“The vast majority of leaders, from small states, from middle powers, and even a few from major powers, recognise the importance of a UN that is a global conversation platform,” Forti said.
Trying to weigh in where the Security Council fails
The UN is juggling multiple conflicts – from high-profile wars involving Iran to the often overlooked catastrophes in Sudan and Myanmar.
In the Ukraine war, the UN says more civilians were killed in the first eight months of 2026 than in the whole of 2025, and even NATO powers now say they worry about spillover into their countries.
Russia has repeatedly vetoed Security Council resolutions, but Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has continued to appear before the UNGA to urge member states to help stop Moscow.
On Wednesday, Zelenskyy spoke for the fifth time before the assembly since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, urging leaders to further tighten economic measures meant to punish Moscow despite its vetoes of Security Council resolutions.
“Many of you here have seen more than once how the abuse of the veto at the UN weakens the world and pushes peace further away,” Zelenskyy said.
In the Israeli war on Gaza, the UN has labelled Israel’s conduct there a genocide, but it has struggled to exercise real agency. Security Council resolutions have been repeatedly vetoed, and UN relief agencies have been targeted by Israel without any accountability.
The ongoing war between the US, Israel and Iran is having economic impacts across the globe and threatens to plunge Yemen back into a civil war.
“From Ukraine, to Gaza, and Sudan, and also with what’s happening now in Iran, the veto problem leaves the UN hamstrung,” said Alanna O’Malley, professor and chair of Global Governance and Wealth and head of the Department of History at Erasmus University.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told Al Jazeera’s James Bays this week that these conflicts were having real humanitarian impacts worldwide, including reduced food access, rising fuel prices, and global inflation.
The UNGA will allow the opportunity for some discussions for parties involved in these kinds of conflicts, but it is unlikely they can reach major agreements, said Forti.
But the assembly is still the only forum where all 193 member states are equal, and nations have tried to invoke new procedures and reach back into historical mechanisms to try and mitigate the veto deadlocks, O’Malley said.
A 1950 resolution, dating from a deadlock over the Korean War, has allowed the UNGA to debate issues vetoed in the Security Council. And in 2022, an impasse over Ukraine generated a new mechanism forcing any permanent council representative – China, France, Russia, the UK, and the US, often called the P5 – to come before the UNGA and explain when it uses the veto.
“The idea is to build more accountability into the system for the P5, to make the veto not just harder to use, but also ensure it uses a lot of political capital,” O’Malley said.
Calls for reforms have only increased since 2023 and Israel’s war on Gaza, O’Malley said, with “unprecedented” majority votes in the UNGA challenging the Security Council.
Getting major powers to buy in
Perhaps the greatest challenge facing the UNGA, though, is remaining relevant as major global powers go their own way.
The administration of US President Trump has pushed through its own Board of Peace, a body that has accomplished few of its goals but has secured Security Council approval and claims to take on responsibilities previously handled by UN agencies, like distributing aid or managing refugees.
Unhappy with the UN, Trump has also imposed sanctions on the body’s special rapporteurs, as well as organisations like the International Criminal Court.
Washington, though, may not be the only government looking to strike out on its own.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is in the US this week, but he will not be attending the UNGA. He last addressed the body in 2021 via video, but this year he will skip it altogether, opting instead for one-on-one talks with US President Trump. China has positive views of the UN, often using the Security Council to weigh in on global issues, Forti said, but it is also looking for alternatives, through venues like BRICS and the SCO, to strengthen multilateralism.
The impetus to look for alternatives to the UN, even Secretary Guterres admits, is driven by the fact that the Security Council is unable to pass binding resolutions in the most controversial situations, because permanent members can simply veto them based on their own interests.
Guterres told Al Jazeera this week that kind of inaction was creating an “environment of impunity”, where the behaviour of major global powers was inspiring middle powers and others to “believe that they can do whatever they want because nothing will happen to them”.
The search for the next secretary-general
Guterres’s term ends on December 31, and the Security Council is expected to announce its recommendation for who will replace him.
“We had a secretary-general who didn’t have a lot of political capital to expend to solve these conflicts, and he hasn’t taken great initiative on a lot of them,” said O’Malley.
Guterres did, for example, draw on rarely used Article 99 powers in 2023 to bring the Gaza issue before the Security Council. But the UN also faces major funding problems, with major donors like the US cutting back, making it difficult to deliver aid in places like the West Bank and Gaza. “So he [Guterres] also has no actual financial capital,” O’Malley said.
Candidates to replace Guterres must win at least nine of the 15 votes from the council, and avoid a veto by any of the P5, to be put before the UNGA for a vote.
Forti said member states are looking for someone to refocus on preventing wars, and also deal with criticism that the UN has become unwieldy and costly.
“They will have to balance the UN’s diplomatic work, its impact, with financial cuts and racing to the bottom,” Forti said.

It features seats that rotate 360 degrees and flip as the ride reaches speeds of up to 76mph, racing through half loops that suddenly become “sheer drops”.

“It’s the design of this ride that makes it inherently dangerous and makes it dangerous in a way that no reasonable rider would expect,” he said. “Time after time innocent people are coming off the ride with permanent brain damage.”

====================================================================================================

New study links evolution to weaker human joints
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
03:52:06 CST
04:52:06 KST

JERUSALEM, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- An international team of researchers has found that human evolution may have left people more vulnerable to joint disease, Israel's Weizmann Institute of Science said in a statement on Wednesday.
In their new study, published in the journal Nature, the researchers examined genetic differences between humans and other great apes, including chimpanzees and gorillas.
The researchers found that humans produce significantly lower levels of glycosaminoglycans, or GAGs, in their cartilage. GAGs are sugar molecules that attract water and help cartilage absorb shocks and cushion joints.
The team found that human cartilage contains about one-third as much GAG material as the cartilage of chimpanzees, gorillas, orangutans and bonobos.
The finding may help explain why osteoarthritis and other joint disorders are common in humans but rare in other great apes, even those that reach old age. Osteoarthritis affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide and can cause pain, stiffness, and disability.
The researchers suggested that the evolutionary change may have contributed to other human traits, including lighter bones and a more flexible brain.
They concluded that the findings could help scientists better understand joint diseases and potentially identify new approaches to their prevention and treatment. ■

====================================================================================================

Study led by researchers at University of Sheffield reveals cancer survival mechanism
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
03:51:58 CST
04:51:58 KST

LONDON, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Researchers have identified a mechanism that allows some aggressive cancers to survive when deprived of their normal energy supply, a finding that could offer a new way to slow tumor growth and improve the effectiveness of existing treatments, the University of Sheffield said on Wednesday.
The study, led by researchers at the university and published in the journal PLOS Biology, focused on aggressive breast and pancreatic cancers surrounded by dense, scar-like tissue known as the extracellular matrix.
According to the university, the extracellular matrix can account for up to 90 percent of the mass of some breast and pancreatic tumors. While the dense tissue restricts blood supply and the delivery of nutrients, cancer cells can adapt by using type I collagen, a major component of the matrix, to help them survive.
The researchers found that when levels of glucose, normally a major energy source for cells, fall, collagen activates signals that enable cancer cells to switch their source of fuel and take up essential amino acids needed for growth and survival.
The process depends on a transporter protein known as LAT1, which helps move amino acids into cancer cells. Laboratory experiments using cellular models showed that blocking LAT1 while disrupting the interaction between cancer cells and collagen deprived the cells of vital nutrients, according to the university.
Dr. Elena Rainero, senior lecturer at the University of Sheffield and lead author of the study, said cancer cells can adapt rapidly, which means a single treatment often fails to eliminate a tumor completely.
"If we can block this collagen-driven survival mechanism, we could slow the growth and spread of cancer cells while making them more sensitive to existing treatments like chemotherapy," Rainero said.
She said such an approach could potentially allow clinicians to use lower treatment doses, reducing severe side effects while improving treatment effectiveness.
The researchers said the findings could offer a promising target for future cancer therapies. ■

WINDHOEK, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Namibia has detected an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) within its designated FMD-free zone in the southern Kharas Region, an official announced Wednesday.
Addressing the National Assembly, Acting Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform Charles Mubita said the outbreak was identified on a commercial farm in the Karasburg State Veterinary District during routine disease surveillance by veterinary officials.
Samples were collected from 11 cattle showing clinical signs consistent with FMD on Tuesday, and the laboratory analysis revealed that 10 of the 11 samples tested positive on Wednesday, he said.
"This state confirms an active FMD outbreak in Namibia's World Organization for Animal Health-recognized FMD Free Zone," he added.
According to Mubita, the ministry has instituted immediate control measures as provided for in the Animal Health Act, No. 1 of 2011, to control and contain the outbreak swiftly.
Effective immediately, the movement of all cloven-hoofed animals and their products within the country has been suspended, alongside a complete halt on the import and export of all cloven-hoofed livestock until further notice.
Additionally, the Directorate of Veterinary Services will issue a detailed Veterinary Public Notification outlining all control measures, he said.
FMD is a highly contagious viral disease that affects cloven-hoofed livestock like cattle, sheep, goats, and pigs. ■

The parties are expected to appeal to the Supreme Court, which has overturned similar disqualifications in previous elections.
The Central Elections Committee is chaired by a Supreme Court justice, but is composed mainly of representatives of parties in the outgoing parliament.

Photo taken with a mobile phone on Sept. 21, 2026 shows a train arriving at Main Railway Station in Bratisalva, Slovakia. Slovakia will cut second-class passenger train fares by 50 percent for one month starting from Oct. 1, Prime Minister Robert Fico announced Wednesday after a government meeting. (Xinhua/Liu Haodong)
BRATISLAVA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Slovakia will cut second-class passenger train fares by 50 percent for one month starting from Oct. 1, Prime Minister Robert Fico announced Wednesday after a government meeting.
The measure, approved on the proposal of the Slovakian Transport Ministry, will initially remain in effect for 30 days. Subsequently, it will be reviewed on a monthly basis, Fico said.
"Slovakia is currently facing a sharp rise in fuel prices with a direct impact on the economy and households, whose costs for private car transport are increasing. One of the possible solutions is to shift from private car transport to passenger rail transport," the ministry said in its explanatory report.
The measure is primarily intended for people who use trains regularly to commute to work or school, or for other daily needs. The 50 percent reduction will apply to all second-class, single-journey tickets, as well as weekly and monthly season tickets.
The temporary fare reduction is expected to reduce railway operators' revenues by about 4.3 million euros (4.9 million U.S. dollars) over the 30-day period, while increasing their costs by around 1 million euros (1.14 million dollars).
The government is also considering measures for regional bus transport. Slovakian Transport Minister Jozef Raz has been tasked with preparing by Sept. 30 a proposal under which the state will reimburse self-governing regions for one third of their spending on suburban bus services if they reduce fares by 30 percent. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Americans' firsthand encounters offer fresh perspectives on China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
03:51:37 CST
04:51:37 KST

by Yang Shilong, Vivien Liu
NEW YORK, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Russell Craig Targove can start singing a Chinese song in New York and expect people around him to join in.
Nearly three decades ago and thousands of miles away in Serbia, Sanja Vasic encountered Chinese culture for the first time when a high school teacher wrote Chinese characters on a blackboard.
For both, seemingly casual encounters developed into lasting connections with China.
MUSIC OPENS A DOOR
In the early 1990s, Targove, a New York entertainer, began hosting karaoke nights at a Chinese restaurant owned by a businessman from China's Hong Kong. He soon started learning Chinese pop songs, marking the start of a decades-long connection with New York's Chinese community.
The Chinese songs opened a door beyond music. Through performances at community events and weddings, he became familiar with traditions ranging from tea ceremonies to wedding toasts.
One song that stayed with him was "The Moon Represents My Heart."
"Everybody knows it," he said. "I can start it, and then everybody joins me."
For Targove, music can create connections even when listeners do not share the same language.
"It's a beautiful thing to see people respect each other's culture," he said. "I am always an advocate for bringing those cultures together."
Chinese music has also reached broader audiences at major New York cultural venues, including Carnegie Hall and Lincoln Center. Performances there have featured traditional instruments such as the erhu, pipa and guzheng.
At an August discussion hosted by the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations on the growing visibility of Chinese cultural influence in the United States, Michael Berry, director of the Center for Chinese Studies at the University of California, Los Angeles, said cultural influence does not necessarily follow a single, top-down path.
"The way it manifests is sometimes unpredictable," Berry said.
"When you touch something that maybe reminds you of your parents -- 'Oh, my father used to love this song' -- it has a bridge," Targove said.
FROM LANGUAGE TO LIVED EXPERIENCE
For Vasic, born in Serbia and now a U.S. citizen, language was the doorway.
As a high school student in Serbia, she watched her English teacher write Chinese characters on the blackboard.
"Something clicked in me," she recalled in a recent interview with Xinhua. "I said, although I don't understand it, I'm going to learn it. I'm going to understand it."
Learning the language led her deeper into Chinese history and philosophy, including Confucian thought and Taoism.
"I think it became an integral part of who I am," she said.
Vasic also traveled extensively across China. Looking back, she said one of the most fascinating aspects of the country was "how it balanced between modernization and continuity."
When she first arrived in 1998, she remembers streets filled with bicycles and small private businesses alongside state-run stores. Mobile phones and digital technology had yet to become fixtures of everyday life.
"The most impressive thing is the transformation, and the scale and the speed," she said.
More recent American visitors have encountered that transformation from a different starting point.
Before New York photographer Delaney Masal first traveled to China, she expected the country she had long seen portrayed in American headlines -- crowded, less developed and unwelcoming.
Instead, the experience "floored" her.
Traveling through east China's Zhejiang Province, Masal was surprised by the scale and bustle of Hangzhou and later by the coexistence of advanced technology with centuries-old towns and landscapes.
Joshua Cuppek, another first-time American visitor, arrived with a different expectation.
"I'd always imagined China would be busy and fast-paced, but everything about it -- the culture, the landscapes -- was calming, almost meditative in its own way," he said.
Such firsthand encounters have become more common as China has expanded visa-free travel. In the first half of 2026, foreign nationals made 17.82 million visa-free entries into China, up 30.6 percent year on year, according to China's National Immigration Administration.
For Vasic, such direct exposure matters.
Learning Chinese, she said, "really enriches your life in ways that people cannot imagine" and "really opens your eyes to the rest of the world."
A DIFFERENT IMAGE OF MODERN CHINA
Technology has created another point of contact.
Speaking at the same National Committee discussion, Shaoyu Yuan, a visiting assistant professor at New York University's Center for Global Affairs, said some young Americans are paying attention to aspects of everyday life in China that received relatively little attention in the United States in the past.
"Everything is about how fast the public transport is, how clean it is, and how developed the electric vehicles are, the mobile payments, the robotics. And China in that case becomes a comparison point," Yuan said.
Vasic has watched another part of that transformation over nearly three decades: Chinese companies moving from producing goods designed elsewhere toward developing their own technologies and products.
That change is also registering in American public opinion. Electric vehicles, batteries, drones, robotics, mobile payments and high-speed rail have become not only technology stories but also windows through which some Americans encounter contemporary China.
A 2026 survey by the Committee of 100 and NORC at the University of Chicago found that 59 percent of Americans favored increased cooperation between the United States and China.
For Vasic, the value of encountering another culture is ultimately more personal.
"We may all speak different languages. We may all have different cultures and different backgrounds," she said. "But we all care for the same things, like our family, our children, our meaningful job, health and hope for a better future."
"I fell in love with the language and the culture, and I never regretted the decision," she said. "I'm still learning." ■

Trump ramps up noncitizen voting prosecutions ahead of midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:51:37 UTC
04:51:37 KST

Trump ramps up noncitizen voting prosecutions ahead of midterms
WASHINGTON, Sept 23 - President Donald Trump’s administration is ramping up criminal prosecutions of noncitizens accused of voting in US elections as he presses claims of widespread election fraud ahead of the November midterms.
The US Justice Department has brought criminal charges against about 20 people this month under a law criminalizing “voting by aliens”, roughly 13% of all prosecutions brought under the statute since it was enacted three decades ago, according to a Reuters review of court records and government statements.
The investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security has mobilized hundreds of agents in all 50 states to aid what a Justice Department official described as a “tier-one priority for the attorney general and for the White House.”
The official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss details of the investigations, said the pace of prosecutions would likely increase in the weeks leading up to the November 3 midterms, which will determine control of the US Senate and House of Representatives.
The spate of recent cases is part of a long-running attempt by the Trump administration to demonstrate that voting by non-US citizens poses a major threat to the security of elections, despite studies showing the practice is rare.
Trump and his supporters say it is part of an organized conspiracy led by Democrats who hope to retake Congress. Trump is pushing Republicans in Congress to toughen up voting requirements.
Critics of the administration allege the claims are aimed at diminishing confidence in the vote and potentially laying the groundwork to challenge election results, with polls showing Trump’s Republican Party could face significant losses in November.
The rhetoric about noncitizen voting is "little by little eroding the trust of the public,” Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar, a Democrat, told Reuters.
Trump administration officials have pointed to the recent cases to push back against Democratic criticism.
“The folks on the other side, the opponents of the president, insist this never happens,” acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told reporters on Tuesday. “When you have dozens of cases that we brought just in the last few weeks, I think that discourages and defeats their characterization.”
A Reuters review published in July found that prior to Trump’s second term, federal prosecutions for alleged noncitizen voting were extremely uncommon. Many defendants were lawful permanent residents, a trend that has continued in the recent cases.
A separate Reuters review published on Wednesday found states may have added more than 30,000 self-declared noncitizens to the nation’s voter rolls since 2000 because of software glitches and clerical errors made while processing their driver's license and state ID applications.
Cases brought by the DOJ in recent weeks allege that defendants registered to vote or cast ballots in recent elections despite knowing they were not US citizens. The recent uptick in prosecutions represents a small fraction of the tens of millions of ballots cast in federal elections.
An official with Homeland Security Investigations, the DHS unit that conducts criminal investigations, said HSI has 1,600 open investigations related to the issue.
A COORDINATED EFFORT
The Justice Department has brought charges against 32 people in the last four weeks for noncitizen voting and related offenses, according to a DOJ spokesperson.
Seven of those cases were brought by the US Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas, where federal prosecutors received help from the office of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for the US Senate and a Trump ally.
In one example of the pressure to bring cases, a top DOJ official told senior prosecutors at US attorney’s offices across the country this month that prosecutors could no longer decide on their own to refuse election fraud cases, according to a source briefed on the conversation.
The deputy attorney general's office, staffed by political appointees, would have the final say if agents with the FBI or DHS felt the evidence warranted charges, the source said.
The directive unnerved some on the call given it has traditionally been career prosecutors who decide whether charges are justified in such cases, according to the source. MS NOW first reported details of the meeting.
A DOJ official said the deputy attorney general's office would not intervene in every case where prosecutors think charges are not warranted, but said department leadership would mediate disputes between prosecutors and agents. REUTERS

‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:51:12 UTC
04:51:12 KST

Google has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a feature Google calls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting.
“AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” wrote Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search, last August. In May, the company said more AI is coming.
As people grow accustomed to AI chatbots, they’re spending more time with Google’s and therefore more time on Google.com. Academic studies are finding that people navigate less to sites beyond Google if an AI Overview can give them a good enough answer, even if the bot cites the sites that feed it. Clicks, also known as traffic, are often the most significant way a website earns money from advertising. Media outlets and website owners are enduring a sustained traffic decline. Large US media companies are suing Google, alleging that AI summaries have redirected and reduced traffic to their sites, cutting into their revenue.
Google said it had not seen a decline in aggregate traffic and that such accusations are based on “flawed methodologies”. Reid, the company’s vice-president of search, wrote last year: “Total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.”
The Guardian asked readers whether Google has improved or worsened in the age of AI and how their habits of searching the internet have changed.
‘Google is better now’
Better, mainly because it leads you in your quest rather than you having to search on yourself. I am happy to have the AI lead me to an answer but the mega caution is that Google AI or any of them are not at all trustworthy. I have had it admit that it was lying to me and apologise! Sionn Achog, retired teacher 76, Dublin
I find that AI responses are more informative than previously, which simply referred the user to other relevant websites. Peter Warb, 75, UK
AI has made Google better. I use AI mode for all my searches. Jose Garcia Jr, 40, recovery coach, Dallas, Texas
AI has improved Google search. The analysis and chat functions are so much more useful than a ranked list of websites that still need to be explored by the user. Reviewing a list of websites is still an option but is very time consuming, and frustrating. Alan Caruana, consultant, 62, Malta
Far more better, faster and real. I search now with confidence, complete assurance and a high degree of accuracy. Eleazar Eke, electrical engineer, 67, Onitsha, Nigeria
Much better. It hasn’t changed my behavior, just getting better and more focused results. Catherine Weber, former political analyst, 57, Oregon
It’s made Google search much better, I find that I rarely actually click on the website links any more. I find information I want much faster and have a deeper understanding of any topic as I can ask questions about it and drill into the areas I’m interested in. Mark Johnson, 52, software engineer, London
Greatly improved it by getting at more arcane info regarding subject matter. Juxtaposition has improved with AI and abstruse knowledge of subjects becomes more accessible to layman. Wonderful tool with power to extend mind through sensing connections and very akin to human thinking. Samuel Lieberstein, 90, retired teacher, Cherry Hill, New Jersey
‘Search has gotten worse’
Search has become worse. Google AI obscures sources and tries to claim information it did not create while diverting traffic from the sources it steals from. Sean Peters, document processor, 41, Portland, Oregon
Every time I search I have to scroll down to find an actual real website to find a full article or discussion or to confirm that the AI summary isn’t making things up. Occasionally when I am feeling particularly bitter, I remember to add the ““-ai”” tag to my search. Ewan Herbert, English teacher, 33, Japan
Worse. I have disabled AI overviews using an extension. Chris Gibson, Dundee
Absolutely worse. I want to be able to decide for myself which results are the most useful and relevant, and we’re no longer able to turn off the AI summary results. Jon Wilkinson, personal trainer, 43, Manchester, UK
‘It’s so bad I quit Google’
Google has been enshittified … I do miss old Google Search and I really hope something of equal capabilities eventually comes to replace it.
The search engine I currently use is good for a lot of things, but if I need to look for something in languages other than English, the quality of the results is much lower. Image search is also not as good as that of Google used to be. Sofia, postdoctoral physics researcher, 30, Lausanne, Switzerland
My first stop now is Duck Duck Go, a pale imitation of Google’s search engine at the height of its powers. Unfortunately, the top results often include Grokipedia entries and other garbage. Craig Garrett, book editor, 52, New York City
I have stopped using Google. I now use another search engine with no AI overviews. Guy Arthur Simpson, writer 66, Spain
I’ve made a conscious effort to find a browser which does not lead with the AI results. Mine is now Ecosia. Dan Jennings, IT, 54, Southampton, UK
I do a lot of research for my studies, and the AI features are a nightmare! I’m still scouring for a decent search engine without any of these ‘AI features’, the last thing i want is to accidentally utilise a water-wasting AI behemoth datacentre when I forget that crucial suffix. I’ve even resorted to using my local library’s resource of legal cases for my work, at least it is trustworthy. Catherine O’Leary, student studying law, politics and sociology, 17, Newcastle Upon Tyne
Google has become almost useless, searches I’ve made in the past which yielded specific results, (news articles, local information, historical references) no longer appear. I no longer submit to Google search first, I go directly to Wikipedia as my first source, then to DuckDuckGo, (with AI disabled) then to Reddit and only to Google as a last resort. Pedro Reyes, 61, Galicia, Spain

Music critic and television host Sergey Sosedov has died at 58, journalist Vadim Takmenev reported on Wednesday.
In an Instagram post, Takmenev referred to the shows “Superstar” and “Vocal-Instrumental Ensemble Superstar” and wrote: “We’re all in shock. This morning we lost our friend Sergey Sosedov, an indispensable part of our team and the heart, soul, and driving force behind ‘Superstar’. We were all supposed to get together this Saturday to watch the first episode of the new season of ‘VIA Superstar’. He was really looking forward to seeing everyone and to the premiere. The entire season will be dedicated to his memory. In memory of the man he was — spontaneous, fair, stubborn, kind, gentle, vibrant, and genuine!”
According to the Telegram channel Shot, Sosedov died in an accidental fall down the stairs while on tour.
Sergey Sosedov was born in Moscow in 1968. He graduated from Moscow State University, where he studied journalism, and worked for the newspaper Rossiyskiye Vesti in the mid-1990s. He became well known for his appearances on the TV-6 show “Akuly pera” (“Sharks of the Pen”), where he interviewed Russian and international entertainment stars. He was also a judge on “The X Factor” in Ukraine and on the Russian television music shows “Superstar!” and “Ty — superstar!” (“You’re a Superstar!”). Sosedov also hosted the NTV talk show “Za granyu” (“Beyond the Edge”).
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Sosedov criticized Russian performers who had left the country. He called for Maxim Galkin and Chulpan Khamatova to be “denounced and put in their place” and called them “disgraceful” artists. Ukraine placed Sosedov on its sanctions list in 2023.

Albert Axelrad, Brandeis Hillel rabbi who championed pluralism and social justice, dies at 87
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:48:59 UTC
04:48:59 KST

Rabbi Albert S. Axelrad, a Reform rabbi, community leader, and political activist who headed Brandeis University’s Hillel Foundation for 34 years, died on Sept. 18. He was 87.
Starting in 1965, Axelrad sought to ensure that students and faculty from all Jewish streams received the logistical support and resources needed to live the fullest of Jewish lives at Brandeis, the only nonsectarian, Jewish-sponsored college or university in the United States.
“Al didn’t just preach pluralism. He lived pluralism,” said Rabbi Peretz Rodman, who first met Axelrad as an undergraduate and later joined his Hillel staff while a graduate student. “For example, there hadn’t been much of an Orthodox presence on campus until the mid-1970s, when he hired an Orthodox rabbi and provided space for that minyan.”
Although dedicated to egalitarian prayer that offers equal roles for men and women, Axelrad often attended Orthodox and other non-egalitarian services, Rodman said. “He would quip that he davened in an egalitarian minyan before praying with the Orthodox minyan, so he’d be ‘yotzei’” — having fulfilled his own religious requirements as a liberal Jew.
Axelrad’s commitment to egalitarian prayer led him to cofound the non-denominational Havurat Shalom in Somerville, Massachusetts. A lay-led, independent congregation that drew on aspects of the counterculture, it served as a model of egalitarianism for what became known as the havurah movement.
A native Brooklynite, Axelrad attended the Yeshivah of Flatbush and earned a bachelor’s degree in sociology from Columbia University. In 1965 he received rabbinic ordination from Hebrew Union College-Jewish Institute of Religion. Soon afterward, he moved to Massachusetts to become the Hillel director and chaplain at Brandeis.
His first years at Brandeis coincided with the movement opposing the war in Vietnam, and Axelrad, a member of the Jewish Peace Fellowship, counseled students who were weighing whether to become conscientious objectors. He also advocated for divesting from South Africa as a means to end apartheid.
Israel and Jews remained at the center of Axelrad’s activism
But Israel and Jews remained at the center of Axelrad’s activism. He was an early supporter of the “two-state solution” through Breira, the first national Jewish organization to advocate for an independent Palestinian state, and passionate about the struggle of Jews locked beyond the Iron Curtain and punished for practicing Judaism.
He made activism to free Soviet Jews central to Jewish life at Brandeis and traveled to the Soviet Union twice to meet Jewish refuseniks. His 1985 book “Refusenik: Voices of Struggle and Hope” chronicles his first visit. In 1984 he wrote “Meditations of a Maverick Rabbi,” in which he explained, among other things, why he performed interfaith marriages.
Axelrad is credited with creating, in the 1970s, the first bar- and bat-mitzvah training programs for Jewish adults who missed out on the ceremony in their youth. These programs became a mainstay in many American synagogues. Other Hillels adopted the annual Jewish Arts Festival he introduced.
After retiring from Brandeis in 1999, Axelrad became the founding director of the Center for Spiritual Life and an adjunct professor of religion at Emerson College in Boston.
Upon learning of Axelrad’s death, hundreds of former Brandeis students — many of them now rabbis themselves — took to social media to recall Axelrad’s pluralistic, the-door-is-always-open style of leadership and the effect he had on their lives. Many called him a bridge-builder and a “mensch.”
Rabbi Bob Carroll, who worked closely with Axelrad as a student board member of Brandeis Hillel and, later, as its president while an undergraduate, said he owed Axelrad “a huge debt of gratitude.
“Probably more than anyone else in my life, when I waver over whether I should have the courage to speak out about something demanding moral courage or sacrifice, to risk my own position or reputation, it is his example and memory that I see in my mind’s eye,” said Carroll, an Orthodox rabbi.
“I haven’t always lived up to his standard. But because of him I at least knew what I should have had the guts to do, or to say. And I was a better human being and a better Jew because of him. Even when our paths diverged.”
Rabbah Riqi Kosovske, the rabbi of the Beit Ahavah Reform synagogue in Northampton, Massachusetts, said Axelrad had a “huge impact” on her life from the moment she became a Brandeis undergraduate.
“One of my earliest memories was singing in the student circle with him at 12:15 p.m. every day at the daily vigil when he was on the hunger strike for divestment [from South Africa], and I would cry watching him as I worried and cared so much for him and was so inspired by him,” she said. “I am grateful for his kindness and the impact he had on me.”
'He would look you in the eye. He was fully present'
Rabbi Ron Kronish was a sophomore when Axelrad began his position at Brandeis. Kronish, who became the student head of Hillel during his senior year, described Axelrad as “a great listener. He would look you in the eye. He was fully present.”
Kronish, who later became a Reform rabbi and an interfaith activist in the United States and Israel, said Axelrad always looked at life through a Jewish lens and that his opposition to the Vietnam War and his involvement in civil rights “came out of his understanding of what it means to be Jewish.”
Larry Sternberg called Axelrad “a consummate mensch — kind, gentle, caring — a good listener, a strong ally and a principled leader.” He first met Axelrad in 1973, when he began his graduate work at Brandeis. Sternberg later served on the faculty at Brandeis and as executive director of the university’s Hillel from 2004-2013.
“He acted on his passions and beliefs, reflecting a commitment to rabbinic activism. At times I found him infuriating,” Sternberg said, “but that never resulted in tension between us. Our bond was strong because Al knew that disagreeing did not diminish our respect for one another. While many rabbis aspire to inspire others, Al was the real deal.”
Axelrad is survived by four children and several grandchildren. Berta Axelrad, his wife of 63 years, died in December 2024.

US drafted memo condemning UK over West Bank sanctions, but it was never released - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:48:52 UTC
04:48:52 KST

In early September, US officials in Jerusalem and Washington prepared a draft statement attributed to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemning plans by the UK, France and Canada to block imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
The September 8 document, previously unreported and which two sources said was driven by David Milstein, an influential aide to US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, proposed that Rubio describe the countries' actions as a series of hostile measures against Israel that contribute to antisemitism.
"These tactics unacceptably draw from the playbook of the antisemitic boycotts, divestments and sanctions movement," the draft document, reviewed by Reuters, said.
The statement was never released.
According to three people familiar with the matter, the White House and the State Department's senior leadership did not support the statement.
The people spoke on condition of anonymity.
Instead, speaking to reporters on September 8 in Florida before traveling to Latin America, Rubio refrained from outright criticism of the decision or any particular country.
"Obviously, we’re not going to do what the UK did. We saw their announcement today, but I don’t have any comment on it right now," Rubio said.
A widening divide between the White House and Trump's senior diplomats in Israel
The episode illustrates a widening divide between the White House and Trump's senior diplomats in Israel about how best to respond to the expansion of Israeli settlements under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government.
It also highlights a growing ideological split within the American right over support for Israel, with polling showing younger Republicans holding an increasingly unfavorable opinion of Washington's closest Middle East ally.
US President Donald Trump earlier this year expressed his opposition to settlement expansion, a growing source of friction with Israel's Arab neighbors, but his administration has put little pressure on Israel to change its policy.
That has at times put him at odds with Huckabee, a Baptist minister who is a staunch supporter of settlements and who refers to the West Bank by its biblical name, Judea and Samaria, a term used by the Israeli government but not formally adopted by the US.
Huckabee's aide Milstein last year advocated that the US impose sanctions on the entire International Criminal Court to convince it to drop war crimes charges against Israeli leaders over the Gaza war - a measure the Trump administration has yet to deploy.
In response to questions from Reuters, a senior US official said the draft statement was not prepared in consultation with the State Department or White House.
The US embassy referred questions, including requests for comment from Huckabee and Milstein, to the State Department.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
US public support for Israel questioned
US public backing for Israel has fallen since the Israel-Hamas War began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017.
While large majorities of Republicans aged 50 and older view Israel positively, younger conservative Americans have grown more critical, a Pew Research Center poll from late March showed. Some 57% of Republicans aged 18-49 have an unfavorable opinion of Israel, up from 50% a year previously.
In December last year, Trump said that he and Netanyahu, whose government has overseen a rapid expansion of settlements, did not fully agree on the West Bank following a meeting with the Israeli leader. That September, Trump said he would not allow Israel to annex the territory.
Violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the territory has risen sharply this year, some of them emboldened by support from Netanyahu's right-wing government, which includes ministers who are themselves settlers.
Huckabee has publicly condemned the violence and called for perpetrators to be prosecuted. He has also said violent settlers were a minority and do not represent the wider settler community.

Sa’ar rejects claim of global consensus against Israel, says UN majority cannot dictate policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:48:44 UTC
04:48:44 KST

Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar acknowledged that Israel currently finds itself in a diplomatic minority at the United Nations but rejected the characterization that there is a broad international “consensus” against Israel.
Speaking to The Jerusalem Post during the ongoing 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, Sa’ar said Israel had been in a minority position at the UN for decades.
“We were in the minority a year ago. We were in the minority two years ago, ten years ago, twenty years ago, and forty years ago,” Sa’ar said.
The opening day of this year’s General Assembly highlighted Sa’ar’s point, as a series of world leaders devoted significant portions of their speeches to criticism of Israel’s policies in Gaza and the West Bank.
“We need to ask ourselves whether we should base our policy regarding our existential interests on the international consensus, or, even if it is not a total international consensus, on the majority view within the international system, or according to our own existential interests,” Sa’ar said.
According to Sa’ar, Israel’s past concessions have not translated into lasting diplomatic credit.
'We have reached a point where we cannot make concessions'
He cited the Oslo Accords, the establishment of the Palestinian Authority and Israel’s 2005 unilateral withdrawal from the Gaza Strip as examples of far-reaching Israeli steps that, in his view, did not produce the expected diplomatic benefits.
“Ultimately we receive no accumulated credit in the international system for these actions,” he said.
Sa’ar said Israel had reached a point where it could no longer continue making concessions simply because of international pressure.
“We have reached a point where we cannot make concessions,” he said.
The comments come as several countries continue to promote Palestinian statehood at the UN. A joint statement issued on Tuesday by the foreign ministers of Turkey, Jordan, Egypt, Indonesia, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates reaffirmed support for a “sovereign, viable, and independent Palestinian State” and called for implementation of a two-state framework.
One of the world leaders who criticized Israel was Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Sa’ar said he did not currently define Turkey as an “enemy state,” stressing that the term is an official designation with practical consequences.
“I do not define Turkey as an enemy state,” he said. “But I cannot ignore the fact that Turkey under Erdogan’s leadership is pursuing a policy hostile toward Israel in the diplomatic arena, including moves in the economic and legal spheres.”
Sa’ar said relations between Israel and Turkey had unfortunately been moving in a negative direction for decades and had intensified during Erdogan’s years in power.
He also pointed to Turkey’s relationship with Hamas as a significant element in Israel’s concerns.
Israel and Turkey have exchanged increasingly sharp accusations in recent months. In July, Sa’ar condemned comments by Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan regarding Israel, calling them a “clear call for genocide.”
Sa’ar was similarly critical of Jordanian statements at the General Assembly.
King Abdullah II used his UNGA address to accuse Israel of changing realities in Gaza and the West Bank, including through settlement expansion, land seizures and what he described as de facto annexation.
Israel was 'not particularly impressed' by 'Jordanian moralizing'
The Jordanian king also criticized Israeli actions in Syria, describing what he called Israel’s regional “appetite” as a threat and saying Syria was a warning sign.
Sa’ar said Israel was “not particularly impressed” by what he called Jordanian moralizing on the Palestinian issue.
“I just want to remind you that, when it comes to international law and Palestinian rights, Jordan is perhaps one of the last countries that should be lecturing others,” he said.
He referred specifically to Jordan’s 1988 decision to sever the legal and administrative ties that had granted West Bank residents Jordanian citizenship, arguing that the move deprived many people of citizenship and associated rights.
Sa’ar characterized the decision as contrary to international law and said it should be considered when evaluating Jordanian criticism of Israel on international-law issues.
Sa’ar also criticized what he described as a bloc of countries that has increasingly coordinated its diplomatic messaging against Israel.
He acknowledged that some of these countries initially came together around goals Israel could support, including ending the Gaza war and securing the release of the hostages.
“But if you look at it, that same bloc frequently issues joint statements systematically criticizing Israel,” he said.

Somaliland delegation eyes Israeli military presence to strengthen cooperation against Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:48:43 UTC
04:48:43 KST

Somaliland and Israel should develop a military partnership that could include an Israeli presence in Somaliland in order to strengthen cooperation against Houthi terrorists, Ahmed Dirie, chairperson of the executive committee of the Israel and Somaliland Friendship Association and head of a visiting delegation, told The Jerusalem Post.
Dirie said he envisioned a relationship in which Israel and Somaliland would assist one another against common threats, arguing that Somaliland’s position in the Horn of Africa and near the Bab al-Mandab Strait gives it particular strategic importance.
Asked whether Somaliland would be open to an Israeli military presence in the country, Dirie responded, “That’s right.”
“Somaliland has a very strategic point in Bab al-Mandab,” he said. “We have a problem there at the moment, and that problem, the only one who can solve it is Somaliland.”
“If they get help from the Israelis, they can beat the Houthis and make it safe,” he continued. “And we can operate in that area easily because of the location they have in Somaliland.”
Dirie’s comments come after months of speculation over whether Israel could eventually establish a military base in Somaliland.
In June, Somaliland Defense Minister Mohamed Yusuf Ali, speaking on the sidelines of a business conference in Tel Aviv, told Reuters that there was no Israeli military presence in Somaliland and no negotiations underway to establish a base.
He did, however, confirm that Israel was training Somaliland military and police personnel.
Speaking to the Post that same month, Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi similarly said an Israeli military presence had not been discussed, but left the door open to such an arrangement in the future.
“I cannot rule out the possibility that it could happen in the future,” Abdullahi said. “If our cooperation continues to deepen, our relationship could develop far beyond where it stands today.”
Earlier this month, Abdullahi told Israel Today that an Israeli and American military presence could have a deterrent effect in the region. Jewish News Syndicate reported on Tuesday that Abdullahi said he hoped the two countries would begin cooperating in the security sector before the end of the year.
Still, Abdullahi also told the Post earlier this month that Somaliland currently has no conflict with the Houthis and that his government had not discussed allowing Israel to use Somaliland territory or airspace for operations against the group.
Dirie calls for mutual military cooperation
Asked whether he envisioned something resembling a mutual-defense arrangement, under which Israel and Somaliland would assist one another if either came under attack, Dirie said, “That’s right. That’s what we need.”
“If anybody was attacked, they have to help each other,” he said.
Dirie repeatedly emphasized military cooperation as central to his vision for the developing relationship. He also described the Houthis as a direct threat to Somaliland.
“The Houthis want to attack Somaliland, and they want to attack Israel. They have to face this together,” he said.
Israel became the first UN member state to formally recognize Somaliland as an independent and sovereign state in December 2025. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar visited the African country the following month, vowing to “vigorously advance relations” between the two countries.
In May, Dr. Mohamed Hagi presented his credentials to President Isaac Herzog, becoming Somaliland’s first ambassador to Israel. Somaliland opened its embassy in Jerusalem the following month.
Dirie said the next chapter in relations should involve “cooperation on everything: business cooperation, military cooperation, peace cooperation, as in protecting each other.”
“Israel and Somaliland are facing the same enemy at the moment,” he said.
Din Moriel, an Israeli member of the delegation, was more explicit about what an Israeli military presence could offer strategically.
“Obviously, them sitting in Bab al-Mandab, in the waterway, it’s right in front of the Houthis,” Moriel said. “So, having a military base there, having military presence there, and being able to use force whenever needed, without sending our airplanes so far across the world, would be very much of a help to Israel.”
Somaliland prepared to contribute up to 2,000 troops to Gaza force
Dirie also referred to Somaliland’s willingness to contribute soldiers to an international stabilization force in Gaza.
Abdullahi, speaking on the sidelines of the MEAD conference in Washington earlier this month, said Somaliland was prepared to provide as many as 2,000 troops if requested, while stressing that the country had not yet been asked to contribute forces.

A New York judge sentenced former Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein to 15 years in prison on Wednesday for sexually assaulting a former production assistant in 2006, following the ex-movie mogul's conviction at a retrial last year.
Weinstein, 74, was convicted in June 2025 of first-degree criminal sexual act for assaulting Miriam Haley at his Manhattan apartment, the culmination of a six-year legal saga that saw his 2020 conviction overturned by New York's highest court. Weinstein has denied assaulting anyone or having non-consensual sex.
Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg on Wednesday praised Haley for her testimony and said he was moved by her courage.
A Weinstein spokesman said in a statement that Weinstein maintains his innocence and strongly disagrees with the sentence imposed by Judge Curtis Farber.
Weinstein was first convicted in New York in 2020 of assaulting Haley and raping aspiring actress Jessica Mann and was sentenced to 23 years in prison. New York's highest court overturned that conviction in 2024, finding that he had not received a fair trial. At his 2025 retrial, jurors convicted him of a charge related to Haley, acquitted him of assaulting former model Kaja Sokola, and deadlocked on a rape charge involving Mann.
Weinstein faces separate California sentence after New York conviction
A third trial on Mann's allegation ended in another mistrial in May. Prosecutors dropped the charge the following month after Mann said she did not want to testify in a fourth trial.
Weinstein, who co-founded the Miramax studio, was separately convicted in California in 2022 of rape and sexual assault and sentenced to 16 years. A California appeals court in June upheld those convictions but ordered him resentenced because the trial judge had considered his since-overturned New York convictions as an aggravating factor.
Weinstein's original conviction was a milestone for the #MeToo movement, which encouraged women to come forward with allegations of sexual misconduct by powerful men.
More than 100 women, including famous actresses, have accused Weinstein of misconduct. He has denied the allegations.
