Why the breakup of the ‘United Kingdom’ can't come soon enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:47:30 UTC
04:47:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Why the breakup of the ‘United Kingdom’ can't come soon enough
Does the recent agreement and declaration of a renewed effort at the constitutional break-up of Britain, launched by the heads of nationalist parties across Scotland, Wales and Ireland, signal the return of the national question to British politics?
Meeting in Cardiff Bay less than a fortnight ago, the leader of Plaid Cymru Rhun ap Iorwerth, Scottish National Party leader John Swinney, Sinn Féin President Mary Lou McDonald and Sinn Féin Vice-President Michelle O’Neill signed a Memorandum of Understanding seeking to revive momentum behind their respective quests for national sovereignty. The Memorandum itself articulated a shared agreement over stronger, fairer economies, the expansion of national energy resources, a commitment to the future of the European Union, and a defence of self-determination.
Coming within months of Andy Burnham’s rise to the top of government, this announcement of intentions, clearly geared towards taking advantage of the Labour leader’s support for devolving power regionally and nationally, was met with polite dismissal. A spokesperson for Burnham made it clear that the Prime Minister was focused on uniting the nation and confronting the cost-of-living crisis rather than on “constitutional debates”.
Whilst the evidence for Andy Burnham focusing qualitatively on resolving the cost-of-living crisis remains remarkably thin, the relative success of Celtic nationalism has always depended on the nationalist parties’ capacity to conjure social content into their strategies.
In 2014, despite the SNP losing the independence referendum by 10 points, the Yes vote, in no small part due to the mass grassroots efforts of the non-aligned Radical Independence Campaign, energised working-class voters on council estates across the country. Across the decade since the referendum, however, the SNP has actively sought to demobilise those sentiments, welding itself far more thoroughly to the technocratic management of the devolved constitutional order.
As Johnathan Shafi has argued in his aptly entitled Independence Captured blog, “behind the scenes, the SNP have acted as a cog in the corporate machine. In 2020 alone, hundreds of secret meetings between multinational corporations and wealthy individuals took place with Scottish Government ministers. The SNP signed off on freeports, subnational tax havens owned by private companies. They sold off Scottish wind energy to foreign capital.”
From their roots in radical leftism and peace politics, the SNP have evolved into a party incapable of inspiring a movement for independence, an issue far less salient to voters than a decade ago. Instead, the party is recovering from its enthralment in a series of high-level corruption scandals involving senior figures such as Peter Murrell and Nicola Sturgeon.
The quest for independence
The recent announcement that Members of the Scottish Parliament will be able to vote on a legal mechanism for an independence referendum should be a significant step towards the break-up of Britain, especially given it was emboldened by the majority. However, the dissonance of an establishment party trying to conjure mass support for independence on establishment grounds does not bode well.
In Wales, the quest for independence is situated in an earlier phase. The 2025 Caerphilly by-election, in which well-known local Plaid Cymru candidate Lindsay Whittle defeated the Reform UK candidate, in some ways prefigured what was to come in the recent elections to the Welsh Parliament, the Senedd. By May 2026, Labour’s century of managed decline, as argued compellingly by Seb Cook, had come crashing down.
Labour’s vote had been cannibalised by Plaid Cymru, which had become the biggest party in the Senedd, five seats short of a majority. Holding off Reform UK, which had increased its number of seats to 34 in its first run at the Senedd, the Welsh nationalists have faced several challenges since forming a minority government.
Having ruled out any commitment to a referendum in this governing cycle, the party has made a significant miscalculation, expecting Labour to operate as Plaid has historically, like the reasonable opposition, reluctantly supporting austerity budgets. The declining establishment party in Wales has given them no such reprieve.
The Irish dynamic remains somewhat different. Whilst, as the late historian Neil Davidson argued, Scottish nationalism emerged as a constituent part of British national identity in the wake of the 1707 Act of Union, Irish republicanism is the distinct and heterogeneous expression of centuries of anti-colonial resistance, articulated and practised by figures as diverse as wealthy Protestants such as Theobald Wolfe Tone and working-class Catholics like Bobby Sands.
The early twentieth-century war of independence saw Republican forces divided by the British state, as Free Staters accepted the British Empire’s partition of Ireland and the erection of a formalised Orange State in the north, exercising sectarian discrimination and oppression against the Catholic minority.
A century later, the republican cause has officially put down the guns, with Sinn Féin commanding the largest bloc in the Northern Ireland Assembly and topping election polls in the Republic of Ireland just four months before an election to the Dáil Éireann must legally occur.
Change must come now
Despite its growing dominance, Sinn Féin reflects a different social base compared to its days as the political wing of the Provisional Irish Republican Army. In the north of Ireland especially, it has increasingly become the party of the Catholic middle class, as parties such as People Before Profit and smaller left Republican outfits chip away at its vote in the working-class Catholic strongholds of Derry and Belfast, as well as some Catholic rural areas.
In the Republic, the Catholic middle class is somewhat more afraid of Sinn Féin, fearing the disruption to their comforts that a potential border poll could bring.
If Sinn Féin is going to win its arguments for a border poll north and south, however, it will have to disregard its framing of Irish unity as “Vote now, change to come later”. The Celtic Tiger may be experiencing a healthier growth pattern than many of its comparators to its east, but its image as a low-tax, low-regulation haven for tax-dodgers and Artificial Intelligence won’t provide the most promising appeal to working-class voters, of Protestant or Catholic descent, in the north.
For independence and unity to be an enticing prospect on both sides of the border, it will require a government geared towards transforming the Irish Republic into a profoundly free and sovereign place for working-class people tout court if the centuries-long colonial sectarianism of Orange state versus Green is to be broken out of.
The existence of left-wing challengers to Sinn Féin, such as People Before Profit, keeping them honest and giving a social content to the independence project not unlike the Radical Independence Campaign, could be central for determining the outcome of Irish politics.
What remains of the imperial British state
It may be counter-intuitive to suggest that the British state might boast of some success for having held on to these three statelets for so long. Without a doubt, the powers that be are evidently capable of great hubris. But the efforts of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, bringing the Provisional IRA to the table, acceding to the popular demands for peace of those in the north of Ireland, instituting the Good Friday Agreement and devolving power to Scotland and Wales have all served to tame and absorb the threats of nationalist projects.
Constitutional devolution transformed nationalist leaders into state managers long before those projects came close to achieving their demands. Andy Burnham, if he is to avoid becoming, in John Swinney’s words, “the last prime minister of the United Kingdom”, will seek to follow in his predecessors’ footsteps, offering up a vision of devolution tempting enough to placate today’s nationalist politicians whilst rescuing what remains of the imperial British state.
In a clear signal of their intention to take advantage of Burnham’s devolutionary impulses, Swinney and ap Iorwerth’s separate agreement between the Welsh and Scottish governments, signed the same day as the Memorandum of Understanding, stated it would "press the case for greater fairness for Wales and Scotland in areas such as the operation of the UK funding arrangements and powers over our constitutional future".
The future of Britain’s break-up, a desirable outcome for democrats and anti-imperialists everywhere, depends on those same nationalist politicians rejecting this tendency and embracing a radicalism which might energise their constituents. In short, as the history of Irish republicanism in particular has shown, the future of Britain’s break-up requires the nationally oppressed and subordinated populace to take national sovereignty as a potential starting point, but by no means an endgame. It’s unclear that today’s nationalist leaders grasp this.
Jonas Marvin is the author of The Breaking of the English Working Class. He also cohosts Life of the Party podcast and blogs at Marx’s Dream Journal.

Zelensky Tells UN Russia Lost Nearly 249,000 Troops This Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:46:27 UTC
04:46:27 KST

Russia lost nearly 249,000 military personnel in the first eight months of 2026 while gaining very little ground, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday.
Speaking during the high-level general debate of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, Zelensky said Russia managed to capture just over 1,000 square kilometers (roughly 386 square miles) of Ukrainian territory.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“And we have already liberated a significant part of it,” he continued.
According to him, Russian President Vladimir Putin had spent about 284 people per kilometer (approximately 736 people per square mile).
Zelensky calls Putin ‘patient zero’
During his UN address, Zelensky repeatedly referred to Putin as “patient zero” – the man from whom the war began to spread.
“The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the word becomes for everyone else,” he said according to a live broadcast from Clash Reports.
According to him, Putin reiterated to senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – who visited both Moscow and Kyiv early September in an effort to broker an end to the war – that Russia would seize the Donetsk region within a few months.
As of July, the Kremlin is seeking to seize all of the Donetsk region while retaining occupied parts of Sumy and Kharkiv regions as permanent buffer zones.
That position would mean Moscow is no longer considering returning occupied land in the northeast in exchange for Ukraine ceding the remainder of Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
Lavrov Tells UN Security Council Russia Won’t Pause the War During Negotiations
However, Ukraine categorically rejects giving up any of its territory as a precondition for a settlement.
“This is probably the 17th or 18th time in five years that he has made this promise,” Zelensky said.
During this year alone, Russia has used more than 2,100 missiles against Ukraine, including more than 950 ballistic missiles, along with 63,000 attack drones.
Sikorski: Russia ‘cannot win’
While Zelensky accused Moscow of abusing its UN veto and threatening Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski framed the escalation as panic.
“You have been trying to conquer Donbas for over 12 years, and Kyiv for over four,” Sikorski said, adding that Russia is running out of resources to sustain its war effort.
“You have been stopped by heroic Ukraine, a country with one tenth of Russia’s gross domestic product (GDP),” he continued, noting that Poland’s economy is almost half the size of Russia’s, while Europe’s is 10 times larger and NATO’s is 25 times larger.
“You cannot win,” Sikorski concluded.
His remarks echo repeated warnings from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who previously said Russia was preparing “very seriously for an escalation of tension” in the region, with autumn and winter remaining key.
On Sept. 18, he also warned that intelligence assessments point to Russian plans for “hybrid” drone and missile strikes on Ukraine’s Western allies, including Poland.
Speaking during the Atlantic Council’s virtual event, “Did Russia intentionally target Western officials?” on Tuesday, former CIA Director David Petraeus said Western officials assess that Russia is losing about 6,000 more personnel each month than it recruits.
The event centered on the Sept. 13 Russian drone strike at the Yahodyn station near the Polish border, where a passenger-train locomotive was hit shortly after a diplomatic train carrying Boris Johnson and other Western officials passed through.
Petraeus was on another train nearby.
Zelensky’s general warning to Russia ahead of winter
The winter, which Zelensky said had fought on Russia’s side for centuries, could now work against Moscow as Ukraine is prepared to reciprocate Russia’s strikes on critical infrastructure.
“This winter could be very harsh for us, but in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too,” he said.
Additionally, Zelensky urged the representatives of 47 countries – including Ghana, Nepal, Tajikistan, India, Yemen, Kenya, Zimbabwe, Cuba, Belarus, Sudan and South Africa – to protect their citizens from Russia’s war.
“They’re your citizens. Take care of them and do not let them end up on another front,” Zelensky said. “Do not let Putin drag you into this war.”
Earlier this month, Amnesty International Secretary General Agnès Callamard said Russia lures foreign nationals into the war with false job offers, coercion and confiscated passports, which amounts to human trafficking, as defined under the UN’s Palermo Protocol.
Over the past several months, Ukraine has been intensively preparing for its fifth winter of Russia’s aggression.
Kyiv is readying its critical sectors amid widespread expectations that Russia will again target the power grid, heating, and water supplies.
Meanwhile, Ukraine continues to appeal to partners for Patriots it urgently needs to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
On Sept. 8, Ukraine signed contracts for about 1,000 Patriot missiles, financed through an EU loan. Separately on the same day, Germany pledged to send PAC-2 interceptors from its existing Bundeswehr (Germany military) stocks.
US President Donald Trump reiterated his previous decision to grant Ukraine the license to produce Patriot interceptors domestically on Tuesday, though no formal agreement was reached.

Freyja is to complement existing missile defense systems and enable larger-scale and cheaper production, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:45:28 EEST
04:45:28 KST

Freyja is to complement existing missile defense systems and enable larger-scale and cheaper production, Zelenskyy says
Kyiv • UNN
The president said that Freyja should become an integrated part of the defense of Ukraine and Europe.
The Freyja antiballistic program does not replace effective missile defense systems, including Patriot and SAMP/T, but is intended to complement them and provide the capability to produce interceptors on a larger scale and at lower cost. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this during his address to the United Nations General Assembly, UNN reports.
Our Freyja program does not replace effective systems such as Patriot or SAMP/T. We want to develop and build a system that can be produced on a larger scale and at lower cost. A system that can be an integrated part of the defense of Ukraine and Europe. One that can help any nation. The global waiting list for antiballistic missiles is enormous, and the threat is growing. Therefore, we need to produce enough systems to protect us, so that every person sitting in this hall could say that my people are protected. This is our approach to security
According to him, today even the wealthiest countries in the world cannot find enough interceptors.
Even those that had been stockpiling them for years have already used their interceptors. Unfortunately, this is the reality. Even in the Gulf countries, where nations are genuinely trying to build a powerful antiballistic system and defense. We need a new program; we need this Freyja, so join us. It may seem that Ukraine is focused only on the war because we talk about defense, weapons, and sanctions, but Ukrainians did not choose this war. We would like to choose not to die
He also reported that Ukraine continues to expand international participation in the program. According to him, 10 countries have already joined Freyja; last week, Ukraine invited Poland to join the program and is also holding consultations with other allies.
We remain open to every country that can make its contribution to developing protection against ballistic missiles
Background
At the beginning of September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy together with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a meeting with the heads of defense companies from partner countries devoted to implementing the Freyja antiballistic program. The meeting was attended by the heads of the defense companies FirePoint, Kongsberg, Weibel, Saab, Diehl Defence, Hensoldt, Thales, Safran, Sener, and Leonardo. The parties agreed on what leaders and government officials should do at their respective levels, and what manufacturers and developers should do at theirs.
What is Freyja
Freyja is a Ukraine-initiated project for a joint European antiballistic system, the first track of the Antiballistic Coalition, which includes 10 states and more than a dozen leading European defense companies. The system is intended to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
The project is being built around the Ukrainian FP-7.x interceptor missile developed by Fire Point, while other components are supplied by European manufacturers. As Fire Point CEO and Technical Director Iryna Terekh told UNN, development has reached the stage of technical integration of the entire ecosystem—radars, a launcher, a data transmission channel, and a command center—and tests are being conducted up to twice a week.

Tap water on paper, no proper accounts, says J&amp;K  probe panel

SRINAGAR: Tap water existing only on paper, people in some areas still having to hire horses for “transporting drinking water to their houses”, water pipes abandoned and littered around at some places are some of the damning observations in the report by a J&K assembly committee that was formed to probe alleged irregularities in the implementation of the Rs 13,000-crore Jal Jeevan Mission scheme in the union territory announced by PM Modi on Aug 15, 2019, with a target of completing it by 2024.The 13-member committee, formed on April 9, 2024, following widespread allegations of irregularities in the implementation of the scheme, tabled its report in the J&K House on Monday.As per the report, overall target achievement of work execution across the union territory was still 37.28 percent.Most of the JJM schemes in Udhampur are “classic examples of good paper work, contrary to field work and ground situation,” it said. “Most of the schemes in Poonch exist on papers.”The report also said that there is no credible record at least produced before the House committee as regards details of water pipes procured, utilized, and left unutilized. “During on-spot visits by the committee water pipes were found abandoned and littered around.”It also said Panchayati Raj institutions were excluded from implementation of the scheme.The JJM scheme aims to provide potable drinking water in taps to all rural homes by 2024.
Around 3,253 water supply schemes have been sanctioned in J&K at a cost of about Rs 13,000 crore.JJM is a 90:10 funding scheme between the Centre and the J&K govt.Officials of the Jal Shakti department said implementation was delayed in J&K as little progress could be made in the initial months following the abrogation of Article 370 on August 5, 2019. They said the administrative transition took about five months, followed by the COVID-19 pandemic, further delaying implementation.
The department told the committee that the model and methods used to implement the JJM in the rest of the country could not be replicated in J&K due to its “difficult geography, limited road connectivity and lack of locally available skilled manpower.” It said the tendering process began picking up pace only after 2022.Ajaz Ahmad Jan, one of the committee members, said despite huge investment, a majority of rural households, especially in Rajouri and Poonch, are still facing hardships in fetching safe drinking water and there has been no benefit of the scheme.

Eisenkot’s Yashar leads Likud, tops Netanyahu in premiership preference: Poll

Zein Khalil,  Mohammad Sio
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party leads Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud by 22 seats to 18 ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 election, according to an Israeli opinion poll published Wednesday.
The Channel 13 survey also found that 48% of respondents preferred Eisenkot as prime minister, compared with 36% for Netanyahu, while 16% said they did not know which of the two was more suitable for the post.
The poll put the governing coalition bloc at 51 seats and opposition parties at 52, while Arab parties received a combined 13 seats and an alliance led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha won four.
A government needs the support of at least 61 members of Israel’s 120-seat Knesset.
According to the survey, Yashar would emerge as the largest party with 22 seats if elections were held now, while Likud would receive 18.
Naftali Bennett’s Beyachad (Together) and Yair Golan’s Democrats would each receive 11 seats.
The Joint Arab List, Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu and United Torah Judaism would each win eight seats.
Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit and Shas would each receive seven seats, while the Religious Zionism alliance led by Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin would take six.
Ofer Winter’s Amcha Yisrael party and the United Arab List, or Ra’am, would each receive five seats.
The poll also showed the Hendel-Zelekha alliance crossing the electoral threshold with four seats, while the Haredi Public party and Benny Gantz’s Blue and White would fail to enter parliament. Blue and White polled below 1%.
Asked about their preferred composition of the next government, 31% backed a broad unity government, 29% preferred an entirely right-wing government and 25% favored a government formed by opposition parties. The remainder chose other options or said they did not know.
The survey questioned 1,503 people and had a margin of error of 2.5 percentage points.
Netanyahu has headed Israel’s current government since late December 2022.
He is on trial on corruption charges, which he denies. The International Criminal Court also issued an arrest warrant for him in November 2024 over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

Forced eviction of 87-year-old 'Maricarmen' despite UN appeal causes outrage in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:44:13 UTC
04:44:13 KST

María del Carmen Abascal had lived in her flat on Sainz de Baranda Street since 1956. Madrid’s Tenants' Union and the UN had opposed the decision to evict her.
Thousands of people have continued to demonstrate in Madrid and other Spanish cities following the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen.
In the capital, police clashed with some protesters during a demonstration organised by the Madrid Tenants' Union. The group criticised the police response and said demonstrators would continue campaigning for the right to housing.
Protesters partially blocked the street outside a controversial luxury penthouse acquired by the Madrid regional government through the publicly owned company Planifica Madrid. They chanted slogans including “We are all Maricarmen”, “Ayuso, resign” — referring to Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso — and “The penthouse for Maricarmen”.
The demonstration, organised through social media by the Madrid Tenants' Union, drew around 10,000 people, according to the Spanish government’s delegation in Madrid.
Protests were also called in cities including Barcelona, Seville, Ávila, Cádiz, Palma, Toledo, Valencia, Guadalajara, Málaga and Huelva, as tenants' groups called for action to stop evictions and address Spain's housing crisis.
Evicted after more than 70 years in her home
María del Carmen Abascal, known to everyone as Maricarmen, is no longer a resident of Retiro in central Madrid. On Wednesday, at 87 years old, she was evicted from the flat at 46 Alcalde Sainz de Baranda Street, where she had lived since 1956.
This was the fourth attempt to evict her and, this time, court officials went through with it after several postponements. Police cleared hundreds of people who had gathered in an attempt to stop the eviction.
Maricarmen's eviction carried out at the fourth attempt
From the early hours of Wednesday morning, dozens of people had gathered around the entrance to the building, until police set up a cordon blocking access to the press and supporters. At around 10:30 am, after an hour of talks between Maricarmen's lawyer and court officers, it was confirmed that the eviction would go ahead.
Officers then removed protesters by force, and an ambulance parked in front of the doorway, with medics entering the building with a stretcher to take the elderly woman out. According to several Spanish media outlets, activists tried to block the eviction in the street, on the stairwell and inside the flat itself. They were removed by police.
Her lawyer, Beatriz Duro, made one final attempt at negotiation, asking for a few days so that Maricarmen could find somewhere to live. The company refused to grant any leeway. “They refused to give her a few hours to remove her belongings,” the lawyer complained.
An old-style regulated tenancy signed in 1956
The roots of the dispute go back almost 70 years. The old-style regulated tenancy was signed by Maricarmen's parents in 1956, with her father as the tenant. After his death, it passed to his wife and, when she died in 2005, there was a second succession in favour of Maricarmen.
The property had belonged to a private family for decades, but it was sold in 2018 and ended up in the hands of Urbagestión Desarrollo e Inversión S.L., a property company based in Madrid and Valladolid that invests in buildings, homes, land, commercial premises, offices and hotels.
The company argued that the second succession was invalid and that the contract had lapsed. The case went all the way to the Supreme Court, which ruled in favour of the owners in March, overturning a first-instance ruling that had backed Maricarmen.
Maricarmen receives a pension lower than the €2,500 monthly rent demanded by the company, several times higher than her previous rent. Maricarmen, who has a disability, was never able to afford that amount.
Urbagestión is also claiming €10,000 from the Madrid Tenants' Union for damages arising from the campaign in support of Maricarmen.
The first eviction attempt was in October 2025 and was halted by the court the day before. There was another attempt on 2 June this year, which was also postponed at the last minute.
The UN called for it to be halted
The UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights called on the Spanish government to stop the eviction and ensure that Maricarmen had access to adequate housing. The request, made in June, was not enough to prevent the eviction.
In Spain's Congress, Socialist spokesperson Patxi López defended the government's actions and shifted responsibility to Madrid City Council and the regional government, which are responsible for housing, noting that the owners had rejected every offer to buy the flat.
Maricarmen is now leaving the home where she had lived since she was 17 and where her parents died. The case brings to a close, as far as the flat is concerned, a years-long legal battle that made her one of the most recognisable faces of Madrid's housing crisis.
Madrid City Council has sought to defuse the controversy sparked by the eviction, insisting that it had already offered Maricarmen various housing options on previous occasions and during earlier attempts to carry out the eviction.
The city's mayor José Luis Martínez-Almeida also stressed that municipal services had contacted her beforehand. He avoided giving further details out of respect for her privacy.
The City Hall housing department maintains that Maricarmen explicitly rejected every accommodation option offered to her. The same situation was repeated on Wednesday after the eviction, when Samur Social again offered her a place in a residential facility. She declined and ultimately chose to move in with relatives.

Berlin Airport briefly suspends flights over drone sighting

Berlin Airport briefly suspends flights over drone sighting
September 23, 2026
Berlin's airport briefly suspended flights on Wednesday evening after a drone sighting, Germany's DPA news agency cited airport and police officials as saying.
A drone was spotted on the Berlin Brandenburg Airport's northern runway at 8:00 p.m. (1800 GMT). Airspace above the airport was closed minutes later and operations were suspended for at least 45 minutes.
Several flights were diverted to Dresden.
As of 9:05 p.m., airspace was reopened but flights were experiencing delays.
Drone sightings on the rise
Drone sightings have become a common occurrence for airports in Europe, with Berlin's airport recording the highest number of sightings in Germany in the first part of the year.
Some 28 drone sightings were recorded during the first six months, as per figures by the German air traffic control (DFS). In seven of those cases, flight operations at the airport were temporarily suspended.
This is a jump from last year, when eight drones were detected at the airport and its surroundings in the whole of 2025, according to DFS.

Hacked FBI data has sensitive information about employees’ intelligence roles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:42:59 UTC
04:42:59 KST

Hacked FBI data has sensitive information about employees’ intelligence roles
- Hacked FBI data by ShinyHunters includes sensitive details about employees' intelligence roles, such as counter-espionage against China, Russia, and other threats, plus personal information like addresses and social security numbers.
- The FBI is investigating the breach, while hackers hold the data hostage, demanding the bureau retract an earlier negative statement about them.
- Experts warn the leak endangers agents and their families, with foreign intelligence and extremists likely to exploit the exposed information, especially on covert operations and human intelligence staff.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – FBI data allegedly stolen by the hacking group ShinyHunters carries granular detail about scores of bureau officials’ job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence, drug cartels, and more, Reuters has found.
The 5,000-line spreadsheet – said by the hackers to represent only a small piece of their claimed two- to three-terabyte trove – includes names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers, and emergency contact details for what they claimed were thousands of FBI employees.
It also includes details of assignments to specific field offices and, in some cases, to units engaged in high-stakes intelligence, security, or counterespionage work.
In a statement, the FBI said it was aware of “a cyber-criminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the FBIJobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information”.
The bureau said the cause of the breach was still undetermined, but that it was “actively and aggressively investigating the matter”.
The hackers said on Sept 22 that they had breached the FBI, stealing data on a large number of current and former FBI employees.
ShinyHunters said it is holding the data hostage until the bureau rescinds an unflattering statement about the group issued in May.
Former FBI counterintelligence operative Eric O’Neill said the data allegedly stolen by ShinyHunters was “a foreign intelligence service goldmine”.
“China would be incredibly interested to know the individuals who are working against it,” said O’Neill, who founded the cybersecurity company Nexasure AI after his stint at the bureau.
He predicted that other hostile intelligence services would be eager to get their hands on the data, along with disgruntled extremists in the United States.
“If I were on that list, I would be very concerned,” he said.
ShinyHunters said in a statement on Sept 23 that it was trying to keep the personnel information from circulating widely in the meantime.
“If the 5,000 sample data records leak, it’s not because of us,” the group said.
Although Reuters has not been able to authenticate the entire spreadsheet, it has been able to individually verify the details of more than 22 people by cross-referencing information in the hacked data with credit records and previous data leaks carried by the dark web intelligence platform District 4 Labs.
Counterterrorism, counterintelligence and surveillance
Some of the assignment details in the ShinyHunters’ data are indistinguishable from what employees themselves might say publicly, noting agents at field offices in Baltimore or Newark, New Jersey, for example.
Others referred to publicly known bureau subdivisions such as the Internet Crime Complaint Centre or the FBI academy at Quantico, in Virginia.
But in some cases, the data referred to FBI units or initiatives that were sensitive or whose existence has not previously been disclosed.
The data names 14 staffers focused on China-related matters, including members of the “China criminal enterprise unit”, the “China tech transfer analysis unit”, and the “China intelligence section”.
Nine others are listed as serving in Russia-related roles, including two in the “Russia Operations Section” and one working on “Russia Critical Infra and Tech Threat”. Three people are listed as working in Iran- or Hezbollah-focused intelligence roles.
Eighteen others are listed as working with “data intercept” or “telecom intercept” technologies, or in the FBI’s “clandestine technical operations” unit, or its “covert access section”, or in video, audio, or electronic surveillance roles.
A further 11 FBI staffers are listed as working in HUMINT, or human intelligence, jobs, including several listed as working in the “Humint program management section”.
Trevor Hilligoss, a former Army investigator who worked with the FBI, said the information tying specific named people to human intelligence work was particularly troubling.
“You don’t have to look far to find examples of undercover agents being harmed when their cover is blown,” he said.
Hilligoss, now the chief intelligence officer for cybersecurity company SpyCloud, said his concerns were heightened by the inclusion of emergency contacts – often spouses or children – “who may have less operational security knowledge than their relative that works in a sensitive field”.
Other targets
ShinyHunters previously claimed credit for the purported theft of millions of business records from video game developer Rockstar Games, the maker of Grand Theft Auto, and an intrusion focused on the education tool Canvas that triggered widespread disruption across US schools.
In May, the FBI said ShinyHunters sometimes used “exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims”.
ShinyHunters said its “threats and claims are very real”, adding that the FBI’s statement was why it targeted the bureau.
Reuters could not verify that all the job assignments were authentic or up-to-date, but it was able to match the career details or titles of eight people whose data was leaked to information in court filings, news articles, or public profiles on LinkedIn or to online posts on sites such as Instagram.
O’Neill, the former FBI operative, cautioned against drawing conclusions about what the hackers hold.
“They’re really trying to scare the hell out of the FBI,” he noted. REUTERS

4 Non‑Anglo Men.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:42:07 UTC

A still from 12 Angry Men (1957, United Artists)
Russian Supreme Court has proposed drastically changing how jury trials operate, including reducing the number of jurors to four and combining them with the presiding judge into a single panel. Reporting by Vedomosti, a business daily newspaper, cites a reform concept presented by Supreme Court Judge Sergei Zelenin.
Currently, the number of people on a Russian jury depends on the court’s level. In lower-level district and military courts, a jury consists of six main and two reserve jurors. In higher-level regional courts, it comprises eight main and two reserve jurors. The new proposal would standardise and reduce the number to just four jurors across all courts.
The most drastic change involves the fundamental principle of jury deliberation. Currently, Russia uses an “Anglo-American” or common law model, where the professional judge and the lay jury make their decisions separately and independently. Judge Zelenin proposed moving towards a “continental” model (used in European countries like France or Germany) featuring a mixed panel.
This new proposed system would feature the professional judge and the lay jurors on a common panel that sits in the deliberation room together. The judge would be able to provide clarifications to the jurors behind closed doors. Proponents argue this will increase “the stability” of verdicts.
Another proposal seeks to streamline trials by abandoning the practice of sending jurors out of the courtroom during procedural or legal arguments they are not supposed to hear. Zelenin’s proposal argues that constantly removing jurors can give them the impression that a crucial part of the proceedings is being hidden from them.
Zelenin also wants to change how juries are selected. He suggests abolishing the practice of dissolving a jury panel due to the “bias of its composition”, a legal mechanism he dismissed as “redundant and inefficient.” Furthermore, the age limit would be relaxed, allowing citizens over 65 to serve if they are willing and healthy enough.
The judge’s summing-up instructions before the jury retires are also proposed to be shortened. Specifically, judges would no longer repeat the prosecution’s charges or summarise the opposing arguments. Zelenin argued that making the judge recount the prosecution’s case can compromise the appearance of judicial neutrality, as the court is not part of the prosecution.
Zelenin justified these sweeping reforms by pointing to inefficiencies in the current system, specifically the lengthy process of selecting a jury and the high rate of jury verdicts being overturned on appeal.
In Russia’s justice system, the conviction rate by professional judges is extremely high, with less than 1% of defendants being pronounced not guilty (excluding guilty verdicts and dismissed cases). Juries, which were reintroduced in modern Russia after the fall of the Soviet Union, have historically been much more likely to acquit defendants. In 2022, a staggering 62% of those verdicts were subsequently overturned by higher courts.

Türkiye-US strategic cooperation expanding across all areas: President Erdogan

Strategic cooperation between Ankara and Washington is expanding across all areas, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Wednesday, adding that Türkiye seeks to turn political alignment into stronger economic ties.
 
Speaking at the Türkiye-US Business Council meeting held at the Turkish House in New York, Erdogan thanked the American Chamber of Commerce, business councils and the Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEİK) for organizing the meeting.
 
"We recently finalized major agreements with the US in energy, aviation and other critical sectors through our joint efforts," Erdogan told businesspeople.
 
“Our strategic cooperation with the US is developing in every area. We want to reflect the harmony we have achieved in our political relations in our economic and trade relations as well.”
 
He said there is significant potential for further cooperation.
 
"The US is now our leading LNG supplier. As a result, we are among the leading countries in Europe choosing American energy resources. We aim to expand this cooperation across the entire energy sector, including nuclear energy," he added.
 
Erdogan said that economic relations between Türkiye and the US should not be viewed solely through trade figures, arguing that a strategic economic cooperation model with Türkiye is needed as the global economic order is being reshaped.
 
Addressing questions from businesspeople about the state of Türkiye’s economic program and progress toward its targets, Erdogan said the program has four main pillars: price stability, fiscal discipline, a sustainable external balance and structural transformation.
 
He said Türkiye had made visible progress in all four areas over the past year despite wars in the region.
 
“Core goods inflation has fallen to its lowest level since 2020, while rent inflation has reached its lowest level in four years. Had it not been for the direct and indirect effects of the war, we would have ended 2026 with inflation in the low 20s. Under current conditions, we expect to end the year at around 28%. We believe 2027 will be a stronger year in terms of disinflation.”
 
Erdogan said Türkiye was also in a strong position on fiscal discipline.
 
He noted that tax reductions had been introduced to protect citizens and the real sector from rising fuel prices, while the budget had nevertheless performed better than its target.
 
The president said Türkiye expects to end the year with a budget deficit equivalent to 3.1% of GDP, compared with an average approaching 6% in comparable countries.
 
He also highlighted Türkiye’s relatively low public debt, saying public debt is below 22% of GDP, compared with an average of around 78% in developing countries.
 
Despite higher energy prices, Erdogan said Türkiye had kept its current-account deficit and external debt indicators below their 20-year averages.
 
 
'We are accelerating investments supporting digital transformation'
 
Erdogan said productivity is the central issue and that structural transformation has therefore been placed at the heart of the economic program.
 
He said Türkiye is pursuing an ambitious green transformation agenda and recalled that Antalya will host COP31 in November.
 
The president said Türkiye is implementing targeted and selective policies to increase value added in industry.
 
“We are accelerating infrastructure investments that will strengthen us in artificial intelligence and support digital transformation. In healthcare, we are providing strong incentives to investors through the industrial zone we are establishing in Ankara. We are moving forward decisively toward our goal of a Terror-Free Türkiye to unlock our regional potential.”
 
Erdogan added that Türkiye is becoming an economy that does not merely react to shocks but invests in resilience, productivity and economic security.
Energy routes are being redrawn
 
Erdogan said the region is heading toward five major economic and strategic shifts as conflicts subside, with Türkiye positioned to play a central role.
 
He said global supply chains are being reshaped, with companies increasingly prioritizing reliability alongside cost, benefiting Türkiye’s industrial base and trade links with Europe.
 
Energy routes are also being redrawn, Erdogan said, highlighting Türkiye’s role in projects such as the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline and TANAP.
 
At the same time, new trade corridors are emerging, with the Middle Corridor connecting Asia and Europe and the Development Road linking the Gulf to Europe through Türkiye, he added.
 
Erdogan said the expected reconstruction of roads, ports, power plants, housing and factories across the region would create new opportunities for Turkish companies, particularly in the construction sector.
 
He also pointed to the growing importance of defense and advanced technology.
 
Türkiye's NATO-standard defense industry has reached the capacity to contribute to the supply security of its allies, he added.

Israeli bulldozers destroy Palestinian olive trees ahead of annual harvest
Palestinian villagers wailed over the mangled remains of their olive trees on Wednesday after Israel's military uprooted them with bulldozers, days ahead of the annual olive harvest, normally a source of joy for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Abd Alfattah Tamimi, who owns an olive grove on village land near Ramallah city, watched as a military bulldozer smashed the top of one of his trees and then tore its roots from the ground.
"All our olive trees, including the newly planted ones, were uprooted. Also our neighbours', they uprooted them all," Tamimi said, adding that he and his neighbours own nearly 9 acres of land filled with olive trees.
"They left us with nothing," he said.
In the past, the military has cited the need to clear land of olive trees to prevent security threats or ambushes on troops.
Palestinian human rights groups reject this, saying the destruction in effect deprives Palestinian farmers of income from the sale of olives and olive oil while uprooting trees they view as a symbol of their connection to the land.
The olive harvest usually begins in the first week of October. Olives are the backbone of Palestinian agriculture, a sector that accounts for around 8% of GDP and more than 60,000 jobs, according to the Palestinian Authority's agriculture ministry.
Palestinian activists and farmers expect this year's harvest to be particularly volatile, amid a record surge in Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians and Palestinian resources in the territory.
Nather Tamimi, another landowner in the area of Deir Nizam village near Ramallah, said the loss of the trees was particularly painful in that it came so close to the start of the harvest.
"From this land, my brothers and I produce 120 drums of olive oil. Our neighbours produce the same," said Tamimi, speaking while looking over his olive grove.
"They uprooted trees everywhere, even between the houses," he said.

Australia's snake season is here. Here's what to do — and what not to do — if you see one
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:36:05 UTC
04:36:05 KST

In brief
- As the warmer months return, Australia's snakes may begin to stir.
- Here's what an expert says about what to do if you find one in your home or yard.
Springtime doesn't just bring a shift in weather and more sunshine; it also marks the start of snake season.
Australia is home to more than 170 land and sea snake varieties, including around 100 venomous species and 12 that are likely to inflict a wound that can be fatal.
In 2024-25, more than 2,100 Australians presented to hospital due to a snake bite, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.
But the Wildlife Information Rescue and Education Service (WIRES) says snakes generally don't attack people unless provoked.
Warmer weather and snakes
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
It's often observed in Australia that snakes seem to go into hiding during winter and return as the weather gets warmer. But is that actually the case? According to WIRES spokesperson and snake enthusiast John Grant, it's a little more complicated than that.
"They actually never go completely into hiding," Grant tells SBS News. "Our snakes, and a lot of reptiles, go into what's called brumation. That's when their metabolic rate slows down somewhat in the colder months for them to be able to conserve energy ... They'll still go out and get a feed every now and then."
But as soon as warm weather arrives, brumation season ends, and snakes start hunting for food and potential partners.
How to tell the difference between a venomous and non-venomous snake
In some instances, you may encounter a well-known animal, such as a green tree snake or a diamond python. These are two of the most common and well-known non-venomous snakes in Australia.
But even if you think you can identify the snake, it's easy to be fooled.
Grant's advice is simple: treat every snake as though it's venomous and don't handle it yourself. Call in a professional to remove it.
"Don't approach it. Don't try to contain it. Don't try to move it. And worst of all, don't try to kill it," he said.
Grant says he knows that some people are very afraid of snakes, but that fear may cause you to act rashly or back the animal into a corner, putting you in danger.
"The worst thing you can do to put yourself at risk is attempting to harm an animal," he said.
"I think another thing that people need to realise is they see us as the predators. They're far more scared of us than we are of them.
"We're not a food source for the snakes in Australia, so they see us as a threat and just keep away. They're going to want to get away from us as quickly as they can."
What to do if you've found a snake indoors
That advice goes double for snakes you may encounter indoors or in your garden. It's paramount to keep yourself and others, and any pets, safely away from a snake that's found its way indoors.
"If it's in your home garden, particularly in our more outer suburb areas where snakes live, although people don't see them, they're still there," Grant says.
"So your cats will be at risk. Your dogs are at risk if you don't contain them because they can get a nasty bite even though (the snakes are) non-venomous, so can humans. So you should just treat everything as if it's venomous."
One thing Grant is very concerned about is that people may try to copy snake catchers they see on social media.
"One of the problems that's happening at the moment is that there are a lot of snake capture videos on YouTube and other channels, and it's giving people the wrong idea that they can do it themselves. The people involved have to be trained."
Snakes and biodiversity in Australia
Grant says another reason to avoid killing a snake that finds its way indoors is that many are protected by law because of their role in maintaining native biodiversity.
"There's a predator for almost every animal, and they're known for keeping the numbers of those down," he says.
Snakes will eat mice and rats, keeping their often large populations under control. Some, like the keelback, eat cane toads too.
"If numbers get out of control, that's the main role that they play. And it's a really big role in making sure that, particularly these days, that vermin (numbers are) kept down," Grant said.
But despite his dire warnings about keeping your distance and respecting a snake's space, Grant can't hide his love for the reptile.
"There's some very rare ones that can't be found anywhere in the world," Grant says. "They're only here, and we're very lucky to have them."

Educated, stressed, in love: Seven charts that show how Australians are really doing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:36:00 UTC
04:36:00 KST

In Brief
- The latest HILDA survey was released on Thursday, finding that cost of living has impacted Australia's wellbeing.
- Australians feel overeducated in their jobs, happy in their relationships, but more fatigued than ever.
Australians are getting more educated, staying home longer and still pretty happy with their partners.
But the cost of living is squeezing households harder than ever, according to the latest Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) report.
The annual survey, released on Thursday, is the largest longitudinal study of its kind in the country, tracking around 17,000 people across 9,000 households every year since 2001. This year's edition draws on data through to 2024 and covers everything from income and employment to relationships and mental health.
"What really comes out quite strongly from the data is the rise in the cost of living and people's incomes not really keeping pace with the rise in the cost of living," Professor Roger Wilkins, co-director of the HILDA survey, told SBS News.
"We've seen that manifest in a number of different ways. We've seen measures of hardship increasing — things like financial stress, housing stress, food insecurity, the inability to afford adequate food," he said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Here are seven charts that sum up where Australians are at.
Half of us are 'overeducated' for our jobs
More than half of Australian workers say they have more education than their job requires — which can be associated with lower job and life satisfaction and an increased likelihood of quitting.
Workers under 25 were most likely to feel overeducated, while a quarter of workers also said they felt overskilled and unable to use their full range of abilities at work.
While it sounds like a negative, Wilkins said it isn't necessarily all bad news.
"It's remarkable how much the educational attainment of the Australian population has increased over the life of the HILDA study since 2001," he said. "We've seen a big increase in the proportion of people with a university qualification, particularly for women."
More than half of Australian women aged 25-44 now hold a university degree.
"So women are now considerably more educated than men in terms of the proportion with a university qualification," he said, adding the trend is likely to continue to increase in the long-term.
We're infected by the love bug
Australians in long-term relationships rated the quality of their partnership highly — an average of 4.3 out of 5 — but clear gender gaps remain.
"Most of men and women who are partnered are quite satisfied with their partner and very much report being in love with their partner, but you do also see a gender divide there in the sense that men do report higher levels of satisfaction with their female partners than females to with their male partners," Wilkins said.
Couples who split housework, childcare and earnings evenly tended to report stronger relationships overall.
Researchers also found a clear U-curve in the perceived strength of a relationship — where it feels strong at first, but gradually declines over 24 years before it finally picks back up, increasing in quality year-on-year and eventually surpassing the love from those early years.
Food insecurity hits 1 in 6 Australians
A huge 18 per cent of Australians — almost 1 in 6 — aged 15 and over experienced food insecurity in 2024 — up from 13.7 per cent in 2020.
Single-parent families, First Nations people, those with a disability or poor health, and smokers were all at greater risk.
"Food insecurity is one of the most vital measures we have for disadvantage, because it shows, in practical terms, just how many people are struggling to access one of the essentials of life," Wilkins said.
It's also proving hard to shake — half of those facing food insecurity in 2020 were still facing it four years later.
Most commonly, that translated to being unable to afford healthy food, being limited to certain foods, or eating less than they felt they should.
Half of 18 to 29-year-olds are still living at home
The rite of passage of moving out of your parents' house in your 20s may soon become a thing of the past.
Back in 2001, 39 per cent of 18 to 29 year olds lived with their parents.
By 2024, after a steady rise over 20 years, that had climbed to roughly half.
A mixed bag of pressures is to blame — but it's not all bad.
"On the negative side, we've had the issue of the rising cost of housing as being a barrier to young people establishing their own household, and also young people taking longer to get into a career track full-time employment," he said.
"On the positive side, one of the drivers is that it's related to the growth in educational attainment — more of us than ever are going on to university," he said, adding that people are also generally hitting adult milestones like marriage and kids later than previous generations.
More fatigue and financial stress
Housing stress hit 23 per cent of private renters and a similar percentage of social housing tenants, while 9.6 per cent of mortgage holders were affected — the highest since 2017.
Across capital cities, 36 per cent of renters and 30 per cent of mortgage holders were spending over 30 per cent of their disposable income on housing, the standard metric for housing stress.
Wilkins said that despite employment participation reaching a record high and unemployment levels remaining low, wages still haven't kept up.
"Incomes are not keeping pace with not just rising prices, but also rising interest rates as well … and more recently, we've had the increases in fuel prices too," he said.
That pressure shows up in wellbeing data too, with Australians reporting less energy and more fatigue than a decade ago.
Mental health also declined among younger Australians, particularly young women, with those aged 25-34 recording a rise in psychological distress that predates the COVID-19 pandemic.
Still, Wilkins said it isn't all doom and gloom in Australia.
"There is quite a lot going right in the Australian community and in Australian society generally," he said.
"Older people's health is better than it's ever been. People are broadly satisfied with their relationships ... by international standards, we have quite a high living standard."
"So on a lot of fronts, there is a positive story to tell about Australian society, but there's also a lot of room for improvement as well."

NATO’s Article 5 is “Deliberately Ambiguous” on Hybrid Threats, Rutte Says

- Category

NATO’s Article 5 is “Deliberately Ambiguous” on Hybrid Threats, Rutte Says
NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause is intentionally vague to prevent adversaries from exploiting red lines, particularly as the alliance faces a growing wave of hybrid warfare, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated on September 23.
Speaking at a Chicago Council on Global Affairs event in Des Moines, Iowa, alongside US Ambassador to NATO Matt Whitaker, Rutte addressed growing concerns over how the military alliance would respond to unconventional, gray-zone aggression, such as the severing of critical undersea cables.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian hybrid warfare blends cyberattacks, disinformation, and physical sabotage—such as arson and drone incursions—across Europe to operate just below the threshold of direct military conflict.
By deploying recruited proxies and criminal networks, Moscow aims to disrupt vital military aid to Ukraine and destabilize Western societies without triggering a full NATO Article 5 response.
“Article Five… is deliberately ambiguous, so we will never exactly tell anyone when Article Five is exactly triggered or not, because we don’t want to make our adversaries any wiser,” Rutte explained to the audience.
While NATO refuses to outline the specific thresholds that would trigger a collective military response, Rutte assured that the alliance possesses a full spectrum of retaliatory options for hybrid attacks. He noted that NATO's responses will not always be a direct “tit-for-tat” mirror of the aggression, but will often be asymmetric.
As a primary example, Rutte pointed to the severing of an undersea telecommunications cable between Finland and Estonia, which prompted NATO to launch the “Baltic Sentry” operation to secure regional waters.
He also highlighted increasing coordinated efforts by allies—including Sweden, France, Belgium, and the UK—to disrupt Russia’s shadow fleet of sanctions-evading oil vessels as another form of asymmetric retaliation that “the Russians hate.”
Beyond hybrid warfare, Rutte used the Iowa address to underscore the deepening threat posed by the collaboration between Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea. He stressed that this unified authoritarian axis requires a dual-theater readiness strategy, defending both the Euro-Atlantic and the Indo-Pacific simultaneously.
To achieve this, Rutte highlighted that European allies are rapidly adopting a historic new defense spending target of 5% of GDP.
This massive influx of European defense investment, he argued, is designed to secure the conventional defense of the European continent, freeing up the United States to project necessary power in the Indo-Pacific without abandoning its NATO commitments.
An unauthorized drone had recently breached the perimeter of the highly strategic US Aegis Ashore missile defense base in Redzikowo, Poland, operating roughly 500 meters from the facility for several minutes before Polish guards reported the incident to a civilian emergency hotline.
The incident has raised significant concerns about the readiness of Polish forces to defend critical infrastructure.

Bentley has unveiled its first electric vehicle, the Torcal — what makes it interesting and how much it costs

Bentley has unveiled its first electric vehicle, the Torcal — what makes it interesting and how much it costs
Kyiv • UNN
Bentley has unveiled the Torcal electric SUV, retaining its signature design and V8 sound. The model's price starts at 230 thousand dollars.
On Wednesday, Bentley unveiled its first fully electric car, betting that affluent buyers want to drive without harmful emissions while retaining the distinctive design features that have defined the British luxury-car brand for more than a century, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The Torcal SUV was unveiled just a few months after Ferrari’s first electric vehicle drew criticism from some of the brand’s fans: it bore little resemblance to the Italian marque’s traditional low-slung sports cars with internal-combustion engines.
By contrast, Bentley’s debut electric vehicle is immediately recognizable as a member of the family. It retains the styling elements of models with internal-combustion engines — right down to diamond-shaped headlights that evoke the traditional radiator grille (although electric cars do not need one to cool the engine).
The car also recreates the sensation of a V8 engine through an accompanying sound based on the sound of orchestral timpani, supplemented by smaller drums whose tempo accelerates as the vehicle gains speed.
We should add
"We have always sought first and foremost to create a Bentley," the company’s CEO, Frank-Steffen Walliser, told Reuters. "We believe people are not looking for a radically different car simply because it is electric."
Apart from Ferrari, the only other major ultra-luxury carmaker already selling an electric vehicle is Rolls-Royce (owned by BMW Group).
Lamborghini, which, like Bentley, is part of Volkswagen Group, has postponed the launch of its first electric vehicle until the end of the decade. British automaker McLaren said last week that it does not plan to produce electric vehicles; both companies attributed the decision to insufficient customer demand.
Bentley previously postponed the launch of its first electric vehicle until 2026 and abandoned its goal of switching entirely to electric power by 2030, saying that customers were not yet ready for such changes.
Unlike Ferrari’s electric Luce, whose price starts at 550,000 euros ($628,000), the Torcal occupies a lower price segment in Bentley’s lineup: its price starts at £173,000 ($230,000). According to Walliser, the model represents "a more affordable Bentley... which definitely opens up new markets."
Bentley is showing the car to existing and potential customers; significant interest has been recorded in Europe, the Middle East and those U.S. states where electric vehicles have a high level of adoption. An advertising campaign marking the model’s launch in China will begin next year.

Ukraine’s Zelenskyy calls for sustained pressure to end ‘Putin’s crazy war’
Ukrainian president urges world leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues to impede its war efforts.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has singled out Russian President Vladimir Putin as the reason for the continuing war between the two neighbouring countries, urging world leaders to sustain economic pressure on Moscow during his address at the United Nations General Assembly.
“For nearly five years now, Russia’s generals have tried to carry out Putin’s crazy war,” Zelenskyy said, adding that no one openly supported this war “except for one man”.
Zelenskyy said Russia had lost 248,000 soldiers over the last eight months in Ukraine, managing to capture “a little more than 1,000 square kilometres [386 square miles] of our territory this year”.
“Putin spent 248 people for every kilometre. Does anyone still think he is smart?” he said, adding that the numbers “are not just statistics. This is about people”.
“We have archived footage of thousands and thousands of Russians losing their lives in kill zones. This is what Putin wants,” he said.
“Something always seems to stop Putin from saying, ‘That’s it. Enough. Peace,'” Zelenskyy said. “Can you even imagine him without war? He is ‘patient zero’, the one from whom war keeps spreading further. ‘Patient zero’ must be stopped,” he said.
Zelenskyy said he expects Russia to intensify its bombing campaign on the country in the coming months and that Ukrainians are prepared for a harsh winter.
“Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us, but in response we will have no choice but to make it harsh for Russia too,” he said.
This month, Ukraine launched its deepest-ever attack into Russia, targeting two Arctic gas condensate facilities more than 3,000km (1,865 miles) from its border. Another attack on Sunday forced a Moscow oil refinery to halt crude processing.
Russia also slammed jet-powered drones into two petrol stations and other sites in Kyiv, killing one and injuring at least seven people on Wednesday.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump has been pushing for an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, blaming the war between the two as one reason behind skyrocketing fuel prices.
Zelenskyy called for sustained economic pressure, saying the money Russia earned through trade “gives this war more time”.
“And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said.
Last week, Trump signed into law a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russia over its war in Ukraine, days after US Congress sent the bill to the White House with rare bipartisan support.
On Wednesday, Zelenskyy also claimed that nationals of 47 countries are fighting alongside Russia in Ukraine, mentioning the two North Korean soldiers captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia’s Kursk region last year, who were sent to South Korea by Kyiv.
“Why should Koreans give their lives in a war in Ukraine?” he asked.
Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that Moscow is prepared to negotiate towards a lasting peace with Ukraine, but won’t just “pause” the war, arguing that such a pause would buy Ukraine and its backers time to line up more weapons.
Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says both Russia and Ukraine have expressed interest in a limited ceasefire that would halt attacks on grain shipments and each country’s energy sectors.

'Compulsory' day devoted to the Pope in Catholic schools sparks controversy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:30:32 UTC
04:30:32 KST

Catholic private schools are being urged to suspend normal classes on 25 September, the day Pope Leo XIV arrives in France.
Just days before the arrival of Pope Leo XIV, who's in France from 25 to 28 September, the decision to hold a "compulsory" school day devoted to the pontiff in Catholic schools is raising questions and has sparked a debate over secularism.
In an internal memo dated 10 September, and revealed by the left leaning daily Libération, the General Secretariat for Catholic Education (Sgec), headed by Guillaume Prévost, asks state-funded private schools under contract to treat Friday 25 September, the day Leo XIV arrives, as a special day and to replace regular lessons with activities focused on the Pope, the Catholic Church and various social issues.
This day must "be compulsory for pupils as well as for all teachers and staff, in the same way as any other school day", the document specifies.
A school day in honour of Leo XIV
In primary schools, the Sgec suggests making paper doves or a mural on peace and introducing pupils to the Vatican and the role of the pope. In lower and upper secondary, pupils will be able in particular to study the speech Leo XIV is due to deliver at UNESCO or work on the theme of the "civilisation of love".
Other activities are proposed around peace, fraternity, artificial intelligence, tackling bullying and preventing violence.
The Sgec stresses, however, that the obligation to attend does not entail "any obligation in terms of belief". Explicitly religious activities, such as prayer or hymns, must remain optional.
To justify holding this day during school hours, the Sgec invokes the rescheduling of the "educational communities day", which is usually held at the beginning of December.
This explanation is contested by Laëtitia Bramoullé, spokesperson for the collective 'Stop aux souffrances dans les établissements catholiques' (Stop Suffering in Catholic Schools), who told Libération that no such nationwide day exists in this form.
Another point of contention is the fact that this day would replace regular classes, even though state-funded private schools under contract are required to follow the national curriculum.
The Sgec, for its part, considers that the educational communities day can "break with the strict framework of the timetabled lesson" and be held "legitimately during school hours". The Catholic body also recommends that teachers' participation be recognised as working time.
"No spiritual time nor any religious practice can be imposed"
Asked by Euronews, the Ministry of National Education recalls that "a state-funded private school under contract may devote school time to a particular theme, such as tackling bullying or introducing pupils to different professions".
"In the private sector under contract, this time may also reflect the specific ethos of the school," it adds.
The ministry nevertheless sets two limits. First, freedom of conscience must be respected: "no spiritual time nor any religious practice can be imposed on pupils or staff".
Second, "the Sgec has no hierarchical authority over schools" and may therefore suggest this initiative, but not impose the suspension of normal lessons for the day. The decision to organise such a day "rests with each school, within this framework", the ministry points out.
Secularism, a debate rekindled by papal events
In France, events linked to the papacy regularly reignite debate over the place of religion in the public sphere.
In April 2025, the government's decision to fly flags on public buildings at half-mast for the funeral of Pope Francis drew criticism. Several political leaders saw it as a breach of the principle of state neutrality, while the executive invoked the pope's status as a head of state.
In 2023, Emmanuel Macron's presence at the Mass celebrated by Pope Francis in Marseille had also prompted reactions. This time, the head of state will not attend any of the Masses celebrated by Leo XIV during his visit to France.
For the open-air Mass scheduled for Saturday in Place de la Concorde and on the Champs-Élysées in Paris, he will be represented by his wife Brigitte Macron and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu, the presidency announced on Tuesday.
Emmanuel Macron will nonetheless welcome Leo XIV on his arrival and receive him at the Élysée.
In France, Catholic education accounts for around 17% of all pupils in primary and lower and upper secondary education, totalling more than 2 million pupils.

OpenAI to provide Ukraine with tools to combat cyberattacks
Technology giant OpenAI will provide the Ukrainian government with free access to its AI-powered cybersecurity system Daybreak to help protect civilian infrastructure such as hospitals and power plants from cyberattacks.
Source: BBC
Details: According to the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA), the country's national cyber incident response team, nearly 6,000 attacks were recorded in Ukraine in 2025.
Daybreak can rapidly identify vulnerabilities in digital systems and help develop measures to address them. Under the agreement, Ukraine will gain access to OpenAI's advanced GPT-5.6 Sol model – a competitor to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable.
George Osborne, former UK Chancellor of the Exchequer and now head of OpenAI for Countries, said: "Protecting civilian infrastructure means defending it against both physical and digital attacks, so people can continue to live, work and access essential services."
Reacting to the news, Rafe Pilling, Senior Director of Threat Intelligence at cybersecurity company Sophos, said Russian offensive cyber operations had been a "key component" of the Kremlin's aggression against Ukraine since 2014.
"Any initiative that strengthens Ukraine's already highly capable, but heavily burdened, cyber defence efforts is a welcome development and could provide a valuable force multiplier," he said.
Jamie MacColl, a senior research fellow specialising in cybersecurity at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told the BBC that Western tech companies have been supporting Ukraine for some time – partly for altruistic reasons, but also because they gain highly valuable data and intelligence in an active conflict environment.
He believes access to Daybreak will be useful, particularly given the scale of Russian cyberattacks targeting the country.
Background: Anthropic foiled attempts by hackers to use Claude to conduct a cyber-espionage campaign against Ukraine that was suspected of being linked to Russia.

US lawmakers propose sweeping AI restrictions with superintelligence ban
Unknown

US lawmakers propose sweeping AI restrictions with superintelligence ban
Legislation seeks to pause advanced AI systems until federal safety standards are established
United States Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Greg Casar of Texas introduced a new bill that would impose sweeping restrictions on the artificial intelligence industry, including banning the development of what is called artificial superintelligence.
The legislation, introduced on Wednesday, comes weeks after top AI industry researchers issued dire warnings that the technology could wipe out humanity within the next decade, according to a wave of industry insiders.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Inside Kazakhstan’s push to become a regional AI centre
- list 2 of 4What’s the US–China AI ‘hotline’ that Trump plans to pitch to Xi Jinping?
- list 3 of 4Wall Street’s Nasdaq hits all-time high as AI frenzy gathers pace
- list 4 of 4As AI leaders warn of catastrophe, US and China shun slowdown calls
The nearly 20-page bill outlines an outright ban on the development of intelligence that can outperform a human being and has the power “to destroy or disempower humanity, including by overthrowing the federal government.”
The legislation would also call for a temporary pause on the development of advanced AI systems until a regulatory body that can oversee and develop safety standards is put in place, as well as establishing a cabinet-level department called the Department of Artificial Intelligence that would oversee the industry.
The proposed agency would be tasked with regulating what are called frontier models — a term referring to the most advanced AI models in development. The agency would ensure the models are not dangerous, and it would be empowered to remove the models from circulation if they do, in fact, become dangerous and supervise their destruction.
The bill would also impose steep penalties for those who violate the superintelligence ban, resulting in 20 years in prison, mirroring comparable punishments for individuals who develop nuclear weapons. It also states that individuals who violate the provisions would be barred from working in the AI industry for 10 years.
For companies, the legislation also calls for what the summary describing the legislation refers to as a “corporate death penalty,” in which charter holders could have their intellectual property and assets seized by the federal government.
The legislation calls for international coordination to institute a global ban. That would include pursuing international agreements, as well as instituting export controls on “artificial intelligence computing infrastructure”.
An uphill battle
Advocates of a pullback like the bill but are sceptical.
“[It’s] unlikely to pass but it’s courageous and much safer than the status quo,” Alex Turner, a former researcher who resigned from Google DeepMind in June, told Al Jazeera.
Concerned that “an artificial intelligence system that exhibits or can easily be modified to exhibit capabilities that match or exceed human cognitive performance and capabilities across a broad range of domains or tasks” is too broad, it might cover current systems. The second definition (disempowerment of govt) seems better,” he said.
The legislation comes as US President Donald Trump told the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday that the US would rename artificial intelligence “super intelligence” in all US government documents.
“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globality scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now, hereinafter called super intelligence. Changing the name,” Trump said in his remarks.
“The use of the word artificial makes intelligence sound fake,” Trump said.
The increased pressure on the AI industry ramped up earlier this month, when Jacob Coxon, a former AI researcher at Anthropic, announced his resignation from the AI giant in a viral social media post outlining the dangers of the technology.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear,” Coxon said.
The bill comes as both OpenAI and Anthropic near initial public offerings on Wall Street, poised for 2027 for OpenAI and potentially November for Anthropic.
