Nawrocki's aide denies 'pay-to-play' claims ahead of New York summit
An aide to Poland's President Karol Nawrocki on Sunday strongly rejected allegations that a private foundation was selling access to the head of state for up to USD 100,000 during his current visit to New York.
The denial followed a joint report by broadcaster Radio ZET and Newsweek Poland. The outlets wrote that a private think-tank, the Centre for Development Strategies, offered corporate sponsorship packages tied to the Polish-American Economic Summit, co-organised by the President's Office, to be held at the Pilecki Institute in New York on Monday.
According to the report, a USD 100,000 'Platinum Package' allegedly promised a one-on-one meeting with the Polish president, while 'Gold' (USD 50,000) and 'Silver' (USD 25,000) packages offered access in smaller group settings.
Blazej Pobozy, an aide to Nawrocki, dismissed the reports on television network TVN24, calling them a "clumsy attempt to attack the president". He said that the president never conditions his participation in public events on commercial payments or paid access.
"Every conference has different tiers or fees for participation," Pobozy said. "The fact that an organiser suggests proximity to certain zones grants specific access is something I can only smile at."
The allegations triggered reaction from Poland's government, which is politically aligned against the president. On Sunday, government spokesperson Adam Szlapka questioned on X whether access to the president could now be secured via "a large enough bank transfer," while Secret Services Coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak described the alleged practices as unprecedented in modern Poland.
Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk also called on the President's Office to clarify the matter "for the good of the office and the state".
The President's Office did not immediately respond to requests for official comment at the time of publication. (PAP)

Russian journalist and YouTuber Yury Dud is now on the state’s ‘terrorist and extremist’ registry. What does that mean legally for his audience?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:26:37 UTC
04:26:37 KST

Russian journalist and YouTuber Yury Dud is now on the state’s ‘terrorist and extremist’ registry. What does that mean legally for his audience?
Yury Dud was added to what?
Yury Dud has been added to the Federal Financial Monitoring Service’s list, with an asterisk next to his name. The asterisk usually means authorities have opened a criminal investigation under a “terrorism” statute. The details of any such investigation remain unknown, but Dud is effectively barred from operating in Russia, and others could face prosecution for engaging with his content.
Wasn’t Dud already banned in Russia?
In April 2022, the Justice Ministry designated Yury Dud a “foreign agent.” Unlike the “terrorist” designation, that status does not ban someone from operating in Russia, though it substantially restricts what they can do. In the summer of 2025, authorities opened a criminal investigation into Dud’s alleged evasion of his “foreign agent” obligations. In November, he was sentenced in absentia to one year and 10 months in a penal colony in that case.
So are Russians breaking the law if they watch his videos?
No.
Russians can still watch Dud’s content and stay subscribed to his YouTube channel or keep following his social media accounts. So far, there are no known cases of anyone being targeted simply for subscribing.
But Natalia Sekretareva, head of the legal department at the Memorial Human Rights Defense Center, said, “Before crossing the Russian border, it’s best to unsubscribe and clear your viewing history: border guards can check devices and, among other things, look for subscriptions to ‘opposition’ content.”
At this link, you’ll find our detailed guide to what else officials may look for on your devices and how to prepare.
What if Russians repost something?
That probably carries a risk. It depends on:
- What content they repost
- Why Dud was added to Rosfinmonitoring’s list
If Dud was added to the list because of an investigation into “justifying terrorism,” the authorities may object to a particular video. Reposting that video could also be treated as a violation of Article 205.2 of Russia’s Criminal Code, and offenders could face up to seven years in prison. Under that scenario, a person could repost Dud’s other videos without the same risk. But Sekretareva told Meduza it was too early to draw firm conclusions:
Since we don’t yet know what he’s accused of, it’s best to be careful.
Does that apply to old reposts, too?
Yes. In Russia, anything posted online could be treated as a “continuing offense” as long as it remains up.
What if Russians post a clip from one of his videos without a link?
It depends on the kind of content they post. If the video is deemed to “justify terrorism,” posting a clip from it could, in theory, be risky even without a link.
But donating is definitely a bad idea for Russians, right?
That’s right. At least if you’re in Russia or still visit from time to time.
Under the law on “financing extremist activity,” you could face up to eight years in prison (or up to 10 years if you used your official position). Under the law on “aiding terrorist activity,” you could face 15 years in prison.
Sekretareva stressed to Meduza that donations to Yury Dud’s personal accounts aren’t the only concern:
You shouldn’t send money to legal entities connected to him, either. In practice, law enforcement officers are unlikely to distinguish between supporting Dud the “terrorist” and funding legitimate journalism through a legal entity connected to him. There have been cases of people facing legal action even for sending their own children money for everyday expenses.

Russia's propaganda center Rybar ran a covert filming operation across multiple European countries, Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD) reported, citing a Czech investigation by Seznam Zprávy. The founder of the project, Mykhailo Zvinchuk, has been under sanctions by the European Union and the UK.
The EU's sanctions justification states that Rybar is a member of a working group established by Vladimir Putin in December 2022 to coordinate Russia's mobilization efforts in connection with the war against Ukraine.
Moscow has recently escalated covert influence operations and disinformation across Europe, yet years of sanctions have not stopped its operatives from working inside the EU. The Rybar case shows how thin the enforcement of those measures remains.
Rybar crew posed as documentarians in Prague
Russians moved freely within the Schengen Area, holding residence permits for EU countries, particularly Germany. They traveled to Prague posing as documentary filmmakers and attempted to record interviews with local experts and politicians. The stated pretext was a documentary series on Europe's sociopolitical situation.
When Seznam Zprávy journalists confronted the film crew at the meeting location, the propagandists fled. The investigation identified Boris Dvorkin as the Moscow-based producer of the operation. One of his projects received funding from the History of the Fatherland Foundation, established by Putin's decree and headed by Sergei Naryshkin, chief of Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).
Operations planned across multiple countries
Similar filming operations were allegedly planned or already carried out in Czechia, Slovakia, Austria, Hungary, Serbia, France, and other countries, the CCD said.
The UK sanctioned Rybar and Zvinchuk in December 2025, citing the network's interference in elections in Moldova and Armenia. It added ten more Rybar staff members in July 2026 for their role in destabilizing Ukraine. In 2024, the US State Department offered a $10 million reward for information on Zvinchuk and eight others tied to the project.

Trump administration to defend its ban of major news outlets in court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:26:03 UTC
04:26:03 KST

US judge delays ruling on White House ban of CNN, MS NOW, Politico
The news organisations are scheduled to make their case to a US district judge on Wednesday afternoon.
US President Donald Trump’s administration has defended his decision to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds, arguing in a court filing that the president has broad authority to determine which journalists can access the complex and that the outlets’ reporting raised national security concerns.
US District Judge Timothy Kelly held the hearing in Washington to consider a request by the news outlets for a temporary restraining order that would immediately reinstate their White House access while a legal challenge they filed on Monday plays out. He did not make a ruling, and it was unclear when he would issue a decision.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3CNN, Politico, MS NOW sue Trump administration over White House ban
- list 2 of 3White House launches ‘Trump TV’ after press bans
- list 3 of 3Rubio defends Trump’s White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico
In a filing ahead of the hearing, Justice Department lawyers said the outlets had failed to meet what the administration described as standards of professionalism and decorum.
“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the filing said.
The White House press office sent letters to the three outlets on Tuesday alleging their coverage involved “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information”.
The letters, filed in court, cited CNN publishing “top-secret” construction details of a bunker beneath the White House’s East Wing, MS NOW coverage of the impact of the Iran war on US military munitions and a Politico report about funding for the White House ballroom that included details about Secret Service security improvements. It also cited Politico relying on anonymous sources for a report describing the Republican congressional midterm convention as a “disaster”.
The filing argues that publishing such information can divert national security personnel and resources as officials assess whether material is classified and determine its security implications.
The administration is also asking the court to overturn a 1977 appeals court ruling, Sherrill vs Knight, which held that White House press access could not be denied arbitrarily or without compelling reasons.
The lawsuit by the three outlets argues that the ban violates their First Amendment rights.
The proceedings are historic, said Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University.
“No president has taken this explicit of a step” to ban entire news outlets because he doesn’t like their reporting, she said. “There have been various presidents throughout history who have grumbled about the press or threatened to take more major steps, but really there was nothing at this level before Trump.”
The case was assigned to District Judge Kelly, who previously ordered the restoration of CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s White House credentials during Trump’s first term. Despite Kelly being a Trump-appointed judge, the president has already expressed his disappointment in the selection.
“They have drawn a great Judge, for them, a man who ruled in favor of Jim Acosta, who now seems to have disappeared from the Planet. The Judge’s name is Tim Kelly, and he was, sadly, appointed by ‘TRUMP,’” the president wrote on Truth Social. “In other words, almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”
An amicus brief was filed by other news groups Wednesday, urging the court to immediately restore White House access to the three outlets. It said, “the targeted expulsion of news media from White House grounds injures the public interest” and that “unassailable First Amendment law makes any viewpoint-based decision to bar reporters from a nonpublic forum constitutionally repugnant”.

====================================================================================================

How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation spreads division and despair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:24:39 UTC
04:24:39 KST

Russian disinformation campaigns are varied in their falsehoods and strategies.
The narratives range from a deepfake Tom Cruise criticising the Paris Olympics to portraying a recent Russian attack on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border as a false-flag operation.
Some efforts are blatant deepfakes, such as stamping the BBC logo on a video wrongly blaming Ukraine for a deadly missile salvo on its own citizens in Kramatorsk four years ago.
The tactics evolve too, from disseminating deceitful narratives through the Telegram messaging platform to “poisoning” AI systems by littering the internet with false stories in the hope they will be regurgitated by chatbots.
It is systematic and Andy Burnham has seen enough, announcing a new anti-disinformation agency, the National Centre for Information Defence.
“We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair,” he said.
Experts say picking off individual examples is the wrong approach and Burnham is right to tackle what he describes as a “poisonous tide”.
Going after isolated examples of disinformation is a “losers’ game”, says Ned Mendez, head of research at Alliance4Europe, a nonprofit that analyses these destabilising threats.
“You can spend all your time looking for a TikTok or a post on X but it’s not an effective use of your day. It’s the infrastructure that is the problem, so this is a step in the right direction, going after the networks,” he says.
Sophie Williams-Dunning, a cyber analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) thinktank, says there is now a “sophisticated ecosystem which exists to exacerbate provokable users for one reason or another”.
Although Burnham is targeting “hostile state information attacks”, this ecosystem does not just include Russia, which likes to amplify “divisive content”, says Williams-Dunning.
It also includes far-right influencers who immediately jump on social flashpoints like the Southport and Belfast riots and individuals simply looking to make money by producing highly engaging content riffing on disruption.
The Burnham announcement is “welcome, if overdue”, says Williams-Dunning, who adds that there will be an accompanying debate about free speech and the right level of government intervention. Inevitably, malign networks will amplify those free-speech concerns, she says.
It is not just Russia deploying information attacks. China and Iran have both used deepfake newscasters to advance their goals.
One recent study, conducted mostly in February by the Social Market Foundation, a British thinktank, found that more than a quarter of posts on X that relate to news were misinformation, a third of which were anti-immigration or Islamophobic.
The UK government defines misinformation as the inadvertent spread of false information, while disinformation is the deliberate creation and spread of falsehoods to create harm or disruption. The two can intertwine to highly disruptive effect.
Labour has become increasingly concerned about Russian disinformation affecting the UK. The Starmer government in May cited information warfare from Moscow when it warned Britain was “confronting an industrial-scale attack on the UK’s and our allies’ information environment, aimed at undermining our security and democratic systems”.
Earlier this year MPs on the foreign affairs select committee called for the creation of a national counter-disinformation centre, in a similar vein to Sweden’s Psychological Defence Agency and France’s Vigilance and Protection against Foreign Digital Interference service.
Experts said Burnham’s announcement at least shows the UK government catching up, although Keir Starmer’s administration showed an awareness of social media’s contribution to unrest by launching the National Internet Intelligence Investigations unit after the Southport disturbances in 2024. Operated by the police, it monitors social media to help local forces “manage public safety threats and risks”.
The UK government has been taking action prior to Burnham’s announcement, however. In May it sanctioned employees of the Social Design Agency and ANO Dialog, Russian entities which it said the Kremlin uses for large-scale interference campaigns.
One example is the Doppelgänger network, so-called due to its technique of imitating the appearance of established media organisations including Le Monde, the Guardian, Der Spiegel and Fox News.
Other examples include the 2023 surge in reports of bedbug infestations in France, falsely blaming Ukrainian refugees. The disinformation leaked into the British press and the French government concluded the stories were being artificially amplified by Russian-linked social media accounts
One of the most longstanding misinformation campaigns has centred on the idea that London is “dangerous” and “lawless”. Analysis of Reddit accounts by King’s College London found the number of such posts rose from 874 in 2008 to 258,444 in 2024.
Robert Topinka, reader in digital media and rhetoric at Birkbeck, University of London, said Russia did not necessarily start such storylines, but enthusiastically amplified them.
He cautioned that counter-disinformation efforts should not assume “people are just being fooled by some sort of outside actor”. Rather, he said, Russia tends to find a point of tension and then create more content around it.
“What really is happening is people are feeling like Britain is run-down – that’s the real source of it,” said Topinka.
AI is adding a new dimension. Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta says AI-generated content is now a “near-standard” part of disinformation campaigns.
The UK thinktank Demos recently highlighted a chatbot “poisoning” campaign where falsehoods published online by a discredited Russian organisation, including the bodies of deceased Ukrainian soldiers being processed into meat products, were repeated by chatbot models.
The National Centre for Information Defence will have a lot of work to do.

A St. Petersburg entertainment venue linked to Svetlana Krivonogikh, who was previously identified as a former mistress of Vladimir Putin, is behind a show being staged this fall at the Bely Mys (lit. “White Cape”) wine center in the southern Russian resort town of Gelendzhik, located on the coast of the Black Sea, The Insider found. The wine center itself is also linked to people close to the Russian leader and has frequently been described as Putin’s “wine Disneyland.”
The show, titled “Wine Cabaret,” is running at Bely Mys. It premiered Sept. 12, with the final performance scheduled for Oct. 10. The event combines cabaret, wine tasting, and a gastronomic dinner:
“Wine reveals itself onstage through music, dance, circus arts, acrobatics, live vocals, lighting, visual imagery, and gastronomy,” according to the description on the show’s website.
Tickets cost between 25,000 and 60,000 rubles ($295 to just over $700).
The wine center itself has previously been linked to Putin’s inner circle. The Bely Mys website domain is owned by a company belonging to a friend of Putin’s from his youth at the Yavara-Neva judo club, The Insider reported this past June. The editorial team also established a link between the new show and other figures close to Putin: the company organizing it is owned by Svetlana Krivonogikh, who was named in a 2020 investigation by the independent outlet Proekt as being the mother of one of Putin’s daughters. In 2016, before the past romantic connection between Putin and Krivonogikh had become known, The Insider identified her as one of the “close acquaintances” who accompanied the then-FSB Director on flights between Moscow and St. Petersburg in 1999.
The current show has been organized by the team behind Leningrad Center, an entertainment venue and performing arts theater housed in the historic former Leningrad cinema building in St. Petersburg’s Tavrichesky Garden. The center’s legal entity is the aptly named LLC Profit (ООО «Профит»). Three-quarters of the company is owned by LLC Relax (ООО «Релакс»), which is wholly owned by Krivonogikh.
Leningrad Center has repeatedly faced criticism over what some viewers described as excessive sexualization in its productions. Its 2021 show LoveSick was billed as the “most provocative and explicit” production staged at the venue, promising audiences “the aftertaste of encounters with a seductive 1930s cabaret dancer, a Victorian courtesan, or a model from Andy Warhol’s studio.” Another production, “Favorites of the Moon,” starred the American actress and former Playboy model Carmen Electra, who had previously performed with the erotic revue Crazy Horse Paris at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas. Audience reviews complained that the show mixed “theater, circus, musical, and striptease, but all of them half-baked,” as well as featuring “unjustified bare breasts” among the performers. Social media posts from “Wine Cabaret” indirectly suggest that the same style has been retained.
Bely Mys, Russia’s largest wine-themed entertainment complex, is located on the waterfront in Gelendzhik. It includes a wine museum, an enoteca boasting the country’s largest collection of Russian wines, more than 10 restaurants, a movie theater, a Wine Academy, and even a civil registry office where marriage certificates can be signed. The complex also has its own yacht marina.
In 2024, the independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo reported that companies linked to Vladimir Putin were involved in building the complex. Developer Veles-Stroy had worked on the reconstruction of “Putin’s palace” at Cape Idokopas, while Alexei Borodin, director contractor Politekhstroy-Svargo, had previously served as an aide to the presidential envoy to the Volga Federal District. The project’s main investor is Bank Rossiya — which is controlled by billionaire Yuri Kovalchuk, another one of Putin’s close personal friends. Bely Mys uses the wine.ru domain, which belongs to Bastion, a company whose beneficiary until the end of 2023 was Taimuraz Bolloyev, a friend of Putin’s from the Yavara-Neva judo club.

S-400 process to take time, Türkiye-US defense cooperation 'essential': US ambassador
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:20:01 UTC
04:20:01 KST

- Tom Barrack says Ankara-Washington relations 'have never been better,' stressing defense cooperation between 2 NATO allies 'essential,' dialogue with Iran 'a step in the right direction'
- Barrack says Trump, Erdogan have 'an amazing respect for each other as leaders', 'a chemistry with each other,' describing Türkiye as 'great friend' of US
- Barrack voices optimism on Iran-US talks, 'region's ready, America's ready. I hope the rest is ready'
US Ambassador to Ankara Tom Barrack said Wednesday that resolving the legal and regulatory issues surrounding Türkiye's purchase of the Russian S-400 air defense system will take time, stressing that defense cooperation between Ankara and Washington remains “essential.”
Barrack told reporters on the sidelines of the 80th session of the UN General Assembly in New York that Türkiye and the US were working through the requirements imposed by Congress regarding the S-400 issue.
"The US Congress is doing a great job. They have so many constituencies that they have to respect," Barrack said when asked about developments on the S-400 and F-35 programs.
He said the S-400 issue was governed not only by the Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA), but also by the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).
He said Türkiye and the US were working to fulfill the requirements of the congressional mandate, which he described as a key part of the process.
Barrack cited a $100 million transaction involving Boeing commercial jets announced recently as an example of economic engagement between the two countries.
"Again, it takes time, but the defense cooperation between Türkiye and the US is essential," he said.
"They're the second-largest NATO ally. We rely on them tremendously for all sorts of regional alliances," he added.  
Trump-Erdogan relationship has 'never been better'
Asked whether informal exchanges between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and US President Donald Trump had produced any new developments in Turkish-American relations, Barrack said the relationship had never been stronger.
"They've never been better," he said.
Barrack explained that the two leaders had already discussed major bilateral issues during their meetings in the previous year, including at the NATO summit.
"We've covered all of the issues. The relationship is continuing," he said, adding that the leaders communicate frequently amid regional tensions.
"So, there wasn't much new territory to cover. It's constant," he said. "The two leaders are very good with each other. They like each other, which really helps."
He said most major issues were handled by ministers and military chiefs, "so, they're in good shape." 
'They have a chemistry with each other'
Addressing informal conversations between Trump and Erdogan during a dinner Tuesday, Barrack said they had mutual respect and strong personal chemistry.
"Yeah, it's amazing. They have such an amazing respect for each other as leaders. But more than that, they have a chemistry with each other," he said.
Barrack added that they communicated effectively despite cultural differences.
"Even though there's this cultural divide, they're very much alike," he said.
He also praised Türkiye's relationship with the US during periods of heightened regional tensions.
"Türkiye has been a great friend to America," said Barrack. "In these very difficult moments when things are tense, you find out who your friends are." 
 'Türkiye is kind of in the middle'
Regarding a meeting with Trump and leaders from Gulf countries, Barrack highlighted Türkiye's geographical position and its connections with multiple regions.
"Türkiye, with its pivotal geographic position and being a hub for everybody, is kind of in the middle between the GCC (Gulf Cooperation Council), Europe, the Caucasus, the Balkans, it's everything," he said.
Barrack said the meeting provided an opportunity for the leaders to engage with Trump and express their appreciation for his efforts.
"Everybody from the notion of saying, let's get on with tolerance and peace in the world and move forward," he said, describing the meeting as worthwhile. 
Barrack says dialogue with Iran is moving in 'right direction'
Asked about the outcome of a meeting with Iran held Tuesday, Barrack said continued dialogue represented progress.
"With every step, every opportunity kind of dialogue, and there's a step in the right direction," he said.
Barrack said US special envoy Steve Witkoff was encouraged by the discussions and highlighted the importance of continuing engagement.
"We're having more discussion, which is the right thing for all of us," he said.
Asked whether he was optimistic about reaching a deal to end the war with Iran, Barrack said he was optimistic because there was no alternative to pursuing a resolution.
"I am optimistic because we have to be optimistic. There's no option," he said.
He described the situation as involving a cultural divide and said both sides had taken courageous positions, while stressing the need for tolerance.
"We just need to find some tolerance between that," said Barrack.
"The region's ready, America's ready. I hope the rest is ready," he added.

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright previously stated that such a ban would not work and could lead to higher prices for gasoline and jet fuel, and also noted that the United States was considering implementing voluntary measures.

Swiss upper house backs tougher capital requirements for UBS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:13:03 UTC
04:13:03 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Switzerland's upper house of parliament backed tougher capital requirements on Wednesday for UBS, the country's largest bank, advancing efforts to strengthen banking safeguards following the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse.
The Council of States voted 29-16 for a provision requiring UBS to back its foreign subsidiaries with Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital equal to 90% of their value.
UBS estimated the measure would require it to hold about $16 billion in additional CET1 capital at its Swiss parent company, according to Bloomberg.
The requirement is a slight easing from the government's original proposal for 100% backing, but remains substantially tougher than current rules.
Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter has said her plan would ensure UBS remains resilient in a potential crisis and protect Switzerland from a scenario in which its largest bank by far could spiral toward collapse.
UBS, which supported an alternative allowing greater use of Additional Tier 1 (AT1) bonds, criticized the decision.
"This political outcome is not a compromise and fails to address the root causes of the Credit Suisse collapse," said the bank, adding that it would focus on protecting its "long-term interests."
The proposed reforms follow the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse, which UBS acquired in an emergency government-backed takeover.
The legislation moves to the lower house of parliament, with a final decision expected no earlier than 2027.

Argentina’s Milei says UN ‘looking the other way’ on Falkland Islands
Argentina steps up its Las Malvinas claim as tensions with the United Kingdom grow over offshore oil drilling.
Argentine President Javier Milei has accused the United Nations of “looking the other way” on Argentina’s long-standing dispute with the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands, known to Argentines as Las Malvinas.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Milei called the islands a “national cause” and took aim at British-backed plans to extract oil from waters Argentina claims as its own.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Why do the Falkland Islands matter to the UK and Argentina so much?
- list 2 of 4Argentina steps up legal campaign against Falkland Islands oil firms
- list 3 of 4Argentinian judge orders suspension of Falklands oil project
- list 4 of 4Argentina’s Left stages ‘March of Anger’ over Milei’s austerity measures
At the centre of the latest dispute is Sea Lion, a major oil project about 220km (140 miles) north of the islands, which Argentina considers illegal. The owners of the project, UK-based Rockhopper Exploration and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum, are expected to begin drilling in the coming months, with production planned for 2028.
Earlier this month, Argentina began sanctions proceedings against 60 companies and individuals linked to offshore drilling near the islands. British officials have rejected the measures, saying the Falklands have the right to develop their own natural resources.
Milei also argues the project runs counter to a 1976 UN General Assembly resolution calling on Argentina and the UK to negotiate over the sovereignty dispute and avoid unilateral action in the meantime.
“Any such activity not authorised by the Argentine Republic … constitutes an unlawful act,” Milei said on Wednesday. He said Argentina had chosen a “peaceful, practical, and effective defence” of its claim.
Along with the sanctions, his government has also announced new funding for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego, Argentina’s southernmost province, to bolster its military presence near the islands.
The Falklands are a largely self-governing UK overseas territory in the South Atlantic. Britain has administered the islands since 1833, but Argentina has long claimed sovereignty.
Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, triggering a 10-week war that ended in its surrender.
The UK says the islanders should decide their own future. In a 2013 referendum, 1,513 of 1,517 voters chose to remain a British overseas territory.
Milei rejected that argument on Wednesday. He said self-determination did not apply because the population had been “implanted by the occupying power” on disputed territory.
The forceful stance is a shift for Milei, who had previously faced criticism from opponents for paying little attention to the sovereignty dispute while pursuing closer ties with the United States.
But the political landscape has changed in recent weeks, as US President Donald Trump has raised the possibility of reconsidering Washington’s position on the islands, though he has stopped short of backing Argentina’s claim.
Milei quickly seized on the opening. Earlier this month, he declared that “winds of change” were blowing in Argentina’s favour and argued that his close relationship with Washington could help advance its case.
Milei’s opponents say he is using the issue to drum up support at home ahead of an expected re-election bid in 2027.
“It’s simply something to look good in the eyes of society or to try to shift the agenda,” Guillermo Michel, a Peronist opposition lawmaker, told Reuters.
But there is little sign so far that the strategy has moved the needle. A study by Buenos Aires-based consultancy Inteligencia Analitica found Milei’s recent televised address on the Malvinas only modestly improved his public image.
His remarks on Wednesday were also part of a much broader attack on the UN. Milei accused the organisation of failing to protect international security and human rights, calling it a “useless organisation” filled with “arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats”.
“Those who follow the rules receive no reward for doing so, while those who break them face no repercussions whatsoever,” he said.
Milei also used the speech to underline Argentina’s close relationships with the US and Israel, saying his government was “unequivocally aligned” with the West and shared a “deep affinity of values” with both countries.
Milei accused the UN of “systematically” voting against Israel while remaining silent about abuses elsewhere. He also condemned Iran and pointed to Argentina’s designation of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a “terrorist organisation”.

Jump forward or back? Let's do the daylight saving time warp again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:11:59 UTC
04:11:59 KST

When does daylight saving time start? Do we gain or lose an hour?
Daylight saving time is looming, with half of Australia about to adjust to a new time zone.
Here's what you need to know before the clocks change.
When does daylight saving time start?
Not this Sunday, but the Sunday after.
Each year, daylight saving time begins on the first Sunday of October.
This year, that's October 4.
Which states have daylight saving time?
- ACT
- New South Wales
- South Australia
- Tasmania
- Victoria
The Northern Territory, Queensland and Western Australia do not observe daylight saving time, so the clocks will not change in those jurisdictions.
Do the clocks move forwards or backwards?
Forwards.
At 2am on Sunday, the clocks will move forward to 3am in jurisdictions that observe daylight saving time.
The clocks will go back by an hour when daylight saving time ends in April.
The clocks in most smart devices will automatically update, so you probably won't have to change the time on your phone.
However, you'll need to adjust the time on your analogue clocks, as well as the clocks on some appliances like ovens and microwaves.
The New South Wales government recommends changing the time before you go to bed on Saturday.
"To kickstart your day and avoid any timing issues, set your watch and household clocks that don't automatically update overnight to the new time before you go to bed," the NSW government website says.
Preparing for the change
The Sleep Health Foundation recommends going to bed 15 to 20 minutes earlier in the three or four nights leading up to the weekend to help your body adjust to the time zone change.
And set your alarm 30 minutes earlier on Saturday and Sunday to prepare yourself.
Don't be surprised if you feel out of sorts for a few days, as experts advise it can take about a week for your body to adjust.
"Daylight saving throws our circadian rhythms out of sync because we are suddenly required to wake at a time when the body clock is still programmed for sleep," the foundation says.
"In general, 'losing' an hour in the spring is more difficult to adjust to than 'gaining' an hour in the autumn when we move the clocks back one hour."
The foundation also recommends:
- Making your bedroom as bright as possible when you first wake up
- Exercising outside in the mornings
- Avoiding exercise just before bed
- Avoiding going to bed hungry or too soon after a meal
Another tip is to spend time outside in the morning light to reset your body clock.
What are the Australian time zones?
We're still in standard time, meaning most of the country falls into one of three time zones:
- AEST: ACT, New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania and Victoria
- ACST: Northern Territory and South Australia
- AWST: Western Australia
But once daylight saving time kicks in, a few more time zones are added to the mix. Here are the main ones:
- AEDT: ACT, New South Wales, Tasmania and Victoria
- AEST: Queensland
- ACDT: South Australia
- ACST: Northern Territory
- AWST: Western Australia
But there are a few exemptions.
For example, Broken Hill operates on South Australia's time zone despite technically being a NSW town.
Then there's Lord Howe Island, a two-hour flight off the NSW coast, which has its own time zone.
Lord Howe Standard Time is 30 minutes ahead of AEST, adding an extra 30 minutes when daylight saving time kicks in.
And don't forget about the cluster of communities in southern Western Australia which have chosen their own time zone.
The pocket is called the Central Western Standard Time Zone, but is more affectionately known as "Eucla Time".
Here, residents operate halfway between WA and SA time zones, but also adopt daylight saving, putting them further out of kilter.
The zone covers a small area of the Nullarbor that stretches from the eastern side of Caiguna to Border Village and is marked in purple on this map:
Does daylight saving time mean a long weekend?
Only for some jurisdictions.
In ACT, New South Wales and South Australia, daylight saving coincides with the Labour Day public holiday on Monday, October 5.
That gives locals a chance to adjust and make sure they turn up to work on time.
However, October 5 is not a public holiday in Tasmania or Victoria, despite them also switching the clocks.
Could daylight saving time become permanent?
As far as we know, that's not a discussion being had in any official capacity in Australia, but it is in the US.
In July, the US House of Representatives passed the Sunshine Protection Act, which would eliminate the need for states to change their clocks twice a year.
However, it has to pass the US Senate to become law and, as the USA Today Network points out, there aren't many more sitting days left for senators to vote on the act before the clocks are due to change in the US in November.
Is there appetite for a similar change in Australia?
When we reported on the Sunshine Protection Act in July, we asked readers whether they support a time zone system that requires two time changes a year and the results were fairly evenly split.
Of the 1,800 readers who voted, 56 per cent said they didn't support a time zone system that requires two clock changes a year.
But this isn't an official poll, and with Australia's population at nearly 28 million, 1,800 voters may not reflect the views of every Australian.

Everything You Need to Know About SpaceX's Wildlife Refuge Land Swap with the Trump Administration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:07:33 UTC
04:07:33 KST

SpaceX has not always distinguished itself as a good environmental citizen. Part of that is unavoidable. You can’t launch 170 rockets per year—as the company did in 2025—without releasing a lot of black soot into the upper atmosphere and creating a lot of light and noise around the launch site, which can be harmful to local wildlife. Environmental organizations have mounted multiple legal challenges against the company over the years to enjoin or minimize its freedom to launch until multiple corrective measures are taken.
Now SpaceX faces another day in court. On Sept. 21 a judge ruled that a proposed land swap with the federal government that would allow the company to expand its launch pads, factory, and related infrastructure into a protected wildlife area in Texas could go ahead. That might have settled the issue but the environmental groups that sued to stop this, plan to appeal—and they believe they have a strong case.
Why did environmental groups sue to stop SpaceX’s land swap?
On June 10, a group of plaintiffs filed suit against the Department of the Interior to block a Trump Administration plan to cede SpaceX 725 acres of land in the Lower Rio Grande National Wildlife Refuge hard up against the company’s Starbase factory and launch site in Boca Chica, Texas, in exchange for 692 acres the company owns in the Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge about 20 miles north of Starbase. The land that would be annexed by SpaceX is not only home to thousands of species of plants and animals including the ocelot, which is endangered in the U.S.; it is also considered sacred by the Native American Carrizo/Comecrudo Nation of Texas, which is a plaintiff in the suit. What’s more, the tract has cultural and historical significance as it includes the Palmito Ranch Battlefield, the site of the last land battle of the Civil War.
The fact that the acreage that SpaceX gets will not be a gift, but rather an exchange for land the company currently owns—taking that latter plot off the table for development—does not solve the problem, says Laiken Jordahl, public lands advocate for the Center for Biological Diversity, the lead plaintiff in the lawsuit. “The whole point of the Lower Rio Grande Valley National Wildlife Refuge is to establish a chain of connected habitats along the river that allows for the migration of ocelots and other wildlife,” he argues. “This will cut out one of the key east-west areas of wildlife connectivity, and in return, we're getting a smaller amount of land in a different area.”
What did the Judge say in its decision that would allow the SpaceX land swap?
On. Sept. 21, Judge Fernando Rodriuguez, Jr., of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas, denied the Center for Biological Diversity’s request for a preliminary injunction that would prevent the move, ruling that the plaintiffs did not have standing to sue. In their filing, the plaintiffs argued that the land swap would cause them irreparable harm since they would lose access to those acres and the freedom to observe wildlife there. The Interior Department countered that the land was already closed to the public as part of its wildlife refuge status, so the plaintiffs suffered no loss.
The plaintiffs, in their filing, anticipated this finding and sought to rebut it in advance with 2014 case law. “[T]he affected individual,” they wrote, “need not always have direct access to the area at issue. Individuals can possess a cognizable interest ‘in observing the landscape from surrounding areas[.]’”
Rodriguez—appointed to the federal bench by President Donald Trump during his first term—was unmoved, and if anything, saw SpaceX as the potentially aggrieved party. The requested injunction, he wrote, “would impose uncertainty into and would result in modifications to SpaceX’s development plans, placing additional hardship on the company’s ability to meet milestones and contractual obligations.”
“We are obviously, extraordinarily disappointed in the judge's decision,” says Jordahl. “This effectively clears the way for the bulldozers to start destroying the refuge land. But the judge did not rule on our overall claims; it was just on the injunction. So yeah, the challenge will press forward.” (The denial of a preliminary injunction falls short of the judge actually ruling on whether the proposed land swap violates federal law—which the plaintiffs claim it does.)
What is SpaceX’s environmental impact?
It’s not for nothing that environmental groups worry about the impact of SpaceX’s south Texas site. That's where the company launches its massive Starship rocket—a 33-engine behemoth that stands 40-stories tall and puts out up to 18 million lbs of thrust, more than twice as much as NASA’s Space Launch System, the second most powerful rocket in the world.
Four minutes into Starship’s inaugural launch on April 20, 2023, it exploded spectacularly, raining debris downward—most of which fell into the Gulf of Mexico. But the mere ignition of the nearly three dozen engines on the concrete launch apron did plenty of harm of its own.
“Impacts from the launch include numerous large concrete chunks, stainless steel sheets, metal and other objects hurled thousands of feet away along with a plume cloud of pulverized concrete that deposited material up to 6.5 miles northwest of the pad site,” the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service wrote in an email to the media at the time. “Approximately 385 acres of debris was found on both SpaceX’s facility and in the surrounding Boca Chica State Park, and a 3.5-acre fire burned on park land south of the launch site.”
Jordahl is not worried just about similar environmental damage, but the harm to be done when those bulldozers he mentions begin to roll.
“I've heard different things [about what SpaceX wants to do with the land], from additional manufacturing areas to warehouses to worker housing,” says Jordahl. “We haven't gotten any clear and obvious plans. But the way that they've been treating the land out there already is telling. They pave over everything. They turn it into an industrial manufacturing zone.” SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
The harm won’t stop there. As SpaceX expands into the refuge, more land that is currently a comfortable distance from the complex will be exposed to the damage the launches can do. SpaceX claims it has cured the problems that made the first launch such a mess, installing a water-cooled metal deflection plate and a retaining wall to control debris. The other 12 Starship launches that have taken place since the inaugural one have indeed caused far less damage to the surroundings.
If that mitigates the environmental damage the rocket can do, however, the planned launch cadence exacerbates it. In August, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk told Aviation Week that he envisions daily Starship launches—carrying crew, satellites, and other cargo to space—as early as 2027. More headsnapping was his 2025 boast on X, that “In about 6 or 7 years, there will be days where Starship launches more than 24 times in 24 hours.”
Clearly, not all of those launches could come from the Texas site, but SpaceX has other launch facilities at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, and dedicated pads at the Kennedy Space Center and the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. A company so large, with more than a $2 trillion valuation, could always build more launchpads at more coastal sites whenever it chooses.
What precedent could the SpaceX land swap set?
The Texas base is making news at the moment, not simply for what it means for this potential development site, but for others elsewhere in the U.S. The Trump Administration is currently pursuing a similar land swap with a private land developer, involving a strip of land in Yosemite National Park for an undeveloped parcel in California so that residents in a planned private housing complex near the park will have easier access to it. Yet another land exchange is under consideration that would open up a federally designated wilderness area on Georgia’s Cumberland island to the construction of luxury homes.
“This [Texas] land transfer is part of a broader scheme by this administration to give away public lands to private interests,” says Jordahl. “The precedent that this transfer will set is extremely concerning when it comes to corporations setting their sights on and taking over public lands across America.

National Trust for Historic Preservation creates defense fund in light of "urgent threats"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:03:37 UTC
04:03:37 KST

National Trust for Historic Preservation creates defense fund in light of "urgent threats"
Washington DC nonprofit The National Trust for Historic Preservation, which sued the government last year over the White House ballroom extension, has announced a $10 million fundraising campaign for legal defence in support of US landmark preservation.
National Trust for Historic Preservation (NTHP) announced the creation of the Historic Preservation Defense Fund today during the 2026 National Preservation Summit.
It is aimed at protecting "the nation's historic places and the laws that safeguard them against urgent threats emanating from Washington", according to NTHP.
"Through the Historic Preservation Defense Fund, the National Trust recognizes the magnitude of the crisis facing us today. And we stand ready to protect what's at stake," said NTHP president Brent Leggs.
"It will provide resources for legal defense, public advocacy, and community action when historic places and the laws that protect them are under threat."
NTHP has been involved in lawsuits over the government's architectural interventions in DC, including a suit to block changes at the White House, which resulted in a ban that was recently lifted.
It said the decision to launch the fund stems from a change in the federal government's approach to preservation.
"Once, we looked to the federal government as a foundational partner in the preservation of the American story," said Leggs.
"We had a shared understanding, even if from different sides of the aisle or cultural contexts, that saving our historical record mattered."
"But as the government divests from this work, it is up to us to take up this charge in earnest."
Trump has denounced the NTHP as "bad for our country".
On its website, NTHP named The White House East Wing and the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts as evidence of federal preservation safeguards being "in jeopardy".
The site of the now-demolished East Wing is currently a construction zone to make way for president Donald Trump's in-progress ballroom extension, and the Kennedy Center recently shut down due to a battle over Trump's plans to rename and renovate it
It also cited the government's proposed Triumphal Arch as an "intrusion" on historic sightlines in Washington DC.
Leggs spoke to the federal government's attempts to rewrite Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which requires federal agencies to consider the effects their projects have on historic US properties.
Currently, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation (ACHP) is seeking to weaken Section 106 regulations, according to NPR.
Leggs said if implemented, the new rules could "dramatically diminish" current legal protections around projects such as the Reflecting Pool and the Smithsonian, both of which have also faced changes under Trump.
"The American public is demanding change and is impatient to see accountability from Congress, the Courts, and the Administration to ensure that no one can violate or weaponize policy to endanger these places," he said.
"It is not an exaggeration to say that this moment is existential."
The National Trust for Historic Preservation is a privately funded nonprofit founded in 1949 and chartered by US Congress to uphold standards in preservation.
Architectural historian Brent Leggs was appointed as NTHP president in June and is the first African American CEO to lead the NTHP.

No, this video doesn't disprove the 9/11 attack on the south tower of the World Trade Center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:01:33 UTC
04:01:33 KST

No, this video doesn't disprove the 9/11 attack on the south tower of the World Trade Center
A former British member of parliament implied that a video filmed from a helicopter on September 11, 2001 shows that no planes actually hit the World Trade Center's south tower, but this claim would be unfounded. The plane that hit the south tower hit the other side of the building, which isn’t visible in the video.
A few days after the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks that took place on September 11, 2001, British former Conservative MP Andrew Bridgen cast doubt on the official narrative when he implied that a plane did not hit the south tower of the World Trade Center. In reality, the south tower was indeed hit by a United Airlines Boeing 767 which had been hijacked by al Qaeda terrorists.
The former MP shared a video on September 15, 2026 that he claimed showed proof that a plane didn’t actually hit the south tower. The video, which garnered more than a million views on X from his post alone, was filmed from a helicopter facing the Twin Towers showing the north tower already in flames. The video then shows an explosion taking place in the south tower, but no plane can be seen. "Where was the plane that caused it?” Andrew Bridgen asked.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
A plane visible in the full version of the video
Bridgen’s claims, however, are wrong. First, if you carry out a reverse image search (check out our handy guide here to find out how), you will see a longer version of the video Bridgen posted on YouTube. The video was filmed live by Chopper 4, a helicopter belonging to the US channel NBC. In this complete version of the video, you can actually see a plane. It appears as a small dot moving towards the south tower just before the explosion.
While the plane’s collision with the tower isn’t directly visible in the video posted by Bridgen, this is because it hit the other side of the tower, which isn’t visible from the helicopter.
Collision on the south side of the south tower
According to a report by the commission set up by the United States to investigate September 11, United Airlines flight 175 crashed into the south face of the south tower after being hijacked by terrorists. However, as shown when we geolocated the craft, the NBC helicopter was filming the south tower from the north, which meant that the plane's collision was hidden by the tower itself.
The moment when the United Airlines Boeing 767 hit the south tower is actually visible in a number of other videos filmed from different angles on September 11, especially the video filmed by cameraman Evan Fairbanks, who was standing at the foot of the south tower. This video, which became one of the most well-known of the attacks, clearly shows a plane striking the south side of the south tower.

Video captures ranger's joyful tears on finding rare night parrot chick
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Rare video of night parrot chick hiding in spinifex tunnel in WA desert
In short:
A young night parrot, one of Australia's most cryptic birds, has been filmed in a spinifex tunnel in remote WA.
The daytime footage captures the elation of a ranger team as they make the rare discovery of the bird in the grassy nest.
What's next?
Rangers for the Ngururrpa Indigenous Protected Area are working with scientists to develop an eDNA program for finding signs of night parrots in waterholes.
Even in the heart of night parrot country it can be rare to actually see one of the world's most cryptic birds.
That is why the discovery of a young night parrot (Pezoporus occidentalis) this year set off an outpouring of emotion in the middle of the Great Sandy Desert in Western Australia.
A new video captures the moment members of the Ngururrpa Rangers and researchers shout-whisper through joyful tears on finding a nestling.
The sighting was even more unique because it happened during daytime, when critically endangered night parrots, as their name suggests, were hidden away.
Night parrots were thought extinct until they were rediscovered in 2013 in Queensland.
While the Ngururrpa Indigenous Protected Area is home to one of the largest populations of the species, this is the first time some rangers have seen a live bird in the area.
Kathryn Njamme, a member of the Ngururrpa Rangers, had previously heard the chime-like call of the bird. She had even seen camera trap footage, an egg and their loose green and yellow feathers.
But she had not laid eyes directly on a living night parrot.
"We was really happy and excited to find a night parrot," Ms Njamme said.
"We all was crying there and holding each other.
"We wanted to show people around the world that there's a night parrot out there in the country."
How the parrot was found
Ms Njamme said during a July trip to the Ngururrpa Indigenous Protected Area she sought help at a spirit tree.
"That's where we asked the Old People to help us find these birds," she said.
"We asked the Old People if they can reveal it for us so we can find them out in the bush when we drew the rain."
A few nights into the trip, there was heavy rain over the desert.
The next morning the rangers went searching among the old-growth mounds of bull spinifex (Triodia longiceps), called "lanu lanu" in Kukatja language, which night parrots are known to use as nests and shelter.
Ms Njamme said that was when ranger Lucinda Gibson found a wet feather in the spinifex.
"She went round to look at that [feather] and she found that burrow [in the grass]," she said.
"That spinifex is a bit grey but she saw little bit of colours on it like yellow and green.
"That's when she noticed that night parrot was in the burrow."
Ms Gibson whistled and gave a hand signal of a flapping bird to Ms Njamme and the rest of the searchers.
Adult night parrots typically sport a coat of green and yellow feathers with black highlights.
But the rangers could see the juvenile bird still had a lot of grey and soft wispy feathers, which helped it blend into the grey interior of the spinifex lump.
Ms Njamme said the parrot may have been perched high in the spinifex because of the damp ground from the rain.
"It was a bit wet on the bottom, that's why he had to move up."
Ngururrpa Indigenous Protected Area coordinator Christy Davies said the parrot was quiet and looked like it was close to the fledgling stage, when a bird learns to fly.
"A lot of young birds and baby birds … unless they're being fed by the parents, they just sit still and don't make a sound," she said.
"So that's what it was doing, just sitting there, not making a sound and relying on its camouflage to protect it."
Turbocharging the search for night parrots
While the moment of finding a juvenile night parrot may seem fortuitous, there is also deep knowledge behind knowing where to look.
By combining what is known about night parrot preferences with cultural knowledge, Ngururrpa Rangers have built a model for finding likely habitat in their region.
The habitat model was developed in a research partnership with the National Environmental Science Program and the Indigenous Desert Alliance.
"A lot of [rangers] have identified areas of likely habitat because they know where that lanu lanu is," Ms Davies said.
"They know where the water sources are and the seasonality of those water sources and where different plants are that form a component of the [parrot] feeding habitats.
"So it's understanding where those different components are that the night parrots need that helps us hone in on particular areas."
Knowing more about where the parrot lives and how many there are will help with conservation efforts to make sure it does not go extinct from threats like feral cats and unmanaged fire.
Rangers are also hoping to use and develop new tools to find the hidden parrots.
An AI tool is being developed to analyse thousands of hours of desert recordings to find likely night parrot calls.
And an environmental DNA (eDNA)analysis technique is in the fine-tuning stage for helping detect if a night parrot has recently used a water source.
Ms Njamme said the eDNA tool could potentially be used by other groups around the country to find and help night parrots.
"We don't see much night parrot, [but] we're trying to look after them."

Mohammad Sio
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted Wednesday to bar the United Arab List party, or Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, from running in the Oct. 27 Knesset election.
The committee approved Ra’am’s disqualification by 18 votes to five, accepting petitions that alleged “the party rejects Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, incites racism and expresses support for an armed struggle against the country or actions of a terror organization against Israel.”
Earlier Wednesday, the committee also voted 19-5, with two abstentions, to disqualify Knesset member Ofer Cassif from running as part of the Joint List on grounds that he allegedly “denied Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state.”
The panel also voted to disqualify Balad party chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh “on the grounds that he supported an armed struggle or actions of a terror organization against Israel.” Israeli media reported that the decision secured a large majority within the committee.
Under Israeli election law, the disqualification of an individual candidate requires Supreme Court approval before taking effect, while decisions barring electoral lists can be appealed to the court.
The petitions were filed by Israeli parties and organizations, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud.
The Supreme Court is expected to review the disqualification decisions ahead of the election.  
There was no immediate comment from Ra’am on the committee’s decision.
Ra’am won five seats in Israel’s 2022 parliamentary election. Polls indicate the possibility of it securing the same number -- or slightly more -- in the upcoming election.
Around 21% of Israel’s population is Palestinian Arab.
The Oct. 27 election is being contested by 38 lists, with parties required to cross the electoral threshold to enter the 120-seat Knesset.
A government must command the support of at least 61 lawmakers in the 120-member parliament.
The disqualification decisions come amid heightened political debate over the role of Arab parties and candidates in Israel’s electoral system ahead of the vote.

‘Journalism must be independent’ to remain relevant – Bangladeshi editor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:58:26 UTC
03:58:26 KST

‘Journalism must be independent’ to remain relevant – Bangladeshi editor
Journalism must remain “independent of political power” and offer audiences verification, context and accountability as social media increasingly competes with traditional news, Bangladeshi journalist and editor Khairul Alam has told RT.
Alam, editor of DBARTA24 and former General Secretary of the Dhaka Union of Journalists (DUJ), spoke to RT on Wednesday on the sidelines of the International Forum ‘Dialogue about Fakes 4.0’ in Moscow.
“Rebuilding public trust begins with one simple principle: journalism must be independent of political power,” he said.
According to Alam, media outlets can restore confidence through transparent sourcing, fact-checking, openly correcting mistakes and giving different sides an opportunity to respond. They must also protect reporters from political retaliation and separate journalism from “political activism,” he added.
Alam pointed to Bangladesh’s 2024 political unrest as an example of how social media can both provide information quickly and amplify false or misleading claims.
“The same platforms can spread misinformation, manipulated videos, old footage presented as new, misleading headlines and politically motivated narratives at extraordinary speed,” he said.
The problem becomes more acute when confidence in traditional media declines, Alam argued, pointing to political pressure and legal cases against journalists in Bangladesh.
The 2024 protests began over civil service job quotas before developing into a broader anti-government uprising that led to the ouster of then-Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. The UN has estimated that as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest. Hasina has since alleged that the US orchestrated her removal after Dhaka refused to allow an American military base on Saint Martin Island.
UN experts raised concerns in 2025 that more than 140 journalists had been charged with murder following the protests. The Committee to Protect Journalists has also documented arrests, criminal cases and other pressure against media workers in the country.
Alam argued that journalists should not face pressure or punishment over their perceived political affiliations, regardless of who is in power.
“Journalism should not become a reward for supporting whoever is currently in power, nor should it become a punishment for having worked under a previous government,” he said.
At the same time, Alam stressed that social media itself is “not the enemy of journalism” and can serve as an important tool for reporters.
Professional media, he said, must instead distinguish itself by providing what social platforms often cannot: “verification, context, responsibility and independence.”

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has stated that Washington would attempt to broker an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, but noted that this is a complex task because both sides have identified energy as a strategic target of their military operations.
Rubio said at a briefing on Wednesday that when it comes to energy from the Russian perspective, the energy-related strikes they face target oil refineries and their oil and gas industry. For the Ukrainian side, energy means its power grid and the approach of winter, with the fear of losing electricity supplies. So, when it comes to energy, it means two different things to different people. Complicating matters further is the fact that energy strikes are central to the tactical actions carried out by both sides.
He noted that Ukrainians strike Russian targets, damaging their energy sector—a key source of revenue. The Russian side, in turn, damages the Ukrainian side by striking its power grid, especially ahead of winter, he said. Thus, the problem lies in the fact that both sides have identified energy as a strategic target of their military operations.
However, according to Rubio, this has global implications regarding oil and gas, as well as a very real and immediate impact on life in Ukraine, especially given these threats.
Nevertheless, Rubio expressed the view that the effort is worth making—it would be beneficial for the world and for both countries alike.

The White House press pool: What is it and how does it work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:57:50 UTC
03:57:50 KST

The White House press pool: What is it and how does it work?
White House banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, after US President Donald Trump complained about coverage.
US President Donald Trump last week announced he would ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House amid coverage that Trump said was unfavourable.
Reporters for the three outlets reported to work over the weekend only to find that their access had been revoked. By Monday, the three organisations had sued the administration, amid allegations the White House violated their First Amendment rights.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4A ‘ban on the free press’: White House bars journalists from three outlets
- list 2 of 4CNN, Politico, MS NOW sue Trump administration over White House ban
- list 3 of 4Rubio defends Trump’s White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico
- list 4 of 4Trump follows in Hugo Chavez’s footsteps to launch his own TV channel
Free speech advocates criticised the White House for yanking their credentials.
“It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the People’s House for criticizing the government. It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move,” Seth Stern, director of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement.
“The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him. The press keeps exposing his corruption and his failures. These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public.”
The White House has nevertheless defended the decision, with US Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also supporting the administration’s position.
On Monday, Bryan Boughton, Fox News’s Washington bureau chief and the chair of the rotating TV pool, announced in a memo that the television networks that participate in the pool would suspend presidential pool coverage following CNN’s removal from its scheduled pool duties, according to reporting from Politico.
What is the pool?
The White House press pool is a group of reporters who follow the president in smaller settings when space restrictions prevent the broader press corps from being on location.
Pool reporters share their reporting with other journalists and news organisations. It provides them with raw newsgathering material, including transcripts of news briefings and information about the president’s, and often his staff’s, whereabouts.
Essentially, wherever the president goes, a small group of reporters is there to document what happens and relay that information to the rest of the White House press corps to use as they see fit for their reporting.
Pool coverage is not intended to be editorialised. It serves as a shared newsgathering resource, allowing other news organisations to report on events they could not directly attend.
Often, the details are fairly mundane, such as what time the president’s motorcade leaves the White House or when he arrives at an event, what time Air Force One lands and takes off, and the remarks the president made before boarding.
For television networks, the pool also provides video and audio feeds that other news organisations can use at their discretion.
The system exists in part because of physical limitations, as Air Force One has limited space for members of the press. There are only 13 seats for reporters on the president’s plane.
Each day, different news organisations are assigned pool duties. The television pool rotates among five networks. Those are ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC. Other parts of the pool include print, radio and new media organisations.
How will this impact other outlets?
Subscribers to pooled coverage include smaller television station groups, streaming networks and international news organisations that may not have their own crews with the president.
That also includes organisations such as C-SPAN and other outlets that rely on pooled video and audio to cover presidential events.
The effect was immediately visible Monday during an event at the White House. The president’s remarks were difficult to hear because there was no TV pool crew providing the usual audio feed.
The memo obtained by Politico said the TV pool would continue providing coverage for other parts of government, including Congress.
How has the pool historically been used?
The pool has been at the helm of coverage of some of the biggest events in recent US history.
On September 11, 2001, pool reporters were with President George W Bush during his visit to an elementary school in Sarasota, Florida, when he was informed about the attacks in New York, and they documented his reaction.
Decades earlier, in 1981, pool reporters were present for the assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan by John Hinckley Jr.
A little less than a decade earlier, the pool also accompanied President Richard Nixon on his historic 1972 visit to China, and in 1963 pool reporters were travelling with President John F Kennedy’s motorcade in Dallas, Texas when he was assassinated.
In 1945, three wire-service reporters who were part of the pool travelled with President Franklin D Roosevelt by train to Georgia and were with him when he passed away there.
