How the U.K. Is Supporting Saudi Arabia In Its Fight Against the Houthis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:57:04 UTC
03:57:04 KST

Saudi Arabia will have assistance from a key Western ally in its fight against Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, as Britain is providing military support to the Kingdom in a bid to help restore stability in the region and ease pressures on the global energy supply.
“We’re working with our friends to try and deliver that de-escalation,” British Defense Minister Luke Pollard said in an interview Tuesday. The “purely defensive” deployment of an RAF Voyager to Saudi Arabia is intended to “ensure there’s no further escalation in the Red Sea, which could further risk our fuel prices,” he added.
The international assistance comes following weeks of fighting between the Saudi-backed government of Yemen and the Houthis, which shattered a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war. The Houthi rebels have made significant advances along the Red Sea coastline as they seek to tighten their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb, a critical maritime chokepoint that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal. With global energy supplies already under strain due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war, the strangling of another trade route could further impact oil and fuel prices.
“Much of our trade, both in goods and in energy, comes through that part of the world. What happens in that part of the Middle East is absolutely vital for our own national security and our own economic security,” Pollard said, explaining why Britain responded to the Kingdom’s request for help.
When talking to reporters en route to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, ahead of his sit-down with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham also cited the cost of living “pressures” at home as a key reason for the support and said he was “acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region.”
Burnham emphasized that it’s a “time-limited agreement in terms of the assistance that we will provide, but we will keep it under review.”
The support extended to Saudi Arabia marks Burnham’s first military deployment since he became Prime Minister in July. However, it’s far from the first time the U.K. has offered assistance to Saudi Arabia, as the two nations share a close military alliance.
How exactly will the U.K. be supporting Saudi Arabia?
The Ministry of Defense on Tuesday confirmed it had agreed to “provide an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft to support Saudi defensive activity” in the region. According to the British Royal Air Force (RAF), a Voyager provides strategic air support by allowing jets and other aircraft to refuel while in flight.
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in defense studies at King's College London, says the Voyager “basically allows the Saudi Air Force to stay in the air over Yemen for longer without having to fly a single sortie and then returning to base.”
“It increases the operational tempo in terms of targeting strikes and being more flexible, and more agile in responding to changing situations on the ground,” he tells TIME.
According to Pollard, the Voyager is set to operate from the British RAF base in Cyprus, which was targeted by Iran earlier this year, and will support the British-built Typhoon jets used by Saudi Arabia. “That will help them with their defensive actions against the Houthis, who have been attacking not just the capital of Saudi Arabia in Riyadh, but also the Republic of Yemen as well,” he said.
Britain has historically held the role of “guarantor for maritime freedom of navigation all around the world,” says Krieg, describing the U.K.’s latest attempt to ease tensions over the Red Sea as an example of the government “stepping up to the plate.”
“We're not just helping a partner in the region,” he adds. “We're also helping ourselves, because the Houthis having the Bab al-Mandeb is not something that the U.K. can tolerate.”
Krieg says the move signifies a small success for Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states as they seek to strengthen bilateral security relationships beyond their traditional reliance on the U.S. This is “the worst security situation the Saudis have been in [for] a very long time,” he notes.
“Gulf states are trying to supplement the existing U.S. capabilities with all kinds of [other] agreements, like the Mecca pact,” he says, referencing a trilateral defense security pact made between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey in August. “The U.K. wants to be seen as being active and being there when a friend is in need.”
The long-standing alliance between the U.K. and Saudi Arabia
The U.K. and Saudi Arabia share an alliance that dates back to almost a century ago.
“It's a very long, strategic partnership,” says Krieg. “It goes back to the early days of the current Kingdom, where Britain, at the time, was still the only superpower in the world, and was controlling the waterways and a lot of the territories in Arabia, including in South Yemen.”
Britain was among the first governments to recognize the independent territories of Saudi Arabia through the Treaty of Jeddah in 1927, which helped solidify the boundaries of the nascent kingdom ahead of the formation of modern Saudi Arabia in 1932.
Decades later, the U.K. supported the Saudi-led military coalition in its campaign against the Houthis from 2015 until the 2022 truce.
According to the Campaign Against Arms Trade (CAAT), the published value of U.K. arms export licenses to Saudi Arabia from the start of the bombing campaign in March 2015 through the April 2022 truce was £7.1 billion ($9.4 billion).
“The two main Western backers of the Saudi Kingdom are the Americans and the British,” says David Wearing, an assistant professor in international relations at the University of Sussex. “From the British and the American point of view, the Middle East is strategically important because it's a huge source of global energy suppliers, oil, and gas.”
In late 2023, the Houthis started disrupted shipping in the Red Sea, targeting cargo ships they said were linked to Israel, in what they described as a show of support for Palestinians in Gaza. Amid concerns over the impact on the world economy, the U.S. and U.K. joined forces in January 2024, striking multiple Houthi targets in Yemen. In April 2025, the U.K. government participated in another joint operation with the U.S. against a Houthi military facility in Yemen.
In March of this year, the U.K. deployed a Sky Sabre, the army’s medium range air defense missile system, to Saudi Arabia to defend the Kingdom against Iranian missile and drone attacks.
The U.K. government's Strategic Export Controls Annual Report of 2025 described the military relationship with Saudi Arabia as a “longstanding” partnership providing “Typhoon, Tornado, and Hawk aircraft, mine countermeasure vessels, and associated munitions, infrastructure, logistics and manpower support packages.”
BAE Systems—a major British defense, aerospace, and security company—said in its own 2025 report that Saudi Arabia was its largest customer by sales in its air business.
How are Saudi Arabia’s other allies responding to the Houthis' advances?
Saudi Arabia has reportedly sought assistance from allies to stave off Houthi advances. France, Pakistan, and Egypt issued strong statements condemning the Houthi attacks, but have not publicly announced new military support for the Kingdom.
Trump is understood to have received requests from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to strike the Houthi rebels. According to the New York Times, Trump reportedly considered launching strikes against the Houthis over the weekend, before ultimately deciding against it. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Asked Tuesday why Washington has held back from striking the Houthis, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it’s “a very dangerous and complex” conflict.
“If it comes down to it, the United States will always stand with Saudi Arabia and support them because we have an agreement with them to do so,” he said, referencing the U.S. economic and defense partnership with Saudi Arabia signed last November, that deepened co-operation between the two countries.
Fears mount over global energy supply as Houthis advance
Global energy supplies have been under increasing strain since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28, as Tehran has leveraged its chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of global oil production flowed prior to the conflict.
In the past few weeks, the Houthis have captured Yemen’s port city of Mokha and the strategic Perim Island, which sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. If the Houthis were to assume control of the strait, shipping companies could be forced to travel via South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope—a longer, costlier route.
The volume of crude oil and petroleum liquids moving through the Bab el-Mandeb increased earlier this year, with the route being used as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. The shipments surged from 5.6 million barrels per day in the first quarter of 2026 to 8.1 million per day in the second quarter, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).
However, recent crossings have been marred by uncertainty over the potential threat posed by the Houthis. Data shared with TIME by Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm, showed an estimated 34 vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb on Sept. 15, a drop from the estimated 53 crossings recorded on July 15th.
A spokesperson for the Houthis on Sept. 11 insisted the waterway will remain free to roam “with the exception of Saudi ships.” Yet concerns among global leaders and shipping companies remain.
Burnham and other U.K. officials have framed Britain’s defensive support partly around the potential economic consequences at home. The average price of petrol rose by 9.1 pence per litre between July and August 2026, compared with a rise of 0.3 pence per litre between July and August 2025, according to data from the Office of National Statistics.
Wearing says that because oil is traded on a global market, supply disruptions in one region can push up benchmark prices worldwide, with those costs cascading through the broader economy.
“What Americans call gas and what we call petrol, if that goes up, think how many goods to market are taken by heavy lorries on petrol. It can push up the price of everything: shipping, road transit, energy, all kinds of industrial production and many consumer products,” he says. “Oil is the lifeblood of the world economy, the longer you restrict the supply, the higher the price goes, the more inflationary pressure there is on everything, and that affects Britain, but it affects the whole system. It's like a heart attack in a human body, suddenly it's not being pumped round."

US drafted memo condemning UK over West Bank sanctions. It was never released
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

US drafted a memo condemning UK over West Bank sanctions. It was never released
WASHINGTON/JERUSALEM, Sept 23 - In early September, US officials in Jerusalem and Washington prepared a draft statement attributed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemning plans by the UK, France and Canada to block imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The September 8 dated document, previously unreported and which two sources said was driven by David Milstein, an influential aide to US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, proposed that Rubio describe the countries' actions as a series of hostile measures against Israel that contribute to antisemitism.
"These tactics unacceptably draw from the playbook of the antisemitic boycotts, divestments and sanctions movement," the draft document, reviewed by Reuters, said.
The statement was never released.
According to three people familiar with the matter, the statement was not supported by the White House and the State Department's senior leadership.
The people spoke on condition of anonymity.
Instead, speaking to reporters on September 8 in Florida before traveling to Latin America, Rubio refrained from outright criticism of the decision or any particular country.
"Obviously, we’re not going to do what the UK did. We saw their announcement today, but I don’t have any comment on it right now," Rubio said.
The episode illustrates a widening divide between the White House and Trump's senior diplomats in Israel about how best to respond to the expansion of Israeli settlements under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government.
It also highlights a growing ideological split within the American right over support for Israel, with polling showing younger Republicans holding an increasingly unfavorable opinion of Washington's closest Middle East ally.
President Donald Trump earlier this year expressed his opposition to settlement expansion, a growing source of friction with Israel's Arab neighbors, but his administration has put little pressure on Israel to change its policy.
That has at times put him at odds with Huckabee, a Baptist minister who is a staunch supporter of settlements and who refers to the West Bank by its biblical name, Judea and Samaria, a term used by the Israeli government but not formally adopted by the US.
Huckabee's aide Milstein last year advocated that the US impose sanctions on the entire International Criminal Court to convince it to drop war crimes charges against Israeli leaders over the Gaza war - a measure the Trump administration has yet to deploy.
In response to questions from Reuters, a senior US official said the draft statement was not prepared in consultation with the State Department or White House.
The US embassy referred questions, including requests for comment from Huckabee and Milstein, to the State Department.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
US PUBLIC SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL QUESTIONED
US public backing for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017.
While large majorities of Republicans aged 50 and older view Israel positively, younger conservative Americans have grown more critical, a Pew Research Center poll from late March showed. Some 57% of Republicans aged 18-49 have an unfavorable opinion of Israel, up from 50% a year previously.
In December last year, Trump said that he and Netanyahu, whose government has overseen a rapid expansion of settlements, did not fully agree on the West Bank following a meeting with the Israeli leader. That September, Trump said he would not allow Israel to annex the territory.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since the 1967 Arab-Israeli War. The United Nations and most countries consider settlements to be illegal under international law governing military occupation. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
Violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the territory has risen sharply this year, some of them emboldened by support from Netanyahu's right-wing government, which includes ministers who are themselves settlers.
Huckabee has publicly condemned the violence and called for perpetrators to be prosecuted. He has also said violent settlers were a minority and do not represent the wider settler community.
Some 500,000 Israeli settlers and 3 million Palestinians live in the West Bank, territory Palestinians have long sought for a future state, along with Gaza and East Jerusalem. REUTERS

Save the Children officially warned by regulator over staff put at risk in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:55:10 UTC
03:55:10 KST

The international aid charity Save the Children has been issued with an official regulatory warning over management failures and misconduct that put staff at its Yemen office at serious risk.
The warning concluded a two-year investigation by the Charity Commission for England and Wales into the running of the office after the death of its safety and security director, Hisham Al-Hakimi, in October 2023 after he was detained by the Yemeni authorities.
The commission said weak governance meant staff at the Yemen office were not properly safeguarded in response to what it called a “live security concern”, and incidents of poor conduct by staff were not addressed.
The warning letter refers to “substantial policy breaches and a lack of accountability” at the office, and said local charity bosses failed to adequately assess and escalate complaints and reports made by whistleblowers.
An internal Save the Children investigation in 2024 after the death of Al-Hakimi found a “negative working culture” in the Yemen office had left staff “disillusioned and marginalised”.
It apologised to staff after admitting it had let them down by failing to properly appreciate the risks facing them amid the deteriorating security situation in the country.
In a statement to the Guardian, Save the Children International said that since 2024 it had made significant changes under new leadership in Yemen to strengthen oversight, improve support for staff and rebuild trust. The charity has closed its north Yemen office because of security concerns.
It said despite its best efforts to understand the circumstances around Al-Hakimi’s detention and his death the challenges in Yemen meant it may never know what happened and why. Another Save the Children member of staff is understood to currently be in detention.
The commission’s warning comes amid a growing humanitarian crisis in Yemen, where the charity has been providing emergency medical help, shelter and drinking water to displaced families.
Official warnings are relatively rare, and are issued when the commission decides breaches of trust or mismanagement in a charity put its staff or beneficiaries at risk. They can be issued where charity trustees are deemed to have acted recklessly or without proper care.
The commission ordered Save the Children International to ensure sufficient resources are in place to safeguard and protect staff and other individuals working with the charity.
Stephen Roake, assistant director for high-risk compliance at the commission, said: “It can be incredibly difficult for charities operating in high-risk, volatile environments and we know that circumstances can change rapidly. However, it is for this very reason that trustees must ensure they have sufficient oversight of their overseas operations.”
In a statement, Save the Children International said it had accepted the commission’s findings of serious shortcomings in governance, management, oversight and compliance with policies and procedures in the Yemen office at the time.
Since 2024, it had installed new leadership in Yemen to strengthen oversight, improve staff support and rebuild trust. It had also introduced detention risk assessments, taken steps to improve incident management procedures and strengthened crisis management.
It said: “We remain committed to learning from this tragedy and ensuring a safe, supportive environment for our colleagues.
“We will continue to work closely with the Charity Commission to address any outstanding matters, while continuing to support our colleagues in Yemen and deliver for children in extremely challenging contexts.”
Save the Children’s Yemen office warned last week that the country faced a “catastrophic humanitarian situation” as a result of escalating conflict, collapsing health services and outbreaks of disease.
More than 1,000 people have been killed or wounded, and tens of thousands displaced by fighting in recent weeks between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces.

EU extends Russia sanctions for three years, lifts restrictions on billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:53:57 UTC
03:53:57 KST

The Council of the European Union has agreed to extend sanctions against Russian individuals and entities for another three years, according to a council statement issued on Sept. 22. As part of the agreement, Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman were removed from the sanctions list.
The remaining restrictions were extended for three years, through Sept. 22, 2029. The existing measures cover more than 3,000 individuals and entities that Brussels says are linked to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The document separately notes that the council “decided not to renew the listings of three individuals and one entity.” The council statement did not name those delisted, but their identities appear in a document published in the EU’s Official Journal. They are:
- Alisher Usmanov, founder of USM Holdings;
- Mikhail Fridman, co-founder of Alfa Group;
- Andrei Falaleev, former rector of Vernadsky Crimean Federal University;
- and Redbird Corporate Services Ltd, a company linked to a vessel belonging to Russia’s “shadow fleet,” the network of ships used to transport Russian oil and other cargo while evading Western sanctions and a price cap designed to limit the Kremlin’s revenue amid the ongoing war.
Multiple media outlets and international news agencies had previously reported that EU countries were discussing the removal of the 62-year-old Fridman and 73-year-old Usmanov from the sanctions list, with reports appearing in The Guardian, Euronews, and Reuters. France and Slovakia had sought Usmanov’s removal, according to the Financial Times, while Luxembourg supported lifting sanctions on Fridman. Latvia was among the countries that opposed the moves.
A spokesperson for Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the EU Council, told The Guardian that the decision was the result of a “difficult compromise” — one that saw the above-mentioned figures removed from the list in exchange for a procedural switch that will significantly extend the time between renewals of the larger sanctions regime:
“Until now, these listings have been reviewed and assessed on a six-monthly basis; today’s decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework.”
Uzbekistan-born Usmanov, who according to Forbes has a net worth of $14 billion (placing him 224th on its list of global billionaires as of Sept. 23), amassed his wealth in the mining, industry, telecoms, and media sectors. He was sanctioned by both the EU and the U.S., as well as Canada, the UK, and multiple other countries in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In its sanctions announcement, the EU described Usmanov as having “particularly close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin” and referred to him as “one of Vladimir Putin’s favorite oligarchs.” Usmanov has denied any association with Putin.
A number of court cases involving Usmanov in Germany have seen the oligarch get the upper hand, with a court in Hamburg upholding a libel lawsuit filed by the billionaire against the newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) this past January. Prosecutors in Munich dropped an investigation into suspected sanctions violations by Usmanov after he made a sizeable charitable payment in 2025, while the Frankfurt am Main public prosecutor’s office closed a separate money laundering investigation into the billionaire in November 2024 after he paid a fine of €4 million.
The Ukraine-born Fridman, co-founder of Alfa Bank, Russia’s largest privately owned bank, has an estimated net worth of $16.6 billion, according to Forbes, which puts him 175th on in its list of global billionaires. Fridman, who also holds Israeli citizenship, was first sanctioned by the European Union on Feb. 28, 2022, four days after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. He was added to the same sanctions list as Usmanov. The UK followed on March 15, 2022, while the United States designated him on Aug. 11, 2023.
After the invasion, Fridman stepped down from his Luxembourg-based holding company LetterOne and also reduced his stake. British authorities have frozen his London properties, including the Athlone House estate, valued at around $100 million.
Fridman founded commodities trader Alfa-Eco in 1989 with entrepreneurs German Khan and Alexei Kuzmichev. The group later formed oil venture TNK-BP by uniting with British energy giant BP in 2003 before selling its stake in 2013 in a deal that brought Fridman about $5.1 billion in cash. Ukraine opened a criminal case against Fridman in August 2023 over alleged fraud linked to Alfa Bank Ukraine and placed him on an international wanted list that December.

Bachelor star Matty J backs mental health screening of new dads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:53:44 UTC
03:53:44 KST

Fathers could receive perinatal mental health screening under new proposal
In short:
Fathers would receive perinatal mental health screening alongside their partners, under one proposal to be canvassed by a parliamentary inquiry.
One in 10 fathers experience postnatal depression, with research indicating that when fathers are better supported, so too are mothers.
What's next?
Fathers and advocates are being encouraged to share their experiences with a Senate inquiry examining postpartum health care.
Reality TV helped Matthew Johnson find love, but then fatherhood brought a plot twist of its own.
The former Bachelor contestant-turned podcast host and father of three, commonly known as Matty J, said one of the most isolating times in his life was when he first became a dad.
"It was this weird juxtaposition of having an amazing partner, having children — something that I'd always dreamed about — but at the same time feeling incredibly lonely and not knowing where to turn to for support," he said.
Johnson, who was recently named Australian father of the year by The Fathering Project, said he found it particularly difficult to find a community of other dads and would often be the only man in the parent group.
"First and foremost, the resources that are currently in place should be tailored initially to mums, but there needs to be more support for dads, who sometimes don't know where to turn," he said.
He said some friends had suffered in silence with postnatal depression, not knowing it was something that could also affect men.
"It is easy for dads to fall to the wayside."
That could be addressed under one proposal to be canvassed by a parliamentary inquiry. It would see fathers screened for perinatal distress or depression alongside their partners and receive follow-up support if needed.
The federal government has established a Senate committee examining postpartum health care in Australia, looking at a range of issues such as mental health, infant feeding, fertility and birth injury.
Many pregnant women are routinely offered mental health screening as part of their care, which helps identify those who may need more support.
But Nicole Highet, executive director of the Centre of Perinatal Excellence (COPE), said only about 2 per cent of men were also being screened.
"We know that the rates of mental health and distress and stressors that fathers face is growing with different pressures, those with mental health backgrounds, those with past trauma or abuse," she said.
"These factors make some dads particularly vulnerable."
COPE's submission to the inquiry will call for more Commonwealth funding to expand screening and follow-up support to more fathers.
Currently men do not always attend perinatal appointments, and follow-up care is difficult to arrange because they are not considered patients.
Dr Highet said if men could be screened at the same time as their partner, health professionals or support services could then review the results and follow up with anyone identified as needing additional help.
She also called for governments and organisations to "think outside the box" by screening dads in workplaces or fathers groups.
"We have the technology available right here and right now to screen fathers but the way that we're doing it in these systems where fathers are not frequenting is preventing them from being offered screening," she said.
Even for mothers, the Commonwealth-funded screening program is currently restricted to public hospitals and family health settings. Dr Highet said it should be expanded to include everybody.
'Imagine the difference'
While there is less research on paternal perinatal mental health compared to maternal data, it is estimated up to one in 10 dads experience postnatal depression or anxiety.
Assistant Social Services Minister Ged Kearney said while she did not want to pre-empt the outcomes of the Senate inquiry, she was looking forward to hearing more about COPE's proposal.
"If we really do care about good outcomes for women and their bubs, then we have to engage dads," she said.
While the inquiry will centre around women's experiences, Ms Kearney said research indicated that when fathers were engaged and supported, mothers experienced better maternal and mental health outcomes.
Research also suggests women are at a greater risk of experiencing violence from an intimate partner during pregnancy and in the postpartum period.
"If we can intervene early and make sure that things like that are picked up and sorted, then imagine the difference that could make for a family unit," she said.
Ms Kearney called for fathers, experts and advocates to share their experiences with the inquiry.
"They will engage if we give them the resources and the services to help them. So let's talk to dads about what that would look like," she said.

More Australians than ever lodging workplace sexual harassment complaints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:53:05 UTC
03:53:05 KST

Human rights commission dealing with record sexual harassment complaints
In short:
Figures reveal a record number of Australians are making workplace sexual harassment complaints, but many are waiting months for cases to be investigated.
The rise is likely due to recent legal reforms and greater awareness of workplace rights, rather than an increase in workplace sexual harassment.
What's next?
There is concern the system cannot keep up with the rise in demand, and more money and expertise are needed to handle cases effectively.
More Australians than ever are lodging workplace sexual harassment complaints.
But behind that rise sits an increasingly urgent challenge: adapting the system so it can respond quickly enough to make a difference.
In 2024, at the age of 19, Heather* thought she had secured her dream career after landing an electrical apprenticeship with a small business in New South Wales.
"I was really thinking about the future and trying to set myself up to buy a house," Heather said.
"I felt it was a stable job that would see me through my life."
But those plans were derailed after Heather said she was sexually harassed by her boss, who she alleged made unwelcome advances, while working away.
Traumatised, she quit the apprenticeship the next day.
Supported by the Electrical Trades Union (ETU), Heather lodged a formal complaint with the Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC).
It took 14 months for her complaint to be formally accepted for investigation and she was only recently assigned a case manager.
"I feel really trapped in the situation,"
"You feel helpless, like it's never going to happen."
Unable to return to an electrical trade, Heather lost nine months of work before eventually finding a new apprenticeship operating heavy machinery.
Her mother, Melissa Unwin, said the lengthy wait has made it difficult for her daughter to move forward, describing the uncertainty as corrosive and damaging to morale.
"You can't see the end in sight," she said.
"I was 100 per cent blindsided. I trusted this guy with my daughter."
Heather's claims are yet to be tested by the commission and are contested by the owner of the business.
System under pressure
The AHRC remains the preferred avenue for many serious workplace sexual harassment complaints, despite lengthy delays there and alternative pathways through state anti-discrimination bodies and the Fair Work Commission.
Employment lawyer Lisa Berton said complainants tolerated longer wait times because the federal system provided access to broader claims, stronger enforcement powers and potentially uncapped compensation.
"If I was acting for an applicant, I would still select the AHRC, even with the delays," she said.
New figures obtained by the ABC show the AHRC received a record 759 complaints under the Sex Discrimination Act last financial year — up 21 per cent on the previous year and 51 per cent over five years.
Of the 460 sexual harassment complaints received in that period, 95 per cent were related to employment.
Complainants waited an average of nearly seven months just to be allocated a case officer.
While the commission had a target to finalise 85 per cent of complaints within 12 months, the latest figures show 49 per cent of workplace sexual harassment matters took longer than a year to resolve.
Data obtained by the ABC also revealed significant differences between jurisdictions.
In Victoria, workplace sexual harassment complaints were typically processed within one to two weeks and resolved in about two months.
By contrast, Queensland reported an average wait of 246 days for allocation and 424 days to finalisation, while in South Australia, complaints were generally allocated within a week.
NSW reported comparatively short delays, with just 84 complaints awaiting allocation and 98 per cent resolved within a year.
The Fair Work Commission received 183 workplace sexual harassment applications in 2024-25.
Monash University discrimination law professor Dominique Allen said the rise in complaints could reflect greater awareness of workplace rights and confidence in reporting, rather than an increase in workplace sexual harassment.
However, Professor Allen said the figures suggested complaint demand was growing faster than the system's capacity to process cases.
"We need more money and expertise put into this so that these claims can be handled more effectively," she said.
The federal government said it had invested $49.8 million in the AHRC since 2022 and would examine the system as part of the upcoming Respect@Work review.
The ETU argued the delays pointed to a deeper problem than growing demand.
The union's NSW/ACT state secretary Allen Hicks said stronger workplace protections only worked if the agencies responsible for enforcing them had enough resources.
"You can have the best laws in the world and if you don't resource the regulatory bodies … then the laws are meaningless," he said.
Unions warn workers walking away
Mr Hicks said the union currently had six members who have been waiting over a year for their AHRC cases to be picked up.
"Young 16 and 17-year-old apprentices who have the courage to stand up and make a formal complaint are put in limbo," Mr Hicks said.
"In construction, witnesses move across six or seven different job sites over 18 months, making it extremely difficult to keep cases together."
Mr Hicks said complaint discontinuance rates at the commission have jumped from 40 per cent to 58 per cent, and a national audit report released in 2025 pointed to delays directly driving workers to give up on their claims.
He said delays threatened broader workforce targets as Australia seeks to add 40,000 more electricians by 2030.
"Stories like this set back female participation by years," he said.
*Heather has been identified by her first name only because of the sensitive nature of the allegations and the ongoing complaints process.

Russian state officials say ruling party United Russia won 58% in last weekend’s parliamentary election. Independent analysts estimate it was really 34–35% without manipulation.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:52:14 UTC
03:52:14 KST

Russian state officials say ruling party United Russia won 58% in last weekend’s parliamentary election. Independent analysts estimate it was really 34–35% without manipulation.
Judging by the reports presented to Vladimir Putin, the recent parliamentary election must have gone very well: turnout was the highest since 2011, United Russia secured the largest State Duma faction in its history, and there were almost no irregularities. But independent analyses paint a very different picture from the one presented by the Central Election Commission: reported turnout was inflated by ballot stuffing and the authorities’ heavy use of state resources; more than half the votes recorded for United Russia appear to have been fabricated; and widespread fraud benefiting the ruling party nearly kept A Just Russia out of the State Duma, so votes had to be added to its tally at the last minute. Meduza reviewed what independent journalists and election analysts have written about the vote. The count is still underway, and experts are working with incomplete data.
- United Russia officially won 58% of the vote — more than in the prewar election of 2021. But analyses by Novaya Gazeta Europe and Important Stories suggest that without manipulation, United Russia’s share of the party-list vote may have been just 34–35%. The journalists reached these conclusions using a method developed by election analyst Sergey Shpilkin. According to Important Stories, roughly 18 million of the 30 million votes recorded for United Russia on paper ballots may have been fabricated.
Sergey Shpilkin is a physicist who began analyzing Russian election statistics in 2007. He based his work on an approach developed by American diplomat John Brady Kiesling, who was the first to study how the distribution of votes among candidates varied with turnout.
Shpilkin’s method rests on the premise that adding large numbers of votes for a single candidate simultaneously increases both that candidate’s vote share and overall turnout. In cases of fraud, data from ordinary polling stations plotted on a graph form a relatively even “cloud,” while data from anomalous stations form a “comet tail” extending toward higher turnout and a larger vote share for the leading candidate.
The method has limits. It can estimate only the scale of ballot stuffing — and only when ballot stuffing far exceeds other forms of manipulation and a substantial number of polling stations count votes honestly. The Shpilkin method does not account for cases in which one candidate is credited with another candidate’s votes or a precinct’s results are fabricated from scratch.
Leonid Volkov, who heads political projects at the Anti-Corruption Foundation, was among those who criticized the method on these grounds: “The Shpilkin method works when there is a clearly defined core of verifiably ‘honest’ polling stations, making it possible to get a good estimate of ballot stuffing and inflated vote totals at the relatively small number of ‘dishonest’ polling stations. But by 2026, the continued trend of extreme, Chechnya-style vote rigging had destroyed that core and blurred its boundaries. And the result we see [even] at polling stations where votes were counted properly can hardly be considered ‘genuine’ [because there was no competitive election campaign before the vote].”

- According to the Central Election Commission, turnout was nearly 60%. Only the 2011 parliamentary election drew higher turnout in modern Russian history, and it ended in protests. But analysts put actual turnout in the latest election at around 40%. They say the official figure was inflated by forcing public-sector employees to the polls — what expert Roman Udot described as pushing the machinery of government to its limit — as well as by ballot-box stuffing and outright fabrication of turnout figures.
- The rescue of A Just Russia has been called the election’s biggest “miracle”: the party was still below the threshold for entering the State Duma after 96% of precinct results had been processed, but had suddenly cleared it by the time 97.5% had been processed. The party’s tally jumped by 67,000 votes in a single hour. Analyst Boris Ovchinnikov believes that A Just Russia would have cleared the 5% threshold in an honest count, but that votes stolen in favor of United Russia had depressed its result. Once this became clear, votes began being added to A Just Russia’s tally instead.
- Experts and journalists did not analyze the remote electronic voting results because they cannot be verified. The system was already a “black box,” and it has since grown even more opaque. Meanwhile, the authorities sought to channel as many votes as possible through it. In Moscow, an “anomaly” left voters without paper ballots for several hours; officials blamed a technical failure. But these elections produced plenty of other “anomalies.”
- At overseas polling stations, where fraud is generally less systematic, United Russia lost in 40 of 152 countries. New People finished first in 39 of those 40. United Russia fared poorly at polling stations in hubs for anti-war Russian émigrés. Its successes came mostly in “friendly countries” — though New People also won in China. United Russia recorded its best result abroad — 79% — in the Central African Republic, where Wagner Group mercenaries remain.

Ker’Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection at the state penitentiary in Huntsville. He is the sixth person executed so far this year in Texas, with three more people scheduled over the next two months.
A jury convicted Ramey of capital murder and sentenced him to death over the shootings of Samuel Roberts, 24, Tiffani Peacock, 18, and Celso Lopez, 38, in the home they shared in the small city of Edna, about 100 miles (160km) south-west of Houston.

The US supreme court rejected a final appeal from Ramey hours before Wednesday’s execution.
Ramey’s attorneys had argued that jurors never heard about how he suffered physical abuse as a child and grew up in poverty. State prosecutors told the court the appeal was “meritless” and argued that evidence showed Ramey had “an escalating pattern of criminal behavior”.
Norman testified at Ramey’s trial nearly two years before being sentenced to death by a jury after pleading guilty to capital murder. He testified that he and Ramey shot the victims. Ramey’s attorneys blamed the shootings on Norman.
Ramey’s former girlfriend testified that she was with him when he threw two pistols into a lake after the killings, and that he told her in detail about his involvement.
Lopez was shot four times, including in the back of the head; Peacock was shot twice in the head; and Roberts was shot five times in the chest, neck and head.

Argentina president attacks UN over inaction on Falkland Islands sovereignty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:50:43 UTC
03:50:43 KST

Javier Milei has condemned the UN as he warned that Argentina would take “matters into our own hands” in its dispute with Britain over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.
In a caustic speech at the general assembly in New York, the Argentinian president criticised the UN for being ineffective when it came to the long-running tensions over the British overseas territory in the south Atlantic known in Argentina as the Malvinas.
“An organisation that set out to defend the territorial sovereignty of its members decided to look the other way regarding the situation of the Malvinas Islands,” Milei said of the UN, adding that Argentina was willing to act unilaterally over recent oil exploration near the territory.
The president criticised the Sea Lion project, a major offshore oil development located in the North Falkland Basin, describing exploitation of the territory’s resources as an “unlawful act”.
The president told the assembly that Argentina would “not remain indifferent to those who exploit resources under illegal foreign occupation”.
“Argentina is not going to sit around waiting for the UN and the international community to live up to their own mandate,” he said. “We’re going to take matters into our own hands.”
Argentina has accused the UK of flouting a 1976 UN resolution ordering both parties to desist from unilateral action on the islands. Milei’s government began sanctions proceedings this month against more than 60 companies and people linked to the oil drilling project.
The Falkland Islands government had approved the field development and production plans for the project, which is a joint venture between an Israel-based energy company and a London-listed oil and gas exploration company.
The UN does not officially recognise either British or Argentine sovereignty and maintains that the archipelago’s status remains a disputed matter that must be resolved through bilateral negotiations. It has repeatedly invited both governments to find a peaceful solution to the dispute that erupted into conflict in 1982 after an invasion by Argentinian forces.
The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentine forces. It cost the lives of 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British military personnel and 3 Falkland Islanders.
“For us, the Malvinas are a national cause,” Milei told the general assembly. The UN, he said, was a “useless organisation whose only purpose is to sustain a cast of faintly arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats”.
“That’s why the Malvinas are not merely an issue between Argentina and the United Kingdom,” he said. “They also raise a question regarding the ability of this organisation to enforce its own resolutions.”
A referendum on the political status of the archipelago was held in the Falkland Islands in 2013. On a turnout of 92%, 99.8% voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.
Milei told the UN delegates that the principle of self-determination should not apply for the Falkland Islands as “the population was implanted by the occupying power on a territory whose sovereignty is in dispute”. “We call on the United Kingdom to resume negotiations with a view to finding a peaceful solution to the sovereignty dispute as required by international law,” he said.
Last month, Donald Trump said he was reviewing the US’s neutral position on the Falklands. The issue was a topic of discussion this week in a first meeting between Trump and the UK’s prime minister, Andy Burnham.
“The clear position is: we will stand firm in the face of any threats,” Burnham said. “We will defend the right of the Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British. I just wanted the president to know directly from me, that’s the clear British position, and he very much understood what I was saying.”

A group of lawmakers in the United States Senate are seeking sanctions against facilitators of Israel’s controversial “E1” settlement programme.
The legislation introduced on Wednesday calls for punitive actions against individuals and groups that support the settlement project, which would link the Ma’ale Adumim and other illegal Israeli settlements to occupied East Jerusalem.

The plan would completely sever East Jerusalem, long seen as the capital of a future Palestinian state, from the West Bank, while effectively cleaving the overall territory in two. 19 Democrats co-sponsored the bill, which was spearheaded by Chris Coons of Delaware, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Ron Wyden of Oregon and Ruben Gallego of Arizona.

Bentley unveils first fully electric car that embraces heritage in "progressive way"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:47:22 UTC
03:47:22 KST

Bentley unveils first fully electric car that embraces heritage in "progressive way"
Car brand Bentley has revealed the Torcal, its first fully electric car. Ahead of its unveiling today, we spoke to design director Robin Page about how the car balances an electric future with the brand's heritage.
Unveiled today at a launch event in London, the Torcal is a fully electric SUV – the first fully electric vehicle by the luxury car company.
Unlike other luxury car brands – most notably Ferrari and Jaguar – Bentley has not radically overhauled the shape for its first electric vehicle.
According to Page, this was to create an electric car that was clearly modern, but also recognisable as a Bentley.
Page told Dezeen his team began talking about direction four years ago.
"That was when we asked, 'Are we doing a car dedicated to an electric language, or should we do another great Bentley with a more modern language – not directly focused on electrification?'"
"We decided that our best route would be to embrace our heritage and DNA, but in a modern, progressive way."
The Torcal has a long wheelbase with a form that evokes previous Bentleys. Page explained that this form stemmed from Bentley's design principles rather than aerodynamic concerns related to electrification.
"With electrification, what mainly drives the form's language is the aerodynamics and the package proportion – aerodynamics directly relates to range," he said.
"The laws of aerodynamics start to give you quite a moulded form and a certain tail, but we decided that aerodynamics shouldn't lead the design. What's dominated the shape is our design principles, and they are based on our DNA and heritage."
The Torcal takes stylistic cues from previous Bentleys, including a continuous bonnet line, expressed rear arches and a prominent grill.
"Outright elegance, the iconic grill, the endless bonnet line, the resting beast – they're our principles, and we've let them dominate the design rather than aerodynamics," said Page.
Although aerodynamics didn't drive the design, Page highlighted the vehicle's range of 600 kilometres.
The grill, inessential in an electric car, is still clearly expressed.
As with the overall design of the car, Bentley nodded to the past. It referenced the grill of the Continental T, but with a modern twist – it can be illuminated in a diamond pattern.
Page said the team decided it needed a grill and that closing it off would feel "like a hand over a mouth", opting for what it considers an art piece.
"[We] decided to celebrate it, to do a piece of art with light," said Paige.
At the launch, the Torcal was presented in a light, yellowy green, another modern update to the brand's heritage.
"The Bentley green is a much darker, solid green," said Page. "We wanted a colour that showed the form, something a bit lighter, this colour works pretty well."
Inside, the car has a wing-shaped dash and natural materials including timber and Merino wool. It has a modestly sized screen – for a high-end car – and numerous physical dials.
"We didn't want to go down the clinical, super modern material route, because you end up with this quite stark, cold feeling inside," said Page.
"It really captures a place you want to be, rather than something you look at and think, 'that's modern'. It needs to be something that feels fresh, but feels comfortable."
Bentley said its choice to make its first electric car an SUV will open up a new market and offer something that other luxury car brands are not doing.
"The reason we're all doing SUVs is that it's a growing market," he said. "We've had a lot of comments from customers who say they could use this Bentley every day."
When it goes on sale later this year, the Torcal will be the first Bentley to feature the brand's redesigned logo, which was revealed last year.

Al industry left to police itself as bleak warnings mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:46:11 UTC
03:46:11 KST

analysis
AI industry left to police itself, as the US, China ignore the UN and bleak warnings mount
Here's a grim question. Which poses the bigger threat to humanity: climate change or artificial intelligence?
Andrew Forrest, who is staking billions on both challenges, has an equally grim answer: "Let's just say that AI will be a lot faster. Maybe a lot less painless."
The Fortescue boss was in New York this week, a place heaving with world leaders and a foreboding sense the world is suddenly at an urgent and critical juncture on AI.
"AI may decide the best way to get rid of climate change is to get rid of humanity," Forrest told the Insiders on Background podcast during a reflective conversation from an office overlooking Manhattan.
If humans don't maintain control of an off button for AI, he said, "it may well decide to have the off button for us".
This bleak warning is not coming from someone opposed to the technology. Forrest was an early and enthusiastic champion of artificial intelligence and now has ambitious plans to invest heavily in the industry's future.
The scale and success of Fortescue's green transition at its Pilbara iron ore operations, it seems, has caught the eye of the world's biggest AI players.
"We've got data centre companies, frontier AI companies, hyper-scalers super interested because our product is green and our product gives some independence from the grid," Forrest said.
At an estimated cost of more than $10 billion, Fortescue is set to deliver more than 2 gigawatts of solar and wind power along with enough battery storage to power fully electric trucks and mining equipment across its operations.
The goal now is to repeat this exercise "many times" over to build renewable-powered, off-grid data centre hubs across Australia.
"If Nvidia wants us to consume their chips and they want to do joint ventures with us, we're going to look at it," he said. "If Anthropic, OpenAI, or any of the other great players — and there are hundreds out there; we're only mentioning a few."
Forrest, it seems, is preparing to dive into the data centre business.
Loading...
The two sides of AI
Forrest's ability to dream big about jumping on board the AI revolution while also acknowledging the technology could end us all is a perfect example of the dilemma being confronted in New York this week.
World leaders, including Anthony Albanese, are looking to AI as a saviour with the capacity to kickstart productivity, drive growth and solve all manner of health and other problems.
There's just that small issue of its potential also to wipe us out.
The joint plea at the UN this week from various middle power leaders, including Albanese, for AI to "remain under human direction, oversight and control" was entirely uncontroversial. Their call for common global safety standards was consistent with how the world might once have dealt with rapidly emerging threats.
But once again the limits of middle-power influence were realised.
AI can be added to the list of things the UN has been unable to control, including ongoing wars and trade battles.
The two big powers who really matter when it comes to AI are ignoring the rest.
China's President Xi Jinping didn't even bother attending the UN General Assembly, skipping it for a direct meeting with Donald Trump at the White House instead.
Trump did attend, using his lengthy speech to forcefully reject the calls for international controls over what he prefers to call "superintelligence".
"I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," he told his nervous fellow leaders, who sat mute through these comments.
Trump and Xi are set to discuss a new "AI dialogue" between the two big powers, with a mechanism to alert each other to incidents that affect national security. It's something, but nowhere near the clear, preventative safeguards middle powers would prefer.
Loading
Al industry left to police itself
On one level, this week's unsuccessful push to put some international controls in place is simply another example of the world we're now in, where the big powers set their own rules and do what they like.
On another level, this is a far more serious fracture, given the stakes facing humanity.
The UN's inability this week to reach any unified position, despite the alarm being raised by the tech industry itself, felt like a pivotal moment.
Albanese, for his part, remains reluctant to criticise Trump on this directly. But clearly, the US president's refusal to accept the risks of rapidly advancing AI and to do something about it is not the outcome the Australian prime minister was hoping for.
As for that grim question on the greatest threat, Trump argues fears about both climate change and AI are simply a "hoax".
The tech industry is now left to police itself.
David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or on iview.

====================================================================================================

Inside the AI machine: How the tech race binds nations into dependence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:44:33 UTC
03:44:33 KST

How artificial intelligence is reshaping global balances of power
• 中文版 | Indonesian •
This is Part 1 of a two-part series. Part 2 — The Human Impact — will be published tomorrow.
ChatGPT and Claude may be the face of AI, but behind the screens lies a complex ecosystem of chips, data, energy and humans.
Across the Asia Pacific, control over those layers is reshaping power, binding allies and rivals into intricate forms of dependence.
This is an artificial intelligence (AI) chip.*
Chips like these power the devices and platforms we use every day: from ChatGPT and Google recommendations, to parking assistance and smartphone cameras.
The most advanced ones contain hundreds of billions of transistors; microscopic switches performing trillions of calculations a second, making them some of the most complex objects ever made.
With parts only a few atoms thick, meaning "a speck of dust" can ruin hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of product, only a handful of companies can produce chips like this.
Their sudden importance has transformed niche technology manufacturing businesses into matters of foreign policy and national security.
But chips are just one piece of a larger machine, without which they are effectively useless.
AI is often portrayed through Silicon Valley and soaring valuations, but these are just the surface layers of what insiders and industry leaders like NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang have popularly described as "AI's layered cake": an international ecosystem of chips, data, energy, models and applications (or some variation of this).
Each layer is dependent on the others: models need data and compute power; computing requires chips; chips operate in data centres; and all of it requires energy.
But here’s the twist: no country controls every layer.
In fact, critical capabilities are so globally dispersed yet concentrated in only a few places, that geopolitical allies and rivals alike are often forced to depend on one another, a dynamic some say has prevented any one country from dominating AI, while also raising the cost of conflict.
Loading...
"The user interface — ChatGPT, Claude — is really just the tip of the iceberg," Robyn Klingler-Vidra, an AI political economy expert who authored a new report on key Asian players, says.
"There are so many enormously valuable layers of the tech stack, spread across 'niche superpowers' in the Asia Pacific, and companies playing with them, that AI underscores something people may not intuitively see: why governments are so concerned about deep trade and critical minerals."
As part of a wider year-long ABC project, we spoke to people across the AI landscape: from everyday users to past and present representatives of major global companies and emerging players — SK Hynix, TSMC, OpenAI, Google, 01.AI and Microsoft — with many others agreeing to speak on background.
Pieced together, their insights tell a story much more nuanced than chatbots and stock prices: a tangled system of power and dependence shaped by resources, diplomacy, and remarkable accidents — and with consequences for Australia.
Underneath the AI hood: Laying it on thin
Loading...
To understand the AI race, we first need to understand how the physical system works and what countries are competing over.
There is no universally agreed version of the so-called AI “stack” — some call it a chain, cake, or ecosystem — but for simplicity, think of it as chips, data, energy and software, with the first three being largely physical.
At the heart of the physical stack are chips, whose importance is difficult to overstate: When you prompt Google or ask AI a question, it’s chips doing the computing behind the scenes.
"Put simply, without exponential advances in AI chips, we would not have today's AI capabilities," Chris Miller, author of the 2022 book Chip War, says.
While US company NVIDIA designs many of the world’s leading AI chips, it does not manufacture them.
That work falls largely to companies such as the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes the majority of the world’s most advanced AI processors. But even TSMC cannot operate alone, and relies heavily on specialised technology and materials from other countries to manufacture them.
“Advanced chip manufacturing is not one thing: Taiwan may make the world’s most advanced AI chips, but it depends on lithography machines from the Netherlands, ultra-pure materials and chemicals from Japan, memory components from South Korea," Gregory C Allen, AI policy expert and founder of Decision Tree, says.
These companies have spent decades, out of the limelight, becoming extraordinarily specialised in different, but often complementary, parts of the chain: relationships that require enormous trust.
"We do not compete with our customers," a TSMC spokesperson says. "That trust allows us to work closely with the world's leading innovators, aligning our manufacturing roadmaps with their product designs years before production begins."
That division of labour has allowed a swathe of companies to become highly specialised, while also concentrating capabilities in a handful of places.
As AI's capabilities grew more powerful, these supply chains became increasingly political, with governments restricting access to chips and the technology needed to make them: as the US famously did in 2022 when it began restricting advanced chip exports to China, just weeks ahead of ChatGPT's public release.
"In a parallel universe where the US never imposed these export controls, China would almost certainly already be the leader," Allen says.
Those restrictions have since evolved, while new ones have spread up and down the supply chain — from Japan, to the Netherlands, to China — profoundly shaping AI's development.
In other words, the geography of today's AI race isn't simply the product of technological competition. It has, in part, been deliberately engineered: a key point we'll return to shortly.
But chips are only one part of the AI stack, meaning even if you secure access to them, they actually do very little on their own.
The power of advanced processors is only fully realised when thousands are combined with high-speed memory and networking, assembled into servers and racks, and connected together inside vast data centres, where the calculations behind our search queries, Netflix recommendations, and map directions actually take place.
Data centres have existed for decades, but the generative-AI boom has rapidly increased their scale, visibility and strategic importance.
"I imagine data centre developers were ambitious, but demand has probably outstripped even what they anticipated," says Klingler-Vidra.
"It's plausible now that data centres were being planned without anyone fully imagining just how data-hungry AI would become."
These facilities are effectively giant computers: warehouses filled with processors, networking equipment and cooling systems, working together to train and run increasingly powerful AI models.
Similar to chips, however, running data systems at scale creates another bottleneck and dependency: energy. Every task takes a sip of power, so data centres require enormous amounts of electricity, along with grid connections, land, cooling and, often, water.
Wherever data centres are built, their appetite for power is reshaping energy systems around them, a pressure countries including Singapore and the US were already confronting before the AI boom.
“China is far ahead in the scale of its electrical system and available power capacity, and computation requires enormous amounts of electricity,” says Ya-Qin Zhang, chair of AI studies at Tsinghua University and former chairman of Microsoft China, noting that China generates more than twice as much electricity as the US and over a third of the world’s supply.
In Australia, similar concerns are only starting to get louder. As data-centre development surges, experts warn the sector could require as much electricity as currently required to power millions of households within a decade.
Nonetheless, only once these systems are in place — chips, data centres and energy — do we reach the layers most people recognise as AI: models, the trained systems that generate predictions and responses, like OpenAI’s GPT, and applications, the software that people use, like ChatGPT.
Companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic operate largely at this visible layer, while depending on the broader international system.
"Partners and suppliers are central to AI progress because compute supply is not only scarce, but must be secured and managed years in advance," a spokesperson for OpenAI told the ABC, noting that the company previously relied more heavily on individual compute providers.
"We now work across a diversified ecosystem, which improves resilience and creates compute certainty, [which] directly affects whether AI can scale."
Zooming out, powerful AI depends as much on specialised chemicals and energy as on computer scientists. Where those dependencies become difficult to replace, technology intersects with economic leverage and geopolitical strategy — a reality reflected in documents like the 2025 US AI Action Plan.
A redrawn Asia Pacific: Divided by politics, united by necessity
On raw numbers alone, the AI balance of power appears fairly straightforward.
The US dominates in data centres, private investment and leading models, while China leads in electricity generation, robotics, research output and manufacturing capacity.
At face value, that suggests a familiar two-power contest; but the concentration of critical capabilities across the stack tells a different story.
We've seen that while the US might dominate in terms of software or chip design, it's Taiwan that dominates advanced-chip manufacturing.
Taiwan's role, however, depends heavily on specialised equipment, materials and chemicals from the Netherlands, Japan and South Korea.
So while the US might lead in design, a shortage of Japanese chemicals or a critical Dutch lithography component can grind the system to a halt.
This isn't theory: it's happened before, and continues to happen.
In 2019, a stoush between Japan and South Korea choked supplies of chipmaking materials; in 2022, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine disrupted half the world's neon supply, sending prices soaring.
Closer to home, Singapore and Australia may seek to become regional data hubs, but those ambitions depend on software, chips and enormous amounts of energy.
In 2019, Singapore had to pause new data centre development for a few years as demand strained limited power, land and water resources.
Development resumed in 2022 under tighter efficiency rules, the same year Singapore began importing electricity from Laos via Thailand and Malaysia.
AI power therefore doesn't simply belong to whoever has the most money or data centres: it can sit inside an obscure chemical or trade agreement that nobody notices until it disappears.
"What happens to the world if Taiwan magically disappears? Economic apocalypse. What happens to the semiconductor world if the Netherlands magically disappears? Less sudden, but still a catastrophe. What happens if you lose the US? Same thing. What happens if you lose Korea? Same thing," Allen explains.
"There are multiple essential nodes in the supply chain, much like there are multiple essential organs in your body: you need all of them."
Those dependencies can also cut across alliances. For example, South Korea, a US ally, supplies critical semiconductor technology while remaining deeply tied to China, even as Washington restricts China's access to some of the most advanced technologies.
This geography reflects a mix of deliberate policy, commercial decisions, political necessity and historical accident.
For example, observers argue that the 2022 export controls intended to limit Chinese AI development have also encouraged greater efficiency and investment in its domestic alternatives, an effect NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has described as the controls “backfiring”.
"It's a double-edged sword," Kai-Fu Lee, founder of Chinese AI firm 01.AI and former head of Google China, says. "When you don't get [top-end NVIDIA chips], you have to figure out ways to make things faster, you're forced to become more efficient."
Dynamics like these — present across the supply chain, from rare earth refining and specialised talent to sub-sea cables and proprietary data — complicate the idea of AI as a simple "race".
"China refines more than 90 per cent of the world’s rare earths: that represents a huge source of power in a system predicated on their availability," Klingler-Vidra says.
"No country controls every layer, so being extremely difficult to replace in one layer may matter more than trying to dominate the entire thing."
For smaller economies, that creates opportunities.
"Instead of trying to do everything and ending up mediocre at everything, find the things you can be world-class at and use them to get everything else you need," Allen says.
"What Australia needs is strategic relevance, and ideally, strategic indispensability, which it can achieve not by building everything itself, but by controlling something the wider system needs."
But strategic importance cuts both ways: becoming indispensable to the stack, also means inheriting the risks and costs.
Opportunities, transparency, and the price of getting it wrong
Nearly four years since ChatGPT's release, public discourse around AI remains dominated by frontier companies — from breakthrough capabilities to warnings about existential danger — with far less attention paid to the systems beneath them.
Observers point out that while some of the opacity is intentional, much of it is a consequence of how the industry evolved: companies may have legal reasons to avoid appearing dominant, while governments may fear economic retaliation from trading partners for speaking bluntly about AI.
“The self-censorship is a real challenge,” Allen says.
“Politically, economically, it's understandable; but if the public don't hear the plain truth, how are they going to know who to vote for or which policies to support?"
In July, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese declared AI a national priority. But some were quick to point out why turning that ambition into policy is much harder than simply attracting investment or building more infrastructure.
No country controls everything it needs. For Australia, the question is therefore not how to become technologically self-sufficient, but where to build strength, and which dependencies it is willing to accept.
One current AI strategy is to capture domestic value through the jobs, skills and infrastructure built to support foreign AI models, like data centres.
But some experts warn investments of this sort risk turning Australia into an "infrastructure enclave" that consumes domestic land and electricity, without guaranteeing the much-needed intellectual property or economic leverage.
They maintain that Australia already has advantages in energy, critical minerals, and industries like mining and agriculture: areas where it could apply AI to capitalise on existing strengths.
"Australia has a lot of data centres, but many are foreign-owned or funded through outside investment, which might make us strong in that layer, but won't necessarily result in the value or leverage that other areas might provide," Vikas Kumar, who authored a recent AI chain competitiveness framework, says.
"The opportunity at hand is to combine AI with sectors where Australia already has deep, in-demand knowledge, to create exportable products and services.
"For instance, if I'm going to Korea, building that relationship would be my number one motivation: securing key components, while offering applications or energy they need in return."
This approach makes AI policy as much about diplomacy as technology and private investment: trade policy, alliances, immigration and energy decisions can shift technological leverage almost as much as breakthroughs in a laboratory.
Several Chinese and American AI companies told the ABC on background they were already working towards new partnerships with major Australian industries, including mining; OpenAI also pointed to its December 2025 initiative with CommBank, Coles and Wesfarmers.
By the same token, observers were careful to point out that interdependence across the stack does not automatically equate to security, as Europe learnt from its reliance on Russian energy.
“It turns out it wasn’t cheap, we just weren’t counting correctly,” Allen says, pointing to similar dependencies like Chinese rare earths, which may be costlier than assumed once “strategic vulnerability” is factored in.
Influence over critical parts of the AI system therefore matters not only to those building powerful AI models and applications, but also to those with the leverage to constrain them.
For now, as major powers bet that leadership in AI will directly translate into wider economic and geopolitical power, the rate and scale of investment across the chain — from energy to chip design to frontier software — continues to be extraordinary, reflecting the sheer size of that bet.
"In the US, we’re spending more on AI every 10 months than the entire Apollo Moon program cost from start to finish over 13 years: it is an astonishing outlay of capital into a technological question mark that could potentially backfire," Allen says.
"The Industrial Revolution reshaped the global balance of power and almost every aspect of human life: you could literally see its impact from space. My prediction is that, with the level of change occurring across the entire AI stack, this is the kind of moment we’re living through now, hence why it feels so ominous."
For Australia, like much of the rest of the world, there is no single technological race to win. There is only a web of choices to negotiate: what to build, what to trade, whom to trust, where to become indispensable, and where dependence becomes dangerous.

We would add

Lavrov Tells UN Security Council Russia Won’t Pause the War During Negotiations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:42:43 UTC
03:42:43 KST

Russia will not halt its aggression against Ukraine even during possible negotiations, Russian Foreign Minister and the Kremlin’s highest-ranking representative Sergey Lavrov said during the United Nations (UN) Security Council meeting on Wednesday.
Russia rejected growing international calls for a ceasefire during a high-level Security Council meeting on Ukraine in New York, held at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Having learned from bitter experience, we will not pause the special military operation for the duration of negotiations in any format,” Kremlin’s highest-ranking representative said.
Ukraine would have kept its 1991 borders if the European nations had not “engaged in their shenanigans,” he continued, echoing Moscow’s long-standing hostility toward the West, just a month after Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day.
Sybiha: ‘Russia is vetoing peace’
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha condemned Lavrov’s comments during the same meeting on Wednesday.
“Fourteen of the 15 members of the UN Security Council support a ceasefire. Only one aggressor is blocking it,” Sybiha said, according to a statement from Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry.
The Security Council is the only UN body whose decisions can be legally binding on member states. The council has 15 members, including five permanent members: the US, UK, France, China and Russia.
Each permanent member can veto a substantive resolution, meaning Russia can block a resolution seeking to order action over the war it is waging against Ukraine.
Russia Must Answer for Crimes in Crimea, Zelensky Says
Russia “illegally occupies the USSR’s seat at this table,” Sybiha said, calling for its removal from the Council.
He then addressed Lavrov directly, presenting three questions to Moscow; Why won’t Russian President Vladimir Putin meet President Volodymyr Zelensky? What did tens of thousands of Russian soldiers lost in August die for? And how, after four years after planning to take Kyiv in three days, is Moscow now burning?
Sybiha also urged members to demand humanitarian corridors for occupied Oleshky in the Kherson region. “If you remember only one thing from this meeting, remember Oleshky,” he said.
Oleshky, cut off from water, food and medicine, remains a humanitarian disaster as Russia failed to uphold the evacuation deal. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukrainian parliament commissioner for human rights, described the city as a “death trap,” with residents frequently risking being blown up by mines just to have a chance to escape through the woods.
On Sept. 16, Lubinets said his office had received 176 appeals regarding the humanitarian situation in Oleshky, and had already verified at least 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.
51 countries call for ceasefire
Fifty-one countries backed Ukraine in a joint statement on Wednesday, urging the Kremlin to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations as large-scale Russian attacks continue in the fifth year of the war.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas delivered the statement at the UN General Assembly, alongside Sybiha and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, according to Democrata.
Earlier that day, Zelensky said Ukraine was ready to support a safe-passage regime for vessels in the Black Sea, provided Russia took genuine and reciprocal steps toward de-escalation.
On Tuesday, during a meeting with US President Donald Trump, Zelensky offered Russia a truce on energy strikes.
