UK shares findings of damning climate crisis national security report suppressed under Starmer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:36:45 UTC
03:36:45 KST

The UK has warned countries around the world that the climate and nature crises and the coming El Niño threaten their national security and defence, presenting foreign ministries with the findings of an explosive report suppressed under Keir Starmer.
Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, made a presentation to the foreign ministers of the EU as well as Kenya and other countries on Wednesday night at a private meeting during the UN general assembly in New York, based on the report by the UK’s spy chiefs that found the collapse of natural systems around the world would lead to conflict, migration and food shortages.
Miliband told the meeting, the first such discussion among foreign ministers, that the coming El Niño, which has been supercharged by climate breakdown, would test the world’s food systems as never before.
“We face an El Niño that is already set to be the most intense in living memory,” he said. “This will intensify climate shocks that compound and cascade across borders, threatening food and water security, displacing communities, putting pressure on markets and scarring economies.”
This year’s heatwaves, bad harvests and food price inflation showed governments what they were in for, he said, and must be dealt with at the highest levels.
“Climate change and nature loss have never been issues for climate and environment ministers alone,” he said. “They are defining challenges for our citizens, our economies, our foreign policy and our national security.”
 With the backing of Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, Miliband presented the research that found the collapse of global ecosystems such as in the Amazon and Congo rainforests, driven by the climate crisis and the destruction of nature, would have impacts on national security around the world.
The joint intelligence committee (JIC) report, revealed by the Guardian, was scheduled to be published last October, but was suppressed on the eve of its launch by Downing Street. A redacted version was issued in January under the Freedom of Information Act, but ministers have continued to resist calls for the full report to be made public.
Richard Nugee, a retired general and security expert, told the Guardian governments must treat the climate as they would other threats to national security, such as sabotage by hostile states.
“If a bridge is washed away, it has the same impact whether it’s done by [a foreign power] or the climate,” he said. “The climate crisis will affect food security, energy security, water security, and lead to migration and potentially the recruitment of farmers to [terrorist organisations such as] Isis. Countries should absolutely be treating this as a national security issue.”
He said it was not surprising that the JIC report was suppressed and redacted, as it was “very rare” for security reports to be published.
Miliband will appoint a new special representative for climate security, as well as a new ministerial taskforce on “the national security and resilience risks of a changing climate and nature loss”, with military and security experts as well as climate scientists.
He also announced £330m for the Global Environment Facility, the main international fund for protecting nature, that will go towards protecting forests, oceans and other critical ecosystems in developing countries.
The closed-door meeting among foreign ministers was convened after Miliband made a public speech on Monday at the UN general assembly that touched on the links between the climate and national security. Soon after taking office in July, the former energy secretary told the Guardian he would put the climate at the heart of UK foreign policy.
On Wednesday night, Miliband said: “The countries fit for the future will be those that see climate and nature as intrinsic to economic and national security. Countries that anticipate risks and invest in resilience before crises hit.
“Countries that seize the incredible opportunities the clean energy transition presents. Countries that don’t just see the connections but act on them.”
He added: “That is why the UK is placing climate and nature security at the heart of our national security and foreign policy decision-making.”
Adrian Ramsay, the Green party MP for Waveney Valley, who has campaigned for the JIC report to be made public, said: “It’s good that the foreign secretary is presenting the findings of this crucial report to ministers from other governments.
“But it begs the question, why are MPs in this country still being denied access to the full report? And, most importantly, why has our government still not published its response to how it will address the stark findings?”

Iran’s Pezeshkian slams ‘terrorist’ US but extols diplomacy in UN speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:36:39 UTC
03:36:39 KST

Iran’s Pezeshkian slams ‘terrorist’ US but extols diplomacy in UN speech
Pezeshkian leaves door open for negotiations, while calling out international community’s double standards.
Iran: Strait of Hormuz won’t be used to ‘impose insecurity on us’
In a defiant speech at the United Nations General Assembly, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian has delivered a sharp rebuke to a threat by US President Donald Trump from the same rostrum the previous day to annihilate the country, but left the door open for diplomacy to end nearly seven months of war.
“The US president called us terrorists but we are the victims of terrorists,” Pezeshkian said on Wednesday.
During his speech, Pezeshkian held up a picture of former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei – assassinated in a joint US-Israeli strike at the start of the war in February – as well as photos of schoolgirls killed in an alleged US air attack on their school in the southern city of Minab.
“They hit us, but we did not bow our heads or bend the knee,” Pezeshkian added.
As the Iranian president began his speech, an official from the US delegation walked out of the vast hall. The Israeli delegation also boycotted the address.
“[Trump] must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only grow in the face of sanctions and increased pressure and bullying,” Pezeshkian said.
But Pezeshkian, a relative centrist in the Iranian ruling system, also left the door open for negotiations, saying, “Iran extends its hands towards the world.”
“We invite the world and call to it, not out of weakness, but out of a deep belief in our own power and steadfastness to cooperate and collaborate out of a deep understanding that no one in this region will have security alone,” he said.
‘Very good meeting’
On Tuesday, Trump said his son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who are both leading negotiations with Tehran, had held a three-hour meeting with Iranian officials.
“They had a very good meeting, a very productive meeting,” Trump told reporters at the UN, adding that he believed there was “a lot of momentum” towards an agreement. Trump later said talks were continuing and that he believed a settlement would eventually be reached.
The remarks came after Trump used his speech before UN delegates to again threaten Iran’s destruction.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” Trump said. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
Strait of Hormuz
Addressing the US naval blockade of Iran and Tehran’s campaign to choke off trade in the Strait of Hormuz, Pezeshkian said Iran would resist what he called US efforts to use the critical sea lane to expand its war on the country.
“In the Strait of Hormuz, we cannot have some free access and gain their independence from that waterway while at the same time use that waterway to impose their aggressions upon us and to impose insecurity upon us; to forbid us access to our own waterways,” he said.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow at the US-based Center for International Policy, said the Iranian president’s speech showed usual flashes of defiance, but notably signalled an appetite for a diplomatic off-ramp.
“Iran wants a way out of this war. They’ve kept the door to diplomacy open,” she told Al Jazeera.
“Reading between the lines of the Iranian president’s speech, it seems Iran may even show some flexibility as far as a return to some sort of agreement that may not be exactly along the lines of the June Memorandum of Understanding that US President Trump doesn’t seem interested in returning to,” she said. The memorandum, which has expired, called for a halt to fighting, lifting the US naval blockade and opening the Strait of Hormuz to maritime traffic.
Compromise still a possibility
Drawing parallels between the US and Israel bombing of Iran and Israel’s attacks in Gaza, Pezeskhian said Israel’s genocide in Gaza “revealed the double standards to which Iran is held by the international community”.
“They kill and we are sanctioned and we are punished,” Pezeshkian added.
Joey Hood, a former US diplomat and ambassador to Tunisia, said the speech leaned heavily into familiar Iranian official rhetoric and represented a lost opportunity to seek compromise.
“Instead of coming to the United Nations with something new and bold, we heard the same things that we’ve heard before,” Hood said, adding that a concrete peace offer or proposal posed to the US in the speech might have focused Washington’s attention.
“That would actually put Donald Trump on the backfoot, and he would have to respond. The Iranian president didn’t do any of that,” Hood said.

RAF jet crashes and explodes in Anglesey moments after pilots eject
Unknown

2026-09-23

An RAF jet crashed and exploded moments after two pilots ejected during a training flight over Anglesey (Ynys Môn) in north Wales on Wednesday.
The aircraft, a Hawk T2, had just taken off from RAF Valley on the west of the island when the incident occurred, witnesses said.
Both pilots parachuted to the ground and were reportedly treated for minor injuries.
A video of the crash shows the aircraft appearing to climb unevenly before the pilots eject. The plane then nosedives towards the ground while trailing smoke and crashing near houses and agricultural buildings, sending an enormous fireball into the sky.
An RAF spokesperson said: “An incident involving an RAF T2 Hawk aircraft, flying out of RAF Valley, occurred near Anglesey. An investigation is under way and we will not comment further at this time.”
The site of the crash, at Pencarnisiog, is less than two miles from the airbase. RAF Valley is home to the air force’s No 4 Flying Training School, which trains fighter pilots using Hawk T2 and Texan T1 aircraft.
A spokesperson for North Wales fire and rescue service said: “Crews and officers attended an incident involving an aircraft in the Pencarnisiog area of Anglesey, working alongside colleagues from Royal Air Force, North Wales police, Welsh ambulance service and Wales air ambulance. The fire is now under control.”
They added: “Members of the public are asked to avoid the area while emergency services continue their work safely.”
Due to the crash, local train lines were closed and replacement buses were running between Bangor and Holyhead.
Pete Bennett, a local resident, told Wales Live it appeared the plane was in trouble as soon as it left the runway. He said: “I knew straight away that it was in trouble. Right on takeoff there was an orange flame, and as it accelerated it was basically on fire.
“As it gained altitude the flame disappeared but it was clearly in trouble. It climbed at an aggressive pitch – like the pilot was trying to gain altitude. It pitched twice violently in the air and then there were two clear, loud bangs. It was probably at around 800ft at this point. The pilots ejected and both parachutes opened.”
He said the explosion caused a “huge wall of fire and black smoke”. He added: “The aircrew came down around halfway between the runway and where the plane crashed, which I’m guessing was around a mile inland from RAF Valley.”
The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said in a post on X: “My thoughts are first and foremost with the pilots. We will provide further updates in due course.”
North Wales police said: “Two pilots are being treated for what are thought to be minor injuries and at this stage there are no reports of any wider damage or injuries.”

US open to Cuba talks on government change, Marco Rubio says

The United States says it is open to speaking with Havana about how it can make a political transition towards new leadership and end a decades-old trade embargo imposed since former leader Fidel Castro‘s communist revolution in 1959 and the US’s recent blockade of the country.
“Cuba has a golden opportunity to place itself on an irreversible path towards a better future,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday in New York City. “We are prepared to be helpful in that regard if they are open to it.”

Washington has previously said that it wants a change in Cuba’s government. Since earlier this year, the US has additionally imposed an oil blockade that has put the country under severe pressure, dealing with fuel shortages and ongoing blackouts. Cuban officials have also blamed it on problems providing food and other basic needs for its population.
Rubio said Washington was willing to work with some Cuban leaders – those whose “hands are not stained with blood”, he said – but also acknowledged that some were “at least publicly quite recalcitrant”.
Rubio, the child of Cubans who fled the country before the revolution, said businesses and investors from the US, including the Cuban diaspora, were ready to step in and help the country transition its economy if progress was made on political reforms.
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump called Cuba a “failed state,” and said his administration was willing to use military power against it when necessary, outlining a string of moves it has made in the region to protect Washington’s interests, including the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
“My administration is also seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba,” Trump said. “Where the communist regime is under great pressure, the biggest pressure they’ve ever been under.”
Trump’s remarks prompted the Cuban delegation to walk out of the assembly.
Cuban officials have denied any talks are going on with the US, which has sought to remove the post-revolutionary government in Havana ever since it came to power in 1959.
Earlier this month, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez called the US embargo against his country a policy of “economic asphyxiation,” and described the blockade as “genocidal”.
The Cuban government says the US embargo cost its economy $8bn between March 2025 and February 2026, the highest figure yet recorded and 7 percent more than in the previous reporting period.
The total does not include some of Washington’s more recent sanctions, including restrictions on the island’s energy supply imposed in January and secondary sanctions imposed in May, said Rodriguez.
Several world leaders at the UNGA criticised the US blockade in their speeches this year, including Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
“In Cuba, the world watches in dismay as 10 million people face collective punishment from an illegal economic embargo and energy siege,” he said on Tuesday.
Every year since 1992, the UNGA has adopted by a large majority a non-binding resolution calling for the lifting of the embargo imposed on Cuba by the US.
In July, a vote on whether to hold a debate on the resolution signalled a slight erosion in support for Cuba in the General Assembly, with 136 member states in favour, nine against, and 30 abstentions – including traditional supporters Germany and Canada.

A demonstration was held on Wednesday in Jerusalem's Paris Square on behalf of the campaign to find Haymanot Kasau.
The demonstration, led by the Kasau family, was initiated as a call for the transfer of the investigation of Haymanot's disappearance to the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency).
The protest follows the Jerusalem Municipality's refusal to permit the abducted girl's family to erect a protest tent.
The Kasau family repeatedly sought approval to establish a tent outside the Supreme Court, near the Knesset, and opposite the Prime Minister's residence.
They are seeking to raise awareness of the disappearance of their daughter, Haymanot Kasau, who went missing on February 25, 2024, at the age of nine, from the Safed absorption center where she lived with her family. She has not been found since.
It has been 941 days since Haymanot's disappearance.
'Investigation is being handled as an afterthought,' campaign claims
Tesfaye Kasau, father of Haymanot, addressed Lahav 433, the Shin Bet, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"About ten days ago, we sat at Lahav 433 and asked question after question, and not a single one received an answer. Those who are supposed to provide answers, those responsible for investigating, didn't answer and simply didn't seem to know.
"Do they have suspects? Do they have a direction for the investigation? Is the investigation focused inside Israel or abroad? Were all checks performed, such as phone geolocations and polygraphs for everyone at the absorption center on that terrible night?
"Nothing. Absolutely nothing. How can this be? How is it that the investigation into the abduction of a girl who has already turned 11 is being conducted like this? How can it be that those who are supposed to protect us act as if there is time? As if Haymanot doesn't need us to save her, as if Haymanot isn't important."
He lambasted the government for failing to handle the investigation, asking once again for it to be handed over to the Shin Bet, before asking the people of Israel to "stay with us and continue to support us so that we succeed in our struggle for a proper, equal investigation."
An earlier statement released on behalf of the campaign said, "The investigation is being handled as an afterthought, having already passed through four different hands without a single lead - which is why the demonstration aims to press the ongoing demand to transfer the case to the Shin Bet."
Haymanot’s parents, Tesfaya and Benchi Kasau, have led a public campaign calling for increased efforts to locate her, including protests outside Lahav 433 offices and a march in Tel Aviv.
Shelly Shem Tov, mother of freed Hamas hostage, grateful and ashamed
Shelly Shem Tov, mother of released hostage Omer Shem Tov, came to speak at the demonstration for Haymanot.
She related to the family by recalling the fears and emotions from when her son was in captivity.
"When the hostages were in captivity, we felt the embrace of the Israeli public; we felt that we were not alone. Now I stand here and look at you, a small group of people, and every single one of you is so meaningful to Haymanot's family. Because feeling alone, feeling abandoned, is simply terrible. I want to thank each and every one of you for not leaving Haymanot's family alone."
She continued, saying, "On the other hand, I feel ashamed because I feel that I too had somewhat forgotten Haymanot and her family. And the same goes for the people of Israel. I am certain it is not out of bad intentions, but because there isn't the sheer force of numbers needed to shake up those who need to be shaken up. I want to say that being a mother whose child is not with her is something I wouldn't wish on anyone.
"Haymanot is not where she ought to be - at home with her family and friends. Haymanot disappeared out of the blue. And because this family doesn't have the words to scream in Hebrew so they can be heard, they lack that strength.
"I appeal to everyone who stood with us during our struggle: come and make this family feel they are not alone. The public needs to be here."

Russia has 2.5 trillion rubles more cash in circulation than at the start of the year. The central bank wants lenders scrutinizing where it comes from.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:30:54 UTC
03:30:54 KST

Russia has 2.5 trillion rubles more cash in circulation than at the start of the year. The central bank wants lenders scrutinizing where it comes from.
The Bank of Russia will issue new recommendations asking banks to look more closely at where their clients’ cash comes from, said Bogdan Shablya, head of the central bank’s Financial Monitoring and Foreign Exchange Control Service.
Shablya said the recommendations would cover organizations and individuals. The central bank has “never opposed cash itself,” he said, but opposes “only the circulation of cash whose origin is unknown, which is why we provide banks with guidance and recommendations.”
Shablya said the recommendations would revise the typologies of suspicious transactions.
“The recommendations will cover everyone. Everything will be in there: individuals, organizations, deposits into accounts, and steps to take during currency conversions. So it will be comprehensive. We plan to publish the document soon,” he said.
The official said cash of “unknown origin” comes from “wholesale and retail markets” — primarily “illegal cryptocurrency exchanges in Moscow.”
Russia has seen a steady shift toward cash since March 2026, according to RBC. Central bank figures show that cash in circulation has increased by 2.5 trillion rubles since the start of the year. The move away from banks and toward cash is linked to businesses’ demand for cash, partly as they adapt to tax changes in 2026.

15 years after being rejected, Aussie animator lands gig at dream studio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

It took this Australian animator 15 years to make it to their dream studio
Ever since they were young, Australian animator Sammy Lewis knew they were destined for a career in claymation.
"It goes way back to when I was about six. A family friend gave me a book on how to make plasticine creatures and I was just obsessed," Lewis tells ABC News.
"For most of my childhood, I was making little plasticine animals and leaving them around the place."
So, for Lewis, when they graduated with an animation degree at Griffith Film School in Brisbane and went on their first European holiday, it just made sense to drop into their dream workplace — legendary British claymation studio Aardman Animations.
"I had my showreel on DVD; that was the style of the time. I detoured the trip to go all the way on a bus to Bristol," Lewis says.
"I got to the reception, handed them my DVD and they were like, 'Please go away. You can't just turn up to an active studio. You need to properly apply through the website'."
Disheartened but not deterred, young Lewis snapped a photo of themselves below the Aardman sign.
Fifteen years later Lewis recreated the photo, this time returning to Aardman not as a wishful student but as an animator on the studio's latest feature film Shaun The Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom.
"I'm a bit happier in one of them," Lewis laughs.
For the kids
Over the past 50 years, Aardman has been pumping out children's classics such as Chicken Run, Shaun the Sheep and Wallace & Gromit — all lovingly rendered in painstaking claymation stop motion.
Following on from 2019's Shaun the Sheep: Farmageddon, which scored an Academy Award nomination for Best Animated Feature, Beast of Mossy Bottom returns to Shaun's farm for a horror-adjacent adventure involving overzealous hair-growing potions and a very unwitting farmer.
For Lewis, the toughest thing about working on the feature was the commute to work.
"I was in a bit of a dream state of getting to work at Aardman, and everything was kind of magical, even the difficult things.
"It was so inspiring to be around so many talented people, animators who've forgotten more than I'll ever learn. There's animators who are still at the studio whose first job was the original Chicken Run," they say.
"And they're all very lovely and happy to share their knowledge."
Stop motion as a longform medium has become an increasing rarity due to the long production time and heavy human investment needed to bring the creations to life, especially in a post-generative AI world.
In 2024, Aardman announced it was cutting 20 jobs from the 400-plus strong workforce after posting a $US720,000 loss for the year. Beast of Mossy Bottom is the first Aardman project to make it to cinemas since the downsizing, after 2024's Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl was released straight to streaming.
A far cry from bouncing fruit or AI slop, Beast of Mossy Bottom is bursting with signs of human life — right down to the visible fingerprints on the colourful characters. Lewis hopes the movie can carry the stop-motion torch for future generations.
"Going forward, for obvious reasons, I think, handmade things and tactile mediums are just going to be so important. There's just a special kind of magic about things that you just know that they have been made by people," Lewis says.
"Sometimes that doesn't even come down to the artist; it's all the people with the money making those decisions. I don't know how we get them to care about stop motion or hand-drawn animation again."
Don't dream it, be it
Due to the enormous logistical challenge of putting together a stop-motion feature, Lewis only saw the Beast of Mossy Bottom in all its glory at a recent screening for friends and family.
"I hadn't seen any of the final music, or the final editing. When you're working on it, you do get to see the whole film, but it's all in rough cut, storyboard sort of animatic form," they say.
There was one part Lewis was particularly excited by — their name in the credits.
"I had some pretty amazing impostor syndrome at the start of production. So, to see my name in the credits is kind of like, 'Yeah, you did it'."
After their adventure in Mossy Bottom, Lewis is now preparing to move from the UK back to Australia to find their next project and reconnect with local animator communities.
It's the same advice they would give any young Australian who is looking to follow in their footsteps.
"Find your people was probably the first big step out of uni. It can be such an isolating time if you're just doing everything by yourself," Lewis says.
"I graduated, worked my sports retail job for almost a whole year,and then was like, wait, this isn't what I wanted. That motivated me to move interstate and find other stop-motion animators. Once I did that, I think we all worked on music videos and silly things. It's just good having your people around you."
Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom is in cinemas now.

====================================================================================================

AI Agents Teamed Up to Cheat at Blackjack. Their Collusion Is Getting Harder to Spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

This week I bring news of a daring casino caper hatched by a pair of rogue AI agents—as well as the clever trick that revealed their antics.
After researchers instructed them to count cards during a game of blackjack, the agents—which were controlled by the same model—developed a spontaneous secret code to help them get ahead. Though the episode happened inside an Oxford University lab, rather than a real casino, it has troubling real-world implications: It suggests that agents deployed in industries like finance and ecommerce could figure out how to partner up and cheat in ways that are difficult to detect.
“When taken individually, these agents may seem entirely [benign],” says Christian Schroeder de Witt, a computer scientist at Oxford University who led the work and who has done pioneering research into agent collusion. “Once put together in a group, they can collude secretly.”
The agents knew their conversations would be monitored, so they devised a way to communicate while avoiding detection. When one agent said, “This dealer’s on a real hot streak! Every hand they pull a monster,” for example, that indicated that the next card would be of a certain value, and that the agent should bet $250. Most interestingly, their communications weren’t picked up by a system designed to spot signs of collusion in agent chatter.
Aaron Rose, a machine-learning researcher who worked on the project, is also an avid card player, and he figured the blackjack table might be fertile territory for devious agent partnerships. “It worked really well,” he says.
Schroeder de Witt’s group eventually figured out how to detect the conspiracy. Using a method known as mechanistic interpretability, they trained a smaller model to recognize telltale activations across the agents’ weights. Using a tool called Narcbench, they tested the approach on some medium-size open-source models and found they could tell when models intended to slip information to each other.
Crucially, however, spotting what was happening involved monitoring both agents—something likely to complicate detection in real-world scenarios where thousands of agents, some operated by different companies, may be deployed.
Carissa Cullen, a PhD student involved with the study, says the next step is to test whether larger models behave similarly. (The agents in the study were smaller versions of US models Llama and GPT-OSS and the Chinese models Qwen and DeepSeek.) The team saw some signs that larger models exhibit less of a detectable signal than smaller models, and they want to know if larger models are more likely to collude, and more likely to be secretive about it.
Evidence that groups of agents are more problematic than agents operating solo seems to be growing. One project, from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, found that swarms of agents were considerably more dangerous when asked to carry out simulated disinformation campaigns and ecommerce fraud. They were better able to adapt to defensive measures, researchers reported.
“The big lesson is that it’s not enough to evaluate agents individually,” says Diyi Yang, a computer scientist at Stanford University who has studied collusion among agents. “Companies should closely monitor inter-agent interactions when agents interact repeatedly, even when their individual incentives seem benign.”
It’s not all bad: Having thousands of agents collaborate on a task made it possible for OpenAI to solve previously intractable math problems. But groups of rogue agents working together have also featured in several recent high-profile hacking incidents. In May, a team of OpenAI agents hacked into the AI research platform Hugging Face, and used a message board to share tips and ideas. Other models, including Anthropic’s Claude and Google’s Gemini, have also carried out alarming safety breaches.
Secret chatter adds a new dimension to this burgeoning problem, and it may not be the end of it. Another recent study, from a startup called Emergence AI, put agents controlled by frontier AI models in a virtual world to see what they would do. When tasked with making money, they repeatedly tried to devise ways to reach humans on the wider internet in order to sell them stuff. Most bizarrely, the agents eventually developed their own kind of slang. “They very rapidly evolved a language,” says Satya Nitta, Emergence AI’s CEO. “We don’t know why.”
The wider world isn’t ignoring problems with agentic misbehavior; it’s a hot topic at this week’s United Nations General Assembly. An independent scientific panel is set to discuss the OpenAI-HuggingFace incident, while Sam Altman is expected to call for international coordination on developing safe AI agents.
Despite this, some industries, including, ecommerce have become testing grounds for agentic AI. This week, for instance, Amazon said it would block Meta’s Muse AI agent from accessing its site, arguing that it violated its terms of use.
Schroeder de Witt says it’s entirely conceivable that agents tasked with finding deals start to work together—perhaps even covertly—in order to get a better deal, or to screw someone over. It will be crucial to study agent collusion and develop detection strategies as they proliferate, he says. “There needs to be more research and understanding of what will happen when we have more agents in the economy,” he says.
This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

China Capital stories reveal how ICBC advanced China’s political goals across four continents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:29:54 UTC
03:29:54 KST

PARTNER STORIES
China Capital stories reveal how ICBC advanced China’s political goals across four continents
ICIJ’s media partners uncovered strategic deals and moves the Chinese bank made around the world to further the political priorities of the party-state.
China Capital, an investigation by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists in collaboration with 23 media partners, provided an unprecedented look into decision-making at the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, one of the most powerful Chinese institutions, at a time of China’s ascendance on the world stage.
The investigation is based on more than 4.8 million confidential records from two of ICBC’s U.K. units. The records provide rare insight into one of China’s most important financial arms, showing how the government’s influence and political priorities often outweigh ordinary banking protocols.
This is the first time that an international team of reporters has examined the inner workings and lending practices of ICBC– the world’s largest bank by asset size. Like many of its state-owned peers, ICBC is notoriously secretive.
“The ICIJ investigation shows how branch structures can be leveraged by foreign bank headquarters to override local compliance officers when state-backed corporate interests conflict with local regulatory obligations,” said David P. Weber, an accounting professor at West Virginia University and former Chief Investigator of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. He urged regulators in the U.S. and the U.K. to implement a cross-border enforcement mechanism that could “reduce oversight fragmentation.”
From New Zealand to Mexico, the 75 journalists who participated in the investigation uncovered previously unknown details about the bank’s involvement in some of their countries’ most important infrastructure projects and natural resources companies, as well as deals with firms linked to China’s military apparatus. Here are some of the revelations they uncovered.
The bank did not respond to reporters’ requests for comment.
How ICBC blended commercial interests with China’s political priorities
ICIJ’s partners across India, New Zealand and Austria found repeated instances where the bank’s political role blended with its commercial interests.
In 2017, Indian and Chinese troops reached a stand-off in the disputed Doklam region at the two countries’ borders, after the Indian government accused Beijing-backed companies of building roads in a territory claimed by China and Bhutan, in violation of a 1980 treaty. The two-month face-off didn’t just have political repercussions, The Indian Express, an ICIJ partner, reported. It also triggered actions inside ICBC’s Mumbai branch, more than 1,200 miles south of the border.
Soon after the news reached the bankers, ICBC “suspended the disbursement of 11 approved but undisbursed loans and bond investments totalling $185 million,” according to internal records. The bank also “organized” Chinese Communist Party members across every department to stay in constant touch with China’s embassy and consulate. The incident exemplifies the bank’s tight links to the party-state and how geopolitical events can influence its lending operations around the world.
Like most Chinese companies, ICBC has a Communist Party committee, an internal cell that ensures its operations advance the party’s interests, and some bankers were internally referred to as “comrades.”
In New Zealand, The Post reported that a Communist Party member who worked as a senior executive at ICBC’s Auckland outpost handled the local accounts of Hikvision, a Chinese surveillance tech company with links to the government. Numerous investigations by researchers and journalists have documented how, since at least 2017, Hikvision has provided surveillance technology to forces in Xinjiang, the Chinese region where Xi Jinping’s government has waged a repression campaign against hundreds of thousands of Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities. In 2020, the U.S. government blacklisted the firm for enabling human rights abuses.
Internal ICBC records describe how Lu Ping, the chief marketing officer of the ICBC subsidiary in New Zealand, “exhibited the outstanding qualities of a communist party member.” “Comrade Lu Ping” was nominated for a company-wide commendation in 2022 for his proactive role “fulfilling cash management needs” in New Zealand for Hikvision and Huawei, one of the bank’s most important clients.
China Capital also uncovered secret links between one of Austria’s most important aviation companies and a top Chinese producer of military aircraft. ICIJ’s partner in Vienna, profil, examined internal 2021 memos that discussed a $230 million loan to Future Advance Composite Components, which is affiliated with the state-owned Aviation Industry Corporation of China.
While FACC, as the firm is known, publicly states that it produces aircraft parts exclusively for the civilian market, its Chinese owner has an “absolute leading position” in China’s defense industry and is the “sole manufacturer of all kinds of military aircraft and airborne equipment” in the country, according to the records.
ICBC bankers also discussed the possibility that the U.S. government could sanction AVIC in the future due to its links to China’s military apparatus. Though some London officers opposed extending the loans due to risk management concerns, they left the ultimate decision to ICBC’s Beijing headquarters. The documents do not state whether the bank approved the loan. AVIC did not respond to inquiries from profil.
Strategic deals revealed across Australia, Ghana, Belgium, the UK and Sweden
As part of China Capital, reporters also examined hundreds of credit application forms and other records that partly explained why ICBC London would want to pursue a deal. The documents revealed the geopolitical nature of some loans.
In Australia, ICBC issued “loss-making or marginal loans” to some of the country’s biggest resources and infrastructure companies, including Rio Tinto, Fortescue and Glencore, as a way of starting long-term relationships that would help advance Beijing’s political goals, the Australian Financial Review found.
The documents show how in 2015, Andrew Forrest, the billionaire CEO of Fortescue, an iron ore miner, made an emergency trip to Beijing to meet with ICBC’s chairman and seek assistance after the company was forced to cancel a $2.5 billion bond issuance because of unattractive interest rates.
Fortescue was struggling financially, but ICBC’s Sydney branch implored the Beijing headquarters to approve the loan at rates close to 30% below those offered by bond investors in the U.S., AFR reported. An internal memo cited Fortescue’s “significant strategic importance for the Chinese steel industry.”
ICIJ media partners in Ghana found evidence of loans awarded for similarly strategic reasons.
Ghana Business News reported how ICBC continued to provide hundreds of millions of dollars to the Ghana Cocoa Board, a government entity that supports and controls the production of cocoa — an important commodity — even though the company lacked transparency and was on a watchlist of borrowers in financial distress.
According to internal records, China stood to benefit from financing the firm, also known as Cocobod, since Chinese trade companies were key buyers and the deal helped cement the political alliance between Beijing and Accra. ICBC’s Brussels branch also participated in the loan to Cocobod, De Tijd reported, suggesting that the overseas units often helped each other when the clients were considered strategic for the bank and the party-state.
ICBC acquired a key role in the China-Africa trade thanks to its 19.7% stake in South African banking giant Standard Bank, The Africa Report found. Chinese authorities have approved the two institutions as joint renminbi-clearing banks — an arrangement that is expected to ease transactions in the Chinese currency across 19 countries where Standard Bank operates, the report said.
The Chinese bank also financed key energy projects in Europe. In the U.K., The Times found that ICBC issued nearly $1.7 billion in loans and borrowing options to U.K. water and energy infrastructure companies, including some that were “highly leveraged, with private owners borrowing heavily against relatively guaranteed incomes to maximise dividends.”
This model could leave water companies at risk should disputes arise over the debts, The Times reported. According to one internal memo, ICBC London’s ability to participate in wind farms financing was “strategically important in order to remain relevant in the UK renewables sector”.
The revelations prompted a debate in the British parliament, with some members of the House of Lords raising concerns about Chinese ownership of water utilities and key local infrastructure.
ICBC also showed an interest in financing Sweden’s top oil producer, Preem, the Göteborgs-Posten found. Internal records show how the bank offered loans to the company, a long-term client, in order to benefit Chinese oil companies and obtain access to Preem’s technology. In an internal document examined by ICIJ’s Swedish reporting partner, a banker noted that the deal allowed ICBC to gain insight into technology used for refining waste oil from cooking and forest biomass into premium oil products — a process of particular interest to China.
Serving Russia’s allies
China Capital also exposed how ICBC used its London operations as a financing hub for companies linked to sanctioned Russian and Belarusian business owners even after Western countries imposed financial sanctions to dent Russia’s military operations in Ukraine.
ICIJ and the Belarusian Investigative Center reported how ICBC London’s clients included a U.K. subsidiary of Zoomlion Heavy Industry Science and Technology, a Chinese construction company. Zoomlion used the subsidiary to partner with Belarusian state-owned company MAZ and build an industrial park near Minsk. The partnership continued even after the European Union and its allies sanctioned MAZ over its ties to Alexander Lukashenko’s regime.
MAZ left the joint venture in 2023, after the U.S. sanctioned the Belarusian firm, but devised a plan to continue supplying heavy vehicles to Zoomlion through an unsanctioned party, according to records obtained by the Belarusian Investigative Center.
MAZ didn’t respond to reporters’ questions. Zoomlion told ICIJ that the company and its subsidiaries operate in compliance with all laws and regulations.
In the Netherlands, Nout Wellink, a former supervisory board member of ICBC who left his post shortly after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, questioned the bank’s compliance culture, according to Het Financieele Dagblad. The growing pro-Russian stance within the Chinese government caused him unease during his nearly four-year tenure on the bank’s supervisory board, Welling said, according to ICIJ’s Dutch media partner.
“I don’t have a clear enough picture of the extent to which international sanctions are also being internalized within the bank,” he said. Speaking to a Dutch radio show, Wellink said that the bank is, “to a certain extent, an instrument of the Communist Party.”

Sybiha at UN Security Council: We are ready for complete ceasefire, but Russia is vetoing peace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:28:00 UTC

Sybiha at UN Security Council: We are ready for complete ceasefire, but Russia is vetoing peace
He made this statement during a Security Council meeting on the agenda item “Maintaining Peace and Security in Ukraine,” according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“Many speeches have been made in this Council. So many right words. But the war drags on.I don’t want to make another speech that will not stop the war. Enough speeches. Enough broken promises. Enough imitation of diplomacy. Enough. This war has to stop. Ukraine wants to end it now — not later. We are ready for a full, unconditional ceasefire. Ready for ceasefires on energy and food. Ready to stop right now, right here,” the Ukrainian foreign minister emphasized.
According to him, 14 out of 15 Security Council members “in one way or another, an immediate ceasefire. Including four permanent members. Including the United States and China.”
“Only one state blocks an end to hostilities. And it is the aggressor itself. Russia vetoes not just a ceasefire. Russia vetoes peace. Putin could have ended this war long ago. But he chooses daily escalation,” Sybiha noted.
He emphasized that Russia’s war against Ukraine poses a global threat.
“This is not a Ukrainian war. Not even a European one. It is a global threat. Preventing the worst scenario depends on everyone in this room, and beyond it,” the minister said.
At the same time, he stressed that Russia is already waging war against Europe—through arson, murders, cyberattacks, disinformation, election interference, the use of energy, food, and migration as weapons, and drones and missiles entering NATO airspace.
“This is not "hybrid." Drop this word. Russia’s war against Europe is no longer hybrid,” added Ukraine’s foreign minister.
The minister also drew attention to the humanitarian situation in the occupied town of Oleshky in the Kherson region.
“If you remember one thing from this meeting, remember Oleshky. Hear their cry for help. Demand Russia open humanitarian corridors. Moscow is the only cause of this disaster, and the only obstacle to ending it,” Sybiha emphasized.
According to him, the Kremlin is repeating the crimes of the past. “And this policy echoes… the genocide of the Holodomor, when the Soviet regime deliberately starved millions of Ukrainians to death. Back then, famine was Moscow’s weapon. It remains its weapon today.”
Sybiha stressed that “this war cannot be stopped by appeasement.”
“This is not the United Nations Impunity Council. Even though Russia wishes it to be. The mission of this Council is to safeguard peace and security,” the foreign minister stressed.
According to him, the international community must step up diplomatic efforts to end the war, demand that Russia agree to a ceasefire, tighten sanctions and cut off its access to technology, as well as counter Russian recruitment, disinformation, and destabilizing actions.
“If Russia vetoes peace, we must veto Russia's war,” Sybiha said.
He addressed Russia’s representative on the Security Council with questions to which the latter would have no answers: “First: why won't your president sit down with our president to end this war now? Second: in August, you lost tens of thousands of soldiers — to seize a few square kilometers. What did they die for? Third: you wanted Kyiv in three days... How did you end up with Moscow burning four years later?” Sybiha said.
He added that “silence will be his only honest answer.”
Sybiha called on the international community to act now to prevent the war from spreading.
“Russia is never as strong as it wants us to believe. And never as weak as we want it to be. Russia is no longer a global power. It’s a global problem. And it requires a global solution,” the minister emphasized.
Addressing representatives of various countries, he stressed the need to stop the war “before Putin enters your home. He is already at the entrance.”
As reported by Ukrinform, on Wednesday the UN Security Council convened to discuss Russia’s war against Ukraine. Ahead of the meeting, more than 50 UN member states called on Russia to agree to a complete, immediate, and unconditional ceasefire and to begin substantive peace negotiations.

‘It sent a message’: anti-migrant feeling pervades Hampshire town where hundreds protested
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:27:33 UTC
03:27:33 KST

Alan Dale was in two minds as he gazed across at Portsmouth harbour in the late September sunshine and reflected on the latest show of force by far-right activists on the south coast against a supposed disembarkation of asylum seekers.
A stone’s throw away, masked followers of the anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas had been cheered on Tuesday night by hundreds of people, many of them local, who had gathered after social media posts suggested authorities planned to land the migrants in the nearby town of Gosport.
The gathering had at least “sent a message”, said Dale, a retired Royal Navy veteran who echoed a common local sentiment that Gosport and Britain more widely had changed, and that migrants were being put “to the front of the queue” for public services.
“Is it going to be heard though? I don’t think so. It’s almost like the government is sticking its fingers in its ears and saying: ‘We are not listening to you.’”
As for the masked vigilantes who answered the call from Thomas – who calls himself “Danny Tommo” and was filmed earlier in the day using a blade to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard – Dale admitted to feeling uncomfortable about their face coverings, but insisted: “With any protest you are always going to get troublemakers.”
Many local people from a block of flats close to Gosport’s marina indeed appeared have swelled the numbers of those who turned up in what senior Reform UK figures, including the Hampshire MP and former home secretary Suella Braverman, had cheered on as a show of “people power”.
But a far-right presence – and hostility towards migrants – was discernible in the town in a part of England where organised activists from their ranks have been building links for a number of years with anti-migrant campaigns.
Most shockingly to outsiders unfamiliar with the depth of vitriol towards migrants among some here, children had been seen and heard chanting “let them drown” into a megaphone.
Red and white far-right posters emblazoned with the word “resistance” and slogans such as “protecting our children’s future” were plastered on lampposts around the bench where Dale sat in Gosport’s Falkland Gardens.
At least two outsiders were among the six people arrested on Tuesday night by police: a 19-year-old and a 36-year-old, both from Salisbury, who were detained on suspicion of aggravated trespass.
In the end, the small boat carrying 51 people docked in Dover, Kent, at about 12.30am on Wednesday after spending 33 hours at sea.
While there was no plan to land them in Gosport, Home Office sources have insisted, the events have once again placed Thomas in the spotlight – even as he faces the prospect of a police inquiry into his knife-wielding at sea – and saw a blurring of the lines between his activities and local protesters who were praised by Reform.
“It’s a depressing situation that so many people turned up but there is another side here as well and you have people in Portsmouth who are organising gigs to raise funds for the RNLI [Royal National Lifeboat Institution],” said a local man who had worked with young people in the area where the protest took place but declined to give his name.
He also cited the fact that Gosport’s nearby Rowner area had been allocated money – as much as £20m – from the government’s Pride in Place initiative, a long-term strategic effort launched under Keir Starmer’s premiership to counter the electoral threat posed by rising nationalism and the far right in areas where such sentiment finds some sympathy.
A diversity of views could be found again on Wednesday morning among those gathered for a Bible study group inside Gosport’s Holy Trinity church, a short stroll from the seafront.
They included the retired priest Margaret Hay, who said the first thought that came to her mind was that Jesus was an immigrant too, while at least one other participant voiced discomfort that many of those crossing the Channel appeared to be men.
The group also included Tyler Palmer, a young churchgoer who watched the protests on Tuesday night from the edge of the crowd.
“We’ve always been diverse here in Gosport and it’s forgotten. Turkish sailors who fought alongside us in the second world war were housed here,” he said.
“But we’re also a naval town and people are very proud. They’re reading things that scare them – whether that’s GB News or fearmongering on social media.
“These are everyday people, your plumbers, your plasterers, who you wouldn’t expect to be at protests.”

Europeans warn of rising Russian sabotage but see no imminent NATO attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:21:38 UTC
03:21:38 KST

Europeans warn of rising Russian sabotage but see no imminent NATO attack
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 23 - Russia is intensifying sabotage, cyberattacks and other hybrid attacks across Europe to undermine support for Ukraine, European ministers said, while dismissing concerns that Moscow is capable of launching a direct assault on NATO.
Speaking on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly this week, officials from countries on NATO's eastern flank said Moscow was increasingly using drone incursions, cyberattacks, sabotage and other covert operations to sow fear, test Western resolve and weaken backing for Kyiv.
"Europe faces a fast proliferation of sabotage attacks and airspace violations," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told reporters. "Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine."
European governments increasingly see Russia's most immediate threat not as a conventional military attack, but as a campaign of covert and deniable actions aimed at unsettling Ukraine's allies and eroding Western unity as the war drags on.
Kallas said Russia appeared willing to take greater risks and argued the answer was to increase pressure on Moscow through tougher sanctions, including measures targeting its "shadow fleet" and military-industrial complex.
"Russia's economy is one of its weakest parts, and we need to increase the pressure on it so that they would stop this war," she said.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said such activity was no longer merely a threat.
"They're not just threats; they're actual attacks," Sikorski told Reuters, citing arson, explosions, drone incursions and what Warsaw says was a deliberate cruise missile violation of its territory.
The Polish Army Operational Command said on Wednesday a Russian military Mi-8 helicopter made a brief incursion into its airspace from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
"Our F-16s are scrambled up almost every day now because you just never know when these drones or missiles that approach might not actually be possible," he said.
Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu told Reuters Bucharest had seen more than 100 incursions by drones or drone fragments onto its territory as Russia intensified attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure near the Danube and Black Sea.
"We do not have data to indicate we're targeted directly, but that doesn't change the responsibility of Russia for the risk it creates," she said.
Romania has responded by closing Russia's consulate in Constanta and coordinating diplomatic measures with European allies, she added.
The Kremlin consistently denies conducting sabotage operations in NATO countries or plotting any confrontation.
NO IMMINENT NATO ATTACK
Despite the incidents, ministers drew a distinction between Russia's covert campaign and the prospect of a direct attack on NATO territory.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told Reuters alarmist predictions of an imminent Russian assault on the alliance were misplaced.
"We don’t see that Russia is able and even preparing for some kind of active military aggression against NATO or the European countries," he said, arguing Moscow lacked the capabilities for such an operation while its forces remained heavily engaged in Ukraine.
He said Moscow's campaign was designed primarily to create fear and divisions within Western societies.
"This is mainly meant for creating fear, fear of escalation, to divide us, to play with our unity," Tsahkna said. "The main message is: Don't let Putin play with the fear of escalation," he said, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said allied intelligence pointed to a risk that Russia could seek to broaden pressure on NATO countries through attacks on critical infrastructure and other forms of hybrid activity.
"There are some considerations on the Russian side to escalate horizontally, so to say, or geographically," Budrys told Reuters.
The ministers said the best way to counter such tactics was through unity, deterrence and continued support for Ukraine, particularly ahead of winter, when Russia is expected to intensify attacks on energy infrastructure.
Budrys warned that "the cold will be weaponized by Russia" and urged European countries to provide more assistance, arguing support remained patchy across the bloc.
Several ministers argued that firm responses had already shown results. Tsahkna pointed to the sharp reduction in serious Russian airspace violations on NATO's eastern flank following a strong allied reaction to previous incidents.
"Putin is carefully watching," he said. "We have lots of leverage, but we just need to have self-confidence and be clear about our language." REUTERS

Russia, Ukraine signal interest in limited cease-fire: Rubio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:21:00 UTC
03:21:00 KST

Ukraine and Russia have both expressed interest in a limited cease-fire covering grain shipments and energy infrastructure, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday following talks with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in New York.
Ukraine and its allies have pressed for a moratorium in attacks on energy infrastructure and for guarantees on Black Sea shipping, fearing Russia could target power and heating facilities this winter.
"I think both sides have expressed an interest in some limited ceasefire that involve grain and energy. Obviously, you know, that won't be easy either," Rubio told reporters.
Russia has given no public indication it is ready to agree to such arrangements, and it was not immediately clear whether Rubio was suggesting movement in his talks with Lavrov.
Rubio said it was a particular challenge that energy strikes were at the core of both countries' tactical priorities in their war, which is now in its fifth year.
Addressing the 15-member Security Council on the sidelines of the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders, Lavrov indicated that Moscow would not countenance any temporary cessation of hostilities.
"Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause, and it wants to use it to pump the Kyiv regime with weapons," he told a council session focused on the war in Ukraine.
Britain, France and Denmark's top diplomats used their speeches to deliver strong condemnations of Russia's war, warning variously of dangerous escalation and the spike in civilian deaths this summer.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was expected to address the General Assembly later on Wednesday, met U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday and said they had discussed a cease-fire on energy-related targets.
Zelenskyy told leaders at a "Crimean Platform" summit on the sidelines of the U.N. that Kyiv was ready for a maritime truce in the Black Sea based on proposals such as those put forward by Egypt, India and Türkiye.
Zelenskiy spoke ahead of the council meeting on Russia's war in Ukraine.
"We are waiting for Russia's response. Ukraine is ready ... to ensure safe shipping and food security in the Black Sea if Russia is ready to take real steps towards de-escalation too. We have to start somewhere," he said.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told the Security Council it was essential that navigation recommence in the Black Sea: "Eleven million tonnes (of food) risk spoiling. The damage will last many years if we don't restore freedom of navigation now."
Top wheat importers in Asia, the Middle East and Africa that count on the Black Sea region for wheat have been finding it hard to secure supplies. Global wheat prices have soared.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told the Security Council that France backed moratoriums on attacks against energy infrastructure and in the Black Sea as a first step toward de-escalation.
Ahead of the Lavrov-Rubio meeting, the Kremlin said there were no grounds for wider peace negotiations, though it remained open to them.
"For now, there are no prerequisites for moving on to a peaceful negotiating track, although we, as the Russian side, remain open to peace talks," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that he would be ready to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin at a trilateral meeting with Trump.

'Breakthrough' archeological find could confirm location of Paris's original settlement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:19:47 UTC
03:19:47 KST

'Breakthrough' archeological find could confirm location of Paris's original settlement
An ancient wall discovered this summer under a hospital in central Paris is thought to be a fragment of city ramparts built by Iron age settlers. Experts say the stone-and-wood structure could confirm the location of the ancient city of Lutetia.
An ancient wall discovered beneath Paris was described as a "major breakthrough" on Wednesday by France's culture ministry, with the archaeological find possibly confirming the location of the city's original settlement.
A roughly 20-metre (65-foot) wall dating from the Gallo-Roman period was discovered in Paris this summer beneath a hospital on the Ile de la Cité, a stone's throw from Notre-Dame Cathedral in the heart of the City of Light.
The stone-and-wood find is thought to be a fragment of the ramparts of Lutetia – the ancient name for Paris – built by the Gallic Parisii tribe which lived along the river Seine in the Iron Age.
The Ile de la Cite has traditionally been regarded as the centre of Lutetia, but a rival theory, backed by archaeological research, contends that it was in Nanterre, a suburb to the west.
Read moreParis neighbourhoods: Inside the historic 1st arrondissement
"We may be looking at one of the most important remains ever discovered for understanding Gallic Lutetia," Culture Minister Catherine Pegard said in a statement from her ministry which was sent to AFP.
"Scientific caution still requires that we verify its function and its chronology, but the convergence of evidence is particularly remarkable at this stage."
Lutetia was first mentioned in book seven of Roman leader Julius Caesar's "Gallic Wars" series, where it was said to be on an island in the river Seine – a vague description that has given rise to many theories about its location.
The wall, uncovered in the course of excavations beneath the Hotel-Dieu hospital, also bears traces of fire, which may correspond to Caesar's account that the Gauls set fire to their town before the Battle of Lutetia against the Romans.
Read moreArchaeological dig at Notre-Dame unearths 2,000 years of history
Through carbon dating technology, the charred evidence is estimated to date from 10-200 BC, the ministry said in its statement – a timeframe that includes the Battle of Lutetia in 52 BC.
The Ile de la Cité, home to Notre-Dame Cathedral, is the largest island in the river Seine in the Paris region and became the centre of the Roman settlement of Lutetia.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

They Used Gas and Beat a Man: Three Military Recruitment Office Employees Detained in Rivne Region

Details

Bentley launches first fully electric car – with fake engine sounds to replace classic growl
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:15:55 UTC
03:15:55 KST

Bentley is launching its first fully electric car – complete with a drum soundtrack to replace the growl of a combustion engine – as part of a £350m investment in its UK business.
The vehicle, an SUV called the Torcal, is Bentley’s cheapest, starting at £173,000, and will be built at its factory in Crewe, securing the jobs of the 4,000 workers there.
Bentley hopes to win over both EV refuseniks and younger customers with a new synthetic engine noise built from drum recordings based on its old eight-cylinder engines. The feature is designed to give “emotion to the car” and “bridge the gap” to new buyers, said Bentley’s chief executive, Frank-Steffen Walliser.
“We expect a younger clientele,” he added, pointing to a more muscular vehicle body shape than previous models and the comparatively low price, which gives “easier access” to the brand, whose cars can cost up to £1.7m for one-off vehicles built to be showstoppers for billionaires.
The Torcal launches into a thin market for fully electric luxury SUVs. Arch-rival Rolls-Royce’s only EV is a two-door coupe called the Spectre, which starts at about £330,000. The recently announced Range Rover Electric – considered part of the premium segment rather than luxury – begins retailing at £154,070.
It also marks a more tentative entry into the EV market than Bentley once predicted. In 2024, it was forced to abandon plans to launch new electric cars each year from 2025 to 2030, citing poor demand.
Walliser said that while early indications showed demand would be strong in the UK, Europe and the Middle East, he admitted: “We managers always say we know but to be honest we don’t know [how much demand there will be].”
There are “no plans at the moment” for a second EV launch, he added. “I revised so many long-term plans in the last 10 years that one has to be careful of it.”
It is the third big funding announcement in just over a week for Britain’s automotive sector. Nissan has said it will invest £170m to build a new model at its factory in Sunderland, while McLaren will spend £500m on a new factory, creating 1,000 jobs and its first SUV.
However, carmakers remain under significant pressure from US tariffs, competition from Chinese rivals and high industrial energy costs. Jaguar Land Rover recently said it would cut 4,000 jobs, citing “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”, while Bentley’s owner, Volkswagen, is cutting 100,000 jobs by 2030.
Asked if Bentley was immune from the cuts at VW, Walliser said: “Immune would be the wrong wording. But there’s a very simple rule in Volkswagen. If you’re successful you can run your business. And we consider we are a successful business … it doesn’t bother me too much at the moment.”
Bentley itself cut 245 jobs in Crewe earlier this year to reduce costs, and sales have fallen by a third since a 2022 peak of 15,200 cars. Walliser said a period of strong margins after the pandemic was a “post-Covid boom … now we are back to normal”.
Walliser said headcount in Crewe will not grow with the investment “for profitability reasons”, but he insisted that “the statement cannot be clearer” about investing in the UK and that the money will partly go towards a new assembly line.
Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said it was the “third win in just seven days for our world-class automotive industry, which truly shows the confidence that businesses have in Britain”.
But Walliser said the landscape remained “difficult” for Bentley suppliers. “We see a lot of impact on especially the smaller businesses,” he said, citing new EU rules of origin and high industrial energy prices both in the UK and Europe. “There’s a lot of pressure,” he said.
The Torcal can travel up to 375 miles on a single charge, and can power up from 10% full to 80% full in 20 minutes using an ultra-fast charger. The car marks the fourth model in Bentley’s lineup, alongside the Continental, Flying Spur and Bentayga.

Bentley Wants Its Torcal SUV to Break the Curse of the Luxury EV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:15:00 UTC
03:15:00 KST

Bentley has taken the covers off its first-ever fully electric car, the Torcal, making it the automaker's fourth model line, joining the Continental GT, the Flying Spur sedan, and the Bentayga SUV. The luxury brand is confident about the launch, too, with Bentley chairman and CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser saying he believes “this is one of the best Bentleys ever.”
When WIRED first reported on the car in July, we said the EV would have more than 300 miles of range. Well, turns out it has considerably more: up to 375 miles (on the WLTP cycle, maybe 330 miles on EPA), and can charge from 10 to 80 percent in just 16 minutes at 400 kilowatts.
Prodigious performance from a motor on each axle sees the five-seat Torcal—smaller than the Bentayga and so perhaps more of an urban SUV—get 888 metric horsepower (PS) and 1,350 newton-meters (Nm) of torque in the sporting S models, resulting in 0 to 60 mph in as little as 2.9 seconds and a top speed of 162 mph. The “core" model drops to 821 PS and 1,194 Nm, with standstill to 60 mph in 3.4 seconds, and a max of 155 mph.
However, luxury brands get worried about their existing client bases when they switch to electric vehicles—look to Ferrari as a prime example—so it's no surprise that Bentley is keen to point out how this new model embodies the finest elements of the brand, just like every other high-end marque does going into electrification. “The Torcal is a Bentley first and foremost," says the launch literature. “In every aspect of its design, technology, craftsmanship, materials, and sustainability, it is a template for future Bentleys, regardless of powertrain.”
The reason for leaning into brand heritage is obvious on dealership lots. The first-ever EV Bentley will roll off the production line into a decidedly twitchy luxury auto market where Lamborghini shelved its Lanzador electric GT—with CEO Stephan Winkelmann stating demand among its buyers was “going almost to zero, if not to zero”—and Mercedes-Benz selling just 1,450 of its electric G Wagen in Europe through April 2025. Rolls-Royce Spectre sales are down nearly by half, with the brand hoping that a model refresh will turn things around.
And make no mistake that the Torcal is aiming for the luxury dollar. At $218,000 or £173,300 for the base model, and $258,200 or £199,300 for the First Edition S, this EV is priced higher than the Range Rover Electric, which has a similar range and starts in the US at $138,000. But a fairer comparison to the Torcal would be the Range Rover Electric Autobiography model, which clocks in at $208,000. Keep that in mind, and it's easy to see that Bentley is trying to take market share from JLR with its new SUV: Spend an extra $10,000, people, and you can drive off in an electric Bentley instead of a Range Rover.
At 4,983 mm long (161 mm shorter than a Bentayga) and 2,016 mm in width, the Torcal is not far off the size of the Range Rover Electric, but the most drastic difference is in height. The Range Rover Electric towers over the Torcal by nearly 20 centimeters. Also, while Bentley insists the Torcal has off-road chops, it's probably safe to say the Range Rover Electric will have it pipped there.
Where Bentley wants the Torcal to pull ahead is in the luxury refinements. Despite being smaller than its stablemate, the Torcal is a powerful, purposeful-looking SUV, with a switchable glass sunroof and newly designed light clusters, which are particularly evident at the rear. Unlike the Bentayga, the Torcal roofline drops down at the back for better aero efficiency.
At the front, undoubtedly the most striking visual element of the car is the new Torcal grille: Ventilation to a traditional radiator no longer needed, the upright front is now a solid wall of illuminated acrylic “crystals” that light up as you approach, and on a night in a rearview mirror on a freeway or mountain road will be deliberately unsubtle, and a far cry from quiet luxury.
Inside, Bentley continues to ram home the high-end message. All-round power doors open up to reveal a mixture of OLED screens and physical switchgear. The central display curves pleasingly downward, reminiscent of the new Cayenne, but there is deliberately no separate passenger screen option.
Bentley brought in Fox Brothers to engineer a wool tough enough to be used to panel some of the interior, which is apparently a world first. An attractive new wood finish developed for the Torcal is formed from 1,000 layers of walnut off-cuts and recycled paper pressed together, then sliced to less than a millimeter thick. The Torcal has new massage and power-folding seats, and an optional Naim 1,780-watt sound system with 28 speakers including seat shakers and headrest speakers, as well as Dolby Atmos 7.1.
What's impressive is the digital trickery Bentley has employed in both audio and visual manners—mirroring the crystal switchgear, Bentley has created animations on the screens that show light passing through cut glass. After trying to do this completely with computer animation, it was decided the effect was not real enough, as the model could not account for minute imperfections in the glass that subtly affect the light patterns cast. So Bentley had to film these animations using real crystal instead. The effect of the central console and instrument panel is striking.
Then to address the sticky issue of driving sound for a pure EV, instead of creating a digital replica of combustion, Bentley decided to shun electronic imitation and re-create the rhythm of a Bentley V8 using real instruments (including drums, viola, and bass guitar) to create a soundscape that, like the glass animations, had subtle variations and tiny imperfections.
Now, this sounds like it might be a terrible idea, but on the very limited demo WIRED heard, it's actually remarkably convincing and will supposedly provide genuine aural feedback to the driver, rather than simply approximately imitating engine notes. Mercifully, for those not looking to keep things rooted in combustion, it can be turned off if you wish. Bentley even went as far as to record indicator sounds (a hammer striking a leather surface) and the digital assistant wake note (the sound of a crystal glass as you run your finger around the rim).
Bentley has thrown in more tech as well: an augmented reality head-up display; a Refresh mode that uses light and air for a “more invigorating” cabin environment; face recognition so the Torcal can set itself up for individual drivers; mobile phone keys; some 25 radars, sensors, and cameras for assisted driving systems; and space detection, where if another car is encountered on a narrow road, the Torcal can automatically reverse to a point it’s already identified to let the car pass.
None of this is, in the world of automotive, groundbreaking anymore. Chinese brands are coming for the SUV sector as well, and are offering much more for much less. Take a look at Xiaomi's new SkyNomads. These stacked SUVs are coming to Europe next year and will massively undercut both Bentley and Range Rover. They have more range, more features, and crucially are thinking about car interiors in genuinely new ways, adding built-in projector systems and seating systems that are reconfigurable. The SkyNomad even has a heated floor, for heaven's sake.
Walliser has a simple answer to this threat from Asia, a threat that is contributing to Bentley's parent Volkswagen Group now cutting 50,000 jobs (though Bentley is doing well financially), and that is to lean into the one thing that Chinese brands cannot copy or improve: heritage. Bentley, founded in 1919, has bags of it. Will it be enough to secure its continued commitment to full-electric cars? Hopefully. But WIRED's not sure that's a winning tactic for the long term.

In his UN General Assembly speech, Iran's president also accused the US and Israel of illegal attacks on civilians as the US delegation walked out. He closed with a direct message to Trump: "Yes they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee."
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the UN General Assembly on Wednesday that Iran had been the victim of terrorism and not its perpetrator, in an address that pushed back against US President Donald Trump's threat a day earlier to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic.
Pezeshkian's speech marked a striking instance of a foreign leader addressing the world body while their country is at war with the host nation.
He opened by holding up photographs of children killed in a missile strike on the Shajarat al-Tayyiba school in Minab on the first day of the war, which resulted in the deaths of 156 people, and of the late Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in the same opening salvo. He also referenced a US strike on a sports hall the same day.
"The US president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism," Pezeshkian said.
"We only seek to live independently. Are we the sources of instability? Those who are committing terrorism and committing crimes, are they the protectors of peace and stability?"
He accused the US and Israel of illegal attacks on Iranian civilians and infrastructure, saying Iran sought military capability solely for self-defence and had no intention of attacking other states.
The US delegation left the chamber as he spoke.
'We did not bend the knee'
Pezeshkian said Iran would not accept that "nuclear knowledge should be the exclusive preserve of a few countries" and described the dispute over its nuclear programme as having no military solution.
Pezeshkian addressed Israel directly, saying "The atomic bomb is in Israel, but the inspectors are in Iran" and "Israel kills, but Iran is sanctioned."
On the Strait of Hormuz, he said Iran would not allow its right to navigation "even in our own waters" to be taken away.
Addressing the broader Middle East region, he said, "No one in this region will enjoy security alone. Either we will build security together, or we will endure insecurity together."
He closed with a direct message to Trump. "It must be understood by Mr Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force," he said.
"Yes they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee."
He claimed Iran had not struck civilian populations, a statement contradicted by documented deaths among mariners and civilians in Iranian attacks across the region since the war began.
US and Israeli officials blasted the speech, saying that it was hypocritical for the Islamic Republic to present itself as the victims of the world.
“I don’t know what standing Iran has to lecture anyone on human rights or the international system when they habitually violate it," US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters after Pezeshkian's address.
On Tuesday, Trump had told the same General Assembly, "Will a deal be made with Iran... or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly?"
After the speech, he told reporters a meeting between his envoys and Iranian counterparts had been "a very good meeting," adding the Iranian side was "not the highest level, but it's something."
Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei dismissed the talks, saying there had been "nothing new" in the exchange.
Rubio echoed that sentiment Wednesday, saying that “it was a continuation of conversations that have occurred in the past.”
“If there’s an opportunity to exchange ideas and messages, we will. And that’s what largely yesterday was, it was positive in that regard," he said. "But ultimately, I don’t want to mischaracterise this as a major breakthrough."
