Russia fabricates Dobropillia encirclement to strengthen its case for Kyiv’s capitulation at UN – ISW
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:13:32 UTC
03:13:32 KST

Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed on 22 September 2026 that it had surrounded Dobropillia, but the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) found no evidence to support the announcement. Dobropillia is a small town in Donetsk Oblast, known as the "pearl of the Donbas" for its coal industry, which has helped make Ukraine's Fortress Belt cities, holding the region from Russians since 2014, per RBC Ukraine.
Ukraine’s Vivaldi counteroffensive in Donetsk Oblast broke the northern arm of Russia’s plan to surround the fortified cities. ISW says Moscow’s Dobropillia claim diverts attention from that setback and portrays Ukrainian defenses as collapsing during the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, held on 21-28 September. The institute says Russia is likely spreading such claims to support its push for Ukraine’s capitulation.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian officers say Russian assault groups are still trying to break through toward Dobropillia, but have made no major gains.
Russia’s encirclement claim clashes with Ukrainian battlefield reports
Russia’s Ministry of Defense has claimed its troops were advancing toward Oleksandrivka, a village northwest of Dobropillia, but published no map to support its account.
At the same time, Ukrainian military observer Kostyantyn Mashovets said Ukrainian troops still held positions south and northeast of the city, which the experts said was inconsistent with the claimed encirclement.
ISW reported that a Ukrainian artillery reconnaissance battalion chief of staff said on 22 September that Russia had made no major advances near Dobropillia. He said Russian commanders kept postponing deadlines because of heavy losses and a gap between their plans and battlefield conditions.
A Ukrainian battalion officer said Russian troops were still trying to slip through Ukrainian lines in small groups.
How Dobropillia fits Russia’s plan to surround the fortress belt
Dobropillia is a transport hub on the southwestern approach to Ukraine’s “fortress belt,” which includes Kostiantynivka, Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk, and Sloviansk. These cities have anchored Ukraine’s defense in Donetsk Oblast since 2022.
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps commander, Andrii Biletskyi, whose corps is conducting the Vivaldi counteroffensive north of Lyman, explained that Russian forces advancing through Dobropillia were meant to join another force coming from north of Lyman, behind the fortified cities, encircling them rather than attacking them head-on.
ISW had already assessed on 16 September that Vivaldi had made the two-sided plan infeasible. In its 22 September report, ISW said Russia’s false claim about Dobropillia partly aims to divert attention from those Ukrainian gains.
Russian assaults toward Dobropillia continue
The setback north of Lyman has not stopped Russia’s push toward Dobropillia. Ukrainian staff sergeant Dmytro Davydenko reported on 14 September a sharp increase in assault groups moving toward the city, sometimes more than his unit could engage. He said Ukrainian troops had mined, blocked, or destroyed the main approaches.
ISW reported that Russia was preparing armor and drone support for possible assaults using armored vehicles this fall. A Ukrainian battalion officer said fog might help Russia move that equipment, although Ukrainian reconnaissance and drones would make it difficult. He said Russian glide bombs continued to strike infrastructure in the area.

Year ago, only 12 Ukrainian brigades could order weapons online. Now, 500 units participate in revolutionary program that has delivered 1.3 million drones to front
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:11:15 UTC
03:11:15 KST

A year ago, 12 Ukrainian brigades could order their own weapons off a state marketplace. Now, more than 500 units can. DOT-Chain Defense, which lets frontline units order necessary supplies using state funds or bonuses with just a few clicks, has scaled across most of Ukraine's Defense Forces, the Defense Ministry said.
The platform is the delivery backbone of Ukraine's soldier-led procurement revolution. It lies in a shift in the philosophy of defense procurement. Ukraine is abandoning the Soviet principle of "fight with whatever is handed down from above" and transitioning to a market-based model that centers on the choice of the individual soldier.
Over its first year, it has put more than 1.3 million drones and other systems into units' hands, worth about $1.9 billion, and the orders show what this war runs on: 84 percent are drones, with electronic-warfare gear and ground robots making up most of the rest. It is also the engine behind the points-for-kills system that lets units bank credit for battlefield results and spend it on their own equipment.
Access jumps from 12 to 500 units
The growth has been steep. DOT-Chain Defense is now used by combat units across the armed forces, the National Guard, the border and special transport services, the police, the Security Service, and Defense Intelligence, says Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik.
Assault regiments and the "Drone Line" project have joined, ordering unmanned systems to their own specifications.
Drones dominate the orders
By the ministry's count, electronic-warfare systems make up 8.6 percent of everything ordered, ground robotic complexes 7.2 percent, and ammunition a sliver at 0.2 percent.
The gear, worth about $1.9 billion, came both through direct marketplace purchases and through the "Army of Drones. Bonus" program, the points system tied to the same platform.
The US copies the model
The approach has drawn imitators. The US has launched its own Amazon-style marketplace for military drones, explicitly modeled on Ukraine's Brave1 Market and DOT-Chain Defense. For Ukraine, the payoff is data: a running record of which weapons work on which part of the front, which the state uses to scale up what performs.

Palestinian villagers wailed over the mangled remains of their olive trees on Wednesday after Israeli forces uprooted them with bulldozers, days ahead of the annual olive harvest, normally a source of joy for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Abd Alfattah Tamimi, who owns an olive grove on village land near Ramallah city, watched as a military bulldozer smashed the top of one of his trees and then tore its roots from the ground.
"All our olive trees, including the newly planted ones, were uprooted. Also our neighbours', they uprooted them all," Tamimi said, adding that he and his neighbours own nearly 9 acres of land filled with olive trees.

Palestinian human rights groups reject this, saying the destruction in effect deprives Palestinian farmers of income from the sale of olives and olive oil while uprooting trees they view as a symbol of their connection to the land.
The olive harvest usually begins in the first week of October. Olives are the backbone of Palestinian agriculture, a sector that accounts for around 8 percent of GDP and more than 60,000 jobs, according to the Palestinian Authority's agriculture ministry.
Palestinian activists and farmers expect this year's harvest to be particularly volatile, amid a record surge in illegal Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians and Palestinian resources in the territory.
Nather Tamimi, another landowner in the area of Deir Nizam village near Ramallah, said the loss of the trees was particularly painful in that it came so close to the start of the harvest.
"From this land, my brothers and I produce 120 drums of olive oil. Our neighbours produce the same," said Tamimi, speaking while looking over his olive grove.
"They uprooted trees everywhere, even between the houses," he said.

After meeting with Trump on Sept 22, Zelensky said that Washington and Kyiv want the war with Russia to end “before winter.”
While the United States and Russian presidents have spoken by telephone on various occasions, the last time they met was in 2025.
On a separate note about the conflict in the Middle East, Rubio warned on Sept 23 that the last thing Israel or the wider region needed was for the West Bank to become a new crisis.
“The last thing Israel needs or the region needs is an additional crisis or an additional friction point, we understand that that’s the case and that’s what’s happening,” Rubio said. AFP

"Hear the cry for help" — Sybiha, at the UN, called on the world to save the residents of Oleshky from a humanitarian catastrophe
Kyiv • UNN
About 2,000 people remain in occupied Oleshky without stable supplies of food and medicine. Sybiha called for pressure to be put on Russia.
Ukraine's Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha called on the world to pressure russia so that the aggressor country would open humanitarian corridors and allow the residents of Oleshky in the Kherson region, who are currently suffering from artificially induced starvation, to be rescued. The head of the relevant ministry made the statement from the podium during his address on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, where the Sixth Summit of the International Crimea Platform was held, UNN reports.
If you remember only one thing from this meeting — remember Oleshky. Hear their cry for help. Demand that russia open humanitarian corridors
What is the situation in Oleshky at present
As of September 23, 2026, Oleshky remains under Russian occupation. The situation in the city is currently critical due to shortages of food and medicine, problems with utility and medical infrastructure, and the absence of a safe mechanism for evacuating civilians.
According to the Ukrainian authorities, around 2,000 people currently remain in Oleshky itself. Before the full-scale invasion, the city's population was approximately 24,000. Dozens of minors are among those still in the city.
One of the most acute problems remains the provision of food. According to the UN Monitoring Mission, there have been no confirmed regular deliveries of food to Oleshky since the end of May. Ukrainian officials and volunteers also report an acute shortage of food, medicines, and other essential goods. The situation with utility infrastructure also remains difficult. The city has serious problems with electricity and gas supplies, and a significant part of the infrastructure facilities has been damaged or destroyed.
Access to medical care is also extremely limited. According to the Ukrainian side, only a few medical workers remained at the local hospital in mid-September. The medical facility's full operation is hampered by shortages of medicines and disruptions to electricity and water supplies.
The evacuation of the population remains a separate problem. As of September 23, no organized humanitarian corridor from Oleshky is operating. The Ukrainian side had previously worked out the technical conditions for conducting an evacuation; however, according to Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, the Russian side did not confirm its readiness to carry out a humanitarian operation. According to him, hundreds of people requiring assistance to leave the occupied territory have already been verified. Leaving independently is also associated with a high level of risk. Roads and adjacent areas may be mined, while extensive destruction makes movement more difficult. There have been reports of people attempting to leave the occupied territory on foot.
What else did Ukraine's Foreign Minister discuss at the UN General Assembly
Given the event's subject matter, Sybiha first addressed the issue of Crimea, which russia annexed back in 2014. He emphasized that the occupation and militarization of the peninsula pose a direct threat to the security of the Black Sea region.
"russia is using occupied Crimea as a base for attacks on Ukraine, and its further militarization poses a threat to the entire Black Sea region," the head of Ukraine's Foreign Ministry emphasized," — Ukraine's Minister of Foreign Affairs emphasized.
After that, he turned to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by the armed forces of the russian federation, which has continued since February 2022.
"This is not a Ukrainian war. It is not even a European war. It is a global threat. Preventing the worst-case scenario depends on everyone in this room — and far beyond it," Sybiha told listeners from the podium.
The Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine clearly expressed the position of official Kyiv: the war must end, and this must happen without delay. The ceasefire, which was supported by 14 of the 15 members of the UN Security Council, should have been the first step toward this. However, Russia, which in the view of the head of the relevant ministry still illegally occupies a seat in the organization as the successor state to the USSR, blocked this proposal.
"Russia is vetoing not only a ceasefire. Russia is vetoing peace," Andrii Sybiha summed up.
Let us remind you
More than 50 UN member states, as well as the EU, called on Russia to agree to a ceasefire and peace negotiations with Ukraine. They also demand the return of civilians and prisoners of war.

UNGA –Joint Statement by the Founding States of the Global Initiative to…
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:07:38 CEST
03:07:38 KST

UNGA –Joint Statement by the Founding States of the Global Initiative to Galvanise Political Commitment to International Humanitarian Law Humanitarian action International law Joint statement On : September 23rd 2026 I am joined today by my esteemed colleagues to address you on behalf of Brazil, China, France, Kazakhstan, South Africa, and my own country Jordan. Two years ago, together with the International Committee of the Red Cross, we launched the Global Initiative to galvanize political commitment to international humanitarian law (IHL). Today we have come together to renew our call to action. The toll of today’s armed conflicts is unconscionable, and there is no time to lose. Civilians in more than 130 armed conflicts across the world face unacceptable realities. Hospitals, schools and homes are more and more often being treated as battlefields. These patterns are not inevitable casualties of war; they are, too often, deliberate choices to disregard the rules designed to protect people caught up in war. The world must not accept such suffering and destruction. It is possible to change course, and state leaders hold such a power. That is why, at the invitation of His Majesty King Abdullah II, the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan will host the High-Level Conference to Uphold Humanity in War on 7 December 2026. Building on the work undertaken through the Global IHL Initiative, the conference will gather state leaders to reaffirm their collective commitment to IHL and translate the momentum generated into action. In this spirit and following broad consultations, a concise and inclusive political declaration will be issued by states at the conference. We invite all states to join the Initiative and all participating states to attend the conference at the highest level. To date, 118 states from all regions of the world have joined the Global IHL Initiative. Twenty-seven of these states have co-led seven thematic workstreams, developing practical guidance on increasing respect for IHL and addressing the challenges posed by contemporary warfare. This guidance builds on a consistent theme that emerged from states throughout the process: the need to preserve and give effect to the protective purpose of IHL. The Global IHL Initiative addresses issues relevant to contemporary armed conflicts and stakeholders worldwide, seeking to ensure the impartial, consistent and universal application of existing IHL obligations. It acknowledges that states bear the primary responsibility for upholding, implementing and applying the Geneva Conventions in all circumstances, including in situations of occupation. Gathered in New York today, we also recognize the important role played by the United Nations and the wider multilateral system in promoting respect for IHL and supporting its effective implementation. Since their adoption in 1949, the Geneva Conventions have helped to protect the lives and dignity of millions of people. However, the suffering witnessed in today’s armed conflicts around the world is a stark reminder that the most fundamental rules of these conventions are not being respected. We call on all world leaders to unite around this shared responsibility at the High-Level Conference in Jordan. The world cannot stand idly by as the basic tenets of international humanitarian law are routinely and systematically violated. We can put an end to the inconceivable and unconscionable suffering and destruction that characterize today's conflicts and work towards peaceful resolutions. Together, we must uphold humanity in war.

Israel's Liberman wants Jordan to run parts of occupied W. Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:07:19 UTC
03:07:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's Liberman wants Jordan to run parts of occupied West Bank
Leader of the Israeli right-wing party Yisrael Beytenu, Avigdor Liberman, suggested on Wednesday that Jordan take control of parts of the occupied West Bank, drawing criticism from several prominent Israeli politicians, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
In an interview with the Israeli right-wing podcast B’Sheva, Liberman proposed transferring security and administrative responsibility for Areas A and B of the West Bank to Jordan, accusing the Palestinian Authority (PA) of having become “bankrupt”.
Referring to the Israeli-occupied West Bank by its biblical names "Judea and Samaria", which are not internationally recognised, Liberman insisted that Jordan should “take security and administrative responsibility”, adding that Amman has “no choice” and could either deploy its military or establish forces under Jordanian command.
The comments have since drawn responses from figures on the Israeli right, including Netanyahu, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Defence Minister Israel Katz, who all criticised the former defence minister’s proposal.
Netanyahu accused Liberman of moving politically to the left and demanded that he withdraw the proposal.
“Liberman, I knew that you were on the left ever since you established a government with [United Arab List party leader] Mansour Abbas,” Netanyahu wrote on social media.
“I know you’re on the left since you’ll establish a government with [Gadi] Eisenkot, Yair Golan, [Naftali] Bennett and the Arab parties. But I never believed you would suggest today that the Jordanian army rule over territories in the Land of Israel. Retract your statement immediately!”
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich also condemned Liberman’s proposal, accusing him of seeking to relinquish Israeli control over the West Bank.
“Listen to Liberman: Someone who presents himself as a right-winger is proposing that we give up our security responsibility in Judea and Samaria and hand it over to the Jordanians,” Smotrich said. “Liberman wants to return Israel to the days of the Jordanian Legion. We must not let that happen.”
Defence Minister Israel Katz also criticised Liberman, further accusing the politician of seeing himself “as a candidate for a rotating premiership” over the proposal.
“Until recently, he proposed that Israel unilaterally withdraw from Gaza and hand Gaza and the Philadelphi Corridor smuggling route over to Egypt,” Katz said. “Now, he is proposing to station a Jordanian army in Qalqilya, near Route 6, and hand Jordan security and administrative control over all Areas A and B in Judea and Samaria, even though Jordan’s declared policy is the establishment of a Palestinian state.”
Following the criticism, Liberman responded that “the only one who declared his willingness to establish a Palestinian state is Benjamin Netanyahu”, referring to the premier’s 2009 speech at Bar-Ilan University in Israel’s Ramat Gan.
The Israeli opposition politician further expanded on his proposal, arguing that Israel should create territorial continuity between all parts of Area C and maintain complete control there, while finding an alternative to the Palestinian Authority’s security and administrative control in Areas A and B.
“I strongly oppose Israel managing the lives of Palestinians in Nablus, Jenin or Tulkarm,” he said. “Therefore, in order to prevent a vacuum that Hamas, Islamic Jihad and other terrorists will enter, an agreement must be reached with Jordan for them to manage Areas A and B, an Israeli-Jordanian confederation.”
The New Arab approached Jordan’s Foreign Ministry for a response to the comments but had not received a response by the time of publication.
The proposal is not the first time Liberman has advocated a Jordanian administrative role in Palestinian areas of the West Bank.
In an interview with Israel’s Ynet News in January 2025, he proposed an arrangement under which Jordan would administer Areas A and B, while Israel would retain control over Area C.
The proposal built on an earlier plan he presented in 2024, under which Jordan would take responsibility for Area A while Egypt would assume responsibility for the Gaza Strip.
On Tuesday, Jordan’s King Abdullah II addressed the UN General Assembly, where he sharply criticised Israeli policies in the West Bank.
“What was once a creeping process has exploded into something far more aggressive,” he said.
The Jordanian king warned of escalating Israeli settler violence in the occupied territory, as well as “land seizures”, settlement expansion and the “forcible transfer” of Palestinians.
He also criticised Israel’s “expansionist appetite”, warning that its military presence in southern Syria posed a regional threat.
His comments came amid continued Israeli military activity in Syria following Israel’s incursion into the country in December 2024 after the fall of the Assad regime.
“This Israeli government's appetite is now a regional threat,” King Abdullah II said. “And today, Syria is the warning.”

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP, keynote speech at UK Space Power Conference
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:05:54 BST
03:05:54 KST

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP, keynote speech at UK Space Power Conference
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting highlighting the importance of space to national security and daily life in the UK.
I’m mindful that I’m at an RAF conference and people may have seen the news this lunchtime so I thought I would just give an update on the crash in the vicinity of RAF Valley in Anglesey this afternoon. A T2 Hawk aircraft went down shortly after take-off, both crew members ejected as you may have seen. I’m glad to say they’ve now been taken to hospital for treatment. And of course, we’re investigating how and why this happened. But for now, our best wishes go to the crew along with our hopes for a speedy recovery.
Turning to the focus of your conference today, let me start with a health warning. I’m mindful of you being talked at all day. I’m a huge Star Trek fan. And so I’ve been very much looking forward to speaking to you today. I know you’ve heard lots of speeches, but we’re near the end, so hopefully you can Klingon. Sorry, there is more.
Joking aside for now, there is no getting away from the fact that we are living in a time of enormous instability and uncertainty. Our adversaries are probing us and testing us on a daily basis. Russia is waging war in Europe. China is reshaping the economic and technological order. Old alliances can no longer be taken for granted. And the threats we face are growing and getting closer to home.
So, against this backdrop, keeping our country safe, the first duty of any government is a greater and more urgent responsibility than it has been for generations. And so my overriding priority as Defence Secretary is to make sure that we build this country’s deterrence and readiness, to be ready, willing and capable of defeating an adversary so that they think twice about attacking us in the first place. That’s not a new idea, but what it takes to maximise and maintain deterrence in the 21st century is changing, because the threats to our security are evolving.
Hostile states buzz our airspace, they map our undersea cables and encroach on our waters, their hackers attack our infrastructure and our institutions, and they threaten us in and from space. Control of the waves was the essential ingredient in 19th century deterrence. That is why Britain built the finest naval power in history. In the 20th century it was control of the skies and so we built a world-class air force to protect us. This century will depend on control of space and so our job is to make sure that our deterrence in space is as strong as our deterrence here on Earth and to modernise our armed forces so that they’re ready to deter and if necessary defeat any adversary and in any domain.
Thanks to the cultural influences of science fiction, people instinctively see space as something of the future. But science facts matter here and now. Our national security, our economic power, most of our daily lives rely on software and hardware hundreds and thousands of miles above us. Space systems are critical to the effectiveness and capability of our armed forces. They’re what give us an operational advantage by enabling our forces to understand, communicate, move and fight as one.
There is no integrated force without space. Satellites are critical to intelligence gathering and missile warnings. They also underpin almost a fifth of the UK economy. We depend on them from everything from weather forecasts, energy supplies and financial transactions to Sat Navs, mobile phone connections and Amazon deliveries. Many people in this room would not have found their way here today without everyday technology that relies on space. The loss of GPS alone would cost our economy £1.4 billion a day.
The loss of everyday conveniences would undermine our daily freedoms and trust in our institutions. If you think that sounds like a bit of a leap, think how we react to the disruption when airports go offline or a train is suspended or mobile banking goes down. A minor inconvenience today can quickly become a long-standing grievance tomorrow. The kind of thing that takes people from the belief that things are unreliable to the conviction that things just don’t work anymore.
And that is the territory upon which populism thrives, which is what our adversaries are intent on fertilising in our country. So, our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries. The threat is growing in scale, speed and sophistication, and challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics here on Earth.
Our adversaries are investing heavily in weaponry that can take out our satellite systems and technology. Between 2019 and 2021, the combined Chinese and Russian operational satellite fleets grew by 70%. This year, it was revealed that two Russian satellites had intercepted the communications of at least a dozen European ones since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. What this shows is that not only do our adversaries have the capability to threaten our national interests and national security, they also unsurprisingly have the intent and that requires us to act.
We know that there are many challenges in defence and that in some areas we are not where we need to be. That’s why we’ve made the biggest investment in defence since the Cold War, with more to come. But at the same time, we should acknowledge that our space operations are already world leading.
We have a number of tools in our arsenal that give us access and freedom of action in space, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities, deep space radar, satellite communications and more.
And one of the joys of the last nine weeks or so in this job has been seeing some of that in action, the extraordinary people, technology and operations that we carry out every day. We can be extraordinarily proud of what defence is capable of doing and there are lots of things I’ve seen in the last nine weeks that I would dearly love to show the public because they genuinely make you proud to be British.
We can be proud of the fact that this small island off the northwest coast of Europe continues to punch above its weight in the world, whether on science and innovation or indeed the capability that we provide even to a great superpower like the United States.
But it’s important to get the balance right, to be self-confident enough, to be proud of what we have, and to be self-aware enough to acknowledge that we know we need to do more. Britain has to keep pace in the new space race, making sure we have the capabilities to control space, defend our assets, and if required, deny the use of space to hostile states.
This was recognised in the Strategic Defence Review, which for the first time put space on a par with land, sea and air as conflict domains. It was also recognised in the Defence Investment Plan, which earmarks more than £3 billion to space capabilities over the first four years. The UK Space Strategy, launched earlier this month, takes this further and puts defence and national security centre stage.
Earlier today, we announced the formation of the UK’s first ever squadron dedicated to our Control of Space mission. Despite my best efforts, the Chief of the Air Staff declined my suggestion to call it Star Fleet Command. And so, No. 3 Space Effects Squadron it is, and what a ring it has to it.
It will have, though, the ability to conduct offensive and defensive operations, to strengthen deterrence, reduce opportunities for coercion and enhance the resilience of our space capabilities. It will also disrupt, degrade and deny hostile activity and defend UK interests in space and on Earth. This new squadron will make sure that our armed forces can protect the satellites our country depends on, deter those who would threaten them and operate with confidence in an increasingly contested domain. Its mission supports our ongoing development of capabilities for orbital warfare, electronic warfare and counter-satellite weapons, all designed with deterrence in mind.
We cannot afford to make the cliché mistake of fighting the last war. More importantly, we would be wrong to prepare only to fight a current war. The rapid advances in battlefield technology and tactics we see in Ukraine is our warning. It would be foolish not to learn the lesson. Things are moving at warp speed. We have to be ready for space as the next battleground, and we are also clear that any capability we have will always be deployed responsibly and consistent with the UK’s commitment to a safe, secure and sustainable space domain. As on Earth, we do not seek conflict, we simply seek to defend our country, our interests, our values and our allies through deterrence.
Those alliances are paramount. None of what we hope to achieve can we do alone. That’s not just true for the UK but for every country. The world is simply too complex and the challenge is too great. My predecessor but one, John Healey, set out a NATO first but not NATO only approach. I think that’s absolutely the right position. The NATO alliance is the cornerstone of Britain’s defence and security and we need a stronger United Kingdom for a stronger Europe for a stronger NATO. Our alliance’s greatest assets in the future are going to be adaptability and innovation.
That’s the lesson from Ukraine and what underpins our focus in space. We have the foundations to succeed. Our space sector is already one of the most creative, productive and commercially successful in the world. is worth around £20 billion and employees upwards of 55,000 people. Our scientists and engineers build instruments that peer to the edge of the universe and will service satellites in orbit. We must continue to push the frontier of defence innovation and nowhere is that more true than in space, the final frontier. And I promise that’s the last one.
Pushing the frontier of defence innovation means that we can sustain our advantage where we have it and build it where we do not. That means expanding Britain’s defence industrial base and deepening our partnerships with world leading businesses and research institutions. This is critical to our security and it also delivers the Prime Minister’s re-industrialisation agenda and his mission for growth in every postcode.
Investment in defence is investment in British industry, in British skills, and in British jobs, almost 70% of which are already outside London and the South East. Expanding our presence in space will provide more opportunities for young people, whether that’s in or out of uniform or in high school jobs and apprenticeships in digital technologies, working in industry as well as in public service, in AI and telecoms and in robotics, national security driving economic prosperity and opportunity, not just making our country better able to defend itself but also making sure we have a country that is worth defending in the eyes and experiences of its people.
So, our country and the NATO alliance are facing a profound challenge. Our security is under threat in a way we haven’t had to contend with for many years. Our adversaries are seeking to divide and undermine us and the risk of miscalculation is all too real. This is as much a challenge in space as anywhere else. This domain is critical to our national security, our military operations and our everyday lives.
And so faced with this new frontier of conflict, we’re putting defence and deterrence at the heart of our approach. We’re committed to peaceful and responsible activities in space, but we will not shy away from defending the interests so vital to our way of life.
And as we meet the threats, and mitigate the risks, we are also seizing the opportunities, cashing in on the defence dividend to re-industrialise our country, create jobs and rejuvenate our alliances. The new space age is here and the UK is ready. So, thank you very much for your hard work and support in this endeavour. Thank you.

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and US Secretary of State Marko Rubio met on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly’s High-Level Week to examine Kiev’s actions that lead to destabilization on energy markets, the Russian Foreign Ministry said.
During the meeting, Lavrov pointed to the need to mend Moscow-Washington relations.
In turn, Rubio admitted that a short-term or temporary ceasefire in Ukraine would not facilitate conflict settlement.
TASS gathered the sides’ key remarks about the recent meeting.
Russian Foreign Ministry’s statement
Discussing the Ukrainian conflict, Lavrov "drew attention to the close coordination between the Kiev regime and its European sponsors."
The ministry said that during the meeting, the sides "examined in detail Kiev’s destructive actions, including deliberate strikes against civilians and cross-border infrastructure, which destabilize global energy markets.
"The Russian side reaffirmed its unconditional commitment to achieving the goals of the special military operation, including through a political and diplomatic settlement of the conflict that addresses its root causes."
Fixing the Russia-US ties requires an honest dialogue to address the most pressing issues: "This requires an honest dialogue on removing 'irritants' and restoring normal working conditions for both countries’ diplomatic missions, including the return of Russian property in the US that has effectively been confiscated."
The Russian side also "stressed the need to restore bilateral relations to a sound footing as soon as possible, in accordance with the agreements reached by the presidents of Russia and the United States," particularly as "discussions intensify on prospects for economic cooperation, cultural and humanitarian exchanges, easier travel between the two countries, and closer ties between their societies and citizens."
Besides, Lavrov and Rubio discussed "the situation in the Middle East, the South Caucasus, Latin America and the Caribbean."
US remarks
Rubio and Lavrov discussed the Ukrainian conflict and bilateral relations in New York, the US Department of State said in a statement.
"Secretary of State Marco Rubio met today with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of UNGA [UN General Assembly]. The Secretary discussed·the Russia-Ukraine war·and the US-Russia bilateral relationship."
Rubio acknowledged that limited or temporary ceasefires in Ukraine would not lead to a settlement of the conflict: "I will say that war is not going to end on the battlefield. That war is going to end - I think everyone acknowledges - with a negotiated agreement, and we all understand that. And the sooner we can reach that agreement, the less things will be destroyed, and the less people are going to die on both sides. That's what the president wants."
In his opinion, both Russia and Ukraine show interest in a number of areas: "I think both sides have expressed an interest in some limited ceasefire that involves grain and energy [supplies]."
Rubio said that although "’it doesn't solve the war," but, in his view, may "potentially alleviate some of the global pressures" in some way.

====================================================================================================

The Pope’s AI Guy Is Worried About ‘Cartel’ Behavior Among Big Labs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:03:00 UTC
03:03:00 KST

Recently, warnings from researchers inside the world’s largest artificial intelligence labs about the rapid pace of development have led to panic about the possibility that the technology could extinguish humanity. Those warnings are predicated on the idea that—propelled by ferocious competition and a rivalry between the US and China—labs are barreling toward superintelligent models whose abilities will far surpass those of humans.
But according to Father Paolo Benanti, a priest who advises the Catholic Church on AI, the handwaving over superintelligence distracts from the need for open debate about how to constrain the companies building the technology. By casting the problem as so complex that only they can solve it, he says, the big labs exclude everyone else from the conversation.
“Ethics cannot be something that belongs to the board of trustees of a company. It’s something that has to be balanced, mitigated in debate in the public square.” Benanti tells WIRED. “We need democratic regulation.”
In an essay published on the heels of the safety warnings, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for new AI models to undergo mandatory third-party evaluations prior to release, and some sort of crackdown on distillation, a process where rival labs train their own AI on the outputs of proprietary models. Others have argued for a total ban on recursive self-improvement, where AI uses its advanced coding capabilities to help develop future iterations of itself.
Benanti is less interested in restricting methods for developing AI, which he fears could quash innovation, and more so in establishing standards that ensure models cannot slip from human control. Whatever shape those standards take, he says, they should not be designed by the labs.
“The narrative of the frontier labs is self-interested, to gain or maintain a position in the market,” says Benanti. When a small group of companies dictates the rules under which an industry operates, he says, “this has a really clear name: a cartel.”
It’s difficult to know how seriously to take grand pronouncements about the capabilities of the latest and future AI models, says Benanti, owing to the overlapping economic, political, and personal incentives at play.
While both OpenAI and Anthropic have supported calls for a slowdown in development, they’re also preparing to go public, and there are many billions of dollars at stake for whoever captures the market. The animosity between the US and China, where the most advanced AI models are being developed, also complicates the picture.
Anthropic declined to comment. OpenAI and Google DeepMind did not respond to requests for comment.
Benanti also takes issue with the way certain corners of the AI industry talk about superintelligence, with the kind of reverence typically reserved for a god: as sophisticated beyond our understanding, practically omnipotent. (OpenAI CEO Sam Altman once said he aspires to build a “magic intelligence in the sky.”) That kind of framing, Benanti says, threatens to skew the discourse about the technology.
“Are we talking about some-thing, or some-one? This is the real difference. It’s not a matter of faith, it’s a matter of mathematics,” he says. “We are not building the next divinity. We are simply deluding ourselves that there is something more than statistical computation [going on].”
By raising questions about what separates man and machine, and how to shield future generations from the negative effects of technology, the advent of AI has the potential to create “a new role for religions in public debate,” says Benanti. “Living the challenge of the time is part of the mission of the Church.”
Though Benanti is a member of the priesthood, he does not formally represent the Holy See, the governing body of the Catholic Church. Instead, he counsels the church in his capacity as a scholar of philosophy, theology, and technology. Benanti tells WIRED he uses AI to help create tools and materials for his university students, but declined to specify how Pope Leo XIV engages with the technology, if at all. (Benanti’s staff say he is bound by an “oath of secrecy.”)
In May, Pope Leo published his first-ever encyclical, a letter that applies religious teachings to the problems of the day and clarifies the position of the Church. He chose artificial intelligence as its subject.
In the letter, the Pope warned against the technocratic logic that runs through the AI industry, which presents “efficiency as the ultimate measure of value,” and casts human beings as “a project to be optimized.” He also called for international collaboration between rival superpowers and AI companies, who he said must set aside the “desire to secure geopolitical or commercial dominance” to ensure that the technology is developed in service of the common good. In one particularly prescient section, he warned of “the danger of humanity becoming a victim of its own achievements.”
The flap over superintelligence and existential risk threatens to distract from the ambitions laid out in the encyclical, says Benanti, by encouraging people to forfeit their say in the direction the technology should take to a small group of mathematicians, computer scientists, and executives at the big labs.
“The first thing is, we need to have brakes, and a wheel,” says Benanti. “That means a significant position of control for human beings over the machine.”

US Invites Putin To G20 Summit In Miami, Rubio Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:02:18 UTC
03:02:18 KST

NEW YORK -- The United States has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to attend the Group of 20 summit in Miami in December, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on September 23, as the Trump administration is seeking steps to reduce fighting in Ukraine.
“We've invited President Putin to the G20," Rubio told reporters after meeting Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. "We think it's an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president but with other world leaders.”
The invitation was the first public confirmation that Washington had invited Putin to the G20 leaders' summit. Russian officials have previously been invited to ministerial-level meetings.
Rubio said the summit could provide an opportunity for Putin and US President Donald Trump to meet; he later made clear to journalists that the meeting had not been agreed. The two leaders have spoken by phone several times since Trump returned to office in 2025, but Rubio said a face-to-face meeting would be more useful if it had a clearly defined outcome.
Before the Rubio-Lavrov meeting, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that a Trump-Putin summit would require preparatory work.
Rubio said Trump's willingness to meet adversaries was behind the decision to invite Putin.
“The president of the United States, this president, is willing to engage and meet with virtually anyone," he said. "If you only meet with people that you agree with, then these are very nice meetings, but nothing happens," Rubio added. "In order to solve problems, you have to meet with people that you disagree with.”
But Rubio cautioned against treating the invitation as evidence that a leaders' meeting or a broader agreement was imminent.
Proposed Energy Truce
Rubio's comments came as Washington was also pressing Moscow and Kyiv to consider a limited cease-fire covering attacks on energy infrastructure and possibly grain-related targets.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called for an end to attacks on energy facilities. After meeting Trump in New York on September 22, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was prepared to halt such strikes if Russia did the same. Reuters reported that an earlier understanding over energy targets had quickly collapsed after attacks resumed.
Rubio said the proposal had been discussed in recent US contacts with both sides, including by US envoy Steve Witkoff and presidential adviser Jared Kushner.
The secretary of state stressed that an energy truce would not amount to a peace agreement. "It doesn't solve the war," Rubio said but argued that it could reduce some of the consequences of the conflict and provide a possible basis for wider negotiations.
"Ultimately, we all want this war to end," he added.
Speaking later in the day during a UN Security Council meeting, Lavrov said Russia would not stop fighting while peace talks were under way.
"We will not pause the special military operation for the duration of negotiations, regardless of the format. Although Europe wants exactly that," he said.
The EU wants to "buy time and replenish the depleted military arsenals of the Kyiv regime," Lavrov added.
Different Targets
When pressed on why Washington was urging Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian energy facilities despite years of Russian strikes on Ukraine's power grid, Rubio acknowledged that the targets serve different purposes.
“When you come to energy for the Russian side, the energy strikes they're facing are [targeting] refineries and oil and gas [facilities]," he said. "For the Ukrainian side, energy means their electrical grid.”
Rubio said Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil infrastructure were aimed at reducing Moscow's revenue, while Russian strikes on Ukraine's power grid were directly affect electricity supplies and other basic services.
That distinction, he said, made an agreement harder to reach but did not make it less worthwhile. "That's why it's not easy overnight to just say let's reach an agreement," Rubio said. "But it's something that I think is worth investing in trying to make that happen."
Kyiv has stepped up attacks on Russian oil facilities in recent weeks, while Russia has continued strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
No Breakthrough With Lavrov
Rubio gave few details about his meeting with Foreign Minister Lavrov and did not announce any agreement.
The State Department said the two discussed the war in Ukraine and US-Russian relations. The meeting took place as Washington seeks to keep diplomatic channels open while testing whether Moscow and Kyiv can agree on limited measures to reduce the fighting.
The Kremlin has said there are currently no conditions for moving to formal peace negotiations, while also saying Putin remains open to contact with Trump.
Rubio also warned that the conflict could spill beyond Ukraine through sabotage, hybrid attacks, or an accident involving military forces.
"One of the concerns we have, among many, about the war between Russia and Ukraine is that it could metastasize and spread into other places," he said.
He cited the possibility of a hybrid or sabotage attack, or an incident involving military aircraft.
"It could grow into somewhere else, be it through a hybrid attack, be it through a sabotage attack, be it through a misunderstanding," Rubio said.
Washington has raised such concerns with European governments, he said, amid heightened fears that the war could generate new flashpoints outside Ukraine.

No pause in Ukraine conflict for peace talks – Lavrov
Moscow will not pause its special military operation while peace negotiations are underway, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday, asserting that a temporary ceasefire only benefits Kiev.
Ukraine and 51 of its allies released a statement on Wednesday demanding that Russia accept an “immediate and unconditional ceasefire” so that peace talks between Moscow and Kiev can take place. The statement, whose signatories included the EU and its member states, the UK, Canada, and Australia, was published before the security council met to discuss the conflict.
“We are not going to have a pause in our special military operation,” Lavrov said during the meeting. “Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause and it wants to use it to pump the Kiev regime with weapons.”

Ukraine and its allies issued their ceasefire demand less than four days after Ukrainian forces launched their largest-ever drone raid on the Russian capital. The attack killed two civilians in its suburbs and damaged an oil refinery, residential buildings, and civilian infrastructure. Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said the “unprecedented” raid involved more than 1,600 UAVs from all directions.
Throughout the conflict, Ukraine has repeatedly followed such attacks with appeals for ceasefire, which Russia has rebuffed. Moscow maintains that it will only cease military action when both sides seek a comprehensive settlement that addresses the root causes of the conflict.
Russia has dramatically stepped up its missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian military and dual-use infrastructure in recent months, in response to Vladimir Zelensky’s 40-day “influence campaign” of long-range strikes on civilian targets.
Zelensky’s stated aim was to foment discontent among the Russian public, but the campaign ultimately ended with the destruction of Ukraine’s Black Sea port infrastructure and an earlier-than-usual start to Russia’s winter campaign against its power plants and substations.
In a statement released after the latest drone raid on Moscow, the Russian Defense Ministry said that the Russian army would further “intensify its high-accuracy strikes against military targets in Kiev” in response.

Israel election committee bars Arab party lists, MKs from October vote
Israel’s Central Elections Committee has voted to disqualify Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, the United Arab List (UAL), the Joint List and Hadash MK Ofer Cassif from running in the 27 October election.
The decisions are not final and must be approved by the Supreme Court, which has overturned most such disqualifications in previous elections.
Israel’s Central Elections Committee is made up of lawmakers, with seats allocated to parties based on their share of the vote in the general election.
Abu Shehadeh
The committee said Abu Shehadeh had supported armed struggle by an enemy state or "terrorist organisation" against Israel and rejected Israel’s existence as a Jewish and "democratic state".
The petition against Abu Shehadeh was filed by National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit party. It cited an article the Balad chairman published a day after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack in southern Israel, in which he described the attack as "an important historic event militarily, politically and strategically".
Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza since then has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and devastated much of the enclave.
Abu Shehadeh said in a video statement that he would not back down.
"This development will not scare us," he said. "Racists are afraid of equality, and Ben Gvir and Netanyahu are afraid of the Arab vote in this electoral battle".
Adalah director Hassan Jabareen argued that the claim Abu Shehadeh supported armed struggle contradicted his decades of public and parliamentary activity. He said the article cited by petitioners contained no call for violence and instead called for a political solution.
United Arab List and Joint List
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, Ben Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit and the Choose Life Forum filed petitions against UAL.
Adalah attorney Suhad Bishara said the petitions against UAL relied on old evidence that had already been reviewed by Israel’s attorney general and security services, which she said had reached conclusions at odds with the claims made by the petitioners.
In 2021, UAL joined a short-lived coalition that ended Netanyahu’s 12-year run as prime minister.
The committee also voted to disqualify the Joint List, which includes Hadash and Balad and represents large sections of Israel’s Palestinian population - descendants of those who remained in Israel after it was created in 1948.
Adalah said the motion against the Joint List relied largely on outdated material, including bills from previous parliaments and positions that had already been examined by Israeli courts. It argued that the motion did not present the "critical mass" of evidence required under Supreme Court precedent.
A separate motion to disqualify Balad as a party was rejected on procedural grounds, according to Adalah, which represented the party before the committee.
Cassif
Cassif’s disqualification followed a petition filed by Likud and was based on the same grounds cited against the other candidates and lists.
A vocal critic of Israel’s war on Gaza, Cassif rejected the allegations during the hearing, calling them "politically motivated". He described the coalition’s portrayal of his opposition to government policy as "support for the enemy, disloyalty and harm to the state" as a "blatant distortion of reality".
Adalah attorney Ariel Remez said Israeli law did not permit barring a Knesset candidate simply for criticising the army and government over alleged war crimes or for supporting a Palestinian state alongside Israel.
In previous elections, the Supreme Court has overturned most attempts to disqualify candidates and parties. In 2019, however, it barred far-right candidate Michael Ben-Ari from running after the Central Elections Committee had approved his candidacy.
The Supreme Court is expected to hear challenges to the latest decisions next week.
Several other petitions are also being considered by the election committee at the Knesset on Wednesday and Thursday, with most challenges targeting Arab parties and candidates.

First fMRI study of mescaline reveals altered sensory filtering and brain networks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:00:28 UTC
03:00:28 KST

A new study has demonstrated that mescaline produced a distinctive pattern of brain changes in awake rats, reducing activity in the cerebellum while increasing communication between it and several other brain regions. The psychedelic also altered responses to a rewarding smell and changed the brain’s ability to filter sounds, with effects varying according to sound frequency. This research was reported in Neuroscience Bulletin.
Mescaline is a psychedelic compound found in cacti. Indigenous communities in the Americas have used mescaline-containing cacti ceremonially for thousands of years. Modern human studies suggest that mescaline can cause altered visual perception, changes in the sense of time and feelings of separation from one’s usual sense of self.
The drug activates serotonin receptors (specifically the 5-HT2A receptor), which are involved in perception, mood and thinking. LSD and psilocybin act on the same receptor, but research increasingly suggests that different psychedelics may produce different patterns of brain activity. Before the current study, little was known about mescaline’s direct effects on the brain.
The researchers were particularly interested in the cerebellum. It is best known for helping coordinate movement and balance, but it also contributes to attention, memory, emotional regulation and the processing of sensory information.
Led by corresponding author Craig F. Ferris of Northeastern University, the researchers studied 24 rats during the brain imaging portion of the study. Half received 50 milligrams of mescaline per kilogram of body weight, while the others received a control solution.
The rats were trained to tolerate the scanning procedure while awake. Researchers used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)—which measures brain activity by tracking changes in blood oxygen levels—to measure immediate changes in brain function, communication between brain regions at rest, and responses to the smell of almonds. Almond was used as a standardized rewarding odor, allowing the researchers to test how mescaline affected the brain’s response to a consistent positive sensory cue.
A separate experiment involved 16 rats to test sound filtering. The animals heard a quiet warning tone at 4, 12 or 20 kilohertz 100 milliseconds before a loud burst of white noise. This test measured prepulse inhibition, in which the warning tone normally reduces the animal’s startle response. The reduction in startle indicates how effectively the brain filters sensory information.
Mescaline reduced the volume of brain areas showing typical increases in activity in 26 of 169 examined regions, with the largest effects concentrated in the cerebellum. It also expanded the volume of areas showing suppressed activity in 33 regions. At the same time, the drug increased the number of functional connections across the brain. The cerebellum showed particularly strong connections with the hippocampus (which supports memory and context); the thalamus (which relays and organizes sensory information); the somatosensory cortex (which processes touch and bodily sensations); and the midbrain (which regulates alertness, motivation and reward).
The rats’ normal response to almond odor was also largely weakened. Brain activity linked to smell, touch and hearing was reduced, while visual regions were less affected. Sound filtering showed a more complicated pattern: prepulse inhibition improved at 4 and 20 kilohertz but worsened at 12 kilohertz.
Ferris, first author Noah Cavallaro, and their colleagues concluded that mescaline did not simply improve or impair sensory filtering overall. Instead, it appeared to change how particular sensory signals were prioritized. They wrote that “this study establishes mescaline as having a distinctive neurobiological profile characterized by cerebellar-selective hypoactivation [reduced activity] coupled with global hyperconnectivity [excessive communication across brain networks].”
Limitations are to be noted. For example, the researchers did not record heart rate, breathing or blood gases during scanning, meaning that some changes measured during the fMRI could have reflected cardiovascular effects rather than altered neural activity. Furthermore, they tested only a single dose of mescaline, and physiological differences mean these results in rats may not fully translate to humans.
The study, “Mescaline Alters Cerebellar Function, Global Connectivity, and Frequency-Selective Acoustic Gating: A BOLD fMRI Study in Awake Rats,” was authored by Noah Cavallaro, Priya Rai, David Akins, Sima Soltanpour, Md Taufiq Nasseef, Richard J. Ortiz, Rachel Utama, Caitlyn R. Cody, Anoushka Mistry, Heather C. Brenhouse, Praveen P. Kulkarni and Craig F. Ferris.

United Nations, New York — At the UN General Assembly (UNGA), the world saw a confident Syrian President, Ahmed al Sharaa, offer a detailed ledger of his Arab country's rise from the ashes of war and mass destruction.
Unlike his first appearance and brief address at the global podium in 2025, Al Sharaa chose to speak at length on Wednesday, informing the UNGA of Syria's diplomatic rebound and fast revival of national institutions.
"Last year, I said Syria came back; today I say Syria is rising," the Syrian leader told world leaders and diplomats on the second day of the UNGA's General Debate.
He highlighted Syria's transition from conflict to hosting more than 60 diplomatic missions, but warned that Israel was trying to destabilise the country through regular attacks, border incursions, and its decades-long occupation of Golan Heights.
Al Sharaa framed regional tensions – particularly between Israel and Syria – as a contest between "good and evil", arguing that usurped land and violated sanctity leave ordinary people to bear the consequences.
Wars and destructions, he remarked, have demonstrated to Syrian people that "injustice does not continue forever", even when truth does not immediately prevail.
The address was meant to present Syria's trajectory away from war and international isolation towards recovery and stabilisation.
Al Sharaa stated that reconstruction in Syria is going on, emphasising his been reunited from his first ever UNGA speech, weapons had been brought under Damascus' authority, sanctions had been lifted, and the administration is conducting operation against illicit weapons, drug trafficking and new partnerships dedicated to public welfare.
'Regional security has to start in Damascus'
Syria, Al Sharaa said, was back on the diplomatic stage, stressing more than 100 states have engaged with Damascus through roughly 4,000 diplomatic exchanges, the capital had welcomed over 60 diplomatic missions.
Syria has re-established itself as a transit hub for international diplomacy and regional security, he argued, "has to start in Damascus".
He spoke about Damascus’ engagement with the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons and the International Atomic Energy Agency, stating "Syria is no longer isolated" following the lifting of US sanctions, the Caesar Act's repeal, and removal from terror lists.
He also touched on production and economy, saying agriculture has neared self-sufficiency, while services and housing have rebounded. Al Sharaa emphasised that 3.5 million refugees had returned and that Syria had shifted "from crisis to opportunity".
The most critical section of his address focused on the occupied territories.
Al Sharaa stated that Golan Heights "will remain Syrian territory" and that any effort to alter its legal status would be nullified under UN Security Council Resolution 497, which declared Israel’s 1981 annexation "null and void".
"While the world is pleased about our return," he said, Israel continues to launch attacks against Syria and undermine its progress.
He cited approximately 500 air strikes and between 100 and 200 incursions, describing the pattern as "reminiscent of an era that we thought was long gone".
He reaffirmed Syria’s adherence to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement, demanded an Israeli withdrawal, and condemned ongoing Israeli military aggression.
Golan Heights and talks
This statement followed remarks made the previous day at the Atlantic Council event in New York, where he noted that security discussions with Israel had reached "almost 90 percent" agreement before Israel withdrew or introduced new preconditions. At the Council, Al-Sharaa recalled a conversation from his November 2025 White House visit with US President Donald Trump.
When Trump mentioned Israeli control over the Golan Heights, al Sharaa said he joked: "Why don’t you give New Jersey to the Israelis? You don’t own the Golan Heights to give it to them, but you own New Jersey. And I believe that New Jersey is full of Democrats, and they are not voting for Trump. So, it will be good to give it to the Israelis. So at least this is something that you own."
He then immediately added that Trump “doesn’t own the Golan Heights" and that "regardless of this joke, the Golan Heights is owned by its own people. It’s neither the Syrian president or the American president or any other person to abandon them or to give them up to others."
Syria and Israel held US-mediated talks in Jordan and France to halt Israeli attacks and incursions, aiming to revive negotiations towards a broader security accord.
Syria sought Israeli forces' withdrawal to pre-December 8, 2024 lines after Assad’s ouster, but talks stalled and contacts ceased entirely following an Israeli strike on a northern Syrian airbase.
Back in the UNGA, Al Sharaa maintained that sustainable peace necessitates a return to the 1974 lines and that Syrian sovereignty over Golan Heights remains non-negotiable.
He also used Quranic phrasing, affirming that Syria would continue to act "to serve God" and that divine justice rewards integrity and finally concluded on a key theme — that truth remains steadfast, falsehood perishes ultimately, and a country previously seen as a source of crisis has now become an island of opportunity.

“When a gambler loses the game, he usually talks more, makes threats and boasts, and tries in some way to weaken the morale of his opponent,” Kowsari said, adding that Iran had become familiar with such tactics over the past 48 years.
He said the United States, Israel and European countries had repeatedly employed similar methods against Iran, adding: “They say whatever comes out of their mouths; therefore, the listener must be discerning.”
The lawmaker said Trump had failed in his confrontation with Iran, despite having portrayed himself as a superpower and seeking to overthrow the Islamic Republic within four days.
Kowsari also described US actions in the region as part of psychological warfare, arguing that if Washington had the capability to defeat Iran, it would not allow the country “a moment of peace.”
Referring to US meetings with the countries of the southern Persian Gulf, he said Washington was seeking to pressure and intimidate them once again, but argued that the United States no longer had the capacity to take significant military action in the region.
The parliamentarian also referred to the conflict involving Yemen, saying Saudi Arabia, despite the vast sums it had spent on defense and security, was now “stuck in a quagmire” and had largely resorted to airstrikes against Yemen.
“Those bombings have produced no results,” he said.
Kowsari said Trump was seeking to portray himself as the victor in order to prevent domestic pressure in the United States from increasing further. He also accused Washington of attempting to create divisions among Iran’s armed forces, officials and people to exploit those divisions in future actions.
Referring to Iran’s defense capabilities, he said: “Where did these missiles come from? Where did these drones come from? Where did these air-defense systems come from?” Kowsari argued that Iran’s military capabilities were the result of planning and development under sanctions.
Kowsari further said Trump was seeking to use his appearance at the UN General Assembly to project the image that the United States remained a superpower. He added that Washington was still seeking to extract economic and political benefits from some countries in the region.
Asked about Trump’s reported interest in meeting Pezeshkian, Kowsari said unequivocally that such a meeting would not take place.
“There will be no meeting with Trump,” he said, adding that Pezeshkian himself knew that such a meeting would not happen. Kowsari characterized Trump’s efforts to establish contact with the Iranian president as ‘a sign of US weakness.’
 
 “The dignity of our president is far above this for him to meet or approach Trump,” Kowsari said.
Kowsari concluded by saying that Trump’s actions would not succeed in influencing the Iranian president. He argued that Trump should be put on trial and, if no venue existed for such a trial, said Iran should “take revenge” against him.

Ukraine Launches Grants of Up to $177,000 for Domestic Prosthetics Technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:57:56 UTC
02:57:56 KST

- Category
- Life in Ukraine
Ukraine Launches Grants of Up to $177,000 for Domestic Prosthetics Technology
Ukraine’s Startup Fund and defense technology cluster Brave1 have launched a grant program offering up to UAH 8 million ($177,507) to Ukrainian developers and manufacturers working on innovative prosthetic technologies.
The “Innovative Prosthetics” program, supported by Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation and the Ministry of Social Policy, Family and Unity, will provide non-repayable state grants to help teams develop and test prosthetic solutions at different stages, from initial concepts and laboratory models to functional prototypes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The initiative comes as demand for prosthetics in Ukraine has remained consistently high since 2022. As of January 2025, around 20,000 people in Ukraine had required prosthetic care since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, according to Interfax Ukraine, citing experts from Protez Hub, a project supporting prosthetics in Ukraine.
At the same time, the domestic industry continues to face challenges, including dependence on imported components, high research and development costs, and lengthy certification procedures. Limited customization options and shortages of specialists in biomechanics, electronics, and industrial design pose additional obstacles.
Against this backdrop, the program will focus on three main areas: upper- and lower-limb prosthetic solutions, including bionic, electronic, and mechanical systems; domestically developed components such as electronics, actuators, batteries, and mechanical assemblies; and technologies for personalizing prostheses, including 3D printing.
Grant amounts will vary depending on the technological readiness of each project. Developers can receive up to UAH 2 million (around $44,000) to test concepts and conduct initial research, up to UAH 4 million ($97,000) to develop laboratory models and conduct engineering and user testing, and up to UAH 8 million (almost $90,000) to build prototypes, carry out laboratory testing, and prepare products for conformity assessment and certification.
“Ukraine has unique experience and, at the same time, an enormous need for the development of modern prosthetic technologies. However, demand alone is not enough for competitive Ukrainian solutions to emerge—developers need resources to go through the costly and lengthy stages of R&D, prototype development, testing, and preparation for certification,” said Iryna Zabolotna, deputy director of Ukraine’s Innovation Development Fund.
Zabolotna said the program is designed to support individual projects while helping develop a domestic prosthetics technology sector capable of producing its own components, adapting solutions to individual needs, and expanding into international markets.
According to the press release, the program is intended as an investment in Ukrainian technologies that could make prostheses more functional, personalized, and accessible to users.
Ukrainian specialists are already developing highly individualized prosthetic solutions for people affected by severe injuries. Taisiia Yarova, an exoprosthetics specialist at the UNBROKEN National Rehabilitation Center in Lviv, creates handcrafted silicone facial prostheses, sculpting and painting customized replacements for eyes, noses, and ears that closely replicate patients’ natural features

When Will Ukraine Start Producing Its Own Patriot Missiles—and Which Ones Will It Make?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:57:56 UTC
02:57:56 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
When Will Ukraine Start Producing Its Own Patriot Missiles—and Which Ones Will It Make?
Ukraine could begin licensed production of Patriot air defense missiles as early as late 2027 or early 2028, with new details pointing to the PAC-2 GEM-T as the interceptor likely to be manufactured domestically.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defense Express on September 23, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine is negotiating with US defense company Raytheon over licensed production of missiles for the Patriot system. Zelenskyy said Ukraine hopes to establish production within approximately one to one and a half years.
The involvement of Raytheon provides a key indication of which Patriot interceptor could be produced in Ukraine. Raytheon manufactures the PAC-2 GEM-T, while the newer PAC-3 family, including the PAC-3 MSE, is produced by Lockheed Martin.
US President Donald Trump previously said Ukraine would receive a license to manufacture Patriot missiles, describing the interceptor involved as a “less modern version,” but did not identify a specific model.
Defense Express assessed that the combination of Trump’s description and Ukraine’s negotiations with Raytheon points to the PAC-2 GEM-T.
The PAC-2 GEM-T is designed to intercept aircraft, cruise missiles, and tactical ballistic missiles. Unlike the PAC-3 MSE, which uses hit-to-kill technology to destroy a target through direct impact, the PAC-2 GEM-T carries an explosive warhead that detonates near its target.
According to Defense Express, the PAC-2 GEM-T is estimated to have an effectiveness of around 60% against ballistic targets, compared with approximately 80% to 90% for the PAC-3 MSE.
However, the PAC-2 GEM-T could offer advantages when expanding production. Defense Express noted that PAC-3 manufacturing depends on active radar seekers produced by Boeing, which represent a potential supply bottleneck. The PAC-2 GEM-T does not rely on the same component.
The timeline for Ukrainian production remains dependent on when the necessary license is obtained and how much of the manufacturing process is ultimately localized.
If the license is secured in the near term, Defense Express estimated that production lines could be operational by late 2027 or early 2028. That does not necessarily mean completed Ukrainian-made missiles would become available at the same time.
The outlet noted that a full PAC-2 GEM-T production cycle could take at least a year. If Ukraine establishes complete domestic production of the interceptor and its components, the first missiles could therefore reach Ukrainian forces in late 2028 or potentially in 2029.
That timeline could be shorter if Ukraine instead produces selected components domestically and conducts final assembly using parts manufactured elsewhere.
No official date for the first Ukrainian-produced Patriot missile has been announced, and the scope of localization remains unclear. The PAC-2 GEM-T identification and the estimated timeline for the first completed missiles are based on Defense Express’ assessment of currently available information.
Earlier, Ukraine reported a severe shortage of Patriot interceptors, with some launchers left idle due to a lack of missiles. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed licensed production in Ukraine with US manufacturers Raytheon and Lockheed Martin as a way to secure a more stable supply of interceptors.

64 street plays spotlight Sacred Defense themes across Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

64 street plays spotlight Sacred Defense themes across Iran
TEHRAN- A total of 64 street theater productions from 26 Iranian provinces are being staged across the country as part of the “Narration of Epic” program, which is being held alongside Sacred Defense Week to commemorate the experiences and sacrifices of the 1980-1988 Iran-Iraq war through the language of theater.
Organized as part of the programs of the 20th International Resistance Theater Festival, the “Narration of Epic” street theater event began on Tuesday, September 22, and will continue through October 1, bringing performances to different cities across Iran.
According to the secretariat of the Resistance Theater Festival, the program has been organized to commemorate the memory of those who fought during the eight-year war and to promote the culture of resistance through street and environmental theater. The performances are being presented in public spaces, allowing theater to move beyond conventional venues and reach audiences in their everyday surroundings.
The organizers say the event seeks to strengthen the connection between epic themes and the general public by making use of the possibilities offered by outdoor performances. It also provides a platform for street theater artists from different parts of the country to present their works and explore creative approaches to subjects related to war, sacrifice, resistance and collective memory.
The participation of 64 productions from 26 provinces gives the program a nationwide character, reflecting the geographical diversity of Iranian street theater and the capacity of artists outside Tehran to contribute to resistance-themed cultural events.
The program is taking place during a period traditionally associated in Iran with the commemoration of the Sacred Defense. The Iran-Iraq war began on September 22, 1980, when Iraqi forces invaded Iran, and continued for eight years before ending in 1988. In Iran, the conflict is referred to as the Sacred Defense, and the anniversary of its beginning is commemorated annually through cultural and artistic programs across the country.
Theater has long been among the artistic forms used in Iran to preserve and reinterpret memories of the war. Alongside stage productions, street theater has provided artists with a way to present historical and social themes in direct contact with audiences in public spaces.
The “Narration of Epic” program is being held as the 20th International Resistance Theater Festival gets underway. The festival officially kicked off in Tehran on September 21 at the Azadi Tower, launching an edition that brings together theatrical works and related cultural and educational programs under the broader theme of resistance.
The 20th edition has been organized under the banner “Iran, An Eternal Stage of Resistance” and includes several sections, among them playwriting, stage theater, street theater, scientific and research activities, workshops and an international section. The festival is being directed by Mohammad Kazemtabar and is being hosted in Tehran and other Iranian cities.
At the opening ceremony, festival secretary Mohammad Kazemtabar announced that more than 20 stage productions dealing with the theme of the recent war would be presented during the festival. The ceremony also featured a tribute to theater, cinema and television artist Kourosh Zarei and the unveiling of “8 Scenes of the Ramadan War,” a collection of eight new plays by Iranian theater writers focusing on the events of the conflict.
The Resistance Theater Festival has developed over two decades as an event centered on themes including the Sacred Defense, the Islamic Revolution and broader concepts of resistance. Its organizers have also sought to expand the festival beyond conventional theater productions by incorporating workshops, research programs and street performances.
The current edition’s call for submissions highlighted themes ranging from the experiences of the Sacred Defense and the lives of martyrs and fighters to Palestine, Gaza, the role of women in resistance and contemporary events. The festival’s research section is also intended to encourage academic and interdisciplinary discussion about resistance theater and its social and cultural functions.
