New fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region raises fears of a return to the country's civil war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:38:00 UTC
02:38:00 KST

Ethiopia: Where does the Tigray conflict go from here?
September 23, 2026
The fighting reported in and around Ethiopia's northern Tigray region marks more than another episode of tension between the federal government in Addis Ababa and the region's leadership. It raises a fundamental question: What remains of the fragile peace established in 2022 — and where does the conflict go from here?
From 2020 to 2022, Ethiopia was devastated by a civil war between the federal government in Addis Ababa and Tigray's regional leadership. The conflict drew in neighboring regions and foreign troops from Eritrea, leading to a humanitarian crisis that displaced millions and left hundreds of thousands dead.
While a peace agreement halted the worst of the bloodshed in late 2022, it left a lot of the political and territorial disputes unresolved.
DW spoke to witnesses in the towns of Abala and Erebti on the border with Tigray who confirmed that new fighting had taken place there between Tigray forces and Ethiopian federal troops. Humanitarian sources also reported clashes in the area. Ethiopian Airlines has suspended flights to the cities of Mekelle, Shire and Axum, citing the "current situation in the Tigray region."
Reports that Tigray forces have taken control of airports in the region could not independently be verified by DW.
For Oslo-based peace researcher Kjetil Tronvoll, however, the latest developments represent a decisive escalation.
"I think the war has already begun," Tronvoll told DW.
German security analyst Gerrit Kurtz of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin also sees the developments as a serious escalation.
"This is a step towards a war," he told DW.
Two competing narratives
The two sides are presenting fundamentally different accounts of what triggered the latest escalation.
In a statement issued on September 23, the National Regional Government of Tigray said its forces had been responding defensively to an attack by the federal government. It accused Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of launching a new "genocidal invasion" and said Tigray forces had been ordered to defend the population.
The Tigray government also accused Addis Ababa of carrying out air and drone strikes and artillery attacks in recent months. It said it had previously refrained from responding to what it described as repeated provocations in an effort to de-escalate the situation.
The allegations could not independently be verified. The federal government, meanwhile, has portrayed the developments as part of a broader coordinated threat involving armed groups opposed to the prime minister.
The competing narratives illustrate one of the central problems facing any renewed peace effort: The parties do not even agree on the basic interpretation of the escalation.
A fragile peace under pressure
The current crisis cannot be separated from the shortcomings of the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. The deal ended two years of devastating war between the federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), but it did not resolve some of the conflict's underlying political and territorial disputes.
Western Tigray remains particularly contentious. The return of hundreds of thousands of displaced people remains unresolved, while questions over Tigray's political representation and its relationship with the federal government continue to fuel tensions.
"The Pretoria agreement stopped the fighting, but it did not resolve the underlying political conflict," Tronvoll says.
At the heart of that conflict is a fundamental disagreement over Ethiopia's political order. The TPLF has traditionally defended a strong federal structure and substantial regional autonomy. Abiy Ahmed's government has pursued a more centralized political model.
The issue is therefore not simply whether individual provisions of the peace agreement are implemented. It is also about competing visions of how Ethiopia should be governed.
Former enemies join forces
The emergence of an alliance of seven armed groups opposing Abiy adds another layer of complexity.
The grouping includes the TPLF, Fano forces from the state of Amhara and the Oromo Liberation Army from another regional state within Ethiopia. Some of these organizations were bitter enemies during the Tigray war. Their decision to cooperate therefore represents a significant political development — but not necessarily a durable alliance.
Kurtz says the alliance has been developing for some time and that some of its leaders have apparently already met.
"It was a very important development," he says. "The alliance has been in the making for a long time."
At the same time, he points to the fundamental differences between its members.
"All the political differences that they have are certainly there to resolve once their overall joint aim is achieved, which is overthrowing the government of Abiy."
Tronvoll similarly describes the cooperation as primarily tactical. The question is whether the groups can turn their shared opposition to Abiy into a lasting political and military strategy.
There is another complicating factor: Eritrea.
The Ethiopian government has accused neighboring Eritrea of supporting the alliance. Eritrea has rejected such allegations. Kurtz says there have been reports of contacts between the armed groups and Eritrea, but stresses that the new alliance itself appears to be a domestic grouping.
The geography of the alliance is another obstacle. Its members operate in different parts of Ethiopia and pursue different political objectives. Coordinating military operations across such distances would be difficult.
Can the escalation still be contained?
The most urgent question is whether the current fighting can still be contained before it develops into another full-scale war.
Kurtz argues that the immediate priority is straightforward: The forces involved in the fighting need to stop.
"Both the Ethiopian armed forces as well as the Tigray security forces are involved in active hostilities right now. So they should stop this," he says.
But bringing the fighting to an end will require more than a ceasefire on the ground. Ethiopia's conflict has become increasingly fragmented. Armed groups are operating not only in Tigray, but also in Amhara and Oromia, two other regional states within Ethiopia. Regional actors such as Eritrea are potentially also playing a role.
Who can mediate?
International actors have repeatedly warned about the risk of renewed conflict. Yet sustained diplomatic engagement has so far failed to produce a new political process.
The United States remains an important actor, according to Kurtz, but he says Washington has not shown sufficient engagement. The African Union, the European Union and other international actors could also play a role.
The challenge is that there is no single actor with enough influence over all the parties.
"It will require a certain coalition of efforts," Kurtz says. He argues that preventing a wider war would require a broader diplomatic push, with international actors dividing responsibilities and coordinating their efforts.
The United Nations General Assembly in New York could provide an opportunity for international leaders to engage directly with the Ethiopian government, he says. But diplomacy would also have to address the armed groups involved in the new alliance.
Tronvoll is similarly critical of the international response so far. He argues that the warning signs had been visible for some time but that international efforts to bring the parties back to negotiations remained limited.
The political problem remains
For the people of Tigray, the stakes are particularly high. The region has yet to recover from the consequences of the 2020-2022 war. Many people remain displaced, infrastructure has been severely damaged and the economic recovery remains fragile.
A return to large-scale war would therefore not simply mean a resumption of an old conflict. It could open a new and potentially broader phase of Ethiopia's wider security crisis, particularly given the simultaneous conflicts in Amhara and Oromia.
The immediate priority is to prevent the latest fighting from developing into a wider war. But any sustainable settlement will have to address the political questions that the 2022 agreement left unresolved.
The key question is therefore not simply whether the war has returned.
It is whether Ethiopia and its international partners can still create enough diplomatic space to prevent the latest escalation from closing the door to a political solution.
Edited by: Andreas Illmer

More than 57,000 women serve as military personnel in Ukraine's Armed Forces, General Staff says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:37:54 UTC
02:37:54 KST

More than 57,000 women serve as military personnel in Ukraine's Armed Forces, General Staff says
More than 76,000 women serve in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, including 57,000 military personnel, while the remainder hold civilian positions, the General Staff said in response to an inquiry from the Kyiv Independent.
While military service for women in Ukraine is voluntary, women aged 18 to 60 with medical or pharmaceutical education have been required to register with the military since October 2023. As a result, they may be called up for military service if they meet the relevant requirements.
Since March 2026, the number of women serving in the military has increased by about 1,000. At the time, more than 75,000 women were serving in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, including 55,000 active-duty service members, according to the General Staff.
As of September 2026, more than 20,000 of the 57,000 female service members hold combat positions, the General Staff told the Kyiv Independent.
"When we talk about 'combat roles,' we shouldn't reduce women's role in the war to simply being in the trenches. Modern warfare encompasses a very broad spectrum of military professions," Oksana Hryhorieva, the gender affairs advisor for the Ukrainian Armed Forces, told the Kyiv Independent.
"These include drone pilots, reconnaissance specialists, medics, signalers, artillerywomen, military psychologists, electronic warfare specialists, and many other roles."
read also
As of 2026, four women in Ukraine hold the rank of general.
Tetiana Ostashchenko, who served as commander of the Medical Forces of the Ukrainian Armed Forces from 2021 to 2023, became the first woman to receive the rank of brigadier general and the first woman to head the military medical service of the Armed Forces. Ostashchenko was promoted to general by presidential decree on Aug. 24, 2021, before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion.
The other two women generals, Yuliia Laputina and Liudmyla Shuhalei, received the rank of major general while serving in the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) in 2018 and 2020, respectively. Meanwhile, Tetiana Podashevska received the rank of militia general in 2004 for her service in the Interior Ministry.
"It is important that a woman in the military today has the opportunity to go through the entire professional path — from soldier to the highest officer positions. And this is a fundamental change compared with the past," Hryhorieva said.
Since the start of the full-scale invasion, the number of women serving in the military has nearly doubled. Yet women have been part of Ukraine's armed forces since the beginning of Russia's war against Ukraine in 2014. They could serve in combat roles in practice, but legal restrictions meant they were officially listed as holding rear-echelon positions until 2018, when those limitations were lifted.
According to Hryhorieva, an important factor was that, with the start of the all-out war, many women realized that defending the state was not a matter of gender, but of personal choice. At the same time, the state opened access to all military specialties and positions to women.
The nature of the war has also played a role, as the modern military is not only about physical strength, but also technology, intelligence, cybersecurity, medicine, communications, and analysis — fields in which women can serve, Hryhorieva added.
"Today, we are seeing not simply an increase in the number of women in the military. We are seeing a change in the culture of the Ukrainian military itself," the advisor said.
"Gender equality in Ukraine's Armed Forces is not about having women make up a 'certain percentage.' It is about ensuring that everyone who is ready to serve Ukraine has equal access to opportunities, positions, and professional development — and that they are evaluated based on their performance, not their gender."

====================================================================================================

Trump’s trap: Solving Hormuz crisis saves Iranian regime, and threats don't work - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:35:58 UTC
02:35:58 KST

US President Donald Trump has threatened Iran with annihilation so many times over the last year that one wonders how anyone in Iran could still take his rhetoric seriously.
Or, as The Wall Street Journal wrote in an editorial on Wednesday, those threats “would be more credible if we and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps hadn’t heard it several times by now.”
Yet we, and the IRGC, have indeed heard them. And then, in nearly the next breath or at the next photo opportunity, we have heard Trump talk about negotiations and, not in so many words, peace in our time with Iran.
The UN on Tuesday was no exception. On the one hand, Trump threatened to obliterate Iran and “drive them into hell, leaving it no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness for generations.” A few hours later, however, he said the US had held “very good” talks with the Iranians.
Could the tough talk simply be a negotiating move? Of course, it could. But Trump is not the only one who knows negotiating tricks. So do the Iranians.
According to various reports, those warm talks between US and Iranian officials produced a proposal under which Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the US lifting its blockade.
The Iranian ploy is reminiscent of the famous hassidic tale in which a poor man, complaining to his rabbi that his house is unbearably crowded, is instructed to bring more and more animals inside. When he is finally told to remove them, the same house suddenly feels spacious.
That, in essence, is what Iran is attempting to do.
A war never meant to be about the Strait of Hormuz
This war was never meant to be about the Strait of Hormuz. Or, at least, it did not start that way. The Iranians made the strait an issue by mining it and firing at ships and oil tankers passing through. The US retaliated by imposing a blockade on Iran – a blockade that is currently strangling the Iranian economy.
Now the Iranians are proposing that Washington lift the blockade in exchange for Tehran ending a crisis it created. A senior Iranian official reportedly said Hormuz could reopen within seven days if Washington reduced military pressure and lifted the blockade.
Sounds tempting, no? Especially since reopening the strait would allow much more oil onto the world market, lowering gasoline prices at American pumps just weeks before the midterm elections in November.
But such an agreement would solve the crisis Iran manufactured, not the underlying crisis that led to the war.
The central issue is not the Strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s surviving enriched uranium, its nuclear program, and its ballistic-missile capabilities.
If Washington lifts the blockade to reopen the strait, what leverage will it retain to compel Iran to surrender its enriched uranium and accept limits on its nuclear and ballistic-missile programs?
Very little, which is precisely the problem.
With the blockade, the US essentially has its foot on the neck of the Iranian economy. If continuously enforced, that pressure could lead to the best possible outcome from both an Israeli and American perspective: regime change.
Only will abandon nuclear project with regime change
According to Israeli intelligence assessments, Iran will truly abandon its nuclear project only if its fundamentalist regime changes. As long as that regime remains in power, it will continue seeking to build its nuclear capabilities, which it sees as its ultimate survival guarantee.
The danger for Israel is clear: The US might prioritize reopening the Strait of Hormuz, partly because of domestic electoral considerations, over addressing Iran’s nuclear capabilities.
Iran is offering to cease its actions that were already condemned under international law, and it is demanding sanctions and blockade relief in return. The immediate economic incentive to accept will be enormous, but a deal focused narrowly on Hormuz would reward Tehran for manufacturing the crisis.
Trump said in his UN speech that he did not care about the midterm elections, and that they were not a factor in his decision-making.
“When it comes to Iran, it doesn’t even enter my mind,” he said.
That should be reassuring. The problem is that so many of Trump’s previous threats against Iran have proved hollow, and the skepticism surrounding those threats inevitably carries over to his statements here.
What the Iranians do not realize, Trump said, is that he is not running in the midterm elections. “I’ll be here for two and a half years,” he said.
And therein lies a core issue.
To get the Iranians to show flexibility, Trump must show that his position will not fluctuate before or after the elections. He must convince Tehran that the pressure will remain regardless of oil prices, polling numbers, or the date on the electoral calendar.
Yet even that is not enough.
The American political system – not merely the Trump administration – must persuade the Iranians that preventing them from acquiring nuclear weapons is a lasting American policy rather than the preference of one president.
That is a much more difficult task.
The Iranians are betting first that Trump will avoid drastic measures just before the midterm elections, because he does not want to disrupt the oil market and send gasoline prices soaring.
Their second and more consequential wager is that even if Trump holds firm now, they need only endure another two years. After that, a new administration could enter office with different priorities and a far more conciliatory approach toward Tehran.
This belief that American pressure can always be waited out is central to Iran’s strategy. It is also why lifting the blockade now would be particularly damaging.
It will be difficult for the regime to outlast Trump if the blockade remains in place and the economy continues to crumble. It will be considerably easier if the blockade is lifted, sanctions are eased, and Iran is given the economic oxygen needed to stabilize the regime and rebuild its military capabilities.
Following the 12-Day War of June 2025, Israel changed its objective regarding Iran. The goal shifted from “merely” damaging and setting back Iran’s nuclear and missile programs to establishing the conditions for the eventual fall of the regime – something that Israeli intelligence assessments said would take between one to three years if military and economic pressure was sustained.
That assessment has not necessarily changed. It may, however, if the blockade is lifted, and Iran receives sanctions relief, thereby allowing the regime to rescue its economy.
Trump’s credibility will not be restored by threatening Iran with annihilation yet again. It will be restored by demonstrating that the US will not exchange long-term strategic leverage for temporary calm and cheaper gasoline.
The jury, however, is still out.

Canadian NDP leader slammed for Yom Kippur message claiming Jews failed 'to stop ongoing genocide'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:35:50 UTC
02:35:50 KST

Canadian New Democratic Party Leader Avi Lewis is facing widespread criticism following a social media post published on Monday at the start of Yom Kippur, with critics alleging that he stated that Jewish people failed to do their part to “stop an ongoing genocide” in Gaza.
Lewis posted on X on Sunday, "Tonight Yom Kippur begins, the most somber moment of the Jewish calendar. It’s a time of atonement - a time to grieve those who have been lost, a time to acknowledge and take responsibility for harms we have caused, individually and collectively. For Jewish people, the personal has always been political and the political always personal. This year I'm reflecting on the fact that we failed to do our part to stop an ongoing genocide committed in our name. There are many other fronts where I have to do the work of repair. But nothing on this scale."
Later that evening, news broke that a gunman had opened fire outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, during Erev Yom Kippur services. Constable Jeff Smith was injured during the exchange of gunfire while protecting the community as congregants took cover inside.
Following the shooting, Lewis published a second post on X, stating, "The shooting outside a synagogue in Belleville is deeply upsetting and has traumatized a community that gathered to pray. It is yet another reminder of the work that remains to create a Canada that is truly safe for people of all faiths, including Jewish people – to worship, to come together, to live without fear. Today, I am sending love and solidarity to the Jewish community in Belleville and across the country on this Yom Kippur, the most solemn and holiest day of the year."
The initial remarks drew immediate backlash from federal politicians, advocacy groups, and commentators, who argued that attributing collective responsibility to Jewish people for the actions of the Israeli government violates standard definitions of antisemitism and endangers communities.
'Holding Jews responsible is despicable,' says Liberal MP
Liberal MP Anthony Housefather condemned the remarks on X, writing that "holding Canadian Jews and Jews across the world collectively responsible for events over which they have no control is despicable."
Fellow Liberal MP Ben Carr similarly criticized the post when speaking to CPAC reporters, calling the comments "irresponsible" for a political leader, and warning that "it's dangerous and it's the type of narrative that is actually contributing to the type of threats that we're seeing levied against the Jewish community."
Advocacy organizations also weighed in heavily on the controversy. The Center for Israel and Jewish Affairs (CIJA) issued strong rebukes, pointing out in a post on X that "libels have consequences," and emphasizing that "when Jewish people are collectively portrayed as complicit in atrocities, that rhetoric can become a justification for targeting Jews here at home."
Mike Fegelman, executive director of HonestReporting Canada, criticized the post online as well, writing that "the criticism of @avilewis is entirely warranted. His Yom Kippur message is a near-perfect example of the hypocrisy at the heart of the anti-Zionist movement," and noting that "he is invoking Jews collectively, on Yom Kippur, and assigning them a responsibility to atone for the conduct of a foreign government."
In The Globe and Mail, columnist Robyn Urback published an op-ed arguing that "Avi Lewis's foolish statement on Jewish people should be disqualifying," emphasizing that assigning collective responsibility to a religious group during their most solemn holiday crosses a dangerous line where portraying Jewish communities collectively as complicit serves as a justification for targeting them at home.
Lewis defends his remarks on Jews
Addressing the controversy during a press conference on Monday, Lewis defended his remarks and rejected accusations that he was blaming Jewish people for Israel's military actions. When asked by a reporter to respond to criticism regarding his post on Gaza, Lewis stated: "Yeah, I did not blame Jews for the actions of the Israeli government. That's simply untrue. Holding Jews collectively responsible for the actions of the state of Israel is antisemitic. I've never done it. I think it's dangerous, and that's absolutely not what I did."
Lewis added, "I spoke as a Jewish Canadian from a place of profound sadness on the day of atonement and a day of the deepest and most solemn reflection in our calendar and said what many, many Jews feel and many Jews have said, that we have not done enough as Jewish people among a family of faiths and communities around the world. Humanity has not done enough to stop an ongoing genocide in Gaza."
Lewis also noted, "I just read today as part of my own reflections three Kol Nidre sermons from rabbis over the last couple of years about the failure of humanity and of Jewish people of the Jewish faith to stop an ongoing genocide."
Concluding his remarks on the controversy during the press conference, Lewis stated: "I come from a religious tradition which has a diversity of views which has debate at the center of our practice and our culture as Jews. I'm not going to police how other people reflect on Yom Kippur. And I think it's pretty ugly to see these partisan points being used to score partisan points like that. I won't be doing that. This was a personal reflection that I know is shared by many people. And just one more time, holding Jewish people collectively responsible for the actions of the state of Israel is not something I would ever do. It's antisemitic, and it is wrong."
The NDP did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

The Federal Administrative Court of Switzerland has rejected the asylum application of Iranian refugee and Jewish conversion candidate Behnam Vali Heydarian, also known as Ben Vali, putting him at risk of deportation to Georgia and potentially Iran, Vali told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.
Vali previously spoke with the Post in August, describing the violent transnational aggression he said Iran had directed against him while he was in Georgia. A convert to Christianity at the time and a prominent figure in the refugee community, Vali drew the regime’s attention after initially being targeted for distributing Bibles in Iran and later for his pro-Israel advocacy following the October 7 attacks.
After being assaulted multiple times, Vali said he was threatened over his continued pro-Israel advocacy, had his bank accounts repeatedly frozen without warning, and was threatened with deportation by a person he believed was a member of Georgia’s security services.
'He was an active, hardworking, kind, and responsible person'
Mikheil Grishashvili, a Jewish community leader and representative of the Peace Synagogue in Georgia, told the Post that Vali has been an active member of the community since 2023.
“He was an active, hardworking, kind, and responsible person, and he very quickly became part of our community,” Grishashvili said, adding that Vali became increasingly involved in Judaism.
Returning to Iran would likely lead to Vali's execution
Aware that returning to Iran would likely lead to his execution due to his open support for Israel, his conversion and his proselytizing, Vali fled to Switzerland, where he had been granted a business visa.
Though Vali entered Switzerland legally, the country rejected his asylum application, stating that he had entered the country illegally and fled from a “safe” country, despite evidence he provided demonstrating what he described as a clear and present threat in Georgia. Offers from Swiss nationals to provide Vali with employment and housing, so he would not burden the system, also went unanswered.
Ibrahim Alvac, the representative of a Swiss lawyers’ bureau representing Vali, told the Post, “The Swiss authorities have ordered his removal to Georgia because he holds refugee status there and Georgia has agreed to readmit him. His Swiss asylum application was not examined on its merits as a claim concerning persecution in Iran. We challenged the decision to return him to Georgia and sought reconsideration, but we have been unable to persuade the Swiss asylum authorities that his personal circumstances make that return unsafe. The negative judgment of 17 September 2026 has made his situation still more troubling.
“Mr Vali Heydarian is living with the uncertainty of a removal order while trying to make his concerns heard through the legal procedures available to him. He has not hidden from the authorities. He has presented his identity, his history and his objections openly.”
“We appealed the reapplication, arguing that based on my individual risks and the problems I faced, they had to assess, analyze, and examine my individual case and circumstances. But they didn’t,” Vali said. “The final answer was that the State Secretariat for Migration had already done its job and that Georgia is a safe country. You can go back to the safe country and stay there. That’s it. That was the final hope that we had.”
Vali said that the entry ban now in place, preventing him from returning to Switzerland, would stop him from seeking refuge throughout the European Union. He said he has also been attempting to contact Israeli authorities, hoping his pro-Israel advocacy and position as a student of Judaism would encourage some protection, but did not receive a response.

NYT shareholders file lawsuit against paper's parent org. over biased Israel reporting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:35:19 UTC
02:35:19 KST

Shareholders of The New York Times filed a lawsuit against the paper’s parent company Wednesday morning, arguing the paper has failed to follow its own editorial standards.
The suit, filed by the State Board of Administration of Florida (SBA) and the National Center for Public Policy Research (NCPPR) in New York County Supreme Court, requests the Times board of directors to release internal records.
The company has refused to produce the records for four months, the majority of which pertain to the paper’s coverage of the Israel-Hamas war.
Requests were first made by the National Jewish Advocacy Center (NJAC), representing NCPPR, on May 29 following the May 11 Nicholas Kristof column titled “The Silence That Meets the Rape of Palestinians," but the NYT has not complied.
Lawsuit alleges that board failed to establish adequate oversight
The new lawsuit, as reported by The Jerusalem Post, notes that the Times’ reputation for independent journalism is "its most valuable" asset and alleges that the board failed to establish adequate oversight mechanisms to ensure compliance with the company’s own editorial standards.
It cites examples of corrections and disputed reporting, including the October 2023 Al-Ahli hospital explosion coverage, claims about Gaza war reporting errors, and concerns raised by a purported newsroom whistleblower who said internal reporting channels did not resolve her complaints.
The whistleblower, who is not named in the suit but who is said to be a Jewish former New York Times newsroom employee with about a decade’s tenure, said that that in the immediate aftermath of Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, staffers spent weeks searching for evidence that Hamas did not use the tunnels beneath al-Shifa Hospital, even after the Israeli military released its own footage of the tunnels in November 2023.
Whistleblower claimed she raised concerns internally
On November 20, 2023, the head of the video department reportedly referred to the tunnels as "alleged tunnels" in the desk’s morning meeting.
The whistleblower claimed she raised concerns internally about what she believed were violations of the Times’ own editorial standards through internal channels, including EthicsPoint, the Standards desk, Employee Relations, and Human Resources, on at least 15 occasions beginning in 2019.
The filing says the whistleblower’s records include allegations that complaints about newsroom standards were not properly escalated, concerns about bias in coverage were not addressed, and senior leadership was aware of some complaints but did not take corrective action.
According to the filing, the whistleblower alleged that the internal complaint system failed to address her concerns and instead turned against her.
The petitioners argue they are not seeking to direct editorial decisions, but want records showing whether the board monitors compliance with the Times’ own standards and manages reputational risks.

Russia’s Supreme Court proposes cutting juries to four members and allowing judges into jury deliberations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:31:26 UTC
02:31:26 KST

Russia’s Supreme Court proposes cutting juries to four members and allowing judges into jury deliberations
Russia’s Supreme Court has drafted a plan to reform jury trials, according to RBC, Kommersant, and Vedomosti.
The proposal would create a panel comprising both jurors and a professional judge. The judge could join the jurors in the deliberation room to clarify issues that arise during voting.
Supreme Court Judge Sergei Zelenin said this would “considerably streamline the proceedings” and reduce the time needed to hear cases.
The proposal would also reduce the number of jurors to four. Until 2018, juries had 12 members. They now have eight members in regional courts and six in district courts and garrison military courts.
The plan would also allow people over 65 to serve as jurors if they are willing and healthy enough. It would simplify jury selection, particularly by ending the practice of disbanding a jury panel deemed incapable of producing an objective verdict.
Zelenin, who presented the proposal, said the current model was an artificial import from the Anglo-American system. “The separation of jurors and the professional judge, including the division of their powers, is primarily a feature of the Anglo-Saxon legal system and alien to the continental tradition,” he said.
Defendants may request a jury trial during court proceedings. RBC says juries most often hear cases involving murder, intentional infliction of serious bodily injury resulting in death through negligence, and armed gang activity.
Researchers at the Institute for the Rule of Law have repeatedly said the acquittal rate in jury trials is roughly 10 times as high as in nonjury trials, where it is below 1%.

The Guardian view on Russian disinformation: a foreign threat that relies on UK complicity | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:30:08 UTC
02:30:08 KST

In November 2020, Barack Obama warned of an “epistemological crisis” facing western democracies. Polarisation and radicalisation were corroding trust in established information sources. “If we do not have the capacity to distinguish what’s true from what’s false, then by definition the marketplace of ideas doesn’t work,” the former US president said.
That vulnerability has grown since then. Democracy’s enemies have become more determined to exploit it. This is the threat that Andy Burnham highlighted in a speech at the United Nations this week. The prime minister accused Russia of waging an “industrial-scale assault” on the UK’s information environment using bot armies and fake websites to spread falsehoods, interfere in elections, foment discord and poison inter-community relations.
The prime minister announced the creation of a National Centre for Information Defence to thwart campaigns of epistemological sabotage by hostile actors. It is an overdue enhancement of Britain’s civil defence capabilities.
Mr Burnham is right to highlight the threat, but he told only part of the story. The Kremlin would be wasting its money pumping out disinformation if large US tech platforms didn’t provide convenient channels for the toxin to spread, if there weren’t a complicit audience in Britain sharing the offending material and if the market for spreading pernicious propaganda weren’t so lucrative. Information warfare is only effective when it exploits structural vulnerabilities in the target society. Far-right material sowing hatred against migrants is most fruitful where the terrain has been fertilised by domestic politics.
Earlier this year, analysis by the Guardian found that more than half of accounts on X that were posting about racially aggravated riots in Belfast and civil disorder in Southampton were based outside the UK. Seven of the most-read tweets originated in the US, including one posted by X’s proprietor, Elon Musk, the world’s richest man.
Mr Musk has been assiduous in promoting a warped, dystopian idea of Britain as a failed state whose culture is being corroded by mass migration. His platform has been invaluable to far-right activists who have mustered gangs of masked men into mobs that obstruct roads, intimidate people and threaten asylum claimants at British ports. Last year, Mr Musk addressed a rally organised by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, where he called for the Labour government to be removed. Earlier this year, Mr Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, travelled to Moscow on a trip funded by the Musk Foundation. He said the purpose of the trip was to “see the beauty of a civilised society”.
Mr Burnham did not address that side of the anti‑democracy equation in his speech, perhaps because he felt that it would be impolitic to impugn US big tech under the president’s nose. Mr Trump is also an originator and disseminator of falsehoods online, but the nature of transatlantic diplomacy prevents a UK prime minister confronting him with that record.
Under the circumstances, it made sense for Mr Burnham to concentrate his remarks on the threat from the Kremlin, but that must not signal the limit of his policy focus. British democracy is indeed under attack from Russia, but an effective campaign to build resilience has to recognise also the complicity of domestic extremists and the digital privileges they enjoy thanks to US technology companies.

The Guardian view on the future of the UN: more embattled, but more necessary, than ever | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:28:51 UTC
02:28:51 KST

The United Nations was created, its charter states, to “save succeeding generations from the scourge of war”. Donald Trump used his address to the general assembly to threaten Iran, another member state, with annihilation again. The charter also speaks of the obligations of international law. On Venezuela, Mr Trump gloated that “to the victor belong the spoils”. His speech in New York on Tuesday might be regarded as an improvement on last year’s only in that it was not an explicit, full-scale attack on the UN itself, merely on its founding principles.
The absences this year are perhaps as telling as the US president’s hostile presence. Vladimir Putin has not attended for more than a decade. Nor has Xi Jinping – but the snub is more striking as he is in Washington to meet the US president. India’s Narendra Modi is not present; nor are Cyril Ramaphosa, Bola Tinubu or Abdel Fatah al-Sisi – the leaders of Africa’s three giants, South Africa, Nigeria and Egypt. While their reasons are various, the gaps speak collectively to Mr Trump’s wrecking capability and the broader challenges faced by the UN.
In a world where “cracks have become canyons”, to quote António Guterres, the body is more necessary than ever, and under greater strain. The outgoing secretary general has struggled with a “might is right” world: an authoritarian resurgence, the rising tide of conflict and a deadlocked security council. Mr Trump sought to supplant the UN with his “Board of Peace” for Gaza before largely losing interest. Even the biggest champions of multilateralism, such as Canada’s Mark Carney, are looking primarily to other mechanisms rather than UN reform.
With extremely limited powers, secretary generals usually fall into mediator or activist roles. Critics argue that Mr Guterres should have been more hands-on in diplomacy, in conflicts such as Sudan, as he was in brokering a Black Sea grain deal in 2022. But he has been a powerful voice of conscience: early to raise the threats posed by AI, passionate in calling for climate action and heartfelt on the suffering in Gaza, Ukraine and beyond. He has also kept the organisation on its feet – no mean feat given the disappearance of essential US funding (though Washington is now paying some of its debt).
The first female secretary general is long overdue and the informal regional rotation would suggest that a Latin American or Caribbean figure may succeed him; Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica and Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett of Guyana have been frontrunners. But major powers may be biding their time, with serious contenders still to emerge. Observers think that there is a real possibility that a successor may not be agreed before Mr Guterres’s departure date of 31 December, underlining the UN’s challenges.
Yet it remains an essential forum, not least for smaller countries to coordinate and campaign – resulting in important action on issues from landmines to global heating and its consequences. And major powers will eventually have to recognise that the case for security council reform, stressed again by Mr Guterres, cannot be ignored for ever. The charter reminds us that the UN was born from the desperation engendered by two world wars rather than a utopian dream. It endures not because of glorious successes, nor because it has avoided glaring failures, but because a world without it would be far worse. The troubles it faces are all the more reason to defend it.
-

Iran sets conditions for resuming diplomacy with US in Qatar-mediated NY meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:28:21 UTC
02:28:21 KST

Iran sets conditions for resuming diplomacy with US in Qatar-mediated NY meeting
TEHRAN — Iran has laid out its conditions for resuming diplomatic engagement with the United States during a meeting between Iranian and American representatives in New York that was held through Qatari mediation, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said.
Speaking to IRNA late Tuesday in New York, Baqaei said the interaction between the two sides took place through Qatar, with the Iranian delegation clearly and explicitly conveying Tehran’s views and conditions to the US side through the mediators.
“The interaction that took place was through Qatari mediation. In fact, the Iranian delegation conveyed its views and conditions to the American side very clearly and explicitly through the mediators,” Baqaei said.
The meeting was held on Tuesday on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, where senior officials and diplomatic delegations from around the world have gathered for high-level discussions on international and regional developments.
Iran outlines conditions for renewed diplomacy
According to Baqaei, Iran’s conditions for resuming diplomacy include an end to fighting on all fronts, a halt to US acts of aggression against Iran, an end to the US naval blockade and economic war against the country, and the release of Iranian assets.
The Iranian spokesman said Tehran had also communicated its conditions for diplomacy through various channels in recent weeks, including its position on issues related to the security of the Strait of Hormuz.
He said the presence of the Iranian delegation in New York provided an opportunity to reiterate these positions and convey them clearly to the American side through the Qatari mediators.
The remarks indicate that Tehran views any potential diplomatic process in the broader context of developments on the ground and the measures taken by Washington. From Iran’s perspective, the continuation of diplomacy is linked to the removal of military and economic pressure against the country.
Araghchi holds bilateral meetings on sidelines of UNGA
Baqaei also said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held separate meetings with officials from several countries on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
According to the spokesman, bilateral relations as well as developments in West Asia and other international issues were among the main topics discussed during the meetings.
The diplomatic activity comes as regional security developments, including issues surrounding the Strait of Hormuz and the broader situation in West Asia, remain prominent topics in international discussions and diplomatic consultations taking place alongside the UN General Assembly.
Tehran responds to Trump’s remarks at UN
Baqaei also responded to remarks made by US President Donald Trump during his address to the UN General Assembly, saying that the comments amounted to “repeated claims and allegations” against the Islamic Republic.
He said the impression shared by diplomats and delegations from several countries present in New York was that the remarks did not reflect strength but rather desperation.
Baqaei further criticized the use of the UN General Assembly — the world’s largest international gathering — as a platform for remarks that are 'unlawful and contrary to diplomatic norms.'
He also criticized threats of military action against Iran, arguing that such threats are incompatible with accepted principles governing international relations.
Iranian delegation walks out during Trump’s speech
According to Baqaei, the Iranian delegation, headed by Foreign Minister Araghchi, left the venue in protest as Trump delivered his remarks.
However, one Iranian diplomat from the Islamic Republic’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations remained in the chamber to follow the proceedings, in line with established diplomatic practice, the spokesman said.
Addressing questions over why the entire Iranian delegation did not leave, Baqaei emphasized the importance Tehran attaches to maintaining its presence at the United Nations.
“Iran’s seat in a forum like the United Nations General Assembly is our stronghold,” he said, adding that leaving that position in response to hostile or offensive remarks would mean failing to fulfill the country’s diplomatic responsibilities.
Iran emphasizes active diplomatic presence
Baqaei’s remarks underscore Tehran’s stated intention to maintain an active diplomatic presence in international institutions while simultaneously challenging US military, economic and political pressure.
The Qatar-mediated meeting between Iranian and American representatives, alongside Araghchi’s bilateral consultations with foreign officials, forms part of Iran’s diplomatic activity on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Former Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years for sexual assault
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:26:39 UTC
02:26:39 KST

Beril Çanakcı
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
A court in New York sentenced Harvey Weinstein, a former Hollywood film producer whose case sparked a worldwide movement against sexual abuse, to 15 years in prison on Wednesday, according to a report by NBC News.
Weinstein, 74, was found guilty last year of sexually assaulting Miriam Haley, a former production assistant on a US television show, at his New York apartment in 2006.
Judge Curtis Farber told Weinstein that he had used force against the victim and had never accepted responsibility for his actions. After serving his prison term, Weinstein will be monitored by authorities for five years and must register as a sex offender.
Haley spoke in court and said the assault had seriously harmed her life. Weinstein, who attended the hearing in a wheelchair, again denied the accusations but apologized to anyone he may have hurt, according to the report.
For decades, Weinstein was one of the most influential figures in Hollywood. His companies produced and distributed well-known films such as "Pulp Fiction," "The King's Speech" and "The Artist." He won an Academy Award, the film industry's top prize, as a producer of "Shakespeare in Love."
His career collapsed in 2017, when The New York Times and The New Yorker magazine published investigations into allegations that he had sexually harassed and assaulted women for years. More than 80 women, including actresses and former employees, have since accused him of sexual misconduct.
The reports led to the #MeToo movement, in which women around the world shared their experiences of sexual harassment and abuse, often by powerful men in business, politics and entertainment. The movement led to investigations and firings in many countries.
Weinstein said all his sexual relationships were consensual. 
Long legal battle
Weinstein was arrested in 2018 and has since remained in custody.
A New York jury first convicted him in 2020, and he was sentenced to 23 years in prison. In 2024, however, New York's highest court overturned the conviction and ordered a new trial.
In the 2025 retrial, the jury again found him guilty in Haley's case but acquitted him of a second criminal sexual act charge involving former model Kaja Sokola. Jurors could not agree on a rape charge involving former actress Jessica Mann. A third trial on that charge also ended without a verdict, and prosecutors decided in June not to pursue the case again.
Weinstein faces a separate case in the state of California. A Los Angeles court convicted him in 2022 of rape and two counts of sexual assault and sentenced him to 16 years in prison. A California appeals court upheld his convictions but ordered him to be resentenced, overturning the original sentence.

Zaluzhny could reach runoff against Zelenskyy and defeat him if presidential elections were held – poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:26:26 EEST
02:26:26 KST

Incumbent Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ukraine's Ambassador to the UK and former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (2021–2024) Valeriy Zaluzhny would garner the most votes if a presidential election were held in the second half of September 2026, according to a survey by the Sociopolis company conducted from September 16 to 21, 2026.
The survey results indicate that 19.1% of all respondents—or 23% of those who would vote and had made a choice—would vote for Zelenskyy, while 19% and 22.9%, respectively, would vote for Zaluzhny.
Next in the presidential rankings are MP and European Solidarity party leader Petro Poroshenko (supported by 8.9% of all respondents and 10.7% of decided voters); Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine and former Chief of the Main Intelligence Agency of the Ministry of Defence Kyrylo Budanov (7.9% and 9.5%, respectively); Third Army Corps Commander Andriy Biletsky (7.2% and 8.7%); former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov (6.3% and 7.6%); and MP Dmytro Razumkov (5.7% and 6.9%). World boxing champion Oleksandr Usyk would be supported by 2.7% of all respondents (and 3.2% of those who would vote and had made their choice), while MP and leader of the All-Ukrainian Union Batkivschyna, Yulia Tymoshenko, would receive 2.5% and 3% respectively.
At the same time, 8.5% of respondents were undecided on whom to vote for, 7.2% would not participate in the vote, and 1.2% would spoil their ballot.
In a hypothetical presidential runoff between Zaluzhny and Zelenskyy, 46.1% of all respondents would vote for Zaluzhny and 28% for Zelenskyy. Among those who would vote and had made their choice, the figures are 62.2% and 37.8%, respectively. Some 16.4% of respondents would not vote, 4.8% would spoil their ballot, and 4.7% were undecided.
In a matchup between Budanov and Zelenskyy, 35.6% of all respondents would vote for Budanov and 26.9% for Zelenskyy. In a matchup between Budanov and Fedorov, 36% of all respondents would vote for Budanov and 26.2% for Fedorov. In a matchup between Budanov and Zaluzhny, 29.4% of all respondents would vote for Budanov and 43.6% for Zaluzhny.
In a matchup between Zelenskyy and Fedorov, 31.7% of all respondents would vote for Zelenskyy and 33.6% for Fedorov. In a hypothetical matchup between Zaluzhny and Fedorov, 45.4% of all respondents would vote for Zaluzhny, while 24.4% would vote for Fedorov.
According to the press service of the research company Sociopolis, more than half of the respondents (53.6%) believe that, in the event of a genuine cessation of hostilities and the scheduling of elections, the presidential and parliamentary elections should be held simultaneously. Meanwhile, 22.2% of respondents believe the presidential election should take place first, and 19% believe the election of Verkhovna Rada deputies should come first.
The survey was conducted using telephone interviews (CATI) based on a random sample of mobile phone numbers among 1,002 residents of government-controlled areas of Ukraine aged 18 and older. The theoretical statistical margin of error for the proportion of a characteristic—at a confidence level of 0.95 and excluding the design effect—does not exceed 3.1% for figures close to 50% and 1.4% for figures close to 5% or 95%.

No signs Chagos deal can be adapted to suit Trump, say UK officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:26:00 UTC
02:26:00 KST

The Chagos Islands deal is on hold for as long as Donald Trump objects to it, UK officials believe, with no immediate signs it can be adapted to suit the US president.
After Trump savaged the three-way plan as “a terrible deal” during a meeting with Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly, the prime minister said he was “confident” the UK would be able to find a solution to revive the idea.
But while efforts are still taking place to do this, there is an acceptance in the government that it is extremely unlikely unless Trump has another change of heart. “Until the president changes his mind there will not be any progress,” one official said. “We are where we are. We were waiting for the president to present a view, which he has.”
The UK signed a treaty last year to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while retaining control of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia, part of the Indian Ocean archipelago, under a 99-year lease. Mauritius was set to receive £165m for three years and £120m a year from the fourth year.
Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, said on Wednesday morning that payments worth at least £120m to Mauritius were on hold given the deal could not go ahead without US support.
“This deal as it is currently constituted can’t go ahead without American support,” Streeting told BBC Radio 4’s Today’s programme. “So we have to get a deal to a place where it commands American support as well as the agreement of the government of Mauritius and our government.”
The US had supported the plan, but Trump changed his mind amid a wider deterioration of relations with Keir Starmer over the lack of UK support for the US attacks on Iran.
Speaking after their first in-person meeting at the UN in New York on Tuesday, Trump praised Burnham but gave no ground on his scepticism about the Chagos deal.
“I don’t support it. I think it’s terrible,” Trump told reporters. “It was a terrible deal. [Mauritius] all of a sudden say they have ownership. Somebody has ownership that never showed up before, after decades and centuries. I think it’s ridiculous.”
Burnham later said he had “inherited the situation” and had told Trump “that we will work to find that resolution between the different sides”. He added: “It was clear that we need to come to that agreement, but I’m confident we can find it working with our US partners.”
Given Trump’s objections appear based on the core element of the deal – the transfer of sovereignty to Mauritius – there appears to be no immediate way forward. The UK government has previously made clear that Washington’s approval is a prerequisite for the plan.
UK officials stress, however, that while Burnham inherited the impasse from Starmer, there is no intention to deprioritise a plan, begun under Rishi Sunak, that the government says is vital to ensure the future of the strategically vital Diego Garcia base, given Mauritian claims to sovereignty of the archipelago.
“It’s not back to the drawing board, as we do need to find a diplomatic solution to this,” another UK official said. “Everyone agrees something has to be done, which is why several prime ministers and even more foreign secretaries have tried to get it over the line.”
Streeting stressed the same point to the BBC, saying: “The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand … I would caution is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world.”

Araghchi holds extensive diplomatic talks on UNGA sidelines
TEHRAN- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called on the international community to hold the United States accountable for its violations of international law and war crimes against Iran, warning that indifference to genocide will have far-reaching consequences for all countries.
Speaking during a meeting with Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis in New York, Araghchi outlined Iran's positions on regional developments following US-Israeli aggression against Iran, as well as the continuation of interventionist measures, a naval blockade, and economic warfare against the Iranian people.
He stressed the responsibility of all countries to safeguard the UN Charter and international law, particularly the prohibition on the use of force, and referred to war crimes committed by the US and the Israeli regime against Iran during their military aggression over the past year and a half.
Referring to Washington's repeated breaches of commitments, including its violation of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, Araghchi said the international community has a responsibility to hold the United States accountable for the consequences of its unlawful actions.
He further pointed to grave violations of international humanitarian law and multiple war crimes, including the tragedies in Minab and Lamerd, stressing the duty of all states party to the 1949 Geneva Conventions to investigate and punish perpetrators.
Araghchi warned that indifference toward genocide and war crimes, along with continued impunity for perpetrators, would have extremely far-reaching consequences for the entire world.
Restoring Hormuz strait security requires end to US' destabilizing actions
Insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz is solely the result of US and Israeli aggression, Araghchi said, stressing that restoring security to the strategic waterway hinges on an end to US actions that create insecurity.
During a meeting with Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein, the two diplomats reviewed the progress of Iran-Iraq cooperation in economic, trade, consular, and security affairs, and stressed the need to expand relations in all areas of mutual interest.
They described safeguarding the security of their shared border as highly important, emphasizing the implementation of agreements reached in this regard and the need for effective measures to counter terrorist activities.
Araghchi outlined the latest developments concerning shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, including the understanding reached between Iran and Oman on establishing safe routes for commercial shipping.
He stressed the need for all regional countries to adhere to the principle of good neighborliness, particularly by preventing aggressor parties from using their territories and facilities to prepare for and carry out illegal and aggressive actions against Iran.
Europeans criticized for double standards over Iran, regional developments
Araghchi criticized European double standards toward regional developments, particularly their response to US and Israeli acts of aggression against Iran.
During a meeting with Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, Araghchi strongly criticized European countries' "double standards" toward regional developments, particularly their silence and leniency regarding the "aggressive actions and crimes" committed by the US and the Zionist regime against Iran.
He said European countries cannot claim to support the rule of law and human rights while remaining indifferent to, or even supporting, overt US and Israeli military aggression against Iran.
The Iranian foreign minister also recalled Iran's responsible approach to diplomacy aimed at removing US pretexts over the nuclear issue, saying Washington's repeated breaches of commitments and its "warmongering" were the main causes of the current insecurity in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
He stressed that the only way to restore peace and stability in the region is to halt the US' illegal and aggressive actions and respect Iran's rights and national interests.
Iran warns Italy over US bases, complicity in aggression
Araghchi warned Italy that hosting US military bases and assisting in preparations for or implementation of acts of aggression against Iran would be considered complicity in aggression and could entail international responsibility for the host states.
During a meeting with Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, Araghchi described the decision by some European countries, including Italy, to host US military bases and any cooperation in preparing for or carrying out acts of aggression against Iran as "very dangerous" and tantamount to complicity in aggression.
Pointing to the continued aggressive and destabilizing actions by the US and the Israeli regime in West Asia, Araghchi said rising fuel and commodity prices in global markets were a direct consequence of the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran.
He stressed that any responsible country should hold the US accountable for continuing its adventurist actions and threatening commercial shipping in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
On human rights, particularly women's rights, Araghchi criticized the double standards of some European countries, saying those who remained silent over the most blatant human rights violations by the Israeli occupying regime in the occupied Palestinian territories have no standing to lecture others on human rights.
Belarus resolved to strengthen strategic ties with Iran
Belarusian Foreign Minister Maxim Ryzhenkov reaffirmed his country's determination to strengthen brotherly and strategic relations with Iran during a meeting with Araghchi.
Ryzhenkov expressed satisfaction with the meeting and described safeguarding the UN Charter and the national sovereignty of countries as a fundamental principle governing international relations.
For his part, Araghchi pointed to the excellent and growing relations between the two countries and stressed Iran's determination to fully implement previous agreements and deepen bilateral and multilateral cooperation.
Strongly criticizing the unilateral and illegal Western sanctions imposed on independent countries, Araghchi underscored the need for Iran and Belarus to enhance coordination and jointly resist political and economic pressure stemming from unilateralism.
Iran, Azerbaijan discuss South Caucasus security
Araghchi and his Azerbaijani counterpart Jeyhun Bayramov discussed security and cooperation in the South Caucasus, as well as bilateral ties and regional and international developments.
The two sides reviewed agreements and understandings reached between the two countries in various economic and trade fields, as well as issues related to security and cooperation in the South Caucasus.
They also stressed the two countries' determination to implement the agreements reached and strengthen cooperation and coordination in line with the interests of the two nations.
Araghchi also explained the latest developments in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, stressing Iran's determination to defend its sovereignty and national interests against illegal US and Israeli aggression and pressure.
Iran urges EU to avoid appeasement of US bullying
Araghchi urged the European Union to play a constructive role in international developments and avoid double standards and appeasement in the face of US bullying, warning that such approaches undermine international peace and security.
During a meeting with EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, Araghchi highlighted Iran's practical commitment to diplomacy as a means of achieving peace and security in the region, saying repeated US breaches of commitments have been the sole factor disrupting diplomatic processes.
He said the European Union had unfortunately, on numerous occasions, chosen appeasement in the face of US bullying instead of adhering to principles it claims to uphold, including the rule of law and respect for human rights.
Iran calls French positions on regional developments unacceptable
Araghchi slammed France's "unacceptable" positions on regional developments, particularly the US and Israeli military aggression against Iran.
During a meeting with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, Araghchi criticized France's "interventionist" positions toward Iran and stressed the need for the French Embassy in Tehran to respect Iran's domestic laws and regulations.
He decried France's double standards on human rights, saying France cannot claim to be concerned about human rights while remaining silent over "crimes against humanity" committed by the US and the Zionist regime against the Iranian people, including the killing of Iranian women and
children, while also cooperating in the implementation of illegal US sanctions against the Iranian people.
Araghchi stressed that Iran seeks relations based on mutual respect and interests with all countries, including France, but will act firmly and decisively in defending its interests and national objectives.
Iran blames Hormuz insecurity on US-Israeli aggression
Araghchi described insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz and disruption to maritime shipping as the direct result of US and Israeli aggression.
During a meeting with Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger, Araghchi stressed that restoring security for maritime navigation in the region requires an end to destabilizing actions and US "economic terrorism."
He also pointed to the continued genocide of Palestinians and the Israeli regime's flagrant violations of international law, as well as the regime's continued aggression against Lebanon and other countries in the region.

Russia is scouting Kyiv and the surrounding region for its next targets, from power substations and railways to hypermarkets and airports. Nikolaievsky Vaniok, a major Ukrainian monitoring channel, says Russian aerial reconnaissance has been mapping specific sites across the capital and Kyiv Oblast, and a national-security official warns that a ballistic strike is being prepared.
The reported scouting fits Russia's pattern of taking apart Ukraine's power and civilian infrastructure as winter nears, with Moscow switching to terror or rear as its tactics of the war.
Signs of preparation are present
Andrii Kovalenko, who heads the National Security Council's Center for Countering Disinformation, has also confirmed Russia is preparing a ballistic strike, with signs of the preparation visible, while its diplomats stall on any real step toward a ceasefire.
Ballistics are the threat Ukraine's air defenses struggle most to stop: in a recent attack on Kyiv's water system, not one of Russia's ballistic missiles was intercepted.
"The enemy is preparing a ballistic strike. Signs of preparation are present," he wrote, adding the warning to "be attentive in the coming days."
The scouting maps the everyday
Nikolaievsky Vaniok, which tracks Russian air activity, says the reconnaissance had lingered over the capital's ordinary machinery.
In Kyiv, it listed traction substations and other rail infrastructure, an Auchan hypermarket and similar stores in the Obolon district, power substations across several districts, a trolleybus depot, and Zhuliany airport.
In Kyiv Oblast, there are substations near Bucha and Irpin, many more that feed the railways, possible fuel depots near Borodianka and in the Bila Tserkva district, and the airfield at Vasylkiv. The account could not be independently verified.
Jet-drone defenses run late
Ukraine is racing to build a large-scale defense against jet-powered drones, the fast Gerans that have strained Kyiv's air cover, but the channel's administrator said the work was moving at "its own pace".
"If we manage a proper counter before winter, that will be very lucky," he added.

France, UK, Denmark urge Russia at UN Security Council to end war on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:21:27 UTC
02:21:27 KST

Merve Gül Aydoğan Ağlarcı
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
The foreign ministers of France, the UK and Denmark on Wednesday urged Russia to end its war on Ukraine, warning that Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and airspace violations are creating wider security risks across Europe.
Speaking at a high-level UN Security Council session on Ukraine, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, who is chairing the council this month, said Russia is “using winter, the cold, and denial of the most basic needs as weapons of mass destruction, targeting civilian population.”
He said Russia is “lashing out at Europe in its entirety” through alleged targeted killings, sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation, adding that repeated airspace violations involving Romania, Poland, Moldova, Lithuania, Estonia, Latvia and Finland mean “there is not one state who is not now ill at ease” because of Russian aggression. He also pointed to a recent incident in Leipzig, Germany.
Barrot warned that Russia, “trampled upon by a permanent member of the Security Council,” is weakening the UN’s authority, and said Ukraine “is ready for peace” but has met only “Moscow’s stubbornness.”
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said sham elections in occupied Ukrainian territory are “a blatant violation of Ukraine’s sovereignty,” warning that “we cannot accept the changing of borders by force.”
He said NATO “is and always will be a defensive alliance” and pledged to “continue to call out and act against Russia’s hostile activity.” Miliband, whose parents fled Poland and Belgium as refugees during World War II, said “it is time ministers told President Putin the truth,” adding that “the Russian people can feel” Russia is “failing” in the war.
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said “if Russia stops fighting, the war ends. If Ukraine stops fighting, it will be the very end of Ukraine.”
He said Denmark “strongly condemns all attacks in violation of international humanitarian law,” warning of a “dangerous spiral of escalation” as civilian infrastructure and energy facilities come under attack ahead of winter.
Rasmussen said attacks on Ukrainian ports and grain infrastructure “threatened trade, livelihoods, and global food supplies,” and cited Germany’s attribution of a “failed hybrid attack” at Leipzig-Halle airport to Russia as one of several “reckless and dangerous acts” affecting Europe.
He said Denmark “will continue to provide financial and security assistance” to Ukraine, pledging support for reconstruction, humanitarian aid and increased pressure on Russia “through tough EU sanctions.”
All three foreign ministers linked the war in Ukraine to broader security risks across Europe and called for sustained diplomatic and economic pressure on Moscow to bring it to the negotiating table.

Emine Erdogan calls for new systems to address environmental crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:17:21 UTC
02:17:21 KST

Türkiye's First Lady and chair of the UN Advisory Board of Eminent Persons on Zero Waste, Emine Erdogan, has highlighted the global environmental crisis in a video message at the opening of the Sustainable Development Impact Meetings, organised by the World Economic Forum in New York.
“Our planet resembles a ravaged mine, the oceans cannot breathe, and cities are struggling to cope with their waste. Therefore, a circular economy is not one of the options before us; it is a necessity for our future,” she said in the video on Wednesday.
The first lady expressed her regret at being unable to attend the gathering and said that current production and consumption systems are not capable of carrying humanity into the future.
'We see zero waste as a key'
Emine Erdogan noted that achieving a transition to a circular economy means strengthening sustainable development, expanding recycling, improving waste management and turning towards renewable energy sources.
“We see zero waste as a key to achieving all of this. Because zero waste is not merely a waste-management approach that individuals incorporate into their daily lives. Zero waste means redesigning our production and consumption models and redefining our relationship with nature,” she said, stressing the need for new economic models to transform the entire system from production to consumption.
“We must establish an order in which people who adopt zero waste in their lives are supported by the right systems, and in which the production of durable, repairable products whose materials can be reused is encouraged,” she added.
“Indeed, we still have a window of opportunity to combat the climate crisis and build a sustainable future. I believe that Zero Waste, which we launched in Türkiye in 2017 and which has now become a global movement, is a transformative force in making the most of this opportunity,” she said.
“With the right steps we take together, I hope we can make a new beginning — one in which we protect our resources rather than consume them, and create value instead of waste,” she added.
Thanking the World Economic Forum for organising the meeting, Emine Erdogan expressed her hope of meeting the participants at COP31, which will be held in Antalya.

Israel blocks 900 wheelchairs for Gaza's child amputees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:16:44 UTC
02:16:44 KST

Breadcrumb
'Calculated effort to destroy Palestinian life': Israel blocks 900 wheelchairs for amputee children in Gaza
More than 900 wheelchairs donated by two Australian charities for wounded and amputee children in Gaza have been blocked by Israel from entering the enclave, with the shipments stuck in storage in Jordan since 2025.
Mohammad Helmy, a Melbourne-based pro-Palestine activist, told The New Arab that Israel's refusal to allow the wheelchairs into Gaza was intentional, accusing authorities of seeking to make life in the devastated enclave "impossible".
“Israel’s blockade of over 900 custom, all-terrain wheelchairs—hand-built by Australian volunteers to help amputee children navigate destroyed streets—exposes a calculated effort to destroy Palestinian life and render life in Gaza impossible,” Helmy said.
“By undertaking non-stop bombardment and then systematically denying the basic medical aid needed to survive it, Israel is actively executing an ongoing genocide. Trapping mobility gear in warehouses while children crawl through rubble is not a security measure—it is a deliberate policy of collective punishment and total destruction directed against the Palestinian people,” he continued.
The restrictions come as the UN has said Gaza has the largest group of child amputees in modern history as a result of Israel's attacks on the territory.
The charity Kids on Wheels Alliance sent two shipments that arrived in Jordan in February 2025, while another shipment from Wheelchairs for Kids arrived in October that year.
The wheelchairs remain at a storage facility managed by the Jordan Hashemite Charity Organisation (JHCO), which said COGAT, the Israeli defence ministry body that oversees the entry of humanitarian aid into Gaza, had blocked their delivery.
JHCO said it filed an application in late February 2025 for the Kids on Wheels Alliance shipments to enter Gaza as part of an aid convoy, but COGAT rejected the request. Israeli authorities said medical equipment and medicines had not been approved for inclusion in that convoy.
JHCO said its application has since remained "pending", with no further updates, leaving the organisation unable to submit a new application for the other shipments.
COGAT has not responded to media requests concerning the Australian donations. However, the Israeli agency has previously said that thousands of wheelchairs have been allowed into Gaza.
The wheelchairs donated by Wheelchairs for Kids are designed to withstand difficult terrain, including the rubble that now covers large parts of Gaza, and can be adjusted as children grow older and taller.
"The sooner they come out of there and get to the kids, the better, and the little kids can get a much better life," Brother Olly Pickett, co-founder of the charity, said in a statement.
"I think there's a lot of children waiting for them who have had amputations, and so they won't be able to walk around or get around. Once they get a wheelchair, they can get out and about, which would be wonderful,” he added.
Australian media reports, citing an informed source outside the region, said Israeli authorities had denied the wheelchairs entry because they considered them potentially "dual use", a classification applied to goods that authorities say could also have military applications.
Israeli rights group Gisha earlier this year published a report saying Israel had arbitrarily classified essential items, household goods and medical supplies as "dual use" since the start of the war on Gaza.
Items subjected to such restrictions have included flashlights, sleeping bags and portable toilets.
Rights groups have warned that restrictions on such goods have serious consequences for civilians, including tens of thousands of Palestinians attempting to recover from injuries and rebuild their lives amid the widespread destruction in Gaza.

ECHR holds hearing in case of 10 Ukrainian children from Crimea missing since 2014
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:13:15 EEST
02:13:15 KST

The European Court of Human Rights held oral hearings in the case "Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union on behalf of ten Ukrainian children v. Russia" concerning children from orphanages in Crimea whose whereabouts have been unknown since 2014.
According to a press release provided to Interfax-Ukraine, the children, who were born between 2009 and 2013 and were in the care of the Ukrainian state at the time of the occupation of Crimea, were incorporated into the Russian system of adoption and foster care after Russia established control over the peninsula.
"When Russia occupied Crimea, these children were between one and five years old. The Ukrainian state was their guardian, and since then it has been unable to get an answer to a simple question: where are they? Today, they are teenagers who may be living with a different citizenship and in foreign families. Justice for them is not just about punishing those responsible. It is the right of every child and their loved ones to know the truth: where they are, who they are with, and who decided that they are no longer Ukrainian. This is the fundamental importance of this case," Head of Bring Kids Back UA Maksym Maksymov said.
The Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union filed the application with the ECHR in January 2023. The court examined the admissibility and merits of the case. According to the applicant, the Russian government did not submit any observations on the case and did not participate in the hearing.
Third parties in the case include, among others, the Ukrainian government and seven Ukrainian and international organizations. The International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute (IBAHRI) urged the Court to take into account the particular vulnerability of children and the context of the occupation.
The ECHR will issue its decision on the admissibility and merits of the case at a later date.
