Race to evacuate war-damaged Gaza buildings after deadly apartment block collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:06:39 UTC
01:06:39 KST

Race to evacuate war-damaged Gaza buildings after deadly apartment block collapse
GAZA/CAIRO, Sept 23 - Officials in Gaza say plans to evacuate people from war-damaged buildings after the deadly collapse of an apartment block last week face major challenges, including a lack of demolition equipment and limited land to relocate residents.
Nearly a year since a ceasefire ended major fighting between Israel and Hamas, officials say tens of thousands of people, with few options for shelter, are living in buildings damaged during Israel's military campaign, despite repeated warnings that they should leave.
In the early hours of September 16, the danger became clear when the Al-Saada building in Gaza City's Al-Rimal neighbourhood collapsed, killing 21 people. At least 45 survivors were rescued from the rubble.
Gaza officials say more than 2,000 buildings have been classified as being at risk. Other war-damaged buildings have previously collapsed, causing casualties, including amid winter storms.
"These buildings now represent ticking time bombs for residents and displaced people in many places," said Husni Muhanna, spokesperson for the Gaza City municipality, adding that this presented a "real danger" with the weather set to deteriorate into the winter.
On Sunday, Gaza authorities announced an emergency plan to evacuate people from 255 buildings most at risk of collapse and demolish them.
An Egyptian-led relief body had offered to provide transport to move those evacuated to designated shelters, said Ismail Al-Thawabta, head of the Hamas-run Gaza government's media office.
But he said the plan faced major obstacles, "including some families refusing to evacuate unsafe buildings despite the warnings, severe funding shortages, a lack of heavy equipment needed for safe demolition, and limited safe land available to relocate displaced people."
SHORTAGE OF EQUIPMENT
Large-scale reconstruction in Gaza has yet to begin, with US-brokered efforts to get Hamas to disarm and Israeli forces to withdraw largely stalled. A population of more than 2 million lives confined to about a third of the enclave, mainly housed in makeshift tents or overcrowded rooms in damaged buildings. Deadly Israeli airstrikes, which Israel says target militants, have continued.
Most of Gaza's buildings were destroyed by airstrikes or bulldozed by Israeli forces, and almost all others have suffered damage.
Palestinian and UN officials blame Israel's restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery to clear rubble and materials and equipment to rebuild homes.
In response to a request for comment, Israel's military said it was committed to minimising harm to civilians and that any activities, including against "terrorist infrastructure", were carried out based on operational necessity.
COGAT, the Israeli military agency that coordinates aid, said entry of heavy equipment and reconstruction materials would not be authorised until Hamas disarmed. It said Hamas exploited humanitarian aid, something the Palestinian militant group denies.
Alessandro Mrakic, head of the United Nations Development Programme office in Gaza, said a shortage of equipment meant people had to dig through the rubble with their hands when the Al-Saada building collapsed, and that oil and spare parts were needed to keep the machinery already in Gaza in service.
He estimated the number of buildings at risk of collapse at 400. "We know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter," he said. "We are running against time."
RESIDENTS SAY THEY HAVE NOWHERE ELSE TO GO
The Al-Saada building was in an area that was hit by Israeli bombardment two days after a Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, triggered Israel's offensive in Gaza. Israel launched heavy airstrikes followed by a ground campaign which it said were aimed at destroying Hamas and its underground network of tunnels.
Mohammad Arafa, head of the Gaza Engineers Association, said that based on assessments by fellow engineers who inspected the Al-Saada building over the past year, its collapse resulted from structural weakness after bombardment damaged several concrete pillars supporting its foundations.
But people had sheltered there because they had nowhere else to go, said Feryal Abu Ghanem, whose daughter-in-law was staying with her family when the building collapsed and was among those killed.
Bassam Naseer, a displaced man living in another damaged building nearby, said he feared the same thing would happen there. "No one is looking after us. The conditions are very difficult," he said.
After the Al-Saada's collapse, the Israel Defense Forces said in a social media post that it had not struck the building during the war. It did not respond to questions about residents saying it had struck the building, or about whether the building had been damaged by strikes on the surrounding area.
Eyad Azzam, who lost his pregnant wife and a 3-year-old son in the Al-Saada building's collapse, showed a video on his mobile phone of another son, Abdel-Rahman, trapped in the wreckage of the building before he was pulled to safety.
Abdel-Rahman, 7, had reached towards his mother, hoping to protect her from fallen rock, his father said. "He put out his hand and it wasn't a rock that had fallen, it was the entire ceiling."
People continued to live under damaged ceilings or columns for lack of other options, Azzam said.
"Today people say, 'This is a dangerous place to live in.' But where shall I go?" he said. "Even in the street there's no place." REUTERS

President De La Espriella orders militarization of Colombian resort city amid gang retaliation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

Laura Gamba Fadul
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella ordered the immediate militarization of Santa Marta on Tuesday night, deploying troops and launching low-altitude air patrols to regain control of the Caribbean port city following a violent offensive by a powerful narco-paramilitary cartel.
The security crisis erupted after the military killed a senior leader of the Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada (ACSN) along with six associates during an operation in the region. In retaliation, the armed group declared an "armed strike," threatening merchants and drivers to enforce a commercial lockout and transport shutdown across Santa Marta and neighboring Cienaga, local media reported.
The intimidation campaign paralyzed the coastal city of almost 600,000 residents, a major domestic and international tourism hub renowned for its beaches and proximity to Tayrona National Natural Park. Local business representatives estimated that around 95% of commercial establishments remained closed Wednesday morning, while public transit services suspended operations and schools closed.
Throughout Tuesday and into Wednesday, armed men on motorcycles set fire to trucks and buses, engaged in sporadic shootouts with security forces, and forced shopkeepers to pull down their shutters.
President De La Espriella traveled to Santa Marta late Tuesday night, posting video footage on social media showing him walking through heavily guarded streets to reassure residents.
"Those who do not submit will be taken down, and I will not allow them to continue bringing our people to their knees through terror," De La Espriella declared, confirming that three suspects had been arrested in connection with the arson attacks and threats.
In office since August, De La Espriella has pursued a militarized strategy against illegal armed groups, backed by enhanced security cooperation with the US. He emphasized that organizations such as the ACSN, Los Pachenca, and the Gulf Clan would face the full force of state power.
"We are going after all those bandits without mercy," the president said.
The ACSN traces its origins to legacy far-right paramilitary groups that originally formed to fight leftist guerrilla forces in the 1990s and 2000s. Today, the heavily armed criminal network finances its operations through international cocaine trafficking, illegal mining, and systematic extortion.

'Too small for the future' defense establishment demands expansion of Israel Navy, as sixth submarine arrives from Germany
There is growing concerne from security officials because despite the arrival of the INS Drakon from Germany, Israel has only 6 submarines, while Turkey has 12 and Greece has 9
With the arrival of the INS Drakon submarine in Israel on Wednesday, the defense establishment is calling for the expansion of the Navy, as currently it is "too small for the challenges of the future."
Israel is currently monitoring the military buildup of various countries in the Middle East with developing naval fleets, such as Turkey and Egypt.
Turkey realized more than a decade ago the potential of the navy. The commander of the Turkish Navy coined the phrase "the Blue Homeland." A doctrine where they see the sea as a sovereign extension of Turkey, including the annexation of its economic waters.
According to an Israeli official, this represents significant potential to increase Turkey’s power projection and strength in the long term. Israeli assessments are that in the future Turkey will have 18 submarines (currently 12 and another 6 are planned), including an independent capability to produce submarines.
At the same time, the Syrian navy is beginning to re-arm with the help of the Turks, which places Israel at a crossroads. According to security sources, there is sufficient time to build up if the proper process is started in the near future. They recommend the acquisition of two additional submarines, semi-autonomous vessels, light Reshef-class corvettes and other means for naval warfare, preparation for combat on the open sea, and more.
The new submarine brings with it new capabilities and it is the largest ever to arrive in Israel. It took nearly 14 years to build the sophisticated vessel, and under the shadow of the war, its arrival in the country was even delayed by several months following Ireland and Norway's refusal to allow training in their maritime territory. It will take another two to three months for INS Drakon to become operational, after the installation of Israeli systems.
A senior official in the security establishment said that the blockage of Bab al-Mandeb should greatly worry Israel, among other reasons because it exposes the Mediterranean Sea to future risks and leads countries and organizations to impose a blockade on the State of Israel. In his definition, the closure of a strait is “asymmetric warfare” due to the circumstances. When the Houthis launch missiles from deep within Yemen toward a very narrow stronghold—it is almost impossible to effectively target them.

INS Drakon: From Germany to Israel
After a journey of about 4,000 nautical miles from Germany, the INS Drakon, arrived in Israel on Wednesday. Upon its arrival, the submarine joins the new generation of submarines built in Germany as part of the security cooperation between the two countries.
INS Drakon is equipped with an Air Independent Propulsion (AIP) system, which enables the submarine to generate energy and recharge its batteries even during prolonged stays underwater, without the need to surface or use external air. The system uses oxygen and hydrogen to produce energy, thereby allowing for an extended duration of covert underwater operations and maintaining operational capabilities over time. This is the third AIP submarine in the Israeli Navy.
The submarine is over 70 meters (230 feet) long and is about 30% larger than the Dolphin-class submarines. Despite its size, less than one-fifth of its volume is visible above the water.
Its arrival marks the completion of the second generation of Navy submarines built in Germany, and signifies another milestone in the longstanding security cooperation between Israel and Germany.
The voyage from Germany to Israel took about a month, along a route of approximately 4,000 nautical miles, which is about 8,000 kilometers. The journey included sailing in the Atlantic Ocean, passing through the Strait of Gibraltar, and continuing through the Mediterranean Sea to Israel.
The construction of the submarine lasted more than 12 years, and after its completion, months of tests and preparations were carried out ahead of its arrival in Israel.
Throughout the project, there was close cooperation between the Israeli Navy, the German Navy, the German Ministry of Defense, and the professional parties involved in the construction of the submarine.
Israeli involvement in the project has been ongoing for about 20 years, through an Israeli project management team operating in Germany, which oversees the planning, construction, and testing processes. The management team is staffed by officers and engineers from the Navy, who come to Germany together with their families for periods of several years. At a later stage, crews from the submarine flotilla also join the project, participating in sailings and evaluations prior to the delivery of the submarines and their integration into the Navy.
Alongside technology, the Submarine Flotilla emphasizes the importance of human capital: submarine crews are required to maintain high levels of professionalism, responsibility, composure, and operational sharpness. The submariners operate complex combat systems and work for extended periods deep at sea and in remote theaters, under conditions of secrecy and isolation from the outside world. Israeli involvement in Germany continues to this day, with an eye toward the next-generation project—the Dakar submarines, which are currently under construction and represent the next generation of the Navy's submarines.

However, the leaders expressed deep concern regarding El-Sayed's candidacy, stating that he "has had every opportunity to meet our request to support our basic needs" but "has declined even to respond." The coalition outlined five core principles candidates must address to guarantee Jewish safety, including for Zionists, protecting identity rights, upholding Jewish sovereignty in Israel, welcoming full political participation, and providing an affirmative vision for the Middle East.
El-Sayed has been criticized for blaming Israel for local issues in Michigan
The letter criticized past remarks by El-Sayed, pointing out that he has called Israelis "bloodthirsty," referred to American support for Israel as "purchased loyalty," blamed Israel for local issues in Michigan, and rejected Israel as a Jewish state. Emphasizing that support cannot be taken for granted, the coalition wrote in their open letter that "every constituency must occasionally remind its party that support is earned, not owed," describing the campaign as "a good faith effort to make our needs unmistakably clear, and to invite any candidate seeking public office — now or in the future — to engage, listen, learn, and grow."

IRGC benefiting from false hopes of renewed negotiations, expert tells ‘Post’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:04:04 UTC
01:04:04 KST

The indirect talks between Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, which many have viewed as a sign of Tehran’s willingness to reengage in negotiations, are only “half” the “truth” of what is really taking place, INSS Iran expert Beni Sabti told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.
For the first time since the memorandum of understanding (MoU) failed in July, Araghchi and the US envoys communicated through mediators, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Sabti said that the talks and promises to open Hormuz meant little when Iran was continuing to attack ships and attempting to assert control over the strait.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday that Tehran was willing to reopen Hormuz provided Washington openly committed to resolving the conflict diplomatically. However, only a day after the statement, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center reported that a cargo vessel was struck, resulting in two casualties.
Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesperson for the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, also confirmed on Tuesday that the Islamic Republic had no intention of abandoning its attempts to control the Strait of Hormuz. The parliament adopted provisions allowing the regime authorities to seize 20% of a vessel’s cargo, or its value, from ships violating Iran’s rules for passage through the strait.
'This is the Iranian way'
“They talk, and they attack, and this is the Iranian way, the terrorist organization way. It is exactly what Hamas did during the war,” Sabti said.
“There were negotiations, but there were also attacks and war. They want all their conditions to be met, and then there will be negotiations or an opening of the strait. They want all of the frozen money released, all the wars, especially by Israel against their proxies and against themselves, to stop, and other conditions,” he noted.
“These seven points cannot be fulfilled, and they know that. So they come for negotiations, but not with 100% desire and will, goodwill, or a true heart. It’s just kind of a theater, a lie that they bring,” Sabti added.
IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi admitted on Tuesday that he viewed negotiations as another strategy of the war, saying that “if the country’s interests require it, negotiations can be part of the battle while we remain prepared for combat… One war is fought with weapons; in negotiations, the war is fought with words, arguments, and diplomatic methods.”
In an interview with Agence France-Presse, Mohebbi also claimed that Iran had tightened its conditions to end the conflict and had refused Washington’s multiple attempts to return to the negotiating table.
The stark difference between Mohebbi’s narrative and what is being portrayed in New York is where the half-truth lies, Sabti explained. Those in New York were “not the relevant people to talk to” as the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is firmly in control of Iran.
'This is the problem of the West'
“This is the problem of the West: They think the entire Iranian regime is one entity and that it is all the same: If you talk to the president or the foreign minister, it’s like talking to the whole regime because this is the way it is in the Western world,” he said, adding that those in the IRGC were profiting from Western naivety and using diplomats to “buy a little more time.”
With reports indicating that Saudi Arabia is restarting operations at its East-West Pipeline, potentially allowing 7 million barrels per day of oil to return to the global market amid growing frustration with the Houthis, Iran’s strategy of holding the strait hostage is slowly failing, he claimed.
With the Iranian economy suffering after years of sanctions that have intensified since August’s Operation Economic Outcast [US President Donald Trump’s “Economic D-Day”], IRGC officials running the country are hoping for some relief as a gesture of goodwill from the West – regardless of whether they have any real intention of following through, Sabti concluded.

This is stated in a joint statement in support of Ukraine issued by 51 member states of the United Nations (UN), with the participation of Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha, during a press briefing ahead of a high-level meeting of the UN Security Council on Ukraine.
"As the Security Council meets to discuss the situation in Ukraine, we reaffirm our shared commitment to the principles of the UN Charter and to peace. We stand in solidarity with Ukraine as it continues to face Russia's war of aggression. We recall that the UN Charter upholds the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of all States, and the inherent right of self-defence," reads the statement, which is available to the Interfax-Ukraine news agency.

The statement notes that after four years, six months, and thirty days of full-scale war, the human toll continues to rise. "We are deeply concerned by Russia's escalation against civilians and civilian infrastructure across Ukraine causing record high number of casualties in the last months, as recorded by the UN. We call for full respect for international humanitarian law, accountability and for the protection of civilians."
In addition, the signatories expressed particular concern over the attacks in the Black Sea. "We are deeply concerned by Russia's escalation against civilians and civilian infrastructure across Ukraine causing record high number of casualties in the last months, as recorded by the UN. We call for full respect for international humanitarian law, accountability and for the protection of civilians."
The signatories of the statement also called on Russia to "ensure the immediate, safe and unconditional return to Ukraine of all arbitrarily detained, forcibly transferred or deported Ukrainian civilians, including children, as well as the complete return of all prisoners of war and the return of all internees, as significant confidence-building measures."
"Ukraine wants peace. We want peace. Russia must stop its aggression, accept a ceasefire, and engage meaningfully in negotiations towards a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in accordance with international law," the signatory countries concluded in the statement.
The statement was signed by: the European Union, Albania, Andorra, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Canada, Costa Rica, Croatia, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Honduras, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Israel, Italy, Japan, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, Montenegro, the Netherlands, New Zealand, North Macedonia, Norway, Panama, Poland, Portugal, Republic of Korea, Republic of Moldova, Romania, San Marino, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom.

Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the quota system was not working and that he was preparing a new migration policy model. Social Security Minister Inga Ruginiene, however, said the current system was strict and functioned effectively.
The quota for this year was exhausted in early September. Business representatives have warned that Lithuania needs a clearer long-term migration policy.
Lithuanian Tatars, also known as Lipka Tatars, have lived in the region since the late 14th century. The Kaunas Mosque, built by the Tatar community in the period between the two world wars, reflects that centuries-old Muslim presence.

A huit mois de la présidentielle, les comptes de campagne déjà sous surveillance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:03:25 UTC
01:03:25 KST

A huit mois de la présidentielle, les comptes de campagne déjà sous surveillance
POLITICO a rencontré Christian Charpy, le président de l’autorité administrative qui aura la responsabilité de valider ou non les dépenses des candidats à l’Elysée.
Christian Charpy aura une vigilance toute particulière sur l’origine des prêts de personnes privées, qui constituent un moyen de se financer en plus des dons ou des ressources de son parti. | CNCCFP
Dans les bureaux sécurisés du 35, rue de la Fédération, à Paris, où les étagères croulent sous les piles de factures et de documents de campagne, l’atmosphère a changé. La course pour 2027 a aussi commencé pour la Commission nationale des comptes de campagne et des financements politiques (CNCCFP), aux avant-postes d’une élection majeure.
"On est sollicités par les équipes de campagne", explique d'emblée Christian Charpy, le président de l'autorité indépendante, à POLITICO. Il prévoit de réunir l’ensemble des représentants des candidats, dès que la liste des personnalités sur la ligne de départ sera connue.
Alors que les dépenses électorales sont prises en compte depuis le printemps, soit un an avant le scrutin, les écuries veulent s’assurer qu’elles sont dans les clous, pour éviter de voir les comptes de leur champion retoqués par Christian Charpy et ses auditeurs.
Advertisement
"Beaucoup de questions portent sur l'utilisation des réseaux sociaux et sur leur inscription dans les comptes", rapporte l’ancien magistrat à la Cour des comptes, passé par la direction de l’Agence nationale pour l’emploi. Pas plus tard que le 22 septembre, la Commission a répondu à Renaissance, le parti de Gabriel Attal, qui voulait des précisions sur le statut des interviews avec des créateurs de contenu.
"La liberté, qu'elle soit d’expression, d’opinion, d’information, est là. C’est compliqué d’incriminer un influenceur qui fait un podcast avec un candidat, s’il n’y a pas de contrepartie financière derrière", acte le haut fonctionnaire. A l’inverse, si le créateur de contenu est payé pour réaliser une interview, l’opération doit être imputée dans les dépenses. Une telle transaction sera d’ailleurs interdite à partir du 1er octobre, date à laquelle la publicité politique est prohibée.
Prévention… et vérifications
Autre signe d’un changement d’époque, sur fond de craintes des ingérences étrangères : les candidats sont invités à faire preuve d’une "extrême vigilance" sur l’origine des fonds qui permettent de faire campagne. Pour les dons aux candidats, ils doivent être faits par des personnes résidant en France ou de nationalité française. Les prêts bancaires ne pourront, eux, provenir que d'une banque située dans l'espace économique européen.
Christian Charpy aura une vigilance toute particulière sur l’origine des prêts de personnes privées, qui constituent un moyen de se financer en plus des dons ou des ressources de son parti. "Est-ce que les prêteurs sont réels, ou sont-ils des prête-noms ? C’est une question qui peut se poser", pointe-t-il.
En cas de doute, le gendarme des comptes de campagne saisit le service de renseignement financier Tracfin pour remonter l’origine de fonds douteux, ou dialogue avec Viginum, l’agence de l’Etat chargée de lutter contre les ingérences numériques, en cas d’opération de déstabilisation "caractérisée".
Lors des dernières municipales, deux candidats LFI avaient fait l’objet d’une attaque extérieure sophistiquée. Le sujet est d’autant plus sensible que certaines formations, comme le RN, peinent à trouver un prêt. Et ce, alors que l’initiative de Matignon de créer un "pool bancaire" pour éviter cette situation a été abandonnée, comme l’a révélé POLITICO.
Advertisement
"Ne pas respecter les règles, c'est prendre des risques"
Le cru 2027 sera également marqué par une dernière nouveauté : la dématérialisation.
Les pièces justificatives et les factures vont bientôt pouvoir être directement déposées sur un site internet. "On pourra plus facilement faire des croisements de fichiers, salue Christian Charpy. Pour faire, par exemple, des comparaisons de coûts entre des meetings ayant accueilli le même nombre de personnes pour des candidats différents. Ce ne sera pas inutile pour se demander s’il y a eu surfacturation ou sous-facturation."
La dernière fois que la CNCCFP a sorti l’arme nucléaire, c’était en 2012, lorsque les comptes de campagne de Nicolas Sarkozy ont été entièrement rejetés. Un cas de figure rarissime, mais que toutes les équipes ont bien en tête. "Ne pas respecter les règles, c’est prendre des risques considérables", fait savoir celui qui a pris son poste l’année dernière.
Pour éviter toute interférence ou ingérence, la Commission a d’ailleurs prévu de louer un grand espace supplémentaire, à son siège parisien, pour accueillir sur place tous les auditeurs au moment où il faudra, après le scrutin, passer au crible l’ensemble des dépenses des candidats. Une précaution qui en dit long sur les menaces planant sur l’élection suprême.
Alexandre Léchenet, Jason Wiels et Judith Chetrit ont contribué à cet article.

What can lead to a pension card being blocked and how to restore access to the money
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:01:48 EEST
01:01:48 KST

What can lead to a pension card being blocked and how to restore access to the money
Kyiv • UNN
Access to pension funds may be restricted by a bank, an enforcement officer, or the Pension Fund of Ukraine. We explain the reasons for the block and the procedure for restoring payments.
Situations arise in life when money from a pension card cannot be used. The reasons vary. For example, a bank may temporarily block the “plastic” for security reasons, so that criminals cannot gain access to the money. Card servicing may be temporarily suspended because the holder failed to contact the financial institution that issued it in time and update their personal data. In addition, there are cases when the bank itself, the State Executive Service, or a private enforcement officer restricts the use of funds in the account.
Sometimes the problem is not with the card. These are cases when the Pension Fund (PFU) stops transferring the pension, even though the bank account remains accessible. The reason determines whom to contact and which documents to prepare.
Why pensioners may lose access to their money and how to restore it is explained by UNN.
Plastic card and bank account: what exactly can be blocked for a pensioner
A pension card is a payment instrument that a person uses to access funds in a bank account. The money is held in the account itself, so if a person’s plastic or virtual card is blocked, the funds themselves will remain available. To use them as before, it will only be necessary to find out the reason for the restrictions and take all steps to eliminate them.
If the bank has restricted the use of the card only, other ways of accessing the funds may remain available. For example, a person may be able to make a transfer using the account details or receive their payment at a bank teller’s desk. Everything depends on the reason for the block and the extent of the restrictions imposed.
A different situation is an attachment of funds. In this case, the ability to dispose of the money in the account is restricted, and replacing the card will not solve the problem.
The suspension of pension payments concerns the further transfer of the pension by the Pension Fund. The card may continue to work, and the holder may use the available balance. Therefore, the absence of a new deposit and an ATM’s refusal to dispense cash require different actions.
Why a bank may block a card for security reasons
A bank may restrict the use of a card if it has reasonable grounds to suspect that unauthorized persons have gained access to it. The purpose of such a decision is to prevent unauthorized debiting of funds. In particular, verification may be required when there are signs that the card has been compromised (for example, when fraudsters may have learned its details or someone carried out recent transactions with the funds without the holder’s consent). In this case, restoring access requires contacting the bank through official channels and completing the prescribed verification.
If the card details have in fact fallen into the hands of third parties, it is advisable to discuss reissuing the “plastic” with the bank. Simply restoring its operation does not eliminate the risk of the stolen data being used again.
Transactions may also become unavailable after a person forgets their PIN and enters it incorrectly three times in a row on an ATM screen or in the bank’s mobile application. In this case, the duration of the restriction and the procedure for restoring access depend on the rules of the particular financial institution.
What happens after the card expires
The card’s expiration may also be a reason for a payment or cash withdrawal to be declined. However, this is not the same as blocking the account or suspending pension payments. First, one should clarify with the bank whether it has extended the card’s validity period and which transactions remain available. If the answer is negative, a new card should be ordered.
It is also worth checking separately whether the IBAN account number has changed. If a pensioner opens another account or switches to another bank, the new details must be reported to the Pension Fund. Replacing a card and changing an account are different procedures.
Outdated personal data: when this may lead to restrictions on using pension funds
Banks are required to verify their clients and keep information about them up to date. Therefore, even a person who has been receiving a pension at the same bank for many years may receive a request to update their details, which they must comply with. In turn, the financial institution may ask them to confirm their passport details, address, or other information in the questionnaire, or to provide documents in place of those that are no longer valid. The specific list depends on the circumstances and the content of the request.
If a client does not provide the necessary information, the bank has the right to restrict debit transactions. Termination of the business relationship may also be possible on the grounds provided for by law. At the same time, the receipt of funds and the ability to spend them are different matters: under certain restrictions, money may continue to be credited, but it cannot be used until the verification is completed.
To avoid this unpleasant situation, notifications about updating personal data should be checked through the official app, contact center, or branch. At the bank itself, one should clarify the list of documents, the deadline for submitting them, and whether the procedure is available remotely.
Which transactions with a pension card may raise questions during financial monitoring
Even if a pensioner receives their lawful state payment on a card, this does not exempt other transactions on the account from financial monitoring. Banks analyze the movement of funds and compare it with information about the client, their income, and the nature of their use of the account.
Questions may arise if the amounts of incoming funds or transfers differ significantly from the person's financial activity known to the bank. In that case, the institution may request an explanation of the nature of the transactions and documents confirming the origin of the funds.
To resolve the issue, it is necessary to determine exactly which transactions require an explanation and provide documents that correspond to the actual circumstances. It is worth remembering that in such cases there is no universal document that automatically removes any restrictions.
Freezing of funds due to debts: where a pensioner should turn
A person's access to money may also be restricted במסגרת enforcement proceedings. One common reason is the compulsory collection of debts for loans, utility services, alimony, or fines.
In such a case, one should obtain from the bank the details of the enforcement proceedings and find out who imposed the freeze. Next, one should contact the state or private enforcement officer and review the decision.
If a pension is credited to the account, it is necessary to confirm the origin of the funds. A bank statement and a certificate from the Pension Fund may be required for this. With these documents, one should raise the issue of the legality of the freeze, its scope, and whether there are grounds for lifting the restrictions.
During martial law, an individual debtor may designate one current account for debit transactions within the limit of two minimum wages per calendar month. The calculation uses the minimum wage established as of January 1 of the relevant year. To exercise this right, a pensioner must write an application and submit it to the state or private enforcement officer who imposed the freeze. It allows the person to use part of the funds (equivalent to two subsistence minimums established by the Cabinet of Ministers in January of the current year — Ed.), but it does not cancel the debt and does not mean that the freeze will be lifted in full.
When the problem is the suspension of pension payments
If the card is working but the pension was not credited on the scheduled date, the reason must be clarified with the Pension Fund. They may, in some cases, suspend payment of the funds on grounds established by law. \Among these are the granting of a pension based on documents containing inaccurate information, failure to receive the granted pension for six consecutive months, or failure to undergo physical identification in cases where it is mandatory.
For persons temporarily residing abroad or staying in temporarily occupied territories, physical identification must be completed by December 31 of each year. The relevant rules have exceptions, including for payments made under international agreements.
For recipients residing in the temporarily occupied territories, the absence of debit transactions on the account for six months may constitute a separate ground for terminating payments if they also did not undergo physical identification during that period.
How to restore access to money on a pension card
The first step is to contact the bank and obtain a clear explanation of what exactly happened: whether the card was blocked, an individual transaction was declined, debit transactions were restricted, or the funds were seized. It is also worth checking whether the pension was credited most recently. Further steps depend on the reason. Security issues, PIN-related matters, reissuance, and updating personal data are handled with the bank. Restrictions in enforcement proceedings should be addressed with the enforcement officer, while the termination of pension payments should be addressed with the Pension Fund of Ukraine.
To resume pension payments, an application, supporting documents, and identification may be required. Available methods of identity verification include video identification and authorization on the Pension Fund of Ukraine's web portal via Diia.Signature. The specific procedure should be clarified depending on the grounds for terminating the payments.
If contacting the bank did not help resolve the issue, a complaint may be filed with the National Bank of Ukraine. To do so, it is advisable to retain the requests, the institution's responses, and documents confirming the circumstances.
Reminder
Earlier, UNN explained how to use an account under seizure during martial law.

EU faces backlash after lifting sanctions on Russian billionaires

EU faces backlash after lifting sanctions on Russian billionaires
BRUSSELS, Sept 23 - The European Union faced a growing backlash on Wednesday for lifting sanctions on two Russian billionaires, with some of its members saying the move undermined a pillar of support for Ukraine’s war effort and that it signalled the bloc would bow to blackmail.
Following pressure from France and despite pleas by Ukraine, the EU agreed on Tuesday to end asset freezes and travel bans on Russian-Uzbek metals tycoon Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, co-founder of one of Russia’s biggest conglomerates.
France privately told partners that Azerbaijan was using Usmanov's sanctions case to pressure Paris over two French citizens held there, three diplomats told Reuters.
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev on Wednesday pardoned a French national jailed for espionage, a move that Paris said was a "humanitarian gesture".
France’s push to lift sanctions on Usmanov prompted Luxembourg to demand the same treatment for Fridman, who has launched a $16-billion claim against it for freezing his assets.
'ONE HELLUVA PANDORA'S BOX'
Bill Browder, a British financier and opponent of Russian President Vladimir Putin, said "every sanctioned Russian oligarch" would now start working with "tinpot dictatorships around the world" to gain leverage to get sanctions lifted.
"France just opened one helluva Pandora’s box," he posted on X.
Other governments felt they had little choice but to accept France’s demand, which Paris linked to national security, in return for the renewal of Russia-related sanctions on about 3,000 other people and organisations for the next three years, diplomats said.
Diplomats from multiple countries said they hoped the long renewal period would prevent others making a similar push any time soon. France was able to push through its demand partly because the sanctions were about to expire.
Within the EU, some of the most strident criticism came from the Baltic states. Latvia initially blocked the move before agreeing to abstain.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told Reuters during the UN General Assembly in New York that the move sent a “very bad signal at a wrong time, when Russia is actually putting more pressure on Ukraine”.
EU diplomats, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss internal discussions, said discontent about the move was widely shared across the 27-nation bloc.
"This is certainly not a glorious moment," one said.
UKRAINE QUESTIONS EU MOVE
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy’s commissioner for sanctions policy, said he was shocked to discover the EU was moving to lift sanctions on the two billionaires.
"I couldn't really believe it. I didn't really see it coming," he said.
He welcomed the three-year rollover but asked: "Is it really worth (it) to de-list two names of this kind of magnitude?"
Asked about the move at a press briefing in Brussels on Wednesday, EU foreign policy spokesperson Christian Wigand underlined the renewal decision and said the bloc would keep applying more sanctions.
"We adopted 21 packages of sanctions. And in parallel, we are also working on a new set of sanctions," Wigand said.
He said the EU wanted to increase pressure on Russia’s military industrial complex and its "shadow fleet" of tankers shipping oil and gas.
The EU's foreign policy arm has proposed about 1,600 additions to the sanctions list. Some diplomats voiced hope that EU member states would swiftly approve the additions, to show the bloc remained committed to sanctions.
Some diplomats questioned France’s explanations for pushing to remove sanctions on Usmanov. French officials often seemed uneasy when defending their stance and when asked by reporters whether the Azerbaijan cases were the real reason for the move.
One senior European official said Paris had lost a lot of credibility, which could make it harder to push initiatives inside the EU as Emmanuel Macron enters his last few months as French president.
Guntram Wolff, a senior fellow at Brussels think tank Bruegel, said the move would not have a major impact on the war in Ukraine but sent "a very negative signal that the EU has been ready to make more or less dubious exemptions at a moment of political pressure". REUTERS

Russian citizen who served as Ukrainian Supreme Court's deputy chief charged with corruption

Russian citizen who served as Ukrainian Supreme Court's deputy chief charged with corruption
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) on Sept. 23 charged Bohdan Lvov, former deputy head of the Supreme Court, with money laundering.
Lvov is one of Ukraine's most scandalous judges. He was fired from the Supreme Court in 2022 due to his concealed Russian citizenship.
The controversy over Lvov's nationality highlighted the necessity of reforming the Supreme Court, which has been engulfed in corruption and other scandals for years.
The NABU did not identify him by name, saying that it had charged a former head of the Supreme Court's commercial division. Lvov served as head of the commercial division and deputy head of the Supreme Court from 2017 to 2022.
A law enforcement source confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that the NABU was referring to Lvov. The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from him and will publish his response once it is received.
In 2021–2022, Lvov acquired assets worth a total of about Hr 26 million ($580,000), including a house and the land it sits on, two apartments, and four plots of land, according to the NABU.
The NABU said it had also charged a former subordinate of Lvov and the subordinate’s mother.
“To conceal the illicit origin of the funds and the assets’ true ownership, he brought his subordinate, who effectively served as his secretary, into the scheme,” the bureau said. “The illicitly acquired property was formally registered in her mother’s name, allowing him to conceal evidence of the crime and launder the assets.”
Lvov was also charged with complicity in large-scale embezzlement in 2025.
As part of the embezzlement case, he is accused of helping the illegal transfer of a state-controlled oil product pipeline to companies allegedly affiliated with pro-Kremlin politician Viktor Medvedchuk in 2017.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty's Schemes investigation project reported in 2022 that Lvov received Russian citizenship in 1999 and still had a valid Russian passport. Schemes cited official information from Russia’s Federal Tax Service and leaked documents from Russia’s official passport database.
Lvov denied the allegations.
Subsequently the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) confirmed that Lvov had Russian citizenship.
In October 2022, Vsevolod Kniazev, then head of the Supreme Court, fired Lvov due to the constitutional ban on judges with foreign citizenship.
The Public Integrity Council, the judiciary's civil watchdog, concluded in 2017 that Lvov did not meet ethics and integrity standards and did not have the right to run for a Supreme Court job. However, the watchdog's conclusion was ignored by the judicial authorities, and he was appointed.
Lvov has been under investigation for allegedly helping a member of the High Council of Justice to extort a $500,000 bribe in exchange for favorable court rulings.
Lvov has also been investigated as an alleged accomplice of ex-High Commercial Court Chairman Viktor Tatkov and his deputy Artur Yemelyanov, who have been charged with organizing the issuance of unlawful rulings as part one of Ukraine’s largest corruption schemes.
The judge denied the accusations of wrongdoing. He has not been charged in the bribery and Tatkov cases so far.
As the Supreme Court's leadership has been engulfed in corruption scandals, the European Union has demanded a reform of the Supreme Court and included it in EU accession requirements.
The Ukrainian authorities have so far failed to implement the reform.
When the current Supreme Court was created in 2017, the Public Integrity Council established that 22.2% of its judges did not meet integrity and ethics standards, and another 28.8% of the Supreme Court judges could have violated ethics standards.
The authorities ignored the conclusions and appointed the judges nonetheless.
Chickens came home to roost in June 2026, when a court sentenced Kniazev, former head of the Supreme Court, to five years in jail for bribery.
According to the investigators, Kniazev instructed subordinates to put the money into 13 bags for 13 Supreme Court judges.
In May 2026, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau charged three incumbent Supreme Court judges and one former judge of the court with receiving bribes in exchange for rulings as part of the same case.

Norway says Europe's 'largest' rare-earth mine plan set for 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:00:41 UTC
01:00:41 KST

The project has been delayed by environmental concerns, particularly over plans to locate mineral-processing facilities in an area of forest.
The Norwegian government says it is aiming to have a plan in place to develop mining facilities at Europe’s largest known rare-earths deposit by the year 2028 at the latest.
The Fen Complex, around 150 km southwest of Oslo, is estimated to contain 15.9 million tonnes of rare-earth oxides, including neodymium and praseodymium, which are used in powerful magnets for electric vehicles, renewable energy technology and defence equipment.
Environmental concerns have long delayed the project. Surveys in the area identified 78 endangered animal and plant species, including rare beetles, trees, mosses and fungi.
Rare Earths Norway (REN), the company that owns the extraction rights, has said the mine itself would be “invisible”, with extraction and crushing taking place below ground. However, surface processing facilities would still be required.
Earlier this year, Norway’s government took over the planning work from the municipality, including the study of alternative locations for surface installations.
“The objective is to have a plan in place by 2028 at the latest, but preferably before then,” Industry Minister Cecilie Myrseth told a press conference on Wednesday.
The government says the Fen Complex could help strengthen European and wider Western supply chains for critical minerals. No rare-earth deposits are currently being mined in Europe, leaving the continent heavily dependent on China for supplies.
Rare earth metals are crucial in the production of products ranging from smartphones and electric cars to fighter jets, and are classified as critical by the European Union.
REN says it hopes to start mining in the first half of the 2030s.

Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski attends opening of 81st UN General Assembly general debate in New York
22.09.2026
On 22 September, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski took part in the opening of the 81st UN General Assembly general debate in New York. On the second day of the high-level week, the head of Polish diplomacy spoke with world leaders about cooperation within NATO, security in the Indo-Pacific, and the Middle East conflict.
World leaders took part in the opening of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. The meeting was attended by Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski and President Karol Nawrocki, who is heading the Polish delegation. The leaders were welcomed for the last time by Secretary-General António Guterres, whose term expires on 31 December. The secretary-general spoke about the changes that have taken place in the world in recent years.
Over the last decade, wars erupted with devastating consequences and dragged on with despicable cruelty. Civilians were targeted. Human rights trampled. Hunger weaponized. Humanitarians killed. International law cast aside. Geopolitical divides have deepened. Inequalities have intensified
said Secretary-General António Guterres, adding that the main crises and challenges facing the world are conflicts, inequality, climate change, and technological changes.
Most of these challenges were also the subject of bilateral talks held by Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski. On the second day of the high-level week, the head of Polish diplomacy took part in a meeting on maritime security hosted by German foreign minister. Minister Sikorski, together with the heads of diplomacy of: Australia, France, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, and the United Kingdom discussed, among other things, strengthening partnerships with Indo-Pacific countries, including strategic relations with Japan and South Korea, continuing dialogue in support of a rules-based international order, and limiting Russia’s influence in the region.
The MFA chief also met with US Senators Jeanne Shaheen and Ruben Gallego. During the talks, the minister emphasised the importance of the presence of US troops in Poland and of military cooperation between the two countries, in particular in the context of the war beyond NATO’s eastern flank. The politicians provided assurances regarding the validity of guarantees under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty.
During the UN high-level week, Minister Sikorski drew attention to Russian provocations:
Putin is trying to provoke NATO in order to justify to his own public opinion why he is sending another half a million of young Russians to war in Ukraine. Russia is sending soldiers, cruise missiles, and drones. Russia is blowing up moving trains, trying to plant incendiary devices on airliners, torching shopping malls, I could go on. ... It might do something reckless and provocative below the threshold of a full-scale war. Therefore, our allies’ warranties are so important for us,
said Poland’s top diplomat.
Security was also a primary topic during Deputy Prime Minister Sikorski’s bilateral meetings. In his conversation with Kazakhstan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Mukhtar Tleuberdi, he stressed that Russia’s aggression against Ukraine poses a threat not only to Poland, but also to the whole region.
With the partners from Africa, the Polish foreign minister exchanged views on the conflict in the Middle East, the situation in the Persian Gulf, and other issues. During a meeting with his Egyptian counterpart, Minister Sikorski discussed, among other things, the development of Polish–Egyptian relations, including economic, agricultural, and scientific cooperation, as well as the University of Warsaw’s collaboration with partners in Egypt, the situation in Yemen, and maritime security in the Straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab.
Talking to Mauritania’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Mohamed Salem Ould Merzoug, Minister Sikorski raised the issue of stability and security of the Sahel, countering illegal migration, and cooperation with the European Union.
On behalf of the EU, the head of Polish diplomacy also met with Cameroon’s Minister of External Relations Lejeune Mbella Mbella. He presented the EU member states’ position on Russia’s war against Ukraine and noted Cameroon’s role in ensuring regional stability in the Chad Basin and the Gulf of Guinea.
Poland’s top diplomat is going to stay in New York until 24 September. He will hold a total of over 30 meetings in diverse formats to discuss, among other things, the future of multilateral cooperation and the need for UN reform. On Wednesday, 23 September, during a UN Security Council debate, the deputy prime minister will present Poland’s position on Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.

Fear of the unknown is linked to lower life satisfaction and heightened death anxiety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:00:25 UTC
01:00:25 KST

New psychology research indicates that a tendency to find unpredictable situations highly distressing is linked to lower overall life satisfaction. This connection appears to be driven by existential factors, with an inability to tolerate uncertainty relating to a reduced sense of life purpose and a heightened fear of death. The study was published in Psychological Reports.
Unpredictability is an inevitable part of human existence, ranging from daily inconveniences to global crises. For some people, navigating these unknowns is manageable. For others, ambiguous situations trigger a response known as intolerance of uncertainty. This psychological trait involves perceiving unpredictable events as threatening, unacceptable, and highly distressing.
Past research has established that an intolerance of uncertainty is associated with worry and anxiety. However, less attention has been given to how this trait relates to a broader evaluation of a person’s existence, known as life satisfaction. Life satisfaction is a subjective assessment of how well one’s current circumstances align with their personal goals and standards.
The research team wanted to explore whether existential concerns act as a bridge between a fear of the unknown and reduced life satisfaction. “In today’s world, individuals face unprecedented levels of unpredictability—ranging from global crises and economic shifts to personal life challenges,” Osman Hatun, an associate professor in the Department of Psychological Counseling and Guidance at Marmara University in Türkiye, told PsyPost. “While prior research has extensively shown how intolerance of uncertainty fuels anxiety and distress, very little attention was given to how it impacts overall life satisfaction through existential processes.”
Hatun and his colleagues focused on two key existential processes: meaning in life and death anxiety. Meaning in life refers to the feeling that one’s existence has purpose, value, and a sense of direction. Death anxiety involves a persistent uneasiness or fear regarding mortality, the process of dying, and what happens after death.
Because death represents the most extreme uncontrollable and uncertain event, the researchers suspected that individuals who struggle with unpredictability might be especially vulnerable to death anxiety. They proposed a potential pathway where an intolerance of uncertainty relates to a weakened sense of meaning in life, which in turn leaves a person more vulnerable to death anxiety, resulting in lower life satisfaction.
To explore these ideas, the researchers recruited 485 adults living in Türkiye through social media platforms. The participants ranged in age from 18 to 63, with an average age of about 32. Most of the sample identified as female, and all participants reported having experienced at least one adverse life event, such as a natural disaster, severe illness, or the loss of a loved one.
The volunteers completed a series of online questionnaires designed to measure the four central concepts of the study. They answered questions about how upsetting they find unforeseen events to assess their intolerance of uncertainty. To evaluate their meaning in life, they rated how strongly they felt their lives had purpose.
The participants also completed a death anxiety scale, answering questions about how much the ambiguity and inevitability of dying made them anxious. Finally, they rated their agreement with statements regarding their overall life satisfaction, providing a snapshot of their subjective well-being. The researchers then used statistical modeling techniques to observe how these four variables interacted with one another, while accounting for the participants’ age, sex, and number of prior adverse life events.
The results indicated a negative association between an intolerance of uncertainty and life satisfaction. In other words, individuals who found ambiguity highly distressing tended to report lower satisfaction with their lives. The statistical models provided evidence for the researchers’ proposed existential pathway.
A higher intolerance of uncertainty was linked to a lower sense of meaning in life. A reduced sense of meaning in life was, in turn, associated with greater death anxiety. Finally, higher death anxiety was related to lower life satisfaction. Together, an intolerance of uncertainty and meaning in life accounted for 27 percent of the variance in death anxiety among the participants. The full model explained 43 percent of the variance in life satisfaction.
Hatun noted that the size of these effects is highly meaningful. “When looking at statistical models, individual indirect pathways might appear modest in number, but the overall picture reveals strong practical significance,” he said. “In psychological research, explaining nearly half of someone’s life satisfaction through a set of related factors is quite substantial.”
The researchers were also struck by the robustness of these existential links. “It was striking that this sequential existential path remained significant even after controlling for participants’ actual cumulative experiences with adverse life events, such as natural disasters, severe illness, or bereavement,” Hatun added. “This suggests that how a person mentally relates to uncertainty can be just as decisive for their life satisfaction as the objective hardships they have lived through.”
The findings suggest that the emotional burden of uncertainty extends beyond everyday worry. People who have difficulty tolerating the unknown may find it harder to maintain a coherent and purposeful view of life. Without a strong sense of purpose to act as a psychological buffer, they may become more preoccupied with mortality, which takes a toll on their overall contentment.
This dynamic highlights the importance of anchoring oneself in everyday purpose. “Because we cannot eliminate uncertainty from the world, trying to control every unknown is often a losing battle,” the researchers explained. “Instead, our findings suggest that the key to protecting our well-being lies in actively cultivating meaning and purpose in our daily lives—whether through core values, relationships, or community connections.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which examined how self-determination and psychological need satisfaction buffer death anxiety rather than modeling an intolerance of uncertainty. That study similarly found that death-related anxiety is linked to lower life satisfaction. Additionally, a 2021 study of older Hindu pilgrims indicated that experiencing a greater sense of meaning in life is linked to lower death anxiety, mirroring the associations found in the new Turkish sample.
However, the results are in tension with a study covered by PsyPost in 2023. That research found that for individuals with high self-alienation, a greater meaning in life was actually associated with heightened death anxiety. The new study, which evaluated a sample of Turkish adults and focused on an overall pathway rather than looking at specific interactions with self-alienation, did not model this reversed effect.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on data collected at a single point in time, meaning it is impossible to determine the true sequence of events. The researchers can observe that an intolerance of uncertainty and life satisfaction are linked through meaning in life and death anxiety, but they cannot prove that one factor directly causes the other to change. Hatun emphasized this constraint, noting that “cross-sectional data show indirect associations rather than definitive cause-and-effect over time.”
He also cautioned against overinterpreting the findings as a mandate for complete control. “A common misinterpretation we would want to preempt is the belief that intolerance of uncertainty directly or inevitably ruins a person’s life satisfaction, or that individuals must eliminate all uncertainty from their lives to be happy,” Hatun said. “Eliminating uncertainty is neither realistic nor necessary; what matters most is the existential buffer—how uncertainty influences our sense of meaning and purpose.”
Another caveat is that the data came entirely from self-report questionnaires, which rely on individuals accurately perceiving and reporting their own feelings. The sample also consisted exclusively of people who had experienced at least one adverse life event. Because trauma and loss can deeply influence existential thoughts, these patterns might look slightly different in a population without a history of severe adversity.
There is also the cultural context to consider when interpreting these results. In Türkiye, family obligations, community connections, and spiritual beliefs often heavily shape a person’s sense of meaning and their attitudes toward mortality. Hatun noted that because the sample consisted of Turkish adults recruited online, “caution should be exercised when generalizing these conclusions across diverse global populations without longitudinal replication.”
To build on this work, the research team hopes to trace these mechanisms in real time and test meaning-centered interventions. “We plan to examine these pathways across diverse cultural contexts and developmental stages, specifically exploring how cultural meaning frameworks—such as family connectedness and spiritual worldviews—serve as protective buffers,” Hatun said. Ultimately, the researchers hope to inform clinical approaches, such as Logotherapy and Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, to help individuals cultivate resilience in an unpredictable world.
Above all, they hope the research fosters a more compassionate view of human struggles with the unknown. “We would like to emphasize that facing uncertainty is a fundamental part of the human condition, rather than an individual flaw or weakness,” Hatun added. “Our study highlights that while unpredictable events are inevitable, how we actively construct meaning in our daily lives provides an essential psychological anchor.”
The study, “Intolerance of Uncertainty and Life Satisfaction: The Mediating Roles of Meaning in Life and Death Anxiety,” was authored by Osman Hatun, Mark D. Griffiths, and Tuğba Türk Kurtça.

PHOTO economic.bg
Font size
Bulgaria’s Finance Ministry is proposing a 33% tax on windfall profits made by banks, payday lenders, insurers, telecom companies and retail chains from 2027, Deputy Finance Minister Lyudmila Petkova said. The tax would be paid in advance.
The threshold for mandatory VAT registration would also rise to €75,000.
The windfall tax is intended to bring additional revenue into the budget and partly offset the cost of higher tax relief for families with children. From 2027, parents with one child would be able to deduct €5,000 from their taxable income, rising to €8,000 for two children and €11,000 for three or more.

PHOTO BTA
Font size
Parliament has lifted the ban, in place since October 31, 2025, on exports and deliveries of petroleum products to the EU, mainly diesel and aviation fuel. The government proposal was approved with 121 votes from Progressive Bulgaria (PB) and will take effect once published in the State Gazette.
Forty-two MPs from Democratic Bulgaria, We Continue the Change, Vazrazhdane and three from GERB-SDS voted against. Another 23 GERB-SDS MPs abstained, while the Movement for Rights and Freedoms (MRF) did not take part in the vote, BTA reported.
The ban was introduced to safeguard Bulgaria’s energy security and keep the domestic fuel market stable following US sanctions on companies in the Lukoil group.
Slavi Vasilev of PB said lifting the ban would not affect diesel prices but would help the refinery and fuel traders.
“At a time when there is a fuel shortage and prices are rising worldwide, you are deciding to lift the export ban and trying to convince us that this is good for Bulgarian citizens,” Assen Vassilev of We Continue the Change said.

Russia Must Answer for Crimes in Crimea, Zelensky Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:58:51 UTC
00:58:51 KST

International order cannot fully recover until Ukraine restores its sovereignty over Crimea – the peninsula Russia illegally annexed in 2014, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, urging Western allies to hold the Kremlin accountable for its crimes.
Zelensky delivered the message at the sixth international Crimea Platform summit in New York, held alongside the high-level segment of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Wednesday, Sept. 23.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“There can be no full return to normality without Crimea, without restoring security, protecting people and lives, freeing the prisoners Russia is holding and returning to the basic principles of international law,” Zelensky said.
“Territorial integrity matters, the sovereignty of states matters,” he continued.
Holding Russia accountable remains crucial
Russia’s violation of international norms began with its seizure of Crimea in 2014, which became a starting point of the wider confrontation now affecting Ukraine, the Black Sea and overall global security.
“We want international law to have real force. We want Russia, which started this war and is stealing the land, to be held responsible,” Zelensky said, speaking about Ukrainian citizens living under Russian occupation in Crimea, parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions and Donbas, and those held in Russian prisons and camps.
Largest turnout in 6 years
This year’s summit drew more than 60 participants, including 16 leaders from every continent. For the first time, Panama and Trinidad and Tobago took part.
Russian Drone Attacks Kill 2, Injure 62 as Explosions Rock Ukraine Nationwide
The president described the Crimea Platform as an enduring diplomatic mechanism rather than a symbolic annual gathering.
The initiative was established as an international consultation and coordination format intended to strengthen the global response to Russia’s occupation and support the restoration of Ukraine’s control over the peninsula in accordance with international law.
It works on maintaining the policy of nonrecognition of Russia’s occupation, defending human rights on the peninsula and coordinating pressure on the Kremlin.
Wednesday’s summit placed particular emphasis on systematic rights violations and the militarization of occupied territories, including the influence of Russian policies on young people and education.
As of Sept. 1, Russia further expanded military training for children, including in occupied Ukrainian territories, and raised the share of mandatory instruction to 50% of school time.
Human right groups warned that the program, planned through 2036, targets both boys and girls to build a future mobilization reserve, while the First Deputy Chairman of the State Duma Committee on CIS Affairs, Viktor Vodolatsky, called for mandatory military training to begin in fifth grade on June 22.
“Let them prepare, but the outcome is inevitable,” he said, citing 2030 as a “relevant milestone” for Russia to attack NATO.
Black Sea security remains a problem
Zelensky connected the ongoing security crisis in the Black Sea to Crimea’s occupation. He said Russia’s transformation of the peninsula into a military base had affected freedom of navigation, food security and energy security.
Ukraine is prepared to take steps to protect shipping and food supplies in the region should Russia demonstrate a genuine willingness to pursue reciprocal de-escalation.
During a meeting with US President Donald Trump on Tuesday, Sept. 22, Zelensky offered another reciprocal energy ceasefire – in this case, on the power grid Ukraine expects Russia to target in the upcoming winter, alongside water supplies.
Although Ukraine consistently calls for the war to end, Russian President Vladimir Putin continues rejecting requests for direct meetings, while oftentimes rejecting and mocking such proposals, deeming them as “pointless.”
Zelensky’s UN schedule
Aside from the Crimea Platform, Zelensky is expected to hold bilateral meetings with the leaders of Australia, Finland, the Netherlands, Norway and Turkey, as well as with NATO secretary general and US policy experts.
He is also scheduled to attend a UN Security Council meeting on maintaining peace and security in Ukraine at 11 a.m. New York time (6 p.m. Kyiv time) before addressing the UNGA’s general debate at about 2 p.m. local time (6 p.m. Kyiv time), according to Ukrinform.

Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years after sexual assault conviction

Unknown Publisher

00:56:14 KST

Harvey Weinstein was sentenced to 15 years on Wednesday after being convicted of sexually assaulting former TV production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006 at his Manhattan apartment.
Haley appeared in court on Wednesday morning and delivered a victim impact statement.
In her statement, Haley spoke about the harassment and humiliation she has endured over the past seven years, saying she was publicly smeared by Weinstein, his defense team, and podcasters she suspects were paid to damage her image.
Haley added that her experience following the assault has “already been a life sentence” for her, and asked the judge to take all of this into consideration.
New York assistant district attorney Nicole Blumberg addressed the court on behalf of the prosecution. She asked the court to sentence Weinstein, 74, to 20 years with five years of post-release supervision, stating he never showed any type of remorse for his crimes.
Weinstein said in his statement he has remorse for Haley. “I live with many regrets and sincerely apologize for my actions,” he said.
Weinstein’s defense had also argued that their client is too sick to serve a long sentence following a diagnosis of several health conditions including blood cancer and heart disease. The defense asked for a nine-year sentence.
Before sentencing, Judge Curtis Farber acknowledged that Weinstein would be remembered not just for producing films, but for being the face of the #MeToo movement. Farber said Weinstein took advantage of Haley’s dreams of working in the film industry.
“You had it all,” Farber said. “Your legacy could have been cemented with greatness. But you threw it all away by assaulting Miriam Haley.”
The latest sentencing comes after years of appeals and retrials in the closely watched case.
Weinstein was sentenced to 23 years in prison in 2020 after a jury convicted him of sexually assaulting Haley and raping aspiring actor Jessica Mann.
But in 2024, New York’s highest court overturned the convictions, saying Weinstein’s trial had been prejudiced by the judge allowing woman who alleged they were sexual assault victims of Weinstein to testify, despite not being plaintiffs in the case.
Weinstein went on trial again in 2025 and was once more convicted of a criminal sexual act involving Haley.
Jurors acquitted Weinstein of a separate sexual assault charge involving former model Kaja Sokola but could not reach a verdict on the rape charge involving Mann. Prosecutors retried the Mann charge earlier this year, but the jury deadlocked in May. The charge was later dropped after Mann said she could not endure another trial.
Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate California rape case.
In June, a California appeals court upheld Weinstein’s 2022 rape and sexual assault conviction. He was found guilty of assaulting an Italian model in her hotel room during a film festival.
He could serve the California sentence before beginning the sentence imposed in New York. Farber said at Wednesday’s sentencing that California will have the final say on whether Weinstein’s sentences run consecutively or concurrently.
The accusations and subsequent charges against Weinstein were one of the biggest factors in launching the #MeToo movement. More than 80 women have come forward with allegations of sexual assault or misconduct against him.

“Facade politics” is making far-right ideas acceptable: AIVD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:55:03 UTC
00:55:03 KST

“Facade politics” is making far-right ideas acceptable: AIVD
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Far-right organisations are using euphemistic terms such as “remigration” to establish racist and discriminatory ideas in mainstream debate, the Dutch security services have warned.
The intelligence agency AIVD and the national counter-terrorism co-ordinator said “façade politics” was designed to mask extremist ideas by expressing them in more palatable language.
Groups such as White Lives Matter, the Active Club Dietsland and the Greater Netherlands Student Union (GNSV) had emerged in the last 10 years under the banner of “identitarian resistance”, itself a euphemism for white supremacism.
“In reality many identitarians are convinced of ‘white superiority’ and show an aversion to other cultures and religions, as well as white people who think differently such as feminists and LGBTI+ people,” the agencies said.
Far-right groups are also infiltrating demonstrations against asylum seeker centres, organising international conferences and influencing political parties.
The right-wing parties JA21, Forum voor Democratie, Geert Wilders’ PVV and the the BoerBurgerBeweging took 30% of the vote between them in last October’s general election. All used the term “remigration” in their election manifestos.
Weekend riots
The report was published after a weekend in which 300 people gathered for an anti-immigration protest in The Hague organised by a group calling itself Wij Zijn Het Volk (“We are the people”).
Protesters made Nazi salutes, chanted anti-Semitic slogans and carried banners with messages such as “blanke mannen vooraan” (white men first).
The demonstration was cancelled after rioters clashed with police who ordered them to remove their face masks. Altogether 24 people were arrested. It was the second year in a row that an anti-immigration demonstration on the city’s Malieveld triggered violent confrontations with police.
The AIVD estimates that “several hundred Dutch people” are involved in right-wing terrorist activity and there is a real chance that some will resort to actual violence.
But they also said the groups were at undermining the democratic system “by stealth”, using social media platforms such as TikTok and X to spread extremist ideas.
“The effect in the long term can be greater than a terrorist attack,” the report said.
