Who is skipping the UN General Assembly — and why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:54:00 UTC
00:54:00 KST

Who is skipping the UN General Assembly — and why
September 23, 2026
Few world leaders would miss a stage like the United Nations General Assembly. Donald Trump, Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Emmanuel Macron are among those in New York for the 81st session of the UN General Assembly — or UNGA81 for short — where the speeches from the green marble lectern make headlines around the globe.
That makes the no-shows all the more surprising. Here is a look at some of the leaders staying away — and why.
Germany: Friedrich Merz
The German chancellor, in his second year in office, would like to be much more present on the international stage and has described himself as a "foreign-policy chancellor." But domestic politics have been keeping him busy. Three German states held parliamentary elections in September and Friedrich Merz is under more pressure as chancellor and leader of the Christian Democrats (CDU) than ever before. In Saxony-Anhalt and Berlin, the CDU was firmly voted out of office, while in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern it failed to enter the state parliament at all — a first since the founding of the Federal Republic of Germany.
Merz is in crisis-management mode at home and seems to want to prevent his opponents from planning a revolt in his absence. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul will speak in his place.
Italy: Giorgia Meloni
Italy's prime minister is in a considerably stronger position than Merz but has said she needs to deal with domestic matters this week. After the NATO summit in early July, Giorgia Meloni said she had just returned from several international summits and had to tackle various issues, including some pending within Italy. She pointed out that Merz had also been absent in 2025 - she too is sending her foreign minister, Antonio Tajani.
South Africa: Cyril Ramaphosa
The South African president has also just attended an international summit — the BRICS summit in India. He said he would not attend the UN General Assembly for health reasons: medics advised him to take time to rest and recover. His office did not disclose details about his condition. South Africa will also be represented at the UN lectern by Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.
Egypt: Abdel Fattah al-Sisi
Along with Africa's largest economy, the second- and third-largest economies on the continent are also not sending their presidents to New York: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi is being represented by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly. Al-Sisi's office did not give a reason for his absence. During his first years in office, from 2014 onward, he regularly attended the UN General Assembly. In 2020, the event was held online because of the coronavirus pandemic and the following year it was a hybrid event, to which al-Sisi sent a pre-recorded video message. He has not attended since the General Assembly returned to in-person meetings.
Nigeria: Bola Tinubu
Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu is the third influential African leader to miss this year's UN General Assembly. His spokesman was quoted by Nigerian media as saying the West African country would be "fully and effectively represented" by Vice President Kashim Shettima. Tinubu, meanwhile, is on vacation: He spent time in the UK in late August before traveling to France.
India: Narendra Modi
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is relatively rarely to be seen at UN General Assemblies. He last took the podium in 2021, since when the world's largest democracy has consistently sent Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar instead. According to Indian media outlets, Modi was reportedly listed as a speaker at this year's gathering before his plans changed. Why he decided not to attend is not known.
China: Xi Jinping
Chinese President Xi Jinping's absence is under international scrutiny this year. As this year's "High-Level Week" takes place, Xi will also be in the US but he will not be going to New York. Instead, he will head straight for Washington, some 300 kilometers away, for a full state visit, including a White House gala dinner and a military parade.
Although Beijing has not framed it this way, the timing suggests that Xi is prioritizing great power diplomacy over the United Nations' multilateral forum. Xi and Trump have serious bones of contention, including over trade relations, artificial intelligence and Taiwan's security situation.
Russia: Vladimir Putin
Russian President Vladimir Putin has also rarely stood at the iconic podium so it comes as little surprise that Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will once again speak for Russia this year. Putin ordered this by decree — and didn't offer a reason for his absence.
Palestinian territories: Mahmoud Abbas
Mahmoud Abbashas clocked up far more UNGA experience than any of those listed above. The president of the Palestinian Authority (PA), who has been in office since 2005, was a regular until Donald Trump's second term.
But last year, the Trump administration denied him a diplomatic visa and has done so again this year.
Yet, under the 1947 UN Headquarters Agreement, the United States is committed to facilitating access to UN headquarters for foreign representatives. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, for example, is still due to speak in New York, despite the US having recently bombed Iran.
In the case of the Palestinians, the US State Department recently said it was extending sanctions "that deny visas to members of the Palestine Liberation Organization and the Palestinian Authority." Abbas plans to address the assembled heads of state and government by video message, as he did last year.
This article was originally published in German.

European Commission Executive Vice President Teresa Ribera on Wednesday signaled support for a woman becoming the next U.N. secretary-general for the first time in the organization’s history.
Writing on Bluesky, Ribera said she was “willing to see a woman leading the U.N.” Her comments come as speculation mounts over who will replace António Guterres in the top job when he steps down at the end of December after completing his second and final five-year term. His successor is due to take office on Jan. 1, 2027.
Four women feature among the seven candidates seeking to replace Guterres: Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan, Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, and Ecuador’s Ivonne A-Baki and María Fernanda Espinosa.
Advertisement
Grynspan topped the latest informal Security Council poll, while Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, Senegal’s Macky Sall and Uganda’s Olara Otunnu are also in the field. All nine previous U.N. secretaries-general have been men.
Ribera’s intervention echoes that of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who said on American comedian Jon Stewart’s podcast Wednesday that “after 80 years of this multilateral order, I think it’s important, it’s fair that we choose a woman, the first woman, leading the U.N. as secretary-general.” Sánchez also called himself a “feminist politician.”
The race is unfolding as U.S. President Donald Trump pressures the U.N. to overhaul its finances and structure. Trump reportedly floated FIFA President Gianni Infantino for the job in July, though the U.S. has not formally nominated him.
The next U.N. chief will inherit an organization facing funding shortfalls and pressure to overhaul its structure, with the U.S. State Department saying in a statement that candidates must “get the U.N. back to basics and publicly commit to the changes we require.”
“The U.S. is not walking away, we’re not turning out the lights, but we are demanding reform,” U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz said last Sunday.
The Security Council must recommend a candidate with at least nine votes and no veto from its five permanent members before the General Assembly can appoint the next U.N. chief, according to organization rules.

Source: a European Pravda correspondent, citing sources in the Council of the EU
Quote from the source: "On 23 September, Coreper adopted the draft Council decision on Ukraine's fulfilment of the conditions for a partial payment of the eighth tranche under the Ukraine Plan of the Ukraine Facility, and ministers are expected to adopt it at the Council of the EU tomorrow."
Details: The allocation amounts to around €3 billion.
To receive the funds, Ukraine has, among other things, completed a step that it had committed to implement in the second quarter of 2025: bringing in legislation on reviewing judges' integrity declarations and the process for verifying them.
Ukraine has also implemented three reforms scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2025, which, taken together, will unlock €368 million for the Ukrainian budget:
- the appointment of a new electricity market operator
- the enactment of legislation supporting the development of efficient and more sustainable district heating
- the enactment of the law on the safety and interoperability of rail transport in Ukraine.
Three more steps that have been approved by the EU relate to Ukraine's commitments under the current eighth tranche and have unlocked €2.292 billion:
- the publication of a resilience assessment of the banking system
- the enactment of legislation on access to information about external engineering works
- the publication of a report on the implementation of state support through the public Agricultural Registry.
Background:
- On 24 August, Ukraine requested payment of parts of the fifth, seventh and eighth tranches under the Ukraine Facility, totalling €3 billion.
- On 30 July, the Council of the EU approved an updated reform plan under the Ukraine Facility, allowing Ukraine to receive €8.3 billion in 2026 to cover budget needs.
- On 31 August, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy appointed another judge to the High Anti-Corruption Court in a necessary step towards unlocking EU funding under the Ukraine Facility.

Polish fighter jets scrambled
The armed forces reacted immediately to the violation of Polish airspace. Fighter jets were scrambled and ground units remained on standby.

"The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence" - the Operational Command of the Armed Forces said.

"The crews of Poland's air defence systems maintain round-the-clock surveillance and remain in constant readiness to ensure the security of Polish airspace" a statement by the Operational Command of the Armed Forces added.
Polish skies under constant surveillance
Wednesday's incident took place on the same day that NATO fighter jets were also scrambled in the morning, in response to Russian strikes on Ukrainian territory.
Because of the threat, residents of the Lublin region received an RCB alert. Operations at the airports in Lublin and Rzeszów were also temporarily suspended.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said at the time that a Russian drone had hit a petrol station in Ukraine near the border crossing at Dorohusk. A similar situation was repeated on Friday morning, when the alert lasted until around 9:00.
Another incident involving a Russian drone was also recorded in September. In the middle of the month, on the beach at Rusinowo near Jarosławiec in the West Pomeranian region, a Russian Gerbera 2 unmanned aerial vehicle was found and recovered from the Baltic Sea.
On 3 September, Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced on X that he had decided to expand the protection of Polish airspace.
This is linked to the increased number of Russian provocations and acts of aggression against Poland.
"Recent weeks have shown that provocations from Russia are taking different forms and pose a threat in places that until now have been considered safe" - the deputy prime minister wrote on his X account.
He also assured that Poland is constantly monitoring the situation on its eastern border.

====================================================================================================

The Woman Winning the Reading Wars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:49:41 UTC
00:49:41 KST

Louisa Moats was at a conference in Daphne, Ala., earlier this year when she was approached by a group of teachers. For the 81-year-old, this was a relatively new occurrence. “They’re poorly paid, they don’t look very healthy, they certainly didn’t have an elite education and I feel this concern and admiration for them as they do this job,” she says, with her characteristic frankness. “They come up to me, with this glazed, starry-eyed look, and thank me as if I, personally, was the conduit to their renewed sense of purpose and competence. I get that a lot now.”
Moats has become a late-in-life heroine, at least in some circles, because of a teacher-training program she wrote decades ago that has become a buzzy property. She is not exactly basking in the attention. “I take it with a grain of salt,” she says, sitting in her remote Vermont lake house. “Behind that is my sense that what I would want them to do is probably not exactly what’s going on in their classroom, but it’s a reasonable enough approximation that it’s making a difference for kids.”
Her skepticism can be forgiven. For a long time, Moats found herself on the losing side of America’s so-called reading wars, the back-and-forth over the best way to teach kids to read. She and her cohort of researchers promote the idea that reading is a skill that must be painstakingly taught, first through an understanding of the way sounds make up speech and get represented as letters, then through explicit instruction on how language works. But the prevailing view, until a few years ago, was that most children would figure out how to decode the letters if given enough encouragement, stimulating material, and context clues, just as they do with speech.
“This is still something I ponder all the time,” Moats says, about why schools chose to teach the way they did. One explanation she has landed on: people did not keep up with the research. “Usually they have not sat down and looked at the evidence—the nature of the evidence, the scope of the evidence, the durability of the evidence—and so they don’t understand what the science is about.”
Interest in “the science” has recently increased dramatically, alongside the level of panic about literacy rates in the U.S. About 4 in 10 American children have not mastered basic reading-comprehension skills by fourth grade, the worst result in 20 years, according to the 2024 National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP). A third of eighth-graders also fall below the reading level expected for their age. The average 12th-grader scores three points lower on a reading test than his or her peers did in 2019, and 10 points lower than those from 1992.
Some of that can be laid at the door of school closures during the pandemic. But it’s a problem with deeper roots: roughly a quarter of young adults (16 to 24) are functionally illiterate, according to the National Center for Education Statistics. Professors bemoan having to assign ever-shorter reading assignments. Time-use surveys report that people from 20 to 34 spend no more than 10 minutes a day reading for pleasure. Grave declarations have proclaimed the “end of reading.”
To combat the decline, states have looked to the few education districts where students are showing improvement and followed their example by enacting what are known as science-of-reading laws. The laws, which have been passed in 42 states and D.C., mostly in the past seven years, mandate that schools use very structured techniques—including foundational instruction on phonics. Many teachers did not learn this approach in college and have to be retrained.
Moats’ program, Language Essentials for Teachers of Reading and Spelling (LETRS), has become the preferred way for schools to meet the requirements. The course is famously long and rigorous. Teachers must delve into language theory and cognitive science before any advice on instruction is given. It isolates 19 vowel sounds and 29 consonant sounds in U.S. English. Moats’ ideas are generally associated with phonology (how words sound), but the program goes deeply into morphology (how words are built of parts) and orthography (how words are written). It’s also relatively pricey. Public contracts and appropriations suggest statewide LETRS rollouts cost up to $1,700 per educator, before factoring in substitute teachers, planning time, coaching, and administration. And it’s not clear that all the knowledge translates into better teaching methods.
But that hasn’t stopped 23 states from purchasing the program, and at least one, Alabama, from paying teachers $1,000 if they did all of it. In 2020, fewer than 25,000 teachers had enrolled in the 155-hour course, according to Lexia, the company that now owns it. In 2025, that number reached 700,000, mostly lower elementary. (There are approximately 1.5 million K-5 educators in the U.S., according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.) Michigan, whose recent standardized test results showed 38.2% of third-graders were proficient in reading, announced this summer it was spending $75 million so that every reading teacher could do the course. (It has already spent $44 million on teachers who did it voluntarily.) “The last three years, I have seen more money from this than I ever expected to see from it,” says Moats, who earns what she calls “a small royalty” on each sale.
Still, whether out of native New England reticence or because she’s almost sure she’s seen this movie before, Moats, now allegedly retired, regards this turn of events with mild suspicion. “It’s humbling, it’s a bit bewildering, it’s a bit surrealistic,” she says. Finally, when asked directly, she adds, “and yes, it’s very gratifying.” Educators may dismiss the idea of the reading wars, claiming teaching is not an us-vs.-them endeavor, but if they are real—and it looks like they are—it sure seems that Moats has emerged as a victor.
She intended to be a folk singer. But having graduated from Wellesley College with a degree in music, Moats needed a job, and her sister got her one in Boston, with a researcher in the emerging field of neuropsychology, who needed people to type up reports. He also needed a lab technician, so he gave Moats a white coat and trained her to administer tests. “That’s how I learned to think about the kids with learning disabilities who were sent to our clinic,” she says. “I learned how to think of them through this neurological lens.”
When Vanderbilt University’s Peabody College offered one of the first fellowships for a master’s in learning disabilities, Moats jumped at the chance to move to Nashville. “I tromped up and down Music Row and got a contract as a songwriter and got a master’s degree in learning disabilities,” she says. “It was fun, and it was completely worthless as far as learning how to teach.” Armed with a balance beam, a chalkboard, and some visual aids, she was hired to “cure” learning disabilities in local schools. “The experience of the total disconnect between what I learned in a master’s program and the realities of the kids and their needs,” she says, has given her sympathy for teachers now realizing that the reading-instruction methods they learned in college might be flawed.
Even though her music career was progressing (she had a songwriting contract with Screen Gems) and her career in special education was opening doors (she had a parent-teacher meeting with Johnny Cash), Moats was not a Nashville type. She found the music industry predatory and missed the snow. (Her daughter Charlotte would later become a Junior Olympics ski champion.) She moved back to her old job at Tufts–New England Medical Center and claims she more or less fell into a doctorate at Harvard, where she encountered the terrifying but brilliant linguist Carol Chomsky, wife of Noam, and Jeanne Chall, after whom Harvard’s reading lab is named. “Chall was the one who got me into understanding how to look at spelling errors in a very detailed and informed way,” says Moats.
She began to observe that children who couldn’t read or spell just did not register the relationship between the sounds in a word and the letters. They struggled especially when the words sounded a little alike but were spelled very differently, as in juice and choose, or spelled alike but pronounced differently as in the s sound in was and saw. Moats came to believe teaching kids to read entails understanding a lot more about the brain and language processing than the average teacher knows.
In the mid-1980s, after a few years of helping struggling readers, from impoverished children to Dartmouth academics, in her private practice in East Thetford, Vt., Moats realized that earlier intervention was needed. So she began to teach teachers, at Harvard and at smaller Vermont colleges. She gave her incoming postgraduates surveys. “The results were appalling,” she says. “They didn’t know anything.” Many had been taught the whole-language theory of reading, which suggested that teaching students to decode words distracted them from understanding their meaning, and therefore students should learn the words as a unit, not by blending graphemes. She wrote an academic paper about it, which was republished by the American Federation of Teachers in 1995.
A few years earlier, another literacy researcher, G. Reid Lyon, had been put in charge of creating and overseeing a federally funded reading-research network, a large multisite program that investigated how children learn to read and why some don’t. He asked Moats to help. “What I needed was a leader and a teacher and a teacher of teachers, which she was extraordinary at,” says Lyon, also now retired in Vermont. “A lot of professors can get up there and quack away, but they don’t really have the wherewithal to demonstrate it. She did.” Moats was assigned to the Washington, D.C., site.
“Boy, did I have impostor syndrome,” she says. “Here I was in this room full of eminences, and I had been reading their work, I’d been citing them, I’d been learning from them.” She also had some hard lessons to learn as a northeastern hippie in a majority-Black school district. “I just couldn’t believe the state of affairs in these schools,” says Moats. “Libraries with no books, no doors on the lavatory, no running water in the sinks.” She labored to get the teachers to trust her. Eventually, one of her assistants took her aside. “She said, ‘You’re the director, you’ve got to look like the director,’” recalls Moats, who favors denim and heavy glasses. “I said, ‘You have any advice?’ She said, ‘Go to Ann Taylor.’” The project was a success, her nine schools’ reading rates soared, and local politicians started to drop by for photo opportunities.
Then national politicians took notice too. The No Child Left Behind Act that President George W. Bush signed in 2002 enshrined the work of Lyon’s team and the National Reading Panel. Moats was tapped to write the teacher-training component of the act’s Reading First initiative, which became LETRS.
Reading First was expensive—about a billion dollars was spent on a few million children—and the law mandated that a report be made of how effective it was by 2008. The news was not great. While students had been taught in a way that research had said was most effective, and first-graders did decode words better, elementary students as a whole were not better at understanding what they read than the students who were not part of the initiative. An Institute of Education Sciences (IES) report on LETRS in particular found that while the training improved teachers’ understanding of language, it did not improve outcomes for students.
Moats is still steaming about that analysis. “You don’t get an impact on student achievement after one year,” she says. “You’ve barely gotten through the professional-development material.” She also notes that after four years of Reading First, many state-level reading analyses showed improvement, especially in high-poverty regions. Nevertheless, Reading First’s funding was not renewed, and states were allowed to go their own way with reading instruction.
It is perhaps reductive to boil this history down to a battle between two women. But it is also true that around the time Moats and her colleagues were doing their work, another approach was ascendant, championed largely by a figure with a lot of the kind of main-character energy that Moats lacks. The founder of the Teachers College Reading and Writing Project (TCRWP) at Columbia University, Lucy Calkins, promulgated the idea of balanced literacy, which purported to be a détente between the phonics camp and the whole-language advocates. Calkins, whose background was in writing instruction, believed that children first of all needed enticing books at a level they could manage and a ton of cheerleading. “I always knew phonics mattered,” Calkins says now. “When kids write, every single minute of what they’re doing shows their phonics.” Nevertheless, the curriculum materials she authored had little phonics, and suggested that teachers use a separate phonics course.
“A lot of people who have a casual acquaintance with the research have persuaded themselves that balanced reading instruction means a little of this, a little of that,” Moats wrote in a seminal essay about balanced literacy in 2000. “Take a cup of phonics from one cupboard, add a half-pint of whole language from the fridge, and the resulting blend will succeed with children while avoiding the battles and conflicts of the ‘reading wars.’ Everyone will be happy, and all will be well. The problem is that it doesn’t work that way.”
This was the world that Margaret Goldberg was introduced to after she completed her master’s degree at UC Berkeley. In 2015, she arrived at a Title I Oakland school and quickly found that the methods she used in higher-performing schools just down the road did not work. After discovering Moats’ essay via Google, she started using more structured literacy methods with some of her classes and took a balanced-literacy approach with others. “I didn’t realize that I was teaching on both sides of the reading wars,” says Goldberg, who co-founded the Right to Read Project in 2019. The results were stark. “All of the ideals of balanced literacy were happening with the kids who were being taught systematically and explicitly how to decode. The students I was teaching balanced literacy to—I was just trying to sell them on reading.”
Eventually, parents, especially those with dyslexic children, who tend to need more explicit phonics instruction, began to protest. Mississippi, which gave all its K-3 teachers LETRS training starting in 2014, was the first state to improve its numbers. By 2019, its fourth-grade NAEP reading score had risen 10 points from 2013—the largest gain of any state during that period. LETRS wasn’t the sole reason for Mississippi’s success. The state also added new practices around teacher coaching and accountability, more student screening and intervention, and held back a bunch of third-graders. But the teacher training was key.
Meanwhile, public-radio journalist Emily Hanford amassed enough evidence against the balanced-literacy methodology to publish a 2018 audio documentary that would become her influential Sold a Story podcast. Politicians, administrators, and even teachers’ colleges took heed. But change, especially to higher education, came slowly. Carol Tolman, one of the co-authors of later versions of LETRS, was an early trainer in the program. At one college, she says, “there was a letter on my podium, just saying, ‘We don’t need the likes of you here. As soon as you leave, this is all going to change and go back.’ I mean, it got really heated.”
Alabama piloted the use of LETRS in 2018, and expanded it to the whole state in 2021, by which time South Carolina and North Carolina were also jumping on board. In 2022 they were joined by Kentucky and Arkansas. In 2021 North Carolina approved almost $50 million to train its K-5 educators using LETRS. Not all of them appreciated it. “I’m all for the science of reading. I’m all for providing structured sequence materials to teachers,” says John Davis, who did the training as a third-grade teacher. But he knew a lot of the material already. And the main curriculum used in his school was not aligned with LETRS methodology. “You spent all this money and time on this training, and it’s not showing up in our reading curriculum?” says Davis. “It just seems like a waste.”
Even Calkins came around—a bit. She rereleased her curriculum materials a few times, adding more phonics emphasis, but criticism of some of the methods she recommended mounted, and after Columbia University detached itself from TCRWP in 2023, she founded her own institute. “I am all for what I’ve learned from the science of reading, and also the new relationships I’ve developed and the new organizations I belong to now,” she says. “All that’s been helpful, but it’s awful to have teachers teaching in ways they don’t believe in.”
Indeed, the prospect of yet more mandatory training brought many teachers zero joy. Lisa Anderson was one of them. She had been an elementary teacher in Minnesota for more than 20 years when she was required in 2022 to undertake LETRS. “Another hurdle, something more to jump through,” she says. “The pendulum’s swinging, we jump on, and let’s see where this one lands.”
That feeling lasted until about halfway into Volume 2. Before she’d even completed the program, she began to implement some of its methods—the school was also using a different curriculum that was more aligned with LETRS ideas—and saw surprising results. Students were starting to read, even many who were floundering. A new emotion emerged: anger. Why had she never been shown this information before? She was moved to write to her alma mater, Bemidji State, and demand a refund of the fees associated with the courses she had taken on teaching children to read. “You didn’t do your job,” she says she told them. (A spokesperson told TIME that the college continually updates its curriculum in accordance with state standards.)
While LETRS’ success has assured Moats a comfortable retirement, she is still hoping that it will pay other dividends. “I hope that maybe we’re getting beyond the reading wars,” she says, meaning that the correct way to teach reading has been established. “But I don’t feel that secure about what it is I’m trying to teach actually taking hold. I think people do the course, but they don’t realize the power of the information.”
Sitting on a chair in her dining room, not far from the guitar on another one, is a spelling sheet from a second-grade child in California that a teacher has sent through asking for help. Moats sighs deeply as she reads it. (“She sighs a lot,” says Lyon.) The child has written all the -igh words (thigh, high, fight) like -ing words (thing, hing, fing). “He’s trying to memorize letters by their appearance. He has no idea about the correspondence between speech and print,” she says. Even today, five or more years after the science-of-reading revolution began and decades after the Reading Panel, “this teacher cannot look at these writing samples and recognize poor phoneme awareness.” (Surveys suggest that even with all the legislation and training, no more than half of K-3 teachers are using science-of-reading techniques.)
LETRS is also hitting critical mass just as Moats cedes control over the quality of the training, to the consternation of some of the earlier employees. “The mission became the money,” says Leta Palmiter, a former LETRS trainer who joined the company shortly after Lexia was bought by the private-equity firm Veritas Capital in 2020. “Not the people who received the training.” A Lexia spokesperson says improving literacy “remains at the heart of everything we do.”
It’s too soon to tell—especially with the interruptions caused by the pandemic clouding the data—whether any of the states that have newly adopted LETRS have managed to improve the reading skills of their students. And even if they do, it will be difficult to tell how much LETRS is responsible. A $4 million five-year randomized study of its effect is under way, but the results will not be available until 2029. A recent analysis by the Kentucky Department of Education found that schools with higher rates of LETRS-trained teachers posted larger gains in reading proficiency than schools with lower rates, but it was an internal study. Meanwhile, NAEP reading scores ticked up a few points for 9-year-olds in 2025 (although not for 13-year-olds), and another national report showed improvement in K-8 reading skills from 2025 to 2026. “I think all this work can only help,” says David Liben, a literacy consultant and one of the authors of the 2010 Common Core standards. “I just don’t think that at this point we have the evidence that we can make a claim that we’re turning a corner now.”
Experts agree that teacher training alone is not a solution for America’s reading ills. “This idea that nobody was teaching phonics, it just is absurd,” says former director of reading for Chicago Public Schools Timothy Shanahan, whose recent book Leveled Reading, Leveled Lives takes aim at balanced literacy, but who is also not sold on its replacement. For every Mississippi, he says, there’s a state like Arkansas, where LETRS hasn’t seemed to make any difference. And the tight focus on teacher training has come at a cost to other urgent problems in education, like truancy. “Is it that the kids are getting poor instruction, or that our attendance levels are so low right now that kids just aren’t learning?” he asks.
Mistakes in education take a long time to show up, and so do fixes. By the time the students who learned how to read from LETRS-trained teachers are in the workforce, the landscape for communication may be unrecognizable. Even now, reading is not as vital to thriving as it was a mere five years ago. There are remarkable new ways to glean information and disperse it. Generative AI can write for us, and books can be read aloud by machines, so some of the disadvantages of being illiterate may be overcome by technology.
But the ability to recognize and manipulate written words will still be a critical skill, say most educators, because it is inextricably linked to thinking. Decades of research in psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, and education suggest that becoming literate changes how people reason, solve problems, organize knowledge, and deliberate on their own thinking. “The mental work that is reading,” says Moats, “is the essence of learning.”

Iran will 'never bend at the knee', Pezeshkian tells UN in defiant wartime address
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian gave a defiant wartime address at the UN on Wednesday accusing the US of terrorism in his country and saying Iran would not "bend at the knee". But as Pezeshkian called for diplomacy, Iranian officials downplayed their talks with US counterparts on the sidelines of the gerenal assembly as "not anything new".

Iran’s president said Wednesday that his people have been “victims of terrorism” by the United States, delivering a rare wartime speech at UN General Assembly a day after President Donald Trump said he could “annihilate” the Islamic republic.
In a defiant speech, President Masoud Pezeshkian held up large photos of the late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and the more than 150 school Iranian children killed on the first days of the war.
“We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” Pezeshkian said at the General Assembly. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. And we defended ourselves with utmost strength. America and Israel attacked us.”
Toward the end of his speech, Pezeshkian called out Trump by name.
“It must be understood by Mr. Trump and those who seek to bully us that we are ready for dialogue and diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force,” he said.
"That the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend at the knee," he added.

He also said one thing that was measurably false: "We did not hit civilian populations.” Mariners and migrant workers in the region have been among the civilians killed in Iran’s attacks since the war began.
Arriving in New York under heavy security and scrutiny, Pezeshkian – who, within Iran’s political landscape, is considered a moderate politician – addressed world leaders a day after Trump used the same stage to suggest he may “annihilate” the Islamic Republic if a deal isn’t reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.

‘Everything we prepared for happened’: When IDF medics became casualties deep inside Syria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:49:21 UTC
00:49:21 KST

If you had asked Capt. M., then the medical officer of the IDF’s 810th Mountain Brigade, what her unit had prepared for most extensively before launching Operation Green-White, she probably would not have had a single answer.
For months, the brigade rehearsed nearly everything that could go wrong while operating deep inside Syria: What happens if several soldiers are wounded at once? How many units of blood should the force carry? Which medical team should move where? And who treats the wounded if the medics themselves are among the casualties?
A year later, they know that the last scenario was not merely hypothetical.
“The people wounded in the encounter were the doctor and medics who had joined the force,” M. recalled.
To understand how the brigade dealt with that predicament, the story goes back to September 2025, when Operation Green-White — which would become one of the most significant missions in the young brigade’s history — moved from the planning table to the field.
Troops from the 810th Mountain Brigade, under the 210th Division, were called into action in the middle of the night for an operation that had been planned for months.
Their target was a series of abandoned commando outposts belonging to the former Syrian regime, some 38 kilometers, or 24 miles, inside Syria. Their mission was to reach weapons left behind following the fall of Bashar Assad’s government, remove them and, above all, ensure they could not fall into hostile hands.
The troops operated at the sites for about five hours, raiding the outposts and locating weapons and other materiel that had been abandoned there.
“We found bombs, hand grenades, explosive devices and various types of missiles,” M. said. “It would be fair to say that the quantities surprised us.”
The discovery changed an operation that had been intended as a one-time mission and prompted a follow-up.
After the troops returned to Israel, preparations began for what the brigade called “Green-White 2” — another incursion into the same sector to complete the mission and remove additional weapons that remained there, again under conditions of complete secrecy.
For M., that meant returning to the medical plan developed for the first operation and reviewing it almost from scratch.
“When we plan an operation like this, I work on the assumption that the most complicated thing that can happen will happen,” she said. “I know I’m sending a force into a dangerous country where evacuation distances are very long. So I need to give it as much independence as possible in the field while remaining close behind and ready for anything that might go wrong.”
That independence begins with determining how many units of blood accompany the force, preparing stretchers, selecting the medical equipment troops carry into the field, identifying potential helicopter landing zones and mapping the medical teams dispersed among the troops. Planners must also determine what to do if any one of those elements suddenly becomes unavailable.
The reason, M. said, is clear from the map.
“At the depth where the troops were operating in the Syrian sector, a ground evacuation could take hours,” she said. “And even when the evacuation is by air, it’s not enough to find the nearest hospital. You have to match the hospital to the type of injury and the medical care the casualty requires.”
“In the case of a serious head injury, for example, I need to know that the casualty is being taken to a hospital that can provide the optimal treatment,” she added.
The distances are compounded by the terrain. The mountainous landscape and weather, which can quickly become extreme, played a major role in the scenarios medical teams rehearsed before Green-White 2 began.
But a central part of the plan was developed not on the ground but in the air.
During preparations, the brigade coordinated with the Israeli Air Force and its elite Unit 669 airborne combat search-and-rescue unit, seeking to reduce as much as possible the time between the first report of a wounded soldier and the moment that person could be evacuated.
“When human life is at stake, regardless of the severity of the injury, every minute matters,” M. said. “We don’t want to arrive at an incident and only then start figuring out how to land a helicopter there.”
“Before the operation, we coordinate, go over the scenarios and create a common language so that when the moment comes, everyone knows exactly what they need to do, when and how.”
When the second phase of Green-White was approved and troops began moving and operating inside Syria, M. sat at the central command post overseeing the mission alongside the officers responsible for providing support from behind the front line.
“It’s crazy,” she said. “You sit in the operations room and watch the forces advance, and you constantly have to know what happens if one of the soldiers is wounded right now. You can be on duty for 48 or 72 hours, and at any moment you have to be able to say where the medical team is, who can reach the casualty, how to evacuate them — and exactly where to take them.”
Then, during the operation, a grenade exploded near 810th Brigade troops.
Five members of the force were wounded, including by shrapnel and the blast. As the situation became clearer at the command post, another detail emerged that made the incident considerably more complicated: All five casualties were members of the medical team that was supposed to respond to such an emergency.
“At the moment they were needed most, the doctor and medics who had gone in to provide treatment became the ones who needed it themselves,” M. said.
But the brigade had prepared for that possibility.
“Because we had prepared for this as well, we had additional teams and medical units in the field,” she said. “We were able to move forward the nearby battalion aid station and send in another team to begin initial treatment.”
Meanwhile, another race began at the command post. Once officials had established a clearer picture of the casualties and their conditions, a helicopter carrying Unit 669 personnel was dispatched.
The airborne medical team needed as clear a picture as possible of the number of wounded and the severity of their injuries before arriving. At the same time, the hospital where they would land had to prepare to receive them.
Amid the complex evacuation effort, M. said, there was another factor that does not always appear on operational charts: The soldiers on the other end of the radio were learning in real time that their friends had been wounded.
“The reports coming over the radio are, in the end, about people,” she said. “You have to handle it sensitively but also keep a cool head. An incident like this can very quickly create pressure, but everyone has to remain sharp and focus on getting the wounded to the hospital as quickly as possible.”
After rapid planning, instructions over the radio and the helicopter’s deployment, the aircraft reached the troops.
“Within a relatively short time, we managed to bring the five wounded from deep inside Syria to the hospital,” M. said. “The team in the field performed well, and we were able to provide the support from behind.”
“In the end, everything we prepared for actually happened in the field,” she added. “Most of the wounded were released from the hospital during that same week.”
For the Mountain Brigade, the operation came during a year that marked a historic turning point along Israel’s frontier with Syria.
Looking back, brigade officials say the weapons removed from the abandoned outposts were part of a security environment that has changed dramatically — even beyond what they had expected — since the fall of the Assad government.
For M., the operation remains one of the greatest tests of her military career.
“You can equip a soldier with the best weapon and the most advanced gear,” she said. “But ultimately, that soldier needs to know that if something happens to him, there are people right behind him who know how to reach him quickly, treat him professionally and bring him home safely.”

IN BRIEF: Key statements from Putin’s meeting with government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:47:41 UTC
00:47:41 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Russian authorities must do everything to live up to the trust shown by the public in the recent elections, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at a meeting with cabinet members.
The head of state also urged officials to explain to the public in greater detail what the digital ruble is and what advantages it offers.
For her part, Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina reported that the mass launch of the digital ruble went according to plan.
In addition, Putin requested a report on the relocation of major state-owned companies' headquarters to the regions.
TASS has compiled the key statements made during the meeting.
The recent elections
Putin noted that Russians turned out to vote despite all obstacles created by the adversary: "I want to thank the citizens of Russia for their participation in this election campaign. It is well known that attempts were made to hinder us and disrupt these elections, as evidenced by constant attempts to breach the air defenses of Moscow and other regions."
According to the head of state, the high voter turnout in the parliamentary elections, despite all interference from the adversary, shows that Russians support the authorities' efforts to strengthen the country: "Such strong public involvement – with a record number of people coming to polling stations to vote – shows that the people of Russia support our efforts aimed at strengthening the country."
Putin emphasized that it is impossible to intimidate Russia, a fact demonstrated by the course of the parliamentary elections, which took place despite all attempts by the adversary to disrupt them: "The queues at polling stations show that it is impossible to intimidate Russia!"
The President noted that the recent elections showed that Russians trust those serving at the front and believe in their devotion to the Motherland and the country's victory: "We certainly understand the times we are living in. And now, I would like to address our soldiers and commanders on the front line. I want you to know, comrades: this vote was for you. People believe in you and in our victory. They believe in your courage, your heroism, and your devotion to the Motherland."
Digital ruble
Putin stated that the digital ruble, the use of which began on September 1, has become a full-fledged financial instrument: "As of September 1, the digital ruble has become a full-fledged payment instrument within the Russian financial system."
The President pointed out the need to explain the difference between the digital ruble and ordinary cashless payments in greater detail to the public: "Because for the average citizen, this is not very clear."
In turn, Bank of Russia Governor Elvira Nabiullina noted that "the launch of the digital ruble went according to plan": "This is an event we prepared for meticulously. Citizens and businesses now have a new, additional tool for payments and settlements. In essence, our country now possesses all components of a national payment infrastructure."
She emphasized that the digital ruble is an entirely Russian-developed product "featuring the highest class of protection and security."
Nabiullina reported that the Central Bank, together with developers of secure SIM cards, is preparing a solution that will allow payments in digital rubles without an internet connection: "However, this is currently under development."
The head of the Bank of Russia stated that citizens had opened nearly 200,000 digital ruble accounts in just three weeks: "That is a significant number for the first three weeks."
She added that 36 Russian banks are currently connected to the digital ruble platform: "So, the digital ruble is gradually becoming part of our lives."
According to Nabiullina, the digital ruble will enable tighter control over the expenditure of budget funds and accelerate the transfer of funds to contractors: "All accounts are opened directly on the Central Bank's platform, creating new opportunities for automating settlements – including ensuring that budget funds are spent for their intended purpose."
The head of the Bank of Russia noted that the regulator intends to "expand the functionality of the digital ruble platform," with solutions for cross-border settlements possible in the future.
In turn, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov stated that opportunities to make payments using digital rubles would increase "as the infrastructure develops."
He noted that the first payments in digital rubles – specifically for taxes and fines – had already been credited to the budget.
According to Siluanov, the Finance Ministry will expand the scope of the digital ruble's use in the budgetary process year by year: "From the perspective of the budgetary process, we will increase and expand the scope of its use with each passing year."
Relocation of state-owned companies to regions
Putin asked for a report on the progress of relocating the headquarters of major state-owned companies to the regions: "I know this process is underway. What is its current status?"
Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov reported that eight major Russian holdings have plans to relocate part of their workforce to the regions: "Their structures comprise 250 companies based in Moscow and 270,000 employees. These include Russian Railways, Aeroflot, Russian Post, Transneft, Rosseti, Rosneft, Inter RAO, and Zarubezhneft. Each company has a plan for how it will proceed."
Expectations from government
Putin stressed that Russian authorities must do "everything to live up to the trust" placed in them by the public during the recent elections.
"A great deal depends on the government – monetary policy, social policy. There are many tasks ahead, and the vote cast by Russian citizens in the State Duma elections shows that this is linked to their hopes that all the goals facing us regarding the crucial areas of Russia's development and strengthening will be achieved," he said.

Trump, Venezuela's Rodriguez discuss debt overhaul, Rubio says
NEW YORK, Sept 23 - US President Donald Trump and Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez discussed restructuring the South American nation's billions of dollars in sovereign debt, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday.
The brief meeting at a reception Trump hosted late on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly came during Rodriguez's first trip to the US since American forces captured then-President Nicolas Maduro in a January raid.
The meeting is the latest sign of a rapid thaw in US-Venezuela ties since Maduro's removal. Washington is backing efforts to reconnect Venezuela with international lenders and support an economic recovery after years of default, sanctions and isolation.
"There's a lot that needs to be fixed in order for Venezuela to be successful," Rubio told reporters. "Debt restructuring is key to that."
Rubio said Venezuela likely faces one of the world's biggest sovereign debt workouts. He said Washington wanted to help, but that the process "has to be done in the right way."
Venezuela announced in May it would begin restructuring its external debt, which has been in default since 2017. The government and state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela together have about $60 billion in defaulted bonds outstanding. Analysts estimate total liabilities, including arbitration awards and accrued interest, could reach $150 billion to $200 billion.
Venezuela has not published full debt data for years, while US sanctions imposed in 2017 largely shut it out of Western financial markets.
POLITICAL CHANGE
Rubio said Washington also pressed for political change. Critics say Washington has sidelined the Venezuelan opposition, dropping demands for free elections in favor of oil and investment deals with the interim government.
"We made that point that in the end, for this project to be successful, it culminates in a free and fair election," Rubio said.
Some US lawmakers have also called for elections, amid criticism that the Trump administration has failed to extract meaningful democratic concessions from Rodriguez's government.
Rodriguez arrived in New York on Monday with a delegation holding talks with US officials, multilateral lenders and companies on energy, mining and debt, sources said.
The head of the Inter-American Development Bank has been working to secure approval for a $2.5 billion loan for Venezuela, Reuters reported on Tuesday, despite resistance from some board members.
Though small relative to Venezuela's overall obligations, such a loan would mark a major step toward restoring international lending. REUTERS

LONDON — Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham is planning to attend a high-stakes Commonwealth summit presided over by King Charles III, three people with knowledge of the conversations told POLITICO.
While Downing Street has not formally confirmed Burnham will go to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) on Nov. 1-4, planning for him to attend has ramped up in recent weeks, said one of the three people. All were granted anonymity to discuss internal conversations.
The biennial summit of 56 countries, most of which once formed part of the British Empire, looks set to be Burnham’s first major diplomatic outing with Charles since entering No. 10 in July. The monarch is the head of the Commonwealth and confirmed last month that he would attend CHOGM.
Advertisement
Some government officials have long suggested that conversations around the U.K. prime minister’s attendance at CHOGM are guided closely by the monarch’s wishes. Burnham and his wife had an audience with King Charles at Balmoral, his Scottish castle, earlier this month. Royal officials say plans are led and decided by the Commonwealth Secretariat and its secretary-general.
The king would have good reason to want backup, as the politics of this year’s summit looks destined to be particularly fraught.
It is being held in Antigua and Barbuda in the Caribbean, many of whose island nations are leading a charge for Britain to pay reparations for its historical role in the slave trade. Last week, Caribbean nations met in Barbados for a conference on reparatory justice.
Calls for reparations dominated the last CHOGM on the Pacific island of Samoa, where Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, insisted the issue was not on the table before other nations confronted him with a communique that mentioned reparations directly.
While U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is also due to attend CHOGM, one of the three people cited at the start of this article said attending personally would allow the prime minister to “lead from the front” rather than watching the debate unfold in his absence.
However, Downing Street’s line on reparations has changed little since 2024. Burnham’s spokesperson said on Sept. 7 that “the U.K. does not and will not pay reparations,” adding: “The transatlantic slave trade was abhorrent, and of course it’s right that we acknowledge the wrongs of the past, but we’ll continue to face forward and work with other countries on our current shared challenges.”
Advertisement
Estimates of the cost of reparations vary dramatically. Campaigners argue they could take many forms other than financial payments, such as climate adaptation and educational programs.
King Charles told the last CHOGM in 2024 that “None of us can change the past, but we can commit with all our hearts to learning its lessons and to finding creative ways to right inequalities that endure.”
Adding another summit to his formal diary would hand Burnham an even busier schedule this fall, a time when he is already due to unveil a 10-year plan setting out his vision for government. CHOGM will take place days after his first government-wide budget, around a week before the COP31 climate summit in Turkey — which Burnham has confirmed he will attend — and the month before G20 leaders meet in Miami in mid-December.
Burnham, who has sought to cast himself as a leader focused on domestic issues, argued at the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday that the cost of living could not be detached from global turmoil. He added: “We sit on the [UN] Security Council. In the Commonwealth … In a divided world, we have the ability to bring people together — and we will. We are going to step into that role.”

WASHINGTON - Four of US President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans called on his administration on Sept 23 to release more than US$15 billion (S$19.2 billion) in stalled national security assistance for Taiwan, as he welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping for a three-day visit to Washington.
US Senators Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, the former Senate majority leader, John Cornyn of Texas, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Thom Tillis of North Carolina wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth expressing concern about the funds.
The letter cites the State Department's failure to move ahead with US$300 million in foreign military financing Congress appropriated for Taiwan, the Defense Department's failure to obligate US$1 billion and the administration's decision to withhold approval for a US$14 billion package of foreign military sales to the island.
"We are concerned by President Trump's description of Taiwan as 'a very good negotiating chip' in engagements with Xi Jinping and the Chinese Communist Party," the letter said.
"It is difficult to imagine how the United States might credibly project influence deterrence in the Indo-Pacific if the price of keeping up diplomatic appearances is denying our partners key deterrent capabilities," the letter said.
The State and Defense departments did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the letter.
Xi is expected to press Trump to halt Taiwan arms sales altogether under a 1982 joint statement during his visit to Washington, sources briefed on the matter told Reuters.
China regularly describes the issue of Taiwan, which Beijing views as its own territory, as its most sensitive and important diplomatic issue, and has repeatedly called for arms sales to stop.
The Trump administration in December approved an US$11 billion arms package to Taiwan, the largest ever. However, a second package, worth some US$14 billion, has been on hold for months.
After a May summit in Beijing with Xi, Trump said he was holding it in abeyance and described it as a "very good negotiating chip”.
Trump's fellow Republicans in Congress rarely question his administration's actions publicly. Three of the senators who signed Wednesday's letter — McConnell, Cornyn and Tillis — are leaving the Senate at the end of this year, with only Murkowski remaining. REUTERS

lume traveler’s lightest caravan hides a pull-out kitchen in its aluminum shell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:45:12 UTC
00:45:12 KST

Lume Traveler has taken one of the bulkiest parts of a caravan interior and pushed it outside. Its new Ranger places the kitchen in a pull-out module along the body, turning food prep into an outdoor act and giving the compact cabin more room to breathe. The aluminum trailer measures 5.19 meters long including its drawbar and just over two meters wide, with an empty weight of 1,150 kilograms.
That move sets up the whole plan. A fixed Auping queen bed fills the rear, while an enclosed bathroom and a small seating area fit into the remaining interior. Designed for two people, the Ranger also gains a pop-up roof that lifts once parked, opening up the low-profile cabin overhead.
images via Lume Traveler
silver outside, softer inside
From outside, the Ranger keeps the silver aluminum skin and rounded body familiar across Lume Traveler’s collection. Inside, the finish shifts toward warmer surfaces. Teak runs underfoot while wool felt wraps the walls and ceiling. Leather appears in smaller details, bringing a more tactile feel to a space where nearly every surface sits within reach.
The bed stays fixed instead of folding away between uses, which gives the rear of the caravan the feel of a tiny bedroom. Storage is tucked into the shell, while power and USB outlets are distributed through the interior. The pop-up roof keeps the trailer low on the road, then changes the volume of the room once the Ranger is set up for a stay.
the Lume Ranger wraps its compact two-person cabin in a rounded aluminum shell
a pull-out kitchen turns the campsite into another room
The outdoor kitchen is the Ranger’s clearest spatial decision. Slide it out and the side of the caravan becomes a work zone, with a countertop and sink alongside two gas burners facing the campsite. Cooking moves into the landscape around the trailer to leave the interior largely given over to sleeping and sitting.
That split shapes how the Ranger is used once it leaves the road. The roof rises above while the kitchen extends from the side, so the compact aluminum shell becomes only one part of the occupied space. An optional awning can cover the exterior cooking area, while an outside shower can add a second service point beyond the body.
a pull-out outdoor kitchen extends from the side of the caravan
Lume trims down its caravan
At 1,150 kilograms empty and 1,500 kilograms at its authorized maximum, the Ranger is Lume Traveler’s lightest model. The company says it can be paired with electric cars rated to tow at least 1,500 kilograms. At 2.04 meters wide, its dimensions also keep the body fairly compact for a trailer containing a permanent bed and enclosed bathroom.
Seen as a whole, the Ranger is built around a fairly simple exchange: move one major function outdoors and the cabin gains space where it is most useful. Its silver body still reads immediately as a caravan, while the plan depends on the landscape around it becoming part of the room. For a trailer this small, that one move changes quite a lot.

Specialists from the municipal enterprise Pleso cleared the storm drain grate, removed the dislodged sorption booms, and installed new ones.

German police official Jürgen Ebner has been selected to become the next executive director of Europol, putting the longtime agency insider on track to lead Europe's increasingly powerful law enforcement body.
EU ambassadors backed Ebner in a Council vote Wednesday, selecting the German from a three-person shortlist after weeks of horse-trading among national capitals.
Ebner currently serves as Europol's deputy executive director for governance and has been acting executive director since Belgian Catherine De Bolle's mandate ended in May. He was widely regarded as De Bolle's right-hand man, making his selection a vote for continuity at The Hague-based agency.
Advertisement
He beat two other senior police officials in the race: Alicia Malo, head of international cooperation at Spain's national police, and Linas Pernavas, director of Lithuania's main anti-corruption law enforcement agency.
Ebner began his career with the German police in 1988 and went on to hold several operational positions at the Federal Criminal Police Office, or BKA, eventually serving in the office of its president.
He moved to Europol in November 2019 after being appointed as deputy executive director responsible for governance. His portfolio has included legal and institutional matters, and he has also served as Europol's security coordinator.
His selection does not quite finish the process.
Ebner will now appear before the European Parliament's civil liberties committee, known as LIBE, which can issue a non-binding opinion on his candidacy. The Council of the EU will then formally appoint Europol's next executive director.
He is set to take charge at a pivotal moment for the agency. The European Commission has proposed significantly expanding Europol's role, resources and technological capabilities as Brussels seeks a stronger response to organized crime, cyberattacks and hybrid threats.

McDonald's will spend big on restaurant upgrades, training to drive growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:44:01 UTC
00:44:01 KST

McDonald's on Wednesday announced plans for its own media network, pricey restaurant upgrades and ways to win over GLP-1 users during an investor presentation at its Chicago headquarters.
In June, the company unveiled its newest growth strategy, McDonald's > NEXT. The pillars of the plan include a new restaurant design, better-tasting food and drinks, consumer-led innovation, and improved hospitality from employees. But until Wednesday, executives had offered few details about how they would implement the plan and how it may affect its financial results over the coming years.
The shifts come as McDonald's U.S. business tries to rebound from sluggish sales and as consumers hit by years of elevated inflation visit restaurants less often. The chain aims to win over more diners at a time the company expects inflation and flat traffic to restaurants overall will persist, CEO Chris Kempczinski told CNBC.
The plan and Kempczinski's comments did not impress Wall Street, as McDonald's shares fell 6% in afternoon trading.
A key part of the strategy is restaurant remodels, which McDonald's mandates roughly every decade for franchisees. The new design features updated PlayPlaces, which were previously being phased out, and more open kitchen layouts. Customers will be able to see their McCafe drinks being prepared.
But the chain will also unveil what it calls Restaurant > NEXT, which includes improvements to equipment, technology and operations. It also will feature "ArchIQ," an artificial intelligence-powered operating system for restaurants. The company said "Archy" can take orders in English and Spanish from customers, saving about 50 labor hours per week, while other elements of ArchIQ can manage inventory and schedule shifts, as well as use scales to assess order accuracy.
"Capabilities such as AI-enabled revenue management and Archy's suggestive sell will help increased average check over time," CFO Ian Borden said.
McDonald's invests in restaurants
All of those upgrades will require steep investment from franchisees. But McDonald's is also planning to provide financial support, through rent relief and actual capital. Through 2036, McDonald's plans to spend as much as $8.5 billion to accelerate franchisees' investment in the restaurant improvement plan.
About $5 billion of that support will happen through 2030. McDonald's is projecting about $1.5 billion to $2 billion in capital spending from 2027 through 2030 to accelerate NEXT, in addition to about $3 billion every year on typical capital expenditures. (In 2025, McDonald's reported $3.4 billion in capital expenditures.)
A standard lobby remodel of a drive-thru restaurant in the U.S. typically costs about $400,000 to $450,000, paid for by the franchisee. The additional investments tied to the plan will be "incremental" to the remodel expenses and cost roughly $800,000 per restaurant, although McDonald's will be providing financial support for some of that, according to Borden. Those investments will be phased, with tech, kitchen and operational upgrades adopted over time as they become available.
Franchisees may protest the franchisor's expectations for their own investment in the restaurants, on top of standard cosmetic remodels. Beef and labor costs are already weighing on their profits.
"We'll get good returns," Kempczinski told CNBC. "Now that doesn't mean to say that there aren't going to be a lot of anxieties, a lot of questions, as there always is around investment. It happens every time we go into one of these cycles, and we'll work with our franchisees collaboratively on that to address their questions."
Kempczinski added that the company is projecting franchisee returns in the mid-to-high 20% range, while corporate returns will be in the high teens.
Plus, McDonald's projects that efficiency improvements will result in an increase of roughly $100,000 in annual cash flow for the average U.S. restaurant, and the initiative will take about four years to return franchisees' investment. Average annual U.S. franchisee cash flow is currently about $500,000, up nearly 50% compared with 2019, boosted by franchisees opening new restaurants, according to Borden.
While McDonald's plans to spend more to fuel restaurant improvements, the company said it aims to cut costs elsewhere, although it did not offer specifics. By 2030, McDonald's is targeting an operating margin in the low-to-mid 50% range. In 2025, the company reported operating margins of 46.1%, according to company filings.
Some of that margin expansion will come from its general and administrative spending. By 2030, McDonald's is projecting that about 1.9% of its systemwide sales will go toward G&A. For comparison, the company is currently forecasting that 2.2% of its systemwide sales will be spent on G&A in 2026.
"At the company, AI will help enable a step-change improvement in corporate G&A," Borden said.
Higher operating margins will also come from increased revenue.
McDonald's is planning to build a media network that involves advertising other businesses on its digital drive-thru displays. Executives said it could grow to become a billion-dollar business. The company has started testing it over the last month at 450 company-owned restaurants. Media networks have become high-margin businesses for retailers like Amazon and Walmart.
McDonald's also has an eye on growing its sales globally. Some of that will come from new locations. Next year, the company expects restaurant openings will make up about 2.5% of its systemwide sales growth.
The company's accelerated expansion will slow in the following years. By 2030, McDonald's anticipates new restaurants will account for only about 2% of growth to systemwide sales.
Menu changes and more chicken
In recent years, the burger chain has leaned into menu items other than its core beef offerings to drive sales, namely chicken and beverages. By 2030, McDonald's wants to grow its global market share in those two categories by about 1.5 percentage points each.
McDonald's already sees nearly $15 billion in system sales from Chicken McNuggets, $4 billion from its McChicken and $2.5 billion from McCrispy menu items, according to Jill McDonald, the company's global chief restaurant experience officer. Altogether, the chain accounts for about 20% of chicken sales out of the entire $130 billion global category.
But McDonald's wants a bigger bite.
To grow its share of chicken sales, the chain plans to introduced hand-breaded chicken options. Chicken specialists like Chick-fil-A, Popeyes and Raising Cane's already hand-bread or batter their chicken for a crispier exterior and better taste. However, the technique requires more time and labor from employees.
U.S. restaurants will soon start piloting hand-breaded chicken menu items, McDonald said.
Other chicken options coming to McDonald's menu include new grilled chicken sandwiches and wraps and new flavors and sauces for Chicken McNuggets.
Likewise, McDonald's wants a bigger share of the global $230 billion beverage category, according to McDonald. Today, it holds a roughly 10% share and is the second-largest coffee player globally. But the category is growing quickly, presenting more opportunities for the chain to grow sales.
"Beverages are no longer just an add-on, but a reason to visit," McDonald said.
In the U.S., McDonald's rolled out an expanded drink menu earlier this year, featuring refreshers, crafted sodas and energy drinks. The chain now plans to launch more beverages in its international markets. It also aims to upgrade the quality of its coffee; U.S. restaurants will receive new espresso machines and the opportunity to customize their drinks with alternative milk choices.
And McDonald's has an eye on new food menu items, too.
"We're exploring bowls, grilled chicken and egg bites to expand protein-forward options across breakfast, lunch and dinner," McDonald's U.S. President Skye Anderson said.
Some of that protein-focused innovation is spurred by the growing adoption of GLP-1 drugs. For several years, investor concerns about how the medication will affect McDonald's sales have weighed on the stock. But executives on Wednesday expressed confidence that the chain will not lose customers because of changes to their appetites. Anderson said that 84% of households with at least one GLP-1 user still visit McDonald's.
"This is an opportunity," she said. "We don't need to win a new base of customers into McDonald's. Instead, we need to keep giving them more reasons to make McDonald's their first choice as their eating habits evolve."
Still, McDonald's isn't abandoning burgers. The company wants to hold onto its leadership in beef, too.
It currently holds onto about 40% share of the $50 billion worldwide beef category, McDonald said. It plans to add its fresh beef Quarter Pounders in more markets outside of the U.S., where it made the shift about eight years ago. Plus, Kempczinski told CNBC that there is even more opportunity in the U.S. to lean into the Quarter Pounder to steal share from its rivals who use frozen beef. The chain also wants to improve the quality of its burgers, building off the success of its "Best Burger" improvements that rolled out in 2024.
To do so, it plans on implementing "Make It Golden," a multiyear training program for corporate employees, restaurant workers and franchisees to ensure consistency, improved food quality and better customer service.
"While there's so much our customers love, we are falling short when it comes to consistent execution," Anderson said.
The emphasis on hospitality comes as customer expectations keep growing, McDonald's Global Chief People Officer Tiffanie Boyd told CNBC.
"People want and expect more because so many things have become more convenient, and so you can't just differentiate on something like convenience alone," Boyd said. "And, as we automate more things in our lives, we're finding that people have a higher expectation around the quality of a human interaction."
The program will begin rolling out on Oct. 5, the 124th birthday of Ray Kroc, who turned the burger restaurant into a global giant.

50+ countries at UN urge Russia to end aggression and agree to immediate ceasefire
This was stated in a joint declaration released ahead of a UN Security Council meeting by EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, an Ukrinform correspondent reports.
The document stresses solidarity with Ukraine and the need to uphold the principles of the UN Charter, including respect for states’ sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity, as well as their inherent right to self-defense.
The statement expresses “deep concern” over the escalation of Russian attacks on Ukraine’s civilian population and infrastructure, which, according to the UN, have caused a record-high number of casualties in recent months.
“We call for full respect for international humanitarian law, accountability, and the protection of civilians,” the document states.
The countries expressed concern over Russia’s attacks in the Black Sea, noting that Moscow is seeking to obstruct Ukrainian grain exports, posing a threat to global food security. They support efforts to reach agreements to ensure freedom of navigation in the Black Sea.
Since March 2025, Ukraine has agreed to a full, immediate and unconditional ceasefire, the statement says.
“We call on Russia to finally do the same as a necessary step toward meaningful diplomacy and negotiations leading to peace,” the statement reads.
The countries also urged Russia to immediately, safely and unconditionally return to Ukraine all unlawfully detained, forcibly transferred or deported civilians, including children, as well as fully return all prisoners of war and internees.
“Ukraine wants peace. We want peace. Russia must end its aggression, agree to a ceasefire and engage meaningfully in negotiations for a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in accordance with international law,” the joint statement says.
Most European countries, as well as Australia, Canada, Costa Rica, Honduras, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, Panama and South Korea, signed the document.
As reported, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha is attending Wednesday’s UN Security Council meeting on the agenda item “Maintenance of International Peace and Security of Ukraine.”
