Ukraine Smashes Russia’s Two-Month Push to Encircle Druzhkivka, 237 Troops Killed
Ukrainian forces have disrupted a Russian attempt to reach key logistics routes and create conditions for the operational encirclement of Druzhkivka in the Donetsk region following a nearly two-month clearing operation involving several Ukrainian units.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s 1st National Guard Corps “Azov” on September 23, Russian forces had been building up in the area throughout the summer with the aim of advancing toward Druzhkivka and launching further attacks in the direction of Dobropillia.
The Russian grouping included elements of the 90th Tank Division and the 8th Combined Arms Army, according to Lev, callsign “Khorus,” commander of Ukraine’s 12th Special Forces Brigade “Azov.”
Ukraine reinforced troops already operating in the sector and launched a coordinated operation involving the Ultima Ratio special reconnaissance unit, the 1st and 6th battalions of the 12th Azov Brigade, the Tuman special forces unit of the 1st Azov Corps, and the Shkval Battalion of the 425th Skelia Separate Assault Regiment. Lasar’s Group of the National Guard provided additional support.
The first Ukrainian assault groups began advancing on August 7 after Russian positions and concentrations were targeted to isolate the area and prevent additional Russian forces from moving forward. Artillery and strike drones were used to support infantry clearing operations.
According to Azov, Ukrainian units sought to destroy or suppress Russian positions with FPV drones, bomber drones, and artillery before sending assault troops forward when direct clearing operations posed an increased risk to personnel.
The operation was complicated by dense vegetation, Russian infantry moving in small groups, and extensive Russian drone activity, which also made the evacuation of wounded Ukrainian troops more difficult.
Azov said the operation resulted in 237 Russian troops killed, 44 wounded, and three captured. The figures have not been independently verified.
The Ukrainian units also reported strikes on Russian artillery during the operation. Lasar’s Group provided fire support to assault units, while earlier Ukrainian operations targeting Russian artillery and armored vehicles helped reduce Russia’s ability to support troops operating in the sector.
The operation prevented Russian troops from reaching logistics routes that Ukrainian commanders said could have been used to threaten Druzhkivka and support an advance toward Dobropillia. According to Azov, losing positions in the area forces Russian forces to search for alternative routes and commit additional time and resources before attempting further advances.
The operation comes as Ukrainian forces conduct broader counteroffensive actions in northern Donetsk region. Ukraine’s Third Army Corps recently reported that its Operation Vivaldi had returned 125 square kilometers of territory to Ukrainian control during several stages of fighting.

Thousands of displaced in south-west Somalia could be in famine by year end, IPC says
NAIROBI, Sept 23 - Thousands of displaced people in Somalia's south-west could experience famine between October and December if El Nino causes worse-than-expected flooding and humanitarian aid remains insufficient, a global hunger monitor said on Wednesday.
Baidoa, one of Somalia's biggest cities, is home to hundreds of thousands displaced by conflict and hunger.
A report by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), an initiative of UN agencies, regional bodies and aid groups, said that 5% of displaced people in Baidoa, or about 26,000, were likely to face starvation and a collapse in livelihoods in October to December.
More than 5 million Somalis, 26% of the analysed population, are already suffering crisis-level food insecurity or worse due to repeated droughts, conflict and aid shortfalls, the report said.
The number suffering food insecurity is forecast at 5.4 million people in October to December.
Food aid is expected to reach only 70,400 people per month in October to December, or 1.3% of those in need.
An estimated 1.92 million children aged 6 months to 5 years will require treatment for acute malnutrition by next June, including 433,000 severe cases.
Somalia last experienced famine in 2011, when around 250,000 people died, and came close in 2017 and 2022. REUTERS

Morocco votes for new parliament amid hopes and concerns over cost of living
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:15:27 UTC
00:15:27 KST

Hopes and concerns over jobs, wages, public services and cost of living dominate Morocco’s parliamentary election as the country prepares for the 2030 World Cup.
Moroccans went to the polls on Wednesday to elect a new parliament in an election shaped by mounting issues but also hopes for better opportunities generated by the country’s thriving economy.
The next government will oversee preparations for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco will co-host with Spain and Portugal, while facing pressure to address everyday worries about unemployment and low wages, as well as issues with housing, schools and hospitals.
Voting centres across the North African kingdom are due to close at 7 pm local time (9 pm CEST), allowing nearly 16 million registered voters to cast ballots for the 395-seat House of Representatives.
A total of 7,288 candidates are standing, backed by 28 parties and alliances or running on two independent lists.
The vote will determine the next prime minister and the makeup of the government, which will serve alongside a powerful monarchy that retains broad authority over strategic affairs.
Morocco’s constitution requires the king to choose the prime minister from the top-performing party in legislative elections.
Since no single party is expected to capture an absolute majority, the winner will need to build a coalition government. Portfolios are split among the political allies, but the palace traditionally keeps key posts such as defence and foreign affairs under royal control.
Еconomy strong, jobs scarce
Morocco’s economy is growing and attracting foreign investment, and new industries are developing. It has also become Africa’s most-visited destination.
The kingdom is a close US ally and maintains strong ties with Western capitals. It is among the few Arab countries that have diplomatic relations with Israel.
Beyond the palaces, seas and mountains that draw tourists from around the world, development remains uneven across the country, economic growth is not creating enough jobs, and 12.7% of Moroccans live in relative poverty.
Politicians have said they have heard these grievances and have proposed solutions in their election manifestos. Many young Moroccans in particular said they have heard such promises before.
Who are the main contenders?
The outgoing government is a coalition of the National Rally of Independents (RNI), the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) and the Istiqlal Party. All three are competing to finish first.
The liberal, pro-business RNI won the 2021 election and has led the government for the past five years. Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch stepped down as RNI leader in February and is not standing for a parliamentary seat. Mohamed Chouki now leads the party.
Both the RNI and PAM have promised to create around 1 million jobs over the next five-year term. The RNI has also proposed a guaranteed minimum monthly wage of 5,000 dirhams (€455).
PAM is the second-largest party in the outgoing parliament. Its main figures in this election include Fatima-Zahra Mansouri, the mayor of Marrakech and urban planning minister, and Fouzi Lekjaa, the budget minister and president of Morocco’s football federation.
The party has proposed exempting salaries below 15,000 dirhams (€1,370) from income tax and providing 100,000 housing options for young people. If PAM finishes first and Mansouri is chosen to lead the government, she would become the first woman to hold the post.
Istiqlal, Morocco’s oldest political party, is led by Water Minister Nizar Baraka. The nationalist, conservative-leaning party has made faster treatment in public hospitals one of its campaign pledges.
The Justice and Development Party (PJD), led by former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, is also trying to make a comeback. The moderate party led the government for a decade before falling from 125 seats to 13 in the 2021 election. It says it wants to reduce the economic gap between Casablanca and other parts of the country.
Other established contenders include the Socialist Union of Popular Forces, the Popular Movement and the left-wing Party of Progress and Socialism, which has campaigned on education and tighter anti-corruption rules.
How does the election work?
Voters receive two ballot papers and choose a party list rather than individual candidates.
Of the 395 seats, 305 are filled through local constituencies. The remaining 90 come from regional, all-female lists. Seats are allocated under a proportional system.
Under Morocco’s 2011 constitution, King Mohammed VI appoints the head of government from the party that wins the most seats.
No party is expected to secure the 198 seats needed for an outright majority, so the winner will probably have to negotiate a coalition. The proposed cabinet must then receive royal approval.
The elected government runs domestic policy and public services, but the king retains broad powers over the country’s overall direction, defence and foreign affairs.
The constitution recognises the right to vote for Moroccans living abroad, but there is no voting by mail or ballot boxes at Moroccan consulates.
Instead, they must travel to Morocco to vote or authorise a registered family member or acquaintance to vote on their behalf.
Counting begins after polls close on Wednesday evening. Preliminary national results are normally announced the following day.
Morocco does not have election opinion polls, so there is no reliable public forecast of which party will finish first. Once the result is known, the leading party will begin talks with potential coalition partners.

Watch a robot dog run a marathon faster than the average human
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:14:55 UTC
00:14:55 KST

Hot on the heels of humanoid robots besting Usain Bolt’s record in the 100-meter sprint is a marathon-running dog bot.
The quadrupedal machine, named RAIBO2, ran the full 26.2-mile marathon course in a single battery charge, finishing in four hours, 19 minutes and 52 seconds—slightly ahead of the human average.
The feat shows how far researchers have come in making these bots energy-efficient. “What matters is energy consumed per unit of distance,” explains the study’s lead author Choongin Lee, a roboticist at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) in South Korea. To make their robot able to complete a marathon without needing a recharge, Lee and his team identified all the areas where walking robots waste energy.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
About two thirds of a robot’s energy budget is lost as heat in the motors and their drive electronics, the researchers found. The rest goes into friction in the gears, feet that slip and the jolt of each footfall.
Lee’s team tackled each issue one by one: The researchers cut the weight of each leg, designed low-resistance motor boards and spent the freed-up mass budget on a bigger battery, combined with motors that produced the same torque for less current. RAIBO2’s walking style was trained through simulation with reinforcement learning, in which the control algorithm was rewarded for setting the robot’s feet down softly and for not allowing it to slip or overheat.
On top of that, RAIBO2 was designed to recuperate and recharge the battery on downhill stretches. The robot is described in a study that was published in Nature on Wednesday.
The result of all this tinkering is that the robot needs less energy to carry a kilogram over a distance of one meter than the average human runner. RAIBO2 travels roughly three times farther per charge than other quadrupedal robots, with a projected range of around 40 miles.
“I’m impressed with their ability to combine efficiency with speed and mobility in a quadruped,” says Sarah Bergbreiter, a mechanical engineer at Carnegie Mellon University, who was not involved in the study.
Katie Byl, an engineer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, who also was not involved in the work, points out that the humanoid robots that were recently seen racing in China needed several battery swaps from a support team jogging alongside. “It’s akin to a ‘mobile pit crew,’” she notes.
Still, Lee’s robot required human help during the marathon. “RAIBO2 is basically running blind,” Byl explains. The robot carried a camera but no software to interpret the road. A human operator had to steer it remotely.
Adding more autonomy will cost power, Lee says. To minimize the loss of energy-efficiency an added electronic brain would cause, Lee’s team is currently working on smaller onboard networks and sensors. “This way the robot can become more capable without a large increase in power consumption,” Lee says.

Netherlands to return to Eurovision 2027 after boycotting Israel’s participation

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:13:40 UTC
00:13:40 KST

The Netherlands will join the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest after boycotting the event this year over Israel's participation, Dutch public broadcaster NPO said on Wednesday.
NPO took over from the original public broadcaster AVROTROS, which formally announced in August that they would not participate in the contest, stating that the event could "no longer be considered neutral" while a participating country, referring to Israel, remains involved in a large-scale military conflict, NL Time reported Wednesday.
In August, AVROTROS director-general Taco Zimmerman stated that the contest was meant to unite people and countries involved in international conflicts, undermining the contest's "neutrality" character, saying, "The Eurovision Song Contest was originally created to bring people and countries together." It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the contest, undermining its neutral character.”
The broadcaster noted that it had returned responsibility for Dutch participation in Eurovision to the NPO. This organization oversees the overall Dutch public broadcasting system.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) had initially set a September 15 deadline for countries to confirm their participation. NPO requested additional time to evaluate its options after taking over responsibility for the Netherlands’ Eurovision entry and was granted an extension until the end of September.
Countries weigh Eurovision return as Bulgaria prepares to host 2027 event
The Netherlands was among five countries, together with Ireland, Spain, Iceland, and Slovenia, that withdrew from the 2026 Eurovision contest in Vienna. Ireland’s broadcaster RTÉ has since said it will also skip and not broadcast the 2027 contest, while Spain and Iceland are still reviewing whether they will participate, according to Eurovoix.
The contest's final semi-final rounds ad grand final will be held in Burgas, Bulgaria May 11-15, 2027 hosted by Bulgarian National Television (BNT) alongside the European Broadcasting Union (EBU).
Reuters and Tzvi Jasper contributed to this report.

Poverty, child labor, and child marriage partially behind Iran’s unfilled classrooms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:13:38 UTC
00:13:38 KST

Thousands of Iranian children of elementary-school age have been unable to receive an education due to financial hardship, Iran’s Education Ministry reported on Tuesday.
Rezvan Hakimzadeh, deputy minister of primary education, said 140,562 students had been identified as not attending school last year, with the majority located in Sistan and Baluchestan, Tehran, Razavi Khorasan, and Khuzestan provinces. Of those children, 54,445 were in the first grade, he said.
Nearly 42,000 of the students had left Iran with their families, while 18,000 were not required to enroll due to disabilities, Hakimzadeh said. Thousands of others were out of school due to family financial hardship, child labor, a lack of adequate guardianship, or enrollment in unlicensed education centers, he added.
There were 86 cases in which a child of elementary-school age was not attending school because they had married, the report said.
Primary school in Iran is for children ages six to 12, while Iranian law generally requires girls to be 13 and boys to be 15 to marry. In some cases, however, a judge’s approval can allow for marriage at an earlier age.
The start of the school year in Iran has drawn greater attention to the country’s rapid demographic change.
According to the Razavi Foundation’s Astan Quds Razavi media site Quds Online, 1.154 million six-year-old children began primary school in Iran this year, about 76,000 fewer than last year.
Iran's challenged demography
Iran’s declining birth rates, delays in marriage and childbearing, economic pressures, and lifestyle changes have all impacted the country’s shifting demography, Quds Online reported.
Alireza Sajedi, head of Iran’s Population Monitoring Center of the National Organization for Civil Registration, told Quds Online the number of births had fallen from about 1.116 million in 2021 to fewer than 980,000 in 2024.
The downward demographic shift could eventually lead schools to reduce both classroom sizes and the actual number of classes in cities, Quds Online reported. In rural areas, however, it may no longer be viable to keep schools open, the report said.

Israel Navy moves toward semi-autonomous fleet with robotic ships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:13:26 UTC
00:13:26 KST

The Israeli navy is moving toward becoming a semi-autonomous force and may eventually become nearly fully autonomous, the IDF said.
It has been reported that the Israeli navy has operated autonomous sea vehicles in recent years, though it is unclear when swarms at sea will be ready to roll out.
Elbit Systems has already been among the Israeli companies developing such technologies, including its publicized 12-meter Seagull autonomous surface vessel, designed to patrol offshore infrastructure for up to four days. It also "incorporates mine countermeasures (MCM), anti-submarine warfare (ASW), maritime security (MS), electronic warfare (EW) and other advanced systems and technologies."
Other countries like France, Singapore, and the Netherlands are also shifting their navies toward more autonomous operations.
Despite those navies' progress, Israel's navy said it is even more advanced in using robots and autonomy.
The need for robots and autonomous operations is clear, given that ships can spend weeks or longer at sea.
Even the most resilient sailors have trouble with this amount of time at sea, and an overwhelming portion of the population is just incapable of doing it at all.
Israel faces growing naval threats from Turkey, Iran, Houthis
In addition, Israel faces growing naval threats from Turkey, and possibly from Iran, the Houthis in Yemen, and others.
The navy said this means it will need more ships in the future to secure Israel's maritime national security interests.
However, the navy does not believe the country or the military will grant it additional staffing power for more ships, so the only stable way to expand Israel's naval fleet sufficiently will involve fewer human soldiers per ship, and eventually zero or close to zero.
At one stage, Israeli soldiers can focus solely on maintenance and safety issues with robots and autonomous systems operating most other systems.
Robots are a double-edged sword
At a later stage, robots may be able to undertake all or much of the maintenance work.
But robots are a double-edged sword.
Enemy forces are also expected to use robots and autonomous systems against Israel.
This will create a number of challenges: land-to-sea and sea-to-sea.
In addition, the IDF is aware that China, Russia, and other countries have explored cutting underwater cables, which foreign reports have confirmed going back to at least 2023 in the Baltic Sea, near Britain, Norway, and at other locations.
Israel is working on and will need to expand its defense of these underwater cables going forward.

The four firms succeeded suppliers called Verona, Kombinat Doshkolnogo Pitaniya, Russotskapital and Shkolnik-Yuz, which had been owned by Prigozhin, the outlet reported.
Ragimov studied with Putin at Leningrad State University, now St. Petersburg State University. Forbes estimated his fortune at $500 million in 2014, citing business interests that included Moscow’s Sadovod market, the Ukraina hotel and the Evropeisky and Panorama shopping centers.

Gaza journalists operating under Hamas media controls were given platforms in Westminster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:13:14 UTC
00:13:14 KST

Gaza-based journalists who worked amid what photojournalist Motaz Azaiza has described as a “Hamas-controlled media environment” were given prominent platforms in Westminster, researcher Emma Schubart of the Henry Jackson Society (HJS) revealed to The Jerusalem Post exclusively on Tuesday.
Schubart’s discovery follows comments made by Gazan photojournalist Motaz Azaiza in a September 3 podcast interview with journalist Ahmed Biqui.
During this conversation, Azaiza mentioned the existence of a Hamas-administered WhatsApp group called Smart, which, he said, included “every journalist working in Gaza.” The group’s icon displayed a Hamas flag and was administered by “the director of media for the Rafah Border Crossing,” who has been identified as Wael Abu Mohsen.
According to Azaiza, the group coordinated media messaging and organized campaigns against journalists whose reporting departed from the sanctioned line.
“It was never a spontaneous thing,” he added.
Gazan photographers 'accustomed to lowering cameras' to criticism of Hamas
Azaiza added that photographers in Gaza had “become accustomed to lowering their cameras” when civilians criticized Hamas.
HJS reported that several journalists who operated within this Hamas-controlled media environment were subsequently welcomed into Westminster and presented to British parliamentarians as authoritative witnesses to the war. Other journalists from this environment have been involved more indirectly with the British government.
For example, Al Jazeera’s Gaza bureau chief Wael al-Dahdouh was hosted in Parliament in September last year.
MPs host Hamas-linked journalists
Hansard [the official report of all Parliamentary debates] records Labour MP Yuan Yang saying on September 10, 2025, that she had “co-hosted an event in Parliament for Wael al-Dahdouh” the previous evening.
During that visit, Dahdouh also met with Labour MP Afzal Khan for Manchester Rusholem (formerly Manchester Gorton), who posted publicly that he had met Dahdouh, calling the meeting “an honor.”
While neither the Post nor HJS has independently verified the membership of the group, Azaiza said it included every journalist working in Gaza at the time.
Then there is Azaiza himself, who on May 15, 2024, addressed a Nakba Day gathering at Westminster Central Hall, yards from Parliament, sharing the event with Sir Alan Duncan, the former Conservative Foreign Office minister.
Additionally, Scottish National Party (SNP) MP Brendan O’Hara co-organized a cross-party panel in a House of Commons committee room in mid-July 2025 with Oxfam GB and the Council for Arab-British Understanding.
Gaza journalist Abubaker Abed spoke alongside Oxfam’s then-CEO. Abed addressed MPs and journalists who were in attendance on conditions in Gaza and called for an end to UK arms support for Israel.
Finally, Al Jazeera and the International Centre of Justice for Palestinians (ICJP) held a sold-out Westminster screening of the documentary Gaza in October 2024, followed by a panel. Al Jazeera Gaza correspondent Youmna El Sayed appeared as a panellist, with MPs and peers attending.
“One of Gaza’s most famous ‘journalists’ has described, in his own words, how Hamas controlled the media environment,” Schubart said.
Schubart noted that this is of great importance to every international outlet that has relied on Gaza-based journalists yet still claims that their reporting is editorially independent of Hamas.
“The question is straightforward: Why were British politicians giving a parliamentary platform to journalism produced under Hamas control?”
Schubart has personally written to the Speaker of the House on these findings. The letter was viewed by the Post.

DOJ defends Trump ban of 3 news outlets, says White House access is a 'privilege — not a right'

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:11:28 UTC
00:11:28 KST

The U.S. Department of Justice late Tuesday evening urged a federal judge not to block President Donald Trump's total ban of three news outlets from the White House, saying, "Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right."
The DOJ, in a new court filing, also said Trump was motivated by concerns about national security in his decision Friday to summarily ban MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House.
The filing came ahead of Wednesday's scheduled teleconference hearing in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., where Judge Timothy Kelly will hear arguments by a lawyer for the outlets, which have asked him to enjoin Trump from continuing the ban as part of a lawsuit filed against him Monday.
"The President has determined that Plaintiffs have reported classified or sensitive information bearing on national security," the DOJ said in the filing to Kelly, who is a Trump appointee.
"The President therefore has a compelling interest in limiting access to White House grounds to organizations that do not pose such a risk to national security," the filing says.
Targeting claims by the media outlets in their lawsuit, the DOJ said that there is no First Amendment right of news reporters to the White House.
The outlets in their suit say that Trump's ban was motivated by so-called viewpoint discrimination, or targeting them for their perceived "motivating ideology or the opinion or perspective."
The DOJ, in its filing, included new letters, dated Tuesday, to the media outlets, giving each of them to chance to contest the initial decision to ban them and the factual basis for the ban.
The letters reference stories published by the outlets that purportedly threatened national security.
"Plaintiffs may submit any response by 5:00 pm on Friday, September 25, 2026," the filing says.
"Otherwise, 'this initial decision will be final."
Disclosure: CNBC and MS NOW are divisions of Versant Media.

US targets Iranian airlines (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:10:41 UTC
00:10:41 KST

US targets Iranian airlines (VIDEO)
Iranian airlines are being cut off from international routes and airport services as Washington steps up pressure on the country’s aviation sector. Several regional connections have already been suspended or restricted, although some foreign flights continue, RT’s Saman Kojouri has reported from outside the Tehran headquarters of Mahan Air, one of Iran’s major carriers.
The US Treasury targeted 27 Iranian airlines earlier this month as part of a broader campaign against the country’s aviation sector. Foreign companies providing services to the carriers risk US secondary sanctions, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that the restrictions would effectively shut Iranian airlines out of international aviation from September 23.
”If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” Bessent said.
The impact is already spreading across the region, according to RT’s Kojouri. Azerbaijan has suspended flights operated by Iranian carriers, while Iraq has reportedly stopped accepting Iranian aircraft. Flights between Tehran and Muscat have also been suspended, while Georgia has said it will comply with sanctions affecting Iranian carriers.
Mahan Air is among the airlines facing the squeeze. Washington first sanctioned the carrier in 2011, accusing it of providing support to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Quds Force (IRGC-QF). The Treasury has since targeted companies abroad accused of providing commercial and logistical support to the airline.
The aviation crackdown comes as Washington ramps up pressure on Tehran while simultaneously pursuing diplomatic contacts on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. President Donald Trump threatened on Tuesday to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” if negotiations fail, saying he faced a “big decision” between reaching an agreement and further military escalation.
Most of the Iranian delegation walked out of the General Assembly hall during Trump’s speech, leaving only one representative seated. The US president defended the nearly seven-month US-Israeli war and accused Tehran of pursuing nuclear weapons and supporting terrorism.
Despite the hostile rhetoric, indirect contacts continued later in the day. US envoy Steve Witkoff said mediators had shuttled between the American and Iranian delegations during “lengthy talks,” while Tehran said it had used the channel to clearly convey its conditions to Washington, including lifting the US naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

One Single Planet: French photographer Yann Arthus-Bertrand on his 'Vivre Ensemble' portraits

00:08:54 KST

Photographer Yann Arthus-Bertrand spoke to Euronews about his Vivre Ensemble portrait project, celebrating the people, diversity and connections that shape contemporary France.
For photographer Yann Arthus-Bertrand, the idea of living together is at the heart of his latest portrait project, Vivre Ensemble, now on display in Lyon.
The exhibition brings together hundreds of portraits exploring the people and stories that make up contemporary France. Arthus-Bertrand began the project with demographer Hervé Le Bras, aiming to document different professions, social classes and family structures in a country he says is changing rapidly.
The photographer says he has photographed around 40,000 people as part of the project, including nearly 1,500 people in Lyon, where a studio photographed visitors over three days.
Known for his aerial photography and his Earth from Above project, Arthus-Bertrand says he has increasingly turned his camera towards people.
“I prefer today to photograph faces rather than landscapes,” he told Euronews, describing the empathy and connection created through portrait photography.
For him, the project is also about including everyone. People can come alone or with their families, regardless of their profession or background.
Arthus-Bertrand says he is particularly moved when visitors tell him that the exhibition “does them good” and that they leave feeling happier. At its heart, he says, the exhibition is about “love” — his love for the people around him.
Looking at the Earth from above, he says, there are no borders, only one planet that we all share. In an increasingly difficult and complicated world, he believes cooperation, sharing and passing things on are essential.
“The more we give, the more we receive,” he says. And for Arthus-Bertrand, the true beauty of the world lies in people who share, give and pass things on: “This beauty is called love.”

Nuclear arms unlikely to be deployed in Lithuania soon despite parliament consent — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:08:53 UTC
00:08:53 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Nuclear weapons will not appear on Lithuanian territory in the near future, despite the decision by the Seimas (parliament) to lift the ban on their deployment, Ruslan Pankratov, a member of the Officers of Russia expert council, deputy chairman of the Union of Political Emigrants of Europe, and a former deputy of the Riga City Council has said.
On September 22, the Lithuanian Seimas approved lifting the ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons within the country. Following a discussion of the issue, the parliament referred a constitutional amendment to the relevant committees for review.
"There is a vast, if not enormous, gap between repealing Article 137 and the actual arrival of nuclear weapons on Lithuanian soil. Decisions to deploy nuclear warheads would require specific consent from the US and NATO, military infrastructure, specialized security and storage procedures, and would entail significant political costs," Pankratov said.
In his opinion, such decisions amount to an "ostentatious demonstration of Lithuania's readiness for the closest possible military-political integration with NATO."
Pankratov also emphasized that the practical value of deploying nuclear warheads in Lithuania for NATO is quite limited.
"The alliance is unlikely to rush the deployment of nuclear weapons right on the Russian and Belarusian borders, as this would sharply increase the risk of actual - rather than merely rhetorical - escalation for its domestic electorate," he explained.

If you read The Diplomat, you probably follow Asia-Pacific affairs – and thus you probably already know that Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to arrive in Washington, D.C. today for a much-anticipated summit with U.S. President Donald Trump.
According to the White House’s itinerary, Xi will land at Andrews Air Force Base on September 23, where he will be personally received by Trump himself. The next day, he’ll receive a formal welcome ceremony at the White House, followed by the actual summit and a state dinner. On September 25, Trump and First Lady Melania Trump will host Xi and his wife for tea; both couples will then visit the National Archives, “where they will view a variety of important records and documents significant to the American and Chinese relationship throughout history.” Then Xi and his delegation will fly home.
What’s most remarkable about this itinerary is what it doesn’t include: a stop in New York, where the United Nations’ General Assembly is currently holding its 81st session. Heads of state and government from around the world are making the trip to New York just for the UNGA, including top leaders from Bangladesh, Japan, Indonesia, Kyrgyzstan, Nepal, Mongolia, South Korea, and Vietnam, just to name a few from The Diplomat’s coverage region.
Meanwhile, Xi is making a trip across the Pacific Ocean and the entire continental U.S. and not bothering to take an extra jaunt up the coast to attend the United Nations’ most important annual event.
Instead, Vice President Han Zheng will be in New York from September 24 to 26 to represent China at the UNGA. According to China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, “On the sidelines of the general debate, Vice President Han will attend the High-Level Dialogue on the Fifth Anniversary of the Global Development Initiative hosted by China, and meet with [the] U.N. secretary-general, president of the 81st UNGA session, and leaders of relevant countries.”
Apparently, these are meetings Xi couldn’t be bothered to attend himself, despite being just an hour’s plane ride away.
Xi’s absence from the UNGA would seem to undermine China’s consistent rhetorical emphasis on the United Nations’ importance. China’s white paper on global governance, released in June 2026, repeatedly emphasized the U.N. as the “core” of the international order. “The United Nations is the primary platform for practicing multilateralism and advancing global governance,” the white paper declared. “Its leading position must be upheld and remain rock solid; its role can only be reinforced, not weakened.”
In the same press conference where Guo announced Han’s trip, the spokesperson repeated a similar line: “The United Nations is the core platform for global governance, and the general debate of UNGA is a vital opportunity for countries to build political consensus and coordinate multilateral actions.” But if the United Nations, and the UNGA, are so important, why can’t Xi be bothered to attend?
Xi has gone to the UNGA just once since becoming China’s top leader in late 2012. He went in 2015, to commemorate the United Nations’ 70th anniversary, and addressed the UNGA in person for the first and only time.
Notably, this coincided with Xi’s last state visit to the United States, when he included attendance at the UNGA within a broader itinerary that saw him also hold a summit with then-U.S. President Barack Obama. That makes the decision not to do the same thing in 2026 all the more notable.
In 2021, Xi gave a video address to the UNGA, in which he announced China’s Global Development Initiative. He has not delivered a speech before the UNGA since.
Perhaps most notably, Xi chose to skip last year’s UNGA – the 80th session. China puts much stock in these round-number anniversaries, pegging trips abroad and major upgrades in bilateral relations to special dates. Remember that Xi took the time to attend the United Nations’ 70th anniversary in person. That wasn’t an aberration – China’s top leader had attended every decennial anniversary of the U.N. since Jiang Zemin in 1995. That made Xi’s absence from the 80th anniversary in 2025 all the more conspicuous.
As I wrote at the time:
Instead [of attending the UNGA], Xi stayed in China, where he “extended festive greetings” for the farmers’ harvest celebration and visited Urumqi to mark the 70th anniversary of the founding of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.
Those events were duly splashed across the front-page headlines of People’s Daily, the official newspaper of the Chinese Communist Party. Premier Li Qiang’s presence at UNGA received just a one-line mention on the front page for September 24.
Xi has also stopped announcing China’s major global initiatives at the United Nations. He unveiled the Global Development Initiative at the UNGA back in 2021, albeit in a virtual speech. But in 2025, Xi chose to announce the new Global Governance Initiative – even more directly related to the United Nations’ mission – at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit held in China a month before the UNGA.
Similarly, China founded its own World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) – “an independent intergovernmental international organization that… aims to promote international cooperation and global governance on artificial intelligence” – rather than working within the United Nations to legitimize its efforts toward the same ends. China announced WAICO at its own AI conference, rather than at the U.N. Global Dialogue on AI Governance held a month earlier.
Meanwhile, as Trump reduces U.S. funding for the United Nations, China hasn’t stepped up to fill the gap. Its own U.N.-assessed contributions have been chronically late and remain a mere fraction of what the United States was contributing prior to Trump taking office.
No matter the lip service China pays to the United Nations’ “core role” in global governance, Beijing clearly prefers to give attention, money, and prestige to settings where it exerts more control. That includes China-led groups like the SCO, but also purely bilateral meetings like the summit with Trump.
Nikkei Asia theorized that Xi’s decision to skip the UNGA was an attempt to position China as a true equal to the United States – a message that apparently would have been diluted by Xi rubbing elbows with leaders from smaller states in New York. That in itself is telling. For all China’s rhetoric about a multipolar world where all states have equal representation – and equal say – in global governance, when push comes to shove Beijing defaults to a different perspective.
As China’s top diplomat put it, fairly undiplomatically, in a heated ASEAN meeting back in 2010: “China is a big country and other countries are small countries, and that’s just a fact.” One of the perks of being a “big country,” as Trump has repeatedly shown, is the privilege of ignoring the United Nations to pursue national interests in other settings.

Power beneath the waves, threats of blockade: Israel Navy’s covert battle with its new submarine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:06:05 UTC
00:06:05 KST

The Israeli Navy is preparing to receive INS Drakon, the country’s sixth submarine and one of the most advanced vessels of its kind, as military officials warn that Israel must rapidly expand its maritime capabilities to confront threats stretching from Iran and the Houthis to Turkey and vulnerable infrastructure beneath the Mediterranean.
The submarine departed Germany on September 1 and is due to dock at Haifa Port on Wednesday ahead of an official reception ceremony Thursday.
Drakon’s arrival is not merely another step in expanding the fleet. Navy officials see it as part of a broader transformation of Israel’s maritime force following the October 7 attack and amid sweeping changes across the region’s seas and strategic waterways.
Those challenges include the confrontation between the United States and Iran around the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi control over the southern reaches of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and potential future maritime tensions involving Turkey and other regional powers.
The stakes are especially high for Israel because 98% of its trade arrives by sea. Israel sits at a strategic crossroads connecting East and West, making open shipping lanes a critical national economic and security interest.
Turkey’s growing maritime power
A senior Israeli security official said Turkey’s naval buildup is rooted in its “Blue Homeland” doctrine, which places control of surrounding maritime areas at the center of Ankara’s strategic thinking.
Turkey has expanded its maritime presence in recent years and is considered a major regional naval power, backed by a domestic defense industry that gives it considerable independence in producing and arming vessels.
Turkey currently operates 12 submarines and plans to add another six in the coming years, according to Israeli security officials.
Alongside the buildup and the need to defend strategic assets above the water, including ports and offshore energy platforms, Israel is increasingly concerned about assets below the surface, particularly communications cables laid along the seabed.
Senior security officials say countries are developing capabilities to locate and damage such infrastructure in different parts of the world.
“The Russians, for example, cut underwater lines and operate using various methods,” one senior security official said.
The official said robotic systems are being developed that can operate at great depths and sever communications cables, potentially causing major economic, security and strategic damage.
No Israeli communications cable has so far been damaged, officials said, but they described previous activity in the eastern Mediterranean that raised concern.
“Several years ago, we saw surveillance and attempts by various actors to monitor and locate Israel’s cables in the eastern Mediterranean,” one security official said.
‘A distinctly Israeli interest’
The Houthis’ activity around the Bab al-Mandab Strait has further sharpened Israeli concerns over freedom of navigation.
A senior security official said the Yemeni terrorists’ control over the southern part of the strait has harmed freedom of navigation and could encourage both states and terrorist organizations to consider maritime pressure against Israel.
“The issue of Bab al-Mandab and freedom of navigation in the Red Sea is a distinctly Israeli interest,” the official said. “Beyond that, it gives both countries and terrorist organizations an appetite to try, for their own interests, to impose a naval blockade on Israel. If you do not respond to this, you create the understanding that such incidents will simply be tolerated or absorbed.”
Officials say a blockade need not involve conventional warfare.
“A blockade on Israel, even a partial one, can be created not only through military means but also through civilian actions such as flotillas,” the official said. “For example, in the latest flotilla that was stopped in Crete, some of the vessels tried to block a ship that was on its way to Israel.”
“The entire issue of the straits began with Bab al-Mandab, continued to the Strait of Hormuz and now everyone is talking about the maritime arena.”
The official said Israel’s response, particularly against the Houthis, should include building maritime coalitions and strengthening cooperation with countries such as Greece and Cyprus, which are also affected by disruptions around Bab al-Mandab.
Navy says it must grow
The IDF is closely monitoring naval developments in neighboring countries, with Turkey considered the most significant but Egypt also receiving close attention.
Security officials say the Israeli Navy will have to expand because its current force remains relatively small compared with the changes taking place around it.
That process takes years. Drakon itself was ordered about 14 years ago. Even after reaching Israel, it is expected to require roughly two months of work to install complex Israeli systems before becoming operational.
New Navy commander Maj. Gen. Eyal Harel has made force buildup a central focus of his tenure and is seeking to expand the fleet, its capabilities and its role in future rounds of fighting.
Security officials say there is currently an asymmetry between Israel’s fleet and neighboring navies, though they argue there is still enough time to make the necessary adjustments.
“There is currently an asymmetry between the Israeli fleet and those around it, but there are capabilities and enough time to make the adjustments needed for the Navy to develop accordingly,” security officials said.
Navy officials distinguish between two key concepts that have gained importance during recent operations, particularly against Iran.
The first is “maritime superiority,” comparable to air superiority, meaning the ability to dominate a defined maritime area for a limited period, impose a tight naval blockade and strike targets within it.
The second is “sea control,” which allows military forces to operate effectively in a given maritime space without completely denying the enemy the ability to act or fire from it.
Officials describe Israel’s current position against Yemen as sea control rather than full maritime superiority.
“At the moment, the Navy is providing an answer to the threats, but if nothing is done, a growing gap will open between Israel’s capabilities and those of the enemy,” one security official said.
Israeli officials also point to U.S. activity around the Strait of Hormuz as an example of the economic power of maritime operations.
“The American operation in the Strait of Hormuz has enormous economic consequences for the Iranians, and every indicator shows that the worsening economic pressure is working,” officials said. “It will take them a long time to recover from something like this.”
They added: “Israel will have to develop capabilities to operate as a significant arm in the next campaign against Iran. Those changes are already underway.”
A new maritime doctrine
As part of the Navy’s transformation, Harel established a special team in May bringing together military personnel, economic researchers and civilian experts to formulate a new maritime security doctrine.
The effort reflects the Navy’s view that maritime security and national economic interests are closely linked, particularly when it comes to keeping shipping lanes open.
The team is expected to submit its conclusions to the IDF chief of staff by the end of the year.
The main changes under discussion include building a stronger intelligence infrastructure, increasing the size of the force, expanding covert capabilities, introducing autonomous vessels and developing more international partnerships.
“We have operated in very distant places where Israel had never operated before until recently,” one military official said. “We remained off enemy shores for extended periods without being detected, sometimes for many weeks, with capabilities operating very close to enemy areas.”
The official said Israel is also assisting U.S. operations around the Strait of Hormuz with intelligence and analysis.
“When it comes to Hormuz, Israel helps with analysis and intelligence because a great power like the United States can have difficulty carrying out precise operations quickly and in a focused way when the target’s window of opportunity is critical,” the official said. “Israel can close fire loops very quickly.”
Israel’s submarine fleet
Since October 7, Israeli submarines have logged about 10,000 hours at sea annually, according to security officials, meaning that at least two submarines are deployed at sea at any given time.
Officials say Shayetet 7, the Israeli Navy’s submarine flotilla, has operated in four new theaters where Israel had never previously deployed submarines.
The vessels carry out intelligence-gathering and strike missions, including operations against the Houthis in the Red Sea, where crews must navigate narrow waterways and areas with limited depth.
“In some cases the submarines dived in areas where, because of the difficult navigation, even a small deviation could cause damage or a collision with an underwater mountain,” one security official said.
Preparations for Drakon’s arrival were themselves accompanied by delays and diplomatic obstacles.
At one stage, Norway and Denmark barred the submarine from operating in their territorial waters for training and testing, according to a senior Israeli military official, even though it was sailing under the German flag.
“That caused a delay of several months in the preparations,” the official said. “The Navy also had to deal with embargoes and boycotts by various countries because of the war.”
Israeli and German crews ultimately conducted training in waters between Sweden and Denmark.
Drakon will become the Navy’s sixth submarine and its third Dolphin AIP-class vessel.
The AIP, or air-independent propulsion, system uses oxygen and hydrogen to generate power and recharge batteries during prolonged underwater operations without requiring the submarine to surface or draw outside air, allowing it to remain submerged and concealed for longer periods.
The submarine is more than 70 meters long and around 30% larger than Israel’s original Dolphin-class submarines. Less than one-fifth of its full size is visible above the waterline.
Its arrival completes the second generation of Israeli submarines built in Germany and reflects the countries’ long-standing defense partnership.
The journey from Germany to Israel covers roughly 4,000 nautical miles, or about 8,000 kilometers, and takes around a month through the Atlantic Ocean, the Strait of Gibraltar and the Mediterranean.
Construction took more than 12 years, followed by months of testing and preparations in close cooperation between the Israeli Navy and German naval and government authorities.
Israel’s involvement in the project has lasted roughly two decades, with a permanent team of Navy officers and engineers working in Germany alongside their families.
For Israeli naval planners, Drakon’s arrival is not the end of that process but the beginning of the next one: building a force capable of protecting Israel’s sea lanes, strategic infrastructure and long-range reach as the maritime arena becomes increasingly central to the country’s security.

UK arms broker jailed for 16 years over missiles and fighter jet deals with Libya and Sudan
A British arms broker who arranged illegal deals to supply ex-Soviet surface-to-air missile systems to South Sudan and fighter jets to Libya during its civil war was on Wednesday jailed in a London court for 16 years.
David Greenhalgh, 68, was convicted in June of 10 counts of involvement in the unlicensed supply of arms, also including AK-47 rifles, battle tanks and hundreds of thousands of rounds of ammunition, between 2009 and 2016.
Greek national Christos Farmakis, 48, was convicted of nine offences, though he was tried in his absence and his current whereabouts is unknown.
Judge Sally-Ann Hales sentenced both men to 16 years' imprisonment, saying they repeatedly sought to breach arms export bans to sell weaponry for significant profits.
Prosecutors said only one charge involved the actual supply of weaponry, with the pair selling a former Ukrainian S-125 Pechora missile system to South Sudan, where Greenhalgh and Farmakis had "very close connections to senior figures."
South Sudan was still formally part of Sudan until it achieved independence in 2011, prosecutor Edmund Burge told jurors at Southwark Crown Court, meaning the semi-autonomous region was subject to a British arms embargo.
Greenhalgh and Farmakis also arranged to supply weapons to Iran, Iraq and Syria in breach of arms embargoes, before Farmakis was arrested in 2016.
Farmakis was caught after using his email address for his job at the government-funded Greater London Enterprise to privately arrange arms deals.
Burge said Farmakis' email account forwarded an email to his boss, which led to the authorities discovering documents relating to plans to sell fighter jets and other arms to Libya in the wake of the 2011 Arab Spring.

Pope Leo XIV to trace back French ancestry, spiritual roots on visit to France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:02:44 UTC
00:02:44 KST

Pope Leo XIV to trace back French ancestry, spiritual roots on visit to France
Pope Leo’s four-day visit to France, which kicks off on Friday, is something of a homecoming for the Chicago-born pontiff, a grandson of European immigrants with family roots in Normandy. His spiritual roots in French Catholicism run deeper still.
The first American pope arrives in Paris on Friday for the start of a four-day trip to France that will feature popemobile parades, an open-air Mass on the Champs-Élysées and a visit to the Sanctuary of Lourdes.
The trip – the first papal state visit since 2008 – is being labelled in France as a homecoming for the Chicago-born pontiff, more than a century after his grandmother left her native Normandy to build a life in the US – and eight decades after his father took part in the D-Day landings.
It will include a visit to Metz in eastern Lorraine, the home region of a 17th-century monk Leo XIV has described as a spiritual mentor, where he will plead for peace in Europe and meet with other faith leaders.
Read morePope Leo to visit a secular France at odds with Catholic views on abortion, euthanasia
“Leo – Robert Prevost before his election as pope – has French connections on both sides of his family tree,” says Christopher White, associate director at Georgetown University’s Initiative on Catholic Social Thought and Public Life, and the author of “Pope Leo XIV: Inside the Conclave and the Dawn of a New Papacy”.
“His surname comes from his French great-grandmother on his father’s side, who was born in Normandy,” adds White. “On his mother’s side, he has both French Canadian and French Caribbean lineage.”
The Pope is, in fact, 40 percent French, according to the genealogy website Geneanet.
“From a genealogical point of view, he is predominantly French,” the website adds. “His roots, on both his father’s and mother’s sides, can indeed be traced back to France.”
Norman origins
A French birth certificate drawn up in Le Havre states that Leo’s grandmother Suzanne Louise Marie Fontaine was born on February 2, 1894, the daughter of Ernest Auguste Fontaine, a pastry chef’s assistant, and Jeanne Eugénie Prévost.
Suzanne emigrated to the United States in 1915, during World War I, bound for New York. Shortly after her arrival, she fell in love with a Sicilian man who was already married – he too had recently arrived in America – named Salvatore Riggitano.
The couple had two sons, but they were unable to take their father’s surname owing to their illegitimate status. Instead, they were named after their maternal grandmother: Prevost.
One of the two boys, Louis Marius Prevost, born in 1920, was the father of the future pope. He served in the US Navy during World War II, returning to his ancestors’ Normandy coast during the D-Day landings in June 1944. He also took part in the Provence landings a few weeks later and had attained the rank of lieutenant by the end of the war.
A generation after Suzanne’s arrival in the US, French was still spoken within the family. The future pope’s uncle, Jean Prévost, taught the language and published a study on Dandyism in France between 1817 and 1839. However, this French culture was not passed on to the following generation.
“The pope’s French is quite poor, even though he is now actively studying the language,” notes Martin Dumont, secretary-general of the Research Institute for the Study of Religions (Irer), part of Sorbonne University in Paris.
White says Leo XIV has shown great interest in his family history since becoming pope.
“At a lunch at the Vatican a few days after his election as pope, he said to the French publisher Marc Leboucher (co-author of a biography of the pope): ‘You'll be able to tell me about my grandfather's origins!’ And then several months later, he met with American historian Robert Louis Gates to better understand his genealogy,” he says.
A rare visitor
Despite this growing interest, the 71-year-old Pope has seldom visited his grandmother’s native country.
“He visited Lourdes twice on pilgrimage: at the age of 19, when he was a student, and again aged 29, when he was a very young priest,” says Dumont, who is publishing a book on two centuries of papal discourse about France, under the French title “La France dans la pensée des papes” (Papal thoughts and views on France).
One of the most visited Catholic shrines in the world, the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes will host the pontiff on Saturday and Sunday. The hallowed site holds “a special place in the hearts of all popes”, says Dumont.
“The faithful come here seeking peace and consolation. There is an element of popular piety that is of paramount importance to Leo XIV,” he explains. “It is true that the pope could have returned on other occasions, but geographical distance got in the way.”
Read morePope Leo to meet clergy abuse victims during upcoming France visit
Robert Prevost was ordained a priest in the Order of Saint Augustine in 1982 in Rome, but he did not remain in Europe for long. He worked for over 20 years as a missionary in Peru, where he obtained citizenship. It was only during his predecessor’s pontificate that he had the opportunity to return to France.
“In 2023, Pope Francis appointed him as prefect of the Dicastery of Bishops, responsible for episcopal appointments worldwide,” says Dumont. “It was in this capacity that he accompanied Francis to Marseille in 2023 and to Corsica the following year.”
Leo's bedside reading
While Leo’s family links with France are ultimately tenuous, the French historian argues that the pope’s spiritual ties with French Catholic figures run much deeper.
Shortly after his election in May of last year, the 267th pontiff sent a letter to the bishops of France to mark the centenary of the canonisation of saints Jean Eudes, Jean-Marie Vianney and Sister Thérèse of the Child Jesus. Its aim, says Dumont, was to encourage French Catholics to delve into their religious history and find inspiration for “a new missionary impetus”.
“These French saints speak to the current pope, who was himself a missionary for over 20 years,” he explains.
During his stay in Paris, Leo will follow in the footsteps of one of his spiritual mentors, the 17th-century French monk Lawrence (Laurent) of the Resurrection, whose book “The Practice of the Presence of God” he recently described as his bedside reading.
Originally from Lorraine in eastern France, Brother Lawrence lived in the Carmelite monastery where the Catholic Institute of Paris now stands, and which the pope is due to visit on Saturday. His writings invite Christians to “think of God regularly in their daily life and entrust everything to Him,” says Dumont.
Though largely forgotten in France, the Carmelite friar has long been popular among worshipers in Britain and the United States, where his writings are bestsellers. The pope has described their message as “a type of spirituality where one simply gives his life to the Lord and allows the Lord to lead”.
In Leo’s case, the path has led all the way to the Holy See – and now back to his grandmother’s homeland.
We do not know whether Suzanne Fontaine, who died in Detroit in 1979 at the age of 85, ever returned to France. Her obituary, published in the press, described her as “a loving grandmother” to her three grandchildren: Louis, John and Robert, the future pope.

‘School reopening ceremony’ added to Iran’s national intangible heritage list
TEHRAN - Iran has officially registered the traditional ceremony marking the reopening of schools as part of the country’s national intangible cultural heritage, the minister of cultural heritage, tourism and handicrafts said on Wednesday.
Seyyed Reza Salehi-Amiri said the ceremony was registered to recognize the role of schools in shaping the historical memory and cultural identity of generations of Iranians.

He made the remarks during a ceremony marking the beginning of the 2026-2027 academic year at Shahid Behzadi Elementary School in Tehran, where a registration plaque was unveiled as well.
The event was attended by First Vice President Mohammad-Reza Aref, Education Minister Alireza Kazemi, Tehran Governor-General Mohammad-Sadeq Motamedian and other officials.
Salehi-Amiri said the school is more than a place for formal education and represents a shared experience that has contributed to the formation of individual and social identities across generations.
“Alongside studying, we should learn from Iran,” he said, urging students to recognize the historical foundations on which the country has been built and preserved by successive generations.
The minister noted that many prominent figures and officials attending the ceremony had once sat in classrooms and behind school desks themselves.
Salehi-Amiri said the national registration of the ceremony reflects the importance of preserving customs and rituals shared by successive generations, describing them as an integral part of Iran’s intangible cultural heritage and cultural identity.

Are We Failing the Youth? A Young Professors Late Reckoning With AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:02:11 UTC
00:02:11 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
I’m a professor who is banning AI in my classroom this semester.
A note of mine recently got a lot more attention than expected. It was a regular Tuesday. I’d been reading some excellent work in the Atlantic by Rose Horowitch warning us that ‘the end of reading is here’. I decided that enough was enough. I needed my classrooms, especially my first year classrooms, to be tech-free.
Allowing the internet to hold me accountable, I told the world that my courses would be changing this semester. The responses and level of engagement surprised me
I started teaching full-time at university level in Fall of 2025. I had just defended my PhD, and I wasn’t at all prepared for the effects of AI on my students’ learning.
When Chat GPT burst onto the scene in late 2022, I was on my fellowship year at Columbia, which meant that I did not teach and received a stipend to support myself while writing my PhD. I vaguely remember panic in what’s app groups from fellow grad students who were not in their fellowship year, who were TA’s (‘teaching assistants’) when Gen AI first became mainstream.
Aside from that, I lived in blissful ignorance. As someone who loves learning, it was a wonderful year for me. I spent most of my days in a library reading and writing, or in a swimming pool swimming and thinking. It’s also the year I met my now husband.
In my bliss, I ignored the panic, in part because I was free to think and write without teaching responsibilities, in part because I was engrossed in my dissertation, in part because I wrongly assumed the panic was exaggerated, that this would all ‘blow over’.
The following years that I served as a teaching assistant, and then primary instructor, at Columbia, I continued to bury my head in the sand. I have always been a lover of books and learning, and I had no interest in the technology.
But more deeply than that, if I’m being honest, I was already exhausted and burnt out trying to get my own PhD written (there are many privileges that come with getting a PhD, and there are many stressors too). I was teaching, finishing up a PhD, and on the job market, sending out far too many applications than should be necessary in the hopes of securing a job to pay my rent and feed myself come graduation.
Was it really on me, in this moment, I thought to myself, a burnt out PhD student, to save the youth from AI and its harms?
Graduate school took a toll on my mental health. Especially in those final years. So, as someone who had finished secondary school (that’s Irish-English for high school) at a time when we used pen and paper for everything, I happily ignored AI right up until I graduated from Columbia with my PhD.
At 17 and 18, I had mountains of notes, ideas, lessons, and thoughts, physically written down and stored away in different parts of my desk. Obviously, it took me hours and hours to write these kinds of notes, but I was studious, loved learning, and took pride in how colourful and organised my notes were.
I had virtually no tech distractions (sure, there was Facebook or whatever, but I was lucky enough to have real friends, who I would spend real time with, and my phone was a block with nothing much on it). I was happy to be tech free.
Moreover, the kind of cognitive and physical labour that was required of me to take these kinds of notes, also meant that these thoughts, ideas, and lessons were not just stored on paper, they were stored away in my brain, which was being appropriately exercised for the kind of cognitive development that an 18 year old brain requires.
In college, I had a laptop —though nothing too fancy — but I would only really use it to write papers. By the time I got to grad school, my laptop got a little fancier (I invested in a Mac) but frankly, I was so immersed in pen and paper, books, and of course, the internet, for most of my life, that when AI came on the scene, it never even entered my mind to use it. In fact, I barely looked at the technology until 2025.
I realise now that my lack of temptation to use AI was an enormous privilege. To be so disinterested in a technology that promised to make my life, thinking, and work more ‘productive’, ‘efficient’, and whatever other lies are sold to us today, reflected decades of dedication from teachers, professors, and parents, to my education and learning.
In my first year as a full professor, I was still tired from graduate school, and didn’t really know how to handle AI use in my classroom. On one side, I would hear people claim that I was not preparing my students for the real world if I banned AI use, a line I was fiercely sceptical of, but figured I should test; on the other side, even when I was banning AI use, I didn’t see the point in policing it in the name of ‘education’.
I was also settling into my first ‘real job’ as people like to say of newly minted PhDs (good one, I’d had several jobs for the past 7 years of my PhD program). Because I already had a lot on my plate. I decided to ban AI in my classrooms, but I was explicit with students that I wouldn’t waste my time policing their use of AI.
As a young professor, I am subject to at least some of the same stressors as my students: a terrible economy, unstable work, the pressure to excel, etc.
Two things happened in 2025. I came on Substack in November and started writing about AI, not in an educational capacity but as it relates to the philosophy of mind and questions of consciousness. I also witnessed troubling patterns in student assignments (the same idea magically appearing in ten different papers, suspiciously well written objections to an argument, that kind of thing).
Moreover, I witnessed push back when I expressed scepticism towards using AI in my own writing. ‘This article could do with a good AI edit’, something to this effect was a comment I received on an early Substack piece. That really stopped me in my tracks.
Is that really what we are focused on today? A good AI-edit?
With all of this going on, and as I wrote more on AI, I began experimenting with the technology myself. I wanted to experience what this technology would do to my brain, how it might change my behaviours, or my thinking, and whether it was in fact true that I was doing a disservice to my students in banning its use in the classroom.
After a year of engaging with this technology, I cannot say I was impressed with the results—and before anyone comes at me in comments, when I say ‘AI’, yes, I mean corporate LLMs, and when I speak to the effects of these corporate LLMs in my own life, yes, I am aware that there are other ways to use the models (that I could, if I wanted to, work to integrate them into my workflow in helpful ways, etc).
My experimentation with this technology was not to figure out how to incorporate it into my workflow in effective ways (I won’t be doing that in any serious way, sorry).
It was to see what happens when you engage with this technology the way the overwhelming majority of people are being told to engage with it (open a chat bot, ask it to help you in a variety of ways, try to prevent it from making bad decisions for you by writing instructions for it, etc).
It was to see what happens when you advertently or inadvertently outsource decision making to it, outsource judgement to it, or give it an inchoate idea and try to expand on it with an LLM instead of with other books, people, and your own imagination.
There is much I could say here, but overall I found its effects were overwhelmingly negative. I noticed my memory foundered on topics that I engaged with LLMs on, far more than on topics that I didn’t. I found it to be so bad at producing good judgement or decision making that I would use up more of my time managing the poor judgements of the machine than actually getting to develop my own good judgement.
I found its ‘ability’ to help form inchoate ideas into richer ones to be poor. I cannot think of a single time that engaging with an LLM on an idea lead to anything other than dead ends and wasted time, something that rarely happens when I follow my own intuitions and creativity in thinking through ideas and projects.
(and yes, for those of you in business, this issue is surely happening whole scale for you too — you can talk to me about this if you like).
I am one year out of graduate school with a one year contract to teach this coming fall, and no promise of a paid income after that.
I am 32 years old since August. That makes me just 14 years older than the 18 year olds who have grown up in a world where LLMs are saturating every aspect of their education. I have no idea what I would have done at 18, if I lived in their world.
I’ve heard from several young people that professors are often critical of them, and consider them ‘lazy’ in their attitudes towards learning and AI.
I find it disappointing that the burden seems to be falling on 32 year old me — who in the grand scheme of things, still feels pretty young, dumb & broke— to step up and turn my 1 year teaching contract into a space where I can facilitate people born just 14 years before me, getting a real education.
I want to be clear, I am not suggesting I am a martyr, that I am the only professor doing this —the amazing support and comments I’ve seen on this note of mine shows me I am far from alone — or even necessarily, that younger professors are feeling the brunt of this issue, more than established professors.
Rather, I am telling my own story in the hopes of highlighting how the education system is failing students and professors alike, albeit with different consequences for each of us. Because what would benefit students more, universities investing in AI, or universities giving contingent professors permanent jobs?
And what would help students more, believing that the system is stacked against them, and that it is all too easy to outsource their education to AI —an education that is increasingly reduced to the pressure of good grades, and preparing them for a job — or believing that our students are ‘lazy’?
It is a convenient myth to believe that 18 year me, or any other 18 year old born in the 60s, 70s, or 80’s, would not have been tempted or allured into using AI had they been born into the social and economic environment that today’s youth have been born into. Our students do not need universities to invest in AI. They need universities to invest in professors. And our students do not need professors to be judging them for their AI use. They need their professors to create the conditions in which students today can get the kind of education that older generations were lucky enough to get.

30 Sasanian silver coins restored in Isfahan workshop

30 Sasanian silver coins restored in Isfahan workshop
TEHRAN - Thirty silver coins dating to the Sasanian period have undergone specialized conservation and restoration at the restoration workshop of the Cultural Heritage Department in Iran’s central Isfahan province, the provincial heritage chief has said.
On Wednesday, Amir Karamzadeh said the coins were transferred to the provincial cultural heritage restoration workshop over the past two months, where each piece was separately examined and subjected to conservation and restoration measures based on its material condition and degree of deterioration.
“The first step in dealing with these objects was to examine the condition of each coin and assess its conservation needs,” Karamzadeh said.
“Historical metal objects exposed to environmental factors over long periods do not suffer from identical types or degrees of damage, so a single treatment cannot be applied to all of them.”
The restoration process included documentation, controlled cleaning, removal of surface deposits and contaminants, and stabilization of the coins’ conservation conditions.
Karamzadeh stressed that the purpose of restoration was not simply to improve the appearance of the coins, but to protect their historical material, control deterioration and preserve their research value.
He also emphasized the importance of documenting historical objects before conservation work begins. Each coin was therefore assessed individually, with its existing condition recorded before appropriate treatment was carried out.
Sasanian coins are regarded as important sources for the study of the history and archaeology of the Sasanian Empire, which ruled much of the Iranian plateau and neighboring territories from 224 to 651 CE. The empire was centered in what is now Iran and Iraq, with its capital at Ctesiphon, near present-day Baghdad.
The Sasanians issued large quantities of silver coins, particularly drachms, which are among the most important primary sources for studying the empire’s monetary and economic history. Their inscriptions, royal portraits and mint marks can also provide information about political authority, artistic traditions and the organization of coin production.
According to Karamzadeh, preserving such objects is particularly important because further damage to their structure or the loss of identifiable features could reduce their documentary and research value.
He said conservation work should control deterioration while preserving, as far as possible, the historical and artistic characteristics of an object and ensuring suitable conditions for its long-term study and storage.
The Sasanian Empire emerged in 224 CE when Ardashir I, a descendant of the Zoroastrian priest Sasan, overthrew the Parthian ruler Ardavan IV. The dynasty remained in power for roughly four centuries until the defeat of its last ruler, Yazdgird III, in 651.
The empire’s economy was largely agrarian, while long-distance trade also played an important role. Sasanian exports included textiles, carpets, leather goods and Persian Gulf pearls, while goods transported from China and India passed through Sasanian territories and were subject to customs duties.
Karamzadeh said conservation activities at the Isfahan workshop have continued throughout the current Iranian year. Since the beginning of the year, 55 historical objects made of pottery, metal and stone have undergone specialized conservation and restoration at the facility.
The restored Sasanian coins will subsequently be maintained under appropriate conservation conditions to support their long-term preservation and future study.
