West Yorkshire criminals using social media to recruit students as ‘parcel mules’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:01:09 UTC
00:01:09 KST

Students are being recruited by criminals to transfer illegal packages containing illegal drugs, prohibited weapons, stolen goods and dirty cash, say police in West Yorkshire.
Organised criminals are using social media platforms including Snapchat, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook to recruit people to help them move illicit goods, particularly targeting students and vulnerable adults.
They offer cash to “parcel mules” to accept criminal packages in what West Yorkshire police has described as a new trend, which could see those not otherwise involved in crime landed with a criminal record.
Parents are being warned to speak to their university age children and advise them against becoming involved with the gangs moving criminal property around West Yorkshire.
The social media adverts typically contain phrases such as “Work from home”, “Easy money”, “No experience needed” and “Earn £100-£500 per week”.
Police are warning that the suspect packages could contain anything from illegal drugs to offensive weapons, as well as stolen goods, counterfeit items or fraudulently purchased products. Some may also contain criminal cash obtained through illegal activities.
Officers have warned that not knowing what is in a parcel may not always protect those handling it from criminal investigation, and ultimately receiving a criminal record.
Depending on what the parcel contains, they may face charges for anything from possession of controlled drugs or prohibited weapons to handling stolen goods or money laundering. Anyone receiving the parcels may also find themselves charged with conspiracy offences.
Officers have said that warning signs to look out for include being offered money simply for accepting deliveries, being asked to use your address without being told why, someone using multiple names or addresses, or being asked to accept a parcel but not being told what is inside it.
Police have also said to be wary of anyone saying “don’t worry it’s legal” without further explanation, anyone pressuring the recipient into making a decision, or saying they want to collect the parcels quickly after delivery.
Officers have said that criminals may talk their victims into accepting packages by saying things such as “it’s just because I’m not home during the day,” or “you’re not doing anything wrong,” or “nobody will ever know.”.
West Yorkshire police Ch Insp Michelle Swift said: “What may seem like an easy favour or a way to get quick cash could leave you facing a police investigation and a criminal record.
“Criminals will often use social media like SnapChat, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook to recruit people to help them.
“If something doesn’t feel right, trust your instincts and report it to us.
“We hope by raising awareness of this type of crime, people will be alert to the risks and tactics used by organised criminals.
“We would particularly encourage parents to have this conversation with their university age children to make them understand this type of trend and the dangers that are associated with it.”
Earlier this year, Lincolnshire police issued a similar warning, advising people to beware of “anyone offering money or favours for accepting deliveries,” as well as parcels arriving addressed to unfamiliar names, and packages arriving from overseas with no clear sender.
The force warned that in some cases, individuals and addresses were being used without their consent, as part of organised fraud or delivery scams.
Anyone who suspects they may have been recruited as a parcel mule is advised to stop involvement immediately, keep messages, emails or screenshots and report their concerns to the police.
Anyone who has received a parcel not addressed to them is advised not to open it, and to contact the delivery company to arrange return or collection.

Bats originated in Europe, rewriting mammals’ family tree, study reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:00:52 UTC
00:00:52 KST

In the northern forests of the Congo-Brazzaville, as the sun slips away, a distinctive honking fills the dusky sky. Every evening, thousands of hammer-headed fruit bats depart their daytime roosts in search of mates, calling out through large, box-shaped snouts that give the flying mammals the appearance of a winged moose. Here, along the Congo River, scientists have been collecting DNA swabs and tissue samples from the bats for years, working deep into the night in spacesuit-like protective gear.
Those hard-won samples are now among the thousands of specimens gathered from bats across the world that have helped to reshape what we know about the bat family tree.
In a landmark study published today in the journal Nature, a team of more than 130 international researchers combed through ancient bat fossils and genomic data from living species to establish that bats likely originated in Europe about 65m years ago – not in Africa, Asia or North America, as had previously been thought.
Rather, it seems that the earliest ancestors of modern bats dispersed from Europe into Africa, then expanded onwards to Asia, the Americas and Australia. The findings also reveal that echolocation, like flight, also evolved near the dawn of bat evolution.
“Bats, on a scale of amazing to amazing, they’re super amazing,” said Sarah Olson, one of the study’s authors and director of health research at the nonprofit Wildlife Conservation Society. “It’s fun to have part of that puzzle piece in the block, and then we can keep finding and adding other puzzle pieces to it now.”
The work is part of a larger global effort known as Bat1K, launched in 2017, which seeks to sequence the genomes of all the living 1,500 bat species – the second most diverse mammal species in the world, and accounting for one-fifth of all mammals. Genomes are an organism’s complete set of genetic constructions, containing all the DNA needed to build, grow and live.
The Nature study ultimately drew on 103 bat genomes from 21 bat families, alongside 44 fossil bats – mostly their teeth – unearthed across the globe.
Olson said their findings lay the groundwork for better understanding bat physiology and, critically, how the mammals have evolved to be so resistant to disease. Bats are often identified as reservoirs of fatal zoonotic viruses, including Ebola, Nipah and Marburg – but the bats don’t get sick themselves.
“How are they living with these viruses that, when they get into us, they cause so much damage?” Olson said. “What we have now is a kind-of code book of life.”
A 2025 study based on the Bat1K genomic work found that early bat ancestors seemed to have excessive immune gene adaptations. “We showed for the first time that these adaptations associated with viral tolerance and disease resistance probably evolved at the same time that all bats evolved,” said the evolutionary biologist Ariadna Morales, who worked on both studies.
Bats are also unique among mammals in that they live exceptionally long for their size, showing few signs of ageing or cancers. Now, scientists say they will be able to investigate the genes driving those traits. What they learn could be a gamechanger for research into human ageing, immunity and disease resistance.
“With the genetic information that we can find in bats, it could be used to develop therapeutics associated with zoonotic disease. And they could also be models to develop treatments for cancer,” Morales said.
Olson added that the research can also strengthen our understanding of “what makes a healthy bat a healthy bat, and what are bats going to be susceptible to?”
About half of the known bat species have unknown or decreasing populations, with 18% of species considered threatened by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature.
Bats are at risk from the climate crisis, habitat loss, and bat persecution and harvesting, said study co-author Liliana Dávalos, a conservation biologist at Stony Brook University in New York. At the same time, bats play an important role in ecosystems, helping to pollinate plants, spread seeds, and keeping insect numbers – particularly mosquitoes, another spreader of disease – in check.
“Unlike most small mammals, all but one bat species have very small litters of one or two pups, so when individuals drop dead from scorching temperatures, or get killed through persecution or harvesting, populations cannot quickly recover their numbers,” Dávalos said.
And while bats have shown resilience to Ebola and Marburg, in Canada and the United States bats have perished by the millions from a fungal pathogen called white nose syndrome, which grows on the skin of hibernating bats.
“This research can help us go back and look at what makes the myotis bat species more susceptible to these fungal diseases,” Olson said. “There may be some interesting findings that other researchers can take from this study … to go back and piece together what’s happening with white nose syndrome.”

My (complicated) relationship with AI: often seductive, occasionally frustrating and always demanding vigilance | Setareh Seyedghorban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:00:52 UTC
00:00:52 KST

I am walking between carriages in search of a cup of tea on a train travelling over 100 miles an hour from Liverpool to London when I see half the people in my carriage in deep conversations with a machine: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini to name a few. I am meant to be on sabbatical, the rare stretch of academic life reserved for slow thinking. Around me, almost nobody is thinking slowly.
This is not limited to a train carriage. Half of the adults surveyed in one US study reported using an AI chatbot, one example of how fast people are entering a relationship with their AI tools, which now receive more of our questions, problems and drafts than our friends and colleagues do.
I am one of them; I research advanced technologies for a living. I sceptically entered this relationship to satisfy my curiosity, and my very first request of ChatGPT was to proofread an email. The second was to plan a four-day holiday, and the third was to compare home loans. I sent that AI-proofread email, took that short holiday, and refinanced our mortgage with a better rate – all based on its advice. The relationship started growing and I started giving it more complicated tasks: summarise an article, collate recent findings on a specific topic and redesign my kitchen. What would have taken hours took only minutes. I trusted nothing and checked every line, as trust in any relationship accrues exchange by exchange. I did not like the kitchen design it produced.
I was not alone; in an experiment published in Science, professionals using AI completed their writing tasks 40% faster and produced writing rated 18% higher in quality. The most interesting finding for me from the experiment sat silently in the middle: inequality between workers decreased.
That hit close to home. English is my second language, and for years I paid copywriters thousands of dollars to proofread and smooth my drafts. These were outsiders with no knowledge of my field or the experience behind my arguments. Now it takes minutes, at any hour of the day, and at a fraction of the cost. For a multilingual academic, it is more than just convenience. It is the levelling of a field that was never level; it is workplace equity.
The relationship is not rosy; at times it is unsettling and frustrating.
The most seductive quality of AI is not its speed to produce lines of code, summarise meetings or synthesise complex patterns. It is its agreeableness and flattery, or what researchers call “sycophancy”, a phenomenon undermining self-correction and responsible decision-making. In a spectacular failure, investor Jason Lemkin watched an AI coding agent on Replit wipe his company’s live database during a code freeze. The agent did apologise for its “catastrophic failure”, using words a genuinely remorseful person would use. In this case, the apology did not restore anything. Replit deployed the fixes and the relationship continued, with caution. Findings from medicine are more concerning. Endoscopists who used AI to detect polyps in colonoscopies saw their detection rate fall six percentage points when they performed the procedure without AI support. Each endoscopist in the study had more than 2,000 colonoscopies behind them; the authors call it deskilling.
In my line of work, editors at one reputable journal looked in their own back yard and found submissions rising and review reports carrying signs of AI writing. They concluded that human judgment is still holding the line, although at the cost of greater effort. They also found researchers writing in a second language, and new entrants to the field, were among the heaviest users. I am one of them, and I know the difference between asking AI to carry my argument into English and asking it to supply one.
AI and its agents are not disappearing, and there is no returning to the world before them. Our relationship with AI only deepens from here. Mine now proofreads and smooths out my writing and acts as my research and personal assistant, but it still does not know what my dream kitchen looks like.
So, where am I landing? Not in a divorce and not in a honeymoon. A real partnership that is sometimes useful and equalising, occasionally tiring, and always demanding vigilance. One thing AI cannot yet do is care; it has no stake in whether I am right. It will argue any side with equal confidence and apologise for any disaster with equal grace. I keep thinking, judging and developing ideas that are and will be stubbornly mine.
Like it or not, we are in a relationship with AI. What we need to ask ourselves is not whether to be in it; it is whether to stay awake inside it or watch our thinking, knowledge and skills decay.

Serious fun time: Making video and board games accessible for all players
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:00:42 UTC
00:00:42 KST

Gamers with visual or motor impairments are increasingly creating their own ways to keep playing as industry giants Microsoft, Sony and ONCE roll out adapted controllers alongside new video and board games.
When it is time to draw a card, Cristian M. Amores does not look at anything: he brings his iPhone up to an NFC tag stuck on the card sleeve and waits for VoiceOver to tell him what he has just drawn. He is blind and, since the end of 2020, has been adapting, card by card, the way he plays "Magic: The Gathering", the collectible card game created by mathematician and PhD Richard Garfield in 1993.
Amores shares the whole process under the name Magic Accesible on social network X, and his case is far from unique: from controllers reprogrammed button by button to board games with raised pieces, accessibility is gaining ground in the industry, although it is still a long way from being a design standard in everything from big-budget video games to after-dinner games.
The Magic deck you read with your phone camera
Amores' first attempt was braille. Using a Dymo-style labeller, he marked each card with a raised number to tell them apart and look up their information in a separate database. It did not work for several reasons: braille takes up space and makes the paper thicker, the deck became too bulky to shuffle easily and, in an official tournament, a marked card can be seen as a signal of one you do or do not want to draw, which automatically leaves you out of the competition.
For that reason he abandoned braille and considered using QR codes, a label that seemed doomed to extinction until the arrival of COVID-19. That QR code was his solution for a while, but it is no longer the one he uses: having to line up the camera without knowing for sure whether it was scanning the card properly made the whole process slower than playing without assistance, so he dropped it too. Now he uses NFC tags, which he only has to bring close to the phone for the screen reader to read out the full card, with no need to aim or wait. "Since then I've made a brutal leap as a player", he sums up.
The project still needs outside help, someone to read any new card aloud to him before he adds it to the database, but it has allowed him to play in shops and at the National Modern Championship (another MTG format) held in Soria in December 2024, where he had his own stand explaining the system. In November 2022, the newspaper "El Mundo" published a feature on his story and, since then, he has been running a podcast with the same name as his social media account, Magic Accesible, in which he interviews other players and developers in the sector.
Amores has not yet played in tournaments with strict rules, only in more informal matches. In Soria, several judges came over to see how the system worked; one of them told him there would probably be no problem in using it in competition.
In another game, a different judge did check the rulebook and confirmed that tournaments ban electronic devices during play except where strictly necessary, an exception Amores believes could apply to him: until a card goes past his phone, he does not know what he has just drawn, and all his cards are marked in the same way. If he ever competes, he says, he will inform the organisers in advance, both because of the adaptations and because he usually needs a little more time per round than the rest.
Asked what single thing he would ask of Wizards of the Coast, the company that publishes "Magic: The Gathering", he does not hesitate: an accessible version of Magic Arena, the official PC client for the game, which would instantly reach blind people everywhere. There is already a community-made mod that achieves this, although, like any unofficial solution, it depends on the company not blocking it or breaking it with an update.
"WotC, let the mod carry on existing", he says plainly, although he admits he himself has not tried it yet. On physical cards he is more sceptical: he imagines cards with a factory-printed QR code that would link to Gatherer, the company's official database, but doubts it would be worth Wizards' while at that scale. "Paper can take anything, but reality cannot", he concludes.
From braille to NFC: the Commander deck a group of friends adapted from scratch
Amores is not the only one to have ended up using NFC tags along similar lines. On Reddit, under the name jerichodarkstar, a group of friends described how they adapted the Commander deck (a format within MtG) of one of them, who had a degenerative visual impairment from birth.
He started playing Commander in 2023, although by then he could only distinguish lands from non-lands by their shape; for everything else he needed someone sitting nearby to read aloud each card he drew. The problem was not only the dependence: as everyone at the table could hear what was in his hand, he played under what the group describe as a permanent telepathy effect that no one else had to deal with.
At Christmas 2025, tired of that disadvantage, they decided to change things. Their first attempt was braille: they embossed, on the outside of each sleeve, never on the card, the name, the mana cost, the type and the power and toughness of the creatures, placing each detail close to where it appears on the original.
The effects were the real problem: the full text of a card will not fit on a single sleeve, so they invented their own system of abbreviations, combined with the contractions already used in braille; "if you read it literally, it sounds like it was written by a caveman", admits jerichodarkstar.
It took them between three and four days to braille the whole deck, but the system did not withstand actual play: after two months, the raised dots were already wearing down, each brailled sleeve ended up double or even four times its normal thickness, shuffling became a nightmare and the deck would not even stay upright in a single pile because of how uneven it was.
They stumbled on the alternative almost by chance. They posted an update on the problem on Reddit, but the post disappeared. The clue came from a comment on the original thread: a user, whom they name with his express permission, told them that the games shop where he played had a blind regular who used NFC tags.
The group started researching and, within days, they had ordered the tags and set up a new system: an NFC tag inside each sleeve, linked via the iPhone Shortcuts app to an individual note containing all the information for that card. When he brings his phone close, the screen reader reads it all through an earbud, without any need to abbreviate and without having to judge the framing.
The difference was drastic: what had taken three or four days with braille could now be done in about three hours per deck. They have been playing like this for almost a year, with four complete 100-card decks in play and two more under construction.
Gloria and Iria: advising publishers from inside and outside disability
In Spain, much of this work is also done by people outside large organisations. Proyecto Glirp (source in Spanish) is run by Gloria and Iria, who began in 2014 with a blog focused on visual impairment, versinlimitesaccesibilidad. Iria has a visual impairment; Gloria handles the technical side and the audiovisual part of the project.
Over the years, board games gradually took over from the rest of the content they published – technology, books, travel – until they became the pair's speciality: they advise publishers and give talks and workshops on cultural accessibility in fields such as tourism and education, and this year they have published their own book, "Jugar sin límites", centred on accessibility in games.
In that book they go over the most common mistakes in table-top design, and, as they explain, they are almost always the same: poor contrast between letters or icons and the background, and a font size which, whether for aesthetic reasons or lack of space, is usually too small.
For Gloria and Iria this is not just a question of sight: "The less effort you have to make to work out what an element says, the faster you will understand it", they explain, so it is also a question of how long it takes any player to grasp what they have in front of them.
As for whether any publisher stands out for solving these problems, they are cautious: they do not see any company that has consistently made these improvements part of its way of working, although they do acknowledge that those specialising in children's games tend to take more care over these details.
The barrier most likely to go unnoticed by people without visual impairment, they say, is not on the board but at the table. Visual impairment has many degrees, from total blindness to significant residual vision, and each player has their own needs; what almost never happens is that anyone asks what assistance they require.
"Many times, the lack of accessibility" in a game can be mitigated simply by speaking or describing what is happening, they point out, without touching a single physical component. A player might not have access to what is on the board, which cards are available or how others are progressing, and it may be enough for the rest of the table to narrate their moves aloud to solve that. They do admit, though, that there are games whose mechanics make even that impossible.
When a publisher approaches them, accessibility is rarely built in from the start. Gloria and Iria describe a sector that is moving forward but without any clear line of continuity: "With some games, more effort is put into making them inclusive and then the next one that comes out can be the complete opposite."
They work with some publishers and authors who consult them during the design process itself, but the more usual scenario is the reverse: they play a title that is already out and, in their review, point out what could be improved and how.
The stage at which they come in does change the outcome. It is not the same to design something inclusive from the outset as it is to add or alter components later on. "If you are just starting to design something" and you already have guidelines or recommendations to improve its accessibility, you avoid having to go back and redo the work to fix certain aspects.
Controllers redesigned piece by piece
Microsoft released its device on 4 September 2018 for 87 euros, developed together with organisations such as AbleGamers, SpecialEffect, the Cerebral Palsy Foundation and the Craig Hospital. Instead of a hand-shaped controller, it is a flat panel with two large buttons, a directional pad and 19 3.5 mm ports plus two USB ports to plug in the switches, joysticks or mounts that many players with reduced mobility already had, and then remap them using an app.
It can be used with a hand, a foot, the chin or the mouth; even the packaging was designed so it could be opened with a finger or with the teeth. In 2025, as part of the Ability Summit, Microsoft added the Xbox Adaptive Joystick, a one-handed controller costing 26 euros that works on its own or as a companion to the Adaptive Controller.
Sony unveiled its answer at CES 2023 under the name Project Leonardo and launched it as the Access Controller on 6 December that year, at 87 euros. It is round, can be used resting on a table or attached to a mount, and has eight buttons and a central joystick, all of which can be swapped for parts of different shapes and sizes depending on each player's strength and range of movement.
It allows up to 30 profiles to be created and two Access Controllers to be synchronised with each other, or one with a standard DualSense, so the inputs from more than one device can be combined. Its weak point, highlighted since launch, is that it does not replicate the touchpad or the motion sensors of the DualSense, which is a drawback in games that depend on them.
Accessibility in video games is no longer a niche
The figures explain why the big manufacturers keep investing in this area. According to the Entertainment Software Association's 2025 annual survey (source in Spanish), 21% of adult players in the United States say they have some form of disability, and nearly half regard it as very important for a game to include accessibility options when choosing what to play.
The World Health Organization (source in Spanish) estimates that more than 1 billion people worldwide, over one in six, have some form of disability (source in Spanish), and Microsoft cited in 2025 a figure of 429 million players with disabilities around the world when presenting its own Xbox tools.
That same year, the ESA, together with Electronic Arts, Google, Microsoft, Nintendo, Sony, Ubisoft and other companies, launched the Accessible Games Initiative (source in Spanish), a common, voluntary labelling system so that a game's shop listing can show at a glance whether it includes adjustable text, large subtitles, narrated menus or remappable controls.
Some titles are already cited as benchmarks: "The Last of Us Part II" added audio description to all its cinematics and an option that turns spoken dialogue into vibrations on the DualSense controller, so that a deaf or hard-of-hearing player can feel the rhythm and emphasis of a line as well as reading it in the subtitles. In Spain, the ONCE Foundation runs a parallel project focused on video games, Ga11y (source in Spanish), which catalogues accessible titles according to the type of disability they address.
When the challenge is telling pieces apart by touch
Beyond home-made fixes, manufacturers and organisations have for years been releasing board games that are accessible straight out of the box. In the United States, Mattel developed UNO Braille with the National Federation of the Blind (source in Spanish), with braille markings on every card and rules downloadable in braille or as an audio narration.
In Spain, ONCE, through its Bibliographic Service and its foundation, has adapted the puzzle "Katamino" with braille pieces and board, the game "Apalabrados" in partnership with Etermax, a domino set with raised tiles, an adapted "Scrabble" and a braille edition of the card game "Virus!", not counting the usual classics: chess and Ludo with raised boards, or Spanish-suited and poker decks labelled in braille.
The same challenge runs through all these adaptations: making the pieces distinguishable by touch, giving boards a tactile dimension and transferring the text on the cards – the hardest part, because it is purely visual – into braille, raised print or, increasingly, a QR code with spoken descriptions so that nobody has to miss out on the game.

Standard brain scans might misread oxygen metabolism in large portions of the cortex
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:00:23 UTC
00:00:23 KST

A small study suggests that the primary method used to map brain activity may often yield reversed metabolic readings. The research reveals that blood oxygen levels do not consistently reflect underlying energy consumption in the brain, challenging standard interpretations of brain imaging. The findings were published in Nature Neuroscience.
Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, is a standard tool for observing the brain in action. When people perform tasks inside an MRI scanner, the machine does not actually see electrical impulses from neurons. Instead, it detects changes in blood oxygen levels across different brain regions.
This measurement is known as the blood-oxygenation-level-dependent signal, or BOLD signal. The conventional interpretation assumes that an increase in the BOLD signal reflects a surge in local brain activity.
Neurons require energy to function, and they obtain this energy by consuming oxygen. Because neurons lack their own energy reserves, active brain areas rely on a rapid influx of fresh, oxygen-rich blood. This physiological process usually supplies more oxygen than the neurons immediately consume, which flushes out deoxygenated blood and creates a positive BOLD signal on the brain scan.
Conversely, a drop in the BOLD signal is typically interpreted as a decrease in brain cell activity. However, anomalies in this relationship occasionally surface in animal research and specialized human brain scans. These anomalies suggest that the link between blood flow and oxygen consumption might not be uniform across the entire brain.
More than two decades ago, scientists developed a theoretical framework to predict how the BOLD signal should behave based on varying levels of blood flow and oxygen consumption. This framework suggested that certain biological conditions could produce a BOLD signal that contradicts the actual energy use of the brain cells. Until now, this theory had not been comprehensively tested across the entire human cerebral cortex.
Researchers Samira M. Epp, Valentin Riedl, and colleagues sought to test whether this standard biological assumption holds true across the entire human brain. They designed a study to directly measure oxygen consumption alongside the standard BOLD signal. Epp is a researcher at the Technical University of Munich and the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg, where Riedl also holds an affiliation.
The investigators conducted a small study involving 40 healthy participants. They asked the volunteers to perform a series of mental exercises while inside an MRI machine. The researchers utilized a specialized imaging protocol called quantitative fMRI. This advanced technique captures the standard BOLD signal while also measuring absolute blood flow, blood volume, and the rate of oxygen extraction from the bloodstream.
The scanning session required participants to engage in an arithmetic calculation task. This specific math task was chosen because prior research shows it reliably stimulates attention-related brain networks while simultaneously suppressing activity in the brain’s default mode network. Participants also completed an autobiographical memory task designed to stimulate the default mode network, as well as a basic visual control task to serve as a baseline.
By comparing the imaging data across these varying mental states, the researchers could track both the BOLD signal and the actual amount of oxygen the brain tissue was metabolizing. To ensure their results were robust, they conducted multiple control analyses. These controls included a replication study with ten participants using matched image resolutions to rule out potential scan distortion artifacts.
The results contradicted the standard biological model in a substantial portion of the brain. When the researchers examined areas showing a positive BOLD signal, they found that the canonical model held true on average. Blood flow increased heavily, supplying an excess of oxygen and generating the expected brain scan signature.
However, the results for areas displaying a negative BOLD signal were unexpected. Based on conventional wisdom, a negative signal should indicate that neurons are resting and metabolizing less oxygen. Instead, the researchers found that oxygen consumption did not decrease in these areas, and in some cases, it actually increased despite the negative BOLD reading.
When examining individual volume units of the brain scan, known as voxels, the discrepancies became even more pronounced. A voxel is a three-dimensional pixel representing a tiny cube of brain tissue. The researchers discovered that in about 40 percent of the voxels displaying a strong BOLD response, the actual oxygen metabolism moved in the opposite direction of the BOLD signal. The team labeled these specific brain units as discordant voxels.
In discordant voxels showing a positive BOLD signal, the brain tissue was actually consuming less oxygen than at rest. In discordant voxels showing a negative BOLD signal, the brain tissue was consuming more oxygen. This means that simply looking at the BOLD signal would lead to a backward interpretation of the underlying cellular energy use in nearly half of the responding brain regions.
The team also identified voxels that exhibited a mixed response. In these areas, the tissue demonstrated a standard, expected blood flow response during one cognitive task but shifted to a discordant response during another task. This flexibility suggests that a single region of the brain can alter its oxygen delivery mechanism depending on the specific cognitive demands of the moment.
The researchers identified two distinct biological mechanisms driving these brain responses. In standard, concordant brain regions, the tissue met its energy needs by triggering an immense increase in local blood flow. This massive rush of blood overcompensates for the oxygen consumed by the neurons, generating the classic positive BOLD signal used in most neuroscience studies.
In discordant regions, the tissue handled its energy needs differently. Instead of relying on a large influx of fresh blood, the neurons simply extracted a higher percentage of oxygen from the blood that was already present in the local capillaries. Because the overall blood flow barely changed, this increased oxygen extraction left a higher concentration of deoxygenated blood in the area.
Deoxygenated blood has magnetic properties that darken the MRI image. As a result, this higher extraction rate caused a negative BOLD signal, even though the neurons were actively working and consuming more energy.
The researchers noticed that these two types of brain tissue function differently even when a person is resting. Discordant regions naturally maintain a lower baseline rate of oxygen extraction. This lower baseline provides them with a built-in reserve of oxygen to draw from when they suddenly need to perform a cognitive task, allowing them to function without demanding a fresh surge of blood from the vascular system.
One limitation of quantitative MRI techniques is that measuring total blood volume can be technically challenging. The method used in the study captures total blood volume rather than strictly venous volume, which can introduce some variation when comparing data between subjects. Additionally, the calculations for oxygen metabolism are primarily validated for the brain’s outer gray matter and are difficult to interpret in the deep white matter.
Readers should not interpret these results as invalidating decades of prior fMRI research. A positive BOLD signal still reliably indicates increased oxygen metabolism on a broad, average scale. However, the exact location and magnitude of that activity may be misinterpreted if scientists rely exclusively on standard BOLD imaging without considering regional differences in blood flow.
Future imaging studies might need to adopt quantitative fMRI methods to accurately map brain function. This approach could be especially relevant for studying aging populations or patients with vascular diseases, where blood flow responses might be altered. Tracking actual oxygen consumption alongside standard imaging provides a more accurate window into how the human brain distributes its energy.
The study, “BOLD signal changes can oppose oxygen metabolism across the human cortex,” was authored by Samira M. Epp, Gabriel Castrillón, Beijia Yuan, Jessica Andrews-Hanna, Christine Preibisch, and Valentin Riedl.

The Second Draft of Yesterday by Kenneth Dhillon
"The Second Draft of Yesterday confronts a building suspended between intention and completion: Herzog and de Meuron's Berlin Modern M20, frozen in construction at the Kulturforum, severing the civic dialogue between Mies van der Rohe's Neue Nationalgalerie and Scharoun's Philharmonie.
"The project asks what an architect's obligation is to an unfinished building, and answers through editorial intervention. Selected structural bays are erased to create civic porosity.
"The retained fabric becomes the ground; the erased voids become civic space. A copper facade records time, and a rotating brick Palimpsest Tower turns the building's logic inward. The pathological becomes propelling."
Student: Kenneth Dhillon
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutor: Alexis Germanos
Email: kennethdhillon[at]outlook.com
Deterritorializing the Railway Station, a Flâneur's Architectural Dream by Anastasia Stachtiari
"Small-to-medium railway stations make up around 80 per cent of the UK's rail network, yet remain underinvested. This thesis addresses this overlooked typology through an ecology of rail travel rooted in Wales.
"Drawing on situationist theory, it develops the concept of rail psychogeography, experienced through the lens of the flâneur, in which the railway journey becomes an experience of drift and discovery.
"The project challenges the present conventional typology, which is driven primarily by operational efficiency, arguing that the urban presence and architectural, social and civic value of small-to-medium railway stations are often underestimated.
"It asks how their components might be reimagined to support unconventional uses of platforms, kinetic crossings and flexible programmes that encourage lingering, wandering and exploration within stations and throughout the rail journey."
Student: Anastasia Stachtiari
Course: Master of Architecture (MArch)
Tutor: Will Judge
Email: anastasia.stachtiari[at]gmail.com
Reviving the People's Floodplain by Catherine Towers
"Located on the Severn Ham floodplain in Tewkesbury, the project proposes a flood-responsive civic and ecological landscape that occupies, rather than resists, seasonal flooding.
"A linear intervention, the Mowing Edge, separates a public commons and water-treatment landscape from restored floodplain meadow and wetland habitats, while functioning as resilient community infrastructure.
"At the threshold between Tewkesbury and the Severn Ham, elevated walkways, floating structures and adaptable public spaces remain accessible throughout changing water levels, supporting ecological restoration, environmental education, year-round recreational uses and flood resilience.
"The proposal reimagines flooding as a civic asset, transforming periods of inundation from disruption into opportunities for occupation, learning and engagement with the historically important landscape."

Learning in the Landscape by Amelia Farman
"Learning in the Landscape reimagines nuclear energy as civic architecture within the Oxford–Cambridge Arc.
"Responding to the rapid growth of artificial intelligence and its escalating energy demands, the project proposes a Centre of Nuclear Learning set within the historic landscape of Stowe.
"Drawing on the tradition of the English landscape garden and the villa as a place of intellectual exchange, the proposal combines research, education and public engagement.
"This thesis challenges the defensive image of nuclear energy, arguing instead for an integrated, culturally grounded masterplan that supports both technological advancement and civic identity."

Finally, a true blue rose exists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

This development could change poetry forever. Roses are red and now they’re also blue.
True blue roses were once thought impossible. Roses can make red and yellow pigments but don’t have an enzyme needed to make blue pigments. At least they didn’t until 2004, when researchers at the Suntory Global Innovation Center in Kyoto, Japan, genetically modified a rose to produce blue pigments. The team inserted the gene for an enzyme that can produce a blue pigment called delphinidin. But those roses were purplish, suggesting it takes more than blue pigment to make flowers blue.
Naturally blue flowers, such as irises, make blue pigments like delphinidin. But they also need almost colorless “co-pigment” molecules called flavone C-glycosides to create their blue hue. Those helper molecules stabilize pigments and make them appear deeper blue. Roses also lack genes for making the co-pigments.
This time, Suntory researchers inserted four genes from other blue flower species into a light pink rose. A gene from Canterbury bells (Campanula medium) allowed the engineered roses to produce multiple blue pigments. Two genes from wishbone flowers (Torenia x hybrida) and one from clustered gentian (Gentiana triflora) made enzymes that produce the colorless helper molecules. The combination of the blue pigment malvidin with a helper called isoorientin made bluer flowers than roses producing only delphinidin, the company announced August 25 at the 32nd International Horticultural Congress in Kyoto. The higher the level of co-pigments in the petals, the bluer the flowers, the researchers found.
Roses making the co-pigments are rated as violet blue based on a flower color chart. The rose bushes continued to produce blue flowers for seven years in greenhouse tests in Japan and three years growing in fields in Colombia.
The achievement is sweet. And the team hopes to further enhance the hue.

Trump’s attacks on media, raised interest rates, and measles deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Trump’s attacks on media, raised interest rates, and measles deaths
Welcome to our press review of events in the United States. Every Wednesday we look at how the Swiss media have reported and reacted to three major stories in the US – in politics, finance and science.
The international media has long struggled to distinguish between the nonsense spouted by US President Donald Trump and his meaningful statements, Le Temps wrote this week. But they are hanging in there, and “as in any democracy, they are continuing to fulfil their mission: to inform”.
Help us improve the press review
As a reader of our weekly press review, your feedback is important to us. Please take two minutes to answer a short survey and help us improve our journalism. This survey is anonymous and all data is confidential.
👉 [Take the surveyExternal link]
The decision by US President Donald Trump to ban several news outlets from the White House reflects the “astonishing drift towards authoritarianism at the highest levels of the American state”, according to one Swiss newspaper.
“CNN, Politico and MS NOW are taking Trump to court,” Swiss public broadcaster RSI reported on Monday, following Trump’s announcement on Friday that he would ban them from the White House for reporting what he deemed fake news. “The three media organisations are seeking to defend their First Amendment rights. […] In support of CNN, the other four American broadcasters that make up the presidential ‘pool’ – CBS, ABC, NBC and Fox News – have decided to cease their coverage.”
But for Le Temps, the solidarity boycott “doesn’t eclipse the astonishing drift towards authoritarianism at the highest levels of the American state – which doesn’t stand to gain much from this either”.
In an analysis on Tuesday, Le Temps wrote that the international media had been “thrown off balance” by Trump and had “long struggled to distinguish between the president’s nonsense and his meaningful statements”. “Willingly or not, faced with the administration’s disdain, public mistrust and a web saturated with misinformation, they are still hanging on. Perhaps the president’s strategy of information overload has triumphed. Perhaps the media could do better. But, at the very least, as in any democracy, they are continuing to fulfil their mission: to inform,” it wrote. “However, the task is becoming increasingly complex.”
The Geneva newspaper noted that a consequence of the ban was that Trump inaugurated the White House’s new helipad on Monday, “shouting into the void – inaudible because no media outlet was there to record his remarks”.
“And this is only the beginning,” it said. “Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday, could take place in an information black hole, with no end in sight. One might take some satisfaction in seeing the biter bit, but while it’s true that the image-obsessed president has little to gain from his decision, neither do the United States. The ‘beacon of the free world’ has fizzled out. No more sound, no more pictures.”
The decision by the US Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate is far more than a monetary policy measure, says Swiss public broadcaster SRF. It’s a “clear commitment to the independence of the institution”.
Kevin Warsh, head of the US central bank since May, “also took the opportunity to clearly distance himself from US President Donald Trump”, SRF said in an analysis.
The Fed raised its key interest rate on September 16 for the first time since summer 2023 owing to persistently high inflation, the Tages-Anzeiger explained. The rate is rising by 0.25 percentage points to between 3.75% and 4.00%.
SRF said that on several occasions Warsh was asked on Wednesday what his message to Trump was with this interest rate rise, given that the president insisted on low interest rates. He was also asked when he had last spoken to Trump. “Warsh laughed off such questions, appearing composed rather than flustered, and explained the actual reasons behind the decision. Namely, that the labour market is stable, that full employment can be said to exist, and that the economy as a whole is robust.”
SRF noted that everything the new Fed chair has done so far has been consistently linked to Trump, “thereby perpetuating the impression that Warsh can’t act independently of the White House”.
SRF concluded that Warsh was therefore “sending a clear signal”. But will it be enough to dispel suspicions of a lack of independence? “It’s quite possible that these suspicions will cling to Warsh like a curse for as long as Donald Trump remains in office.”
The recent announcement of Pennsylvania’s first measles-related deaths in decades has ignited a public feud among politicians and health officials who disagree over the role of the contagious disease in the fatalities, Swiss media reported last week.
Authorities in Pennsylvania confirmed last Tuesday a fourth death linked to measles, Swiss public broadcaster RTS reported. “This is the latest in an outbreak that has reached levels not seen in the country for 35 years.”
All of these deaths occurred among unvaccinated individuals, the local Department of Health said.
Measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000 thanks to vaccination, but it has been making a strong comeback for several years, against a backdrop of falling vaccination rates and growing mistrust of health authorities, RTS said. “Although the vaccine is compulsory in the US, people across much of the country can circumvent the rule by citing religious or even philosophical grounds,” it explained. “These non-medical exemptions have surged since the Covid-19 pandemic and the explosion of vaccine misinformation. Consequently, when measles enters unvaccinated communities, outbreaks can occur.”
Since the start of 2026, more than 3,294 confirmed cases of measles have been recorded in the US (as of September 10), a level not seen since 1991, RTS said. The top three states were Pennsylvania with 637 cases, South Carolina with 670, and Utah with 526.
These deaths have fuelled a heated dispute between Pennsylvania’s Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, and Donald Trump’s health secretary, Robert Kennedy Jr, who is known for his anti-vaccine views, Le Temps wrote last week. “On Tuesday, Shapiro accused Kennedy on X of fuelling unfounded fears about the vaccine and downplaying these deaths.”
According to Shapiro, Kennedy allegedly ordered the country’s leading health agency not to include these four deaths in its figures, “no doubt because they don’t fit with his misleading narrative”.
Le Temps said Kennedy denied these accusations, denouncing what he saw as the “politicisation” of these deaths, some of which he has questioned as to whether they were actually linked to measles.

El Niño could cause 451,000 more heat deaths compared to normal year, group says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:58:48 UTC
23:58:48 KST

El Niño could cause 451,000 more heat-related deaths compared to normal year, group says. Map shows areas at risk.
An estimated 451,000 more people could die as a result of excessive heat in the first nine months of the current El Niño compared with a typical year, according to a report from the University of Chicago's Climate Impact Lab.
"That's on top of the impacts from droughts, wildfires and flooding expected from hotter temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns as this El Niño could become the strongest on record," the research hub said in a news release Wednesday.
Map shows which regions face highest risks
Countries across the Global South are forecast to see the greatest impacts, with Nigeria, Sudan, Niger and Chad expected to record more than 65,000 heat-related deaths combined. The Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, Cambodia and Indonesia are expected to record close to 40,000 deaths collectively, while Brazil and India could also see high death tolls, according to researchers.
The projected global toll "is such a large number that it can be numbing, but it is made up of parents and children, grandparents and neighbors, people going to work, caring for families, and living their lives," Michael Greenstone, a cofounder of the Climate Impact Lab, said in a statement.
El Niño is a climate pattern characterized, in part, by above-average ocean temperatures in a portion of the Pacific Ocean near the equator. It influences extreme weather events across the globe, in different ways and to varying degrees depending on the region. In some places, the onset of El Niño correlates with intense heat, drought and flooding, which can be even harsher when El Niño is particularly powerful, like it is this year.
Meteorologists have warned of the current El Niño's potentially historic consequences since it developed at the start of the summer. The World Meteorological Organization forecast earlier this month that this El Niño could become the strongest on record, with its most severe impacts still ahead.
The U.N. agency predicted the "supersized" phenomenon won't reach its peak intensity until closer to the end of 2026. The U.S.-based Climate Prediction Center expects El Niño will likely remain in place through the Northern Hemisphere's winter season, and possibly last into spring.
Greenstone said the Climate Impact Lab's report "allows decisionmakers to see exactly where emergency actions can be taken to save tens of thousands of lives in the coming months." It can also help humanitarian organizations decide how to allocate emergency funds and other resources. It emphasized that "heat warnings, health outreach to vulnerable populations, cooling centers and hydration stations, worker protections, and expanded health system capacity can all help people cope with extreme heat."

What the too-big-to-fail  Swiss parliament vote means for UBS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:58:45 UTC
23:58:45 KST

What the too-big-to-fail Swiss parliament vote means for UBS
The wrangling over UBS bank has led to a decision in the Swiss Senate. Parliamentarians voted in favour of fairly tough capital requirements.
What did the Swiss Senate decide today?
UBS must be significantly better capitalised than it is at present. UBS is to underpin its foreign subsidiaries with 90% hard capital. This decision came about after months of wrangling. Twenty nine Senators voted in favour of this proposal, with 16 against.
What does this mean?
For UBS, this represents a doubling of its capital buffer. A 45% core capital ratio currently applies to its foreign subsidiaries. It has various options for raising the additional capital. For example, it could issue additional shares, retain profits or downsize its subsidiaries.
Who wins with this outcome?
Finance minister Karin Keller-Sutter is likely to be largely satisfied even though the government’s stricter proposal did not get through. But neither did the significantly weaker alternative proposal recommended by the Economic Affairs Committee of the Senate.
More
How to tame UBS without making the bank toothless
Before the vote, Keller-Sutter told the Senate: “We should not repeat the mistakes that were made in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis.”
She had already described her own 100% capital ratio proposal as a compromise. However, she also asked that Senators support the 90% proposal “if necessary”.
What does UBS have to say about this?
For the bank, the decision is a defeat. In a statementExternal link, the bank said: “This political outcome is not a compromise and does not address the root causes of the Credit Suisse collapse.”
The statement also notes that the bank would have to hold around $15 billion in additional hard capital should the proposal be implemented.
Bank CEO Sergio Ermotti had personally been campaigning against the government’s proposal for months. Most recently, on Tuesday – at the same Swiss Finance Forum as Keller-Sutter – he said that current regulations were strong enough.
He also appealed to people’s emotions: “We are not just a risk to Switzerland. It is disrespectful to talk about us in this way.”
More
Why a monster UBS bank scares Switzerland
Does the bank now have a financial problem?
No, it could manage the capital build-up. It made a profit of $7.8 billion last year, and a further $5.8 billion in the first half of 2026. If it were to retain profits and not pay out dividends, the build-up would be completed relatively quickly.
The bank’s concerns relate much more to its competitiveness. It is afraid of falling out of favour with its shareholders.
What happens next?
Following the Senate, the House of Representatives will decide on the bill. This will happen in December at the earliest. There could also be a referendum. It could take anywhere from a few months to several years before UBS is required to comply with the new rules.
The Senate debated three options: 100% backing of UBS foreign subsidiaries with core capital, 90% backing, or a 50/50 option.
In the third case, half of the capital would have been covered by AT1 bonds. These can be converted into equity capital or even written off in a crisis, above defined limits, to stabilise the bank.

Six arrested after anti-migrant protest at Gosport marina

Unknown Publisher

Six people have been arrested after anti-migrant protesters gathered at a marina in Hampshire in the mistaken belief that a small boat was due to arrive.
Heeding calls from the far-right campaigner Daniel Thomas, hundreds of protesters gathered early on Tuesday evening at Gosport in Hampshire, aiming to disrupt any disembarkation of asylum seekers. The Border Force vessels carrying them landed instead in Dover early on Wednesday.
Thomas, who styles himself as Danny Tommo, spent Tuesday afternoon in a speedboat in the Channel broadcasting his pursuit of the asylum seekers to more than 100,000 people.
He is facing a police inquiry after using a blade to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard.
Hampshire police said two men from Salisbury, aged 19 and 36, had been arrested on suspicion of aggravated trespass; and four people from Gosport – two men aged 33 and 67, and two women aged 31 and 32 – were held on suspicion of assaulting an emergency worker.
The 67-year-old was also held on suspicion of careless driving.
Police are “conducting inquiries” into footage of Thomas slashing the side of an inflatable boat while a member of a rescue team was still on it, then sailing away shouting: “Traitors.”
The arrests were made after unions representing Border Force staff discussed security concerns with the Home Office following increasingly aggressive tactics by anti-migrant activists.
The discussions followed attacks on Border Force vehicles and attempts to record and identify staff members by some anti-migrant activists.
The Home Office plans to use public order powers to stop the harassment and possible doxing of government staff who pick up small-boat arrivals at sea.
Lucy Moreton, of the Immigration Services Union, said: “Following several conversations with the ISU regarding staff safety, the Home Office is working with local police and MoD [Ministry of Defence] to ensure that staff, and migrants, are properly protected using existing police powers and civil service support networks.”
Fran Heathcote, the general secretary of the PCS union, which represents Border Force guards, said: “PCS unreservedly condemns this life-threatening and criminal behaviour. Our members do an important and dangerous job and this inference is reckless in the extreme.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “We have been clear that groups creating fear and intimidating communities cannot be allowed to operate with impunity.
“Police should make full use of the powers available to them to deal robustly with criminality and ensure communities, staff and those in their care are protected.
“Recent events demonstrate the need to learn lessons and adapt our response to new tactics, ensuring police have the tools, intelligence and operational plans needed to act quickly and effectively.”
Some of the protesters in Gosport wore black clothing and face coverings, and chanted “send them back”, wrongly assuming the boat would be guided to the Hampshire coast.
In fact, it docked in Dover, Kent, at about 12.30am on Wednesday after 51 people onboard reportedly refused help from a French ship and spent 33 hours at sea.
It emerged on Tuesday that a second small boat had arrived on UK shores within the last 24 hours without being detected and intercepted.
The boat reached Samphire Hoe, near Dover, on Tuesday afternoon. Border Security Command has detained 21 migrants so far.
On Monday, five people were detained and passed to Border Security Command after a dinghy made it to shore at Folkestone, also in Kent.
The defence minister Luke Pollard dismissed suggestions the government had lost control of the border.
“Our borders are secure, but we want to make them stronger,” he told LBC Radio, adding that a Home Office investigation was under way into what had happened.
A man was found dead on a beach in northern France on Wednesday, French authorities have said.

Ukrainian partisans say they have sabotaged the railway signaling that keeps Russian troops supplied on the Lyman front. The ATESH movement reports that its agents disabled four relay cabinets on a line through Voronezh Oblast that carries military cargo to Russian forces there, delaying ammunition to three regiments.
The strike was timed to help Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, the counteroffensive the Third Army Corps is running near Lyman in northern Donetsk. In its first phase, the operation cleared 75 square kilometers of Russian infiltrators and de-occupied another 10.
Cutting the rail line that feeds the Russian units facing that offensive is, by ATESH's account, part of the same fight, targeting the supply line rather than the front.
Four cabinets go dark
The sabotage hit a rail corridor running through the Voronezh, Novovoronezh, Liski, and Ostrogozhsk areas of Voronezh Oblast, a route ATESH says Russia uses to move military cargo toward the Lyman axis.
Relay cabinets house the switching gear that runs a line's automatic signals. Knocking them out can freeze traffic on a stretch of track without a single explosion, and ATESH says its agents disabled four of them. As with the movement's other claims, the account could not be independently verified.
Ammunition backs up
By ATESH's telling, the signaling failure delayed shipments of ammunition and engineering materiel to the 1st and 15th Guards regiments and the 254th Motor Rifle Regiment. Russian commanders, it said, had to rush in repair crews and divert resources to guard the infrastructure. A delayed shipment, far behind the front, can be felt at it, where an assaulted position waits for the ammunition that does not arrive.
ATESH hunts the supply lines
ATESH is a network of pro-Ukrainian agents operating inside Russia and Russian-occupied territory, and it has increasingly gone after the rail and power infrastructure that sustains Moscow's war. This month, the group also said it knocked out the power supply of a plant in Voronezh that makes components for Russian missiles.

Putin says election turnout shows Russians support military agenda
MOSCOW, Sept 23 - President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday that high turnout in last weekend's parliamentary election showed that Russians support their armed forces fighting in Ukraine and the authorities' efforts to protect national security.
Putin had framed the election, held from September 18 to 20, as a test of public support for the 4-1/2—year war in Ukraine and for his avowed determination to fight on until key military aims are met.
Near complete results on Monday showed the pro-Putin ruling United Russia party had retained its decisive majority in the national parliament in a tightly controlled political system that excluded most candidates who oppose the war.
Russia's Central Electoral Commission put turnout at 59.3%, which the TASS state news agency said was higher than in most recent elections for the State Duma lower house of parliament.
Commenting on the results publicly for the first time, Putin said: "Such a high, even record, number of people who came out and voted shows that the people of Russia support our efforts aimed at strengthening the country."
During part of Wednesday's televised speech, he addressed soldiers on the front line directly: "This vote is for you. People believe in you, believe in our victory, believe in your courage, in your heroism."
The pro-Putin United Russia party is set to control 355 seats or nearly 80% of the 450 seats — a record number — in the Duma after winning more than 57% of votes, the near-complete results showed on Monday. REUTERS

Queen Ursula’s new ‘boyfriend’ should make Putin smile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:50:20 UTC
23:50:20 KST

Queen Ursula’s new ‘boyfriend’ should make Putin smile
European Commission president and unelected de facto “queen” of Europe, Ursula von der Leyen, can’t get enough of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Her annual “State of the European Union” address last week should have been called “State of my crush on Mark Carney.” It seemed to transform into one giant excuse to gush about him while he sat in front of her, as she mused aloud to “Dear Mark” about her vision of some kind of “associate EU membership” for Canada. It reminded me of a kid back in grade school who once did an entire speech on “seals” in French class, just so he could constantly repeat the French translation of the subject, “phoques,” at a rate of once per sentence.
“President Metsola, Prime Minister Carney, Honorable Members,” she began. “Mark, your presence here is a symbol of the enduring friendship between our people. Our cultural, historical and personal links run deep within the fabric of our societies.” That’s what we used to call a group date to hide your crush. Only the group here consists of Canada’s 41 million people and the EU’s 452 million.
“Dear Mark,” she continued. “I said we must urgently reimagine our partnerships… We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well.”
Carney may be glad that ocean she speaks of is there, as it seems to be perhaps the only thing preventing her from camping out on his front lawn at this point. For his part, Carney has made it clear that he’s playing the field, and that any commitment is welcome in that context.“We’re not looking to become a member of the European Union,” Carney said, unequivocally. “What we are looking – and will begin discussions for – is a unique alliance between Canada and the European Union.” In other words, he isn’t looking to flee Trump’s 51st state threat in favor of Canada willingly being the EU’s 28th.
No one in their right mind can blame him. You have to think that Carney – the former central banker of both Canada and the UK, and the onetime head of the G20’s Financial Stability Board in Basel – knows an economic basket case when he sees one. And it’s one thing to hang out, have a good time, and fill your boots. But it’s quite another not to have the total freedom to just zip up and peace out when the next inevitable self-imposed meltdown comes along. Which is at about the rate of one a week, at this point.
A lot of the EU’s problems come down to a lack of accurate foresight and an inability to prioritize by coordinating their agenda with existential reality. Had European leaders been more adept at doing so, they might not need Carney to stand there in front of the EU Parliament and explain that it’s okay not to kiss Washington’s behind to their own detriment. Or that dating around allows for a more chill approach to all relationships.Until recently, anyone adopting this position in either Canada or Europe would immediately be subject to a proctology exam, accused of being some kind of secret tool of the Kremlin. EU officials have repeatedly warned that fragmentation and multipolarity that de-centers the Washington-led agenda hinders Western unity to the benefit of rival powers such as Russia.
But Carney is basically saying that it benefits any country to pursue strategic non-alignment. He’s cutting deals with Europe and with BRICS countries. He said to a standing ovation at Davos earlier this year that it was important to be “pragmatic in recognizing that progress is often incremental, that interests diverge, that not every partner will share all of our values. We are engaging broadly, strategically, with open eyes. We actively take on the world as it is, not wait for a world we wish to be.”
This isn’t a guy who’s into nation-building beyond his own. Ursula may think that she’s acquiring Canada and its resources for Europe, but she’s also importing, first and foremost, a political instinct that the bloc has long lacked. Carney is now articulating – to resounding applause – a position that, until recently, was far more closely associated with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s worldview than the one that orbits around Washington.
Still, Carney is singing from the EU’s hymn book on Ukraine and Russia right now. He’s also literally negotiating for Canada to get some defense manufacturing revenues from the EU’s massive fear-driven spending spree on its defense security blanket. It’s not hard to see a profit motive here. Nor in the fact that he’s literally pitching for Europe to replace Russian natural resources with Canadian equivalents.
So right now, Canada and Russia are positioned as competitors on the global economic playing field. At least for the time being. But that won’t always be the case once he’s secured the bag. Carney – now officially the most popular prime minister in Canadian history at 70% approval – got himself into that position by ditching right-left ideology for pragmatism. He could turn out to be an important interlocutor for Russia with the West. Someone who’s blunt, action-oriented, and doesn’t much honestly care what you do as long as it doesn’t annoy him. Ursula is clearly smitten with Carney. And if her new boyfriend ends up showing Europe how to be a little less cliquey about engaging with the rest of the world, then perhaps there’s hope for us all yet.

Dutch to end Eurovision boycott, despite Israel's continued participation
The Netherlands will end its boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest, despite Israel's continuing participation in the annual song contest. They withdrew from the 2026 competition, along with Ireland, Spain, Iceland, and Slovenia, due to Israel's ongoing genocide in Gaza.
The Dutch public broadcaster, NPO, said Wednesday it would step in to replace a company that had pulled out over Israel's participation.
"The Dutch public broadcaster will once again take part in the Eurovision Song Contest from 2027 onwards with a Dutch participant. An independent team of experts will carefully guide the process surrounding the act," said the NPO.
In August, the AVROTROS broadcaster, which selected the Dutch entry and broadcast the show, had pulled out, saying the event can "no longer be considered neutral" given Israel's genocide in Gaza.
The broadcaster said the contest provokes "mixed feelings" in the Netherlands, but claimed it had "explicitly asked the EBU to once again make the unifying character of the festival an important part of the event," despite Israel's inclusion in the contest.
In August, organisers announced they were excluding any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.
But when it pulled out, AVROTROS had said those changes did "not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored".
Next year's contest will take place on May 15 in Bulgaria's Black Sea city of Burgas.
