Trump pushes Russia-Ukraine ‘energy truce’: Can it work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:49:04 UTC
23:49:04 KST

Trump pushes Russia-Ukraine ‘energy truce’: Can it work?
Talks of a possible halt in attacks on energy facilities come as strikes on such targets continue unabated.
A proposal by US President Donald Trump for an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine appeared to be gaining ground this week when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was “ready” to make an agreement.
Trump has blamed the Ukraine-Russia war for the current record rise in diesel prices in the United States, which has become a major issue as the country approaches midterm elections in November.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Putin’s party wins supermajority in Russia’s parliamentary election
- list 2 of 3UN General Assembly 2026: Who is speaking and when?
- list 3 of 3Russian strikes on Ukraine kill three as Zelenskyy arrives for UN summit
Trump and Zelenskyy met for 40 minutes on Tuesday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York to discuss efforts to end Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
In comments to reporters at the UN headquarters, Zelenskyy said Kyiv would halt strikes on Russian energy facilities if Moscow stopped targeting Ukraine’s energy systems as well. “If they don’t want us to attack their diesel and refineries, we are ready – if they will not attack our energy system, our electricity, heating system, water supplies,” he said.
The Trump-Zelenskyy meeting comes as a barrage of attacks on energy facilities by both Russia and Ukraine continues unabated, raising questions over whether such a truce could indeed be reached – and whether it could hold.
Here’s what we know:
Why are Russia and Ukraine targeting energy facilities in particular?
This year, Ukraine has massively expanded strikes on Russia’s oil industry, using long-range drones to strike refineries and other energy facilities at sites up to 3,000km (1,865 miles) from the Ukrainian border. The aim is to disrupt Russia’s energy industry, which it relies on to fund its war effort.
A September 20 attack forced the Moscow oil refinery, which processed about 230,000 barrels of crude a day in 2024, to halt crude processing, the Reuters news agency reported, citing industry sources. Also this month, Ukraine launched its deepest-ever attack into Russia, targeting two Arctic gas condensate facilities more than 3,000km (1,865 miles) from its border.
On Wednesday, Russia slammed jet-powered drones into two petrol stations and other sites in Kyiv, killing one and injuring at least seven people. Ukrainian oil company Ukrnafta said Russia had hit one of its petrol stations in the capital, the sixth such facility attacked in recent weeks.
Zelenskyy also warned in a post on Telegram on Tuesday that Russia was planning “a new massive attack” against his country.
What does an ‘energy ceasefire’ mean?
A bilateral energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia would involve a mutual halt of attacks on all energy-related targets in each other’s countries. What remains unclear is whether both sides can agree on the preconditions for it being set in place.
The Kremlin previously welcomed the US proposal for an energy moratorium while also calling for such measures to be extended to Russian seaborne energy exports and sanctions.
On Wednesday, Zelenskyy said, “Both the US and Ukraine want to see this senseless Russian war ended before winter.” But he also insisted that there could not possibly be any discussion of easing sanctions against Russia “when Ukrainians live every day under the threat of missile and drone attacks”.
Why is Trump involved in this?
This week, Trump expressed concern about the extensive damage done by Ukraine to Russia’s fuel-processing capacity, which he said is stoking diesel prices and “hurting the world”. On Sunday, he asked Ukraine to stop hitting Russian diesel refineries in particular.
But Trump’s intervention to halt Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy facilities appears to contradict his administration’s general approach to Russian energy.
This month, the US Congress passed a new bill that gives Trump sweeping powers to impose sanctions on Russia’s crude exports as well as steep tariffs on buyers of Russian energy.
Analysts say that Trump’s approval ratings have slumped to a record low at home, and he is now likely hoping an energy ceasefire could reduce petrol and diesel prices at US pumps ahead of the November midterm elections.
Furthermore, amid fears that Russia will try to cripple Ukraine’s heating and power facilities as winter approaches – as it did last year – Zelenskyy has asked Trump for additional Patriot air defence missiles, the only weapon in Ukraine’s arsenal capable of downing Russia’s ballistic missiles.
A halt to attacks on energy facilities, instead, would ease that pressure on Washington, whose supply of Patriots is being depleted by the US-Israel war on Iran.
But while such a ceasefire could lower prices, it would also likely aid Russia’s war economy, analysts said.
“The ongoing sales of Russian fossil fuels continue to finance Russia’s war against Ukraine,” Amanda Paul, senior policy analyst at the European Policy Centre (EPC), told Al Jazeera.
“Rather than putting the emphasis on the impact of Ukrainian strikes on fuel prices, Trump should be putting greater pressure on Russia to end its attacks and bring the war to an end,” she said. “Trump himself is responsible for stoking high energy prices, due to the repercussions of the US-Israel war on Iran and the subsequent blocking of the Strait of Hormuz.”
Marnie Howlett, an associate professor of international relations in Eastern Europe and Eurasia at the University of Oxford, said that by pressuring Zelenskyy, Trump was placing emphasis on the wrong actor in the war.
“It is Russia’s – not Ukraine’s – responsibility to end the attacks,” Howlett told Al Jazeera. “The Russian Federation has repeatedly broken ceasefire agreements, so the war will continue until it agrees to recognise Ukraine’s territorial sovereignty.”
Could Trump bring about an energy ceasefire?
Christopher Pool, a researcher at the Department of War Studies at King’s College London, said Trump actually holds little leverage over the Ukrainian deep-strike campaign and has been “mysteriously reticent” to put pressure on Russia.
“A truce is more likely to be agreed because of pressures on both Ukraine and Russia caused by the war itself,” Pool told Al Jazeera.
“Ukraine is facing the hardest winter of the war, and memories of the brutal winter last year, when heating and electricity cuts were commonplace whilst temperatures dropped to minus 25 degrees Celsius [minus 13 degrees Fahrenheit], are fresh in Ukrainian minds.”
At the same time, Russia is facing its own energy crisis as a result of the Ukrainian deep-strike campaign. “The Kremlin may fear its effects on certain sections of the Russian population whose support, or apathy, is crucial for its survival,” the researcher added.
“The Ukrainian deep strike campaign therefore not only degrades Russia’s capacity to prosecute and escalate its war, but brings the war home to the very people the Kremlin is trying to shield from its effects.”
Could such a truce hold?
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, no ceasefires have been successfully maintained between the warring sides. During his presidential campaign in 2024, Trump claimed he would end the war in Ukraine very quickly if he resumed office as US president. However, this has not happened.
While Trump said last week that the two countries had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy facilities, strikes resumed almost immediately.
In May, Trump announced a three-day ceasefire to mark the end of World War II for the Russians. Russia announced a ceasefire for May 8 to 9 to coincide with commemorations of the Soviet Union’s victory over Nazi Germany, while Ukraine announced its own proposal for an open-ended ceasefire beginning on May 5.
But Moscow and Kyiv both quickly accused each other of violating these ceasefires. Talks deadlocked over Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, with Kyiv saying it would not pull troops back from parts of the region it controlled.
Ukrainian and Russian officials met in Turkiye for the first direct talks in years in May 2025, hoping to move forward on a full and unconditional ceasefire. The Istanbul talks resulted in an agreement to swap 1,000 prisoners of war each, but stopped short of the most urgent objective of halting the hostilities.
A previous round of talks in Istanbul in March 2022, soon after Russia invaded Ukraine, also failed to de-escalate the conflict and establish a diplomatic route.
Analysts say it is unlikely that a Trump-brokered energy ceasefire would be any different. “Russia is not interested in such a plan,” Paul said, as Moscow has been known to double down on attacks on energy facilities during the winter season.
“The Kremlin will exploit ambiguities in an energy truce by claiming that Ukraine violated the agreement and using that as justification for renewed attacks,” she said.
“Any deal would need clear rules, independent verification and a precise definition of what constitutes a violation – which will be hard to achieve.”
According to Pool, “Kyiv is likely to hold to its end of the bargain as long as Moscow does likewise.”
“Whether Russia does the same would be a reflection of how seriously the Kremlin takes the ongoing threat to the bubble in which urban and middle-class Russians have, to date, been able to live,” he said.

Russian forces have captured approximately 890 square kilometers (344 square miles) of Ukrainian territory since the beginning of 2026, while Ukraine’s Defense Forces have recaptured around 800 square kilometers (309 square miles), President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Zelensky presented the figures in an interview with The Wall Street Journal published on Tuesday, Sept. 22.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This year, he [Russian President Vladimir Putin] captured about 890 square kilometers [344 square miles], while we de-occupied 800,” Zelensky said.
“So, in different directions, he gained an additional 90 – let’s say 100 – square kilometers [34-39 square miles] during the year,” he added.
The figures represent gross gains made by the two armies on different parts of the front, rather than Ukraine retaking precisely the same territory seized by Russia.
Zelensky says Russia paid heavily for limited gains
According to Zelensky, Russia’s net territorial advantage in 2026 is significantly smaller than the amount of Ukrainian land its forces captured in previous years.
He said Russian troops had previously occupied between 3,000 and 4,000 square kilometers (1,158-1,544 square miles) of additional territory annually.
“You can understand the price of these 100 square kilometers [39 square miles] – it is very high,” Zelensky said.
“He is neither winning nor losing, but his society is losing people and money for the sake of some 100 kilometers,” the president added.
Confirmed Russian War Dead Top a Quarter Million
Zelensky estimated that Russia had suffered approximately 270,000 personnel losses in 2026 involving troops who would not return to the battlefield. He did not provide a breakdown of those he described as killed, missing, or permanently unable to fight.
Neither the territorial nor casualty figures presented by Zelensky could be independently verified. Battlefield estimates frequently vary because military authorities and monitoring groups use different methods for counting contested areas, cleared territory, and settlements under partial control.
Ukraine reports counteroffensive gains
Ukraine has reported several successful counteroffensive operations during 2026, particularly in the southern regions and along the border between the Kharkiv and Donetsk regions.
In May, Zelensky said Ukrainian forces had already recaptured approximately 590 square kilometers (227 square miles) since the beginning of the year. The figure increased to 745 square kilometers (288 square miles) by August, when he announced that Ukrainian troops had liberated 26 settlements across three regions.
More recently, Ukraine’s Third Army Corps reported further gains during Operation Vivaldi near Lyman in the northern Donetsk region.
Ukrainian forces liberated Shandryholove and Derylove and took full control of Drobysheve, according to the corps. Its commander, Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky, said the broader operation recovered approximately 125 square kilometers (48 square miles) of territory.
Near Kupiansk in the Kharkiv region, Ukrainian troops also regained positions around Zapadne and cleared several additional square kilometers from Russian forces.
Earlier territorial claims have sometimes differed from independent battlefield assessments.
In February, Ukrainian Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrsky said Ukrainian forces had regained as much as 400 square kilometers (154 square miles) in the south, while the Institute for the Study of War had independently confirmed approximately 169 square kilometers (65 square miles) at the time.
The difference reflected contrasting methodologies, incomplete public information, and delays in confirming control over contested areas.
Despite Ukraine’s counterattacks, fighting continues along the roughly 1,200-kilometer (745-mile) front, with both armies attempting to advance in different sectors. Zelensky’s figures suggest that the front has shifted considerably at the local level during 2026 while producing relatively little net territorial change nationwide.

Could a Left Party government in Berlin expropriate large real estate companies?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:49:00 UTC
23:49:00 KST

Could Berlin expropriate large real estate companies?
September 23, 2026
The socialist Left Party, which won the Berlin election on September 20, was the only major party on the ballot that said it would implement the results of Berlin's 2021 referendum, when 57.6% of Berliners voted to expropriate the apartments owned by real estate companies that own more than 3,000 units.
But the federal government has said they won't let it happen. So is it even possible? And how did we get here? DW explains:
- 
	What did the Left Party say about expropriation?
The Left Party was one of the main supporters of a successful, years-long grassroots campaign called "Deutsche Wohnen & Co. enteignen," ("Expropriate Deutsche Wohnen").
Deutsche Wohnen is a major property developer that owns over 140,000 units across Germany, and 100,000 in Berlin alone.
The campaign and the Left Party argued that by expropriating this and a handful of other major companies like it, the Berlin government could put some 270,000 apartments in Berlin into public ownership, and make them available at affordable rent prices. Other estimates put the number at around 240,000.
The argument struck a chord, as surveys showed that housing and rent prices were the biggest concerns for Berlin voters in the recent election.
Some 25% of rented property in Berlin is already in public ownership, through state-owned companies like Berlinovo. The expropriation measure would likely push that up to over 30%.
- 
	The 2021 referendum — what was the question and what came out of it?
The original referendum, held in September 2021, asked Berliners to vote yes or no on a five-point plan:
- Socializing the apartments owned by the major property companies
- Administration of the properties by a public-law entity
- Administration of the properties with participation from both city officials, renters, and local communities
- Ban on any re-privatization
- Compensation for the property companies "significantly below" the market value of the property
The referendum did not oblige the state government — at the time a coalition of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the Greens, and the Left Party — to immediately implement the plan.
Instead, the then-SPD Mayor Franziska Giffey put together a 13-person expert commission, including former justice ministers and constitutional law experts. This was given the task of establishing whether the plan conformed with the German constitution, or Basic Law, and how the compensation could be organized.
In 2023, the commission concluded that expropriation was legal and possible, though budget questions still needed to be clarified.
By then, a new conservative-led government, headed by the Christian Democratic Union's (CDU) Kai Wegner, had been voted into office, and announced that it would not expropriate any real estate companies, regardless of what the commission said. At the same time, it emerged that the Berlin CDU was receiving hundreds of thousands of euros in donations from property companies.
Instead, the government said it would draw up a socialization law that would define the conditions for the socialization of property, while ruling out expropriation. A draft law was completed in December 2025.
The Deutsche Wohnen Enteignen campaign rejected this idea as pointless, and had in the meantime gathered legal experts to draw up its own expropriation and socialization law, and promised to start another campaign to force a referendum to implement that.
- 
	The legal basis for expropriation: Articles 14 and 15 of the German constitution
The original campaign founded its plan on articles 14 and 15 of the German Basic Law.
Article 14 says that, while the right to property is guaranteed, "expropriation shall only be permissible for the public good."
Article 15 states: "Land, natural resources and means of production may, for the purpose of nationalization, be transferred to public ownership or other forms of public enterprise by a law that determines the nature and extent of compensation."
As far as the campaigners are concerned, the law they have drawn up covers those two bases.
But, while Article 14 is implemented often enough (for example, when the state wants to build a new highway), Article 15 has never been implemented at all. It is new legal territory, and no one is quite sure what would happen if it were tried.
Some legal experts say the plan would contravene European law. Housing companies would almost certainly fight the measure in court and demand more compensation than the government is willing to offer.
- 
	'Not happening' — Chancellor Merz vows to prevent expropriation
Chancellor Friedrich Merz responded to the Left Party's election victory immediately by promising to draw up a federal law banning state governments from expropriating property.
"It's not just about banning something here in Berlin," Merz said at a press conference in the aftermath of the Berlin election. "It's about sending a clear message to international investors, which is: There is no expropriation of private property in Germany."
However, it's unclear whether the federal government has the power to impose such a law. Germany's Constitutional Court once ruled that the federal government cannot pass a law simply to prevent a state from governing in the issues it wants.
- 
	What now?
The Left Party still has to enter into coalition negotiations to form a government in Berlin. Its most likely coalition partners are the SPD and the Greens, and given the opposition from the federal government and the massive controversy over the issue, the expropriation plan could become a major sticking point.
Whatever happens, the Left Party itself acknowledges that expropriation and socialization would take a while to put into practice, and it would be even longer before it had a measurable effect on Berlin's overall rents.
In the meantime, it has drawn up a number of laws that it hopes will tackle the problem more quickly, such as a rent cap.
In any case, Berliners themselves appear to have gone a little cold on the idea. Despite the Left's electoral success, a recent poll by infratest-dimap found that only 37% of Berliners are still in favor of expropriating real estate companies.
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

EXPLAINER - UN General Assembly: What did world leaders say about AI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:48:14 UTC
23:48:14 KST

Artificial intelligence emerged as a major theme at the opening of the UN General Assembly, with world leaders warning about everything from autonomous weapons and disinformation to concentrated technological power and job disruption.
But there was little consensus over what should come next.
US President Donald Trump rejected international attempts to control AI and emphasized competition and rapid development, while several other leaders called for common rules, international safeguards and greater government oversight.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres issued perhaps the starkest warning, saying humanity is increasingly transferring power to machines and insisting that decisions over life and death must remain under human control.
Here is what leaders said about AI at the 81st UN General Assembly.
Trump used his Sept. 22 address to reject international efforts to establish global controls on artificial intelligence.
“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme of control for the Artificial Intelligence being spoken of so much now -- hereinafter officially called ‘Super Intelligence.’”
He announced that US government documents would refer to AI as "super intelligence," arguing that the word “artificial” made the technology sound less significant than it was.
He framed AI development as a strategic race, saying the country that wins the technology would gain a major advantage.
“Whoever wins SI, whoever wins Superintelligence wins,” Trump said, adding that the US was ahead of China and intended to remain so.
Trump said he would not slow AI development, arguing that it could become more significant than previous technological revolutions.
“I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution,” he said. “We will only encourage superintelligence. We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.”
At the same time, he said the US would monitor the technology through the Justice Department and other law enforcement agencies and would encourage its development “safely and responsibly.”
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan called for an international legal framework on AI.
“The time has long come to establish a common international legal framework for artificial intelligence,” Erdogan said.
He called for work to be accelerated to prepare and bring into effect a UN international convention on AI.
“It is important to accelerate efforts to prepare and bring into force a United Nations International Convention on Artificial Intelligence.”
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham highlighted both the potential benefits and risks of frontier AI.
He said AI was already speeding up cancer diagnosis in the UK and could help transform healthcare, education and the economy, while also becoming a vital tool for security.
“AI will also be a source of disruption to the way we live and work – and a multiplier of risk,” he warned.
“Fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance" Burnham said, arguing that elected governments should retain responsibility for those choices.
He announced that Britain would put AI at the heart of its G20 presidency in 2027 and work toward “a single set of global principles and standards” to ensure transparency, access, preparedness and safe AI development.
Burnham said the challenge was to harness AI’s economic and scientific benefits while avoiding the upheaval and inequality associated with earlier industrial transformations.
French President Emmanuel Macron warned against allowing the US and China, or a small group of technology companies, to dominate decision-making on artificial intelligence.
"There are some who wish to make us believe that only two powers, the US and China, will be making the decisions. They want us to believe that just a few economic actors will make all the decisions.”
He called for countries to develop their own AI capabilities and for greater oversight of AI models, saying they should not become dependent on a handful of private companies.
Macron also backed international cooperation on AI, including the development of an open-source frontier model that countries could share.
“Rather, we must come together to build an open-source frontier model, a cutting-edge model,” he said.
Macron pointed to Europe’s efforts to establish rules and principles governing AI as an alternative model.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva called for stronger regulation of Big Tech and artificial intelligence, warning against what he described as an unchecked technological race.
“It would be an unforgivable historical omission not to address the challenge of regulating the big techs and artificial intelligence,” Lula said.
He accused a small group of “techno-oligarchs” of promoting “a race with no ethical boundaries” and bypassing the UN and its scientific panel on AI.
Lula also called for greater corporate responsibility, saying companies that are aware of the risks of their products were shifting the burden of dealing with algorithms onto families.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb described artificial intelligence as a technology that could reshape science, the economy, politics and security.
He called for humans to retain control over its development.
“Artificial intelligence is the most consequential technology in the history of mankind,” Stubb said. “Humans can and should be in the driver's seat.”
He said countries faced a choice over how to approach AI: “We can compete, cooperate, or slow down,” adding that he believed cooperation was the best path.
Stubb said Finland and Norway, together with other countries, had launched a call for companies, governments, regional organizations and the UN to develop mechanisms to control frontier AI models.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that humans are “increasingly handing power to machines,” pointing to the growing role of AI and autonomous weapons in decisions once reserved for humans.
He said AI was rapidly concentrating power in data, computing capacity and algorithms, while advancing faster than humanity’s ability to understand its consequences.
“The danger is not technology. The danger is technology without accountability,” Guterres said, calling on governments to take responsibility for managing AI risks.
He urged countries with the greatest AI capabilities to share information on emerging safety risks, cooperate on testing and evaluation, and work toward common safeguards.
Guterres also called for a multilateral AI risk-management framework backed by credible and independent oversight, saying artificial intelligence must be “shaped by humanity, with humanity and for all humanity.”
The UN chief outlined particularly strong safeguards concerning children and warfare.
“Children must never become the test subjects for unregulated systems,” he said.
He added that “life-and-death decisions must never be surrendered to machines,” declaring: “Killer robots must have no place in our future.”
Kenyan President William Ruto raised another dimension of the AI debate: technological dependence and ownership.
In remarks at a high-level AI Middle Powers Coalition meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Ruto said African countries needed to move beyond consuming AI products and instead develop, own and shape systems that reflect their languages, economies and societies.
“We must not reproduce the old extractive economy in digital form. Africa cannot provide the minerals, energy, data, content and talent of the AI revolution, only to import the resulting intelligence at a premium.”
Ruto called for greater investment in African computing infrastructure, skills, research and governance capacity.

Indian embassy celebrates Ayurveda Day, highlights Iran cooperation
TEHRAN - The embassy of India in Tehran hosted a ceremony on Wednesday to mark National Ayurveda Day under the theme “Ayurveda for a Healthier Tomorrow,” bringing together diplomats, physicians, media representatives and enthusiasts of traditional medicine.
In his opening remarks, Indian Ambassador to Iran Vishwesh Negi said Ayurveda Day is observed to promote and revive the ancient Indian system of medicine, which is rooted in natural healing and a holistic approach to well-being.
Negi said the annual observance, initiated by the Indian government in 2016, seeks to raise international awareness of Ayurveda and its potential role in disease prevention and health promotion.
He also highlighted growing cooperation between Iran and India in traditional medicine, noting that the two countries have signed a memorandum of understanding between India’s Ministry of AYUSH and Iran’s Ministry of Health and Medical Education to build on their shared heritage of herbal and traditional remedies.
The ambassador referred to developments at the 16th BRICS Health Ministers’ Meeting in Chandigarh in July 2026, where traditional, complementary and integrative medicine was included in the agenda for greater cooperation among member states. The meeting’s declaration called for stronger collaboration in research, evidence generation, quality and safety.
Elsewhere in his remarks, the Inian envoy said the Ayurveda sector has experienced substantial economic expansion over the past decade, with the Ayurveda economy growing from $2.85 billion in 2014 to $43.4 billion in 2023, according to figures cited in his remarks.
He also highlighted the “Strategic Roadmap for Making Ayurveda Global,” released by NITI Aayog in July 2026. The roadmap sets out a phased strategy for expanding Ayurveda internationally, with emphasis on research, education, exports, regulatory alignment, international cooperation and quality standards.
Speaking at the ceremony, Paola Amadei, Italy’s ambassador to Iran, shared her experience of visiting India and spoke about the country’s rich culture and its traditional medical heritage, including Ayurveda.
Dr. Alireza Yargholi, a physician specializing in Persian medicine, addressed the historical and conceptual links between Persian medicine and Ayurveda. His presentation examined the two traditions from the perspective of shared concepts, historical exchanges, research and opportunities for future cooperation.
Dr. Arman Zargaran, an international affairs adviser at the Center for Iranian and Complementary Medicine of the Ministry of Health and Medical Education, discussed Iran-India cooperation in traditional medicine, including previously signed memorandums of understanding and ongoing joint activities.
Dr. Sohrab Dehqan, meanwhile, spoke about his studies of Ayurveda in India, the principles of the traditional medical system and his personal experiences.
Ayurveda derives its name from two Sanskrit words: “Ayur,” meaning life, and “Veda,” meaning knowledge. The system developed on the Indian subcontinent thousands of years ago, with roots in the Vedas, and traditionally seeks both to maintain the health of healthy people and to treat illness.
Speakers at the ceremony emphasized that Ayurveda is not presented as a rejection of modern medicine, but as an approach that places particular emphasis on prevention, daily routines, digestion, sleep and maintaining balance between body, mind and spirit.

KATHMANDU, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The recent devastating mudslide in Nepal is expected to affect the country's economy in the current fiscal year 2026-27, with the economy projected to grow by 4.1 percent, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) said on Wednesday.
In its latest Asian Development Outlook, the ADB said Nepal's economic growth is expected to moderate in the current fiscal year compared with its earlier projection, as severe disasters in August damaged transport infrastructure, hydropower facilities and other productive assets.
The mudslide and its aftermath are expected to disrupt trade, tourism, agriculture and local economic activities, weighing particularly on industrial and services-sector growth during the first quarter of fiscal year 2026-27, which began in mid-July.
The damage to critical infrastructure and productive assets is likely to constrain economic activity in the short term, while disruptions to transport and other supply networks could further affect businesses and the movement of goods and people, the ADB said.
According to the Rapid Disaster Needs Assessment (RDNA) report prepared by a joint technical team of the National Planning Commission and the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the recent mudslide is estimated to have caused losses of 2.69 billion U.S. dollars.
However, reconstruction and rehabilitation spending is expected to partly offset the economic impact of the disaster by supporting demand and helping restore damaged infrastructure, according to the ADB. Increased investment in hydropower expansion is also expected to contribute to economic activity.
The RDNA report said an estimated 4.77 billion U.S. dollars will be required for the reconstruction and recovery of affected infrastructure and assets.
The reconstruction effort could, however, put additional pressure on public finances as the government increases spending to restore infrastructure and productive capacity damaged by the floods.
Public debt is expected to increase further in fiscal year 2026-27 as additional resources are mobilized for reconstruction and recovery. Nepal's public debt had started to rise substantially after the country mobilized domestic and foreign debt for the reconstruction following the 2015 earthquake.
"Despite higher financing needs, Nepal remains at low risk of debt distress," the ADB said. ■

China Focus: German auto executives call for deeper cooperation with China on NEVs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:44:48 CST
23:44:48 KST

HAIKOU, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- German auto industry executives and experts have called for deeper cooperation with China on new energy vehicles (NEVs), batteries, artificial intelligence (AI) and automated driving, saying the two countries could draw on their respective strengths as the global auto industry undergoes a rapid technological shift.
Speaking at the ongoing World New Energy Vehicle Congress 2026 in Haikou, capital of south China's Hainan Province, participants pointed to the complementary strengths of the two countries, with Germany bringing engineering expertise, quality, safety and global industrial experience, and China offering rapid innovation, digital ecosystems, battery technology and smart mobility.
Hildegard Müller, president of the German Association of the Automotive Industry, said China is not only an important sales and sourcing market but also a key location for innovation. She called for closer exchanges in battery technologies, charging infrastructure, intelligent manufacturing, software-defined vehicles, automated driving, hydrogen and AI-based mobility.
"Combining our strengths can accelerate more sustainable, intelligent and customer-oriented mobility worldwide," she said.
China has been the world's largest NEV market for years.
The country's NEV production and sales reached more than 7.43 million and 7.44 million units, respectively, in the first half of 2026, up 6.7 percent and 7.3 percent year on year, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers.
NEV exports, meanwhile, surged to over 2.35 million units during the period, a 120-percent increase from a year earlier.
The rapid growth has made China increasingly important not only as a market and manufacturing base but also as a center for automotive research and development. That shift is reshaping how German automakers operate in China.
Ralf Brandstätter, chairman and CEO of Volkswagen Group China, said the company's strategy had evolved from "from Europe, for China" to "in China, for China," and now toward "in China, beyond China."
He said Volkswagen has localized not only its products but also its ability to create them, with its Volkswagen Group China Technology Company (VCTC) in Hefei developing next-generation NEV technologies.
"German engineering precision, Chinese innovation speed, Volkswagen scale" is the combination Volkswagen brings to China, he said.
Volkswagen has invested more than 3.5 billion euros in Hefei, capital of east China's Anhui Province, where VCTC, its largest R&D center outside Germany, is located. In August, Volkswagen Anhui's 100,000th intelligent electric vehicle rolled off the production line there, marking another milestone in the German automaker's electrification push in China.
Drummond Jacoy, head of Mercedes-Benz China Research, Development and Procurement, said Sino-German automotive cooperation is moving from a focus on scale toward higher-quality cooperation.
"China is no longer only an important market, but an important part of the global automotive innovation network," he said.
Mercedes-Benz is deepening cooperation with Chinese technology partners and applying AI across its value chain, while its joint research with Tsinghua University has spanned AI, road safety and autonomous driving.
Jacoy called for joint development, validation and deployment across intelligent driving, software, batteries, low-carbon supply chains, testing and the circular economy, saying the two industries could move "beyond collaboration to co-creation."
While speakers acknowledged competition, market pressure and geopolitical uncertainty, they stressed that these challenges make dialogue and cooperation more important, not less.
"Competition and cooperation have always gone hand in hand in the automotive industry," said Christian Ach, president and CEO of BMW Group Region China, who added that China and Germany have maintained close ties for many years.
Germany has remained China's largest trading partner and biggest source of foreign investment in Europe. Data from the German Economic Institute show that new German direct investment in China amounted to roughly 7 billion euros in 2025, well above the roughly 4.5 billion euros recorded a year earlier.
The World New Energy Vehicle Congress, held under the theme "Transformation & Upgrading, Resilient Growth," runs from Sept. 22 to 24. ■

Strengthening port air defense, insurance, vessel escort services could improve security of shipping in Ukraine – experts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:44:42 EEST
23:44:42 KST

Strengthening air defense at ports, developing insurance mechanisms, and the possibility of providing escorts for merchant ships in the Black Sea – these measures could improve shipping and the state of Ukrainian exports, according to a report by the United Ukraine analytical center presented to Interfax-Ukraine on Wednesday.
In particular, an expert at the center Ivan Us expressed the view that Ukraine should work with Turkey to explore the possibility of Ankara enlisting partners to escort merchant ships in the Black Sea.
"Turkey can enlist partners it deems necessary to escort ships," Us said at a press conference titled "Enclosed sea: Mutual blockade of Black Sea ports of Ukraine and Russia as instrument of war."
Among the priority measures, the expert also cited strengthening the ports' air defense, since without port infrastructure, ships will not be able to safely enter them.
He identified the development of insurance mechanisms as a second priority, since without insurance against war risks, ship owners, he said, will lack sufficient incentives to call at Ukrainian ports.
The document's recommendations include a proposal to create a state-run mechanism for insuring military risks, specifically "a joint EU-G7 pool with a sovereign backstop to cover the lives of crews."
It is also proposed to introduce monitoring based on AIS and satellite data, a public incident registry, and a rapid investigation mechanism.
As for the possibility of imposing a moratorium on attacks against merchant ships, crews, and civilian port infrastructure – unlinked to sanctions or political packages – the authors of the document believe there is a chance, albeit a small one.
"But we must fight for these opportunities, because everything hinges on the details and the positions of the parties. If Russia is most concerned about fuel shortages and the resulting social tensions, as well as attacks by Ukrainian defense forces on oil refineries, while the world prioritizes grain security, Ukraine prioritizes the broader complex," an expert on political and security issues and head of the United Ukraine analytical center Ihor Popov said.
An international political scientist and co-founder of the United Ukraine analytical center Anton Kuchukhidze said Ukraine is ready to consider relevant proposals regarding critical infrastructure, provided that Russia implements reciprocal measures.
He also noted the need to develop alternative export routes, particularly through Poland and Moldova.
As noted in the document, in the first half of 2026, 24.6 million metric tonnes of cargo passed through the ports of Greater Odesa, while 2.7 million metric tonnes were transported via alternative routes covering the Danube, rail, and road transport, although in 2023, approximately 29 million metric tonnes of cargo passed through the Danube route.
"So, in principle, there are alternatives, but it's clear that this is more complicated," the expert said.
Political scientist Petro Oleshchuk and international affairs expert Dmytro Levus recalled the three previous phases of Ukrainian ports' operations following the start of full-scale Russian aggression. During the first stage, from February 2022 to July 2023, the ports were closed; this was followed by a year-long Black Sea Grain Initiative, during which 32.8 million metric tonnes of grain were exported before Russia withdrew from the initiative.
Starting in August 2023, the Ukrainian Maritime Corridor was established, through which 150 million metric tons of cargo – including 90 million metric tonnes of grain – were exported, and 6,000 ships were handled. However, due to intensified Russian attacks on both ports and ships, its operations were nearly halted by the end of July 2026.

Chinese police dismantle transnational fraud ring with 257 suspects detained
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:44:39 CST
23:44:39 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese police have dismantled a transnational fraud ring that allegedly targeted many elderly people, leading to the arrest of 257 suspects in China and three Southeast Asian countries, the Ministry of Public Security (MPS) said Wednesday.
Since July, police in northeast China's Jilin Province have arrested 101 suspects under the MPS' direction. Through international law enforcement cooperation with police in Laos, Singapore and Cambodia, another 156 suspects were apprehended, the ministry said.
The suspects have been successively escorted back to China, it added.
Jilin police first identified the alleged fraud ring in January after an investigation found that the gang had fabricated investment projects, hired technology teams to develop fraudulent mobile applications, and used online platforms to attract potential victims and recruit members.
The gang allegedly targeted elderly people over an extended period, resulting in numerous victims and more than 6 billion yuan (about 888 million U.S. dollars) in suspected funds, according to the ministry.
The case marked the latest progress in China's efforts to strengthen cross-border law enforcement against telecom and online fraud.
On Monday, the MPS announced that Chinese and Malagasy police have carried out their first joint operation targeting telecom and online fraud, dismantling multiple criminal dens in the Malagasy capital Antananarivo and other areas.
In recent years, China has strengthened law enforcement cooperation with more than 30 countries, including Spain, the United Arab Emirates and Myanmar, to combat cross-border telecom and cyber fraud, developing cooperation mechanisms and achieving results in joint efforts against these crimes.
Since 2023, China and Myanmar have conducted joint operations that led to the dismantling of four major criminal gangs in Myanmar's Kokang region. Earlier this year, police authorities from China, the United States and the United Arab Emirates conducted their first joint law enforcement operation, resulting in the arrest of 276 suspects.
Cooperation with Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Malaysia, Indonesia, Sri Lanka and other countries has also led to the arrest and repatriation of more than 20,000 telecom and online fraud suspects this year.
Earlier this month, China initiated the International Alliance Combating Telecom and Cyber Fraud, with 46 founding member countries. The alliance is an intergovernmental organization designed to promote cooperation among law enforcement agencies in tackling transnational telecom and cyber fraud and related crimes. ■

South Africa's consumer inflation rises to 4.4 pct in August

22:44:33 CST
23:44:33 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- South Africa's annual consumer inflation edged up to 4.4 percent in August from 4.3 percent in July, official data showed Wednesday.
According to Statistics South Africa (Stats SA), the consumer price index was unchanged month on month.
Housing and utilities and transport were the biggest contributors to annual inflation, rising 5.2 percent and 8.8 percent, respectively. Insurance and financial services increased by 5.7 percent.
Annual inflation for food and non-alcoholic beverages rose to 1.1 percent in August from 0.9 percent in July, marking its first increase in nine months. Fish and other seafood inflation accelerated to 7.5 percent from 6.6 percent, while meat price trends were mixed, Stats SA said.
Meanwhile, annual transport inflation eased slightly to 8.8 percent from 8.9 percent in July, mainly due to slower fuel inflation, which declined to 20 percent from 20.6 percent. Petrol prices fell 2 percent month on month, while diesel prices rose 3.1 percent. ■

Asian Games | Day 4: China's teen swimmer Yu completes hat-trick, DPR Korea dominates in weightlifting to open gold account
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:44:20 CST

by sportswriter Li Jia
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's 13-year-old swimmer Yu Zidi completed an individual event hat-trick at the 2026 Asian Games here on Wednesday, while DPR Korea opened its gold medal account thanks to female weightlifters.
Yu continued her stunning performance at the Games, claiming her third gold by winning the women's 400m individual medley after victories in the 200m fly and 200m IM. She led all the way to touch in a Games record of 4:28.56.
"I gained a lot from this Asian Games but there were also some regrets," she said.
Meanwhile, 19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo claimed his third title by winning the men's 200m freestyle before helping China win the mixed 4x100m medley relay for his fourth. Zhang surged in the final meters to overtake South Korea's Hwang Sunwoo, setting a new Asian record of 1:43.49.
Also in the pool, Peng Xuwei won the women's 100m backstroke in 59.30, while Yu Yiting edged out teammate Zhang Yufei by just 0.03 seconds to win the women's 100m butterfly in 56.41.
Adding to China's medal haul, Tang Qianting set a Games record of 1:04.98 to win the women's 100m breaststroke.
The only remaining swimming gold the day went to Japan's Shoon Mitsunaga in men's 100m fly in a Games record time of 50.56, who narrowly defeated China's Xu Fang.
China advanced to the quarterfinals of the men's football as group winner, after securing a 0-0 draw against the United Arab Emirates in its final group match.
Head coach Antonio Puche praised his squad's resilience. "This group has been extremely difficult," the Spaniard remarked. "Every match has been very tough, and today was not different." China will next face Thailand in Saturday's quarterfinals.
The athletics competition kicked off Wednesday with the men's and women's half-marathon race walks. China's Shi Shengji claimed the men's gold medal, while Yang Liujing took the women's crown.
In gymnastics, China defended both men's and women's team titles, while in equestrian, Olympic rider Alex Hua Tian retained his individual eventing title.
In table tennis, China's women's team advanced to the final after sweeping DPRK 3-0 in the semifinal. The men's team similarly dispatched Chinese Taipei 3-0, setting up a gold-medal clash against host Japan. Meanwhile, mixed doubles star pair Wang Chuqin and Sun Yingsha cruised past Chinese Taipei's Feng Yi-hsin and Yeh Yi-tian 3-0.
On the badminton courts, both China's men's and women's teams made the finals after beating India 3-1 and Indonesia 3-0 respectively. Women's world No. 1 An Se-young won her singles match, but that's not enough to prevent South Korea from losing 3-1 to Japan in the women's team event.
China also continued its dominance in shooting. Jiang Yiting landed a commanding victory in the women's skeet competition. She later teamed up with her teammates to capture the team gold in the event. In the women's 10m air pistol team event, China's trio of Shen Yiyao, Jiang Ranxin and Yao Qianxun won another gold.
Gao Xiaobin and Yao Yang each captured a wushu gold medal to add two more to China's medal tally.
DPR Korea finally secured the delegation's first two gold medals in weightlifting.
Ri Song Gum won the women's 49kg category, setting three world records. She lifted 94kg in the snatch and 121kg in the clean and jerk for a dominant total of 215kg.
"I'm really, really happy. I don't even know how to put it into words," said Ri, who secured her third consecutive Asian Games title.
Later, Kang Hyon Gyong gave DPRK the second gold of the day in the women's 53kg. The 27-year-old lifted a total of 223kg, breaking five Games records along the way.
After four days of competition, China leads the medal table with 48 gold, 20 silver and 10 bronze medals. Japan sits second with 15 gold, 25 silver and 27 bronze medals, followed by South Korea with eight gold, eight silver and 25 bronze medals. ■

China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:44:10 CST
23:44:10 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The South African Reserve Bank (SARB) on Wednesday raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 7.25 percent, citing heightened inflation risks amid renewed fuel price pressures and persistent global supply shocks.
The Monetary Policy Committee unanimously decided to raise the rate, with the decision effective on Sept. 25, according to the central bank.
SARB said escalating tensions in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine conflict were disrupting energy and food supplies, contributing to a large and persistent global supply shock.
The central bank raised its near-term inflation forecasts mainly due to higher fuel prices. Headline inflation is expected to rise above 5 percent later this year and early next year before easing as the fuel price shock recedes, and is projected to return to around the 3-percent target toward the end of 2027.
"A few months back, it seemed that the fuel-price shock might be unwinding, but now it has intensified," the statement said.
SARB also lowered its forecast for South Africa's economic growth this year to 1.2 percent from 1.4 percent, after the economy contracted by 0.2 percent in the second quarter. It expects growth to rebound in the second half of the year, while risks to the outlook remain tilted to the downside.
The rate hike came as South Africa's annual consumer inflation edged up to 4.4 percent in August from 4.3 percent in July. ■

‘A triumph of money, filth, and hypocrisy’: EU decision to lift sanctions on Russian billionaires Fridman and Usmanov draws backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:42:34 UTC
23:42:34 KST

‘A triumph of money, filth, and hypocrisy’: EU decision to lift sanctions on Russian billionaires Fridman and Usmanov draws backlash
The European Union maintains a large sanctions list drawn up in response to Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. It includes more than 3,000 people and companies. EU countries used to review the list every six months. On September 22, they agreed to extend it for a full three years, but with an important caveat: two billionaires with close ties to Russia, Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov, were removed from the list. Both men had long sought to have the sanctions lifted, both through European courts and other means. The final decision on their cases was political rather than judicial: Luxembourg intervened on behalf of Fridman, who has filed a lawsuit against the country for a huge sum, while France intervened for Usmanov and, in exchange, received a pardon for one of its citizens who had been convicted in Azerbaijan.
The lifting of European restrictions on Fridman and Usmanov has outraged figures in the Russian opposition in exile, Ukrainian officials, and some European politicians. Meduza has collected their reactions, presented here with minor cuts.
Russian opposition
Vladimir Kara-Murza
opposition politician
Shame on you [in the European Union].
Yulia Navalnaya
leader of the Navalny-founded Anti-Corruption Foundation
It turns out that for Europe, it doesn’t matter whether you support the war or not, or whether you’re friends with Putin or opposed to him. In the end, it seems, what matters far more is how much money is in your bank accounts.
If you’re rich, have a couple of yachts and the right connections, apparently your sanctions can be lifted without much trouble. But if you fled Russia with little more than a few belongings because of political persecution or the draft, because you don’t support the war, it’s a different story: you might be denied a visa, refused a bank account, faced with a mountain of obstacles, and effectively pushed back into the arms of Putin’s system. And accused of supporting the war on top of it.
Thanks to the European Commission for yet another reminder that in big politics, money still speaks louder than principles, and the fates of ordinary people often end up somewhere near the bottom of the list of priorities.
Leonid Volkov
head of political projects at the Anti-Corruption Foundation
On Fridman, this is simply a mistake. He hasn’t done anything, hasn’t changed anything, hasn’t even spoken up. Lifting his sanctions “just because” is foolish. Four years ago I proposed, and I still believe, that clear and transparent mechanisms should have been created for exiting sanctions for entrepreneurs like Fridman, in exchange for concrete steps to weaken Putin’s regime: everything from condemning the war to providing substantial help to Ukraine. That was entirely achievable, but it was never done.
On Usmanov, this isn’t just a mistake, it’s a moral catastrophe, and a double one at that. First, Usmanov is no “rank-and-file oligarch.” He is one of the key people in the system. And it’s not just that his personal kept man is former president and current drunken bully Medvedev, but also which assets Usmanov bought up on behalf of and at the direction of the Kremlin for censorship and lawlessness: from MegaFon to Kommersant. Remember: “I don’t use the internet, I develop it”? Well, Usmanov is one of the people who developed it into its current state.
Second, Usmanov achieved the lifting of sanctions through hostage-taking. Azerbaijani dictator Aliyev helped out as a friend, detained French citizens, and France came running to sort things out. Great! The path out of sanctions has been shown: expect new hostages!
In 2022, Leonid Volkov signed a letter to the European Commission asking that sanctions against Mikhail Fridman and other senior Alfa Group executives be lifted. The letter proposed that the EU adopt “a clear and simple set of criteria” for removing people from the sanctions list. “These criteria could be tied to a public condemnation of the war, compensation for damages, and severing ties with Putin and his regime,” the letter said.
The letter became public in 2023. Volkov called it his “major political mistake” and stepped down as head of the international Anti-Corruption Foundation, ACF International, though he remained one of its key figures.
Meduza wrote in detail about this story here.
Maria Pevchikh
former head of the investigations department at the Anti-Corruption Foundation
What a colossal, planetary-scale disgrace this lifting of sanctions on Fridman and Usmanov is. As I said a couple of years ago, when I proposed trading yachts for political prisoners (which for some reason caused quite a scandal), if that isn’t done, the sanctions will simply be lifted for nothing. There will be no yachts and no political prisoners released. That is exactly what is happening now.
A triumph of money, filth, and hypocrisy. Some people, to get a measly work visa in Europe, have to bend over backwards proving they’re sufficiently anti-war, that none of their relatives, down to a seventh cousin, work for Putin’s regime, and produce stacks of convictions handed down in absentia in Russia. But these two assholes, pardon my language, haven’t said a single word against the war, and yet, please, come on in, cruise around on your yacht, live in your villas, no problem at all.
Vyacheslav Gimadi
head of the legal department at the Anti-Corruption Foundation
Putin’s oligarchs Usmanov (against whom I won at the European Court of Human Rights over Navalny’s investigation into Medvedev’s corruption) and the no less notorious Fridman are being removed from EU sanctions. How could this happen? These decisions are made unanimously, meaning any of the 27 countries can block them regardless of the “interests of the majority.” That’s what the Hungarians, Austrians, and Slovaks did, and now apparently France too, from what I’ve read. This vulnerability and pliability, I believe, diminish the institution itself, since it encourages terrorists to pressure individual countries, or maybe even offer them [financial] incentives, though I have no proof of that, and to blackmail them. Other people on the list will surely want to follow the same successful path.
Ivan Zhdanov
former director of the Anti-Corruption Foundation
If the European Union adopts this decision (or has already adopted it), it will collapse the entire system of personal sanctions. Today I sent an urgent letter through whatever channels I had, describing Usmanov’s personal role in the persecution of Navalny and of me (my first criminal case was over Usmanov) and his funding of the warmonger Medvedev. A terrible injustice and an abandonment of its own values [on the part of the European Union].
Alexey Navalny had long been in conflict with Alisher Usmanov. Their dispute began in 2017, when the Anti-Corruption Foundation released an investigation titled On vam ne Dimon “He Is Not Dimon to You,” about Dmitry Medvedev’s alleged corruption. The film said that Usmanov had given a charitable foundation linked to Medvedev a mansion in the Rublyovka area. Navalny called this a bribe, and Usmanov sued him and won. The court ordered the film removed from all platforms, but Navalny and his associates never complied.
In 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Anti-Corruption Foundation published a “list of corrupt officials and warmongers” naming 6,000 people. The foundation proposed adding them to Western sanctions lists for strengthening Putin’s regime and supporting Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Usmanov, like Fridman, is on this list.
That history may explain why current and former Anti-Corruption Foundation representatives have been so vocal in criticizing the decision to lift sanctions on Fridman and Usmanov.
Ukrainian authorities
Volodymyr Zelensky
president of Ukraine
At a time when Russia is carrying out brutal attacks on our people – and even now, during the UN General Assembly, air raid alerts are ongoing in many regions because of drones and ballistic missiles – signals about lifting sanctions on individual Russian oligarchs are self-defeating and counterproductive. Wars end through resolve and strength, not concessions to the aggressor’s entourage. I’m grateful to [European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen] for her readiness to work on adding more Russian names to the EU sanctions lists. These are the kinds of steps that bring a just peace and guaranteed security closer.
Andrii Sybiha
foreign minister of Ukraine
The decision to remove Usmanov and Fridman from the sanctions list is shameful and entirely unjustified. Moscow is celebrating, having gotten exactly what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the European Union, and a split among Europeans. I call on all EU member states to declare now that they will impose their own national sanctions against these two individuals.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk
Ukrainian presidential commissioner for sanctions policy
We consider the EU’s decision not to extend sanctions against Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman very strange. […] Lifting restrictions on individual Russian businessmen should not become a new practice. That is why we will keep proposing new sanctions measures, in particular regarding Russian oligarchs connected to Russia’s military-industrial complex.
European politicians
Pina Picierno
vice president of the European Parliament
The decision to delist Usmanov and Fridman is disgraceful, cowardly and completely unacceptable. But let’s be crystal clear about where political responsibility lies: with the Member States in the Council, not the Commission.
Under the EU treaties (such rules that must change!), the High Representative proposes sanctions, working with the Commission on their economic aspects. But restrictive measures can only be adopted unanimously by the Council.
This unanimity rule makes the EU fragile and weak. We need a politically strong, sovereign Europe: one that is more than the sum of its Member States.
Andris Kulbergs
head of Latvia’s government
Latvia agreed to a compromise but is not changing its principled stance.
We opposed the removal of Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the European Union’s sanctions list until the very end. […] However, the government had to make a responsible decision. The choice was between changing the status of two individuals and risking the loss of the entire sanctions regime. That is why Latvia’s representative will abstain in the vote. […]
Latvia is not backing down. The Foreign Ministry has been instructed to prepare the legal grounds for imposing national sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman.
Mindaugas Sinkevičius
prime minister of Lithuania
Oligarchs are part of Russia’s war machine. The regime’s “wallets” must not be allowed to feel at ease in Europe while Ukrainians are being killed. I have instructed the relevant authorities to initiate the process for imposing national restrictive measures on Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.
Margus Tsahkna
foreign minister of Estonia
The EU has just extended sanctions against nearly 3,000 individuals and entities linked to Russia’s aggression for another three years. This is a significant achievement, as it reduces the risk of future sanctions renewals becoming hostage to political bargaining.
However, to secure this agreement, sanctions against two prominent Russian businessmen, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, both known supporters of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, were lifted.
Estonia did not support this decision and abstained from the vote. We will now impose national sanctions on both individuals. Russia has not changed course. Neither should we.
Maciej Wąsik
member of the European Parliament from Poland
A compromising of the EU. Russian billionaires Usmanov and Fridman have been removed from the sanctions list. Only Latvia protested. Where was the Polish government? Where was the Polish protest?

Zelenskyy says Ukraine ready for ‘energy ceasefire,’ calls for trilateral meeting with Putin, Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:41:48 UTC
23:41:48 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on U.S. President Donald Trump to organize a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying the world leaders need to move "as quickly as possible" to bring an end to the war.
Zelenskyy spoke with Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.
The high-stakes meeting provided Ukraine's president with a rare sit-down opportunity to discuss ways to bring an end to Russia's full-scale invasion, further U.S. air defense support and security guarantees for Kyiv.
A winter package of Patriot missiles and licenses to produce the weapons domestically were two priorities for Ukraine over the coming months, Zelenskyy said.
"President Trump, our teams, and I spoke about how to end the war. This is the priority. We are ready. I'm not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire," Zelenskyy said overnight via social media, providing a roundup of his comments to reporters at the General Assembly.
Ukraine's president confirmed Kyiv is ready to agree to an energy truce on the condition that Russia does not attack its energy, electricity and heating infrastructure as well as its water supplies.
Trump has previously called on Ukraine to stop targeting Russian oil refineries with drone strikes, which he says are "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions from the Ukraine and Iran wars propel U.S. diesel prices to a record high.
In a post Monday on Truth Social, the U.S. president said Russia had "unfortunately lost control" of its diesel oil industry due to the war.
"I think the most important move President Trump can make – he can organize a trilateral meeting where the leaders can raise all the sensitive issues and try to end the war," Zelenskyy said.
Asked whether his comments mean he's prepared to meet directly with Putin and Trump to bring an end to the war, Zelenskyy replied: "I'm ready. I said it, I'm ready anytime when all the sides will be ready. I think we all need to move as quickly as possible."
CNBC has contacted a White House spokesperson and Russia's embassy in London for comment and is awaiting a response.
A meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy before expert-level discussions have taken place would be a waste of time, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday, according to Russia's state-run news agency RIA Novosti.
"Regarding Putin's meeting with Zelensky, our position is well known. Putin said that Zelensky, if he wishes, can come to Moscow," Peskov said.
Zelenskyy: Xi has 'influence on Putin'
On his meeting with Zelenskyy, Trump told reporters that he had spoken with his Ukrainian counterpart about finding a solution to end Russia's war. He also referenced a diplomatic push to bring an end to the conflict during his speech to General Assembly delegates.
"We will get that one done," Trump said.
Diplomatic talks have stalled as the U.S. has shifted focus to its war against Iran, although negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff traveled to Ukraine for the first time for talks with Zelenskyy earlier in the month.
Ukraine, which has stepped up its strikes on Russian oil facilities and logistics infrastructure in recent months, also called on Trump to discuss ways to bring an end to the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Wednesday.
"I said to the President, very openly, that we think if he also engages President Xi – he has influence on Putin. If we want to end this war, not just in messages, we all have to work 24/7 for this, for the people," Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine has insisted that Russian energy sites are legitimate military targets as it continues to resist Russian forces that invaded the country in early 2022. Russia's Defense Ministry has said it is planning "massive strikes" on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, amplifying fears of another winter assault.

Ukraine’s new drone ferries FPV drones deep behind Russian lines and releases them there. It costs about $9,900 and does three other jobs too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:38:52 UTC
23:38:52 KST

A Ukrainian company has disclosed a small aircraft that can bomb a target, relay radio signals, carry FPV drones behind enemy lines, or strike on its own. The KARA, a fixed-wing drone made by Ukrskytechnology, is listed on Ukraine's state Brave1 Market in three tiers, from a bare airframe to a ready-to-fly aircraft, Defender Media reported.
One airframe does the work of several, and it goes for some $9,900. The marketplace it sits on, Brave1 Market, has processed more than $235 million in orders, lists over a thousand products, and lets frontline units buy gear even before a weapon clears formal codification.
One airframe does four jobs
What the KARA does depends on how it is kitted out. Fitted one way, it drops cargo; another, it works as a signal repeater to extend a unit's radio reach; another, it ferries FPV drones deep into the enemy rear to be released; and another, it carries out strikes itself. Buyers choose among an empty glider they equip themselves, a Plug-N-Play version with basic electronics installed, and a Ready-To-Fly model.
The drone flies light and far
The specifications are modest but flexible, according to Ukrskytechnology. The KARA has a tactical radius of 70 kilometers, and a stated endurance of 2.5 hours, cruises at 90 kilometers per hour and tops out at 120, and works at 200 meters but can climb to 3,000.
It runs on either an electric motor or a combustion engine, and carries two payload blocks of up to three kilograms each under the wing. Launched by catapult and landing like a plane, it takes 10 minutes to set up.
The marketplace lists it now
The KARA is being prepared for codification, the formal approval that clears a weapon for standard state procurement, but it does not have to wait for that to reach the front. Brave1 Market was built precisely so that units can buy proven kit fast, without waiting on the slow pipelines of the past, and the KARA is already there for the price of a used car.
