From Vimeo to WeTransfer: How Italy’s Bending Spoons built a tech empire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:24:14 UTC
23:24:14 KST

Bending Spoons’ revenue more than tripled in two years as it acquired brands including Evernote, WeTransfer and Vimeo. Euronews Next looks at how the Italian company grew so quickly and whether it can keep going.
As Europe looks for ways to retain tech talent and build global businesses, an Italian company has quietly grown into one of the continent’s biggest tech success stories.
You may not know the company’s name, but you have likely used one of its products.
Founded in Milan in 2013, Bending Spoons has acquired a string of familiar digital brands, including Evernote, WeTransfer, Vimeo and Eventbrite in recent years.
Its annual revenue rose from $387 million (€338 mn) in 2023 to $1.31 billion (€1.14 bn) in 2025.
In July, the company went public on New York’s Nasdaq stock exchange.
So how did a company many people have never heard of come to own so many familiar names?
How has Bending Spoons grown so quickly?
Most tech companies try to invent a product and persuade people to use it. Bending Spoons often restructure an established product with a recognised name and existing customers that it believes could perform better under new ownership.
After a purchase, it may reorganise teams, rewrite software, redesign the product and change its marketing or pricing.
“We rearchitect the technology, product, and organisation, all of which is designed to speed up innovation, benefit customers, and strengthen business performance,” Nicolle Wasserman, People Operations lead at Bending Spoons, told Euronews Next.
Bending Spoons continues to develop the products it buys. It acquired, for instance, the video-editing app Splice in 2018 and the AI photo app Remini in 2021, then added new features to both.
The company says it has its own software engineers and tools for payments, data analysis and product testing that it uses across acquired businesses.
Large-scale layoffs have also repeatedly followed Bending Spoons’ acquisitions.
After it bought the note-taking app Evernote in early 2023, the company laid off most of its US- and Chile-based employees that July as it moved operations to Europe.
In 2024, it also said it planned to cut around 75% of the workforce at the file-sharing service WeTransfer, amounting to roughly 260 of its 350 workers.
Subscriptions are the main source of income across Bending Spoons’ portfolio, accounting for 84% of its revenue in the first quarter of 2026, according to company filings. By March 2026, its products reached more than 500 million monthly active users.
Buying more businesses is also different from growing the ones it already owns.
“Acquisition-led growth should not be confused with organic growth,” Yoram Wijngaarde, founder and CEO of global tech data firm Dealroom, told Euronews Next.
According to analysis from Dealroom, Bending Spoons’ acquisitions account for most of the dramatic increase in Bending Spoons’ revenue, although businesses it owned earlier have also grown.
Expansion in Europe
Bending Spoons is also expanding the teams behind its products. This week it opened an office in Warsaw, joining its headquarters in Milan and offices in London and Madrid.
The company said it had received 50,000 applications from candidates in Poland so far this year and plans to recruit locally for work across its businesses.
The Warsaw opening puts a concrete European dimension on a company whose products and customers span the world. But its wider significance, Wijngaarde suggested, lies in the kind of business it has built from Europe.
“Europe can be the buyer and operator of global software businesses, not just where companies are built before being acquired from abroad,” he said. “The contribution includes operating expertise and talent in Europe—not simply acquired assets. This complements, rather than replaces, building new companies.”
That does not mean other European firms could reproduce its results merely by buying software companies.
“Others can follow, but capital alone is insufficient,” Wijngaarde said. “The hard part is repeatedly improving products and economics while retaining users through major changes.”
Can it keep growing?
Keeping up its current strategy could become harder as Bending Spoons buys larger and more varied businesses.
Wijngaarde said the strategy could falter if Bending Spoons overpays for acquisitions, takes on too much debt or buys businesses it is less equipped to run.
“Cost savings are finite; ultimately, customers must keep finding the products worth paying for,” he said.
Whether it can keep growing will depend on whether users find those products worth staying with after the changes.
Higher prices or less free access could prompt them to leave, although Wijngaarde said the effects need to be assessed product by product.
The major staff reductions do not necessarily mean the products will stop improving, according to him. The measures to watch, he said, are “product quality, useful features and retention, not just headcount or margins”.

India to begin mass production of new laser anti-drone system — newspaper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:23:35 UTC
23:23:35 KST

NEW DELHI, September 23. /TASS/. India’s Defense Research and Development Organization (DRDO) plans to begin mass production of a new mobile laser system designed to destroy drones, The Times of India reported.
The 30-kW laser system is capable of intercepting unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) at a distance of up to 5 km. In August 2025, the platform underwent successful testing and will be ready for mass production in a few months at one of the DRDO’s partner companies.
This new development will allow the Indian Armed Forces to reduce their reliance on more expensive air defense systems to counter the threat posed by UAVs.
Previously, the DRDO developed a 2-kW laser weapon for destroying drones, which is already being manufactured by defense companies Adani, Astra, and Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL). India has also developed a 10-kW laser weapon for engaging aerial targets, with production contracts awarded to Larsen & Toubro and BEL.
As part of India’s ongoing Sudarshan Chakra program to develop a multi-layered air defense system, the DRDO is working on the development of 50-kW and 100-kW laser systems.

Higher fuel bills are costing the EU €270 million a day on average, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:22:26 UTC
23:22:26 KST

Diesel accounts for most of the extra road fuel cost. T&E estimates that an EU diesel driver paid €142 more over the period it studied, while a German long-haul truck faced an extra €236 a week.
Since the start of the Iran war, higher road fuel prices have cost the EU an estimated €53 billion, according to a report published on Wednesday by Brussels-based environmental group Transport & Environment (T&E).
Most of that extra cost — €40 billion — came from diesel. T&E estimates that higher road fuel prices have added an average of €270 million a day to transport costs, including €203 million a day for diesel. The remaining €67 million a day is attributable to petrol.
The estimates compare costs during the war with the same period last year, adjusted for inflation. They cover the 28 weeks to 6 September.
“Europe is the most reliant major economy on diesel,” T&E says.
Diesel and gasoil account for about 43% of the oil products used in the EU by volume — around 16 percentage points above the global average and roughly twice the US share. Nearly four in 10 passenger cars on EU roads ran on diesel in 2024.
Road transport used 77% of the EU’s diesel and gasoil that year. Cars accounted for the largest share of road use, followed by heavy trucks and buses, then vans. Diesel is also used in farming, construction and some homes, though fuel used by machinery off the road is not included in T&E’s €203 million daily road diesel estimate.
For drivers, the increase is substantial. T&E estimates that the average EU diesel car driver paid about €142 more over the period it studied than in the comparable period last year. By 14 September, filling a 50-litre diesel tank cost about €30 more than before the war, it says.
Businesses face higher bills too. An average German long-haul diesel truck incurred about €6,000 in extra fuel costs over the period, equivalent to €236 a week, according to T&E. That is an example based on a German truck, rather than an average for trucks across the EU.
Why has diesel become so expensive?
Crude oil prices have risen sharply since the war began, but the price of diesel has risen faster. The conflict has disrupted fuel production and exports from the Middle East, while attacks on Russian refineries have further reduced global supply.
T&E says diesel and gasoil exports from the Middle East and Russia together fell by almost 75% in August compared with a year earlier. The gap between the price of crude oil and wholesale diesel exceeded $100 a barrel in early September, against a typical range of $10 to $30. That points to a shortage of refined diesel as well as more expensive crude.
The weighted average EU diesel price reached €2.159 a litre on 14 September, the highest in the European Commission’s series dating back to 2005.
ECB experts told Euronews Business last week that, based on fuel futures at the time, diesel refining margins were expected to peak in October. That was a forecast for margins, not a prediction of when pump prices would peak.
Supply could tighten further in autumn as demand for heating oil, farm machinery and freight rises while refineries carry out seasonal maintenance. The US is also considering a full or partial ban on diesel exports. President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he supported the idea, but no ban has been announced. Such a move could make it harder for Europe to secure supplies.
What could reduce diesel costs in Europe?
Using the International Energy Agency’s previously recommended measures to cut consumption, T&E estimates that four measures together could cut diesel demand from cars by 15% in the short term. These include increased working from home where possible, supported by T&E’s calculation that three additional remote working days per week could reduce a driver’s fuel bills by up to 20%.
Further measures include lowering current motorway speed limits, investing in better public transport and providing advice on fuel-saving driving, including maintaining tyre pressure.
In the longer term, the group argues that electric vehicles would reduce Europe’s exposure to oil price shocks. It estimates that nearly eight million electric cars in the EU avoided the use of about 46 million barrels of oil in 2025, saving €2.9 billion in oil imports.

IDF: Drakon submarine has stronger weapons, longer underwater capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:22:08 UTC
23:22:08 KST

The German-made INS Drakon submarine, which will be officially accepted in Israel at a ceremony on Thursday, has stronger weapons and longer underwater capabilities than prior Israeli submarines, according to the IDF.
The Drakon submarine is the sixth submarine to join the Israeli Navy’s fleet in recent years and the third of the Dolphin class – specifically, the Dolphin II variant equipped with an Air-Independent Propulsion system.
This AIP system allows the submarine to generate energy and recharge its batteries while submerged for extended periods, with no need to surface or access external air.
Earlier submarines could only remain submerged for a couple of days, eventually a couple of weeks, but the Dolphin-II class Drakon can do so for much longer.
Part of the Drakon’s system utilizes hydrogen and oxygen to generate energy, which enables the submarine to extend the duration of its covert underwater operations and maintain operational capability over time.
The submarine measures over 70 meters in length, making it approximately 30% larger than the original Dolphin-class submarines. The section visible above the water accounts for less than one-fifth of its total size.
While neither Israel nor the German company ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS) has revealed why the Drakon has an expanded design or confirmed what new systems it has installed, experts have speculated that the expanded design could include new capabilities – such as possible vertical launching systems (VLS).
These systems, if present, could substantially increase the submarine’s potential uses by enabling it to deploy additional weapons, cruise missiles, unmanned underwater systems (UUVs), intelligence equipment, or special operations capabilities.
Some experts have speculated that the expansion could also relate to launch cells, but the precise internal configuration remains unknown.
What has been published is that the Drakon has 10 torpedo tubes located in the bow: six standard 533 mm tubes and four oversized 650 mm tubes. The wider tubes can launch heavier weapons, specialized equipment, and even UUVs.
According to reports, the submarines are able to deliver nuclear weapons. Multiple foreign publications have noted that Israeli submarines are part of a triad of nuclear deterrence that Israel possesses, along with land-based and air-based weapons.
During Defense Ministry Director-General Amir Baram and other senior defense officials’ stay in Germany in December 2025, they made new progress regarding the ongoing submarine deals, which have unique offensive and defensive capabilities, The Jerusalem Post reported at the time.
Though Israel has never publicly admitted to possessing nuclear weapons, former prime ministers and others, notably Ehud Olmert, have at times slipped up and alluded to such a weapons program.
The arrival of the Drakon completes the second generation of Israeli Navy submarines built in Germany, which Israel has said symbolizes the long-standing defense partnership between the two countries.
The voyage from Germany to Israel covers a distance of approximately 4,000 nautical miles (8,000 kilometers) and took the Drakon just over three weeks, but it can also take up to a month.
Possible delays due to various diplomatic maritime issues Israel has encountered
There may have been delays due to various diplomatic maritime problems that Israel has encountered, which have been publicly reported since the beginning of the Israel-Hamas War.
Departing from the TKMS shipyard in Kiel, Germany, the Drakon transited across part of the Atlantic Ocean near Western Europe and passed through the Strait of Gibraltar to the Mediterranean Sea.
The vessel’s arrival in Israel was the culmination of over 12 years of development, including months of trials and preparations.
Close cooperation was maintained throughout the project among the Israeli Navy, the German Navy, and the German Defense Ministry, as well as the German professionals involved in the submarine’s construction.
Israeli direct involvement in joint naval projects with Germany continues
Israeli involvement in the project has spanned approximately 20 years, managed by an Israeli project directorate operating in Germany that oversaw the design, construction, and testing phases.
Officers and engineers from the Israeli Navy served in the project directorate, relocating to Germany with their families for periods of several years. Submarine squadron crews joined the project at a later stage, participating in drills at sea, testing, and the process of judging the ship’s readiness and delivering it to the Israeli Navy.
Israeli direct involvement in joint naval projects with Germany continues, looking ahead to the next generation of submarines – the Dakar-class – which are currently under construction and have an expected delivery start date in 2031.
The Drakon incorporates advanced technological capabilities that expand the Israeli Navy’s operational toolkit, enabling it to operate across a diverse range of arenas and missions.
Beyond the technology, the submarine squadron relies on its human capital – young crews demonstrating high levels of professionalism, responsibility, composure, and operational sharpness.
Submariners operate complex combat systems over extended periods in distant maritime theaters, working in challenging conditions of secrecy and isolation from the outside world.

As many as 17 people killed by bear attacks in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:21:30 UTC
23:21:30 KST

KRASNOYARSK, September 23. /TASS/. The number of people killed by bear attacks in Russia in recent months has risen to 17. Such attacks have occurred in the Siberian and Far Eastern federal districts, according to TASS estimates.
The highest death toll was recorded in the Krasnoyarsk Region in Siberia, where six people have died in bear attacks. Three people have been killed in each of the Tomsk and Irkutsk Regions, while two deaths have been reported in Buryatia. Fatal bear attacks on people have also been recorded in Altai, Kamchatka and the Khabarovsk Region.
Forest fires in the Krasnoyarsk Region and a poor pine nut harvest were among the reasons for the large number of bears coming into contact with people. The latest case was reported on September 23, when a bear attacked a guard at a truck parking lot in northern Krasnoyarsk Region.
Overall, TASS estimates that bears have approached populated areas in 41 Russian regions in 2026. The situation has been particularly difficult in Eastern Siberia. Bears have approached schools and military units and tried to enter private homes in the north of the region. Bears have also been spotted in popular tourist recreation areas in Krasnoyarsk, including the Gremyachaya Griva eco-park, near the Krasnoyarsk Pillars National Park and in an upscale cottage community in the Udachny neighborhood.
A heightened-alert regime has been introduced throughout the Irkutsk Region, while a curfew is in effect in Baikalsk. A heightened-alert regime has also been introduced in the city of Abaza in southern Khakassia, where, according to local authorities, bears have placed the city under "de facto siege." Regional authorities plan to extend the regime to the entire republic.

US sanctions could make ICC operations impossible, lawyer says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:20:49 UTC
23:20:49 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. US sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) could make its day-to-day operations and investigations impossible due to restrictions related to the US financial system and technology, Artur Gulasaryan, an associate professor at the Kutafin Moscow State Law University (MSAL), told TASS.
Reuters earlier reported, citing two sources, that US President Donald Trump’s administration had prepared a full package of sanctions against the ICC as an organization and planned to announce their introduction soon.
"Cutting the ICC off from US technology and the financial system makes it impossible to conduct its day-to-day operations and investigations," Gulasaryan said.
The lawyer explained that due to the sanctions, the ICC could lose access to US financial and technology services without special authorization from the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). "The financial aspect of the restrictions involves the inevitable blocking of dollar correspondent accounts and transactions, which, under strict banking compliance rules, effectively isolates the ICC from the international settlement system and makes standard cross-border payments impossible," he said. "The court’s operations are further paralyzed by the severe deterioration of its IT infrastructure: due to OFAC restrictions, the institution loses legal access to US-licensed software, cloud data storage services and secure communications systems."

23:19:45 KST

At least 16 former and serving senior officials in Russia’s regional and municipal executive branches have been killed after going to war against Ukraine, The Insider has calculated based on data from open sources. The tally includes officials ranging from deputy heads of municipal districts or urban districts to deputy governors. Ten of the 16 had been convicted or were facing criminal cases before going to war, mostly on bribery and abuse-of-office charges.
The latest known case is that of former Belgorod mayor and Belgorod Region deputy governor Konstantin Polezhayev. The Kremlin-aligned media outlet Kommersant reported his death on Sept. 22, citing two people close to the former official. One said Polezhayev had served in an assault unit and was killed in a missile strike in the Kharkiv Region.
Polezhayev served as mayor of Belgorod from 2015 to 2019 before becoming a deputy governor. He was detained in 2023 on charges of bribery, with state investigators alleging that a construction company gave him two luxury SUVs, a Porsche Panamera, and a Range Rover worth a combined 18 million rubles ($214,000) in exchange for favorable treatment connected to government contracts. In August 2024, a court sentenced Polezhayev to five years in prison, after which he signed a contract with Russia’s Ministry of Defense.
In April 2025, the independent Belgorod-based outlet Pepel reported that Polezhayev was allegedly only formally listed with a BARS reserve unit and was in fact still living at home. It is not clear when he was actually first sent to the front.
The other casualties
Of the 16 cases of officials’ deaths identified by The Insider, three involved figures who had held positions at the deputy governor level. Sergei Efremov, who was then serving as deputy governor of Primorsky Krai, was killed in early 2025 in Russia’s Kursk Region. He had overseen domestic policy in the region while also commanding the Tiger volunteer unit. Former Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug deputy governor Alexei Zolotukhin, who had been responsible for security in the regional government, volunteered for the war after leaving office and was killed in 2026. The third was Polezhayev.
The Insider found three more cases involving senior city officials. Former first deputy head of Yugorsk Dmitry Krylov signed a contract with the military and commanded an assault platoon before being killed in battles for Avdiivka in February 2024. Former Chelyabinsk Deputy Mayor Sergei Reprintsev went to war after being arrested in a 10 million-ruble ($119,000) bribery case and was killed in May 2025. Former Magnitogorsk Deputy Mayor Dmitry Gavrilov, who had been sentenced to 10 years in prison for bribery, also signed a contract with Russia’s MoD and was subsequently killed in Ukraine. His death became public only in September 2026.
Another 10 cases involved the heads and deputy heads of districts and urban districts. Igor Ustyuzhanin, the former head of Manturovo, was killed after going to war after receiving an 8.5-year prison sentence for corruption. The former head of the Ketovsky District in the Kurgan Region, Alexander Noskov, also joined the Russian army from prison, where he was serving a six-year sentence for abuse of office; he was killed in Ukraine in February 2024. The former head of the Tsimlyansky District in the Rostov Region, Vladimir Svetlichny, had been convicted of abuse and exceeding his authority; he was also killed after being deployed to the front.
Former first deputy head and acting head of the Kortkerossky District in the Komi Republic Alexander Arteyev, who had received an 11-year prison sentence for bribery, embezzlement, and abuse of office, was killed in June 2024. The former head of the Perm Region’s Gornozavodsky District, Alexander Afanasyev, who was sentenced to three years for abuse of authority, signed a contract in December 2024 and was later killed. The former head of the Tselinny District in the Kurgan region, Alexander Sytov, was declared dead in summer 2026. Before the war, he had been sentenced to seven years in prison for bribery, fraud, and embezzlement, including the theft of 100,000 rubles ($1,200) collected for mobilized soldiers.
Fyodor Ivashchuk, head of the Ulchsky District in the Khabarovsk Region, resigned in March 2025, voluntarily signed a contract with the Russian army, and joined the BARS-8 Khabarovsk unit. He was killed that August while carrying out a combat mission. Aidar Zagirov, deputy head of the Uchalinsky District in Bashkortostan, was also serving under contract and was killed during a combat mission. The former deputy head of Novorossiysk’s intracity district, Oleg Skornyakov, signed a contract with Russia’s Ministry of Defense in spring 2025, went missing several months later, and was officially confirmed dead in March 2026.
Former deputy head of the Tugulymsky Urban District in the Sverdlovsk Region Sergei Utkin, who had been sentenced to eight years in prison for taking an especially large bribe, signed a contract with the Russian army while incarcerated and was also killed at the front.
Ten of the 16 were involved in criminal cases
Ten of the 16 officials The Insider identified had faced criminal prosecution before going to war. Nine — Polezhayev, Gavrilov, Ustyuzhanin, Noskov, Svetlichny, Arteyev, Afanasyev, Sytov and Utkin — had been convicted. Reprintsev was under investigation on charges of bribery when he signed his contract.
The Insider reported in 2024 that the war had allowed some former officials to leave prison or put criminal cases on hold, former Vladivostok Mayor Oleg Gumenyuk and former Khakassia Deputy Governor Sergei Novikov prominent among them. Some later returned to Russia after serving their allotted time in the military.
The tally does not, however, include former Krasnodar Region Deputy Governor Sergei Vlasov. Reports of his death surfaced in spring 2026, but Kommersant found that Vlasov was officially listed as missing and that his body had not been found.
The Insider also excluded judges, security officials, election commission members, heads of individual administrative departments, members of parliaments at all levels, and officials killed by shelling or mines while performing their civilian duties. The count includes only serving or former executive officials at the level of deputy district head or higher who entered military service or joined volunteer formations.
A broader count now includes at least 51 dead
If the count is expanded beyond senior executive officials, the number is significantly higher. In February 2025, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty counted at least 32 Russian government officials who had been killed in Ukraine. That category included election commission officials, members of parliament at various levels, and a federal judge in addition to government officials.
In June 2026, the independent outlet Meduza found open-source reports of at least 16 additional deaths that were published after RFE/RL had completed its project, bringing the minimum estimate to 48. Since the Meduza study was published, at least three more deaths have become publicly known: those of Alexander Sytov in July, Dmitry Gavrilov in September, and Konstantin Polezhayev on Sept. 22. Using the broader definition of “government representatives,” the minimum toll now stands at at least 51, according to The Insider’s calculations.

News
€50 fuel compensation to be paid to 550,000 people amid rising fuel prices
Wednesday 23 September 2026 16:11
Wednesday, 23 September 2026, 16:11
PHOTO BTA
Font size
More than 550,000 people on low incomes will receive a one-off payment of €50 to help offset increased household consumption costs resulting from higher fuel prices. The measure is part of a new government support scheme for the most vulnerable people and families, the government press service announced.
The one-off compensation will be available to individuals and families with incomes below the poverty line who receive social assistance; children and young people up to the age of 21 without parental care who are leaving residential social services; people receiving heating assistance during the current winter season; and families raising children with permanent disabilities.
The compensation will be paid automatically by the Social Assistance Directorates across the country, using the same method by which recipients receive their other forms of social assistance, either into a bank account or by post.
Recipients will not be required to submit an application to receive the funds.

Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti
on Wednesday called for changes to the way national statistics
agency Istat compiles its data after the government suffered a
significant setback related to a budget-deficit figure.
                                    
                                       
				Istat said Tuesday that Italy's deficit-to-GDP ratio for 2025
was 3.1%, confirming the provisional figure it gave in April and
dashing hopes the country would be able emerge from its EU
excessive-deficit infringement procedure.
                                    
                                       
				The government had been hoping the figure would be revised down
to within the 3% threshold allowed by the EU's budget rules.
                                    
                                       
				"While rooted in specific statistical requirements, the
continuous updating of ISTAT data undeniably has a significant
impact on national budgetary decisions, as it modifies—after the
fact—the parameters used in the European fiscal surveillance
procedure and in the preparation of public finance documents,
which are even more sensitive to changes in light of the new
European economic governance," Giorgetti said during a
question-time session in the Lower House.
                                    
                                       
				"The Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF) has repeatedly called
for regulatory changes to strengthen the data collection system
already in place—which is not always compatible with the
requirements for compiling the accounts—particularly regarding
public-private partnership (PPP) operations involving a very
large number of public administrations."

Burnham stands by claim UK is ‘in hock’ to bond markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:17:49 UTC
23:17:49 KST

Andy Burnham has said he still believes the UK is far too exposed to global shocks, defending comments last year when he said the UK should be less “in hock” to the bond markets.
He said the comments had been deliberately misinterpreted by the former prime minister Keir Starmer and his advisers and said his aim was not more borrowing and spending but a far more resilient economy.
Burnham’s comments in an interview with the New Statesmen last year made waves before the Labour conference because of the then Greater Manchester’s clear ambitions to replace Starmer as prime minister.
In a fresh interview with the magazine on Wednesday, he said he had intended to highlight how vulnerable the UK was to global price fluctuations. Government borrowing has climbed again over the past months as energy prices have risen in response to continued deadlock on the Iran war.
The UK government borrowed a higher than expected £18.3bn last month, putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, as he prepares for next month’s budget.
Burnham said he wanted to build an economy that was far less vulnerable. “I mean, the point about the bond markets, it holds – in that what I was saying was the country has left itself over-exposed,” he said, telling the magazine he was arguing for a “much more streamlined, productive state”.
He said criticism from Starmer and the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, was unjustified. “They couldn’t understand why I was saying some of the things that I was saying … [They] didn’t know what to do with it, but they did what they always do, which is they pulled one line out of it and then framed that one line within their world, rather than the one that I was talking about.”
Burnham also addressed criticism from the Conservatives after he said during an exchange at prime minister’s questions that national security “should not come at the expense of social security” – which opponents said showed he was not willing to cut the welfare budget to fund increased defence spending.
“It oversimplifies the political discourse that we need to have, doesn’t it?” he said.
Burnham, who will address his first Labour conference as prime minister in Liverpool next Tuesday, said he would set out his political vision, which would be a break from the economic and political mainstream of the past 40 years.
“It’s about control,” he said. “If you strip it back, and all the fluff and, you know, the verbiage, you can actually strip it back to one word, which is control.”
He said that would be a business-friendly approach, rather than purely statist. “People aren’t going to come in and invest in a significant way where the place isn’t functional and it’s in major decline,” he said, saying it was the state’s job to “create the optimum conditions for private-sector investment”.
“We’ve just got to get that belief back into Britain that, yeah, we know what we’re about, we know what we stand for, that is what we’ve always been, so we can do it again.”
In attempts to calm jittery bond markets, Burnham has previously said his budget would “stick to the fiscal rules” on debt and borrowing set out under Reeves, “but at the same time we will help reduce cost of living pressure on our constituents”.

A Tunisian activist's journey from Gaza flotilla hero to jailed hunger striker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:16:45 UTC
23:16:45 KST

A Tunisian activist’s journey from Gaza flotilla hero to jailed hunger striker
TUNIS, Sept 23 - A year ago, Wael Naouar stood on the deck of a boat at Sidi Bou Said port on Tunisia's Mediterranean coast, waving to thousands of supporters before setting off to try to deliver humanitarian aid to Gaza by breaking Israel's naval blockade.
Today, Naouar is more than a month into an open-ended hunger strike in a prison outside Tunis, demanding that the charges of financial misconduct against him and three other activists arrested with him be dropped.
"I don't understand why they arrested him. My son did nothing wrong," Naouar's mother, Hamida Dridi, told Reuters during an interview in the family home, weeping as she sat before a large photograph of her son.
Critics say the arrests mark another milestone in a campaign against activists, journalists and opposition politicians, who flourished after 2011 "Arab Spring" pro-democracy protests but have been targeted since President Kais Saied accumulated power in 2021.
The government denies the prosecutions are political and Saied says freedoms are guaranteed, the judiciary is independent, and no one is above the law.
VIDEO OF CONFRONTATION WITH ISRAELI SOLDIERS SPREADS ONLINE
A longtime political activist and critic of Tunisia's authorities, Naouar had spent two decades protesting against unemployment and pursuing social justice before shifting his attention to the Palestinian cause during the war in Gaza.
When Israeli soldiers intercepted his boat, one of a few dozen that sailed as part of the Global Sumud Flotilla initiative that also included Swedish activist Greta Thunberg, a video clip showing him confronting them spread widely online.
Naouar was detained in March with three other Sumud Flotilla organisers on charges of money laundering and misuse of donated funds, which they all deny.
There is broad support in Tunisia for the Palestinian cause, including from authorities, but the arrested men's lawyers say they are being targeted over their activism because of their popularity. Authorities say the case is part of an apolitical judicial and financial investigation.
Naouar's lawyer, family members and civil society groups say his health has deteriorated. He is "in a very critical health condition and on the verge of death," said Bassem Trifi, president of the Tunisian League for Human Rights.
A prison spokesperson did not immediately reply to requests for comment on Naouar's case and condition.
DETENTION DRAWS PROTESTS
Naouar's detention has inspired protests in the streets of the capital, including one last week that ended with 14 arrests.
"He is on hunger strike, and the authorities are doing nothing," Tunisian artist Mounir Troudi said at that protest.
For Naouar's family, the political arguments are less urgent than the question of whether he makes it back home alive.
"The laughter is gone. The atmosphere in our family is gone," his mother said.
His brother, Nabil, said that if anything happened to him he would hold the president and justice ministry responsible.
In Tunisia, there is no direct line of contact for media to the presidency or justice ministry. The prime minister's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. REUTERS

Moroccans head to polls amid economic uncertainty to decide next parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:16:37 UTC
23:16:37 KST

Moroccans vote in parliamentary elections amid economic uncertainty
More than 15.8 million registered voters are choosing among 27 political parties to determine the nation’s next government.
Millions of voters went to polls in Morocco on Wednesday to determine the makeup of the House of Representatives, the parliament’s lower house.
Twenty-seven political parties are competing for 395 seats in the country’s 12th legislative election since independence in 1956.
Almost 16 million people are able to vote, with 55 percent residing in urban areas and 45 percent in rural regions, seeing a mix of concerns among voters.
Economic frustrations
While King Mohammed VI will maintain most executive powers, the new government will manage many public affairs for the coming years.
Once the votes are counted, the king will appoint the head of government from the leading party, but they will still need the support of 198 deputies – an absolute majority – to gain parliamentary confidence.
The election comes at a time of mounting challenges for the country, with the economic situation creating discontent and frustration, Mohammed Masbah, head of the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis, told Al Jazeera.
“The upcoming elections will have special importance because they come in a context tied to a social and economic crisis, especially high prices and the cost of living on one hand,” Masbah told Al Jazeera.
“On the other hand, there is a state of frustration among broad segments of society, especially the youth. The Gen Z protests last year, as well as the attempt to cross towards Ceuta a few weeks ago, demonstrate this crisis.”
The introduction of a new financial system designed to support candidates aged 35 could encourage more youth participation. But the nearly six million Moroccans residing overseas, many of them younger citizens, will have to appoint a proxy in Morocco to cast their vote.
There is also an upcoming key milestone for the country with the 2030 World Cup, which requires huge investments. What will remain in the minds of most voters is the state of the economy and inflation, which have impacted the living standards of many Moroccans.
“I believe the upcoming elections will produce a government majority whose primary function will be to address these imbalances, especially the economic ones related to the high cost of living in Morocco,” Masbah said.
“Regarding the issues that were raised and discussed by the majority of political parties, whether represented in the government or the opposition, they are the issue of employment and high prices.”
Two of the main parties competing in the election, the National Rally of Independents and the Authenticity and Modernity Party, have put these issues at the front of their campaigns in what has been a heated election.
“Of course, this is the main topic, but in the public debate, we also noticed conflicts, especially between the top two parties currently running the government,” Masbah said. “We noticed mudslinging and accusations of squandering funds and stealing candidates, which may increase voter alienation from voting today.”
Despite the tense conditions, Morocco’s Public Prosecution has recorded a significant drop in election-related complaints compared with the 2021 vote.
But legal amendments that criminalise digital offences for the first time – including the dissemination of fake news and false allegations intended to defame candidates or voters – have been introduced. The digital space became the primary arena for violations this year, accounting for 22 complaints.
Masbah said that despite a mood of frustration in Morocco over the government’s inability to manage key economic and social issues, turnout is expected to remain steady, as it has been over the past 20 years, due to structural factors.
“Electoral and voting behaviour in Morocco is not primarily linked to electoral programmes and promises [of parties], as much as it is linked to the stable bloc formed by Moroccan deserts and villages, which relies primarily on a network of notables who have influence and the ability to win voters’ voices through utilitarian voting,” Masbah said.
“I expect that if there is a decline in the voting rate – and this is likely – it will not be catastrophic or a sharp decline, given the consideration I mentioned earlier, which is the focus on notables and traditional elites in winning over voters.”

Golan Heights will remain Syrian territory: Al Sharaa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:16:20 UTC
23:16:20 KST

Syrian President Ahmed al Sharaa has said the Golan Heights will remain Syrian territory, rejecting Israel’s annexation measures as invalid under international law.
Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Sharaa said attempts to impose “facts on the ground” could not undermine Syria’s sovereignty or the applicability of international law.
“The Golan will remain Syrian land,” he said, referring to UN Security Council Resolution 497, which declares Israel’s 1981 decision to impose its laws and administration on the occupied Golan Heights “null and void”.
Al Sharaa also referred to a UN General Assembly vote in December 2025 in which 123 countries backed a resolution concerning the occupied Syrian Golan. He thanked countries that supported it and urged those that abstained to reconsider their position on Resolution 497.
He accused Israel of carrying out nearly 500 air and artillery strikes, more than 1,200 incursions and around 300 arrests and detentions of Syrians, saying the actions threatened Syria’s stability and defied international consensus.
Al Sharaa said Damascus remained committed to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and continued to call for Israeli forces to withdraw to the lines held before December 8, 2024.
He rejected what he described as Israeli attempts to impose “new facts on the ground”, saying such actions across the region undermined security and stability.
The address marked Al Sharaa’s second consecutive appearance at the UN General Assembly. He attended the 80th session in September 2025, becoming the first Syrian president to participate in the gathering since 1967.

H&N JSC — formerly Danone Russia and now operating under the Logika Moloka (lit. “Milk Logic”) brand. Zakriev, a nephew of Kadyrov’s, has served as the company’s CEO since July 2023.
Aptar Vladimir’s financial statements, which have been reviewed by The Insider’s editorial team, indicate that the company remains highly profitable. Revenue totaled about 1.75 billion rubles in 2025, virtually unchanged from the previous year, while net profit rose about 7%, from 502 million rubles ($5.9 million) to 537 million rubles ($6.4 million). Its net profit margin was close to 31%.
The Vladimir plant manufactures plastic packaging products. Russian certification registries list lids, caps, and dispensers among its products. Aptar itself includes the Vladimir facility in its Beauty division and lists it among the group’s Russian manufacturing sites.
Aptar Europe Holding is the French subsidiary of U.S.-based AptarGroup. The group operates in more than 20 countries and reported sales of about $3.8 billion in 2025. Its Russian business has operated since 2003.
H&N JSC, which has now been given control of the Aptar plant, itself came under Russian government control through the same temporary-management mechanism. In July 2023, Putin placed Danone’s Russian business under the control of Rosimushchestvo, Russia’s federal property management agency. After that, Zakriev was appointed head of the company.
In March 2024, Putin removed the assets from temporary management, and Danone later sold its Russian business to Vamin R. As The Insider previously reported, citing an investigation by the investigative project Sistema, assets worth more than 1 billion euros ultimately went to structures linked to Kadyrov’s circle, with a significant portion of the purchase financed using money from the former Danone business itself.
Russia’s temporary management mechanism for foreign-owned assets has been in place since April 2023. Formally, the foreign owner retains legal ownership while a manager appointed by Russian authorities receives broad powers to run the business. In practice, the arrangement has already preceded foreign companies losing control of their Russian assets, as occurred with Danone. On Sept. 17, Putin used the same mechanism to place the Russian businesses of Auchan, Nestlé, and FM Logistic under the management of L.E.V. Management. The Insider found that at the time, the company was still listed on a registrar’s website among ready-made joint-stock companies being offered for sale — the price was 450,000 rubles ($5,340).

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Italian police discovered €3.2 million (over $3.6 million) in cash concealed inside the walls of a house during an operation targeting an alleged mafia-linked criminal organization near Naples.
The money, mostly in €50 banknotes wrapped in plastic, was recovered after officers broke through the walls of a property in Caivano. Eleven luxury watches worth more than €127,000 were also found.
Italian news agency ANSA reported earlier this week that the operation targeted 34 suspects, with 23 ordered into custody and 11 placed under house arrest.
Investigators believe the organization was linked to the Angelino clan, which operates in Caivano and Casoria, and was involved in drug trafficking and extortion.
According to ANSA, collaborators of justice played a decisive role in the investigation, during which Carabinieri found €3.2 million in cash while searching the home of a person believed to be among the group’s leaders.
The investigation, which covered activities between 2021 and July 2025, also detailed how alleged drug-selling operations were organized, with regular deliveries and payment schedules.
Investigators said some dealing operations were largely managed within families to limit the involvement of outsiders.

curved mirrored steel walls multiply one tree into forest at infinite grove pavilion in shanghai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:15:09 UTC
23:15:09 KST

Infinite Grove pavilion reflects a single tree into infinity
One tree becomes an endless forest in Infinite Grove, a traveling pavilion by Chang Hao Studio in Shanghai. Two curved mirrored–steel walls reflect a single tree back and forth, creating a forest with no visible edge. First presented in spring at the 2026 Shanghai International Flower Festival, the pavilion has since moved across the city, pairing the same structure with different trees for each season.
One tree, multiplied, shapes a forest within two walls
Infinite Grove is a pop-up pavilion built by Chang Hao Studio around a single tree. Two curved mirrored-steel walls multiply it through reflection, while a circular entrance reveals only part of the interior. Frosted panels diffuse daylight into a soft haze, making it difficult to distinguish the real tree from its reflections.
Inside, the tree appears above while its repeated reflections surround the visitor, incorporating their own figure into the mirrored landscape. The experience unfolds through three stages: a partial view through the circular opening, the first glimpse of the reflected forest, and the realization that the entire scene originates from a single tree.
Infinite Grove multiplies a single tree into a forest of reflections
The traveling pavilion forms A garden for the city
Infinite Grove was selected by Xiaohongshu (RED) Design Week for the 2026 Shanghai International Flower Festival, held from April 18th to May 10th, 2026. The expanded festival brought gardens beyond traditional exhibition grounds and into shopping districts, parks, and streets across two main venues and ten sub-venues throughout Shanghai.
The pavilion was installed at the Huangpu main venue in Xintiandi among more than forty themed gardens. The festival received approximately 29.5 million visits. Within the dense urban setting, Infinite Grove uses a compact footprint to create an interior that appears much larger than its physical dimensions.
two curved mirrored-steel walls create the pavilion’s endless landscape
A Chinese garden of framed views and borrowed scenery
The design draws on two principles of the classical Chinese garden: framed views (kuangjing) and borrowed scenery (jiejing). These are used as spatial strategies rather than historical references. Traditional gardens often use a small doorway or window to frame a landscape beyond its apparent scale. Infinite Grove applies the same approach through its circular entrance, withholding the full view until the visitor enters.
Here, the borrowed scenery is the tree itself. Reflections extend it beyond the limits of the site, turning a pavilion only a few steps across into a forest-like interior.
the real tree becomes difficult to distinguish from its reflections
Curved mirrored steel, frosted panels, and a living tree
The pavilion uses a compact material palette of curved mirrored steel, frosted panels, and a single living tree. The mirrored walls create the repeated landscape, while the frosted panels filter daylight and soften the interior.
The structure is prefabricated in a factory and requires no foundations. On site, it is simply positioned in place, limiting its impact on the ground. The completed pavilion can be transported on a single truck, allowing the entire structure to move between locations.
a circular opening frames a partial view of the interior
Chang Hao Studio composes A pavilion that travels
Infinite Grove is designed as a mobile installation, with its central tree changing according to the season and setting. At the flower festival in spring, a flowering azalea stood at the center, its blossoms multiplying across the mirrored walls to create a forest of color.
For its second site in summer, the azalea was replaced by an olive tree. Its silver-green foliage and twisting trunk gave the reflected landscape a lighter character. The structure remained unchanged, while the different tree produced a new spatial and visual environment.
The pavilion continues to travel through Shanghai as a mobile installation, with each new tree reshaping the forest created inside the two mirrored walls.
the compact pavilion creates an interior that appears to extend beyond its physical limits
frosted panels diffuse daylight across the mirrored pavilion
a single tree appears repeatedly across the pavilion’s curved walls
azalea blossoms multiply across the mirrored walls to create a forest of color
a flowering azalea formed the center of Infinite Grove in spring
different trees reshape the reflected landscape while the pavilion structure remains unchanged
the circular aperture draws on the framed-view tradition of Chinese gardens

Netherlands pushes EU action to safeguard ICC from further US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:14:59 UTC
23:14:59 KST

The Netherlands has asked the European Commission to prepare a "blocking statute" to protect the International Criminal Court (ICC) from possible further US sanctions, the foreign minister said on Wednesday.
In an interview with Dutch daily De Volkskrant on the margins of the UN General Assembly in New York, Tom Berendsen expressed his concern over continued pressure on the ICC and court officials.
He said new sanctions are possible. "We are preparing for anything."
"Within the European Union, we stand strong together, but outside of it, there are individual countries that feel the US is increasing the pressure, and they cannot simply ignore that," said Berendsen.
His remarks came after The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday that US President Donald Trump's administration is preparing to implement expansive economic sanctions against the court.
Saying that the US has never supported the court, Berendsen added there is now a "massive" hardening of attitudes that could make the institution’s functioning impossible.
"We will do everything we can to protect the court," he noted.
Berendsen added: "The Netherlands has asked the European Commission to prepare the blocking statute so that we can deploy that drastic measure. We are prepared to use it."
What is blocking statute?
The blocking statute is a legal mechanism designed to protect EU companies and individuals from the extraterritorial application of specific third-country laws, primarily secondary sanctions imposed by the US.
"The blocking statute is the last resort we have. As long as we can protect the ICC in other ways, we will do so," he said.
Berendsen noted that drastic measures should not be used just to send a signal, as it could lead to the situation "escalating even further."
Last month, the US imposed sanctions targeting ICC President Tomoko Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye. This move sparked backlash across European countries, including the UK, France and Germany, as well as from the presidents of the European Council and European Commission.
The measures are part of sanctions against the ICC imposed by US President Donald Trump in February 2025.
The ICC said nine of its 18 judges, both deputy prosecutors, its former prosecutor and one staff member are currently under US sanctions.

US-backed board unveils $2.45B Gaza reconstruction plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:14:00 UTC
23:14:00 KST

The U.S.-backed Board of Peace unveiled a $2.45 billion, six-month plan Wednesday to begin rebuilding devastated Gaza and establish Palestinian governance, as political deadlock continues to stall implementation of President Donald Trump’s cease-fire framework.
At a meeting of the group’s board, the governors unveiled a 66-project blueprint to get things started while acknowledging enormous hurdles that must still be overcome. The projects include ambitious infrastructure, education and health initiatives that are designed to support Trump’s 20-point plan to end the Israel-Hamas war.
"The need is immense,” the board said, noting that full reconstruction from the physical damage across Gaza will cost roughly $35.2 billion over the medium term and another $71.4 billion in the next 10 years.
The cease-fire, which took effect on Oct. 10, was meant to clear the way for a broader process to rebuild Gaza under the guidance of the Board of Peace. The plan included additional Israeli military withdrawals from Gaza, the disarmament of Hamas, the arrival of an international peacekeeping force and a new apolitical Palestinian government to administer the territory’s day-to-day affairs. It also envisioned an ambitious program for rebuilding war-ravaged Gaza.
But the U.S.-backed plan has largely stalled. While the cease-fire halted the heaviest Israeli attacks and humanitarian conditions have improved, the Israeli military has expanded its control of Gaza and now occupies some 60% of the territory and continues to kill civilians. Hamas has not given up its weapons. The international military force and new government still have not entered Gaza, and reconstruction has not begun. The vast majority of Palestinians continue to live in tent camps or ruins of their former homes.
The board’s high representative, Nikolay Mladenov, has said progress hinges largely on Hamas disarming - a step the group has refused to take so far. But he also has pressed Israel to scale back its attacks.
A key question the board faces today will be not only laying out plans for reconstruction, but a timeline for the deployment of the international force and new government, plans to disarm and bringing badly needed building materials into the territory.

Al-Sharaa vows Golan Heights will remain Syrian in UN speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:11:01 UTC
23:11:01 KST

At an Atlantic Council panel the day before, the Syrian president said he openly told Trump he had no right to recognise Israeli sovereignty over the Golan, quipping that the US president should give New Jersey to Israel instead.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa vowed in front of the UN General Assembly Wednesday that the Golan Heights region will remain Syrian despite Israel's claims over the strategically important territory.
"Any attempts that violate our sovereignty, violate international law, will be stopped. Golan will remain Syrian territories," al-Sharaa said at the UN meeting of world leaders in New York.
The US had been the only country to recognise Israel's annexation of the Golan Heights in 1981, which it captured from Syria in 1967, until Colombia's new hard-right government in August recognised Israel's claim.
The UN maintains that the plateau is Syrian territory under Israeli military occupation, previously declaring Israel's 1981 annexation of the territory "null and void".
In July UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres reiterated that the Golan Heights were part of Syria, describing Israeli occupation as "totally unacceptable".
Al-Sharaa also used his second turn at the UN rostrum since ousting former dictator Bashar al-Assad in a blitz offensive in December 2024 to denounce repeated Israeli strikes on his country.
"Israel is launching attacks against Syria. There have been 500 air strikes, more than 1,200 incursions, and 300 detentions. This is at odds with the orientation we're seeing at global level," he said.
"It is reminiscent of a era that we thought was long gone."
Yet Al-Sharaa held out hope that "the opportunity for peace and security is available to those who wish to live in peace, a just peace that maintains the rights of all."
Golan Heights — or Jersey City Heights?
Speaking at an Atlantic Council panel in New York on Tuesday, moderated by former senior US national security official Brett McGurk, al-Sharaa recounted telling US President Donald Trump directly that he had no right to recognise Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights.
"Why don't you give New Jersey to the Israelis?" al-Sharaa said he told the US president.
"You don't own the Golan Heights to give it to them, but you own New Jersey, and I believe New Jersey is full of Democrats, and they are not voting for Trump," al-Sharaa quipped.
"So it will be good to give it to the Israelis. At least this is something that you own."
"The Golan has its people," al-Sharaa told McGurk, who served under four US presidents including Trump, adding that neither the Syrian nor the US president had the right to cede it.
Trump — who has openly shown his admiration for al-Sharaa — formally recognised Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights in 2019 during his first term.
Al-Sharaa derived his nom de guerre Abu Mohammad al-Jolani from his family's origins in the Golan.
At the Atlantic Council panel, al-Sharaa said Syria and Israel had held several rounds of direct talks, some facilitated by the US, and had reached "almost 90% of agreements" before Israel pulled back or introduced new conditions.
"It's not appropriate that what happened on 7 October set Israeli policy for Syria," he said. "Israel needs to change its policy because it's creating problems around it in order to maintain its security."
He accused Israel of twice bombing Syria's presidential palace and targeting airports since he came to power in December 2024.
"Since the fall of the former regime, Israel is repeating its attacks and aggressions against Syria. It is occupying new territories, territories that have been occupied after 8 December 2024," al-Sharaa said.
"Will that bring security to Israeli citizens? I believe the problem is with Israel, not with Syria."

Defeat against North Korea is unacceptable to me: Abdi

Unknown Publisher

Defeat against North Korea is unacceptable to me: Abdi
TEHRAN - Hossein Abdi, head coach of Iran’s U23 football team, described his side’s heavy and unexpected defeat to North Korea as unacceptable.
Iran had taken the lead against North Korea at the Asian Games, but eventually suffered a 4–1 defeat and were eliminated in the group stage after finishing below North Korea on goal difference, missing out on a place in the quarterfinals.
“First and foremost, I apologize to my dear people. This result is unacceptable to me. This is the first time we have faced such a result in an official match at this level. I believed we could achieve a different result,” Abdi said.
“We could have produced any other result—except this one! I apologize to everyone who expected and believed that we could advance to the next stage,” he added.
The Iran U23 coach criticized his players’ mentality, saying: “My feeling is that the players entered the game with the mindset that we had already secured qualification for the next round. But, to be fair, North Korea were one of the teams we expected to face a difficult game against from the outset. The Koreans played very good football, and they deserve congratulations.”
“It is disappointing because we could have maintained our advantage in what appeared to be one of the toughest groups of the tournament—a group in which it was unclear until the final day which teams would advance. Unfortunately, we were unable to produce the performance we expected today or earn the points we needed. In any case, this is my apology to my dear people.”
“I hope we can do better in the future and that this experience will help us take a better path. The players need to understand that nothing is decided before a match is over, and no result is certain until the final whistle,” Abdi concluded.

====================================================================================================

On Taiwan, US ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Is Not Dead Yet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:08:00 UTC
23:08:00 KST

Under the longstanding policy of “strategic ambiguity,” the U.S. government has refused to say ahead of time whether or not it would send American forces to help defend Taiwan against an attack from China. Some analysts say the Trump administration has rendered this policy ineffective by generating doubt that U.S. forces would intervene.
To cite just one example, the title of a September 14 analysis by columnist James Crabtree in Foreign Policy proclaimed that “Trump is killing ‘strategic ambiguity’ over Taiwan.” Crabtree argued that based on “signals from Washington,” the United States is “inching more toward a position of nonintervention.” Similarly, geopolitical risk analyst Shahn Louis said “the era” of strategic ambiguity “is over.” Michael Schiffer, a former U.S. deputy assistant secretary of defense for East Asia, argued that “strategic ambiguity is no longer a sustainable or effective policy.”
Multiple opinion polls show the belief among Taiwan’s people that the United States would ride to the rescue has decreased since 2025. The reasons for this loss of credibility are not hard to find.
Trump has repeatedly made four points about Taiwan, all of which call into question a robust U.S. response to military action by Beijing. The first is that Taiwan is vastly smaller and less important than China. Second, he says Taiwan is indefensible – too close to China and far from the United States. Third, Trump thinks Taiwan free-rides on U.S. defense. Finally, he complains about Taiwan allegedly stealing America’s semiconductor industry. Shortly before he took office for the second time, Trump said he would respond to a Chinese invasion of Taiwan with economic sanctions.
On top of this, Trump avoids antagonizing Beijing over the Taiwan issue, presumably to clear the way for a China-U.S. bilateral economic deal. During his keynote speech at the 2026 Shangri-La Dialogue, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth did not mention Taiwan, a change from his speech the previous year. The unclassified version of the 2026 U.S. National Defense Strategy also does not mention Taiwan by name.
After his May 2026 meeting with Xi Jinping, Trump criticized the Taiwan government for allegedly flirting with independence due to the presumption of U.S. support. “[W]e’re not looking to have somebody say, ‘Let’s go independent because the United States is backing us,’” he told Fox News.
For good measure, Trump announced that he was delaying a large arms sale to Taiwan already approved by Congress, calling such sales a “very good negotiating chip” in talks with China. He also dismissed the Six Assurances, part of U.S. policy toward Taiwan since the Reagan era.
The idea that strategic ambiguity has lost its usefulness, however, is wrong. Despite particular statements by Trump that are adverse to Taiwan, U.S. policy remains broadly supportive of Taipei.
The Pentagon’s 2026 National Defense Strategy said the United States will “erect” and “sustain a strong denial defense along the First Island Chain.” Even a cursory look at a map indicates that aspiration is meaningless without a U.S. intent to prevent China from absorbing Taiwan.
The large arms sale is delayed, but not canceled. This latest package of armaments is all business, not symbolic. It includes weapons systems appropriate for the scenario of an attempted amphibious invasion by the People’s Liberation Army (PLA): HIMARS rockets, ATACMS missiles, ALTIUS loitering munition drones, Javelin and TOW anti-tank missiles, and mobile howitzers.
U.S. military transits through the Taiwan Strait continue, albeit about half as often as during Trump’s first term.
U.S. security cooperation with the Philippines and Japan, highly relevant to deterring China from moving aggressively against Taiwan, has deepened during the second Trump administration.
The United States got access to, and set aside funding to develop infrastructure in, additional base sites in the northern Philippines, close to the Taiwan Strait. The annual Balikatan military exercises were larger than ever before in 2025 and 2026 and brought in Japan and Australia. U.S. forces deployed NMESIS and Typhon missile systems to the Philippines. The stridency of China’s complaints about these deployments indicate they present problems for Chinese planners.
Washington’s plan to upgrade U.S. Forces Japan to a joint force combat headquarters has proceeded under Trump’s second administration. U.S. and Japanese armed forces increased their interoperability in 2025 and 2026 through more integrated command-and-control structures, more complex joint exercises, and more sharing of data. The United States started supplying Tomahawk cruise missiles to Japan. Washington and Tokyo are engaged in serious discussions about Japan producing warships or components for the U.S. Navy to help it close the gap with China’s production.
Strategic ambiguity still holds because what look like indications of U.S. abandonment of Taiwan are relatively superficial, while substantive investment in capabilities that could deter China continues apace.
The stances of the Joe Biden presidency and the second Trump administration are different. Biden said on four occasions that the United States would militarily intervene in a cross-strait war, placing him close to an unambiguous pre-commitment to intervention. Trump is closer to the other end, a pre-commitment to non-intervention.
Both, however, represent forms of strategic ambiguity. One president seemed committed and the other reluctant, but who knows what either of them would actually decide to do at crunch time. Beijing still cannot confidently assume a Trump-led United States would not intervene in a Taiwan scenario despite Trump seemingly indicating reticence to do so.
Chinese analysts consider Trump to be unpredictable. They cannot be sure he will act in a way consistent with his past statements. The Chinese remember how quickly Trump turned on them in 2020. In January, he said “our relationship with China now might be the best it’s been in a long, long time.” Later in the year, largely over the COVID-19 pandemic, Trump regularly berated China with statements such as “I’m very angry at China” and “The world is now suffering as a result of the malfeasance of the Chinese government.”
There are, nevertheless, reasons to doubt the American commitment to defend Taiwan, and these reasons go beyond the current U.S. presidential administration.
First, the demographic trend in the United States is increasingly anti-war. Gen Z Americans, born 1997-2012, are significantly less fearful of China attaining a stronger global position and less likely to see China as an adversary. The succession of unpopular wars against Afghanistan, Iraq and Iran further strengthens the aversion of Americans toward getting embroiled in foreign conflicts.
Second, the costs and risks of maintaining U.S. strategic pre-eminence on the western Pacific Rim against the determination of China to achieve regional supremacy are rising. The United States already dominates the Western Hemisphere. The rationale for dominating the Asia-Pacific, as well, is that doing so makes war less likely and opens the door for U.S. commerce. This rationale is less persuasive, however, if China supports international trade and if opposing China’s aspirations for “rejuvenation” makes war more rather than less likely.
Military analyst Jennifer Kavanaugh’s September 10 proposal for a “Second Island Chain strategy” attracted much attention. Kavanaugh, a member of the “restrainer” camp in U.S. foreign policy, argued that to reduce the risk of war with China while still protecting the most vital U.S. interests, Washington should end its alliances with Japan, South Korea, Australia, and the Philippines, pull most of its military forces out of the region, and announce that it will not intervene to protect Taiwan in a cross-strait war. Expect arguments such as this to grow in volume and frequency.
Finally, the U.S. defense industrial base is currently unable to compete with China’s productivity. This weakness is not easily fixed, even with an increased defense budget. As the modernization of its armed forces have made China a near-peer adversary of the United States, China’s advantage in manufacturing capacity becomes potentially decisive in a theoretical China-U.S. war.
Recent wargaming suggests both China and the U.S. would suffer huge losses in a conflict. Even where the U.S. “wins,” China is better placed to quickly rebuild and rearm its forces, giving Beijing hope that it would prevail in a second round. If American leaders conclude the math leaves them without a path to victory, they will reconsider whether an intervention is feasible.
But for now, Beijing would be reckless not to assume that both the United States and Japan would militarily oppose an attempt to conquer Taiwan. And Xi is not reckless.

Kremlin-backed executives have officially taken control of the Russian operations of French retail giant Auchan, home improvement chain Lemana Pro and French logistics operator FM Logistics.
Ilya Berdnikov, a former official at Russia’s state property management agency Rosimushchestvo, will head Auchan Retail Russia after President Vladimir Putin signed an executive order last week placing it under temporary state management, the newspaper Kommersant reported.
Sources familiar with the matter said Auchan Retail Russia’s former CEO Asya Balabay will stay on to manage daily store operations under Berdnikov’s supervision.
Denis Isayev, the son of former State Duma lawmaker Rizvangadzhi Isayev, will take over at Lemana Pro, according to Kommersant. As with Auchan, the former CEO of the home improvement chain, previously known as Leroy Merlin, will remain at the company and work with Isayev.
FM Logistic, meanwhile, will be headed by Yevgeny Nenashev, a former housing official in the Moscow region. It was not immediately clear whether Oleg Alkhamov, who had served as CEO since 2021, would stay at the company.
Last week, the Russian assets of the three companies, along with those of Swiss food giant Nestlé, were placed under the temporary control of L.E.V. Management, a little-known firm headed by a former police general.
Nestlé Russia will continue operating under CEO Denis Voityuk within the new government oversight structure.
Alexander Shokhin, who heads Russia’s largest business lobby, has said that the latest seizures of Western companies should serve as “preemptive signals” to European officials amid ongoing discussions on whether to use frozen Russian funds in the West to help finance Ukraine.
“In my view, decisions of this kind are largely connected to demonstrating that if you do this, we have retaliatory measures,” Shokhin, who heads the pro-Kremlin Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs, told state media.

TEHRAN- Abbas Khatibi, deputy of Iran’s transportation infrastructure construction company, announced that the executive work on the 162-km Rasht–Astara railway, the missing link of the North–South Corridor, has begun.

The Commission is set to formally back Albania's 2027 accession deadline in a new roadmap, which is also due to include a list of key deliverables Tirana will have to prioritise to complete the process by the end of next year.
The European Commission is working towards closing the books on Albania's accession process by December 2027 — a timeline Tirana has long touted, and that is now set to receive formal recognition in the EU's upcoming enlargement roadmaps, EU officials told Euronews.
The Commission is preparing a roadmap to confirm Albania's stated goal of closing all negotiating chapters by the end of next year, and to lay out priority deliverables to plug the remaining accession gaps.
Albania has set the end of 2027 as its target for completing accession negotiations, a timetable Prime Minister Edi Rama and other senior officials have repeatedly described as an agreed plan with the European Commission.
But while Commission officials have backed the ambition, the EU executive does not typically set deadlines for accession, since enlargement is meant to be a merits-based process.
"As you know, enlargement doesn't work with dates. But the more the country is coming towards the end of the technical part of the accession, the more we can say about it or the more we can use the years," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in July.
That is set to change soon. In her State of the Union address to the European Parliament last week, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a series of "roadmaps" for candidate countries.
"We will soon be proposing roadmaps for the candidates that have made most progress," von der Leyen said, mentioning Ukraine, Moldova and the Western Balkans as countries whose future lies in the EU.
The roadmaps are expected to set out an indicative timeline to give candidate countries a clearer sense of direction, echoing the 2002 enlargement strategy that paved the way for the "Big Bang" accession of 10 new members.
The roadmaps will be folded into the Commission's enlargement package, its annual health check on the accession process, expected in late October, which also includes country-specific assessments and recommendations for next steps.
In this context, the Commission is drafting a closing benchmark assessment report that assesses whether a candidate country has met the benchmarks set for it to be considered to have met accession requirements, notably in justice and the rule of law, the so-called "fundamentals."
In Albania's case, the plan is to include a list of key deliverables spelling out the reforms and measures needed to close the remaining benchmark gaps.
That was already the case for Montenegro, where the Commission used the closing-benchmark process to pin down the concrete reforms and results it needed to deliver.
The deliverables list is meant to clearly signal to candidate countries where the priorities lie, pushing them to complete the missing steps.
"Essentially, the Commission saw that this approach worked well with Montenegro and they want to replicate it," an EU official told Euronews, asking to remain anonymous given the sensitivity of the discussion.

TAF Industries signed a joint-venture memorandum with Danish firm Upteko for production but says bureaucracy is slowing the process. Meanwhile, Resist.UA agreed to invest in BlueShadow, a Danish maritime-defense startup whose founder commanded a US nuclear submarine and whose engineering team works largely in Ukraine, Defender Media reported.
Ukraine's defense industry has outgrown much of its own 2022-era hardware in two years of rapid wartime iteration, but a government fee of 20-30% on export permits and over 200 stalled co-production bids have left the country's foreign arms sales far behind battlefield demand. Deals like the two in Denmark route Ukrainian technology into allied markets without waiting for Kyiv's export apparatus to catch up.
Ukrainian first-person-view drones, made on Danish soil
Drone maker TAF Industries plans to produce its first batch in Denmark by the end of 2026, through a joint venture with local firm Upteko. The two signed a memorandum in August 2026, but paperwork on both sides has slowed things down.
"We need to pass a fairly large number of bureaucratic procedures to make it possible," chief business development officer Mykhailo Diachenko told NordicDefenceWatch.
He called the year-end target reachable, "though maybe it will look more like a miracle."
TAF wants footholds in other countries that support Ukraine. It has started the process in Norway and is negotiating with Sweden's Recas. Diachenko said the goal is local production plus sharing Ukrainian combat experience and technology with European partners. TAF builds FPV drones, with capacity near 1 million units a year.
A Ukrainian fund bets on Odesa's sea defense
Ukrainian fund Resist.UA signed a letter of intent to invest an undisclosed sum in Danish maritime-defense startup BlueShadow's €2 million ($2.29 million) pre-seed round, the company announced. BlueShadow's software collects data from maritime sensors, commercial feeds, and open sources, merges them into a single operational picture, and uses AI to detect threats, Defender Media reported.
The company has also built an open software platform it says can help intercept Shahed-type drones. BlueSentry, designed to protect ports, offshore wind farms, undersea cables, and maritime borders from hybrid attack, is one product that the company plans to launch in the Baltic and North seas in October. BlueDragon, now in prototype testing with Defense Ministry certification targeted for late 2026 and deployment planned for spring 2027, is designed to defend Odesa with autonomous swarms of armed sea drones meant to shoot down Russian attack drones.
Founder Charles Maher is a former US Navy submarine commander who ran a nuclear-powered boat, Defender Media reported. Almost his entire engineering team works in Ukraine, drawing on more than 15 Ukrainian suppliers. Resist.UA this summer launched Resist 2.0, an Estonia-based fund aiming to raise €50 million for Ukrainian defense-tech companies.
