‘Dangers of Israel and Zionism’: Morocco’s Islamists seek comeback as country votes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:41:30 UTC
22:41:30 KST

Polling stations opened across Morocco on Wednesday for parliamentary elections taking place against a backdrop of deep frustration among millions of young people in a country whose economy is growing but where unemployment and inequality remain persistent problems. Nearly a year after unusual Gen Z-led protests were met by a sweeping crackdown, the discontent resurfaced dramatically this summer when tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in hopes of reaching Europe.
Morocco is a constitutional monarchy headed by King Mohammed VI, who retains extensive authority over strategic policy, particularly foreign affairs and defense. The election therefore is not expected to fundamentally alter the balance of power in Rabat, but it will determine the government responsible for much of the country’s day-to-day policymaking over the next five years.
That government will also oversee the final stages of a vast infrastructure drive ahead of the 2030 FIFA World Cup, which Morocco will co-host with Spain and Portugal. The International Monetary Fund estimates investment in transportation and tourism infrastructure through 2030 at about 190 billion dirhams, or roughly $20 billion, including railways, airports, stadiums, roads and projects in host cities. The scale of the undertaking has led some Moroccans to dub the next administration the “World Cup government.”
Under Morocco’s constitution, adopted after the 2011 Arab Spring protests, the king must appoint the prime minister from the party that finishes first in the parliamentary election. The 395-seat House of Representatives is elected, and the prime minister then seeks to assemble a coalition, but the monarch retains decisive influence over strategic policy and presides over the Council of Ministers.
Voting began at 8 a.m. local time and was due to end at 7 p.m., with preliminary results expected the following day. Turnout, particularly among younger voters, is being closely watched as a gauge of public confidence in elected institutions. Of about 26.7 million Moroccans of voting age, roughly 15.8 million are registered to vote. Only 4% of registered voters are aged 18 to 24.
The numbers reflect a broader political challenge. Morocco has attracted foreign investment, developed major industries and become Africa’s most-visited tourist destination, but the benefits of growth have been uneven. Youth unemployment among those aged 15 to 24 reached about 37% in 2025.
That frustration erupted in September and October 2025 in Gen Z-led demonstrations demanding better healthcare, education, employment opportunities and social justice, as well as the resignation of Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch. Thousands were arrested or prosecuted following the unrest.
The crackdown did not eliminate the underlying discontent. At the end of July, roughly 70,000 people crossed or attempted to cross into Ceuta by land and sea in one of the largest such movements into European territory in years. Ceuta’s leader later told European lawmakers that about 100 people had died during the rush. Most of those who entered were subsequently returned to Morocco.
Ayoub Lasli, a lifeguard from Casablanca who was among the young Moroccans who swam into Ceuta, told The Associated Press he had no intention of voting. “I don’t care about politics and elections, and I don’t want to care,” he said.
Siham Azeroual, a 32-year-old environmental activist from the Atlas region, voiced similar frustration, describing the political system as a “complete circus” and saying she had little hope that the election would bring meaningful change.
Others remain more optimistic. Ayoub Belaidi, 23, who also tried to reach Ceuta, said the Gen Z movement could still translate into political change if younger Moroccans are genuinely heard. “Following the Gen Z movement, if young people’s voices are truly heard, change will happen,” he told AP.
Economic concerns have dominated much of the campaign. The National Rally of Independents, or RNI, and the Authenticity and Modernity Party, or PAM, both members of the outgoing governing coalition, have promised major employment initiatives. The RNI has pledged to create 1 million jobs over five years, while PAM has also made employment, housing and purchasing power central to its platform. The two parties have nevertheless traded accusations over rising food prices and other government shortcomings.
Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch, the billionaire businessman who has led the government since 2021, is not seeking another term after stepping down from the leadership of the RNI earlier this year.
That has opened the question of who might emerge as Morocco’s next prime minister. One of the most closely watched names is Fouzi Lekjaa, Morocco’s budget minister and president of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation. Lekjaa, who became nationally prominent as Moroccan soccer enjoyed unprecedented international success, joined PAM’s political bureau in July.
Lekjaa’s profile rose sharply after Morocco became the first African and Arab team to reach a World Cup semifinal in 2022, and his role in preparations for the 2030 tournament has made him an unusually prominent figure in both sports and government.
But at one PAM rally, supporters openly backed another possibility. “We want a woman as prime minister,” activists shouted, referring to Fatima-Zahra Mansouri, 50, the mayor of Marrakech and urban planning minister. If PAM finishes first and the king chooses Mansouri, she would become the first woman to serve as Morocco’s prime minister.
Another potential candidate is Nizar Baraka, leader of the conservative Istiqlal Party and Morocco’s water minister. Baraka is the grandson of a prominent figure in the country’s independence movement, and supporters portray his party as a defender of traditional Moroccan values.
Former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane is also seeking a political comeback. Benkirane leads the Islamist Justice and Development Party, or PJD, which suffered a crushing defeat in the 2021 election, collapsing from 125 seats to just 13 after years as the dominant force in government.
Israel has become a prominent theme in the PJD’s campaign. Morocco normalized relations with Israel in 2020 while the PJD headed the government, as part of the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords. Benkirane has since called that decision a “mistake” and is campaigning for the relationship to be severed.
The campaign comes just days after Morocco and Israel agreed to deepen their ties, including plans to elevate their diplomatic missions to full embassies, appoint ambassadors, expand flights and pursue additional economic agreements. The measures were announced after Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita and Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar met in New York in talks hosted by U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz.
At a campaign rally in Marrakech, Benkirane warned supporters about what he called “the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco.”
“We have to speak up,” he said. “If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people.” The remarks also underscored the limits of what any election result can change: foreign policy ultimately remains under the king’s authority.
More than two dozen political parties are competing for the 395 parliamentary seats, but some groups argue that the limited authority of elected institutions makes participation meaningless.
The far-left Democratic Path has called for a boycott, arguing that the vote does not meet what it describes as the “minimum conditions of democracy and fairness.”
“The elections will not give us a parliament that expresses people’s will, and the government will not have any decision-making power,” party leader Jamal Berrajaa said, adding that more than 30 party members had been arrested after urging people not to vote.
Al Adl Wal Ihsane, an Islamist movement that is banned but tolerated by authorities, has issued a similar call. “Elections in Morocco are used to produce sham institutions that cannot perform their functions,” said Abdelwahed Moutawakkil, head of the organization’s political department.
For Morocco’s political establishment, the immediate question is who will form the government charged with steering the country through the massive preparations for 2030. For many of its young citizens, however, the more fundamental question is whether voting can change the conditions that drove thousands into the streets last year and tens of thousands toward Europe this summer.

TPLF forces take control of airport in Ethiopia's Tigray as tensions deepen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:41:24 UTC
22:41:24 KST

Semih Kemal
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Forces of the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) have taken control of Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle, the capital of Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, according to local media reports.
TPLF forces, which have been engaged in renewed clashes with the federal government, seized control of the airport, local media reported. Neither the federal government nor the TPLF has yet issued a statement on the airport's status.
Ethiopian Airlines said in a statement that flights to Mekelle, Aksum and Shire had been temporarily suspended due to "the current situation in the Tigray region." The airline said it would announce a date for the resumption of flights at a later time.
The suspension effectively cut air links to the three cities following reports that the TPLF had taken control of the Mekelle airport.
The development came days after seven armed groups and political organizations from different parts of Ethiopia, including the TPLF, announced the formation of an alliance against the federal government. The announcement raised concerns over a possible return to civil war.
The groups announced the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, also known as the Alliance for Survival, in a joint statement Sunday. They accused Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's Prosperity Party government of driving the country toward widespread conflict, humanitarian distress and political instability, warning that Ethiopia faces the "danger of disintegration."
The alliance includes the TPLF, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Ogaden National Liberation Front. It also includes the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front, the Benishangul Peoples' Liberation Movement and the Gumuz Peoples' Democratic Movement.
The groups said their immediate objectives were to remove the current administration and establish an "inclusive transitional government" under a shared charter aimed at ending ongoing hostilities and initiating broad constitutional dialogue.
They also called on other political and civic organizations and members of the federal security forces to join their efforts.
The Ethiopian government has not publicly responded to the alliance's announcement. 
Tensions rise in Tigray
The latest developments follow renewed tensions between the federal government and the TPLF despite a 2022 peace agreement that ended the two-year Tigray war.
The conflict between federal forces and the TPLF began in 2020 and ended with the signing of the Pretoria peace agreement in South Africa in November 2022. Hundreds of thousands of people are estimated to have died during the war.
However, disputes have persisted over the implementation of the agreement, the status of Tigray's forces and the ownership of contested areas in western Tigray. Fighting has recently intensified again between forces linked to the federal government and the TPLF.
The TPLF is seeking the implementation of the 2022 peace agreement, the return of displaced people and a resolution to the status of disputed territories in Tigray.
The TPLF was Ethiopia's dominant political force for nearly three decades before Abiy became prime minister in 2018.
The OLA has fought federal forces in Oromia since 2018. The Fano armed movement fought alongside government forces during the Tigray war before turning against the federal government after authorities sought to disarm regional forces.
Armed conflicts have also continued in parts of the Amhara and Oromia regions, while tensions in Tigray have increased in recent months.
Experts have warned that the renewed clashes and the formation of the anti-government alliance could trigger another civil war in Ethiopia.
The Ethiopian Media Authority has also indefinitely suspended Tigray Television after it broadcast live Sunday's announcement by Zemene Kassie, head of the Amhara Fano National Movement, according to local news outlet Addis Standard.

In eastern Poland, a railway line for freight trains was blocked with concrete blocks - an investigation has been launched
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

16:40:59 EEST
22:40:59 KST

In eastern Poland, a railway line for freight trains was blocked with concrete blocks - an investigation has been launched
Kyiv • UNN
In the Lublin Voivodeship, two freight trains crashed into concrete blocks on the tracks but did not derail. The police are investigating an act of hooliganism.
In eastern Poland, unidentified individuals blocked railway tracks with concrete blocks in the Lublin Voivodeship. Police report an attempt to provoke freight trains to derail. UNN reports this, citing Onet Wiadomości.
Details
The incident occurred on Tuesday evening, September 22, in Jedlanka, Łuków County. According to the authorities, two freight trains traveling in opposite directions collided with concrete blocks lying on the tracks.
According to TVP Info, the incident occurred on a line used for freight transport. One of the trains was carrying fuel. As an RMF FM reporter learned, the trains were not carrying any hazardous materials.
According to RMF24, the trains involved were a 24-car train traveling from Konin to Biała Podlaska and a 22-car train traveling from Małaszewicze to Kutno.
The trains did not derail, and no driver was injured. The locomotives’ front snowplows were damaged.
A preliminary examination conducted at the scene under the supervision of the prosecutor’s office found no explosive materials.
Rail traffic at the scene was suspended for several hours.
Investigation launched
Law enforcement officers are currently investigating an offense under Article 173 of the country’s Criminal Code, which consists of causing a traffic accident.
"Due to suspicions of a breach of railway infrastructure security, police officers from the Łuków County Police Headquarters, criminal investigators from the Lublin Voivodeship Police Headquarters, and counterterrorism officers from the Lublin Police Headquarters carried out operations at the scene," the Łuków County Police Headquarters said in a statement.
Marcin Kozak, a spokesperson for the District Prosecutor’s Office in Lublin, later told PAP that the concrete blocks placed on the tracks in both directions had resulted from the demolition of a nearby railway station. "Following the preliminary investigation, it was ruled out that this was part of a terrorist act. No explosives were found. Most likely, we are dealing with an act of vandalism. Police have already reported similar incidents at this location in the past," the spokesperson explained.
What Tusk said
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk commented on the incident. He said the initial reports "are not particularly alarming, as this does not look like a very professional operation." "We do not ignore any such event, especially because it could lead to another tragedy," he added.
Update
Earlier, Poland had already reported sabotage on the railway route used to deliver aid to Ukraine.

					The technical storage or access that is used exclusively for statistical purposes.
					The technical storage or access that is used exclusively for anonymous statistical purposes. Without a subpoena, voluntary compliance on the part of your Internet Service Provider, or additional records from a third party, information stored or retrieved for this purpose alone cannot usually be used to identify you.
				
			 
			
				
				
					The technical storage or access is required to create user profiles to send advertising, or to track the user on a website or across several websites for similar marketing purposes.

Pakistan's jailed former PM Khan's sons told DW the authorities are cracking down ahead of new PTI protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:39:00 UTC
22:39:00 KST

Pakistan: Khan family arrests raise stakes ahead of protests
September 23, 2026
Family members of Pakistan's former Prime Minister Imran Khan are concerned about the 73-year-old's health in a Rawalpindi prison and accuse authorities of preventing him from accessing appropriate medical care.
Khan's London-based sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, told DW they had received "little to no information" about their father's health.
"When we last spoke to him on the phone back in March, he said that he had lost 85% of the vision in his right eye and that despite his complaints, it was neglected for months," they said.
The brothers added that their father was being held in a tiny cell and has been allowed outside for only one or two hours a day. They also allege that he was kept in isolation from family, lawyers, and a personal physician for 10 months before he was briefly allowed to see two of his sisters.
Meanwhile, the opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party's has planned a protest march on September 27 to exert pressure on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's government for Khan's release.
Sons demand family access and medical care for Khan
Khan's sons have urged authorities to allow their father access to a personal physician and to restore regular access to his family and phone calls.
"We are asking the Pakistani authorities to obey the Supreme Court orders immediately and shift our father to Shifa International Hospital so that he can be assessed by independent doctors," they said.
Khan's sisters detained as PTI plans new protests
From jail, Khan remains at the center of Pakistan's political confrontation between the PTI and the country's powerful military. He remains a popular political figure in Pakistan, despite being ousted from office in 2022 a parliamentary no-confidence vote.
Khan's three sisters were detained in the Punjab capital of Lahore on Monday ahead of the planned PTI protest march.
The detention orders cited concerns that the sisters were a threat to public safety and maintenance of public order. All three were ordered to be held for 30 days under a public order ordinance.
Khan's sons told DW the arrests were intended to intimidate their family and supporters before the planned protest rally.
"Our family members who have been arbitrarily taken into custody must be released immediately," they said. "The abductions of our family members in the middle of the night, with no reason given, were purely to intimidate them."
Khan was ousted as prime minister in 2022 and jailed the following year on what he says are politically motivated corruption charges. His PTI party says it has faced an ongoing government crackdown.
Pakistan government calls for 'order'
Pakistan's government rejected these claims and said that its priority was to maintain public order during the planned protest.
Authorities have stepped up security preparations in Islamabad and Rawalpindi, deploying thousands of police personnel and placing shipping containers and other barriers at key entry points.
Talal Chaudhary, Pakistan's minister of state for interior, warned that the government would not tolerate unlawful activity or actions threatening lives and property.
"If you are a peaceful citizen, come to Islamabad from any route, come 100 times," he told DW. "But if you come as terrorists, we will not let you leave."
In 2024, pro-Khan protests on the streets of Islamabad turned violent. Demonstrators breached high security zones and clashes with security forces left six dead. When Khan was arrested in May 2023, nationwide PTI support rallies also led to violence, with military and government buildings suffering damage. Several people were killed and hundreds injured.
"The right to protest does not give the right to attack," Chaudhary said.
Arrests could 'galvanize' PTI supporters
The PTI has said the September 27 protest will call for respect for constitutional and political rights.
Michael Kugelman, a South Asia analyst at the Washington-based Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars, told DW that the arrests would likely further energize Khan's supporters.
"The arrests will galvanize what is already an angry and anxious Khan support base," he said.
He added that the detention of Khan's sisters, who Kugelman said were"prominent advocates" of Khan's cause had placed his family at the center of the confrontation between the government and the PTI.
Khan's base is "concerned about the state of his health, and for his sister to be detained will increase the chance that protesters take to the streets on the 27th," he added.
Zulfi Bukhari, a senior PTI leader and close aide to Khan, said the arrests were meant to create fear but would not prevent the party from mobilizing its supporters across the country.
"What they [the government] don't realize is all they are doing is creating more hatred for themselves among the public," he told DW.
Bukhari described the current repression as the most severe the PTI has faced. "This crackdown seems the more brutal," he said, adding that the government was acting out of frustration.
"They are fueling a fire that will soon be out of their control," he asserted. "They can keep attacking us, and we will continue to resist. This protest will go on, and many more after it," he added.
As Pakistan's government faces several challenges, including economic malaise, conflict with the Afghan Taliban, and fallout from the Iran war, further domestic unrest would be an unwelcome complication.

Tripolitsa massacre: Why the wound hasn't healed for over two centuries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:37:40 UTC
22:37:40 KST

More than two centuries after Greek insurgents stormed the then-Ottoman administrative capital of the Peloponnese in southern Greece, the Tripolitsa massacre remains a historical wound that continues to fester in the collective psyche of the Turkish people.
The Greek revolt in the Morea resulted in the massacre of tens of thousands of Muslim Turks as well as Jews who had lived in the Peloponnese for centuries.
Independent historians put the number of civilians and soldiers – Turks, Albanians and others – slaughtered inside the overcrowded city of Tripolitsa, the historical name for the Greek city of Tripoli, as high as 40,000.
Following the beginning of the Greek Revolt in February 1821, Muslim and Jewish families from the surrounding countryside sought safety in Tripolitsa because the city was fortified.
But Greek rebel forces surrounded the city and eventually entered it to carry out a killing rampage as part of a wider campaign that emptied the Peloponnese of its long-settled Muslim and Jewish communities.
Ali Fuat Orenc, a professor of history at Istanbul University, says the Tripolitsa massacre was not a chaotic wartime excess, but a calculated atrocity.
“The massacres at Tripolitsa were an atrocity deliberately orchestrated by Greek gang leaders and insurgents,” he tells TRT World.
Although the city’s Muslim population agreed to surrender after months under siege, the Greek gangs failed to honour the agreement, he says.
“The Muslims were massacred en masse,” he notes.
That broken pledge by the Greek gangs was only the beginning of their atrocities against the long-settled Muslim and Jewish populations.
The city was then “looted down to the very last rusty nail”, followed by a cultural erasure.
“All historical artifacts, including Muslim tombstones, were destroyed, and the cultural heritage was obliterated,” Orenc says.
“There is absolutely no doubt that all of these were premeditated acts,” he notes.
Western commentators watched the massacre unfold, but raised few objections.
Afterwards, the massacre was downplayed, or even ignored, in European commentary, experts say.
“The primary reason why Western commentators and political leaders overlook or downplay the Tripolitsa massacre is that the Greek insurgents… enjoyed the unconditional support of Europeans,” Orenc says.
Europeans framed the Morea Revolt as a religious war and, therefore, extended “unconditional support for the Christian Greek insurgents against the Muslim Turks”.
Volunteer fighters from the European continent took part in the massacre.
“Europeans were complicit in the massacres,” Orenc says.
That European silence over the original complicity continues to date in some ways.
“Their ancestors were accomplices to the perpetrators of these killings,” he says, while referring to the present lot of philhellenes, a term reserved for the unsuspecting admirers of Greece and its culture and history.
‘An inhuman atrocity’
Independent-minded researchers who studied the massacre wrote about systematic killing, in stark contrast to the romantic image of a classical Greek revival painted by the so-called philhellenes.
“For three days, the civilian population was ruthlessly butchered,” wrote William St Clair, prominent British historian and author.
“Women and children were tortured and dragged through the streets before being killed,” he wrote.
According to George Finlay, a Scottish historian, the atrocities committed in Tripolitsa could not be justified by the necessities of war.
“Helpless and unarmed people, women and children, were systematically slaughtered for days. This was not a victory, but an inhuman atrocity,” he wrote.
In his memoirs, Theodoros Kolokotronis, leader of the Greek uprising, was unapologetic.
“From the time I entered the city until I reached the palace, my horse's hooves never touched the ground; all along the path, we were riding over corpses,” he wrote.
“Not a single living Turk was left in Tripolitsa,” he added.
Statements from the Turkish foreign ministry calling the killings a “black stain” on European history, coupled with scholarly work on the destruction of Ottoman culture, keep the subject alive in Turkish public life.
However, the massacre is described in Greek writings in a totally opposite way.
“In modern Greek textbooks, the period of the 1821 uprising is characterised as a revolution,” Orenc says.
In fact, it is placed “on par with the French Revolution”.
When the killings appear in textbooks at all, they are framed as the inevitable result of so-called “oppression endured under centuries of Ottoman hegemony”.
“Greek textbooks fail to provide sufficient information… about the Muslims and Jews living in cities across the entire Peloponnese (Morea) – all of whom were erased from history,” he says.

British arms broker jailed for 16 years over missile, fighter jet deals with Libya and Sudan
- David Greenhalgh was jailed for 16 years for illegal arms deals supplying missiles, fighter jets, and weapons to South Sudan, Libya, and other embargoed countries between 2009 and 2016.
- Greek national Christos Farmakis was convicted in absentia for nine offences linked to arms trafficking, with his whereabouts currently unknown.
- Authorities uncovered the deals through Farmakis' work email, revealing attempts to breach arms embargoes and profit from selling weapons during conflicts in Libya and South Sudan.
AI generated
LONDON - A British arms broker who arranged illegal deals to supply ex-Soviet surface-to-air missile systems to South Sudan and fighter jets to Libya during its civil war was on Sept 23 jailed in a London court for 16 years.
David Greenhalgh, 68, was convicted in June of 10 counts of involvement in the unlicensed supply of arms, also including AK-47 rifles, battle tanks and hundreds of thousands of rounds of ammunition, between 2009 and 2016.
Greek national Christos Farmakis, 48, was convicted of nine offences, though he was tried in his absence and his current whereabouts is unknown.
Judge Sally-Ann Hales sentenced both men to 16 years’ imprisonment, saying they repeatedly sought to breach arms export bans to sell weaponry for significant profits.
Prosecutors said only one charge involved the actual supply of weaponry, with the pair selling a former Ukrainian S-125 Pechora missile system to South Sudan, where Greenhalgh and Farmakis had “very close connections to senior figures”.
South Sudan was still formally part of Sudan until it achieved independence in 2011, prosecutor Edmund Burge told jurors at Southwark Crown Court, meaning the semi-autonomous region was subject to a British arms embargo.
Greenhalgh and Farmakis also arranged to supply weapons to Iran, Iraq and Syria in breach of arms embargoes, before Farmakis was arrested in 2016.
Farmakis was caught after using his email address for his job at the government-funded Greater London Enterprise to privately arrange arms deals.
Burge said Farmakis’ email account forwarded an email to his boss, which led to the authorities discovering documents relating to plans to sell fighter jets and other arms to Libya in the wake of the 2011 Arab Spring. REUTERS

The British Royal Air Force is creating its first space squadron to protect satellites from attacks
Kyiv • UNN
The UK's new space squadron will counter threats in orbit and protect critical satellites. It will be equipped with electronic warfare capabilities.
The Royal Air Force is creating the first specialized unit to counter hostile threats in space and protect British satellites. The new squadron will use, among other things, electronic warfare capabilities to suppress, degrade and disrupt hostile activity. This was reported by the British Ministry of Defence, writes UNN.
Details
As noted, the new No. III Space Effects Squadron will be the first unit in the United Kingdom tasked with disrupting, degrading and preventing hostile threats in space.
The squadron will protect critical satellites that provide navigation for British ships, mobile phone connectivity and missile attack warnings
The new squadron will bring together specialists from all branches of the armed forces to counter hostile activity in orbit and protect satellites.
The squadron will use, among other things, electronic warfare technologies. It will carry out both offensive and defensive missions and will gradually expand as new capabilities emerge.
Previously, the British RAF had two specialized space units. No. I Space Operations Squadron is responsible for space operations, while No. II Space Warning Squadron is responsible for monitoring and warning of threats in space. The new squadron is intended to directly counter such threats.
The UK government also plans to invest £880 million by 2030 in space intelligence, surveillance and control capabilities in space.

Taiwan Cement Corporation (TCC), one of the world’s largest cement producers, is set to become a strategic investor in PJSC Ivano-Frankivskcement (IFCEM), Ukraine’s leading cement manufacturer. The deal marks a rare example of a global industrial group investing in a Ukrainian manufacturing asset while the country remains at war.
The IFCEM deal brings one of the global cement industry’s heavyweights directly into Ukraine’s reconstruction effort, where cement and concrete will play a central role in future infrastructure projects.

The transaction will be carried out between the owners of the Ukrainian group and TCC Group EMEA Holdings B.V., the Netherlands-based subsidiary of TCC Group Holdings Co., Ltd., according to an IFCEM statement published on Wednesday.
On the sellers’ side are CemInWest S.A., a Swiss company and IFCEM’s majority shareholder, along with the owners of three affiliated companies: Ivano-Frankivskdakh LLC, Krugips LLC, and Krumix LLC.
TCC will receive a 100% stake in the businesses which is valued at €750 million ($857 million), Focus Taiwan reported, citing press conference comments made by TCC Group Holdings Vice President Shelly Yeh.
Completion of the transaction remains subject to antitrust clearance and other regulatory approvals in the relevant jurisdictions, as well as customary closing conditions, the company said.

IFCEM has an annual cement production capacity of 4.3 million tonnes (4.7 million US tons) and, together with its affiliated companies, employs about 2,500 people, according to their website.
However, the group produces not only cement under the IFCEM brand, but also concrete and reinforced-concrete products under KRUBETON, fiber-cement roofing under FIBRODAH, façade materials under AEROPANEL, dry building mixes under KRUMIX, and gypsum plasterboard under KRU GIPS
TCC, with a history of more than 70 years, operates more than 40 production sites with an aggregate cement capacity exceeding 112 million tonnes (113 million US tons) per year and employs about 13,800 people, according to the release. IFCEM’s capacity is equivalent to roughly 4% of TCC’s.

Centuries-old water channels unearthed during construction in Tartu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:34:00 UTC
22:34:00 KST

Centuries-old water channels unearthed during construction in Tartu
Archaeologists excavating the site of Tartu's planned Siuru cultural center have uncovered centuries-old drainage channels in remarkably good condition.
At the 10,500-square-meter archaeological excavation site in central Tartu, experts uncover historical objects almost every day. Piece by piece, the finds are building a clearer picture of life in what is now Tartu's Central Park centuries ago. The largest discovery so far is a system of drainage channels and wells.
"You don't find such a well-built system every day. Because we can investigate a very large area at once, we have the rare opportunity to excavate so much of it. We have already uncovered more than 20 meters of one longer section, including the drainage wells," said Keiti Randoja, head of the archaeological excavation.
The wooden channels were built to carry away wastewater and rainwater. Dating from the 18th or 19th century, they mark the site of a former suburb that probably included a courtyard.
"Organic material generally decomposes in the ground, but the soil here has less oxygen and has preserved the wood better. If the logs are well preserved, we can saw off disks for samples and determine, even to the exact year, when the trees were felled and when the channels may have been built," Randoja explained.
The channels will not remain where they are for much longer. Tartu City Museum will decide what happens to them.
"They have generally taken some wooden items to the museum. For example, they dismantled a barrel so they could reassemble it there. They will decide whether they already have enough finds of this kind. In any case, the channels will be photographed and measured, but Tartu City Museum will decide where they ultimately go," said Siuru director Aavo Kokk.
The excavation area will soon be expanded, including toward the Emajõgi River. Archaeologists suspect the drainage system continues in that direction. Finding an ancient boat as they move toward the river would be an added bonus. Archaeological excavations at the Siuru site will continue until the end of next year.

Old American armor, new Ukrainian brain: Skelya regiment nears completion of M1117 unmanned conversion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:33:16 UTC
22:33:16 KST

Ukraine's 425th Separate Assault Regiment Skelya is converting American-made armored vehicles into remotely operated platforms as part of its "remote infantry" concept, head of the regiment's innovation support group Edhar Vinnik wrote in an exclusive column for 24 Kanal. The approach rests on a simple principle: if a machine can do the job, no soldier should risk their life doing it, Vinnik argued. The regiment established an Innovation Center to develop unmanned systems and robotic platforms, Militarnyi reported.
The M1117 is the second vehicle Skelya has converted to unmanned control—after completing the Novator armored car in June—and the regiment's approach won a Defense Ministry DELTA innovation competition on 31 August 2026, earning approximately $33,700. The pattern suggests Ukraine's cheapest path to unmanned ground capability may not run through purpose-built robots but through vehicles already in service, upgraded with off-the-shelf hardware.
M1117 conversion nears completion
The regiment is in the final stages of converting the American M1117 Guardian into a remotely controlled platform. The 4x4 vehicle has been in Ukrainian service since 2023.
"The project of remote control of the American armored wheeled vehicle M1117 is in the final stage," Vinnik said.
This is Skelya's second such conversion. In June, the regiment completed a similar project with the Novator armored car. The Novator received multiple communication channels: Starlink, LTE, and Silvus radio systems. Vinnik argued the conversions prove that remote control can scale to any vehicle in service, if the hardware supports it.
Software ties the system together
Without adequate software, all unmanned platforms would remain isolated machines, Vinnik noted. The regiment's IT Innovation Department develops proprietary software for coordinating unmanned systems. One solution replicates functionality similar to R2D2—a network data-relay infrastructure that enables remote equipment operation. Using off-the-shelf routers cut the cost roughly fourfold.
"Without adequate software, all these drones and ground systems would remain just separate machines," Vinnik said.
The cost reduction matters for scalability, Vinnik argued. A technology that exists in one copy is a demo—one cheap and reliable enough for hundreds of crews is a capability. The regiment measures its progress by one number, he wrote: how many soldiers were not sent where they could be killed or wounded.
Why old armor gets a second life
The M1117 Guardian—built on the Cadillac Gage Commando chassis from the Vietnam War era—exemplifies the trend. The regiment's Innovation Center, established in autumn 2025, won a Defense Ministry DELTA innovation competition on 31 August 2026. Skelya's approach reflects a broader Ukrainian trend of converting existing vehicles into unmanned platforms rather than building robots from scratch. The National Guard's Khartiia Corps earlier converted a 12-ton US-made M113 armored personnel carrier into an unmanned platform for remote demining and logistics, fitting it with anti-drone armor and a mine flail. Ukraine is also rebuilding Soviet BRDM-2 armored scouts into remotely operated robotic platforms, and three units recently received Kaban—a bolt-on kit that turns ordinary vehicles into uncrewed ones.

Slovakia's Fico draws fire over NATO Article 5 remarks
September 23, 2026
"I'm afraid of war," Robert Fico told medical students at a teaching hospital in Presov last week.
"What is happening in Europe today, what we're hearing and seeing today, is that the military conflict in Ukraine has got out of control," he went on, warning them that Europe faced the possibility of a wider war.
He asked the students to imagine Slovakia being told to prepare "5,000 soldiers, 10,000 soldiers" who would go somewhere to fight "without us even knowing whom they are fighting, or why, or what for."
Then he turned to Article 5 of NATO's founding treaty, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
"I do not want Slovakia to be part of any military conflict because of some Article 5," Fico said.
"Yes, we are in NATO. We value that. Cooperation and fulfilling our obligations matter to us. But as prime minister, I will do everything to ensure that Slovakia is never drawn into a military conflict."
The remarks prompted uproar from the Slovak opposition and also a spat with Petr Pavel, president of neighboring Czechia and former chairman of NATO's Military Committee.
"If anyone says they're glad to be a member of NATO … but are unwilling to get involved if anyone else is attacked, then they have not understood the word solidarity," Pavel said.
Fico replied that he understood that Pavel, as a former NATO general, would like to fight, while he himself preferred peace.
The impact on Slovakia's standing
The Slovak prime minister's fear of a wider war is shared by many Europeans. But critics at home gave his remarks short shrift.
"Isn't he a prime minister? Isn't he the leader of a country? Is he not supposed to lead people instead of expressing fears?" asked former Slovak Foreign Minister Miro Wlachovsky, now a distinguished fellow at the GLOBSEC think tank.
"My question for him as prime minister is: OK, even if the situation is as bad as you are saying, what I want to hear from you is how the country is prepared. What have you done for preparedness? Who will come to our aid in case we are attacked?" Wlachovsky told DW.
Asked whether Fico's remarks could damage Slovakia's standing among its allies, Wlachovsky replied: "It's already done."
Political background to Fico's comments
Analysts see a clear political context to Fico's remarks.
The Slovak prime minister will face a difficult reelection fight next year. Some observers believe Fico is trying to steal votes from the extreme-right Republika party, which is viscerally hostile to NATO and the EU and opposes military support for Ukraine.
Wlachovsky compared Fico's rhetoric to that of Hungary's former Prime Minister Viktor Orban and the current Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, both of whom have presented themselves as the candidates of peace.
Babis was heavily criticized during his unsuccessful 2023 presidential campaign after questioning during a televised debate whether the Czech Republic should send troops to NATO ally Poland if it came under attack.
What is NATO's Article 5?
Oana Lungescu, a distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute and a former NATO spokesperson, told DW that Article 5 was "the most solemn pledge that a country can make to another."
But its central purpose, she said, was deterrence: convincing a potential aggressor that it would face the alliance together, rather than an isolated member.
"This is about solidarity, standing together, underpinning deterrence and therefore avoiding war," she said. "NATO is a defensive alliance. It's not an offensive alliance."
Nor would invoking Article 5 automatically send every member's troops into combat, she said.
The North Atlantic Council, where every ally is represented, would assess an attack and decide by consensus whether it constituted an Article 5 situation — Slovakia's voice would be equal to that of its 31 partners in that room, she said.
Once consensus was reached, each country would then assist the attacked ally by taking the action it deemed necessary, which might — or might not — involve armed force.
Article 5 has been invoked only once, following the September 11, 2001 attacks on the United States.
Lungescu pointed to one of NATO's initial responses: sending AWACS surveillance aircraft to patrol US skies and help prevent another attack.
She pointed out that Slovakia already benefits from the same solidarity Fico appeared to question. The country hosts a NATO multinational battlegroup established after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with personnel from several allies alongside Slovak troops.
Its purpose is to deter an attack on Slovakia.
'Exactly what Putin wants'
For former Slovak Defense Minister Jaroslav Nad, the danger lies in allowing that fear to dictate policy towards Ukraine.
"This is exactly what Vladimir Putin wants," said Nad, who was defense minister from 2020 to 2023 and is now head of the non-parliamentary opposition Democrats party.
"He wants citizens in the EU and NATO to believe that if EU and NATO countries continue to support Ukraine, this escalatory situation might lead to a Third World War or something like that," Nad told DW.
Nad was in office when Slovakia decided to hand over its entire fleet of ageing MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine. Fico's government later sought a criminal investigation into the transfer; prosecutors closed the case, finding no crime.
"Even when I was defense minister, I heard this not only from ordinary people but also from some ministers around the table: that we shouldn't help Ukraine with this or that equipment or capability or ammunition, because it might create a difficult situation in terms of escalation towards Russia," he went on.
"None of that happened."

Bear attacks kill 6 in Siberian region this month, prompting negligence investigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:31:33 UTC
22:31:33 KST

Burç Eruygur
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Bear attacks have killed six people in Russia’s Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk this month, prompting a criminal investigation into alleged negligence by local authorities, investigators said Wednesday.
The region’s brown bear population has grown to more than 26,000, about 2.5 times its previous level, the Investigative Committee of Russia’s branch covering Krasnoyarsk and neighboring Khakassia said in a statement on Russian social media platform Max.
Residents submitted more than 120 reports of sightings across more than 15 districts, including the regional capital, Krasnoyarsk, the committee said.
It noted that despite numerous warnings of danger, local authorities “failed to take measures to regulate the predator population or prevent them from appearing in areas inhabited by people.”
“As a result of the improper performance of duties and a lack of adequate oversight, six fatal brown bear attacks on humans were recorded in September 2026 within the Yeniseysky, Sosnovoborsky, and Yermakovsky municipal districts of Krasnoyarsk Krai,” it said.
Investigative actions are currently underway to establish all the circumstances of the crime, with a criminal case opened over “negligence,” it added.
“The investigation will include a legal assessment of the actions taken by officials responsible for responding to the presence of bears in inhabited areas,” it said.
Meanwhile, Dmitry Buchenik, deputy head of neighboring Khakassia, said Wednesday that Abaza was “effectively under siege” by bears, with sightings reported from all directions.
He said bears were driven away from an area near the town bridge and three were killed during the operation.
Bear attacks have killed 17 people across Russia’s Siberian and Far Eastern regions in recent months, according to state news agency Tass.
On Tuesday, Vladimir Mazur, the governor of the neighboring Tomsk region, announced restrictions on mass events, excursions and tourist gatherings in forests following an increase in bear encounters on Telegram. The restrictions will remain in place until at least Nov. 1.

Golan Heights will 'remain Syrian', President Ahmed al-Sharaa vows at UN
Syria's President Ahmed al-Sharaa told the UN Wednesday that the contested Golan Heights region would "remain Syrian" despite ongoing military occupation by Israel. The Syrian leader also used his second turn at the UN rostrum to denounce repeated Israeli strikes on his country.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa insisted at the UN Wednesday that the Golan Heights region will remain Syrian after Colombia last month recognised Israeli sovereignty over the strategically important territory.
Read moreUN General Assembly live: Iran’s Pezeshkian tells UN his country is ‘victim’ of US ‘terrorism’
"Any attempts that violate our sovereignty, violate international law, will be stopped. Golan will remain Syrian territories," al-Sharaa said at the UN meeting of world leaders in New York.
Colombia's new hard-right government in August recognised Israel's claim over the Golan Heights, which it captured from Syria in 1967.
The United States had until then been the only country to recognise Israel's annexation of the territory in 1981.
The United Nations maintains that the plateau is Syrian territory under Israeli military occupation.
In July UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres reiterated that the Golan Heights were part of Syria, describing Israeli occupation as "totally unacceptable".
Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz responded by saying that the Golan Heights would remain under Israeli sovereignty "forever".
"My clear response to the Syrian president, who made bombastic declarations from the UN podium: The Golan under Israeli sovereignty is an inseparable part of the State of Israel forever," Katz said in a video statement.
Al-Sharaa also used his second turn at the UN rostrum to denounce repeated Israeli strikes on his country since the fall of former dictator Bashar al-Assad.
"Israel is launching attacks against Syria. There have been 500 air strikes, more than 1,200 incursions, and 300 detentions. This is at odds with the orientation we're seeing at global level," he said.
"It is reminiscent of a era that we thought was long gone."
But he held out hope that despite repeated "aggressions" by Israel, "the opportunity for peace and security is available to those who wish to live in peace – a just peace that maintains the rights of all."
During a discussion at the Atlantic Council on Tuesday, al-Sharaa said Syria wanted a peaceful solution with Israel and that negotiations between the two countries had resolved nearly 90 percent of the outstanding issues needed for a security agreement.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Moscow Fortifies Power Plants With Concrete After Retaliatory Ukrainian Drone Strike
Russian authorities have begun installing concrete barriers around a thermal power plant in Moscow, apparently seeking to protect the facility from possible drone strikes.
This was reported by Militarnyi on September 23, citing eyewitness footage from Astra recorded at the site.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The fortifications are being installed around the combined heat and power plant 8 (CHPP-8) on Volgogradsky Prospekt. The footage shows concrete-block structures being erected around parts of the energy facility.
Astra indicated that the barriers may later be supplemented with anti-drone nets. The protective structures appear intended to prevent drones from reaching critical equipment or reduce damage from a direct impact.
The measures come as Russian authorities prepare energy infrastructure for possible retaliatory Ukrainian drone attacks during the heating season. The source did not report whether similar concrete fortifications were being installed around other Moscow power plants.
Similar protective measures have also appeared at Russian oil refineries, where anti-drone nets and metal frameworks have been erected around individual installations. These structures are designed to intercept incoming drones before impact or limit damage to refinery equipment.
The fortification effort at CHPP-8 became public shortly after one of the largest Ukrainian drone and missile barrages against the Moscow region to date, launched overnight into September 20.
That attack hit a major refinery in Kapotnya, which supplies roughly 40 percent of the region's petroleum product demand, igniting a large fire and underscoring the vulnerability of energy sites now drawing sustained attention in Ukraine's long-range campaign.

Ukraine Has Chance to End War With Russia Before Winter, Zelenskyy Says
Unknown

Ukraine Has Chance to End War With Russia Before Winter, Zelenskyy Says
Ukraine has a chance to end Russia’s war before winter, but reaching that goal will depend on US political will, increased pressure on Moscow, and additional American military technology, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Wall Street Journal on September 23, Zelenskyy outlined the conditions he believes could create an opportunity to reach what he described as a just peace within the next two months.
“We have a chance to stop and end this war before winter, if… There are several ‘ifs.’ Of course, the first ‘if’ is always will. The will of the United States, especially the president. It is precisely about the political will to end this war,” Zelenskyy said in the interview.
At the same time, the Ukrainian president said political will alone would not be sufficient to change Russia’s position and called for additional pressure on Vladimir Putin.
The second condition, Zelenskyy said, is access to US technology and additional weapons, particularly air defense interceptors needed to protect Ukraine during the coming winter.
“The second ‘if’ is technology. We need some technologies from the United States. We have our experience, we are always ready to share it, but we need something from the US. We need a ‘winter package’: missiles for Patriot systems. Only the US produces them now,” Zelenskyy said.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Zelenskyy raised the proposed “winter package” during his meeting with US President Donald Trump in New York on September 22, requesting additional weapons and Patriot air defense capabilities. Zelenskyy also said he expects Washington to pursue an agreement aimed at stopping attacks on energy infrastructure.
Kyiv has made additional Patriot interceptors one of its main defense priorities ahead of winter. Zelenskyy previously said Ukraine had calculated a requirement of around 300 Patriot missiles for the winter period—approximately 100 per month.
Ukraine has also been discussing licenses that would eventually allow Patriot interceptors to be produced domestically. Zelenskyy has said, however, that securing missiles for immediate use remains a higher priority because establishing new production capacity would take time.
Zelenskyy had previously said Ukraine was prepared to take reciprocal de-escalation steps if Russia stopped targeting Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and food exports.

Germany's oldest party, the center-left SPD, is in a difficult position following its success in the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania state election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:28:00 UTC
22:28:00 KST

What Germany's SPD can learn from its election success
September 23, 2026
Following state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, two of Germany's 16 federal states, the mood within the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) is oscillating between relief and frustration, confidence and bewilderment.
"The SPD is clearly capable of winning more than 30% of the vote," party co-leader Lars Klingbeil said jubilantly in Berlin. "This result in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is an encouragement for the entire Social Democratic movement."
As Klingbeil put it, Manuela Schwesig, the SPD state premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and her party had shown "how to make up ground, how to fight, and how, with the right issues and the right approach, to stage a comeback and ultimately win people over through that effort."
What Klingbeil conveniently omits is that Schwesig's success was also because she distanced herself as much as possible from the federal government's policies, and by extension from the SPD at the national level, which it governs in coalition with the center-right CDU/CSU alliance of the Christian Democratic Union and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union under Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Meanwhile, the national government has become more unpopular than any of its predecessors.
Focus on the SPD's traditional values
Schwesig scored points above all with her opposition to parts of the federal government's pension reform plans. At the post-election review meeting in Berlin, she intensified her criticism, launching a pointed attack on the chancellor. She argued that 81% of people in her state consider the reforms unfair and that Merz is misjudging the situation.
On election night, Friedrich Merz made clear that he was all the more determined to stay the course. "The reforms must go ahead," the chancellor said. "Of course, this puts all of us in a difficult position. What needs to be done now requires courage, resilience, and patience. I will demonstrate those qualities as leader of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country."
Schwesig had a clear response. "My advice to the chancellor, if he wants to regain people's trust, though I'm not sure that's still possible, is that he needs to engage with the reality on the ground." She argued that Merz must ask himself what needs to change. "There can be no business as usual."
SPD's Bas and Klingbeil struggle to chart a course
The SPD, and above all its leaders, Lars Klingbeil and Bärbel Bas, now find themselves in a dilemma. Both serve as cabinet ministers in Merz's government and therefore help implement policies that many SPD members are increasingly questioning.
At the same time, they are accountable to their party and must ensure that SPD priorities are reflected in government policy. The success Schwesig achieved with her unequivocally critical stance is now putting them under considerable pressure.
Following her electoral victory, Schwesig has emerged as one of the most influential figures within the SPD. Many party members would like to see Schwesig become the party's next leader.
She already appeared to be embracing that role as she stood before the microphone at the post-election review, dressed head-to-toe in red and exuding confidence. By contrast, Bas and Klingbeil appeared almost defensive, seeking to strike a balance between criticizing the coalition and supporting it.
"If people in our country perceive reforms as something that threatens their way of life and leads only to things getting worse, then it is not just our communication that needs to improve. In some areas, the substance of the reforms themselves needs to change as well," said Klingbeil.
Bas called for both a "reality check" and a "fairness check" on the reforms, arguing that they must be workable in practice and socially equitable.
Show confidence, uphold Social Democratic values
Will that be enough? Calls for the SPD to be "more like Schwesig," in other words, to assert its own positions with greater confidence, are growing ever louder within the party. The only question is how much dissent a governing party can afford to show. "Nothing would be more damaging than allowing this coalition to collapse over a policy dispute at this point," Bas warned. Solutions, she argued, "are possible within this coalition as well."
At a leadership committee meeting on the morning after the state elections, the SPD leadership adopted a strategy paper. Across nine key points, it sets out the priorities the party intends to champion in government. One section is headed "Real Change Instead of Simply Cutting Spending," while another is titled "An Affordable Life for All."
The SPD wants inheritance tax reform to ensure that the resulting revenue can fund a "genuine education initiative." On pension reform, the paper states that important questions remain unresolved regarding phased retirement and the right to retire without pension reductions after 45 years of contributions.
The SPD leaves no doubt about its stance: "The lifetime achievements of people who have paid into the system for many years must continue to make a difference."
It remains unclear whether the CDU/CSU will respond to these demands. The same is true of the simmering debate over whether Bas and Klingbeil should be replaced at the helm of the party.
Pressure continues to come from Philipp Türmer, leader of the Jusos, the SPD's youth wing. "I'm not saying that the two of them are the problem, but at the moment they're not part of the solution either," he told German broadcaster RTL and its news channel ntv.
Türmer and others had called for a special party conference that could have paved the way for replacing Bas and Klingbeil. Instead, the party will hold a convention in December, a smaller party gathering that cannot elect or remove party leaders.
From now on, however, SPD members are likely to judge their leaders even more by how effectively they defend the SPD's positions in government and whether they can restore the party's appeal among voters.
This article was originally published in German.

Japan is reaching for the sword again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:27:13 UTC
22:27:13 KST

Japan is reaching for the sword again
In recent months, there’s been a distinct sense of ‘historical déjà vu’ – from Germany’s interest in long-range missiles to the development of hypersonic missile technologies in Japan. The first question that comes to mind is whether revanchism is emerging more than 80 years after the defeat of the fascists and militarists in WWII. However, this question is quite complicated, so for now, we will focus on a more practical issue: Japan’s military-technical buildup. Below, we will attempt to assess the significance of this shift in Japan’s strike capabilities and understand the direction in which the country is heading.
By the end of the 20th century, Japan had become one of the strongest and most loyal allies of the US in the Pacific region. The Japan Self-Defense Forces are equipped with American aircraft, missiles, interceptors, and other weapons. Japan is the first and to date the only country in the world to manufacture Patriot surface-to-air missiles under license, and it is the first foreign recipient of Tomahawk subsonic cruise missiles.
On July 29, 2026, the first test launches of Tomahawk cruise missiles were conducted in the Pacific Ocean from the Kongo-class guided-missile destroyer JS Chokai, equipped with the Aegis system. These tests mark the beginning of the Japanese Navy’s adoption of American long-range cruise missiles. The program to acquire these missiles is quite ambitious: Japan plans to equip four additional Aegis-capable destroyers – JS Kirishima, JS Haguro, JS Myoko, and JS Atago—with these state-of-the-art missiles, with the long-term goal of upgrading all other destroyers of this class. In total, the acquisition of 400 missiles (Block IV and Block V variants) is planned by the end of the 2027 fiscal year. This arsenal significantly alters the capabilities of the Japanese Navy, given that such cruise missiles can strike targets at ranges of up to 1,600 km. Furthermore, this is merely an interim solution pending the adoption of domestically developed missiles with similar or superior specifications.
Japan is currently working on several missile projects, with a particular focus on hypersonic technologies. Japan has already concluded an agreement with Australia to conduct joint tests at Australian missile ranges, which offer the necessary facilities for testing long-range missiles; the development of several strike missile projects is scheduled to begin in 2027.
One of the major initiatives is the project to develop a submarine-launched hypersonic missile capable of striking land-based targets. The missile is expected to be versatile, capable of being deployed from both Japanese Navy submarines and surface ships. Japan justifies the deployment of such missiles on submarines by citing the need for retaliatory strike capabilities in the event of an external attack. Naturally, Japan is pointing to the growing capabilities of China’s navy and missile forces. For its part, China is also actively enhancing its capabilities in light of a possible confrontation with the US and Japan.
While the hypersonic missile project is currently in the preliminary design phase, it draws upon Japan’s existing experience in developing various types of missiles and submarine-based vertical launch systems, as well as ambitious programs to build new missile-equipped vessels and, eventually, nuclear-powered submarines. In 2023, the Japanese Ministry of Defense signed a contract with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries for the development of a submarine-launched guided missile; a separate official program launched that same year is focused on developing an indigenous hypersonic guided missile; the work is set to continue through 2031. These programs are essentially aimed at creating preliminary designs for future missiles and developing hypersonic technologies in general; however, following the research phase, Japan will move on to developing specific missile models. The potential for this already exists.
What about launch platforms? Currently, the Japanese Navy operates several Aegis-equipped destroyers and non-nuclear submarines; they could carry a limited number of missiles. However, this would not be sufficient for mass deployment.
In 2027, the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force is set to commission the lead ASEV-class destroyer into service. Though the destroyer is modestly designated as a “missile defense ship,” it is in reality a guided-missile cruiser. It will measure approximately 189 meters in length and 25 meters in beam, with a standard displacement of around 12,000 tons. This makes it significantly larger than the current Maya-class destroyers or even US Ticonderoga-class guided-missile cruisers. Each vessel will carry 128 modular vertical launch system (VLS) cells capable of housing Standard Missile shipborne guided missiles, anti-ship missiles, and strike missiles – ranging from the Tomahawk to future domestically-developed hypersonic missiles. Plans currently call for the construction of two such ships. The speed of construction is impressive: one ship is set to be built in three years. This will be the most heavily armed missile-carrying warship in the Pacific.
And what about nuclear-powered submarines? Recently, Japan’s Ministry of Defense officially included nuclear-powered submarines in its defense posture review, paving the way for Tokyo to assess the feasibility of building such vessels alongside its conventional fleet. Strict restrictions on the military use of nuclear energy had previously been in place in Japan, but in regard to submarines, this particular constraint is now being quietly lifted.
Naturally, such a move would logically expand Japan’s underwater operations in the Western Pacific; from a shipbuilding perspective, Japan certainly has the capacity for it. Nuclear propulsion would allow Japanese submarines to remain submerged for virtually unlimited periods, effectively neutralizing potential Chinese undersea superiority. The US would, of course, be Japan’s primary industrial partner in this endeavor, though the UK or France could also share their expertise in nuclear submarine construction. Following Japan’s lead, South Korea is also considering the development of nuclear submarines. While Japan blames China, South Korea cites the threat of North Korea. In both cases, it looks like the arms industry lobby is actively seeking an outlet for its manufacturing capacity.
But that’s not all – there is also the aviation sector. Alongside the UK and Italy, Japan is participating in the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP) to develop a sixth-generation fighter jet. The program aims to finalize the aircraft’s requirements and technical specifications by the end of 2027. Furthermore, the Excalibur flying test laboratory and the demonstrator aircraft are scheduled to begin testing by the end of 2027. These efforts are critically important for Japan, as it decides which joint initiative to participate in and whether it should launch its own program to develop a next-generation fighter jet
Therefore, by the 2040s-2050s, the capabilities of the Japanese armed forces could change beyond recognition. Japan could possess nuclear-powered submarines, a missile-armed fleet, a modern air force, ground-launched and subsonic long-range hypersonic and cruise missiles.
Finally, experts believe that, if necessary, Japan could quickly produce nuclear weapons. This would take only a few months. The country possesses a highly developed nuclear industry and nuclear energy sector – with stockpiles of plutonium and other materials, as well as all the requisite technologies. Japan also has nuclear weapons delivery systems at its disposal. In short, all the prerequisites are in place, though strict constitutional constraints currently remain in effect. However, if one threshold is crossed and the decision to build nuclear submarines is made, one might expect this nuclear trend to continue in the direction of classified research and weapons development. A highly advanced nation like Japan could develop nuclear weapons quickly and covertly.
That’s the ‘samurai sword’ slowly but surely emerging from the East. How should we react to it? Sound the alarm and deploy weapons, or call for peace and dispatch ballet troupes? Perhaps, both. Let’s hope that we’ll never have to use the weapons, but be prepared just in case; as for ballet, it’s always a good idea.

Freelancing in the Netherlands? First get your tax sorted!
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:27:01 UTC

Partner content
Freelancing in the Netherlands? First get your tax sorted!
Setting up your own business or going it alone as a freelancer takes a lot of time and energy, and it is easy to forget some of the things you need to do. For example, if you are considering becoming a ZZP’er, how can you make sure you keep on the right side of the taxman?
Dealing with BTW
One of the first bits of paperwork you will be confronted with if you go into business in the Netherlands is dealing with BTW — omzetbelasting, or value added tax. “What people often forget is that they do have to submit their VAT return every three months even if they have only just started in business,” says Andra Radu, from Taxmo, an online bookkeeping and tax platform for freelancers, which largely focuses on helping internationals.
“Your first VAT deadline can arrive sooner than you expect. Starting a business doesn’t necessarily mean you have three months before you need to think about VAT. Depending on when you register, the VAT quarter may already be underway. And even if you haven’t made much money yet, you may still have a return to submit.”
Using a smart bookkeeping software, like that developed by Taxmo, means you can produce and send your invoices, keep a record of suppliers and upload the invoices they have sent you, calculate your personal expenses, and deal with your VAT and your income tax on one all-encompassing platform. You don’t even have to fill in the tax office’s own forms because Taxmo does it for you.
Understanding tax terminology
For many internationals, the difficult part isn’t running the business itself, it’s understanding the language and administration around it. You must file a VAT return if you are registered as an entrepreneur with the tax office (and have been assigned a VAT number starting with NL), if you are a ZZP’er — or freelancer — or if you are running a VOF, BV, or eenmanszaak (partnership, limited company, or sole proprietorship).
The jargon can seem incomprehensible and Dutch tax terms, unfamiliar deadlines and different rules for different types of clients can make a relatively simple freelance business feel much more complicated than it actually is.
Tax rules for freelancers
One rule freelancers may not be aware of, for example, is the KOR — yes, more jargon — the small business ruling, which, simply put, means that if you book annual turnover of less than €20,000 a year, you may be able to avoid dealing with VAT altogether.
Qualifying for the KOR doesn’t automatically mean it’s the best choice for your business. If you have significant business expenses, being unable to reclaim VAT on them can make a difference. It’s also worth thinking about how quickly you expect your business to grow rather than looking only at your turnover today.
“Business expenses are another area where new freelancers can easily get confused,” says Andra. “Keeping track of invoices, receipts and expenses from the beginning makes life much easier when it’s time to file, particularly when you’re still learning which costs actually count.”
Cross-border VAT
As an international freelancer, you may well have clients in other countries, and that’s something you’ll need to sort out too when keeping on top of your taxes. “This is particularly relevant for internationals, who often continue working with clients outside the Netherlands after setting up here,” Andra points out.
“You might have a Dutch client, an EU client and a US or UK client in your first few months of freelancing. How you handle VAT can depend on where the client is based, whether they’re a business or consumer and what you’re selling, so it isn’t always as simple as adding 21% to an invoice.”
File your tax returns yourself
Of course, smart software cannot solve all problems. There will always be situations where professional advice is useful, particularly as a business becomes more complex. But freelancers with relatively straightforward businesses don’t necessarily need to outsource every VAT return or routine piece of administration.
“Becoming a ZZP’er does not mean you need to understand every part of the Dutch tax system yourself or hire an expensive accountant for every filing,” says Andra. “Our platform has been designed specifically for the Dutch situation, to make sure you can do as much as you can yourself. We are all Dutch taxpayers even if we don’t speak the local language, or at any rate not much. Paying tax is not something you can avoid, but you can make it as easy as possible.”
Find out here how Taxmo helps freelancers handle bookkeeping, VAT and income tax in the Netherlands, without having to become Dutch tax experts themselves.

Two plants make 70% of Ukraine’s steel. Russia hit both. Then ports closed, rail costs rose 30%, and the EU’s carbon tax kicked in
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:26:37 UTC
22:26:37 KST

Russian missile strikes shut down or damaged four of Ukraine's largest steel plants in August and September, halving steel output and prompting the operator of the country's largest plant to call on the government to pass a dedicated rescue plan, RBC-Ukraine reported.
Russia's full-scale war has already cost Ukraine the Azovstal plant in Mariupol, one of its largest steel mills, and more than two years of disrupted production across the sector. The latest strikes hit plants that produce the bulk of remaining capacity, concentrated in a single month, in what the industry describes as a deep crisis for a sector that supplies 6% of the country's GDP.
Steel output halved as missiles hit plants producing 70% of Ukraine's steel
The 11 August strike on Zaporizhstal killed seven workers and injured 21 as they headed for a shelter, Metinvest said; a second ballistic strike on the plant followed on 27 August. Two died and 13 were injured at ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, and five were killed at Kametstal. Russia also hit the Dnipro Metallurgical Plant. On 12 September, Russia struck both Zaporizhstal and ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih again with ballistic missiles.
Zaporizhstal and Kametstal, both part of the Metinvest group, stopped entirely. ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih—Ukraine's largest steel plant—partially shut down. Zaporizhstal and ArcelorMittal alone produce more than 70% of Ukraine's steel.
August steel production fell to 277,000 tons, down 57.3% year on year and 39.4% from July, according to Ukrmetalurhprom data cited by GMK Center. Rolled-metal output dropped to 270,000 tons.
Strikes, a port blockade, and rising costs hit at once
The strikes came on top of a Black Sea port blockade that has shut down maritime exports of iron ore and steel since late July. A 30% increase in rail tariffs took effect on 1 August. Alternative routes—rail through western border crossings, Danube ports, and roads—can carry at most 50% of what the Black Sea ports handled, GMK Center analyst Andrii Hlushchenko said. Steelmakers also have to compete with farmers for that limited rail capacity.
Rail exports of iron ore and metals dropped 2.5 times in the first 15 days of September compared with the same period last year, Ukrzaliznytsia said. Shipping iron-ore pellets through European ports costs $50–60 per ton, making many deliveries unprofitable.
The steel sector generated 6% of Ukraine's GDP last year, brought in 13% of all foreign-currency earnings, and paid UAH 27 billion (about $606 million) into budgets between January and July. Deputy chair of the parliamentary economic committee Dmytro Kysylevskyi called the situation "a perfect storm."
Meanwhile, Türkiye re-rolls Russian slabs and sells the resulting steel on Ukraine's domestic market. China uses cheap Russian energy to undercut Ukrainian prices.
"We are effectively importing Russian metal in the form of finished products," Ukrmetalurhprom President Oleksandr Kalenkov said.
ArcelorMittal calls for a Cabinet rescue resolution
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih CEO Mauro Longobardo said the government should pass a dedicated Cabinet resolution assigning specific tasks and deadlines to multiple agencies at once.
"No single agency can solve the full set of problems. Without a single document with assigned responsibilities and deadlines, each issue is dealt with in isolation and stalls," ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih representatives said.
The resolution should cover EU negotiations on deferring the carbon border tax (CBAM) until at least the end of martial law plus one year, restoring steel quotas to last year's level, stabilizing rail tariffs, securing long-term electricity contracts for industry, and launching anti-dumping investigations against Turkish and Chinese imports, Longobardo said.
Ukraine's Economy and Environment Ministry said it is in talks with the European Commission on easing CBAM and expanding quotas. A Cabinet source told the outlet that Black Sea trade negotiations with Russia are possible in October, after the Duma elections that ended on 20 September.
