Economic Watch: Chinese motorcycles pick up pace on new-energy track
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:09:33 CST
22:09:33 KST

CHONGQING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- In an exhibition hall in southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, an electric off-road motorcycle drew a crowd of onlookers. Nearby, retro-styled e-motorcycles, urban commuters and high-performance electric bikes stood in rows, waiting for their turn in the spotlight.
But the motorcycles were not the only things attracting attention. Buyers moved from booth to booth, stopping to examine batteries, motors and intelligent control units -- the components powering a new generation of electric two-wheelers.
The scene at the 24th China International Motorcycle Trade Exhibition offers a glimpse into a broader shift in the country's motorcycle industry: new-energy models are no longer a niche attraction. They are drawing increasing attention from manufacturers and buyers.
Held in Chongqing from Saturday to Tuesday, the exhibition brought together 1,120 exhibitors and more than 100 global motorcycle and electric vehicle brands, showcasing over 3,000 vehicles. Thousands of international buyers and dealers from more than 80 countries and regions came to explore new Chinese products.
For manufacturers, the change is reflected in the products on display. Electric motorcycles are being developed for an increasingly diverse range of uses, from intercity long-distance travel and performance-oriented commuting to competitive racing and off-road riding.
And their push is extending beyond China's borders. Some brands have already gained a foothold in European and American markets, with their electric motorcycles now sold across dozens of countries and regions.
"Electric motorcycles represent the future trend," said Hernan Holguin, a Colombian buyer, as he weaved between different booths, taking a close look at Chinese electric motorcycles.
For buyers like Holguin, the appeal goes beyond the exhibition floor. Rising fuel prices, growing urban transportation needs and a booming express delivery sector are driving South American markets to turn to Chinese e-motorcycles, he said. He hopes to reach cooperation agreements during his trip and bring more Chinese e-motorcycles to Latin American markets.
The growing interest is also drawing attention from industry insiders.
New-energy motorcycles will become an important part of urban transportation in many countries and regions, said Zhang Hongbo, secretary-general of the China Chamber of Commerce for Motorcycle (CCCM). As technology advances, the industry is moving toward greener and smarter development, he said, adding that Chinese new-energy motorcycles are expected to see further growth in global markets.
Analysts say the country's vast and well-established motorcycle industry is expected to provide a solid foundation for the growth of the electric motorcycle sector.
China is the world's largest motorcycle producer, with an industrial chain valued at nearly 500 billion yuan (74.6 billion U.S. dollars). According to the CCCM, the country produced more than 22.1 million motorcycles and sold nearly 21.97 million in 2025.
Chongqing, a major production hub where roughly one in every three motorcycles made in China rolls off the production line, offers a close-up view of the industry's evolution.
Here, fuel-powered and electric motorcycles are developing side by side. Major manufacturers such as Zonsen and Shineray are accelerating their new-energy plans, while battery makers are also rolling out new technologies and products, gradually broadening the industry's electric offerings.
In the first half of this year, Chongqing exported 117,000 electric motorcycles and mopeds worth 515 million yuan. Export volume jumped 130.5 percent year on year, while export value increased 66.6 percent, statistics from the municipal commission of economy and informatization show.
For many manufacturers, the next step is clear: bringing electric models into their product lines.
Founded in 2024, ZXMOTO rapidly built a presence in the market with large-displacement fuel-powered motorcycles. Now, it is turning its attention to electric models.
The company has already secured the necessary qualifications and related R&D is well underway, its founder Zhang Xue said at the event.
As more manufacturers embrace electrification, industry experts see potential for electric motorcycles to follow the growth trajectory of China's electric auto industry.
The motorcycle sector can follow, replicate and even surpass the electrification path of China's automotive industry, said Chen Qingquan, an academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering, noting that both vehicle and battery technologies have now reached a mature stage.
"The era of rapid development for the electric motorcycle industry has arrived," Chen said. ■

JUBA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- South Sudan President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional government on Tuesday evening, ahead of the country's first elections scheduled for December.
The presidential decree dissolved South Sudan's national legislature and state governments, removed the first vice president and four other vice presidents from their posts, and named a caretaker government to manage the transition to the Dec. 22 elections.
Riek Machar, who holds the post of first vice president, has been suspended since September 2025 and is on trial on charges including treason.
The presidential decree, which was broadcast on the state-run South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation, stated that Kiir will remain president throughout the election period until a newly elected leader is sworn in.
Parliament passed amendments to the National Elections Act on Monday, and Kiir signed them into law on Tuesday. The amendments allow the president to stay in office during the election period and remove all vice presidents appointed under the 2018 peace deal.
According to the decree, the judiciary and security institutions will remain intact, while presidential advisers and envoys will continue serving directly under Kiir's authority.
Government ministries and state institutions were instructed to transition immediately to caretaker status to ensure operational continuity.
Kiir appointed caretaker ministers to oversee key ministries, including presidential affairs, cabinet affairs, foreign affairs, defense, interior, justice, national security, finance, petroleum, trade, information and communications technology, East African Community affairs and peacebuilding.
South Sudan gained independence in 2011 but was soon plunged into a devastating five-year civil war.
General elections are scheduled for Dec. 22, having already been postponed twice. ■

Feature: At 55, Pakistani table tennis player makes Asian Games debut
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:09:01 CST
22:09:01 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- On a table tennis court filled with young athletes, Nosheen Aslam stood out.
At 55, she was the oldest player in the women's team competition at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, competing alongside athletes decades younger.
Then she picked up her paddle.
Nosheen represented Pakistan in two team matches on the opening day of the women's competition on Sunday. She did not play in Pakistan's final group match the following day, but her presence in Nagoya had already marked a personal milestone.
It was her first Asian Games. It was also her first time traveling abroad for an international competition.
"The Asian Games is my dream," Nosheen said. "It's a great event, very well organized. All the people are very nice, and it's a great experience for me. I'm enjoying it."
The experience was a dream come true for Nosheen, but it also came with plenty of nerves. "I was very nervous, and I didn't perform very well," she said.
The results did not go her way, but after their matches ended, Nosheen and her teammates gathered courtside for photographs, smiling and enjoying a moment that meant far more than the score.
Nosheen is from Lahore, the capital of Punjab and Pakistan's second-largest city. She took up table tennis 12 years ago, when she was already a mother of three boys, and quickly fell in love with the sport.
"It makes me active. It makes me fit, and I enjoy playing table tennis," she said.
Her three sons all play cricket. Many of Nosheen's table tennis partners and opponents, meanwhile, are around the same age as her children. One of her teammates in Nagoya, Aleena Khan, is just 15.
But once Nosheen steps onto the court, the age gap disappears.
"Every time I play, I feel happy and forget the worries of my life," she said. "Age is just a number. I think table tennis is a sport of skill. If your skills are good, then nothing else matters."
Finding time to train has never been easy. As a mother and a working woman, Nosheen has had to juggle table tennis with caring for her children, cooking and work.
She often trains at night, squeezing practice into whatever time she can find after finishing her daily responsibilities, and has kept at it for years.
Nosheen's experience also reflects how table tennis is developing in Pakistan. In Lahore, there are many clubs with good facilities, and both boys and girls regularly play the sport. Nosheen also enjoys helping younger players learn basic techniques.
The sport is also reaching younger players through schools.
A pilot of the International Table Tennis Federation's School Program began in late 2025 and has since expanded to six countries across four continents. In Pakistan, the program introduced table tennis as a regular school sports activity at four schools, involving 80 students.
The initiative aims to make table tennis part of school life and promote skills such as confidence, teamwork and discipline.
For Nosheen, the growth of the sport means more young players are coming through, making competition increasingly challenging.
She spent two to three months preparing for the Asian Games, with her husband and children encouraging her throughout. But in Nagoya, facing younger players competing at a high level, she could see the gap.
Despite the losses, Nosheen left Nagoya with another target in mind. Retirement is not yet on her mind. Her next goal is the South Asian Games, scheduled to be held in Pakistan next April.
"I think my physical condition is still good," she said. "Maybe I can play for another two or three years."
Then she smiled and added: "Maybe next time my performance will be better." ■

WHO warns DR Congo Ebola outbreak still uncontrolled as cases surge in North Kivu
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:08:57 CST
22:08:57 KST

KINSHASA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) remains uncontrolled despite signs of improvement in some affected areas, as cases have risen sharply in the eastern province of North Kivu, a senior World Health Organization (WHO) official said Wednesday.
Marie Roseline Belizaire, director of the WHO emergencies program in the African region, said during an online press briefing. The country had recorded 7,773 confirmed cases, including 3,759 deaths as of Monday, according to the DRC health authorities.
"We are beginning to see the first encouraging signs of progress," Belizaire said.
Between Aug. 31 and Sept. 20, cases declined by about 26 percent in Ituri Province, the long-time epicenter of the outbreak, and by around 15 percent in Haut-Uele Province. North Kivu, however, recorded a 73-percent increase over the same period, she said.
"This clearly shows that the outbreak continues to evolve differently across the affected areas," Belizaire said, noting that each of the seven affected provinces has its own transmission pattern.
"The outbreak is still not under control," she said. "This outbreak continues to pose a significant risk to regional and global health security."
Children under five remain particularly vulnerable, with a case fatality rate of more than 60 percent, compared with around 40 percent among adults, according to the WHO official.
While contact follow-up has improved to nearly 88 percent, too many new infections are still being detected without a known epidemiological link, highlighting persistent gaps in surveillance, she said.
Belizaire stressed that the response must now focus resources on areas where transmission and risks are highest while maintaining essential health services.
"We must consolidate the progress made in Ituri, strengthen the response in North Kivu and other emerging hotspots, detect cases earlier, reduce community deaths, and maintain strong cross-border preparedness," she said.
The outbreak, declared in May, has become the largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. ■

MP warns Britain’s deterrence against Russia is its people
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:08:51 BST
22:08:51 KST

Graeme Downie MP says Britain is already in an unconventional war with Russia and argues that “our deterrence is our people” as skills shortages test the UK’s defence resilience.
Britain has been fighting an unconventional war with Russia for at least a year and is not yet doing enough to prevent that confrontation becoming a conventional one, Labour MP Graeme Downie has warned.
Speaking at the ADS Skills Conference, the MP for Dunfermline and Dollar argued that the country’s ability to deter Russia ultimately depends not simply on weapons and equipment, but on whether Britain has enough skilled people to build, maintain and operate them. Downie said Scotland’s position at the gateway to the North Atlantic and the High North demonstrated the scale of the challenge.
He said: “It shows why the UK has been in an unconventional war with Russia for at least the past 12 months and I don’t believe our government, society or economy is doing what it is necessary to prevent that becoming a conventional war.”
Downie pointed to pressure across a range of domains, citing Russian drone activity affecting NATO allies, attacks around the Ukrainian and Polish border, the foiled attack on Leipzig airport, threats to subsea infrastructure and disruption affecting parts of Germany’s energy network. His wider argument was that responding to those threats requires industrial depth as much as military hardware, particularly the ability to replace equipment, sustain production and maintain forces during a prolonged crisis.
He said: “Vladimir Putin must see a resolute, informed and resilient British population. A strong, skilled, innovative population that they do not want to challenge.”
Downie added: “If armies win battles and economies win wars then our workforce secures peace. Our deterrence is our people.”
He spoke on shipbuilding in his own constituency as an example of the pressure facing the defence industrial workforce. Downie said: “Three hundred. That is how many welders Babcock was forced to recruit from the Philippines to work on the construction of the new frigates just down the road at Rosyth. That should be a national embarrassment.”
He acknowledged that overseas recruitment had provided a practical solution which allowed work to continue, but questioned why Britain was not producing enough workers domestically for those roles. He said: “These are highly skilled jobs. They are well-paid jobs. But why are we not producing enough of the people to do those jobs ourselves?”
ADS has told the Scottish Affairs Committee recently that it is monitoring around 10,000 live engineering vacancies across Scotland, with shortages spanning welding, fabrication, steelworking, plating and electrical, mechanical and systems engineering.
Downie also rejected arguments that higher defence spending should be funded by cutting welfare, saying national resilience depended on the strength of society as a whole. He said: “I have heard glib suggestions that cutting welfare is the route to security. Give people less so our armed forces can have more stuff. I utterly reject that. Because deterrence is not about stuff.”
He added: “You do not improve your deterrence by taking food out of the mouths of children.”
The MP also directed criticism towards the division of responsibilities between Westminster and Holyrood. Defence policy is reserved to the UK Government, while skills and economic development are devolved. Downie described the argument that defence was therefore someone else’s responsibility as “technically true. It is strategically inadequate.”
He also referred to plans for two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges in Scotland, saying they “need to be created right away”. Industry itself, he argued, also had to take more responsibility for fixing the skills shortages it regularly identifies.
With only around one in six Scottish employers offering apprenticeships in 2024, Downie challenged companies complaining about recruitment difficulties to explain what they were doing to create the workforce they required. He asked: “What are you doing to create the skilled people you need?”
Downie added: “Employers need to be part of the education system, not simply consumers of its output.”
He closed by returning to the central warning of his speech, arguing that building skills and industrial capacity should itself be treated as part of national deterrence. Downie said: “We are in an unconventional war with Russia and we must do everything to make sure that doesn’t become a conventional war that could cost hundreds, thousands, millions of lives.”
He added: “We must deter that and our deterrence is our people.”

Project Sunrise update: Qantas to launch non-stop flights between Sydney and New York from 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:08:03 UTC
22:08:03 KST

Passengers will spend 18 hours in the air on the specially configured Airbus A350-1000ULR aircraft.
There’s not long now until the world’s longest flight between Sydney and London takes off with passengers for the first time in October next year.
And now travellers have yet another ultra-long-haul route to look forward to, with Qantas confirming it is set to launch non-stop services between Sydney and New York in mid-2028.
The Australian airline has said that the flights will cut more than three hours off the total travel time compared with one-stop services today. Tickets for the inaugural flight will go on sale from August 2027.
Dubbed “Project Sunrise”, flights will be operated by specially configured Airbus A350-1000ULR aircraft which are fitted with an additional 20,000-litre fuel tank to allow for 22 hours in the air.
The first test aircraft successfully completed a 24 hour and 24 minute flight from Melbourne to Toulouse in July.
The name for the project is a reference to the “double sunrise” flights operated by Qantas between Crawley in Western Australia and RAF Base Koggala in what is now Sri Lanka during WWII.
Inside the Project Sunrise cabins
Passengers aboard the Sydney to London services will spend a whopping 18 hours in the air – a daunting prospect for many, we’re sure.
But cabins aboard these planes have been designed to keep passengers feeling fresh despite the long distances.
“Flying these distances is only worth doing if our customers arrive feeling their best, and that belief has shaped everything we've built,” Qantas Group CEO Vanessa Hudson said.
“Over the past decade, working alongside experts, we've designed the aircraft and the onboard experience around the science of ultra long-haul travel, from the lighting to the meals to a world-first Wellbeing Zone. This is a fundamentally different way to fly.”
Passengers in all classes will have access to the “Wellbeing Zone”, which has guided on-screen movement programmes you can complete using the integrated stretch handles, as well as refreshments.
Economy cabins have 140 seats in a 3-3-3 configuration with a larger seat pitch than current Qantas aircraft.
In economy plus, the seat pitch is 34 inches, while business class passengers have an 80-inch flat bed.
First class customers have the same bed set up, as well as a separate reclining armchair and a full-length wardrobe.

OECD lifts 2026 global economic growth forecast to 2.9% despite Iran war disruption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:07:13 UTC
22:07:13 KST

The OECD has nudged up its forecast for global growth this year to 2.9%, saying the world economy has absorbed the energy shock from the Iran war better than expected, but it warned that persistent inflation, rising bond yields and the risk of a longer conflict continue to cloud the outlook.
The global economy is proving sturdier than feared.
In its interim outlook published on Wednesday, the OECD raised its 2026 growth projection by 0.1 percentage point from June, concluding that the world economy "has weathered the energy supply shock triggered by the conflict in the Middle East better than expected."
That still marks a clear slowdown from the 3.4% growth recorded last year, and the OECD also trimmed its forecast for 2027 by 0.1 percentage point to 3%.
The upgrades were broad.
The US is now expected to grow 2.2% this year and the eurozone 1%, both up 0.2 percentage points, while Japan's forecast rose by the same margin to 0.8%. China's projection was left unchanged at 4.5%, and the G20 together is expected to expand 3.1%.
Within the eurozone, the OECD expects Spain to grow by 2.6% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027, ahead of the other countries covered in its September update. Germany is forecast to grow by 1.1% in both years, Italy by 0.9% and 0.6%, and France by 0.4% and 0.7%, respectively. The eurozone as a whole is expected to grow by 1% in each year.
Energy prices have soared since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February, but several factors softened the blow.
The OECD pointed to sizeable oil inventories, extra supply from producers outside the Gulf and discretionary government support measures, while broader financial conditions, including rising stock markets and continued access to credit, have remained supportive.
Heavy investment in AI has also bolstered production and trade, and the organisation said it could yet deliver stronger growth than projected.
The risks ahead
The relief comes with caveats.
Central banks have begun raising interest rates to contain inflation driven by high oil and gas prices, which have pushed diesel and other fuel costs to multi-year highs. Headline inflation in G20 countries is projected at 4.1% this year, while the OECD expects it to reach 3% in the eurozone.
Meanwhile, government bond yields in EU countries including Germany and France have climbed to multi-year highs, raising borrowing costs for countries already carrying heavy debts and deficits.
In Europe, these higher borrowing costs, alongside targeted, temporary energy support, are putting further strain on public finances.
Looking beyond Europe, the OECD warned that "rising bond yields underline more than ever the need for enhanced efforts to contain and reallocate government spending, improve public-sector efficiency and strengthen revenues to ensure longer-term debt sustainability and maintain the ability of governments to react to significant shocks."
It also flagged a prolonged war, weather-related supply shocks from a very strong El Niño hitting harvests and food prices, and AI investment returns that could disappoint as the key risks that could weaken growth.

Brazil has record number of Indigenous candidates for general election

"We Indigenous women need to have a voice, and we need to occupy decision-making spaces. Swiss archaeologists uncover rare medieval heating system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:06:35 UTC
22:06:35 KST

Swiss archaeologists uncover rare medieval heating system
Archaeologists in Basel have uncovered an almost intact medieval hot-air heating system during renovation work at the site of the former Gnadental monastery, a find described as unique in Switzerland.
The heating system was uncovered in the courtyard of the former vocational school at Petersgraben 52, it was announced on Wednesday. It was located beneath the walls and mortar floors of the former medieval convent of Gnadental and is thought to have heated the community’s dining hall.
+ Why Switzerland is an archaeological treasure trove
Based on architectural and historical considerations, the experts dated the system to the 13th to 14th centuries. According to a statement, the structure consisted of an underground chamber lined with stones for heat storage and a firebox channel beneath it. Warm air flowed into the room above through eight closable openings.
A unique find in Switzerland
Such stone-chamber air-heating systems are extremely rare in Switzerland. The Basel find is said to be unique due to its almost complete state of preservation and is also considered one of the most significant examples in Europe. The find is to be incorporated into the renovation project at Petersgraben 52.
More
Structures of 11th-century castle discovered in Switzerland
Gnadental Convent was built around 1231 outside the city walls of the time for the Franciscans. But they moved to the newly founded Barfüsser Convent just 20 years later. The buildings then housed Cistercian nuns and Poor Clares. The monastery took its name in 1279 from lay sisters from Gnadenthal near Niederwil, Aargau. These were incorporated into the Order of the Poor Clares and remained there until the monastery was dissolved in the wake of the Reformation.
More
Unearthing a cemetery from the Middle Ages
After the Reformation, some of the convent buildings continued to be used. In 1573, for example, a granary was built using building materials from the convent, particularly from the church. At the end of the 19th century, the granary was demolished to make way for the vocational school. This marked the disappearance of the last visible remains of the monastery. It was only the recent excavations that brought these remains back to light.

Britain puts space at centre of defence buying revolution
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:06:31 BST
22:06:31 KST

National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce says space is one of the first portfolios under Britain’s new procurement structure, as Defence seeks to become a much more active customer for UK industry.
Britain is placing space among the first major capability portfolios under its new defence procurement system, with National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce promising a more direct role for government in buying, developing and exporting UK space technology.
Speaking at the UK Space Power Conference, Pearce said the National Armaments Group, the new organisation he leads, had been created to bring together 15 organisations from across and outside Defence in an attempt to change procurement, supply-chain management and innovation. Pearce, a former chief executive of Inmarsat, described space as central to future warfighting, arguing that modern forces increasingly depend on satellite communications, positioning, navigation and timing, intelligence and surveillance.
He said: “As warfighting becomes more mobile, more digitally enabled, more autonomous, and more integrated, space capabilities are the red thread, bringing it all together into warfighting readiness and advantage.”
The Defence Investment Plan commits nearly £13 billion to enhanced military space capabilities over the next decade, Pearce said, while the new procurement structure is intended to give Defence greater control over how that money is converted into operational capability. One of the first capability portfolios established by the National Armaments Group is specifically focused on space, headed by Rear Admiral Tony Williams.
Pearce said the new model would give his organisation greater authority over the design of what Defence buys, responding to requirements generated by the frontline commands and military headquarters. Some requirements would be met by buying existing equipment, while others would require more specialised development.
He said: “Sometimes, I hope much more, we will go shopping and buy off the shelf. Sometimes we’ll need to develop the most exquisite of capabilities for advantage, and this applies as much to the space sector as any other market.”
The wider reform is also intended to make it easier for smaller companies to enter the defence market. Pearce said a new Office for Small Business Growth would provide a gateway into Defence and reiterated the ambition to increase annual business with small and medium-sized companies by more than £2.5 billion by 2028.
Defence is also preparing a finance and investment strategy and creating a Defence Investment Unit intended to attract more private capital into the sector, from venture investment through to infrastructure and conventional banking.
Pearce drew heavily on his own experience in the commercial space industry, including a decade leading Inmarsat and an earlier period working in venture capital. He said Defence needed to become a better customer for technology companies, particularly during the difficult transition between an innovative idea and an operational product. Under the new structure, the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory and UK Defence Innovation are being brought together within National Armaments Defence Innovation, covering activity from science and research through to later-stage development.
Pearce said £400 million a year had been committed to UK Defence Innovation, describing the funding as effectively creating a £2 billion defence venture capital organisation inside the department. He said closer links were also being created with frontline rapid-capability organisations so that military users could work with companies while technologies were still being developed.
Pearce said: “Expect to see a lot more problem statements coming out from us to solicit ideas from you.”
The objective, he said, was to move promising technology more rapidly through development and into procurement rather than allowing programmes to become trapped between experimentation and a formal equipment programme. His speech also contained unusually direct criticism of the Government’s previous relationship with the British space industry.
Reflecting on his years at Inmarsat, Pearce said successive attempts to build a stronger national space industrial strategy had struggled because Defence had not acted as a sufficiently consistent customer.
He said: “One of the things we struggled with was really to get the UK government to come on board as a major development customer of the UK space industry, to really lend its heft and its buying power to liberate the potential of our industry.”
Pearce added: “It is very clear to me at the time that the elephant that was not in the room was MOD. We couldn’t get MOD to the table.”
He argued that government had historically been stronger at producing industrial strategies than following them through with sustained purchasing and investment. Now responsible for a substantial part of Defence’s investment budget, Pearce said he intended to use that purchasing power differently.
He told industry: “Finally, ladies and gentlemen, I have the invest budget. You have the ideas.”
International collaboration will remain a central part of the approach. Pearce said British systems must be interoperable and increasingly interchangeable with those of allies, while the UK would use NATO, the European Space Agency and bilateral partnerships to encourage greater industrial coordination.
He said stronger allied integration should not be viewed as reducing sovereign capability.
Pearce said: “Building stronger collective capabilities does not diminish sovereignty; it strengthens it. It creates resilient, distributed capabilities, helping share the risk and increase the reward.”
Closing his speech, Pearce said space capabilities were now central to Britain’s ability to deter conflict and, if deterrence failed, to fight it.
He told the industry audience: “I firmly believe that space capabilities sit at the heart of the UK’s ability to deter, and if necessary, to fight and win. So bring it on. Let’s work together. Let’s spend my money on your capabilities.”

====================================================================================================

Samar Yazbek's Your Presence is a Danger to Your Life on Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:05:49 UTC
22:05:49 KST

Breadcrumb
'It seemed as though we had entered hell': Samar Yazbek's chilling Gaza testimonies in Your Presence is a Danger to Your Life
There are sentences in this remarkable, painful book that imply an entire universe of horror. Like this: "We brought my daughter’s leg and buried it next to her brother and sister." Or this: "A boy was blowing air into a dismembered woman’s corpse, trying to bring her back to life – she was his mother."
Your Presence is a Danger to Your Life – the title is taken from the flyers dropped by the Israelis minutes before they bombed civilian targets – documents the Gaza genocide, or at least the genocide as experienced by 26 men, women and children interviewed at length throughout 2024 while they were receiving medical treatment in Qatar.
The interviewer, editor and shaper of these narratives is the Syrian novelist and non-fiction writer Samar Yazbek.
Yazbek has already produced three documentary texts from the Syrian Revolution and war – Woman in the Crossfire and others.
In the introduction, she explains how the destruction of Gaza reenacted for her the destruction of Syria. She hints at the continuum of experience between the two disasters, and describes her work as "testament to a dream of justice for those living beneath the grindstone of this violent era."
But there are key differences, terrifying "novel details" involving the technological sophistication of the Israeli genocidaires and their "algorithms of murder."
Many of the witnesses are householders hit at home in the midst of family life. A child asks for a sandwich, and then, in a flash, life is irretrievably broken.
"My brain couldn’t interpret what had happened" is a phrase repeated by several. "It seemed as though we had entered hell" is another.
Some witnesses are doctors, nurses, or volunteers who helped in hospitals. They recount Israeli soldiers bombing maternity wards, storming the intensive care department, methodically destroying the medical equipment.
One doctor is forced into the role of human shield. Several witnesses remember Israeli soldiers torturing the maimed and dying in their beds.
There are descriptions of dismemberment, of heads split open, of cats red-faced from human meals. Someone recalls "a grandmother as gentle as the breeze … innocent children, splendid as roses, evaporated in an instant;" others talk of children who bleed to death alone, or children who lose their entire families: parents, grandparents, siblings, cousins, aunts and uncles.
For the survivors, or semi-survivors, there is endless pain, vomiting after drinking poisoned water, the stink of sewage, of infected, maggot-filled wounds, of corpses rotting under the rubble.
There is the shame of being unable to stop screaming in a room full of strangers.
'Things that cannot be spoken'
Yazbek preserves the creative uses of Palestinian war idiom in the witness accounts. For instance, the popular word for a vacuum bomb is ‘shafat’ — meaning ‘suction’ — an idea which is then animated: "It took no more than two seconds to suck up twenty-five souls."
One of the accounts ends with the words, "And then there are all the things that cannot be spoken." This silence contains both general and specific meanings.
In general, as Yazbek writes in her introduction, "humans are capable of brutalizing each other in ways that challenge language’s very capacity of expression." More specifically, women witnesses would describe to Yazbek rapes and sexual abuse perpetrated on other women, but never on themselves.
None of this can be described as easy reading. The accounts provoke a visceral response, and sometimes the reader feels a near compulsion to put the book aside, go for a walk, and observe the emotional tumult it has unleashed.
Horror, grief and rage are natural responses to the reality expressed here. And yet there is a contrary compulsion to keep reading, to know the worst of it, to bear witness alongside Yazbek. Each distinct Palestinian voice, full of character, leads us through the maelstrom.
Yazbek understands genocide as an erasure: "The erasure of dismembered bodies; the erasure of our ability to see clearly; the erasure of the profound act of bearing witness to the agony of others; the erasure of language."
This book, then, no less than the writing of Primo Levi and other survivors of the Holocaust, seeks to transform erasure into narrative.
The effort to do so is particularly valuable given the welter of Zionist propaganda erasing the past and present existence of Palestinians.
To render them invisible and inaudible, Israel has prevented international journalists from entering Gaza and has assassinated at least 267 Palestinian journalists since 7 October 2023, according to the International Federation of Journalists.
A history of erasure
The attempted erasure of Palestinians and their rights reaches back through the repeated military assaults and the quarter-century-long siege of Gaza, back through the decades of massacre and dispossession, all the way to the erasure of hundreds of villages and towns that marked the birth of the Zionist state.
In this book, unlike in her documentations of Syrian suffering, Yazbek largely erases her own presence in favour of the Palestinians she so carefully listens to.
She notices the most pertinent details of their narratives and closely reproduces the idiomatic style and substance of their voices. What emerges is the eloquence of ordinary people under extraordinary pressure, a testament to Palestinian resilience, and a record of one of the greatest crimes of the age.
Unlike the crimes in Ukraine, Syria or Sudan, this one has been funded and armed by the United States and rhetorically supported by most Western governments and media outlets. In other words, the states that until recently claimed to promote universal human rights and international law have abandoned that pretence in order to stand with Zionist barbarism.
This has obvious implications for us all, not just Palestinians.
The genocide is still underway today, though more slowly, and will continue until we finally move to stop it.
"For over seventy years," says Abu Yahya, father of two murdered and two maimed children, "everyone has abandoned us."

Tsikhanouskaya warns Russia could use Belarus for new attacks on Ukraine
Unknown

Exiled Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said the threat of Russia using Belarusian territory to launch new attacks against Ukraine is "a real possibility," as reported by Ukrinform on Sept. 23.
"If Russia at some point again wants to attack Ukraine in any way from the northern border, then (Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenko) will be very happy to provide territory, logistics, and Belarusian infrastructure to help Putin achieve his goals," Tsikhanouskaya told Ukrinform on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has increasingly warned that Russia might open a new front against northern Ukraine and attempt to draw Belarus deeper into the war.
Lukashenko, who allowed Russian forces to use Belarusian territory as a staging ground for the 2022 Kyiv offensive, denied such plans on May 21 and proposed a meeting with Zelensky in either Belarus or Ukraine.
Tsikhanouskaya said Belarusian infrastructure is already being used to support Russian drone operations, including logistics and equipment for directing drones.
The comments come after Ukrainian officials said on Sept. 14 that Russia is using Belarusian infrastructure, including LTE networks and repeater stations, to help maintain stable signals for Shahed-type drones during attacks on Ukraine.
Tsikhanouskaya also said repeaters were being installed along Belarus' borders with Ukraine and EU countries, which she warned could facilitate future Russian attacks or provocations.
She added that Lukashenko has benefited economically from Russia's war, claiming that more than 500 Belarusian companies produce components, including optics and microchips, for the Russian military, supply petroleum products to Russia, and help Moscow circumvent sanctions.
Tsikhanouskaya also pointed to Belarus' cooperation with Russian online retailer Wildberries, saying the Belarusian regime was developing warehouses for the company.
Wildberries has become a target of Ukraine's long-range drone campaign in recent months. Ukrainian forces struck at least several of the company's logistics facilities across Russia in July and August. Zelensky said some of the targeted warehouses were being used to supply the Russian military, including with navigation equipment and components for drone production.
Tsikhanouskaya said Lukashenko would like Russia to win the war because Moscow is his main political and economic ally. She argued that a weakened Russian President Vladimir Putin would mean less support for the Belarusian regime.
Belarus held military exercises near its borders with Poland and Lithuania from Sept. 15 to 18, the Belarusian Defense Ministry said on Sept. 15.
The Belarusian Defense Ministry described the drills as "defensive" and said they are aimed at improving the military's ability to "protect the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity."
Belarus is also building new railway infrastructure in the country's southern Gomel Oblast that will be capable of receiving military trains carrying personnel and heavy equipment, the Belarusian Railway Workers' Community reported on Aug. 24.

UK growth outlook weakened by rising energy prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

22:05:18 KST

The UK’s economic growth forecast for next year has been downgraded as the prolonged conflict in the Middle East pushes up energy prices and weighs on the global economy.
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said the UK economy is expected to grow by 1 percent in 2027, down from its previous forecast of 1.1%.
However, the organisation upgraded its forecast for 2026, predicting growth of 1.1 percent, compared with 0.9 percent in its previous outlook.
The OECD said stronger domestic demand had supported the UK economy in the short term. But higher fuel prices were expected to weigh on growth in 2027, with the impact depending on how long supply disruptions caused by the conflict last.
Oil stockpiles and supplies from outside the Gulf states have so far helped cushion the effects on economies, the OECD said.
The OECD expects global growth to be 0.1 percentage points lower next year as a result of the conflict and other risks. Australia, Canada and the euro area are among the economies facing weaker prospects.
It also warned that climate-related supply shocks, including those associated with a strong El Nino, could affect agricultural production and push up food prices.

‘They told me to go back to my country’: Inside the UK’s wave of racism

Unknown Publisher

‘They told me to go back to my country’: Inside the UK’s wave of racism
From street attacks to political rhetoric, xenophobia is becoming an everyday occurrence.
Manchester, United Kingdom – Agnes Peters, a care worker from Manchester, vividly remembers the moment she was targeted for her race.
“I was coming back from work,” she said, her voice low from a table in a Manchester library’s cafe. “I was in my uniform … and they told me to go back to my country, used racial slurs against me and threw things from the car as they drove slowly past,” she said. “People were watching and recording.”

Only one bystander reproached the abusers for “throwing stones” at Peters, she said, remembering the incident last year.
Racists have become emboldened, she said, describing the rise of xenophobia in the United Kingdom.
“They feel like if they come out in public and embarrass me, a Black person, it gives them supporters,” she said. “They’re no longer sitting on the fence. They’re out there actively trying to pull people down.”
While the nature of racism that emerged after Brexit has persisted, focused on those trying to enter the UK irregularly, other minorities have also been at the sharp end of discrimination.
Earlier this month, Oxfam, Amnesty International and 152 other groups issued a joint statement calling for the government “to act immediately” over what they described as the normalisation of racist violence in the UK.
“Levels of racist violence and intimidation that were once considered extreme are now becoming weekly occurrences across the UK”, they said, reflecting on “the consequences of years of growing inequality, underinvestment in communities and public services, and political and media narratives that have normalised racism, anti-migrant sentiment and Islamophobia.”
Migration and racism
The issue is never far away from the headlines.
In recent days, far-right activist Daniel Thomas, described as an “outright racist” by UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, filmed himself slashing an inflatable rescue boat in the Channel – while a rescue worker was still on board.
His group, Patriot Platform, has caused chaos during anti-migrant actions at the ports of Dover and Portsmouth, and he has suggested bringing “thousands” of his black-clad members to the Oxfordshire village of Piddington, where some are resisting government attempts to house asylum seekers.
Other English towns have also seen anti-migration protests, often featuring crowds of masked men engaging in anti-social behaviour.
“They’ll say they’re anti-immigration.” Nahella Ashraf, a Manchester organiser with Stand Up to Racism, said, describing how right-wing protests outside of mosques or hotels housing asylum seekers inevitably result in arbitrary attacks on individuals based on their skin colour.
“And actually the truth is, whether it’s the guys in balaclavas and black outfits in Portsmouth or Dover, or whether it’s the English Defence League marching on our streets many years ago, we know that wherever they go, there are attacks on Black people … That hasn’t changed.”
Political mainstreaming
Increasingly, hateful rhetoric is being politicised.
Commenting on Piddington, Sarah Pochin, an MP with the far-right Reform UK, claimed in an interview that migrants and refugees posed a threat to “indigenous white women”.
“Mainstream discourse has a role in normalising right-wing discourse,” said Paul Jackson, a professor and researcher on the hard right at the University of Northampton.
“Politicians are quick to absorb the sentiments of the extreme right and, by using it in their discourse, normalise it. However, this doesn’t seem to build their base, so much as draw people to the further right-wing extremes. I mean, why would you go for a party aping the extreme, when the real deal is available?”
Earlier this month, Reform UK’s self-styled “shadow Home Secretary” Zia Yusuf was accused of racism after writing on X that Labour figure Sagal Abdi-Wali, tipped to run in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, was born in Somalia.
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds called the post “pretty straightforward racism”.
In 2025, then-Conservative shadow Justice Secretary Robert Jenrick was criticised for saying he had not seen “another white face” during a visit to Birmingham, while earlier this year his successor, Nick Timothy, described a mass Muslim prayer event in Trafalgar Square as “an act of domination”.
Aurelien Mondon, of the Reactionary Politics Research Network at the University of Bath, noted “a clear link between the emboldening of the most extreme actors on the far right and over two decades of mainstreaming of far-right discourse by mainstream actors”.
“We cannot on the one hand have mainstream media and politicians prioritising far-right issues and discourse and then claim to be surprised when the far right rises or gets emboldened,” he said. “The responsibility in this situation is squarely with those who had the most power to stop it and consciously decided to fuel it instead.”
Rising tides
According to a recent YouGov poll, Reform would secure 21 percent of the vote if a general election were held tomorrow, while Labour would reach 23 percent. Support for Restore, which is further to the right than Reform, was predicted at 4 percent.
The hard right is also making gains in Germany and France.
“Populist anti-immigrant rhetoric in Parliament [in the UK] has consequences for public safety,” said a spokesperson for the independent educational charity, the Institute of Race Relations (IRR).
Mainstream political parties “have capitulated to the hard-right agenda when it comes to the onslaught against migrants and refugee rights”, they added.
In Manchester, Ashraf said while the far right may be better funded and, through various social media networks, have a stronger platform, there is still cause for optimism.
“We are still the majority,” she said.
“And although they use their platforms to really push out hate and division, I think we’re still winning,” she added. “We know every time we do an event in support of refugees, people come up and we meet new people constantly.”
At a recent school event, she said children approached her to offer their books to refugees.
“That is a message of hope. And those are stories you never hear.”

A Russian military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace on Wednesday morning, the operational command of Poland’s armed forces has announced.
The incident is the latest in a series of airspace violations by Russia, which have also involved drones and, most recently, a missile. It follows recent warnings by the Polish government that Moscow has been planning further “provocations” intended to test NATO’s defences and unity.

On Wednesday afternoon, Polish operational command announced that, shortly after 11:00 a.m. that day, an Mi-8 helicopter belonging to the Russian armed forces had briefly entered Polish airspace near the town of Braniewo, after crossing from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
The helicopter did not travel further than 300 metres into Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds. In response, the Polish military scrambled fighter jets and placed ground forces on standby.
“The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defences,” wrote operational command. At the time of writing, Russia has not commented on the incident.
Today’s violation appears to be the first publicly reported instance of a Russian military helicopter crossing Poland’s land border. Last year, in two separate incidents, a Russian Su-24 bomber and a naval helicopter flew over Poland’s territorial waters in the Baltic Sea.
In 2023, two helicopters belonging to the armed forces of Belarus, a close ally of Russia, briefly entered Polish airspace before crossing back over the border.
On one night in September last year, around 20 Russian drones entered Poland over its eastern borders amid Russian attacks on Ukraine. Polish and allied forces shot down some of them, while others hit the ground without causing casulaties.
In July this year, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload entered Polish airspace before landing in a field in eastern Poland.

In recent months, Poland and other NATO countries have been warning of Russian plans to carry out further “provocations” intended to test the alliance’s defences and unity, saying that they could include border and airspace violations.
In recent weeks, Poland has regularly intercepted Russian aircraft that have flown close to Polish territorial waters in the Baltic Sea. This month, Russian drones have repeatedly hit targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including a passenger train travelling from Kyiv to Warsaw.
Just last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental.

Damaged data centers cause internet outages

Kwaśniewski says what could prompt Putin to seek ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:02:00 UTC
22:02:00 KST

Kwaśniewski says what could prompt Putin to seek ceasefire
Former Polish President Aleksander Kwaśniewski expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Perhaps it is precisely psychological changes and a shift in public sentiment in Russia that could prompt Putin to accelerate his search for a ceasefire,” Kwaśniewski emphasized.
He noted that, in his view, the psychological resilience of Russian society is the most interesting factor when assessing Russia’s ability to continue its war against Ukraine.
“How long will society be willing to accept this ‘special military operation,’ which is a real war and costs thousands of lives? This is not only about those killed, but also those who return wounded,” the Polish politician said.
According to Kwaśniewski, the war is increasingly being felt directly on Russian territory.
“Thanks to the development of Ukrainian technologies, residents of Moscow, St. Petersburg, or somewhere in or beyond the Urals suddenly saw that this is not something you can simply watch on television. This is not a TV series. This is something they are already experiencing themselves,” he said.
In his view, Ukrainian attacks could gradually erode the sense of detachment from the war in Russian society – the principle of “my home is at the edge” [meaning that one is unconcerned with matters outside one’s immediate surroundings].
“And the question is how long this society will be willing to simultaneously accept a deteriorating economic situation, casualties and a direct threat? I think this is Russia’s main vulnerability today,” Kwaśniewski emphasized.
At the same time, he stressed that the political resilience of Russia’s system remains high. According to him, Putin has managed to consolidate power to an extraordinary degree over the years.
“Perhaps this will sound strange, but he has a stronger position today than Stalin once had,” Kwaśniewski said.
He explained that, despite his powerful repressive system, Stalin had to take the Politburo [the main government group in the USSR] into account, whereas the current Russian president effectively has no parliamentary oversight, independent media or civil society capable of limiting his power.
Kwaśniewski assessed Russia’s economic resilience as moderate. He noted that the country’s transition to a wartime economy had allowed the Kremlin to continue the war despite enormous costs.
“They have been able to wage this war for the fifth year now, despite the colossal costs. The sanctions are working, but their effect is limited,” he said.
At the same time, Kwaśniewski believes that Russia’s economic situation will deteriorate with each additional year of the war.
He also stressed that he does not expect peace on terms that are fair to Ukraine as long as Putin remains in power.
“He wants to have all of Ukraine within his sphere of influence, and he will not change this thinking because it is his worldview,” Kwaśniewski emphasized.
According to him, the Russian president wants Ukraine to remain a buffer between Russia and Europe and to be within Moscow’s sphere of influence rather than that of the West.
“And this needs to be said loudly to the world, because there is an impression that they do not fully understand what this war is about. And it is precisely about this: not a quarter or half of Ukraine – but all of Ukraine, which, in Putin’s understanding, should be part of ‘greater Russia,’ that is, remain within the Russian sphere of influence,” Kwaśniewski said.
He also expressed the conviction that even the signing of a peace agreement would not necessarily mean the end of Russia’s hybrid war against Ukraine.
“I don’t think further manipulation on political issues or exploitation of Ukraine’s vulnerabilities will stop,” Kwaśniewski said.
At the same time, in his view, Russia has already encountered something Putin did not expect – the strengthening of Ukrainian national consciousness.
“He will not be able to subjugate Ukraine, for example, through political manipulation. Terror can subjugate part of a territory, but not the entire country,” the former Polish president said.
As reported by Ukrinform, former Polish President Aleksander Kwaśniewski criticized U.S. President’s Special Envoy Steve Witkoff over his statement that he has “full trust” in Vladimir Putin.

Ukraine’s new draft Civil Code would give people the right to disconnect from work communications during weekends and other non-working hours, Verkhovna Rada Chairman Ruslan Stefanchuk said.
The proposed “right to informational peace” would mean employers and colleagues could not contact people about work-related matters during their days off.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Stefanchuk announced the proposal during the official presentation of the new draft Civil Code of Ukraine.
The draft significantly expands protections for personal non-property rights, including the rights to life and health, reproductive rights, reputation, and privacy.
It also addresses rights linked to modern communication technologies, including messengers, websites, audio and video calls, and artificial intelligence.
For the first time, the code would also introduce a “right to be forgotten,” which Stefanchuk said would protect people from being permanently pursued over mistakes they made as children.
“When a person has a day off, they should not be disturbed over matters related to work communication,” Stefanchuk said.
Other provisions would regulate property rights, intellectual property, and AI, including copyright, patents, licenses and works or other objects created with AI.

EKRE politician hit with copyright claim after using Alo Mattiisen song in political ad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:01:00 UTC
22:01:00 KST

EKRE politician hit with copyright claim after using Alo Mattiisen song in political ad
On June 8, a political ad posted on EKRE Vice Chair Mart Helme's Facebook page used Alo Mattiisen's song "Isamaa ilu hoieldes" without permission, prompting a damages claim.
The claim totals €6,531.40, including legal fees. The damages sought amount to €5,000. That figure is based on what songwriters generally charge to allow their works to be used in similar political ads.
"The information came from various songwriters and advertising agencies that have produced similar ads," copyright holder Mariita Mattiisen-Puusepp said in a written response prepared with her lawyer. There is no standard price list: Each songwriter asks what they consider reasonable and the client either agrees or declines.
"An approximate going rate has nevertheless emerged and that is what we based the claim on," Mattiisen-Puusepp wrote. "In this case, a very important fact is that I would not have given permission for Alo Mattiisen's works to be used in any political party's advertising."
Claim remains outstanding
Helme had until August 24 to meet the claim but has yet to do so.
Through his lawyer, Helme told Mattiisen-Puusepp that he does not manage his Facebook page, had therefore done nothing wrong and would not pay the requested amount. He also reportedly did not answer when asked who manages the page.
Mattiisen-Puusepp and her lawyer wrote to Helme that the page is designated as a politician's page and displays both his email address and EKRE's website. They said his claim that he has no connection to the page was neither credible nor plausible.
Mattiisen-Puusepp and her lawyer also drew Helme's attention to Facebook's rules, which state that a person with a page on the platform is responsible for ensuring, among other things, that it complies with applicable law, regardless of who actually posts to it.
Third persons cannot create pages for strangers in Facebook
Mattiisen-Puusepp said that, as far as she knows, only a politician can create a Facebook page designated for that politician. "Facebook checks this very strictly to prevent third parties from creating official pages for politicians or using someone else's name for any purpose," she said.
Mattiisen-Puusepp added that if Helme does not meet the claim, they will take the matter to court. "The infringement is well documented. The amount of damages can then be settled in court," she said. Intellectual property is property like any other, she added, and even though the post has since been deleted, the damage has already been done.
ERR was unable to reach Helme for comment before publication.

Britain’s far-right violence comes to us direct from the 1970s. But so does the solution | Taj Ali
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:00:50 UTC
22:00:50 KST

There it was: a pool of blood spreading across the pavement. A section of the high street had been cordoned off and a uniformed police officer gestured for bystanders to move along. It was the long hot summer of 1976, and a racist murder had stunned Southall in west London.
“What has happened here, officers?” asked Suresh Grover, then a curious 22-year-old, later to be widely known as a leading racial justice activist. “Go away, it’s just Indian blood,” was the response. Grover was soon to learn that 18-year-old Gurdip Singh Chaggar, an engineering student, had been stabbed to death by racist thugs the night before.
The late 1970s was the era of “Paki-bashing”: homes, shops and places of worship were attacked, while south Asians – young and old – were murdered on the streets. That day, Grover acted instinctively, taking some paint and daubing the pavement near the blood with the words: “This racist murder will be avenged. We’ll get you racist scum.”
This is the story of working-class youth who refused to turn the other cheek. From Southall to Sheffield and from Brick Lane to Bradford, the Asian youth movements were set up to physically defend communities from racist attacks. It was because of their heroic efforts that many of us in diverse towns and cities have grown up in safer environments.
But more than 50 years on, that racist violence has returned with shocking ferocity, a deterioration traceable to the summer of 2024, which marked some of the worst racist rioting in living memory.
In Hartlepool, a young south Asian man was walking down a street when he was punched in the face. Onlookers cheered, laughed and yelled racial slurs. “A Paki got banged,” one shouted, as those around him began to smash the windows of small businesses and kick down the door of a nearby house. In Middlesbrough, a group of white men stopped motorists and questioned them about their ethnicity, asking whether they were “white” before letting them through. In Rotherham and Tamworth, racist mobs tried to burn down hotels housing refugees.
And now? A seemingly relentless rise. Every five days, a mosque in Britain is attacked. The rhetoric of the far right has been mainstreamed.
After years spent researching and writing a book on the rich and proud tradition of political activism in the south Asian community, it seems clear to me that we cannot fight racism in silos. We must build broad movements that transcend racial and religious divides.
The Asian youth movements had a belief in the concept of political blackness as a banner that people of colour could unite under. To Tariq Mehmood, an Asian youth movement member who was born in Pakistan but raised in Bradford, there was no real difference between south Asian, African and Caribbean people: they were all the same to those who wanted to harm them. “We were called ‘black bastards’ on the streets,” he recalled. “We were commonly united with our African and Afro-Caribbean friends. They didn’t know they were black until they came here — I didn’t know I was a ‘Paki’ until I came to Bradford. We were united on those common issues of our oppression.”
They saw themselves as part of a broader working class. The Sheffield Asian Youth Movement and the Indian Workers’ Association, for instance, sent minibuses of their members to picket lines during the 1984-85 miners’ strike. They stood with white working-class communities fighting to save their industries, providing much needed financial support while challenging prejudice in these communities. Grover tells me that more than a decade after that strike, Kent miners were still attending Punjabi Sikh weddings in Southall because of the links that were built during that dispute.
These were movements rooted in their communities and strategic in their organising. They monitored the far right and mapped out who was most vulnerable to racist attacks. The Sheffield Asian Youth Movement had a big thick folder called the “fascist file”, in which they would compile information on local racists.
But things changed. As the 20th century wore on, anti-racist activism was increasingly institutionalised as the struggle moved from the streets to council chambers and boardrooms. Where we once had grassroots anti-racist movements rooted in communities, we now have a race-relations industry in which a few people are paid to tackle discrimination. We also have the rise of self-proclaimed community leaders under the policy of state multiculturalism who often speak on behalf of entire communities. Too often, they become the prism through which authorities engage with ethnic-minority communities.
A revival of grassroots anti-racist movements is long overdue. But it must be of this time, attuned to the changing circumstances of 2026. Racism is not experienced equally. Class, gender and geography all matter. A hijab-wearing Muslim woman is more likely to be a victim of Islamophobia than a Muslim man. Those living in smaller, more isolated ethnic-minority communities are more vulnerable to racist attack. First-generation migrants have greater insecurity than the grandchildren of migrants. An effective anti-racist movement must reflect on these challenges and prioritise those most vulnerable to racist violence.
The good news is that we are starting to see a revival of this approach. A few months ago, I spoke alongside Grover at the launch of the Nottinghamshire Solidarity Network, which is taking a strategic approach to anti-racism by organising county-wide to ensure smaller ethnic-minority communities are not left isolated. A week later, I spoke at the launch of the Greater Manchester Workers’ and Tenants’ Association. Its members understand that the far right feeds on deprivation and despair in working-class communities, and they are seeking to organise on the basis of class in an attempt to offer a counter-narrative to that of division and hate.
All of these movements, past and present, understand that racism will not be defeated from above. It will only be defeated by us – ordinary citizens who refuse to look away.
- 
  Taj Ali is a journalist and historian and author of Come What May, We’re Here to Stay: the Story of South Asian Resistance in Britain

‘It’s inescapable’: will new revelations about enslavement force Britain to finally confront its past?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
13:00:49 UTC
22:00:49 KST

Over the past 10 days, a series of registers, documents and reports have been published, all revealing the scale of Britain’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade. The overall picture is one of a nation powered by enslavement and investment in it. This week, I spoke to Chris Osuh, a community affairs correspondent at the Guardian, about these new revelations and Britain’s persistent difficulty in confronting its own history.
Last week, a Register of British Slave Traders, compiled by historians, was published. Its length and detail exposed that the British financial system was much more involved in enslavement than previously thought. Scrolling through the names is chilling in its prosaicness. There are owners and co-owners of slaving voyages from London to various locations in the Caribbean. There are investors in the Royal African Company, an English trading company that trafficked more Africans to the Americas than any other. There are ordinary people – soap boilers and cheesemongers, surgeons and diplomats – all with various interests, shares, ownerships and investments in the trading of Africans. The register is 636 pages long.
The commodities they traded and profited from were also named a few days later. Earlier this week, the Former British Colonies Enslavement Registers was published, making almost 4 million records of enslaved people across 20 former British colonies searchable to the general public.
People will have different responses when perusing these accounts. But I was most struck by seeing the names of those who were sold into hundreds of years of enslavement and suffering, expressed through the banality of trade and profit details. The relics of the entire system: the ledgers, the neatly written names of the enslaved and their children, reduced to units. Grappling with these records vertiginously brings you face to face with a history that does not feel distant or unrelatable, but something intimate and familiar. This was a business.
Chris draws another parallel between these accounts and the present: there is still a persistent impulse to minimise what happened. “The common thread, to put it bluntly,” he says, is “the same tendency to minimise African pain, suffering and labour. That is something that cuts across centuries. It just expresses itself in different ways.”
“Once upon a time it expressed itself with justifications of slavery,” Chris tells me. “Now it expresses itself with ‘we don’t have to apologise, we don’t owe you anything’.”
Why disavow this part of British history?
Britain is a nation with a vast cultural appetite for its history – from period dramas, to Henry VIII, to the world wars of the 20th century. So I am always astonished by the absence of enslavement from mainstream historical accounts. If you are a nation interested in documenting your past, forget about the morality of it, you would surely be interested in including a system that played a significant role in Britain’s politics, economy and industrialisation for almost 250 years. Perhaps there has been an offshoring of enslavement in the British collective consciousness, in the same way slavery was geographically offshored to British colonies.
Chris says that these blind spots partly result from the ways that history has been leveraged for national fantasies. There is a perpetual culture war surrounding British history, Chris says, “where one side uses history to engage in a kind of national myth making that makes everybody feel good about their identity. This approach values a heroic narrative in which you are always the good guy.” I am reminded here of the scholar and first prime minister of Trinidad and Tobago Eric Williams, who remarked that “British historians wrote almost as if Britain had introduced Negro slavery solely for the satisfaction of abolishing it.”
In the competing historical practice, history is about learning from the past and preventing future mistakes. In 2023, the Guardian published the Cotton Capital series on its founders’ links to enslavement in Manchester, England. In response to these revelations, it launched the 10-year Legacies of Enslavement programme, which included the creation of the Long Wave and Chris’s role.
“There is a huge blind spot about the reality of empire in the UK,” Chris tells me. “It’s a strange blind spot. It’s almost a taboo. You’re not really supposed to connect the dots. You’re not supposed to ask: ‘Where was Manchester getting its cotton from? Where were the ships from Liverpool going? The insurance industry and stockbrokers in London – what were they selling shares in? Why is there a place called West India Docks’?”
The interesting thing, Chris has gleaned from his reporting, is that “there was much more transparency at the time. Church of England clergy were basically saying ‘we need to colonise for gain’s sake, because England is overcrowded’. That ‘Africans are the fittest hands for plantation work’. Churchmen saying ‘we use African bodies for our support and happiness’. They were not pretending.”
That clarity has become obscured over the years by an enveloping myth about Britain. One that has resulted in, Chris says: “a lot of amnesia about inconvenient histories.” This notion that Britain has built itself alone is challenged by honest accounts of its past, which show that the building of modern Britain was made possible by the unpaid labour and resources of millions of people. Chris tells me: “They interfere with this idea of an island nation that punches above its weight.”
It’s time to face the facts
The old myths are colliding with these new accounts. “The scholarship is thriving on different continents,” Chris says, and he describes much of it as an evidence-based account of “who did what, where, and the impact”. Black scholars are at the forefront, but they are joined by white scholars in Europe and America. “This takes it from a place where critics can argue that this is driven by Black self-interest,” Chris says. “Critics would love to frame this in terms of identity, or minimise what happened and make it ideological. But beyond the desire for justice, there is a desire for knowledge.”
By resisting this knowledge, we are denying ourselves a full understanding of Britain’s past, and its present. “This was a commodification of human life on a scale that has never been seen before or since, and an industrialisation of the process sustained by prolonged violence and cruelty,” Chris tells me. He emphasises that these histories show us how that dehumanisation was made possible, with people treated as objects, property, products, as units to generate capital. “It’s inescapable.”
But people and institutions still do want to escape it, not just to avoid shame, but to avoid material loss. As Caribbean nations increasingly mount reparations claims, these records bring us closer to establishing a legal picture of liability.
Even those who refuse to engage with a moral argument must face the fact that there is a case here. “The backlash is being kept alive because it goes to the heart of two things so dear to western societies,” Chris says. “Their identity as heroic, and their money.”
