Al-Qudwa, Hamas, Islamic Jihad and Dahlan join together for Palestinian elections
Multiple sources told The New Arab that a political alliance to contest the Palestinian legislative elections has been formed in Cairo, bringing together the Palestinian Democratic National Gathering, the Reformist Current of the Fatah movement, Hamas and Islamic Jihad. It is expected to be officially announced within two days.
Nasser al-Qudwa, head of the Palestinian Democratic National Gathering, told TNA that currently underway in Cairo is a push for the formation of a non-factional national list to participate in the Palestinian Legislative Council elections scheduled for November.
"Bilateral and multilateral meetings and contacts have taken place over the past two days between the Palestinian Democratic National Gathering, the Reformist Current in the Fatah movement, Hamas and Islamic Jihad. An agreement was reached to form a non-factional national list that includes a broad spectrum of Palestinian national figures and anyone who wishes to be part of this expanded national list," Al-Qudwa added.
He further said efforts will continue in the coming days to draft the political statement and determine the names of participants for the electoral list.
The meetings were attended by Nasser al-Qudwa, head of the National Current; Mohammed Dahlan; Hamas Political Bureau members Hussam Badran and Zahar Jabarin; and Islamic Jihad Secretary-General Ziad al-Nakhalah.
These political groups, along with the Democratic Front and Popular Front, took part in a meeting in Cairo on 20 August, where they discussed the idea of an expanded, non-factional national list to contest the legislative elections.
Reportedly, the Popular Front requested more time at the time to consider the matter and present it to its organisational bodies. It later announced a political initiative, the main feature of which was the establishment of a transitional national council.
However, the initiative received no response from President Mahmoud Abbas and the Fatah movement.
"The formation of the list of names and the political statement will be postponed until after the above alliance receives a response from imprisoned Fatah leader Marwan Barghouti," one source told TNA.
Asked whether Barghouti's rejection would lead to the alliance not being formed, the source said, "We know that Barghouti does not want to head a list in the Legislative Council elections because he has decided to run in the presidential elections, and we are waiting to hear what he will say over the next two days."
The source stressed that "the alliance will continue".
It appears that the Popular Front has not only been absent from this alliance but has also yet to decide whether to participate in the Legislative Council elections.
Informed sources also told TNA that contacts between the Popular Front and the "Alliance for Change and National Liberation" list have ceased, indicating that the Popular Front will not be part of this electoral alliance.
The Alliance for Change and National Liberation brings together a group of national and independent elites and figures and grassroots groups, the National Initiative Movement, and the "Palestinian Popular Conference 14 Million".
The Central Elections Commission set the nomination period from the morning of Saturday, 26 September, until the evening of Wednesday, 7 October, and outlined several conditions; these include that nominations must be submitted only through electoral lists, with individual nominations not accepted; and an electoral list must be formed by a party, a coalition of parties or a group of voters for the purpose of participating in elections for membership of the Legislative Council.
The commission also stipulated that the list of candidates must be closed in terms of the order of names, with the seats won by each list distributed among its candidates according to the order of their names on the list, with the first candidate followed by the next, and so on.
The electoral list's nomination application must be submitted through the list coordinator and authorised representative, who represents it in all matters before the commission, including submitting all applications and documents on its behalf to the commission.

Lithuanian minister decides to close visa centres in Central Asia over ‘terrorism risks’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

Lithuania will close external service centres in several Muslim countries in Central Asia and Europe, citing potential national security and terrorism risks, Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said Wednesday.
“I have made the decision to close the branches of the external service provider in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Bosnia and Herzegovina,” Katelynas said in a Facebook post.
The centres process applications for residence permits and initiate migration procedures for foreigners seeking to come to Lithuania. Katelynas said an assessment of security risks and the threat of terrorism found no justification for continuing their operations.
“When the State Security Department warns of potential terrorism risks and has already identified individuals from Central Asia with radical views or links to terrorism, the state cannot wait for a risk to become an incident,” Katelynas said.
He said Lithuania did not plan to open new external service centres in other countries following the closures.
The decision comes as Lithuania has tightened controls on labour migration from Central Asia. Migration Department Director Indrė Gasperė said Tuesday that the number of workers arriving from the region had increased in recent years, but applications from Central Asian citizens seeking to enter Lithuania for employment are currently no longer being accepted. The department said the external service centres had been suspended after receiving very large numbers of employment-related applications.
Lithuania’s 2026 quota for foreign workers is 24,706. Once the quota is exhausted, temporary residence permits for employment can generally be issued only when additional statutory conditions are met, including higher salary thresholds or employment in certain high-value, shortage occupations.
The closures will also affect Bosnia and Herzegovina, where Lithuania opened an external service provider centre in October 2025 as part of a broader restructuring of the countries in which foreigners could apply for Lithuanian residence permits and national visas.
As of September 1, nearly 227,000 foreign nationals held valid residence permits in Lithuania, according to Migration Department data. Ukrainians accounted for about 80,000, followed by nearly 48,000 Belarusians and about 13,000 Russian citizens. Uzbekistan had about 12,600 citizens with valid permits, while India and Tajikistan accounted for about 9,400 and 7,500, respectively.
The number of Central Asian nationals living in Lithuania has grown significantly in recent years. Official data show that the number of Uzbek citizens holding valid residence permits rose from about 10,500 at the beginning of 2026 to more than 12,600 by September 1, while the number of Tajik citizens increased to about 7,500.

In Taiwan, a Disaster Exercise Prepares for Conflict, Too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:29:00 UTC
21:29:00 KST

In the seaside town of Taitung, four hours from Taipei by train, Taiwan’s premier national disaster preparedness exercise simulated a response to a 7.3 magnitude earthquake – layered with variables Taiwan could face in a conflict contingency. This year’s drill marked a critical operational shift, moving past standard disaster response to stress-test Taiwan against cascading, multisystem failures alongside expanded participation from regional and international partners.
The base scenario estimated damage to 43 bridges and nearly 1,800 buildings, along with 63 casualties. Search-and-rescue teams and fire departments from seven cities and counties in Taiwan conducted a full-scale mobilization southward, while everyone on Taiwan’s cellular network received mobile alerts testing the national alert system. What was once a routine annual drill has evolved into a vital benchmark for Taiwan’s ability to manage crises requiring a whole-of-society response and international assistance.
Since 2018, the “921” exercise has commemorated the devastating September 21, 1999, Chi Chi earthquake, but its scale, complexity, and visibility increase each year. The evolution of the 921 exercise reflects Taiwan’s shift toward unscripted, full-scale scenarios modeled on U.S. curriculum. What used to be a photo-ready display of capabilities is now a deliberate effort to integrate civil government officials, military field medical teams, the private sector, and NGOs into a unified command system responsible for coordinating life-saving rescues, medical treatment, sheltering, and long-term recovery.
Particularly notable is the Taiwanese government’s willingness to test unfamiliar concepts and navigate uncertainties in front of an international audience. The 921 exercise integrates international teams and observers, many of whom face similar natural – and geopolitical – threats. The active international participation marks a key distinction between this drill and Taiwan’s Urban Resilience exercise held in June. During this year’s 921 exercise, 180 international participants brought gear and equipment to the island, working alongside local teams for three days, including the exercise’s first overnight, 24/7 continuous operation.
A Japanese Disaster Medical Assistance Team (DMAT) coordinated with six Taiwanese DMATs, formed by local hospitals and supervised by the Ministry of Health and Welfare. In an adjacent tent, American and Taiwanese medical teams simulated joint field care.
Additionally, 100 international observers traveled to each exercise site to observe the capabilities on display. Beyond Taiwan’s warm hospitality during events like this, international partners get to visualize what a civilian-supported response might look like during conflict – and how they might see themselves in it.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Interior aimed to establish and test a humanitarian assistance and disaster response (HADR) corridor during the 921 exercise, embedding regional allies directly into its civil resilience planning. Taiwan’s emergency responders practiced working together to salvage trapped vehicles from floodwaters in a riverbed and conducted field medical treatment alongside teams from Japan, the Philippines, and Turkiye. The exercise is also of great interest to Nordic partners like Finland, which sent firefighters to bring back lessons as they rebuild their own civil defense plans alongside a volatile neighbor.
Taiwan faces strong typhoons and regular earthquakes, requiring a professional and ready emergency response mechanism. Organizers have now begun to smartly layer these exercises with wartime injects – the scripted crisis events used to test responders. One drill simulated rescuing a downed foreign fighter pilot from the mountains, transporting him to a multinational field hospital, and then airlifting him to a Taiwan Coast Guard vessel. I watched on a livestream, powered by mobile communication units, as a stretcher was lowered onto the ship off the coast.
Each September, the 921 exercise grows in scale and complexity as responsibility rotates among cities and counties. Familiarizing jurisdictions with this integration is essential preparation. Taiwan sits between two tectonic plates, the Philippine Sea Plate and the Eurasian Plate, and the train from Taipei to Taitung runs through the East Rift Valley. Taitung could easily be isolated in an extreme disaster caused by an earthquake, so it’s important to test local capability.
Beyond the natural disaster threat, China conducts continuous drills along the coastlines of Yilan County, where 921 took place in 2025, and Taitung County in the southeast. Equally serious for Taiwan’s preparation is practicing the mobilization of its resources and testing the HADR corridor with these potential, aggressive operations in mind.
Taiwan’s government also wants to be ready to assist its neighbors, as reinforced in President Lai Ching-te’s remarks closing the exercise.

NATO Keeps Article 5 Trigger ‘Deliberately Ambiguous’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:27:39 UTC
21:27:39 KST

NATO will not publicly define the exact point at which an attack would trigger its collective-defense clause as doing so would help adversaries calculate how far they can escalate without provoking an allied response, Secretary General Mark Rutte said.
Rutte made the remarks during a Chicago Council on Global Affairs discussion in Des Moines, Iowa, on Tuesday, Sept. 22.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The discussion, moderated by Chicago Council President Leslie Vinjamuri, also included US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker and focused on the alliance’s future and its importance to American security.
“Article 5 is deliberately ambiguous, so we will never exactly tell anyone when Article 5 is exactly triggered or not,” Rutte said.
He explained that the uncertainty is intentional because NATO does not want to provide its adversaries with information that could help them design attacks that remain just below the alliance’s declared threshold.
NATO keeps response options secret
Rutte said NATO has all the response options it needs to counter hybrid threats, but warned that some allied actions would remain invisible because they would not be made public.
The alliance’s response would also not necessarily mirror the original attack, he said. NATO could use either symmetric measures – responding through similar means – or asymmetric ones involving a different type of political, economic, cyber, or military pressure.
According to Rutte, allies could select measures designed to impose costs without revealing their full capabilities or intelligence.
Ukraine’s Battle-Tested Drones Could Soon Be Made in America
NATO has stated since 2016 that hybrid actions against one or more members could lead to a decision to invoke Article 5. The alliance’s official policy does not define a fixed threshold, leaving each incident to be assessed individually.
Hybrid warfare can combine cyberattacks, sabotage, disinformation, economic pressure, covert operations, and limited military actions intended to cause damage while complicating attribution and avoiding a conventional NATO response.
What Article 5 requires
Article 5 establishes that an armed attack against one NATO member is considered an attack against all members.
However, activating the provision does not require every ally to take exactly the same action or automatically declare war. The treaty says each member must assist the attacked ally by taking whatever action it considers necessary, which may include the use of armed force.
NATO’s official explanation of Article 5 says the alliance determines whether an incident constitutes an armed attack on a case-by-case basis.
The provision has been invoked only once, following the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks against the US.
Rutte has previously emphasized that the collective-defense commitment itself is clear, while NATO deliberately avoids publishing detailed conditions for its activation.
Russia tests the threshold
The comments come amid growing warnings that Russia could use deniable drone or missile incidents, cyberattacks, and sabotage to test NATO’s willingness to defend its members without launching a conventional invasion.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said intelligence assessments indicated Moscow could stage “hybrid” drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine and then present them as accidents.
According to Tusk, such operations could be intended to persuade European societies that Article 5 is “more theoretical than practical” and undermine confidence in NATO’s collective defense.
Rutte’s remarks appear designed to counter that strategy by warning Moscow that remaining below an assumed military threshold would not guarantee the absence of an allied response.
NATO, he indicated, could retaliate through measures its adversaries might not immediately see or connect to the original attack.

Erdogan at UNGA: A reminder for Palestinian statehood and a push for global reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:26:46 UTC
21:26:46 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s address to the 81st United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday ranged across the genocide in Gaza, Israel’s expansionist designs, the Russia-Ukraine war, the Black Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the South Caucasus.
Read alongside his 2025 UN address, his Bloomberg article and his diplomatic meetings in New York, the 2026 speech, however, points to a broader shift in Turkish foreign policy.
Türkiye is pairing its long-standing criticism of the problems in the international system with clearer proposals for how those problems might be addressed.
The strongest continuity between 2025 and 2026 is Palestine.
Erdogan’s 2025 speech focused on Gaza, criticism of Israel’s genocidal war and wider revisionist regional posture, recognition of a Palestinian state and mobilising the international community.
That line remains intact in 2026, but the agenda has broadened to include maintaining the ceasefire, moving to its second phase, rebuilding Gaza, developments in the occupied West Bank, UNRWA and the two-state solution.
His emphasis on hospitals and basic infrastructure in Gaza also fits within this wider framework.
The Palestinian file therefore shows a shift from immediate crisis management towards reconstruction and long-term recovery from the genocide.
The more striking change lies in Erdogan’s criticism of the United Nations.
“The world is bigger than five” has long been one of the most consistent arguments, aimed primarily at the representation problem in the Security Council and the privileges of its five permanent members.
In 2026, a more concrete model sits behind that criticism. Erdogan’s Bloomberg article is particularly important here.
The proposal is clear: abolish the veto privilege, avoid expanding the hierarchy by granting permanent status to additional states, end permanent membership and have Security Council members elected by the General Assembly for fixed terms.
That takes Türkiye’s criticism beyond the power of the five permanent members.
What is being questioned is the principle of permanent privilege itself. Ankara’s answer is a structure based on elections, rotation and broader accountability.
In Erdogan’s 2026 message, objection is turning into institutional design.
Regional issues
The same pattern can be seen in another prominent concept: regional ownership.
In the President’s formulation, regions facing crises should make greater use of their own political and diplomatic capacities.
His reference to the Mecca agreement – signed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan as a regional defence mechanism – is particularly significant in this context.
The same logic appears in the insistence on “Libyan leadership and ownership,” support for regional dialogue in the Balkans and the search for a process emerging from within the region around the Strait of Hormuz.
This should not be read as Türkiye abandoning the Western security architecture for a single alternative bloc.
Erdogan also underlined Türkiye’s importance to European security.
What is emerging looks more like an interconnected security strategy: NATO membership continues, while regional defence mechanisms, bilateral partnerships and mediation diplomacy expand alongside it.
Security crises in Türkiye’s neighbourhood tend to affect Türkiye directly, making regional stability a central motivation of Ankara’s foreign and security policy.
Regional ownership also has an operational dimension: because the UN cannot respond equally effectively to every subregional crisis, greater regional responsibility is presented as one way to support its core purpose of maintaining international peace and security.
The New York meetings broadly reflected this framework and highlighted another concept: connectivity.
For Erdogan, roads, trade, energy routes and joint production are not just economic issues, but also instruments of security and stability.
From Iraq’s Development Road to transport routes across the South Caucasus, the idea is simple: the more economically connected countries become, the stronger their shared interest in preserving stability.
That is why transportation and trade being discussed alongside security in Erdogan’s meeting with Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze of Georgia at the Turkish House, and his emphasis on Türkiye-Georgia-Azerbaijan cooperation mechanisms, matter.
Ukraine and beyond
One of the most concrete technical themes is the relationship between food security and Black Sea security.
From Ankara’s perspective, the Russia-Ukraine war now extends beyond ceasefire diplomacy.
The safety of commercial vessels in the Black Sea, the uninterrupted movement of grain to world markets and open maritime routes are directly linked to global food security.
Türkiye’s search for a new Black Sea navigation mechanism involving Russia and Ukraine is therefore significant.
Ankara’s approach is familiar: instead of trying to solve the entire war through one grand agreement, it looks for narrower areas where the two sides may still have overlapping interests.
The 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative was the clearest example: it functioned while the war continued, allowed Ukrainian grain to reach international markets and was framed by Türkiye as a contribution to global food security.
In 2026, the same method is being carried into a broader maritime security framework centred on commercial shipping, safe navigation and food security.
This reflects Ankara’s preferred mediation model: develop technical mechanisms during conflict and use them to help create conditions for larger political agreements.
This is also where Türkiye’s approach to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) becomes relevant.
Türkiye has nominated former Food, Agriculture and Livestock Minister Mehmet Mehdi Eker for the post of FAO Director-General, putting forward its first candidate for the organisation’s top job.
Eker brings a decade of uninterrupted ministerial-level experience in food and agricultural governance.
Ahead of the 2027 election, Eker has presented his candidacy to bring Türkiye’s experience in agriculture and food security to the international stage, drawing on the country’s long-standing experience adapting its agricultural sector and food systems to climate crisis, one of the defining global challenges of our time.
The Black Sea initiative and the FAO candidacy are separate developments, but together they form a meaningful pattern: Türkiye is seeking to protect food and commercial flows through the Black Sea while putting forward its own candidate to lead a key institution of global food governance.
Seen this way, Black Sea navigation security represents the operational dimension; protecting grain flows and supply chains, the geoeconomic dimension; and the FAO candidacy, the institutional dimension.
Ankara is seeking to deepen its role in shaping both the institutions and the methods through which crises are managed.
The climate agenda fits the same pattern.
Presenting COP31 as an implementation-focused summit, emphasising access to financing and technology transfer for developing countries, and inviting leaders to Antalya in New York show how messages from the UN podium are reinforced through bilateral diplomacy.
Together, these issues reveal the central question of Erdogan’s UN speech: How should power, responsibility and decision-making capacity be distributed within the international system?
Palestine, the Black Sea, Libya, the South Caucasus, UN reform and food security may look separate.
Yet Erdogan’s speech connects them through a common approach that also speaks to this year’s UN theme of rebuilding trust.
In 2025, Türkiye’s message was shaped more heavily around taking positions on ongoing crises, drawing attention to the shortcomings of the international system and emphasising Ankara’s mediation capacity.
That line remains in place in 2026, but it is now accompanied by more concrete proposals at the operational and implementation levels.
Regional ownership, connectivity, functional mediation, collective deterrence, food security and broader representation in international institutions are increasingly becoming complementary parts of the same foreign policy narrative.
That is what distinguishes Erdogan’s 2026 speech. Long-standing objections and criticisms are increasingly being translated into concrete proposals.
Türkiye is seeking to build on its role as an actor that balances between crises and acts as a mediator.
Developing regional security and connectivity architectures, keeping strategic trade routes open, taking on a greater role in global food security and securing stronger representation in international institutions are becoming mutually reinforcing elements of that broader ambition.

Alice Weidel lebt in einer gleichgeschlechtlichen Partnerschaft mit Kindern – ein scharfer Kontrast zum traditionellen Familienbild der AfD. Wie reagiert die Parteichefin, wenn Spitzenkandidaten wie Ulrich Siegmund ihr Lebensmodell öffentlich abwerten und Parteikollegen gegen sexuelle Minderheiten hetzen? Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler analysieren einen internen Kulturkampf, in dem Weidel zunehmend ins Visier der eigenen Leute gerät.
Trotz historischer Wahlerfolge in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern und Berlin brodelt es hinter den Kulissen gewaltig. Ein brisantes internes Strategiepapier des Wahlkampfmanagers Daniel Fiß rechnet gnadenlos mit dem Spitzenkandidaten Leif-Erik Holm ab und fordert einen radikaleren Kurs. Die Recherche zeigt, wie extreme Kräfte die Gunst der Stunde nach der Wahl nutzen, um unliebsame Funktionäre aus dem Weg zu räumen.
Ein Blick nach Österreich offenbart zudem tiefe Risse im europäischen Rechtsaußen-Bündnis. FPÖ-Chef Herbert Kickl inszeniert sich plötzlich als israelfreundlich und erntet dafür heftigen Gegenwind von AfD-Politikern, die von „Schuldkult“ sprechen. Zudem ordnet die Folge eine bemerkenswerte Geschichtsumdeutung ein und klärt, warum Alice Weidel Adolf Hitler öffentlich als „Linksradikalen“ bezeichnet.
„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?
Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.

Ukrainian Startup Fund and Brave1, with the support of the Ministry of Digital Transformation and the Ministry of Social Policy, Family and Unity, are launching the Innovative Prosthetics grant program.
According to the Ministry of Social Policy, the maximum grant for one developer is UAH 8 million.
The amount of funding will depend on the technology readiness level: up to UAH 2 million for idea testing and research; up to UAH 4 million for creating a laboratory sample and conducting engineering and user testing; and up to UAH 8 million for creating a prototype, laboratory testing and preparing the development for the next stage of conformity assessment and certification.

Once packed with world leaders, Netanyahu’s UN trip shrinks to six hours and no Trump meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:24:11 UTC
21:24:11 KST

Over the years, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has attended the annual United Nations General Assembly many times, delivering speeches from its famous podium and meeting leaders from around the world. But since Oct. 7 and the war in Gaza, Israel’s international standing has deteriorated, while Netanyahu has become an increasingly controversial figure abroad. The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for him over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
In the past, a UN visit could serve as an opportunity to meet leaders and advance diplomatic initiatives, much like the summit U.S. President Donald Trump held Tuesday with leaders from Arab states. This time, however, that does not appear to be the case, with the Prime Minister’s Office citing “scheduling constraints” to explain the absence of meetings. Netanyahu’s diplomatic room for maneuver at the UN has narrowed sharply. His last speech was boycotted by 77 countries and delegations, and, as far as is known, he has generally avoided travel outside the United States because of the arrest warrant, with the exception of a visit to Viktor Orban’s Hungary last year and a secret visit to the United Arab Emirates during Operation Roaring
Throughout his years in office and his visits to the UN, Netanyahu has delivered speeches that became deeply etched in the public memory, including his 2012 “bomb speech” and his call to the Palestinians a year earlier to “let’s talk dugri,” using the Hebrew word for speaking frankly. The trips were also used for meetings with U.S. presidents over the years: Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, Joe Biden and Donald Trump, whom Netanyahu also met during one of his more recent General Assembly visits.
It may seem almost unimaginable today, but in late September 2023, roughly two and a half weeks before the Hamas massacre, Netanyahu met Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who has since compared the prime minister to Hitler. At the time, the two discussed the possibility of normalization with Saudi Arabia.
Netanyahu’s first UN visit as prime minister, rather than as Israel’s ambassador to the organization, came in September 1998, more than two years after he was elected. During that trip, he met Palestinian Authority chairman Yasser Arafat and then-U.S. President Bill Clinton at the White House, where Clinton urged the two to return to the peace process ahead of the signing of the Wye River Memorandum later that year.
During the same visit, Netanyahu also met then-UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan, as well as other leaders from around the world. That stands in contrast with more recent visits, during which he has avoided meeting current UN Secretary-General António Guterres. The 1998 trip was Netanyahu’s only visit to the UN during his first term as prime minister.
Eleven years later, in September 2009, roughly six months after returning to the premiership, Netanyahu again flew to New York for the General Assembly. His speech focused primarily on the Holocaust and Iran.
During that visit, he met then-U.S. President Barack Obama and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, with the American president once again urging the sides to pursue peace. Against the backdrop of the publication of the Goldstone Report, which criticized IDF conduct in Gaza during Operation Cast Lead, Netanyahu also met European leaders in an effort to contain the fallout from the report. He also met then-UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon.
Netanyahu went on to visit the UN many times over the years. Iran was generally at the center of his speeches and public statements, and despite his efforts to push the Palestinian issue to the sidelines, some of the leaders he met sought to revive diplomatic efforts aimed at resolving the conflict.
Netanyahu also met leaders considered more friendly toward Israel, as well as leaders from Africa and South America as part of efforts to strengthen Israel’s ties with countries on those continents. He held meetings with leaders from other regions as well. In 2014, for example, he met Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the first meeting between Israeli and Indian leaders in a decade.
In 2017, Netanyahu met Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in New York on the sidelines of his UN visit. That same year, Netanyahu also met U.S. President Donald Trump, as well as Japan’s Shinzo Abe, Panama’s Juan Carlos and Rwandan President Paul Kagame. A year later, he again met Sisi and Trump.
By late September 2023, roughly two and a half weeks before Hamas’ surprise attack, Israel’s international standing and Netanyahu’s own position were very different from today. Netanyahu met Erdogan, as noted, and also held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, about a year and a half after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
He also met German Chancellor Olaf Scholz, with whom he discussed the sale of Israel’s Arrow 3 missile defense system to Germany.
During the same visit, Netanyahu met UN Secretary-General António Guterres, who has since become a harsh critic of Israel and was later declared persona non grata in Israel. Netanyahu also met then-U.S. President Joe Biden.
Since the outbreak of the war, Netanyahu has attended the UN General Assembly twice, in September 2024 and again last September. His upcoming appearance will be his third General Assembly visit since Oct. 7.
In 2024, Netanyahu cut his visit short following the assassination of Hezbollah Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah. During the trip, he met Dutch Prime Minister Dick Schoof and Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić, both considered friends of Israel. Netanyahu did not meet leaders who, even at that stage, were sharply criticizing Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip.
Last September, Netanyahu addressed the UN and met Argentine President Javier Milei, who also lit a ceremonial torch at Mount Herzl during Israel’s Independence Day celebrations, as well as Paraguayan President Santiago Peña, considered a prominent supporter of Israel.
Netanyahu later met Trump at the White House, the fourth meeting between the two during Trump’s second term.
On the upcoming visit, no meeting between Netanyahu and Trump is expected, nor is a meeting with billionaire Elon Musk, despite earlier discussions about one.
Netanyahu is scheduled to land in the United States on Thursday morning at a military airport in New Jersey, about a two-hour drive from the UN headquarters in New York. His speech is scheduled to begin at 2 p.m. New York time, 9 p.m. in Israel.
In an unprecedentedly short stay for an Israeli prime minister visiting the United States, Netanyahu is expected to spend only about six hours in New York. He will not stay overnight and is scheduled to fly back to Israel that evening. Netanyahu will also not bring journalists with him aboard the prime ministerial aircraft.
The short visit is due to concerns over possible security incidents and demonstrations expected against Netanyahu in New York, including protests by pro-Palestinian groups and Israeli demonstrators. At the same time, pro-Israel demonstrations by Jewish supporters are also expected.
Netanyahu’s speech is expected to focus largely on Iran and, according to officials, will include “a series of revelations about Iran and its efforts to rebuild.”
A senior official said the speech is expected to last about 40 minutes and will also include references to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has called Netanyahu the “architect of the genocide in Gaza.”
Mamdani’s remarks also prompted concerns in Israel over whether he would allow the prime ministerial plane, Wing of Zion, to remain at the airport until Netanyahu finishes his speech.
Netanyahu is also expected to strongly condemn the International Criminal Court in The Hague, which issued arrest warrants for him and former defense minister Yoav Gallant.

Loneliness and social isolation cost you up to six years of healthy life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:23:24 UTC
21:23:24 KST

Loneliness and social isolation could shorten the number of disease-free years a person has left, and men and women aren't affected in the same way.
Social isolation refers to limited contact and participation with others, while loneliness is a subjective experience of feeling disconnected from the world around them. While the two are not the same, a new study published in the journal Nature Communications has found that both are associated with fewer healthy years of life.
On average, loneliness and social isolation cost people around six disease-free years, taking a toll on both physical and mental health, researchers found after analysing data from over 270,000 adults between the ages of 40 and 69.
“Overall, the study found that social isolation and loneliness can have a significant impact on disease-free life expectancy,” said lead author Lu Qi, professor at Tulane University.
The study found the associations were stronger for the loss of years free of mental disorders — depression and anxiety — than for years free of physical diseases such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, chronic respiratory disease, neurodegenerative disease, and cancer.
The good news is that maintaining a healthy lifestyle can mitigate the negative impact of social isolation. The bad news — it does not appear to compensate for the damage caused by loneliness.
At age 50, individuals experiencing both loneliness and social isolation lived fewer years free of major chronic diseases compared with those experiencing neither.
How are men and women impacted differently?
Men and women do not suffer from loneliness and social isolation in the same way, and that is also reflected in the impact those have on their health. Because women may prioritise emotional connection, their mental health struggles are more strongly linked to loneliness, while men’s mental health shows a stronger association with social isolation.
Among women, loneliness and social isolation meant 2.4 years spent in worse physical health and 3.7 years in worse mental health, while for men it meant 1.7 years of physical disease-free life lost and 5.8 years of mental disorder-free life lost.
Males were more likely to experience both loneliness and social isolation, had a lack of social, material, and economic resources, and had a lower healthy lifestyle score.
The authors noted that this gender gap may be explained by differences in how men and women obtain support and achieve psychological well-being, with men tending to rely more on physical presence and frequent social interactions and women more on emotional support.

Warming Himalayas: Nepal’s Climate Justice Test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:23:00 UTC
21:23:00 KST

The recent floods in Nepal exposed the growing vulnerability of Himalayan communities and the widening gap between the scale of climate losses and international support. The devastating Himalayan disaster of August 26, 2026, has left Nepal facing enormous reconstruction costs. The critical question for the global community is whether climate finance will be treated as a matter of justice, instead of charity.
The high-altitude glacier collapse in the northern part of Langtang/Lirung Mountain caused a Himalayan tsunami that killed more than 1,451 people as of September 19, 2026, left 5,786 missing, and affected about 1.6 million people in five districts of Nepal, according to the government’s situation report.
The Nepali government has rescued 13,784 people and mobilized security forces for rescue operations. It assessed damage to 41 motorable bridges, 3,702 private houses, roads, and 12 hydropower projects.
The recently released Rapid Damage and Need Assessment (RDNA) estimates total damage and losses at more than $2.66 billion. About $4.72 billion is required for reconstruction and rehabilitation, while $5.7 million is needed for immediate relief and short-term rehabilitation over the next six months.
The flood damaged 7,570 private houses, 48 public buildings, 18 schools, seven health facilities, and 30 cultural heritage sites. About $685 million will be required to rehabilitate the social sector.
But the cost of physical damage does not capture the full social impact. Children, women, and senior citizens have suffered severe psychosocial impact, while marginalized communities have become further marginalized. These “costs” have been undermined or overlooked in the assessment report.
Scientists working with World Weather Attribution (WWA) described the disaster as a “catastrophic rock-ice avalanche that transitioned into a debris flood in the Himalayas along the Nepal-China border.” They said climate change and rising temperatures in the Himalayan region contributed significantly to the disaster. Floods in the Himalayan region have become more frequent and more devastating in recent years.
The government of Nepal has written to the Loss and Damage Fund, seeking reparation for the impacts of climate change and calling on polluters to provide compensation and justice. The Loss and Damage Fund said Nepal should provide sufficient evidence about the causes of the flood. Its board will consider providing up to $20 million in compensation. Compared with the estimated losses, the proposed support is small.
The World Bank has also offered concessional loans to Nepal. Members of the civil society and youth are demanding grants as reparation rather than loans. They have been demanding climate justice, focusing on the causes of glacier melt in the Himalayas, known as the “Third Pole” and a source of water for large numbers of people in the region.
Campaigners argue that the climate crisis is a fundamental human rights issue linked to the right to life and a sustainable environment. They are also calling for climate finance to be treated as justice rather than charity and for a regional framework across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region to share information, establish early-warning systems and develop institutional mechanisms.
Ten young people began a hunger strike on September 18, 2026, at the base camp of Mount Manaslu. They are demanding assessments of future glacial lake outburst flood risks, regular joint monitoring of lakes along the China-Nepal border, and climate compensation and justice for Nepal, which has to bear the costs of climate-related impacts to which it has not contributed.
Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah is attending the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, where he will raise the issue of climate crisis impacting Nepal. It is an opportunity for Nepal to present the context and causes of the recent disaster internationally. Foreign Minister Sisir Khanal has already left for the UNGA and is due to attend side events in New York. He is also expected to appeal for international support to overcome the crisis.
Civil society and the public have raised concerns about delays in rescuing people trapped in a hydropower tunnel, saying the government did not allow international experts to assist during the early phase of the rescue. They have also raised concerns about delays in search operations.
Nepal will need to amplify its demands for climate justice, including through the Loss and Damage Fund, while ensuring accountability and transparency in the use of funds. The federal government’s initial hesitation to collaborate with local governments also created tensions between federal and provincial governments.
The internally displaced are being housed in 27 holding centers in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading, where 1,743 people are living. The government has offered $98 (15,000 Nepali rupees) per family member to stay outside the holding centers for four months.
The disaster gives Nepal an opportunity to raise concerns about climate change at the global and regional levels. Communities living in river basins and near glacier lakes remain at high risk. Nepal should seek timely information-sharing from the international community to reduce those risks, while international partners can provide technology for faster warnings.
Existing early-warning technology and knowledge may not be sufficient to predict disasters of this kind. Investment is, therefore, needed not only for recovery but also for research and knowledge exchange. Digital technology and empowered communities could help reduce vulnerabilities.
Nepal also needs people-centered development to cope with such disasters, including the exchange of knowledge on infrastructure capable of withstanding harsh Himalayan conditions. Nepal, China, and India need to minimize human activities that directly or indirectly affect the ecology and environment of the Himalayas.
Community-led initiatives, respect for indigenous knowledge and participation in development could help sustain the region’s ecology and reduce degradation.
Small states such as Nepal need global support to rebuild after large-scale disasters. The Government of Nepal also needs to prioritize community rebuilding in future interventions rather than focusing on the business community.

AI, trade, Taiwan and climate: what will and won’t be on agenda at Trump-Xi summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:21:47 UTC
21:21:47 KST

The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are meeting in the US this week. It is Xi Jinping’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade. The last time the Chinese president was hosted in Washington (by Barack Obama in 2015), the issues on the agenda included cybercrime, technology, the climate crisis and human rights. The star of the day was Ne-Yo, who serenaded Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, with Peng reportedly singing along at the state dinner.
This time, Xi is meeting Donald Trump, who has overhauled the world order and recalibrated the US-China relationship. Trump is contending with a China that is in a much stronger position than it was 10 years ago. Here are five things to look out for at this week’s US-China summit.
Artificial intelligence
Although AI was surprisingly absent from talks the last time Xi and Trump met, in Beijing in May, it is expected to be high on the agenda this week. There are calls for the two leaders to agree some sort of AI safety framework to prevent the technology – about which there have been dire warnings in recent weeks – from spinning out of human control. But Trump has called warnings about safety a “hoax”, and although Xi has called for “safety and security in AI development”, China sees AI as the key to unlocking its own national potential and bristles at US efforts to contain its progress.
The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, recently suggested that the two countries establish a mechanism to communicate on major AI safety issues. Xi and Trump may discuss further details. But Amanda Hsiao, the China director at the Eurasia Group, says: “The question that’s going to raise is just how is it going to be operationalised, and will it be effective. Because the US and China have had a long history of having crisis hotlines, and they haven’t always been effective.”
Trade
The biggest thorn in the US-China relationship is trade. When Trump launched a global trade war last year, with the biggest target being China, it risked bringing the world economy to its knees. China reciprocated with tariffs on US goods approaching 150% and unveiled a host of other retaliatory measures, most notably restricting the export of rare earths that are vital for US manufacturing.
Since then, a temporary truce in the trade war, and Trump’s war in Iran, have stabilised the US-China trading relationship, with the source of global economic pain coming from the Middle East rather than China. But the truce is set to expire in November. With Trump and Xi expected to meet two further times this year, there may not be a trade deal announced at this week’s summit. But although China has weathered the trade war better than expected, with exports to other countries booming, finding a longer-term agreement to restore the flow of goods to China’s biggest market will be a high priority for Xi.
Taiwan
China’s ambassador to the US, Xie Feng, published an article on Wednesday outlining “four red lines” for the summit. First on the list was Taiwan.
Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, has become an increasingly sensitive topic for Beijing. China wants to isolate Taiwan on the world stage and put pressure on the US to reduce its support for Taiwan’s defences, both of which would make it easier for it to annex the island. After the May Xi-Trump summit, Trump agreed to delay a $14bn package of weapons sales to Taiwan, calling it “very good negotiating chip”.
Beijing rejects the idea of bargaining over Taiwan, describing it as a domestic Chinese issue. Nevertheless, says William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, “the Chinese side definitely feels that Trump is a rare US president that might offer a rare window of opportunity for them to influence American policy on Taiwan, specifically on defence support”.
The leaders may discuss conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, but China has been unwilling to get meaningfully involved in peace negotiations.
Human rights
Second on Xie’s list was democracy and human rights. In Trump, Beijing has found a US president who is less interested than any of his predecessors in lecturing China about its human rights record. In 2015, Hillary Clinton, the former secretary of state, called Xi “shameless” for hosting a UN summit on women while “persecuting feminists” at home. Barack Obama, then the US president, skipped Xi’s session.
Trump is unlikely to echo such sentiments, even though some in his inner circle, most notably his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, are sharply critical of China’s policies.
But Trump may raise individual cases. In May he raised the case of Ezra Jin, a detained Christian pastor, which seemed to contribute to Jin’s release from prison weeks later. Yufang Rong, the wife of a US nuclear scientist who has been imprisoned in China since late 2024, said this week that the White House had assured her that Trump would ask Xi to free her husband. Trump may also raise the case of Min Zin, a US expert on Myanmar, who was arrested in China in June.
The most difficult and high-profile case, however, is that of Jimmy Lai, a British pro-democracy activist who was jailed in Hong Kong on national security charges. Despite promising to secure Lai’s release during his presidential campaign in 2024, Trump conceded in May that Beijing was unwilling to budge on Lai’s case, calling it “a tough one”.
Climate crisis
Notably absent from this week’s talks will be any meaningful discussion about the climate crisis. Tackling the climate emergency used to be described as one of the few areas where the US and China could meaningfully cooperate, with China’s huge strides in decarbonising its economy seen as an area where it could show leadership on US-endorsed goals. But Yang says: “The climate conversation is just not really a topic that Trump is interested in talking about.” Not only has Trump withdrawn the US from the Paris agreement but Beijing and Washington are too divided on a host of issues to talk about cooperation. “They are coming into this summit with very little agreement or consensus in common,” says Yang.

As Xi meets Trump, who’s winning their trade war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:20:40 UTC
21:20:40 KST

As Xi meets Trump, who’s winning their trade war?
The trade war has been a cornerstone of Trump's second presidential tenure but failed to bring down deficits. Meanwhile, China clocked a mammoth trade surplus despite barriers.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to hold talks with United States President Donald Trump at the White House during his state visit – the first by a Chinese leader in more than a decade – as the world’s two largest economies are locked in an ongoing tussle over trade and artificial intelligence.
Trump is expected to welcome Xi on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews outside the US capital, Washington, DC, in a rare gesture for a high-stakes three-day visit by the Chinese leader.
He ramped up tariffs on Chinese goods after returning to power in 2025, and has since imposed curbs on the sale of AI chips to Beijing as the two nations compete for supremacy in the AI race.
The future of their fragile trade truce will be high on the agenda when the two leaders meet on Thursday. US trade with China fell sharply in 2025, with trade declining nearly 30 percent compared with the year before.
But China’s trade with other countries has seen a sharp rise, with Beijing registering a $1.2 trillion global trade surplus last year.
So, what will be on the agenda of the talks, and who is really winning the US-China trade war?
Where does the US-China trade war stand?
A Congressional Research Service report noted that as of July 2026, Chinese goods in the US faced a tariff rate of 36.5 percent, while US goods entering China were taxed at 31 percent. These tariff rates are averages, not product-specific.
The rate varies sharply by product. For example, Chinese copper and its products faced an effective rate of 73.6 percent in June 2026, while aluminium and its products faced 65.2 percent, iron and steel items about 50 to 58 percent and vehicles and auto parts 44.4 percent. These figures show the variety of tariff layers applicable to specific products.
China, meanwhile, maintains a 10 percent additional tariff on US imports on top of its normal tariffs and product-specific duties. For example, US crude oil faces 20 percent, LNG 25 percent, soya beans 13 percent, and US beef can face up to 77 percent.
Soon after resuming office in January 2025, Trump imposed a 10 percent duty on Chinese goods over fentanyl and immigration concerns, leading to the ongoing trade war. Beijing responded with levies on US coal, LNG, crude oil, and autos, as well as additional curbs on exports of five metals key to defence and clean energy.
By April 2025, the trade war escalated, with Chinese goods attracting 145 percent tariffs while Beijing imposed a 125 percent levy on US imports, in addition to curbs on rare-earth exports.
The rivals struck a tariff truce after talks in South Korea, which is due to expire on November 10.
However, the truce has not prevented Washington and Beijing from engaging in trade curbs. Last month, the US banned imports of humanoid robots produced in China, sanctioned Chinese shipping operators over alleged handling of Iranian fuel, and imposed restrictions on other sectors, including a threat to sanction Chinese AI firms.
Beijing said it was left with “no choice but to take necessary countermeasures”, unveiling a package that sanctioned US firms and curbed exports of drones and their tech to the US.
Is the trade war limited to tariffs?
No, the tariffs are only one aspect of a broader economic and technology rivalry between the US and China.
The trade conflict also includes sanctions, entity lists, investment restrictions, and research restrictions, alongside turning supply chains into instruments of economic pressure.
China’s leverage is concentrated in critical minerals, and it has restricted exports of rare earths – crucial for semiconductor manufacturing and AI. Beijing controls almost 90 percent of global processing and refining capacity, and that dominance makes these restrictions particularly consequential for electronics, electric vehicles and defence equipment.
Meanwhile, Washington’s main leverage is advanced technology. The US restricts China’s access to advanced semiconductors and chipmaking equipment, although the policy has become more selective in recent months.
Earlier this month, the US started a trial against Huawei, accusing the Chinese tech giant of stealing technology.
How has it affected US-China trade?
According to the latest US Census Bureau data, US-China bilateral trade has fallen by 29 percent – from $584bn in 2024 to $415bn in 2025.
The contraction has continued into this year: trade between the two countries reached $222bn in January-July, down 14.5 percent from the same period in 2025 and 31 percent from January-July 2024.
The decline is driven mainly by lower US imports from China. US imports fell from $194bn in January-July 2025 to $156bn in the same period in 2026, which is 34.6 percent less than the corresponding period in 2024.
China’s imports of US products remained virtually unchanged year-on-year at $65bn in the first seven months this year, but fell about 20 percent compared with 2024.
The US goods trade deficit with China fell from $297bn in 2024 to $203bn in 2025. Between January and July 2026, it stood at $91bn, but the significant decline in the deficit is driven by the US importing fewer Chinese goods rather than selling them more.
Has the trade war hurt China?
While US-China bilateral trade took a hit, Chinese exports have increasingly been redirected towards other markets as Beijing took advantage of Trump’s tariff war against countries around the world.
China’s total goods exports rose 6.1 percent in 2025, reaching about $3.77 trillion, according to its National Bureau of Statistics.
Chinese exports to ASEAN countries rose 14 percent in 2025, to about $660bn, making it Beijing’s largest export market. Exports to the European Union countries rose 9 percent, to about $560bn.
In the first half of this year, Chinese exports rose 13.4 percent, their 11th consecutive quarter of growth, according to government statistics. For instance, China-ASEAN trade reached $744bn in the first seven months, up 24.7 percent from a year earlier.
China is selling more to Asian, European, African and Latin American countries as it moves up the value chain behind electric vehicles, batteries, electronics, machinery and other high-tech goods.
Until August this year, China had a goods trade surplus of about $820bn – already approaching the mammoth 2025 full-year surplus of roughly $1.2 trillion.
Has the US trade deficit gone down under Trump?
Well, no. Though the central argument behind Trump’s tariff regime was anchored in reducing Washington’s trade deficit, the goods-and-services trade deficit has remained stagnant.
The US government data show that the goods deficit was $1.201 trillion in 2024, before Trump’s presidency. In fact, it rose to $1.235 trillion in 2025, an increase of 2.8 percent in Trump’s first year of the second term.
Since the bulk of tariffs came into force in April 2025, the US goods trade deficit widened further in the corresponding months of 2026.
Between May and July 2025, the US recorded a combined goods trade deficit of about $277bn, according to Census Bureau data. In the same period in 2026, the deficit reached $325bn, an increase of 17.4 percent.
The deepening trade deficit was larger in each month: $105bn (2026) versus $92bn (2025) in May, $101bn versus $84bn in June, and $119bn versus $101bn in July.

Feature: China draws on painful lessons to reclaim Asian Games volleyball crown
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:20:31 CST
21:20:31 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Trailing 19-13 in the third set of Tuesday's Asian Games women's volleyball final, China faced an unexpected challenge. Despite holding a 2-0 lead, the team was suddenly under pressure as host Japan threatened to extend the match.
For China's young squad, the situation presented another test of resilience it had developed since a painful defeat to Thailand in last month's Asian Championship final.
Just 23 days after that setback, China overcame Japan to claim its 10th Asian Games women's volleyball title, completing a remarkable turnaround for a team still finding its feet on the international stage.
Assembled in April 2025, the squad had endured its biggest disappointment when it surrendered a 2-1 lead against Thailand in the Asian Championship final, missing out on both the continental title and a direct berth at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
"The defeat to Thailand at the Asian Championship hit us really hard," outside hitter Zhuang Yushan acknowledged.
Since resuming training in April this year, the players had focused on winning the Asian Championship and securing the continent's direct Olympic qualification berth. Falling short left the squad struggling to recover emotionally.
But with the Asian Games approaching, there was little time to dwell on the defeat.
"We returned to Beijing after the Asian Championship with only around two weeks to get ready for the Asian Games," captain Gong Xiangyu recalled.
"The team was in a low mood for a while. With such a short gap between competitions, we needed to address our issues quickly and rise above the hardships."
The opportunity to demonstrate their progress came in the Asian Games semifinals, where China faced a full-strength Thailand side less than a month after their previous encounter.
Once again, China took a 2-1 lead before Thailand forced a deciding set. This time, however, the Chinese players held their nerve, dominating the fifth set 15-6 to advance to the final.
The victory reflected both tactical adjustments and improved mental resilience.
"We had to rely on training to turn things around," said 18-year-old middle blocker Wang Aoqian.
During the Asian Championship final, China had struggled to contain Thailand's attacking combinations, with its blockers frequently caught out by the Thai setter.
Wang acknowledged that hesitation had undermined her performance.
"I was hesitant and overthinking my blocks at the Asian Championship. After reviewing the game, my coach urged me to trust my reads," she said.
The improvement was evident in the rematch, where China outscored Thailand 11-4 in blocking points and recorded a 17 percent blocking success rate, compared with Thailand's 8 percent.
China's serving also disrupted Thailand's reception, creating opportunities for its blockers, particularly in the deciding set.
The team made adjustments in attack, reducing its reliance on individual hitters and using drop shots and varied attacking angles to unsettle Thailand's defense.
Thailand's defensive performance had been a major factor in its Asian Championship victory, but China finished the semifinal ahead in both total digs and digging percentage.
Beyond the tactical improvements, the tournament demonstrated the team's growing ability to handle pressure.
Tuesday's final against Japan provided another example.
Holding a 2-0 lead, China appeared to be closing in on gold before Japan fought back in the third set. The hosts established a 19-13 advantage, threatening to extend the contest.
With Japan gaining momentum, 20-year-old outside hitter Dong Yuhan came off the bench and helped China regain its attacking rhythm.
"I simply went out to play aggressively without overcomplicating things," Dong said.
Supported by Gong's effective serving, Dong converted four of her eight attacking attempts into points, helping China close the gap.
"We shook off the mental burden and played fearlessly. We came in looking to challenge them, with no extra distractions," she said.
Wu Mengjie, who delivered important attacking contributions in both the semifinal and final, said the team had learned to approach difficult situations with greater composure.
"We braced ourselves for hardships. When these moments arrived, we remained composed and level-headed," she said.
Japan fielded a less-than-full-strength squad in the final, and China's victory did not necessarily represent a fundamental transformation in its technical ability. Nevertheless, the tournament provided evidence of improved preparation and growing maturity.
With an average age below 22, many of China's players have only recently begun competing at the highest international level. Over the past year, they have experienced their first Asian Championship, World Championship and Asian Games, learning to cope with both the disappointment of defeat and the pressure of competing for major titles.
For Zhuang, the ability to recover from setbacks was as important as the gold medal itself.
"China's women's volleyball spirit is about never surrendering, just as we showed in the third set versus Japan today. If you don't give up, you stand a chance," the 23-year-old said.
That determination has long been associated with China's women's volleyball team.
The country's five consecutive major international titles in the 1980s established the foundations of its success, while its Olympic triumphs in Athens in 2004 and Rio de Janeiro in 2016 reinforced that legacy.
In Athens, China recovered from two sets down to defeat Russia in the final, ending a 20-year wait for Olympic gold. 12 years later, it overcame host Brazil, the Netherlands and Serbia in the knockout rounds to reclaim the title in Rio.
For Gong, one of the experienced players guiding the current generation, Tuesday's victory carried particular significance.
Now in her 10th year with the national team, the captain collected her third Asian Games gold medal.
"I cherish my decade-long career with the national team deeply. Not everyone gets the chance to train here every single day. This is my third Asian Games, and also my third Asian Games gold medal personally. I am truly grateful for this opportunity to keep winning glory for our country."
Standing alongside Gong on the podium was 30-year-old veteran Wang Mengjie, with a new generation of Chinese players celebrating behind them.
For Zhuang, their responsibility extends beyond winning individual tournaments.
"We didn't let the loss at the Asian Championship break us. We cannot let the legacy of China's women's volleyball team be tarnished on our watch. It is our duty to uphold it," she said. ■

21:20:31 KST

URUMQI, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- While drones and tractors hum across China's autumn harvest, fields in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region are filled with a very different sound: "Baa."
As a 200-hectare seed zucchini plantation enters its harvest period in Karamay in northern Xinjiang, 10,000 sheep have been sent into the fields in batches to graze on weeds and vines. A clip featuring the white sheep wandering and feeding in the yellow-green fields has become a hit on social media.
Similar scenes are playing out across Xinjiang's main seed zucchini-growing areas. In Shuanghe City, farmer Chen Weiwei has also welcomed the four-legged animals into his fields. "They walk around, eat weeds and make harvesting easier," Chen said.
They are not intruders but helpers.
Seed zucchinis are pumpkin-like plants grown specifically for their white seeds. The skin and flesh are not eaten. The seeds are a popular snack in China and can also be pressed for oil.
The plants grow thick with vines and leaves, hiding the yellow zucchinis beneath. The sheep trample the vines and graze on leaves, exposing the zucchinis to sunlight directly. After several days, the zucchinis grow stronger and the vines wither away.
The field then becomes open after weeds and vines are cleared by the flocks, putting plump zucchinis in plain sight.
Chen said the sheep's "contribution" also includes their manure, a natural fertilizer that helps improve the soil.
More importantly, the sheep do not eat the zucchini. Its skin is hard and thick, so that people have to smash it on the ground to break it.
As pastures in the mountains begin to dry up in early autumn, local herders move their flocks to the zucchini fields. Farmers set up yurts and fences, turning the fields into temporary pastures for a few days.
It is a win-win business, and no money changes hands. The herders save on feed, the farmers save on weeding, and the sheep get a free meal.
Chen has grown seed zucchinis for six years. For him, the old methods were slower and costly. Stopping irrigation to dry out the vines would take more than 20 days, and mechanical harvesting alone would cost over 30,000 yuan (about 4,447 U.S. dollars).
Maidbaye, a herder in Karamay, raises more than 200 sheep. He said the arrangement would save him nearly 10,000 yuan on feed costs.
The "sheep helpers" are part of a broader push toward green, circular farming. Local officials said other methods include turning corn straw into animal feed and returning manure to the soil. The goal is to reduce reliance on chemicals.
China's newly revised Agriculture Law includes a chapter on green agricultural development, calling for a nationwide green transition. It gives priority to ecological circular agriculture, promotes the recovery, harmless treatment and comprehensive utilization of agricultural waste. It also encourages the circular agriculture integrating crop production with livestock breeding.
With policy guidance, this farming wisdom is expected to be taken up more broadly, with animal helpers being seen working alongside machines more often, and other fields across China echoing with the sound "Baa." ■

Alexandria Governor Ayman Attia receives an interview with Xinhua in Alexandria, Egypt, Sept. 22, 2026. "We hope Chinese companies will establish a manufacturing base here and take advantage of local investment opportunities," Alexandria Governor Ayman Attia said recently. (Xinhua/Yao Bing)
ALEXANDRIA, Egypt, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- "We hope Chinese companies will establish a manufacturing base here and take advantage of local investment opportunities," Alexandria Governor Ayman Attia said recently.
In an interview with Xinhua on Tuesday, Attia expressed hope to deepen cooperation with China in industry, trade, logistics, and education, while welcoming more Chinese companies to invest in the governorate.
As a major Egyptian port city, Alexandria has distinctive advantages in economic and trade cooperation with China. Attia said the historic Mediterranean city has extensive economic ties and is well-positioned to handle trade flows from China to Egypt, Africa, and the wider region.
Chinese investors are already operating in Alexandria's industrial sector, the Egyptian official said. "Our relations have deep historical roots and broad prospects for cooperation."
Attia said Egypt has made significant infrastructure progress under President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, noting that improvements in Alexandria's roads, energy, and transportation have created favorable conditions for investment.
In addition to its infrastructure, Alexandria has a well-trained workforce capable of meeting the technological needs of various industries, an important advantage in attracting investment, he added. "We welcome Chinese investors from all sectors with open arms."

Chinese-language education should not be confined to universities, Attia said. Some schools have already introduced Chinese to children at an early age, and he hopes to expand such programs to give more young people the chance to learn the language.
"Chinese is a very important language with a long history and a promising future," Attia said, adding that it is vital for Egyptians to learn it, and that Alexandria offers ideal conditions for learning and using the language. ■

“We remain convinced that the crisis in the Gulf can be resolved through diplomatic means, through reopening the Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, in order to avert war,” the Qatari emir said.
Qatar was doing “everything in our power to address the conflict in the region through diplomatic means," he added.
On Gaza, Sheikh Tamim stated that what had happened there was “genocide in every sense of the word."
“There can be no talk of a just international order as long as Palestine remains in its plight," he said, adding that the scale of the destruction had not been matched by the international response.

Erdoğan renewed his demand for UN Security Council reform, arguing that decisions affecting more than 190 countries should not depend on its five permanent members.
He repeated his long-standing slogan that the “world is bigger than five” and said international law should not be applied differently to strong and weak countries.
Jordan says international inaction is a choice
Jordan's King Abdullah contrasted the international response to Israel with the sanctions, asset freezes, embargoes and diplomatic isolation used in other conflicts.
When it came to Israel, he said, resolutions had repeatedly remained on paper.
He called the failure to act a political “choice” and said the problem was not a lack of available tools.
The Hashemite kingdom's monarch accused Israel of seizing land, expanding settlements and allowing settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, and said that forced displacement constitutes a war crime.
He described Gaza and the occupied West Bank as two parts of an effort to make a viable Palestinian state impossible.
King Abdullah said decades of managing the Israeli-Palestinian conflict instead of tackling its causes had allowed temporary measures to become permanent policy.
He also warned that Israeli actions in southern Syria, including territorial expansion around water resources, posed a direct threat to Jordan’s northern border and water security.
On Iran, King Abdullah said the war was hurting trade and investment and raising energy and food bills worldwide.

China tightens control over orphine-related substances
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:19:59 CST
21:19:59 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese authorities announced on Wednesday that the entire class of orphine-related substances will be placed under control as non-medicinal narcotic and psychotropic substances.
The measure will take effect on Oct. 1, 2026, according to the Ministry of Public Security, the National Health Commission, and the National Medical Products Administration.
China has previously placed the entire categories of fentanyl-related substances, synthetic cannabinoids and nitazene-related substances under control.
The production, trading, transportation, use, storage, import and export of such substances are prohibited for all entities and individuals, according to management rules for non-medicinal narcotic and psychotropic substances.
China has expanded its controls over such substances. From July 1, 16 additional non-medicinal narcotic and psychotropic substances have been brought under control.
Meanwhile, the country has also strengthened its controls over precursors of fentanyl-related substances.
In November 2025, China added 13 types of precursors for fentanyl-related substances to its export control list and applied country-specific measures to the United States, Mexico and Canada. In May 2026, three additional types of fentanyl-related precursors were added to the list applicable to those three countries.
Also on Wednesday, Chinese judicial and law enforcement authorities issued guidelines on handling criminal cases involving fentanyl-related substances, emphasizing severe punishment for such crimes in accordance with the law.
Law enforcement efforts have been intensified against the illegal trafficking of precursor chemicals and other sensitive substances.
The Ministry of Public Security said in May that, since 2025, Chinese police had solved 29 criminal cases involving such materials, arrested 157 suspects, and seized 720 kg of drugs, 1.3 tonnes of new psychoactive substances, 0.9 kg of stimulants and 27.7 tonnes of non-scheduled precursor chemicals. ■
