Men with less modest self-views are more likely to feel victimized and support men’s rights activism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:00:25 UTC
21:00:25 KST

Men with a less modest view of themselves tend to feel that men as a group are unfairly disadvantaged compared to women. This sense of victimhood predicts a greater willingness to support and participate in men’s rights activism, according to new research. The findings were published in Personality and Individual Differences.
To understand this connection, it helps to look at two psychological concepts at the center of the research: trait modesty and group-based relative deprivation. Trait modesty refers to how people evaluate themselves in relation to others. People with high trait modesty generally view themselves as being no better than anyone else. On the other hand, people with low trait modesty tend to feel superior and entitled to special privileges, viewing themselves as better than those around them. This shapes how they interpret situations involving social comparisons.
Group-based relative deprivation is the perception that a person’s own group is being unfairly treated or disadvantaged compared to other groups in society. This feeling often triggers anger and resentment. To experience it, an individual has to compare their group to another, appraise their group as disadvantaged, and view that disadvantage as unjust. In the context of gender, it captures a sense that men are losing power or status they are rightfully entitled to.
Researchers have increasingly documented how men adopt a sense of victimhood and how entitlement fuels backlash against gender equality. For example, a 2021 study indicated that many people now believe sexism primarily targets men rather than women, capturing a core grievance of the men’s rights movement. Building on this idea, a 2022 study showed how men in the men’s rights movement construct a sense of victimhood to build a collective identity that justifies their protests and organizing.
Adding to this picture, a 2024 study provided evidence that male entitlement predicts a willingness to engage in both peaceful and aggressive actions to defend men’s societal status. Similarly, research covered by PsyPost in 2024 found that traits like narcissism and psychopathy were associated with lower support for feminist attitudes.
The new research, led by Joanna Lindström, a psychology researcher at Uppsala University, and Morgana Lizzio-Wilson, a lecturer in social, political, and feminist psychology at the University of Exeter, sought to pinpoint whether low modesty is a specific personality trait linked to these feelings of unfair deprivation and a willingness to engage in men’s rights activism.
“I was initially interested in understanding why some (but not all) members of structurally advantaged groups perceive that their group is unjustly disadvantaged, despite statistics and history suggesting otherwise,” Lindström told PsyPost. “This led me to show that low modesty was linked to feeling deprived among men (but not women), and among White Americans (but not Black Americans),” she explained, referring to a previous study she conducted. “We then wanted to examine whether modesty and feeling deprived as a man could also explain men’s willingness to engage in men’s rights activism.”
The researchers tested this idea in two separate stages. In the first study, the team recruited 195 White American men through an online platform. The participants completed a standardized personality questionnaire designed to measure trait modesty. They also answered a series of questions measuring group-based relative deprivation, indicating how frustrated they felt about men being supposedly disadvantaged in modern society.
Next, the researchers measured the participants’ support for and intention to engage in men’s rights activism. They separated these potential actions into two distinct categories. Conventional political actions included activities accepted within a social system, like advocating for law reform or joining a men’s rights organization. Extreme or non-traditional actions included behaviors that deviate from societal norms, like participating in a protest that might turn violent or supporting those who use physical aggression for the cause.
The team found that men with lower trait modesty were more likely to report feeling that men are an oppressed group. This feeling of deprivation, in turn, predicted higher support for both peaceful and extreme activism. Deprivation was a stronger predictor of conventional activism, while having low modesty itself was a stronger predictor of a willingness to engage in extreme, non-traditional activism. The results suggest an indirect pathway: low modesty leads to a heightened sense of relative deprivation, which then fuels a desire to engage in activism.
“Aspects of men’s personality and perceptions of social context both have a role to play in shaping men’s support for men’s rights activism,” Lindström said. “That is, trait modesty predicts how men appraise their treatment as a group in society more generally, which, in turn influences whether they support and want to personally engage in actions that further men’s ‘rights and opportunities.'” “Put another way, the findings highlight that high modesty may protect men from perceptions of deprivation and men’s rights activism in turn,” she added.
In the second study, the researchers expanded the project to include 492 men, split almost evenly between White and Black Americans. The authors wanted to see if the connection between modesty and activism existed across different racial groups. While the men’s rights movement is often stereotyped as being exclusively White, emerging scholarship has highlighted the presence of a Black manosphere, where Black men engage in online conversations about men’s issues and articulate similar narratives of gender-based disadvantage.
The researchers also tested whether making the idea of male disadvantage highly visible would alter the results. Participants first completed the same measure of trait modesty used in the first study. Half of the men were then asked to take a minute to reflect on the ways men are disadvantaged relative to women, and write four sentences about it. The other half acted as a comparison group and wrote four sentences about their morning routines. After this writing task, all participants completed the measures of deprivation and activism.
The experimental writing task did not change the underlying personality effects. Across both White and Black participants, low modesty consistently predicted a stronger sense that men are unfairly deprived. Just as in the first study, this sense of group deprivation predicted a greater willingness to support and engage in men’s rights activism.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that personal feelings of disadvantage drive hostile sexism toward women. However, the new study specifically measures how group-based deprivation predicts support for collective men’s rights activism rather than individual sexist attitudes.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting the results. The experimental writing task in the second study did not actually increase feelings of relative deprivation compared to writing about a morning routine. This suggests the specific writing exercise might not have been strong enough to affect participants’ views, or that trait modesty exerts a stable influence regardless of the immediate situation.
Also, the researchers note that low modesty shares some overlap with narcissism. Future research is needed to untangle exactly how much of this effect is driven by low modesty alone versus related narcissistic traits, like a desire for authority or a tendency to exploit others. The study also focused exclusively on White and Black men. The authors point out that other minority groups, such as Asian American and Latino men, face unique racial and cultural pressures that could alter how modesty and feelings of deprivation interact.
Finally, the studies were conducted entirely in the United States. Cultural norms around modesty and gender vary widely across the world, meaning these patterns might look different in other countries. More research is needed to see if these psychological pathways hold true in different cultural contexts.
“Given the correlational nature of the data, we also cannot determine a causal link between personality, perceptions of relative deprivation, and men’s rights activism,” the researchers noted. “We know that these things are linked and have explanatory power, but we need to conduct a further experimental study to determine if one variable causes the other, and in which order.” For instance, they explained, “does heightened relative deprivation causally increase men’s rights activism, or does engaging in men’s rights activism/collective action color men’s perceptions of their group’s status in society.”
“We don’t want to convey that the manosphere and men’s rights activism can be explained purely by personality,” the researchers emphasized. “It’s also important to remember that personality is malleable – just because men lower in trait modesty are more likely to perceive men as deprived in society and support/engage in men’s rights activism doesn’t mean that their modesty perceptions can’t change. Cultivating higher modesty may be a key avenue for protecting men from the manosphere’s influence.”
Looking ahead, the researchers are continuing this line of inquiry, including work with the EMMELO project an EU-funded initiative examining the role of masculinity in extremist movements. “We are currently conducting research where we show that modesty and feeling deprived (individually and as a man) predict men’s support for manosphere figures in the U.S. context,” they said. “We aim to design interventions that may decrease men’s support for—and engagement in—the manosphere, which are informed by our ongoing work on the role of modesty and relative deprivation in underpinning endorsement of the manosphere.”
The study, “Low modesty and feeling deprived as a man: A psychological explanation of men’s rights activism,” was authored by Joanna Lindström and Morgana Lizzio-Wilson.

There were violent scenes in Madrid on Wednesday as riot police fought with protesters trying to prevent the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her apartment in the Retiro district.
Hundreds of protesters had gathered, many of them overnight, in an effort to block the fourth attempt to carry out the eviction. Activists from the Madrid and Barcelona tenants’ union, and celebrities including the actor Carlos Bardem and the singer and actor Ana Belén, joined the protest.
Police fired rounds of teargas and made repeated baton charges as they tried to open a path for a judicial committee to carry out the eviction order, which was eventually executed on Wednesday morning. The tenant, known simply by her first name, Maricarmen, is about to turn 88.
Demonstrators chanted “Ayuso’s attic for Maricarmen”, a reference to the scandal surrounding the Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso’s alleged purchase with public money of a €6.3m residential apartment for her use as a temporary office.
Behind the building’s locked door, more protesters occupied the staircase leading to Maricarmen’s flat while neighbours handed out snacks and offered the demonstrators the use of their bathrooms.
When a developer bought the building Maricarmen had lived in for 71 years, she was offered the chance to buy her apartment for €247,000 (£212,000), an impossible sum for a pensioner.
They then raised her rent from €500 to €1,650 a month, while she receives a state pension of €1,350. An unnamed “prominent” writer offered to pay the €1,150 difference indefinitely but their offer was ignored.
In a video recorded by the local tenants’ union before the eviction, a tearful Maricarmen said: “Good morning, everyone, I thank you for the action you are taking, spending the whole night sleeping in the street. Please, keep going, but don’t hurt one another. This has to be peaceful.
“I can still hear all your noise. A hug to everyone and to all the people who are supporting me in this cruel struggle against a person who wants to make money but who should not forget that they have parents and that one day they could find themselves in the situation that unfortunately I am in.”
The original 1956 contract for the flat was in Maricarmen’s father’s name. When he died, the apartment passed to his wife, and on her death in 2008 it was then sublet to Maricarmen. The landlords, Urbagestión SL, successfully argued in the supreme court that this subletting was invalid and that the contract was no longer valid. Urbagestión SL has been approached for comment.
Speaking at the scene, Aldo Reverte, a spokesperson for the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions, said: “Maricarmen’s case is just one more example of what happens when housing is put in the hands of landlords. The difference is that a lot of people have become aware of her situation and the tenants’ union has shown that we can fight this type of barbaric behaviour.”
However, for all their efforts, the protesters were unable to stop the eviction. Beatriz Duro, the lawyer representing Maricarmen, said: “The owner isn’t prepared to negotiate or accept any sort of offer. We have asked for a place where we can take Maricarmen’s personal belongings.”
So far this year, 4,000 evictions have been carried out in Spain.

Syria begins ‘new phase of revival’, President Al-Sharaa tells General Assembly
Syrian President Ahmad Al-Sharaa told the UN General Assembly on Wednesday that his country “is rising” on many levels, thanks to the strength of its people.
In his second address to the General Debate in New York, he said Syria has begun to reclaim “its place among nations and States” through the diplomatic bridges it has built – proving “to the whole world that the security of the East is woven in Damascus and cannot be established without it”.
Mr. Al-Sharaa said Syria has been “united from north to south”, with weapons in the hands of non-State groups brought fully under Government control, security institutions rebuilt, sanctions lifted, reconstruction and investment projects launched, and a process of transitional justice – and efforts to determine the fate of the missing – well underway.
‘Destruction has ceased’
“In Syria’s journey through the conflict between good and evil, the war has laid down its burdens, the bloodshed has stopped, and the destruction has ceased,” he said.
“Syria has begun its journey of recovery and revival, quickening its pace, confident in its path.”
He said his country was waging an open war against cross-border criminal networks, including drug and human trafficking, adding that the consolidation of security and stability had produced “a reality in which the walls of isolation are crumbling”.
“Recovery has returned to this wounded country, bringing with it the voluntary and dignified return of more than three and a half million displaced people and refugees, transforming Syria from a crisis batted between nations – into an opportunity for good around which nations can unite,” he said.
‘Golan will remain Syrian’
Mr. Al-Sharaa said Syria’s national constants were becoming ever more firmly rooted “through the force of law and the will of the people”, insisting that the Golan “will remain Syrian land, and all annexation measures are null and void under the force of Security Council resolution 497”.

The Syrian premier rejected repeated and ongoing Israeli incursions into his country and “its persistent attempts to impose facts on the ground and its expanding attacks in the region, which undermine security and stability”, affirming his country’s commitment to the 1974 disengagement agreement between Israel and Syria, which established the UN observer force, UNDOF to maintain the ceasefire.
A “historic opportunity for peace” exists, he said, “for those who wish to live in peace – a just peace that preserves the rights of all”.
Looking to the future
The Syrian President concluded his address by saying the long-running civil conflict in his country “taught us that truth is strong in itself, even when weakened, and that falsehood is weak, even when it prevails”, stressing that Syria was continuing to rebuild itself and restore its pride and dignity.
“Today, we stand at the 81st session to affirm the reality of progress and revival. And at the 82nd session, we will meet again to build together the fruits of a strategic partnership: a partnership that has established Syria as an international actor that creates prosperity, a regional model that leads stability, and a heart pulsing with life that opens its doors to the future,” he said.

DR Congo Ebola outbreak toll exceeds 3,700 deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

DR Congo Ebola outbreak toll exceeds 3,700 deaths
More than 130 days into the latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), health experts said on Wednesday that response efforts have been scaled up significantly and “the first encouraging signs of progress” are now being seen.
In an update, the UN World Health Organization (WHO) said that in the last 21 days, cases of infection fell by approximately 26 per cent in province of Ituri and by 15 per cent in the province of Haut Uele.
However, over the same period, North Kivu province recorded a 73 per cent increase, clearly indicating that the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak has a different transmission profile in the seven affected provinces where it has been confirmed.
“While cases and theft are declining in some provinces, they continue to rise in others,” said WHO Regional Emergency Director for Africa, Dr Marie Roseline Belizaire.
“Those patterns show the outbreak is still not under control and remain spread across a wide geographic area. One of our greatest concerns is that too many people are still dying before reaching treatment.”
Dr Belizaire explained that around one in three new cases of infection are only identified after people have died outside Ebola treatment centres, in the community.
“These are lives that could potentially have been saved through earlier detection and timely access to care,” the WHO medic said, adding that every death in the community increases the risk of further transmission among family members, caregivers and others involved in traditional burial practices.
Children at most risk
Although adults account for most confirmed cases of infection, children under five have the highest case fatality rate, at more than 60 per cent, compared with approximately 40 per cent among adults.
Ebola infections in children under 5 are proving very hard to detect because they “can't necessarily explain their signs and symptoms as well as adults, and the presentation (of symptoms) may be confusing,” added WHO medic Dr. Catherine Smallwood.
Youngsters also account for a disproportionate share of those dying in the community and in health facilities where Ebola is not diagnosed in time.
“We must do more to identify sick children earlier and ensure that they receive appropriate treatment without delay; early detection save lives,” Dr Belizaire stressed, in an online update from Kinshasa.
Ongoing efforts to ramp up the disease outbreak response have contributed to higher success in tracing contacts of infected people, now at almost 88 per cent.
But “too many new infections are still being detected without a known epidemiological link; closing the surveillance gap is essential, and we are to detect cases earlier, trace their contact, and interrupt every chain of transmission,” Dr. Belizaire insisted.
Expanding response
The UN agency and partners continue to expand their reach across affected provinces, with nearly 1,400 treatment and isolation beds across 49 Ebola treatment centres. In addition, there are 25 laboratories capable of processing up to 2,500 tests every day.
However, infrastructure alone will not stop the outbreak, she said.
“Our response is no longer simply about the scaling up everywhere; it is about directing teams, expertise, and resources to the areas where transmission is greatest and where the risks are high.”
Speaking from Beni in North Kivu, WHO’s Dr Smallwood highlighted the “massive mobilization” of responders in recent weeks, in response to the worrying spread of infection in rural areas of DR Congo.
However, although new health centre or Ebola treatment centre beds are becoming available every day, “the big challenge now is finding the partners that can work within those health facilities…The human resources gap is one of the biggest gaps,” Dr. Smallwood explained.
The WHO medic underscored the need to shift the response “from the big urban centres of Beni, Butembo and Katwa in North Kivu to the province’s remote villages.
“Distances are really long and it takes a long time for patients to be referred into the urban centres,” she said. “So, we really need to put priority on decentralising the response to where the cases are into the villages and into the local areas.”
Ebola facts
Ebola disease is a severe, often fatal illness affecting humans and other primates.
The virus is transmitted to people from wild animals (such as fruit bats, porcupines and non-human primates); it then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected people. It can also be transmitted by contact with bedding or clothing contaminated with these fluids.
The average Ebola disease case fatality rate is around 50 per cent, according to WHO. Case fatality rates have varied from 25 to 90 per cent in past outbreaks.
The first Ebola disease outbreaks occurred in remote villages in Central Africa, near tropical rainforests.
The 2014–2016 Ebola virus disease outbreak in West Africa was the largest and most complex Ebola outbreak since the virus was first discovered in 1976.
There were more cases and deaths in this outbreak than all others combined. It also spread between countries, starting in Guinea then moving across land borders to Sierra Leone and Liberia.

UN health agency calls for investment boost to save young lives from cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

UN health agency calls for investment boost to save young lives from cancer
More children and young people are beating cancer, but progress remains uneven across regions and age groups, highlighting the need for increased investment to boost survival rates.
That’s according to the UN World Health Organization (WHO) which has released complete country comparable baseline data on five-year survival estimates for lymphoid leukaemia – a cancer that affects the blood and bone marrow.
The data, covering 194 nations, informed the findings of a report published in May – Measuring Survival, Driving Change – that examined global efforts to address inequalities and ensure more children and adolescents defeat a cancer diagnosis.
“Childhood cancer is one of the clearest indicators of health system performance,” said Dr. Roberta Ortiz, Childhood Cancer Medical Officer at WHO.
Marked disparities
Each year, approximately 400,000 people worldwide aged 19 and under, develop cancer. Even though most childhood cancers are highly treatable, survival depends on where patients live.
In high-income countries, survival rates now reach between 80 per cent and 90 per cent, compared with closer to 40 per cent in countries with weaker health systems.
The report described this gap as “one of the greatest health inequities of our time.”
Survival rates vary
WHO noted that the Western Pacific and Europe have reached some of the highest estimated survival levels, while Africa and parts of the Eastern Mediterranean face persistent challenges linked to inequities in timely diagnosis, access to essential medicines and high-quality care.
The report also showed that adolescents aged 15 to 19 face a wider survival gap than children aged 14 years and younger, with the divide most pronounced in low and middle-income countries.
For the younger group, the median five-year survival for lymphoid leukaemia is 66.7 per cent while older teens have a nearly 39 per cent chance of beating the disease.
Delays in diagnosis, gaps between paediatric and adult services, and limited evidence on adolescent cancer care are among barriers in this regard.
Adolescents also face different types of cancer than younger children and therefore require different kinds of care.
WHO stressed that “strategic investments in infrastructure, training and equitable service delivery can dramatically improve survival.”
Saving more young lives
Measuring Survival, Driving Change – was published in May by WHO’s Global Initiative for Childhood Cancer (GICC), which was established in 2018.
Having the complete dataset for the report allows the UN agency and governments to monitor commitments to boost overall childhood cancer survival to at least 60 per cent by the end of this decade.
In a powerful example of the convening power of WHO, the data marks the first time that survival estimates have been produced using a common methodology across all WHO Member States, thus providing a standardised baseline to track progress, compare performance and identify areas where investment is most needed.

Right to development: A blueprint for unmet promises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23

Right to development: A blueprint for unmet promises
Ahead of the 40th anniversary of the groundbreaking Declaration on the Right to Development this December, world leaders gathered at a High-Level Week meeting on Wednesday to map progress made and the 21st century challenges still ahead – from narrowing the digital divide to levelling the AI playing field – as the UN chief presented a “blueprint” to address promises that remain unfulfilled.
What you need to know:
- The declaration broke new ground in the universal struggle for greater human dignity, freedom, equality and justice when the UN General Assembly adopted it in 1986
- The declaration can help provide guardrails on issues from AI to internet access, as well as accelerate the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development
- A legally binding treaty on the right to development has been in the works since 2018
Watch live on UN Web TV:
What is the declaration?
Adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1986, it makes access to development an inalienable right.
While a legally binding treaty has been in the works since 2018, the declaration states that everyone is “entitled to participate in, contribute to and enjoy economic, social, cultural and political development, in which all human rights and fundamental freedoms can be fully realised”.
The declaration unequivocally puts people at the centre of the development process.
Read the full declaration here.
‘A call to action’
UN Secretary-General António Guterres told world leaders the declaration’s anniversary is more than a moment of reflection, “It is a call to action.”
For millions around the world, promises made in the declaration remain unfulfilled, “yet we know how to make it real,” he said, pointing to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) that “provide the blueprint to leave no one behind”.
Under the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the 17 SDGs contain goals and targets that are lifting people out of poverty and protecting their rights.
Progress since the declaration’s adoption has been driven by the foresight, dedication and resilience of countries, communities and activists of all ages, he said.
Extreme poverty has fallen dramatically, nearly half the world is now covered by some form of social protection, people are living longer and scientific and technological advances have transformed lives and livelihoods and expanded opportunity, he noted.
New tests await
But today, the promise of development faces new tests, Mr. Guterres said, from widening inequalities and persistent food insecurity to rising debt, conflicts and economic instability that are impeding development and economic growth.
In addition, the climate crisis is reaching devastating new levels each year, reminding the world that there can be no development on a degraded and unhealthy planet.
While the digital revolution and artificial intelligence hold enormous potential to improve lives, these frontline technologies can also be drivers of exclusion and division.
“The declaration unequivocally establishes development as a right and puts people at the centre of the development process,” he said.
“Development, human rights and peace are not separate ambitions. They advance together. In today’s divided world, this vision can still unite us, and the Sustainable Development Goals are the roadmap to get us there.”
Read our explainer on the right to development here.
What does people-centred development look like?
UN agencies have long integrated human rights into projects around the world.
The right to development extends to people enduring humanitarian crises and beyond – from war zones to disaster recovery.
Here’s what putting people first means:
- Colombia: Indigenous Peoples’ groups have participated in the South American country’s peace accords
- Gaza: Women engineers are turning e-waste into opportunity
- Nepal: Lethal floods in August wiped out communities that are now recovering and rebuilding better, with support from UN agencies
- Morocco: Vocational-training programmes are helping women launch income-generating activities in Morocco
- South Sudan: UN peacekeepers built a reservoir to accommodate communities that had been fighting over scarce water resources
- Venezuela: UN agencies partnered to respond to deadly twin earthquakes in June
Snapshots from around the world
Afghanistan: The UN World Food Programme (WFP) operates school feeding programmes, including in Zabul province, Afghanistan, where hunger persists.
Haiti: Deadly gang violence has triggered widespread displacement across Haiti. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) supports ongoing humanitarian efforts, including mobile clinics to serve those in need.
Ukraine: More than four years after Russia’s full-scale invasion, nearly half of the country is contaminated with landmines.The UN Development Programme (UNDP) supports volunteers and specialists working to de-mine land to make it safe again for living and farming.

LIVE: OpenAI and Anthropic to brief Security Council as AI guardrails debate intensifies

With warnings mounting that the world may be losing its grip on systems built to outthink us, Yoshua Bengi, a recipient of the prestigious Turing Award and one of the godfathers of machine intelligence, said the dangers of AI beyond human control represent an unprecedented threat for countries “that none can contain alone and that does not respect the borders we defend.”
What you need to know:
- Concerns are mounting about the rapid growth of AI, which is being used widely, from classrooms to battlefields, with few guardrails in place
- UN efforts include establishing the Global Digital Compact to foster cooperation in governing digital technology and AI, and the UN-backed Independent International Scientific Panel on AI

UN’s ‘sacred covenant has been broken’, Argentina’s Milei tells General Assembly

UN’s ‘sacred covenant has been broken’, Argentina’s Milei tells General Assembly
Argentine President Javier Milei told the General Assembly on Wednesday that the UN has broken the “sacred covenant” on which it was founded, failing at what it was meant to do – while excelling at things beyond its remit.
In his third address to the General Debate, Mr. Milei said he would speak in a “constructive spirit” about three issues: what the organization should have done and failed to do, what it should not have done but did anyway and its position on artificial intelligence (AI).
He said the UN had become a “useless organization whose only purpose is to sustain a caste of fatally arrogant parasites masquerading as well-intentioned bureaucrats”, accusing it of allowing chaos, violence and terrorism to flourish, sheltering dictatorships, while Member States systematically voted against Israel.
‘Lacking consequences’
Turning to the Falkland Islands (Malvinas), which he called a “national cause”, the President said the UN had looked the other way while unilateral changes continued despite resolution 31/49, adopted 50 years ago.
“There’s no shortage of words or resolutions. What is lacking is consequences,” he said.
Mr. Milei said the Sea Lion project was moving towards oil extraction on the Argentine continental shelf under British licenses that Argentina “rejects as illegal and illegitimate.”
He repeated Buenos Aires’ position that self-determination “does not apply in this case, since the population was implanted by the occupying power on a territory whose sovereignty is in dispute”.
Argentina had submitted protests, sanctioned companies involved in oil extraction on the disputed continental shelf and sent a sovereignty defense bill to Congress, he said, again calling on the United Kingdom to resume negotiations.
‘Anarchy and tyranny’
Mr. Milei said the UN had built “a bureaucratic leviathan” to decide how citizens should live, and singled out the pandemic, calling forced lockdowns “a global experiment in social control disguised as science” – the reason, he said, Argentina had left the World Health Organization (WHO).
Argentina had embraced free enterprise capitalism, was rebuilding its military and had “unequivocally aligned” itself with the West, the United States and Israel, he said, condemning Iranian attacks on Israel.
Avoid ‘pre-emptive’ AI regulation
On AI, he said every technological revolution had brought fears about jobs that never materialized and that Argentina would “stand at the forefront of freedom” with “a commitment not to regulate pre-emptively”, limited liability for companies operating with AI agents and tax incentives.
Argentina would keep taking part in multilateral fora in good faith, he said, “but we mustn’t confuse cooperation with subordination.”
“No nation is guaranteed a place in history,” he said. “We believe that Argentina still has a great story ahead of it. And we have decided to go out and claim it.”

Zelenskyy urges stronger pressure on Russia, warns war’s impact is spreading beyond Ukraine

Zelenskyy urges stronger pressure on Russia, warns war’s impact is spreading beyond Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Wednesday called for intensified pressure on Russia to end its war against Ukraine, arguing that Moscow continues to incur massive losses while prolonging a conflict whose consequences are increasingly being felt far beyond the battlefield.
Addressing the UN General Assembly’s annual debate, the President said the war “must be ended” and maintained that Russian President Vladimir Putin remains its sole driving force.
“For almost five years now, Russian generals have been trying to carry out Putin's crazy order to seize our eastern land, the Donetsk region,” he said.
Mr. Zelenskyy argued that Russia has suffered enormous losses for limited territorial gains, claiming nearly 249,000 Russian troops had been killed or seriously wounded during the first eight months of this year.
“It's madness,” he said. “But they still keep going.”
Conflict spreading beyond Ukraine
The President warned that the repercussions of the war are spreading beyond Ukraine’s borders, pointing to the involvement of North Korean forces fighting alongside Russia.
He said North Korean troops had suffered heavy losses and argued that Pyongyang was receiving military benefits in exchange, including improved missile and drone capabilities.
“A war that was not prevented in time, was not stopped in time, and for which Russia was not punished in time, keeps spreading and spreads evil with it,” he said.
Mr. Zelenskyy also warned that Russia continues to threaten countries beyond Ukraine, including Moldova, Poland and the Baltic States, while showing “no respect” for the sovereignty of countries in the South Caucasus and Central Asia.
“The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said.
Targeting Russia’s war machine
The Ukrainian leader stressed that Kyiv's objective is not Russia's oil industry itself but Moscow's ability to finance and sustain the war.
“Our target is Russia's ability to finance this war, to drag it out, to make it more brutal and more destructive,” he said.
He called for continued sanctions, restrictions on trade with Russia and sustained international support for Ukraine through defence assistance and joint weapons production.
“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time,” he added.
Building security through innovation
Mr. Zelenskyy said Russia has launched thousands of missiles and tens of thousands of attack drones against Ukraine since the start of the year, including ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones.
In response, Ukraine is expanding production of interceptor drones and developing new air defence capabilities with European partners through an anti-ballistic initiative known as ‘Freya’.
He presented Ukraine's rapidly growing defence industry as a potential security resource for other countries, highlighting cooperation agreements on drone technology and integrated defence systems with international partners.
His vision, he said, was one of “peace through protection”.
Defending freedom
Acknowledging the toll of the war on Ukrainians, the President said his country's fight was fundamentally about survival and independence.
“Ukrainians did not choose this war,” he said. “We choose not to die, not to lose our country, our families, not to lose our independence, our freedom. And we are defending ourselves.”
Looking ahead, Mr. Zelenskyy warned that rapid advances in military technology and artificial intelligence could make future conflicts even more dangerous. He urged the international community to end existing wars before warfare enters a new technological era.
“Patient zero must be stopped,” he said, referring to President Putin. “Limit his room to act, limit his money, limit his war.”

Guterres calls on countries to set clear timelines for transition away from fossil fuels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Guterres calls on countries to set clear timelines for transition away from fossil fuels
“We are the first generation with the tools to end the fossil fuel age – and the last who can avert climate catastrophe,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said on Wednesday, calling on countries to draw up credible roadmaps with clear timelines to transition away from fossil fuels.
Key points
- G20 countries, responsible for around 80 per cent of global emissions, must lead the transition
- Climate finance should reach $1.3 trillion a year by 2035, with at least $300 billion mobilized annually for developing countries
- New initiatives announced around power grids and critical minerals, alongside a renewed push on early warning systems
The appeal came in the middle of High-Level Week at UN Headquarters in New York, where the UN Climate Summit 2026 brought together leaders from major economies, vulnerable countries and major energy producers – alongside consumers – to push for faster climate action and greater cooperation.
“The world is crying out for climate justice – in mitigation, in adaptation, in finance. We must answer that call with action,” Mr. Guterres urged.
The UN chief decried the fact that greenhouse gas emissions continue rising when they should be plummeting.
“Fossil fuel expansion continues – defying science, economics, and common sense,” he said, adding that fossil fuel companies are “banking windfall profits – while everyday people foot the bill.”
Scientists now expect the world to temporarily exceed the 1.5°C limit for warming above pre-industrial levels set under the 2015 Paris Agreement. The challenge, the UN chief said, is to make that overshoot as small and as short as possible.
There is a way out
“Fortunately, we have a way out. Because the crisis is accelerating – but so are the solutions,” he underscored. Renewables, he said, are the cheapest, fastest, and most secure source of new electricity almost everywhere. Clean energy has gone from alternative to unstoppable”.
Mr. Guterres called for renewable energy capacity to triple, energy efficiency to double, faster electrification, sharp cuts in methane emissions and an end to deforestation. He also warned that the rapidly growing electricity demand, including from artificial intelligence, must be met with more renewable energy, grids and storage.
“I call on every country to develop a credible roadmap to transition away from fossil fuels – with clear timelines,” he said.
The G20, responsible for around 80 per cent of global emissions, must lead, he emphasised, reiterating that the transition must also be fair, creating jobs and strengthening social protection while allowing developing countries to shape it and share in its benefits.
A revolution in finance
Mr. Guterres called for at least $300 billion a year to be mobilised for developing countries, with developed countries taking the lead, and for overall climate finance to reach $1.3 trillion annually by 2035.
He also called for polluters to pay, debt burdens to be eased when disasters strike and developing countries to have a stronger voice in the international financial system.
The goal, he said, is to “match the revolution in energy with a revolution in finance”.
That finance is also needed for countries already dealing with impacts they cannot avoid. “Without adaptation, droughts become hunger crises; storms become debt crises; and heatwaves become killers”.
Across all fronts the Secretary General expressed that climate action depends on protecting its foundations: science and truth, international law and cooperation.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has confirmed that protecting the climate is an obligation, Mr. Guterres noted, while no country can decarbonise the global economy or shield itself from climate chaos alone.
Grids, minerals and early warnings
The Summit also put forward three initiatives aimed at some of the practical barriers slowing climate action.
The new Global Grids Accelerator will initially focus on Africa and Southeast Asia, where renewable energy is expanding faster than the electricity networks needed to carry it.
More than 2,500 gigawatts of renewable projects are currently waiting for grid connections worldwide.
The Accelerator will bring governments, financial institutions and technical partners together to help move priority grid projects towards financing and implementation.
A second initiative under the Task Force on Critical Energy Transition Minerals, will begin work in Guinea, Indonesia, Madagascar, Nigeria, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Demand for minerals including copper, lithium, nickel and cobalt is expected to almost triple by 2030. The mechanism is designed to help resource-rich developing countries create more value and jobs at home, while strengthening governance and environmental safeguards.
Finally, the Early Warnings for All initiative , launched in 2022, has mobilized around 2 billion to ensure everyone on Earth is protected by an early warning system by the end of 2027. More than 160 countries are receiving direct support.

Rohingya refugees deserve a future beyond survival, not endless displacement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Rohingya refugees deserve a future beyond survival, not endless displacement
Nine years after the mass displacement of the Rohingya from Myanmar, their situation remains one of the world's most protracted and complex refugee crises, marked by years of persecution and uncertainty over the prospect of returning home.
Against this backdrop, senior UN officials on Wednesday renewed calls for a durable solution that would enable Rohingya refugees to return home safely and with dignity, while ensuring justice and accountability.
UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih, a keynote speaker at a high-level event held on the sidelines of the 81st session of the General Assembly, reminded participants that nearly 1.2 million Rohingya refugees remain in Bangladesh.
“An entire generation is growing up in exile…Conflicts continue in Myanmar. Conditions for voluntary, safe, and dignified, and sustainable return do not exist at the moment.”
In August 2017, Myanmar's military launched a crackdown in the country's western Rakhine state, forcing hundreds of thousands of Rohingya Muslims to flee across the border into Bangladesh, where the vast majority remain refugees.
Life in limbo
The Secretary-General's Special Envoy on Myanmar, Julie Bishop, lamented that for children born in 2017, displacement now encompasses their entire childhood.
“It's estimated that over 30,000 children are born into the camp each year.”
The Myanmar envoy said women and girls living in the camps face growing risks of gender-based violence, including from armed groups and criminal networks, while access to protection services is declining.
“The young are losing hope.”
UN officials commended Bangladesh for its extraordinary hospitality and generosity but cautioned that the international community cannot stand by while the country continues to host the world's largest refugee settlement.
“When funding disappears, needs do not disappear with it. There is less food, less education, fewer opportunities, greater pressure on health and other essential services, and more desperation for families,” the UNHCR chief said.
Without prospects for a safe and dignified future, Rohingya refugees face increasing risks of exploitation, trafficking, forced conscription and dangerous sea journeys.
The growing cost of displacement
In his address, Prime Minister of Bangladesh Tarique Rahman drew attention to the growing costs of prolonged displacement, both for the Rohingya and for host communities.
“Prolonged uncertainty and disruption are creating new challenges and security risks, including human trafficking, migrant smuggling, drug trafficking, and other transnational crimes.”
He thanked international partners for their support but stressed that generosity cannot become an excuse for political inaction.
“Nor can Bangladesh be expected to shoulder this responsibility indefinitely.”
“The crisis originated in Myanmar; its solution lies in Myanmar,” the Prime Minister said.
Pursuing a durable solution
President of the General Assembly Khalilur Rahman expressed concern that familiar patterns of violence and persecution continue to cast a long shadow across Rakhine state and the rest of Myanmar.
“Civilians face indiscriminate attacks, air strikes, arbitrary arrest and detention, torture, enforced disappearances, forced recruitment, destruction of homes and civilian infrastructure, and the denial of humanitarian assistance.”
The Assembly President underscored the importance of sustained political attention to keep the Rohingya crisis high on the international agenda. Predictable humanitarian assistance, he said, would also remain critical.
UN officials also pointed to the genocide case before the International Court of Justice (ICJ), brought by The Gambia against Myanmar, stressing that justice must be an integral part of any lasting solution and that momentum towards accountability must not be lost.
Hope beyond survival
“Victims deserve to see that we, as an international community, are doing our utmost to avoid a repeat of past horrors,” PGA Rahman added.
Mr. Salih said refugees deserve a future that goes beyond survival.
Drawing on his conversations with Rohingya refugees, he said many continue to hope for a return home, but that return must mean more than simply crossing a border.
“It means returning with rights, being able to move freely, to go to school, to work, to access services, the ability to live alongside other communities without fear,” and have a pathway to citizenship.
“Our responsibility is to help make that future possible,” the UNHCR chief added.

Equality ‘ends at the doors of the Security Council’, Kenya’s Ruto tells General Assembly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Equality ‘ends at the doors of the Security Council’, Kenya’s Ruto tells General Assembly
Kenyan President William Ruto told the General Assembly on Wednesday that the sovereign equality the UN proclaims is contradicted by its own structures, urging Member States to reform the Security Council and an international financial system “built for another age”.
Addressing the General Debate, Mr. Ruto said Kenya spoke “not from despair in this institution, but from conviction in its possibilities”, adding that “multilateralism works when nations summon the will to make it work”.
However, he said the world recorded 65 State-based armed conflicts last year, 13 of them full-blown wars, with nearly a quarter of a million people killed in organised violence and disputes increasingly “frozen, deferred or decided by force”.
‘Permanently excluded’
Every nation has one vote, Mr. Ruto said, yet five hold a permanent power on questions of war and peace that the other 188 do not: “The equality proclaimed in this assembly ends at the doors of the Security Council.”
Africa’s 54 Member States, more than a quarter of the assembly, have no permanent seat on the Council, he said: “Permanently discussed, yet permanently excluded.”
He warned that confidence in the consistent application of international law was weakening in parts of the world.
“International law cannot be invoked loudly in one crisis, cautiously in another crisis, and disregarded when convenient,” he said.
Seventeen years after intergovernmental negotiations on council reform began, he said, “we should not accept that reform is impossible because it is difficult.”
‘Capital must not price prejudice’
Turning to finance, Mr. Ruto said global public debt reached a record $102 trillion in 2024, and 46 developing countries now spend more on interest than on classrooms and medicine.
“The hospital competes with a creditor. The classroom competes with debt service,” he said.
Citing a UN Development Programme (UNDP) estimate that subjectivity in credit ratings has cost African countries some $75 billion, he said developing countries borrow at rates two to four times higher than developed ones. “Capital must price risk. It must not price prejudice.”
“Africa does not come to plead. We come with a proposal,” he said, pointing to the continent’s minerals, renewable energy and youthful population – and Kenya’s planned $16 billion refinery in the coastal city of Lamu, capable of producing 700,000 barrels of oil a day.
“This is not a plea for special treatment. It is a proposition for shared prosperity,” he said, emphasising that a more industrialised, food-secure, better-connected and self-financing Africa can be a stronger partner to the world.
He closed by calling for “not a United Nations of some nations”, but one “where every nation has a voice, every people have a stake and every child has a future”.

Online reports described the "mobilization" of a pilgrim at the border after Rosh Hashanah — border guards explained the situation
Kyiv • UNN
The man was a Ukrainian citizen and was wanted among persons liable for military service. The border guards handed him over to the National Police for verification.
Information spread in the media about the alleged mobilization at the Ukrainian border of an Israeli citizen who was returning after celebrating Rosh Hashanah, but this does not correspond to the actual circumstances of the incident: the man was a Ukrainian citizen and was wanted by the military conscription authorities. He was handed over to the National Police for verification. The State Border Guard Service reported this on September 23, UNN writes.
Details
The SBGS emphasized that, when crossing the state border, foreign citizens are not checked by border guards to determine whether they are registered for military service in Ukraine. In addition, the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine does not carry out mobilization measures at state border crossing points.
"In connection with the dissemination in the media of information about the alleged mobilization at the border of an Israeli citizen who was returning after celebrating Rosh Hashanah, we report the following. (...) During border formalities, it was established that the person in question also holds Ukrainian citizenship. At the same time, the relevant records of persons liable for military service contained information that he was wanted," the SBGS said on social media.
In accordance with the powers and procedures established by law, the border guards, as stated, "handed the man over to representatives of the National Police of Ukraine for further verification."
Thus, the information about the mobilization of a foreign citizen directly at a border crossing point does not correspond to the actual circumstances of the incident
Additional information
Earlier in September, the news channel "Ha-Pargod" on social media reported that a 49-year-old Hasid who was returning to Israel after celebrating Rosh Hashanah in Uman had allegedly been detained at the Ukrainian-Romanian border and allegedly mobilized into the Ukrainian army.

US Set To Unveil Next Steps for Trump-Backed Armenia-Azerbaijan Transit Corridor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:58:11 UTC
20:58:11 KST

NEW YORK, United States -- The United States is set to unveil the next stage of its effort to develop the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, or TRIPP, a planned transport and infrastructure corridor through southern Armenia that Washington says could open new trade routes between the South Caucasus, Central Asia, and Western markets.
Senior State Department officials told reporters that the New York event on September 23 will focus on the institutional and financial mechanisms needed to move TRIPP from last year's Armenia-Azerbaijan peace initiative toward implementation.
The event is expected to bring together the foreign ministers of Armenia and Azerbaijan, representatives of the five Central Asian states -- with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan showing particular interest -- US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Republican Senator Steve Daines, and executives from more than 40 companies, many of them American.
Officials said the event will highlight how TRIPP aims to "pop the cork" on the Middle Corridor, unlocking a westward trade route that connects Europe to Central Asia while reducing reliance on transit through Russia, China, and Iran.
The gathering will also feature the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund, which officials said will invest in opportunities arising from TRIPP and the wider Trans-Caspian trade route. The fund operates at arm's length from the US government under a White House-appointed board and receives grant funding from the State Department. It is distinct from the TRIPP Development Company, the joint US-Armenian corporate entity being established to develop and oversee the corridor.
'A Major Security Issue'
TRIPP is intended to provide unimpeded access between Azerbaijan proper and its Nakhchivan exclave through Armenian territory while respecting Armenia's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and security.
"This becomes a major security issue for us," the official said, describing the removal of existing trade "choke points" as a central objective.
The transit route will be developed and managed by a US-controlled company, giving Washington exclusive rights while effectively excluding Russia from a strategically important project in one of its traditional spheres of influence.
The project emerged from an August 2025 White House summit at which Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinian and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed a US-brokered joint declaration aimed at ending decades of conflict between the two South Caucasus neighbors.
Armenia and Azerbaijan fought two major wars over Nagorno-Karabakh, an internationally recognized part of Azerbaijan that for decades had a predominantly ethnic-Armenian population. Azerbaijan regained full control of the territory in 2023, prompting almost all of its ethnic Armenia population to flee. The two sides agreed on the text of a peace treaty in March 2025, but a final agreement has yet to be completed.
Officials said there have been no cease-fire violations since the August summit and pointed to limited trade in fuel and agricultural products as evidence of growing economic integration. According to them, Azerbaijani fuel supplies have contributed to an estimated 20 to 30 percent decline in Armenian fuel costs.
They noted there had been more interaction between Washington and Baku during the previous 13 to 14 months than during the preceding 13 to 14 years.
A senior State Department official said Yerevan and Baku were acting as though peace were "inevitable," although additional steps remain before a final agreement can be completed. Washington intends to develop TRIPP in parallel with that process, arguing that greater economic integration could help remove remaining obstacles.
Physical Construction Still Some Way Off
Despite plans to move TRIPP toward implementation, construction of the roughly 43-kilometer section through Armenia is not yet ready to begin. The section is expected to include a railway, road, pipelines, electricity infrastructure, and digital data links.
The senior State Department official said Azerbaijan has already been building infrastructure toward the Armenian border at its own expense, while Turkey is similarly developing infrastructure up to the border. The remaining section through Armenia is still to be developed.
“We're not there yet,” the official said when asked how soon physical construction of the Armenian section could begin. The administration hopes to begin looking for business and investment opportunities by the end of 2026 or the first quarter of 2027.
The railway will take longer. A feasibility study is expected by the end of 2026 or early 2027, after which companies will be able to bid. The official said completing the railway would likely take at least 18 months, complicated by difficult topography.
Electricity connections could come sooner. Discussions are already underway, with officials expecting electricity operations to begin in 2027, potentially linking the Armenian and Azerbaijani grids with wider Central Asia, Turkish, and European regional networks. Passenger rail is also planned.
TRIPP Leadership
The briefers provided more detail about the planned structure of the TRIPP Development Company (TDC) but no names for its future leadership.
The TDC is being established as a corporate joint venture between the US government and Armenia. The senior State Department official described it as a first-of-its-kind arrangement in which the US will hold a majority stake, with its own board, voting procedures, and management. Several legal matters still need to be finalized before the company can formally be announced.
Projects involving rail, roads, electricity, oil, gas, and data will go through regular tender processes for construction or concessions. The US Development Finance Corporation (DFC) has been involved in the legal and institutional setup, but the TDC itself will operate as a separate US-Armenian corporate entity.
The United States is prepared to invest once feasibility studies establish that individual projects are commercially viable. The State Department is financing part of the feasibility work, with engineering firm AECOM set to present investors with projects unlocked by TRIPP during the event on September 23.
'A Difficult Neighborhood'
Officials described TRIPP as an alternative to existing east-west routes, with the proposed corridor offering Central Asian trade another route to Western markets that bypasses Russia and Iran.
The senior State Department official said Washington had held discussions with regional competitors but declined to characterize their private views.
"There have been numerous conversations with all of the competitors in the region," the official said, adding that Washington was aware of the potential for "hard conversations" in what officials called a difficult neighborhood.
The event is intended to mark a shift from the 2025 peace initiative toward implementation, with more than 40 companies attending.
The project still requires completing feasibility studies, legal arrangements, financing, tendering, and ultimately construction.
While Washington says Armenia and Azerbaijan are on an "irreversible path to peace," their final peace agreement has yet to be completed.
The US nevertheless intends to develop TRIPP alongside the peace process, arguing that greater economic integration could help remove remaining obstacles. As the senior State Department official put it, the focus is on "what happens the day after the piece of paper."

Britain has suspended its €139 million-a-year lease payments for the Diego Garcia base while ministers try to reshape the agreement into one Washington can accept, with the Conservatives calling for it to be scrapped altogether.
Britain will go back to the drawing board on its agreement to return the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said on Wednesday. The move comes a day after US President Donald Trump attacked the deal during his first meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
The two leaders met on Tuesday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. With Burnham sitting beside him, Trump said he expected the British leader to reconsider the "terrible deal". Burnham nodded and replied "yep".
Burnham, who succeeded Keir Starmer in July, later told broadcasters that Britain would "work hard" to resolve the issue and that he was "confident we can find it working with our US partners".
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting said Trump's objections were "not news to us". But he said the president's latest remarks "provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing".
"So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where we can support it," he said.
Streeting also confirmed that Britain would not "at this stage" make the annual payments of at least £120 million (€139 million) it had agreed to pay Mauritius to lease back the military base on Diego Garcia.
Months of US opposition
The agreement, reached last year between Starmer and the Mauritian government, would hand the Indian Ocean archipelago back to Britain's former colony. Britain would then lease the strategic US-UK base on Diego Garcia for 99 years, with the option to extend. Britain announced in April that the plans were on hold.
Trump first backed the pact but later turned against it, calling it "an act of great stupidity", and it has caused friction with his administration for months.
Starmer defended the agreement by arguing that international legal rulings had cast doubt on Britain's claim to the islands, and that only a deal with Mauritius could secure continued US and UK use of the base.
Britain held on to the Chagos Islands when Mauritius became independent in the 1960s. It removed thousands of islanders, who have since brought a series of compensation claims in British courts. In 2019, the International Court of Justice concluded that Britain unlawfully separated Chagos from Mauritius when ending colonial rule..
'Ostrich strategy'
James Cartlidge, defence spokesman for the opposition Conservatives, said the agreement "should be binned entirely".
Streeting rejected that approach. He told Times Radio: "The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand and hoping it (will) go away ... is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world."
Jack Pannell, a senior researcher at the British Foreign Policy Group think-tank, told AFP that Burnham's focus with Trump would be on "the big international issues", such as AI regulation, Ukraine and the Middle East.
"Success for Burnham means avoiding this issue becoming a millstone around his neck while he pursues his other foreign policy priorities and focuses on his domestic agenda," Pannell said. "The chances of a breakthrough on this issue are slim, and that may suit the prime minister just fine."
Also on Tuesday, Trump signed a security agreement with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark that will allow the US to build two military bases in southern and eastern Greenland.

Russia’s use of jet-powered drones has spiked eightfold within three months since June, according to the Ukrainian Air Force.
The drones, powered by turbojet engines and with flight characteristics comparable to some cruise missiles, have created new challenges for Ukrainian air defense, as Kyiv has resorted to more expensive means, including Western F-16s and air-to-air missiles, to intercept them.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
On television on Wednesday, Air Force spokesperson Yuriy Ihnat said that Russia has used around 7,700 of such drones since their initial deployments, with numbers rising in recent months.
As reported by state media Ukrinform, the total number of jet-powered drones launched in June was 350, which rose to 1,500 in July and 2,850 in August.
For September, about 1,900 have been detected thus far, a week before the month is over, as Russia also began launching the drones in non-stop waves in the same month as a new tactic that complicates Ukrainian air defense.
Prototypes of the jet-powered drones were first seen in 2025, before systematic launches began in the summer of 2026.
Ihnat said the spike suggests Russia has managed to evade sanctions and source foreign components needed to build the drones – partly contradicting recent intelligence reports suggesting Russia’s challenges in sourcing Chinese jet engines used to power the drones.
“This suggests that the enemy is not stopping, that they are finding opportunities to purchase those jet engines, other components, and assemble them on Russian territory,” Ihnat said.

Hacker arrested over cyberattacks on at least two Latvian companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:55:16 UTC
20:55:16 KST

On the 15th of September, Latvian State Police arrested a hacker born in 2003 on suspicion of carrying out cyberattacks against at least two Latvian companies for financial gain.
One attack against a company was recorded as early as February this year, while another cyberattack with a similar modus operandi was detected in early September against household appliance and smart device repair company TSC, which is part of the LMT group, the State Police reports.
The hacker gained unauthorised access to some of the personal data stored in the database and attempted to extort money in exchange for not disclosing the data further. Information available to the State Police indicates that the suspect did not distribute the data obtained in the cyberattacks.
In both cases, the man born in 2003 has been formally recognised as a suspect, and investigations in the criminal proceedings are continuing.
While investigating criminal proceedings concerning a cyberattack on a company’s website in February this year, the First Division of the State Police Cybercrime Combating Department analysed the nature of the attack and the attacker’s “modus operandi”, which indicated a connection to the recent attack on the TSC website.
Investigators established that the suspect used an automated attack tool to identify a vulnerability,
after which he gained access to the website’s database and exported information, including restricted-access data.
The attack was carried out using virtual masking tools to conceal the attacker’s actual location. After completing the attack, the hacker contacted the company using an anonymous email account created specifically for this purpose and demanded payment in exchange for not distributing the stolen data further.
By analysing and investigating the cyberattack on the TSC website, with support from the LMT Security Service and CERT.LV, investigators were able to quickly establish and verify the circumstances of the case. This enabled the State Police not only to identify a potential suspect, but also to link the two incidents and determine the suspected hacker’s location.
On the 15th of September, law enforcement officers arrested the hacker, a man born in 2003, and carried out several other procedural actions, including a search at an address in Riga.
During the investigation, police obtained evidence and information concerning other cyberattacks
allegedly carried out by the suspect against various companies in Latvia and abroad. Investigations into these incidents are continuing.
Based on information obtained during the investigation, there are grounds to believe that, thanks to the swift action of the State Police, the personal data obtained without authorisation was not passed on to third parties.
The First Division of the State Police Cybercrime Combating Department succeeded in linking the two cases, and the detained man has been formally recognised as a suspect in both criminal proceedings.
The cases are being investigated under Section 241, Paragraph two of the Criminal Law for unauthorised access to an automated data processing system for financial gain; Section 183, Paragraph one for extortion; and Section 243, Paragraph three for disrupting the operation of an automated data processing system and unlawfully handling information contained in such a system for financial gain.
In investigating the suspect’s motives, police established that the cyberattacks did not target specific companies. Instead, automated attack tools were used to scan various websites and online resources in search of vulnerabilities.
The State Police therefore urges all companies to assess their online resources and ensure that appropriate security measures are in place to minimise the risk of similar incidents occurring in the future.

Can Baghdad ever bring Iraq's militias under state control?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
11:55:03 UTC
20:55:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Can Baghdad ever bring Iraq's militias under state control?
A relative pause in fighting between the United States and Iran that ended in early September has brought the region back into a state of geopolitical tension.
As the exchange of strikes, retaliations, and signalling between Washington and Tehran continues, there is a heightened expectation from Washington that the US pullout from Iraq should coincide with Iranian-backed militias in the country being disarmed.
A looming US withdrawal
At a meeting at the White House in July, Iraq’s new prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, met with President Donald Trump and indicated that Baghdad would work to disarm the pro-Iranian Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF).
“The fact that both Trump and Zaidi are following through means this is a bipartisan vision in the United States and a continued commitment from Zaidi, who took over the premiership from Sudani as the Coordination Framework’s candidate,” Hamzeh Hadad, an Adjunct Fellow with the Center for New American Security, told The New Arab.
The withdrawal of US forces now places a greater burden on the government in Baghdad to determine the future of the PMF.
“The US pullout removes a key lever for Baghdad and forces tougher bargaining at home,” Dr Inna Rudolf, Senior Research Fellow in the War Studies Department at King’s College London, told The New Arab.
“Coalition forces had been both an excuse some factions used for pursuing greater autonomy but also a tool Washington could use to push for change.”
The US continues to pressure Baghdad for the disarmament of the PMF through diplomatic channels, but the threat of further sanctions and tariffs has been floated by the Trump administration.
On 21 September, Zaidi requested more time beyond the 30 September deadline agreed with the United States, and the next day it was announced that it would be pushed back to 30 June 2027.
Baghdad will now have nine months to continue negotiations with the factions while avoiding potential US financial or economic sanctions.
“The Iraqi government needs to have a more honest dialogue with Washington about its situation and vision,” Haddad told The New Arab.
“But this needs to take place without wishful statements from the Iraqi side that they backtrack on, as they already have to deal with strong foreign pressure on the issue.”
The plan to dismantle and reorganise the PMF fighters into existing brigades and retire older commanders who have served since 2014 will reportedly start implementation in January 2027.
The government also intends to establish a new directorate to monitor the integration.
Zaidi's disarmament push
Iraq’s new prime minister has sought to strengthen Baghdad’s image as a government that can rein in corruption, ensure security, and pursue economic development with the international community.
“Zaidi, entering politics, a new face, with no prior experience in public office, wanted to build on the US backing that saw him come to power, and so he boldly stated that he would enforce a deadline for armed groups outside of the state apparatus to disarm,” said Hadad.
The Iraqi government is currently waging a campaign to curtail the PMF’s power in the country. In mid-August, Iraqi security forces detained a senior commander from the Nujaba Movement, one of the primary Iranian-backed militias that make up the PMF coalition.
“There is a different understanding between what constitutes armed groups outside of the state apparatus in Iraq than in Washington,” Hadad noted.
Hiba Abdulwahhab, an Iraqi researcher and analyst, told The New Arab, “The relationship between the Iraqi government and these factions resembles a Catholic marriage, a union with no easy divorce. They are deeply intertwined politically, institutionally, and economically”.
An uncertain security situation
The US military will also be removing the air defence systems, including Patriot and C-RAM systems, from the Kurdistan Region. The depletion of US air defence system interceptors during the conflict with Iran has contributed to the declining security situation.
In March 2026, Kataib Hezbollah, one of the key factions of the PMF, released a two-minute video that went viral showing an FPV drone flying over the Camp Victory complex near Baghdad International Airport, a site that continued to host US and NATO-linked facilities.
A drone attack that Saudi officials reported originated from Iraq struck the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia on 11 September. Baghdad later confirmed the pipeline attack came from Iraqi territory and dismissed security officials responsible for Maysan Province near the Iranian border and closed the area’s border crossing.
Still, some PMF groups have sought out a political advantage by appearing to adhere to the government’s calls. One militia, Asaib Ahl al-Haq, announced over the summer that it formally withdrew from the PMF coalition and handed over its weapons to the government.
Other groups, such as the Sayyid al-Shuhada Brigades and the Nujaba Movement, have stated they will not turn over their weapons, saying that certain conditions had to be met before they did so.
“[Zaidi’s] reasoning is that there will be no more American forces present in Iraq and therefore no more excuse for armed groups to exist after that,” Hadad told The New Arab.
Dr Rudolf agrees. “Losing that pretext gives negotiators cleaner rhetorical space to press for stricter control as it strips the factions of their usual talking point that foreign troops justify armed resistance outside the formal chain of command.”
Finding a path to disarmament
Iraqi leaders have advocated for the PMF to function as a state security institution and slowly reduce their political nature.
In May, the militia of prominent Shia cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, Saraya al-Salam, announced it would begin disarmament and integrate into the state. While this group is not technically part of the PMF and Shia Coordination Framework, it could be interpreted as a sign of the direction the wind is blowing in Iraq.
However, it is likely that the groups will utilise this approach to reposition themselves without totally surrendering their arms.
“The most likely outcome is therefore adaptation and repositioning rather than genuine disarmament,” Abdulwahhab told The New Arab.
“Weapons could remain in faction-controlled depots, be transferred to affiliated units, or be placed nominally within the PMF’s official structure without being brought under effective government command.”
Observers of Iraq are right to be sceptical that the PMF will do little else other than rebrand and retain their loyalty to informal chains of command and external ties with Tehran.
Regarding the extension of the disarmament deadline, Abdulwahhab said, “The progression raises serious doubts about the government’s ability to act against factions deeply embedded in Iraq’s political and security institutions”.
She added, “The extension is more likely to give Iran-aligned factions time to reorganise and protect their networks than to give the government the power to disarm and dismantle them,” further noting that Baghdad had to take concrete steps now, otherwise June 2027 may bring another postponement rather than a resolution.
Some positive steps have been taken, but it is still early in the process to understand how far Baghdad can go.
“Without tangible incentives and accountability mechanisms, ‘integration’ will feel like administrative rebranding,” Rudolf said. “The public will see it as window dressing.”
The long-term outlook will depend on the future of the financial and military support from Iran as well as Baghdad’s own ability to assert control over the militias.
For now, the government in Baghdad will have to navigate the post-US withdrawal environment on its own.
Christopher Solomon is a Middle East analyst, researcher, editor, and writer based in the Washington, DC area. He is the author of the book In Search of Greater Syria (Bloomsbury)
