Europe’s centrists are finally paying the price of their extremism
The centre’s blind adherence to austerity has devastated European societies.
Friedrich Merz has been German chancellor for less than a year and half, and his approval ratings are at record lows. His centre-right Christian Democratic Union of Germany (CDU), which just lost one state election and was obliterated in another, is in free fall across the country.
The German media cannot talk or write about anything else, blaming Merz for weak campaigning, for boxing himself into an unpopular coalition with the social democrats, for failing to energise the youth as the ultraright Alternative for Germany (AfD) has. All true, all secondary.
What is actually dying in Germany is not just a hitherto dominant party, but the image of centrist politicians as moderate technocrats. After three decades of this facade of moderation and competence, it is now becoming clear that they were neither moderate nor competent.
Alas, first gradually, then suddenly, the masks are falling to the ground, and now the majority can see them for what they have always been: Zealots ruthlessly pursuing dead-end, misanthropic policies that have gutted German society’s capacity to sustain itself and brought it to the verge of an unnecessary war on European soil.
Zealotry dressed in a grey suit and speaking in a soothing voice, repeating ad nauseam that “there is no alternative,” doesn’t look like zealotry until it starts to fail at an epic scale. What changed recently, with inevitable repercussions at the ballot box, is that the deindustrialisation and stagnation caused by the centrists’ extremism has become impossible to ignore.
The AfD did not surge because, overnight, millions of Germans had an epiphany that made them more susceptible to fascist tropes. Its ranks swelled because years of austerity made the German people stare in the face of a loss of status and a high probability of real poverty. Is it any wonder that the ultra-right succeeded in creating an electoral tsunami out of the longing for a return to a fictional golden past – a past lacking the “suspicious” stranger: The Muslim, the Jew, the trans?
It is the same story from Berlin to Paris to London. French President Emmanuel Macron’s centrism has single-handedly pushed France to the edge of a far-right presidency. He made promises of a French renaissance that is impossible, given the shackles of the monetary union with Germany that lacks the necessary democratic and political union.
He has piled tax breaks on the ultra-rich few at a time when the many have struggled to pay for the petrol that their cars need to get them to work. He has raised the retirement age to 64 at a time when impoverished workers’ life expectancy is no more than 72 years.
He has never seen a rent-seeking banker that he has not warmed up to. And all along, he has countenanced no deviation, no compromise, no democratic argument about alternatives.
In the United Kingdom, the centrist Tory-Labour duopoly has also embraced the same austerity policies. In the 1980s, Conservative Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher’s wanton vandalism of British industry and her financialisation of homes and utilities made the UK a cesspit of mind-numbing inequality, with a burgeoning import-based service economy and real estate spivs living parasitically at the expense of the vast, disenfranchised majority.
However, it was Tony Blair’s Labour government that sealed this victory of Britain’s oligarchic rentier class by devising innovative ways to continue the gutting of public goods, while completing the unshackling of the City of London bankers. Naturally, as in Germany and France, the politics of fear and loathing are on the march in the UK.
Everywhere, it is the same mechanism: Parties that called themselves sensible, pragmatic, and centrist have pursued one of the most doctrinaire economic programmes in European history – and pursued it with a rigidity, an intolerance of dissent, and a contempt for democratic contestation that the actual political extremes of the 20th century would have recognised as their own method, even if they had rejected the content.
I want to be precise about what I mean by extremism here, because it is not a rhetorical flourish. An ideology is extreme not so much because of where it sits on a left-right spectrum, not even because of the extreme impact of its policies on the majority, but because of how it treats disagreement: As illegitimate, as a problem to be managed rather than a proposition to be responded to.
By that test, Europe’s centre has been the most extreme political formation since the end of World War II. It has built a currency union explicitly designed to remove economic policy from the reach of elections. It has enabled electricity cartels to rob people and businesses blind. It has labelled anyone proposing an alternative “unserious”, “populist” or “anti-European” – regardless of whether that alternative makes economic sense.
In 2015, as the minister of finance of Greece, I had the privilege of experiencing in person the European centrists’ casual extremism. After five years of a failed stabilisation programme that cost Europeans more than an annual Greek gross domestic product, the people of Greece voted for Syriza, which I was a member of, in January 2015 to renegotiate financial terms that even bankers admitted were ludicrous.
And how did the centre respond? They crushed us. Not because they disagreed with our proposals but because, as Christine Lagarde, then the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, put it to me, they had put so much political capital into the Greek programme that they could not go back.
To understand the nature and causes of the centre’s extremism, I can think of no better case study than the late Wolfgang Schauble, Germany’s finance minister, with whom I negotiated in 2015. His entire career was organised around a (not illegitimate) fear that Paris would capture the Bundesbank and use the deutschmark, the German currency, to pay for French-style deficit-funded policies across Europe.
Once French President Francois Mitterrand convinced German Chancellor Helmut Kohl to agree to a European Monetary Union and a single currency (the euro) in return for France’s consent to Germany’s reunification in 1989, Schauble and the Bundesbank went into overdrive to prevent the French from usurping Germany’s currency.
In this they succeeded by designing a monetary union featuring no fiscal union, no democratic political union, no banking union, and no shock absorbers, so that the German control Schauble couldn’t legislate directly was built into the plumbing instead.
It was not prudence. It was a man convinced, with the zeal of a convert, that there was exactly one correct economic morality and that anyone departing from it – French socialists, Greek pensioners, Italian voters – had to be constrained by architecture since they could not be trusted with a vote. Fiscal Calvinism is the correct term for it.
And the French socialists? Deluded that they could still command the new currency for their purposes, they applauded. And so a new fiscal Calvinism was embedded at the heart of the European Union, in the eurozone – and, lest we forget, Calvinism is not a synonym for moderation.
When in the autumn of 2008 the global financial crisis began, our Calvinist monetary union faced an almighty shock without any shock absorbers. The sequential bankruptcy of the Franco-German banks and almost every eurozone government was inevitable.
And how did Schauble, with every European centrist in tow, respond? Not just by doubling down, but by putting on display an extreme authoritarianism that most Europeans thought had been expunged from Europe in 1945.
Consider the following: After we came to power with an overwhelming mandate, I suggested to them that we sit down and find a compromise. Schauble reacted with a classic extremist line: “Elections cannot be allowed to change economic policy!”
A few months later, Schauble and his minions forced our government to accept a new loan – a new credit card – that would be given under conditions of crushing austerity so that we could pretend that we were repaying our previous credit cards.
When we insisted this was a matter for the Greek people to decide through a referendum, the centrists in authority blackmailed Greece to accept their terms of surrender by practising what I called – and still characterise as – financial terrorism: They effectively shut down Greece’s banking system by having the European Central Bank freeze financing for Greek banks.
Was Schauble demonstrating cruelty to the Greeks? No. He was imposing harsh austerity – discipline, he called it – on us because he wanted to bring it to Spain, Italy, France and, eventually, to Germany. And how did the European centrists, including the social democrats and the Greens, respond? They went along with Schauble’s extremism.
By now it should be clear why the centre is not holding across Europe. Their extreme austerity threw Europe’s economy into a depression. Panicking, the centre reacted by getting the European Central Bank to print mountain ranges of euros – which they gave to the bankers to hand over to Big Business, which did not dare invest it, as the masses were impecunious and, thus, unlikely to buy new high value-added goods. Instead, corporate executives used the money to buy back their own shares and bolster their bonuses, while inequality went through the stratosphere.
This is the mess that Merz inherited. A Germany whose industrial model is kaput because its businesses did not invest during the 15 years their executives were getting rich through austerity for the many and money-printing for the oligarchy. The result is that, today, Volkswagen cannot sell cars, and Merz is forced to transfer its production lines to Rheinmetall to manufacture tanks that not even the Ukrainians want.
Is there a parallel with the 1920s and 1930s? Yes, though not the lazy one where a single leader plays Hitler. The real parallel is in the shape of the orthodoxy: The gold standard then, fiscal austerity now, each treated not as one policy among several but as a fact of nature, defended with a fervour that brooked no dissent even as it visibly deepened the depression it was supposed to cure.
Then, as now, the mainstream parties were not moderates flanked by extremists; they were themselves the immovable ideological core, and it was precisely their refusal to entertain any alternative that left “extremist” as the only label available for anyone who did. The tragedy repeating itself is not that fascism is marching back in uniform. It is that a political culture calling itself the sensible middle keeps behaving like a sect – intolerant, doctrinaire, certain of its own necessity – and keeps being surprised when voters who are refused a legitimate alternative eventually take the illegitimate one on offer.
Merz’s collapsing numbers are not a verdict on his personal charisma. They are the bill finally arriving for a centre that mistook its own fanaticism for moderation and called everyone who noticed a threat to Europe.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Microamp establishes cooperation with the faculty of electronics at the Military University of Technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:02:43 UTC
19:02:43 KST

Microamp, a global leader in resilient 5G mmWave connectivity for real-time operations, and the Faculty of Electronics at the Military University of Technology (MUT), a premier academic and research institution based in Warsaw, Poland, have signed a cooperation agreement. The inaugural meeting for this joint initiative took place on 4 September 2026. One of the initial outcomes of this collaboration is the delivery of the Microamp 5G mmWave Starter Kit to the Faculty, which will serve advanced research and educational purposes.
Key representatives from Microamp attended the meeting, including Dr Marcin Góralczyk (Chief Technology Officer) and Adam Olesiński (Head of RAN Solutions). The Faculty of Electronics at MUT was represented by Col. Prof. Jan Kelner (Dean of the Faculty of Electronics), Lt. Col. Dr Jarosław Wojtuń (Deputy Director of the Institute of Communications Systems) and Dr Paweł Skokowski (Head of the Mobile Communications Systems Department) alongside staff members.
The delivered Microamp 5G mmWave Starter Kit is a comprehensive solution enabling the rapid deployment of a fully functional LDI/LPD mobile architecture. The Microamp mmWave wireless platform consists of radio access network elements, mmWave RAN software, a core network and user equipment. Operating in Standalone mode, the system is fully compliant with the 3GPP standard. The network supports n257, n258 and n261 bands across the 24.25-29.5 GHz frequency range, ensuring throughput exceeding 4 Gbps and latency below 5 ms.
The Microamp mmWave network will be extensively utilised in scientific and research activities conducted by the Faculty of Electronics staff, particularly in developing specialised publications and reports for international NATO working groups. Furthermore, the provided solution forms a foundation for joint research initiatives and projects. This Microamp mmWave system will also facilitate commercial scientific research, proactively addressing the current demands of the industrial market and the defence sector. Access to the complete 5G mmWave environment creates an opportunity to practically verify advanced communication scenarios essential for civil and military applications.
Within the academic framework, the Microamp 5G mmWave Starter Kit will support specialised training sessions and laboratory classes dedicated to the latest connectivity standards. The supplied mmWave wireless platform will allow students to acquire practical skills in configuring, deploying and testing 5G mmWave architectures. Access to this Microamp solution will enable the completion of diploma and design projects, including experimental research on wave propagation, network architecture optimisation and the integration of specialised end devices.
Establishing cooperation with the MUT Faculty of Electronics marks a vital step for Microamp in developing expertise within modern telecommunications. The provided mmWave system will enrich the laboratory facilities of the Faculty and integrate academic education with the practical application of modern 5G connectivity.
About Military University of Technology
The Military University of Technology (MUT) in Warsaw is a public academic institution established in 1951. As a military-civilian university, MUT educates cadets and civilian students while conducting advanced research and development in engineering, technical, exact and social sciences. MUT serves as a strategic research and development facility for the Polish Armed Forces and a leading innovation centre for national security and defence.
The Faculty of Electronics at the Military University of Technology is one of the leading academic and research centres in Poland, specialising in advanced technologies across electronics, telecommunications, radar systems, electronic warfare and communication systems. The Faculty conducts scientific research, implementation projects and educational programmes for both the defence sector and civilian industry.
About Microamp
Microamp is a global leader in resilient 5G and 6G mmWave connectivity for real-time operations. The company designs, builds and delivers ultra-high-capacity, near-zero-latency end-to-end networks powered by its own purpose-built radios. By merging deep-tech know-how with a broad portfolio of technology partners, Microamp empowers industries, system integrators, MNOs, DSPs, governments, and research institutions worldwide. Its networks support applications requiring deterministic performance and high-uplink throughput, in both commercial and defence sectors, where resilience, security and jamming resistance are crucial. Engineered for the most demanding environments, the Microamp system supports critical infrastructure, ports, logistics hubs, public transportation, media production, mass events and specialised military missions.

Azerbaijan pardons French national after EU drops sanctions on Usmanov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:01:32 UTC
19:01:32 KST

Azerbaijan pardons French national after EU drops sanctions on Usmanov
BAKU, Sept 23 - Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev pardoned a French national jailed for espionage on Wednesday, a day after the EU lifted sanctions on Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov following what diplomats said was pressure from Baku.
The Frenchman, Martin Ryan, had been serving a 10-year prison sentence in Baku following a spying conviction in March. It was not immediately clear whether he had been released.
Three European diplomats told Reuters that Paris had privately indicated that Baku was using Usmanov's sanctions case to pressure France over two French citizens held in Azerbaijan.
French weekly Challenges identified the second jailed French national as Anass Derraz, an employee of French water management company Saur. Derraz, who was sentenced to 12 years in prison in 2025 on corruption charges, was not on the list of pardoned prisoners on Wednesday.
An Azerbaijani diplomat last week rejected suggestions of a pressure campaign as "categorically unfounded", saying Baku had openly supported Usmanov's removal from Western sanctions lists because it viewed the measures against him as unjust.
Relations between Baku and Paris have long been strained by France's support for Armenia, Azerbaijan's historic rival. Ties between Azerbaijan and Russia have also deteriorated since the accidental downing of an Azerbaijani passenger jet by Russian forces in December 2024.
SANCTIONS DELISTING CAUSED RIFT IN EU
The delisting of Usmanov and fellow Russian billionaire Mikhail Fridman was the first time the EU removed sanctions on the wealthiest members of Russia's billionaire elite who had not publicly condemned the war in Ukraine.
The decision exposed divisions among EU governments that had hoped a recent change of government in Hungary would help forge a more united stance towards Moscow after years in which former Prime Minister Viktor Orban complicated efforts to renew sanctions and support Ukraine.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy told a press conference in New York after meeting US President Donald Trump that the lifting of EU sanctions was a result of Russia's work to break the West's unity in supporting Ukraine.
"Maybe these two oligarchs are now very happy. But they do not know us, they do not know me. I come with the same surnames to Europe again," Zelenskiy said.
The EU imposed sanctions on Fridman, who was born in Soviet Ukraine, and Usmanov, born in Uzbekistan, in 2022, after Russia sent its troops into Ukraine, including travel and transaction bans and asset freezes within the bloc.
Both men made their fortunes following the collapse of the Soviet Union in the 1990s and later on created their business empires with Fridman focusing on oil and banking and Usmanov on metals and telecoms.
Since the start of the war, Fridman, who holds an Israeli passport, mostly stayed out of Russia, while Usmanov spent time between Moscow and his native Uzbekistan, wielding his influence in the post-Soviet world to help remove sanctions.
The Organization of Turkic States, which includes Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Turkey, sent letters to EU leaders and the US president calling for sanctions to be lifted.
Usmanov, who once held a minority stake in Arsenal football club, graduated from the same prestigious diplomatic school in Moscow as presidents of Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan and knows them in person.
Ryan, the Frenchman pardoned on Wednesday, was arrested in December 2023 and accused of gathering information about Azerbaijan's military cooperation with Turkey and Pakistan.
Before his arrest, he worked in Azerbaijan for a food-import company that also provided consultancy services.
Aliyev's office said Ryan was pardoned alongside 14 Azerbaijani citizens, two Turkish nationals, a dual Russian-Israeli citizen and a Pakistani citizen. REUTERS

‘Who wants a pistol? Raise your hand.’
At the Old Tucson theme park in Tucson, Arizona, visitors step out of their normal lives and into the city’s past. Or, more accurately, a funhouse mirror of the past that plays up the cowboy romance and tamps down the drudgery and poverty to cultivate a good ol’ time. Over the course of a day, the US directors Sue Ding and Sarah Garrahan capture visitors enjoying the park’s many attractions, including shooting games, live shows, rides and, of course, the opportunity to cosplay as sheriffs, outlaws and saloon girls in the old-timey photography studio. Throughout, park guests discuss what draws them to Old Tucson. Whether it’s movie mythos, a longing for a simpler, ‘less political’ era, or just the fun of escapism, there’s an undeniable allure in stepping into a romanticised past that never quite existed.

Gruesome East Jerusalem murder: woman allegedly kidnapped, killed and hidden in barrel

10:00:59 UTC
19:00:59 KST

New details have emerged in the killing of 61-year-old East Jerusalem resident Fatma Rajabi, whose body was allegedly concealed inside an industrial barrel near the home of the man suspected of murdering her.
The suspect, Saleh Othman, a technician in his 60s from East Jerusalem, turned himself in to police after Rajabi had been missing for five days. According to investigators, he confessed during questioning, reenacted the killing and led officers to the location where her body had been hidden. During his interrogation, Othman told investigators: “I was drunk at the time of the murder.”
New footage has also emerged showing what police suspect were Othman’s actions after the killing. He is allegedly seen attempting to withdraw cash using Rajabi’s credit card.
Police suspect the killing may have stemmed from a financial debt amounting to tens of thousands of shekels. Investigators also believe Rajabi and Othman knew each other before her disappearance.
Rajabi was last seen leaving her home and later entering Othman’s work vehicle. From that point, she disappeared.
Investigators suspect Othman killed her while they were traveling and later transported her body to an area near his home in the East Jerusalem neighborhood of At-Tur, where he allegedly concealed it inside a barrel.
Her disappearance triggered a five-day search operation involving Jerusalem District police officers, Border Police forces and hundreds of volunteers.
Searches were conducted in several areas, including near Abu Ghosh and Mevaseret Zion, while investigators simultaneously tried to reconstruct Rajabi’s final movements and gather surveillance footage and other evidence that could indicate what had happened to her.
During the search, Rajabi’s family criticized the police response, arguing that efforts to locate her had begun too late.
Police rejected the allegations, saying extensive forces and resources were deployed as soon as the missing-person report was received.
The breakthrough came after five days, when Othman surrendered to police. According to investigators, he confessed during questioning, reenacted the killing and led police to the location where Rajabi’s body had been concealed.

Republican jitters grow as unpopular Trump fuels midterm ‘bloodbath’ fears

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:00:47 UTC
19:00:47 KST

Donald Trump pulled out all the stops at the Republican party’s midterm convention two weeks ago. In speeches aimed at the voters who will soon decide whether to keep Republicans in control of Congress for the final phase of his presidency, the president dangled $5,000 checks, and warned the United States would turn into a “communist country” if Democrats are elected.
The unprecedented political gathering amounted to a Hail Mary pass at retaining control of Congress, which history indicated Trump’s Republican allies had always been likely to lose in the 3 November vote. Two weeks later, with election administrators in several states already sending out mail ballots, there is no indication the gambit has worked.
Polls have continued to show Democrats with an edge on the generic ballot, a key indicator of voter sentiment in congressional races, as well as in some key Senate contests such as North Carolina and Georgia, both states where Trump won two years ago. Forecasters have moved their ratings of other battleground races almost uniformly in Democrats’ favor, despite Republican-led states’ concerted effort to redraw House districts in the party’s favor.
Trump’s approval ratings remain low, with some surveys finding him plumbing new depths. Prices for gasoline and diesel have started climbing again amid the ongoing war with Iran, prompting the Republican Senate stalwart Chuck Grassley of Iowa to publicly encourage the president to do more for farmers, whose businesses have been particularly hard hit by the conflict’s economic shocks.
Top Republicans suddenly appear worried about the fortunes of incumbents standing for re-election in some of the reddest states in the country. Last week, vice-president JD Vance campaigned in Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century, but where Adam Hamilton is seen as a strong challenger to the Republican incumbent Roger Marshall.
Back in Washington, the extent of the House GOP’s jitters became clear when Democrats forced a vote on a war powers resolution to end the fighting with Iran, and three Republicans who had not backed the previous five efforts supported this one, ensuring its passage.
“This midterm is going to be a fucking bloodbath,” said Nancy Mace, the outgoing congresswoman who was among the trio of new converts, and predicted that her party would not keep control of the Senate and House of Representatives when ballots are tallied in a month and a half.
In the days that followed, more Republicans in competitive races came out against the Iran war.
“The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for Michigan’s open Senate seat, said in a campaign ad released on Monday. Ashley Hinson, the congresswoman who is running to represent Iowa in the Senate, wrote on social media “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end”. She had voted against the Democratic war powers resolution, as had John James, the congressman who is the Republican nominee for governor of Michigan, but on Tuesday, the Detroit News reported he told reporters: “We need to end this war quickly. Because war is terrible, and no one likes war.”
Democratic operatives have long maintained that Trump was leading the GOP’s congressional majorities into oblivion, and are now being joined in that prediction by veteran politics watchers, who see the toxic combination of rising prices, poor approval ratings and dampening enthusiasm among voters as likely fatal for Republicans’ hopes of keeping control of the House, if not the Senate.
“We are seeing a dramatic souring and just overall level of anger at the broken promises of Trump and House Republicans, like, issue after issue after issue. Like, people are just unhappy right now,” said a Democratic strategist who did not want their name to be used.
Talk has even re-emerged of a “blue wave” in November that will see Republicans lose in deep-red corners of the country.
“Republicans should brace themselves: the three most plausible outcomes are that it will be bad, really bad, or truly horrible,” wrote the veteran analyst Charlie Cook.
Yet not everything is necessarily going Democrats’ way. In the battle for the Senate, Republicans have grown increasingly optimistic about their Senate candidate winning in New Hampshire, which some major forecasters now view as a toss-up. The party may also have come out ahead in the mid-decade redistricting push, and definitely has more financial resources this year than the Democrats – a reversal from most midterms prior.
“House Republicans are running with a more favorable map, historic fundraising, stronger candidates, and a commonsense agenda, while Democrats are burdened by unelectable far-left nominees and deeply unpopular policies that make their path to the majority far more challenging than the pundits suggest,” said Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee.
After much speculation about when he would act, Trump’s Maga Inc Super Pac has started spending its $400m war chest, buying $15m in advertisements to support the Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas senate race. Fairshake, a Super Pac connected to the cryptocurrency industry, will reportedly spend $30m against Sherrod Brown, the Democratic former senator from Ohio and cryptocurrency adversary seeking to return to the chamber, after the industry spent $40m to see him defeated in 2024.
Republicans and their allies have thus far put $384.5m into Senate races, to Democrats’ and their supporters’ $112.7m, according to data compiled by political analyst Rob Pyers. In the House, Republican supporters have spent nearly $65.7m to the Democrats’ $51.1m, but Politico has reported that much of that money has gone to districts where Trump won two years ago, a sign that the GOP is playing defense.
Winning the Senate will require Democrats to oust at least four Republicans in states that Trump won in 2024. The House seems an easier target for the party, since the GOP controls it by a low single-digit majority.
House Republican leaders including the speaker Mike Johnson nonetheless insist that voters will expand rather than disband their majority in November. They note that 23 Democrats represent districts that voted for Trump in 2024, a number that has increased due to GOP-led states’ redistricting, while only eight Republicans represent districts that backed Kamala Harris. The party also believes that voters are still too disenchanted with Democrats overall to put them back in charge in the Capitol.
“Voters might not like Trump. They might not even like Republicans. But the polling shows that they hate Democrats even more,” a Republican strategist said on condition of anonymity.
In a statement, Julie Merz, the executive director of the House Democrats’ campaign arm, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, acknowledged the party’s fundraising struggles but said they were still on track for a return to power.
“We are confident we’re poised to win the majority, and that’s why Republicans in deep red territory are running scared,” Merz said. “If Democrats want to break the Republican gerrymanders in the south and get the largest majority possible, more resources ensure we can flip those seats too. We need more cash.”
Money isn’t everything, as Democrats know – Harris and her supporters outspent Trump and his allies in 2024, a year of resounding Democratic losses. And many of the factors that will decide the election outcome may already be baked into the result, said John T Woolley, co-director of the American Presidency Project at the University of California, Santa Barbara.
“Inflation, employment rates – they’re just not going to change a whole lot. So the kind of thing that’s left, the seats, those are fixed, [you] can’t change that stuff. So the only thing that’s left is the president’s approval,” Woolley said.
“What that means is the president has to shift swing voters, independent voters, voters who don’t identify as either Republican or Democrats.”
But that group, too, appears to have soured on the GOP: a New York Times and Siena University poll released last week found 57% of independent voters were planning to vote Democratic in the midterms, and just 34% for Republican candidates.

Gretchen Carlson on press under Trump: ‘It’s my hope journalists will start speaking up’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:00:45 UTC
19:00:45 KST

Donald Trump has achieved something rarely seen in Washington: uniting rival television networks against him. When he banned CNN and MS Now – along with Politico – from the White House, their competitors suspended shared coverage of the US president’s events.
Gretchen Carlson, a journalist, author and former Fox News host, hopes this will not be the only example of solidarity from a White House press corps facing what she describes as an “outright onslaught” from the administration.
In a phone interview with the Guardian before the media ban news, Carlson, 60, called on reporters to push back against Trump’s brazen misogyny, which has included calling female reporters “stupid”, “piggy”, “incompetent” and “a horrible person”.
“That’s highly offensive to any human being, much less journalists whose job it is to cover the president with respect and dignity,” said the co-founder of Lift Our Voices, a non-profit that aims to end the silencing of voices in the workplace. “To be called those kinds of names and still have to maintain your composure and do your job is something that no journalist should have to endure.”
She called for solidarity across the White House press corps in response to the president’s sexist insults.
“It’s my hope that other journalists will start speaking up when that happens and repeat the question that was asked, because it likely wasn’t a stupid question,” she says. “It was likely an appropriate question that many Americans want the answer to like, when will the Iran war end? My hope is that the questions will be asked until they are answered and that it’s not just from the one who’s attacked.”
Carlson also urges the media to take a more robust approach with Trump despite the risks of being barred in the future. “It’s also my hope that journalists will say: you can’t speak to people that way. Now, I’m not naive, I understand there’s a conundrum here for journalists, because this is all about access to the president of the United States and access to this administration. If you speak up and cross this president, he’ll come after you.
“But we have to find a happy medium here because the end result is allowing this to continue is the promulgation of misogyny in our society.”
One potential barrier to collective action is an influx of “Maga” media outlets, ever ready to ask the president favourable questions and unlikely to speak up on behalf of “mainstream media” colleagues. The president can call them at any moment to blunt the momentum of the questions coming his way.
Carlson acknowledges the point but responds: “There’s still plenty of other journalists who might. There is the White House Correspondents’ Association. They were able to plan a second dinner after the assassination attempt so they could certainly come together and decide that they’re going to have a certain reaction to those kinds of attacks.
“When you get attacked like that and another reporter just goes on to the next question, it makes it look like there’s nothing wrong and so if you’re watching this press conference, you normalise that then, and you’re like, oh, I guess that’s how we should treat everyone.
“It’s damaging to young men about how they can treat women and young women about how they feel they should be treated. We’ve been trying to raise up our young women for generations and we’re doing a great job of it and now, all of a sudden, you can just treat women like this and nobody says anything?”
As if channeling the 1960s-set TV drama Mad Men, Trump has repeatedly singled out Kaitlan Collins, the chief White House correspondent of CNN, complaining: “I don’t think I’ve ever seen a smile on your face.” Carlson notes it is not the kind of comment he would ever make to a man.
“Ask any woman on the street how many times have you been told in your life you need to smile more. Barf. I mean, really? We’ve all heard that before: put a smile on your face and just go out there and deal with it. No. That’s like, you go in to negotiate for higher pay, the man just asks for it, the woman has to put a smile on her face in order to get it. It is such an old school way of looking at the different gender types and the way in which we respond to a request if it’s by a man or a woman.”
Carlson rejects the implication that women in media should maintain a happy demeanour when asking tough questions about conflict, economic strife or foreign policy. “She’s not supposed to be smiling when she’s asking tough questions of the president of the United States.
“You’re not supposed to be smiling when you’re out as a journalist covering a triple murder or raging wildfire. There’s plenty going on in America right now where we don’t need to smile about it – high gas prices, high grocery prices, the Iran war, tariffs.
It is almost 10 years since Trump was first elected. It is also 10 years since Carlson sued Roger Ailes, then the chief executive and chairman of Fox News, for sexual harassment. In the following weeks more than 20 other women came forward with allegations that Ailes had abused them. The #MeToo movement, raising awareness of sexual misconduct by men, was in the ascendancy.
Despite the regression personified by Trump, Carlson sees evidence of progress in unexpected places – notably in the Capitol Hill campaign surrounding the disclosure of files relating to Jeffrey Epstein, who exploited and trafficked underage girls. The effort produced an unusual alignment between Democrats and Republicans, demonstrating that survivor advocacy can break through.
“It was an amazing bipartisan movement,” Carlson notes, citing Democrat Ro Khanna and Republicans Thomas Massie, Marjorie Taylor Greene, Lauren Boebert, and Nancy Mace.
For Carlson, the driver of this breakthrough is a fundamental shift in public opinion. A decade ago, she contends, victims of high-profile abuse were routinely dismissed or discredited. Today the baseline has changed.
“The most credit goes to the survivors because they keep pushing forward,” she says. “A lot of times people say to me that the #MeToo movement is in a downward spiral because we’re still not getting all the files released and people aren’t being held accountable. But I look at this as a leader in this movement and say we have to look at the progress.
“People actually believe the Epstein survivors now. Ten years ago, they would not have believed them. Every time they come to the Hill and hold a press conference, they take the power right back.”
Despite the rise of the “manosphere”, “trad wives” and a tsunami of online misogyny, Carlson rejects the narrative that the movement against workplace abuse has stalled or been defeated by reactionary cultural backlash.
“It’s very easy to say the #MeToo movement is dead when you look at all the negative stuff,” she admits. “I’m not naive enough to say that everything is perfect right now–it’s not. But movements ebb and flow. If you look at any major cultural movement, whether it was the civil rights movement or women getting the right to vote, these things did not happen overnight. There were many ups and downs.”
Carlson points to legislative milestones that have altered employment law across the US. Through Lift Our Voices, she spearheaded the passage of two pieces of federal legislation in 2022 that curtailed forced arbitration clauses, preventing corporations from hiding systemic abuse behind secret, binding proceedings.
“People ask me every single day: how did you do that?” Carlson reflects. “These are the kinds of things we have to focus on. Yes, there are blips along the way and hurdles to overcome, but we have to keep pushing forward. There have been laws passed, and state laws passed banning non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) completely for these types of things.”
Her focus remains the total elimination of contractual silencing mechanisms – such as non-disclosure agreements and non-disparagement clauses – that allow toxic workplace cultures to persist in secret.
Carlson insists that workplace safety and anti-silencing reform must remain strictly non-partisan. When high-profile misconduct allegations surfaced surrounding Democratic candidate Graham Platner in Maine, Carlson condemned attempts by some Democrats to shield their own candidates from accountability.
“There is no room for hypocrisy with regard to this kind of behaviour, and the American public is onto this,” she asserts. “The idea that you want to not call out this behaviour because it’s a Democratic candidate and you’re a Democrat is wrong – and the same thing on the flip side.”
At Lift Our Voices, the rule is evaluate the conduct, ignore the party label, she says. “We believe women and we take politics out of it. By the way, it’s been proven all across the board that politics has nothing to do with sexual harassment or sexual assault.
“Before somebody decides to do either of those to you, they don’t ask you what party you’re in. They don’t care. This is about power.”

SEOUL DESIGN AWARD OPENS LIVE EVALUATIONS AND GLOBAL VOTING
Chosen from over 1,200 submissions across 91 countries, the Seoul Design Award 2026 top 10 finalists showcase global projects driving sustainable daily living. Built to honor designs that support balance between people, society, and the environment, the competition elevates work tackling urgent social and ecological challenges. In a shift from traditional closed-door judging, the 2026 program brings the ten shortlisted teams to the Dongdaemun Design Plaza in Seoul on October 14 for on-stage evaluations.
Expanding public involvement in the selection process, the organization has officially launched its online global public voting phase, inviting audiences worldwide to cast their votes alongside the expert jury. The integration of real-time jury assessment with global public voting turns the award into an open, interactive exchange on the future of sustainable design.
Seoul Design Award and Conference 2026, Kampung Mrican Phase 1 revitalizes a dense riverfront community in Yogyakarta | all images courtesy of Seoul Design Award
NINE-MEMBER JURY LEADS ON-STAGE EVALUATIONS
Established as a key initiative within Seoul’s UNESCO Creative City of Design legacy, the award measures projects by their social utility and ecological impact rather than commercial gain. The top 10 live competition features a nine-member international jury on stage, including industry leaders Mauro Porcini (President & Chief Design Officer at Samsung Electronics), Sungwon Jee (CMO & Executive Vice President at Hyundai Motor Company), Andrea Cancellato (Director of ADI Design Museum), and Martin Zelger (CEO of DAAily platforms AG / designboom). In an expansion of this year’s program, three designboom Special Prize winners will be recognized, receiving dedicated editorial coverage to give both the projects and designers global visibility.
The announcement forms part of the broader Seoul Design Conference 2026: THINK · MAKE · CHANGE, a full-day event hosted at DDP exploring how creative fields respond to global shifts. Beyond the live competition, the conference features presentations from the inaugural ESG Design Impact Award recipients, including Hyundai Motor Company, Patagonia, athome, and RHINOSHIELD, focusing on corporate sustainability systems. A dedicated session co-hosted with the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) will examine policies and global frameworks for circularity in electronics.
Closing the event, Session 3 offers a first look at the World Design Congress Seoul 2027, culminating in a ceremony to unveil its official brand identity. Designed to reflect dynamic connectivity and circular thinking, the visual identity sets the direction for Seoul’s next chapter as a global design epicenter, showing how visual communication and strategic action can inspire long-term change.

SCALING MATERIAL INNOVATION FOR A CIRCULAR FUTURE
The top 10 finalists reflect a clear shift toward community-driven resilience and circular design systems. Focused on social impact, key projects support vulnerable populations and local action: Otter Newborn Warmer offers a portable conductive device to prevent neonatal hypothermia in low-resource healthcare settings, while WheeLog! functions as a crowdsourced accessibility platform that allows wheelchair users to map urban mobility barriers. In urban and cultural settings, Kampung Mrican Phase 1 applies targeted interventions to revitalize a dense riverfront village in Yogyakarta, Na-Eh Karen Cultural Market establishes a community-owned forest food hub celebrating Indigenous Karen identity, and Suber Design converts recycled cork into circular furniture produced by disadvantaged groups.
Suber Design turns recycled cork into circular furniture, merging material innovation with social inclusion
In parallel, industrial and material innovations among the finalists demonstrate how circularity scales across manufacturing, waste, and marine management. Lavazza Group’s Tablì redefines capsule coffee through a single-serve system using pure coffee without plastic or aluminum waste. Meanwhile, LAKAT Sustainable Sneakers transforms pineapple agricultural by-products and natural rubber into footwear. On a systemic scale, Process-Controlled Waste Sorting Rear Module | ET35 connects public recycling drop-offs directly to frontline sanitation operations, SMALLrevolution creates a closed-loop tracking mechanism that turns plastic waste into documented raw materials, and Reef Tiles by ReefCircular uses region-specific computational design to restore fragile marine ecosystems.

Scientists discover previously unknown “mitochondrial plaques” in Alzheimer’s disease brains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:00:15 UTC
19:00:15 KST

Scientists have identified a previously unrecognized feature of Alzheimer’s disease in the form of clustered, damaged cellular power plants within nerve fibers. These structures, dubbed “mitochondrial plaques,” appear to arise from a breakdown in the brain’s cellular waste disposal system. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that targeting these newly discovered plaques alongside traditional therapies might offer a more comprehensive approach to slowing cognitive decline.
Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive brain condition that causes memory loss and cognitive impairment. For years, therapies have largely targeted amyloid plaques, which are abnormal clumps of protein that accumulate outside brain cells. But these treatments only offer limited benefits, leading researchers to explore other cellular changes occurring in the disease.
One area of interest involves mitochondria, the tiny structures inside cells that generate energy. When mitochondria become damaged, cells rely on a recycling process called mitophagy to clear them out. During mitophagy, damaged mitochondria are delivered to lysosomes, which are acidic compartments that act as the cell’s waste disposal system.
If lysosomes fail to function correctly, cellular garbage can pile up. A 2026 preprint study indicated that these cellular waste-disposal compartments begin failing early in Alzheimer’s disease, even before classic amyloid plaques form. This early failure helps explain why damaged mitochondria might accumulate rather than being properly degraded.
In this new study, researchers set out to map exactly how and where this mitochondrial recycling goes wrong. “One of our earlier studies suggested that mitophagy, the process by which cells remove damaged mitochondria, may be impaired in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) brains,” Xiuli Dan, a research assistant professor in Paul Robbins’ lab at the University of Minnesota, told PsyPost.
“However, the evidence at that time was largely indirect,” Dan explained. “We were looking at changes in proteins involved in mitophagy and the accumulation of damaged mitochondria, but we did not yet have a way to directly measure mitophagy or determine which regions of the brain were most affected.”
The project to directly visualize mitochondrial degradation in specific brain regions spanned multiple research institutions. “This work was initiated in Dr. Bohr’s lab at NIH and completed at Dr. Robbins’ lab at UMN after I moved here,” Dan noted.
To explore these questions, the scientists used genetically modified mice designed to develop Alzheimer’s-like symptoms. These mice were also engineered to express a fluorescent tag in their mitochondria that glows green in neutral environments but shifts to red when placed in acidic lysosomes. This color-coding allowed the researchers to track exactly which mitochondria were being actively digested and which were simply floating in the cell.
“Using this model, we made an unexpected observation that acidic mitochondria accumulated prominently and specifically in AD mouse brains,” Dan said. “This unexpected finding motivated us to investigate these accumulations further, which ultimately led to our identification and characterization of mitochondrial plaques.”
The team examined brain slices from these mice at various ages using high-resolution microscopes. They also studied a second mouse model of Alzheimer’s disease and examined postmortem brain tissue from human Alzheimer’s patients to verify their findings.
The researchers observed large, abnormal accumulations of mitochondria in the cortex and hippocampus, regions of the brain important for memory. They named these massive clusters “mitochondrial plaques.” These structures were multilayered and much larger than typical mitochondrial recycling spots seen in healthy cells.
These mitochondrial plaques were found specifically within swollen, damaged sections of nerve fibers. Approximately 60 percent of the material inside a typical mitochondrial plaque was acidic, meaning it had been swallowed by lysosomes. The remaining portion consisted of mitochondria sitting in a neutral environment, waiting to be degraded.
Tracking the mice over time showed that mitochondrial plaques appear as early as 15 weeks of age, roughly the same time amyloid plaques begin to form. Initially, the brain tries to compensate by sending more lysosomes to break down the mitochondrial buildup. But the lysosomes in the Alzheimer’s models lacked the necessary acidity and enzymes to digest the waste, causing the mitochondria to pile up.
Over time, these mitochondrial clusters often grew into and merged with amyloid plaques, creating what the researchers described as mixed plaques. Around 60 percent of the local amyloid precursor protein was found trapped inside these mitochondrial clusters. However, the study indicates that mitochondrial plaques can also exist completely independently of amyloid plaques, especially in the early stages of the disease.
To confirm that this is not just a phenomenon unique to mice, the team examined postmortem hippocampal tissue from human Alzheimer’s patients and age-matched healthy controls. The human Alzheimer’s brains contained the same large, mitochondria-rich clusters tightly associated with lysosomes. This feature was entirely absent in the healthy brains.
“The major takeaway is that mitochondrial plaques, or MPs, are a previously unrecognized pathological structure in AD, composed largely of mitochondria that become trapped and are not properly degraded inside neurons,” Dan explained.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study heavily relied on mouse models and a simplified cell-culture system to track the timeline of mitochondrial buildup. These models provide a controlled way to observe brain changes over time, but they do not capture the full complexity of human Alzheimer’s disease.
There are a few things to keep in mind regarding the exact sequence of events. While the images and molecular tests suggest that mitochondrial accumulation happens first, followed by a failed lysosomal response, the study cannot definitively map the entire chain of causality. Other pathological features, such as tau protein tangles or chronic inflammation, might also play overlapping roles in disrupting the brain’s waste disposal systems.
“Importantly, our findings suggest that MP formation is not simply a problem of lysosomal degradation,” Dan said. “The process appears to begin with an abnormal accumulation of mitochondria, followed by impaired lysosomal processing and clearance.”
“We hope this provides a new way to think about mitochondrial pathology in AD and may eventually help identify new biomarkers or therapeutic targets,” she added.
Future research will need to explore whether treatments designed to boost lysosomal acidity and improve mitochondrial recycling can prevent the formation of these plaques. Addressing both amyloid plaques and mitochondrial plaques simultaneously could provide a more effective strategy for preserving brain function.
The study, “Mitochondrial accumulation and lysosomal dysfunction result in mitochondrial plaques in Alzheimer’s disease,” was authored by Xiuli Dan, Deborah L. Croteau, Wenlong Liu, Xixia Chu, Ross A. McDevitt, Paul D. Robbins, and Vilhelm A. Bohr.

Korean dating show featuring AI and human contestants sparks fascination in China
Some question if AI provides an almost perfect partner will people still be able to accept friends and family who have flaws
A South Korean dating reality show exploring human-AI romance has triggered curiosity and attention in China over how artificial intelligence could reshape people’s understanding of intimacy and love.
In August, Seoul Broadcasting System (SBS) launched My AI Partner: Strange Love, the country’s first dating reality show focused on human-AI relationships.
The programme follows three participants – a cartoonist, a television host and an actress – as they form emotional connections with AI companions tailored to their ideal types, from appearance and voice to personality.
Existing only on tablet screens, these AI companions retain memories of previous interactions and operate independently; the production team provides only technical support without intervening in their decisions.

You Actually Don’t Need to See That Movie in IMAX
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:00:08 UTC
19:00:08 KST

2026 has, without a doubt, been the year of IMAX. That’s due in large part to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, which broke countless box office and IMAX records after its release in mid-July. But it’s not just The Odyssey. Films like Project Hail Mary and the year’s biggest blockbuster, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, played in the format, and IMAX theaters will be full through the end of the year, thanks to the final installment in the Dune franchise. In August, lines formed around the block at the AMC theater in New York City’s Upper West Side as people waited to secure coveted tickets to see Dune: Part Three in IMAX 70mm—even though the movie doesn’t come out until mid-December.
But I would argue this fervor is misplaced. I would go so far as to say that IMAX is overrated.
This trend didn’t come out of nowhere: IMAX has been on the rise in the past few years, as post-pandemic audiences are increasingly drawn to movie theaters for spectacle and eventization that can’t be replicated at home. In 2025, moviegoers flocked to see films like Sinners, One Battle After Another, F1, and the final Mission: Impossible in IMAX. The gold standard for cinephiles is the ultra-rare IMAX 70mm screening, which requires a projector large enough to play the giant 70mm film reels (unlike standard IMAX screenings, which use digital projection). Only 26 theaters in the United States can project 70mm IMAX, and the competition to get tickets to films like The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three at those theaters has created a resale market that rivals popular sporting events and concerts.
IMAX’s popularity has been a boon for the box office and great for the movie industry, which has struggled to regain audiences after the COVID-19 pandemic. However, it’s also caused feelings of FOMO in those who aren’t able to secure tickets, or who don’t live near an IMAX theater (let alone the rare theater that can project IMAX 70mm). And many so-called IMAX theaters in the country are not actually true IMAX, meaning people paying extra for those screenings in “LieMAX” auditoriums aren’t even getting all the benefits of the format.
This summer, social media sites were flooded with people sharing photos and videos of their Odyssey viewing experiences, looking for advice on how to secure a coveted ticket, or searching for one to buy off of someone else. There was a pervasive feeling of: If I’m not seeing The Odyssey in IMAX, am I really seeing it at all?
While seeing a movie in IMAX is undoubtedly a great experience, it’s not necessary to enjoy a movie—or to be a true cinephile. At the end of the day, you’ll still get all of the intended narrative and emotional impact in a “regular” theater, even if you aren’t getting the full IMAX screen ratio. A 2014 study by psychologists Andreas M. Baranowski and Heiko Hecht compared sizes of screens with regard to viewer immersion and found that, while larger screens were more immersive, when participants were asked to evaluate the movie they had just seen, the screen size did not affect their answer.
Filmmakers understand this as well. Though they might prefer you to see their movie in IMAX, they ultimately shoot with all formats and audiences in mind, knowing that not everyone will see it in IMAX. (Some people will even watch it on the backside of a plane seat!) When framing shots—even on an IMAX camera—they keep anything essential to the narrative in the core ratio that most people will see the movie in.
Despite all the jokes about “watching a movie as Christopher Nolan intended,” in a recent interview with 60 Minutes, the director said he didn’t mind people watching his movies on iPads. “I’m very much in favor of and in awe of the easy access that we have now to films, for people to be able to immerse themselves in film and film history,” Nolan said in the interview, drawing a comparison to his childhood spent learning about film through VHS tapes.
In the 2020s, movie projection technology is the best it’s ever been. If IMAX isn’t your jam, or if you can’t secure tickets, there are plenty of alternative ways to see movies that are better than all of human history has ever had access to. Dolby is a great option, with its enhanced color and immersive sound, and 35mm and 70mm screenings are plentiful among theaters around the country if you prefer to get the film experience.
So, it doesn’t make you less of a cinephile if you can’t get to an IMAX screen (especially one that can show 70mm IMAX), or if you prefer to not view a movie in IMAX. For people with sensitivities to loud noises or bright lights, it may not be the best option.
There is a difference, but it isn’t enough to stop you from enjoying the film. I saw The Odyssey twice: once in IMAX 70mm, and once in 70mm on a “regular” screen, and enjoyed the non-IMAX experience much better, as it felt less visually and auditorily overwhelming. The same sentiment can be found on various subreddits devoted to moviegoing.
At the end of the day, no matter what theater you choose to view a film in, as long as you’re having fun and actively engaging with the work, you’re doing it right.

The Next Four Years Will Decide the Ocean’s Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:00:05 UTC
19:00:05 KST

This summer, the ocean sent us another warning. In August, global sea-surface temperatures reached their highest level on record. Days later, the most comprehensive assessment of coral reefs ever published showed that increasingly frequent marine heatwaves are leaving reefs less time to recover between bleaching events. Global hard coral cover has declined by 9.5% compared with the 1980-2009 average, driven primarily by human-induced climate change.
For me, this is deeply concerning, but also a reason to act. I come from Seychelles, an archipelago of 115 islands off the coast of East Africa where the ocean is inseparable from our lives, livelihoods, and future. It supports the food we eat, the jobs people depend on, and the resilience of our economy.
During my years in office, I saw what is possible when governments make ocean protection a political priority. In 2020, during my presidency, Seychelles designated 30% of its waters for protection, years before the world adopted the global goal of protecting 30% of land and ocean by 2030. That experience taught me that ambitious conservation is possible when political commitment is matched by action.
With fewer than four years remaining until 2030, the international community needs to bring that same determination to protecting the global ocean.
Since governments adopted the global goal in 2022, countries have made important progress. Nearly 20% of land and inland waters are now designated as protected or conserved, and existing commitments could bring terrestrial protection to around 27% by 2030.
But the picture at sea is very different. Around 10% of the global ocean is currently designated as protected or conserved, and existing commitments would raise that figure to only around 12% by 2030.
The next phase of this global effort must therefore put much greater emphasis on the ocean. Governments need to establish more marine protected areas, strengthen national commitments where ambition remains too low, and move rapidly from targets to protection in the water.
This matters far beyond conservation. Healthy marine ecosystems support fisheries and food security, sustain livelihoods and economies, store carbon, and help protect coastal communities from climate impacts.
The recent coral findings make the consequences of delay clear. Marine heatwaves are becoming more frequent, leaving reefs less time to recover. Recovery is still possible, but ecosystems need time and the right conditions to recover.
Climate action remains essential, but reducing pressures such as overfishing, pollution and damaging extraction can give vulnerable ecosystems a better chance of recovery. Well-designed and properly managed marine protected areas can give nature the space and time it needs.
But drawing a boundary on a map is not enough. The 2026 Ocean Protection Gap Report finds that while around 10% of the global ocean is designated as protected or conserved, just 3.5% is assessed as effectively protected. A protected area cannot fulfill its purpose if damaging activities continue, management is weak, or long-term finance is missing.
In Seychelles, we are confronting this challenge ourselves. Having designated more than 30% of our waters for protection, we are now undertaking the harder work of turning those protections into results in the water. Our Marine Spatial Plan Initiative is legally binding, including no-take areas where extractive activities are prohibited. But effective protection also requires management, monitoring, enforcement and long-term resources.
The next four years, through the end of 2030, must therefore be about both expansion and effectiveness. Success should be judged by area on a map, and by whether biodiversity recovers and communities continue to benefit from healthy ecosystems.
National action alone cannot close the ocean protection gap. The high seas account for roughly two-thirds of the global ocean, yet only a very small share is protected. Species migrate across borders, currents connect ecosystems, and damage in one part of the ocean can have consequences far beyond it.
The High Seas Treaty changes what is possible. For the first time, governments have a global legal framework capable of enabling marine protected areas beyond national jurisdiction. Seychelles became the first African country to ratify the treaty because island states understand that protecting our own waters is not enough. Our future also depends on the ocean we share.
Governments now need to turn this legal breakthrough into protection in the water by advancing an ambitious first generation of high seas marine protected areas, supported by strong science, effective governance, monitoring, and sufficient finance.
Ambition must also be matched by resources. The new assessments estimate that around $16 billion is needed each year for marine protection under the 30% target, compared with only around $1.8 billion currently spent. Without the resources to manage them, protected areas risk remaining protected on paper rather than in practice.
As leaders gather at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, ocean protection should be part of discussions about climate resilience, food security, and economic stability. COP17 next month in Armenia will soon provide another opportunity for governments to confront where progress is falling furthest behind.
In 2019, I spoke from beneath the Indian Ocean because I wanted world leaders to understand that we could not leave the environmental problems we have created for another generation to solve.
That warning is more urgent today. But there are also reasons for hope. Countries have shown that ambitious conservation is possible. This June, French Polynesia announced an expansion that will bring 1.4 million square kilometers—around 30% of its waters—under full protection from extractive industries once implemented. Samoa and Portugal have also made meaningful increases in effective protection over the past year.
We now understand more about what effective protection requires. And with the High Seas Treaty in force, we have a powerful new means of safeguarding the ocean we all share.
The years between now and 2030 must be a turning point for ocean protection. We need to protect more of the ocean, protect it well, and seize the opportunity of the High Seas Treaty. If we do, we will not only safeguard biodiversity, but strengthen food security, climate resilience, and livelihoods for generations to come.

Press review: Trump, Zelensky signal Russia deal interest as Moscow eyes fresh US dialogue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Trump and Zelensky seek a deal with Russia as Washington retains significant leverage over Kiev, Moscow sees scope for renewed dialogue with Washington amid a more pragmatic US approach to the UN, and Iran strengthens cooperation with Russia as its conflict with the US continues. These stories topped Wednesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Trump, Zelensky signal interest in Russia deal as US retains leverage over Kiev
Donald Trump and Vladimir Zelensky met in New York on September 22. The US president said Ukraine wanted to reach an agreement to resolve the conflict and raised the prospect of further direct contacts with Vladimir Putin. Kiev, meanwhile, hopes for increased military support despite another round of scandals stemming from high-profile investigations involving members of Zelensky’s inner circle. Corruption in Ukraine’s defense industry may be linked to the interests of Kiev’s Western sponsors, the Russian Foreign Ministry told Izvestia.
Following the public portion of the talks, the US president said he expected Russia and Ukraine to reach an agreement. According to Trump, he has repeatedly discussed possible terms of a settlement with Vladimir Putin, among others.
A possible halt to strikes on energy facilities was also among the topics discussed. The US president previously said that Russia and Ukraine had allegedly agreed to refrain from such attacks, although no official confirmation followed and the strikes continued.
The White House’s push for an energy ceasefire is driven not only by the president’s peacemaking ambitions but also by decidedly pragmatic considerations. Ahead of the US congressional elections, Trump wants to lower diesel prices, as voters are highly sensitive to rising fuel costs.
The United States still has considerable ability to influence Kiev’s position on a wide range of issues, according to Rodion Miroshnik, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s ambassador-at-large for crimes committed by the Kiev regime.
"The United States continues to sell enormous quantities of weapons and provide intelligence. It wields significant diplomatic weight on many issues, so if Trump has the desire to state his position on this and put pressure on Zelensky, he is entirely capable of doing so," he told Izvestia.
However, the upcoming exchange of views on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly is unlikely to produce results, former Ukrainian lawmaker Igor Markov believes. In his view, a single meeting in New York will not substantially change the situation as long as European countries continue to finance Kiev and support its current approach to the conflict.
Izvestia: Moscow sees potential for renewed US dialogue as Washington shifts to pragmatic UN policy
At their upcoming meeting in New York, Sergey Lavrov and Marco Rubio will discuss further cooperation at the UN, the Russian Foreign Ministry told Izvestia. Moscow and Washington have long struggled to find common ground on contentious issues at the organization. However, US policy at the UN has become more pragmatic since Trump took office, while raising the issue of cooperation at the UN to the ministerial level will give fresh impetus to Russian-US dialogue, the ministry stressed. A new round of talks on normalizing bilateral relations will take place in the near future. However, experts believe that a thaw in relations between the two countries should not be expected.
"During the upcoming meeting between Sergey Lavrov and Marco Rubio, issues concerning cooperation between the two countries at the United Nations will be among the topics discussed. As permanent members of its Security Council, Russia and the United States have enormous potential for developing cooperation. Unfortunately, it remains largely untapped," the Russian Foreign Ministry stressed.
The ministry also noted changes in US policy at the UN. "Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, Washington’s policy at the UN has taken on a more pragmatic character. Against this backdrop, our main disagreements are not with the Americans but with the Europeans, who continue to take radical and ideologically driven positions in line with the broader policy pursued by EU officials in Brussels," the ministry added.
However, experts see little prospect of a swift resolution to the crisis in bilateral relations. Ignatyev stressed that the new restrictions hinder improved relations and that this key irritant cannot be eliminated within the framework of the UN General Assembly. He was referring to the "sanctions from hell" package signed by Trump on September 18, which imposes secondary tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas. By threatening China, India, and Turkey with tariffs, Washington is seeking to force them to completely abandon Russian energy supplies.
New arms deliveries to Ukraine could become a key point of contention at the talks. According to Gleb Ignatyev, a lecturer at the School of Politics and Governance at the HSE University Faculty of Social Sciences, if Moscow raises the issue, the White House could theoretically halt the next stage of military assistance approved at the summer NATO summit.
Vedomosti: Iran sees deep mistrust of US as key obstacle to settlement while expanding ties with Russia
Iran has been under unprecedented US military and economic pressure for six months, since late February. It began with a decapitating strike against Iran’s military and political leadership and intensive US and Israeli bombardments, followed by a naval blockade. No lasting ceasefire has been achieved, and as a result, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has yet to resume, Iranian Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary Kazem Jalali said in an interview with Vedomosti.
Speaking about supplies of various products from Russia, including grain, amid the US-organized blockade, Jalali said the situation had helped strengthen economic ties between Moscow and Tehran. "This has helped develop economic cooperation and relations, and we cannot deny that. For several years now, we have been trying to import all necessary and essential products and goods through our northern neighbors, including Russia. We are making every possible effort to expand economic cooperation with Russia," he said.
"At the same time, the pressure our adversary is exerting on us by trying to draw our neighboring countries into the blockade may help and contribute to the development of both our countries - Russia and Iran," he said.
Jalali also discussed the previously announced construction of the Rasht-Astara railway as part of the North-South International Transport Corridor. "The North-South International Transport Corridor is one of our largest projects with Russia. We launched it in 2023. The volume of goods transported along it is growing every day. The second route is the Caspian Sea," he said.
Another major area of Russian-Iranian cooperation is nuclear energy, primarily the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant. "The second and third phases of the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant are currently being carried out [in addition to the first operating power unit, which entered commercial service in 2013]. We are working together on these projects, and the project is progressing," he said.
Jalali also addressed the prospects for a settlement with the United States. He attributed the failure of the previous attempt at reaching an agreement through Switzerland to Washington’s conduct during the negotiations. "The reason for the collapse of the previous agreements reached in June is, I think, obvious to everyone - the American side did not respect the negotiations. The Americans began to deceive us," he said. "All of this clearly shows why all these negotiations ended in failure. Thus, Iran’s wall of mistrust toward the US has, unfortunately, become very high," Jalali added.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Non-resource sectors gain share of Russian tax revenues
Over six years, revenues to Russia’s consolidated budget more than doubled, from 20.7 trillion rubles ($246.05 bln) to 45.4 trillion rubles ($539.64 bln), excluding the new regions, according to a study by the Analytical Credit Rating Agency (ACRA). The share of revenues generated by industries unrelated to mineral extraction is gradually growing. Experts told Rossiyskaya Gazeta they see signs of an emerging structural shift toward non-resource sectors but caution that it is not yet a sustainable trend, with its durability depending on continued growth, efficiency, and export potential in non-extractive industries.
Federal taxes and fees account for the bulk of revenues, or about 90%. Revenues under special tax regimes increased amid growth in the number of small and medium-sized businesses and self-employed individuals, although their share remained modest at 4% in 2025. Among individual taxes, personal income tax revenues showed steady growth amid an increase in the overall wage bill and the introduction of a progressive tax scale, the agency noted.
Three industries - mineral extraction, manufacturing, and trade - remain the main contributors to the budget, together generating more than half of revenues. In 2025, revenues from manufacturing increased by 15% and those from trade by 11%, while revenues from mineral extraction fell by 20%.
According to experts, it is too early to speak of a sustainable structural shift toward non-resource sectors. "It is still too early to describe the transition toward a non-resource model of tax revenues as an established trend - it is more of an emerging tendency, and its durability will depend on how sustainable growth proves to be within the non-extractive sectors themselves," deputy chairman of the Bureau for the Protection of Entrepreneurs’ Rights at the Moscow branch of OPORA Russia and head of the AIP Audit and Consulting Group Sergey Yelin told the newspaper.
Mikhail Khachaturyan, associate professor at the Department of Strategic and Innovative Development at the Financial University under the Russian Government, also noted that while the increase in the share of non-resource sectors has been substantial, it remains subject to fluctuations and could result in a return to the traditional situation in which extractive industries generate the bulk of revenues. At the same time, he said, the increase in the efficiency and export potential of non-resource sectors over the past six years is evident, pointing to structural changes that could make the economy more resilient to external shocks in the future.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Global diesel crisis drives up prices as Russia’s export ban shields domestic market
Diesel fuel shortages have been recorded in Europe, the United States, and some countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America, while diesel prices have risen worldwide. Russia has not been spared from the increase, with prices at gas stations rising 23% over the past year. Despite the ban on diesel exports, Russia remains part of the global market. Experts told Nezavisimaya Gazeta Russia’s diesel export ban has taken about 10% of supply off the global market and helped shield domestic consumers from surging global prices, but it is also weighing on refining margins and oil production.
The crisis stems from a shortage of diesel supply directly linked to geopolitics. Global refining capacity was already barely sufficient before this year, but the Middle East conflict has taken local oil refineries offline, halted petroleum product exports from the Persian Gulf, and reduced the supply of crude oil to refineries in other countries. Less oil means less finished fuel. More diesel is exported and imported worldwide than gasoline, at a ratio of approximately 60 to 40. Russia’s ban on diesel exports has also had an impact. Yury Stankevich, deputy chairman of the State Duma Committee on Energy, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta that the reduction in Russian diesel exports has effectively removed roughly 10% of global supply from the market.
The situation in Russia is different. As noted above, the country has completely banned diesel exports since the beginning of August, with the restriction currently in place through the end of September. The measure was prompted by unscheduled refinery repairs following UAV attacks, which reduced fuel production. Russia had been producing 40% more diesel than it consumed, and the ban effectively guaranteed sufficient supplies for the domestic market while putting downward pressure on prices, which did indeed decline slightly in September, Rossiyskaya Gazeta writes.
Sergey Tereshkin, CEO of Open Oil Market, told the newspaper that the diesel export ban cuts refining margins while also constraining oil production. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), Russian oil production fell to 8.36 mln barrels per day in August 2026 from 8.56 mln barrels per day a month earlier. The expert believes that the fundamental conditions for lifting the ban are already in place.
