EC on 'SIR split' row: Poll Panel says 'queries' raised by commissioners 'part of standard practice'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:48:59 UTC
18:48:59 KST

EC negates report of differences in commission over SIR
NEW DELHI: The Election Commission on Wednesday conceded that “operational queries or inputs” were raised by election commissioners S S Sandhu and Vivek Joshi on matters including the special intensive revision (SIR) exercise, but insisted that these pertained to the draft stage and were “part of standard administrative practice aimed at safeguarding voter rights”.Claiming that the “suggestions" given by the commissioners were for further improving the electoral process and part of a decision-making process before a final decision, the EC stressed that differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution, "Not only the three commissioners, but every officer of the commission is fully authorised to give his suggestions...for improving the electoral system,” EC said in a statement put out following news reports in a section of the media, alleging that the two elections commissioners had raised written objections 14 times in 10 months, to steps taken by the commission, and even written separately to Cabinet secretary against “gradual centralisation of the electoral roll database"."Highlighting certain specific internal notes/observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives give only one part of the picture. In recent months, the Commission has taken numerous decisions, issued instructions, introduced around 40 new initiatives and undertaken many electoral reforms including the conduct of electoral roll revision (including SIR) across the country.
All these decisions are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full Commission in the past one year,” the commission stated.The statement reiterated that EC, a constitutional body functioning under the strict mandate of Article 324 of the Constitution, statutory roles and established institutional conventions, operates as a multi-member constitutional body, "Written notes, observations, technical suggestions and internal checks-and-balances are standard, ongoing practices designed to ensure complete transparency, legal compliance and operational rigour,” it noted.The commission said all official orders, decisions and administrative directions issued by the Commission carry full legal sanction and follow established statutory procedures under The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023."The Commission has recently successfully conducted major elections of Bihar, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Assam and West Bengal and election-related exercises during this period. This work involved wide-ranging administrative and operational machinery and many Commission approvals and instruction,” it was stated.On the commissioners’ alleged objection to centralisation of the electoral roll database or ERONet/ECINet, with restricted access to electoral registration officers (EROs) who are authorised under the Representation of the People Act to decide on addition of deletion of names in the electoral roll, the Commission said digital platforms such as ECINet operate under strict data security protocols to prevent unauthorised tampering, manipulation, etc.
"IT security checks and audit controls are standard cybersecurity measures implemented across national databases. Statutory authorities, including EROs and district election officers (DEOs), function as per statutory powers for registration and deletion under law,” said EC.The poll body signed off saying that it “remains fully committed to executing its constitutional duties with complete integrity, recognizing its vital role in advancing our democracy”.

United Kingdom announces action on disinformation and global AI standards
The United Kingdom will fight disinformation at home and abroad, and work to ensure global safety standards for artificial intelligence (AI), new Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday evening in his first address to the United Nations General Assembly.
Mr. Burnham said recent years have seen “an industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment” in both the UK and many of its allies.
He told world leaders that “Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fears”, including through the use of bots, fake websites and falsified news articles.
Election interference, AI threat
“They’ve amplified far right narratives. And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 General Election,” he alleged. “We also know that they have tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of horrific events.”
False information shared online helped to spark riots following the fatal stabbing of three young girls at a dance class in the town of Southport in July 2024.
Mr. Burnham maintained that the Kremlin spends roughly $1.7 billion “on manipulating information”, noting that British companies and institutions have also suffered cyber-attacks.
“And we know that AI will multiply the threat,” he added.
Fighting disinformation, shoring up security
The Prime Minister said the UK will establish a new National Centre for Information Defence that will detect, attribute and disrupt information attacks while supporting and defending its democracy.
The UK will also use its experience to help other countries, having assisted Moldova with protecting elections against alleged Russian interference.
“As more elections approach across Europe, more nations are grappling with these issues – some for the first time,” he said.
“So, we’re ready to share our understanding of how these actors work, and how we can respond – because this is vital for our collective security and resilience.”
UK-US partnership on AI
On artificial intelligence, Mr. Burnham described Frontier AI – the cutting edge of the technology – as “one of the most significant challenges and opportunities of our age”.
He announced that the UK is developing a new AI defence partnership with the United States to protect critical national infrastructure.
Support for global AI principles
He stressed that fundamental decisions on AI “are too important to be left to chance” and “must be taken by elected governments who serve working people.”
In this regard, the UK will bring the right people together to deliver on the potential of AI for good while also dealing with the risks.
“And we will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness – and to ensure that AI development is safe,” he said.
The UN continues to uphold that the best way to address AI risks is to bring countries together to adopt shared principles and commitments on AI governance.

The Organization Fighting Ebola Has Never Been More Worried
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

Ebola hasn’t gone away. In fact, the ongoing outbreak in Africa is among the most concerning epidemics the organization trying to tame it has ever seen.
“Other than Covid, which affected the whole world, this is the thing that has frightened me the most,” says Nicole Lurie, who has worked for Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations since 2017 and now serves as executive director for preparedness and response and the US director.
More than 7,000 people have contracted the Bundibugyo Ebola virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo since May, around half of whom have died, according to government data compiled by the World Health Organization.
“This is the most rapidly growing Ebola outbreak that we’ve seen. It’s probably on pace to be the worst the world has ever seen,” Lurie tells WIRED, “and it’s quite terrifying.”
While health officials were able to end the outbreak in Uganda through contact tracing, isolation, and clinical care, instability in the DRC means cases continue to climb. Millions of people have been displaced by ongoing violence, which has made contact tracing a “struggle,” according to Lurie. Matters have only been made harder by a distrust of outside humanitarian workers, which has made isolating and treating cases difficult. Locals have attacked Red Cross volunteers, destroyed medical equipment including ambulances, and delayed safe burial teams.
“I don’t think we’re going to be able to bring this to an end without a vaccine,” Lurie says.
Shortly after the first Bundibugyo cases were reported in May, nonprofit CEPI redirected $100 million of internal funding to develop a vaccine. That money helped fund scientists at the Serum Institute of India to manufacture doses of Oxford University’s ChAdOx1 BDBV vaccine at record speed. That and Moderna’s vaccine candidate, also supported by CEPI, have entered safety trials, with efficacy trials expected to start this month.
Though CEPI sees a vaccine as key to ending the epidemic, it’s likely that any trials, which require contact tracing, will still face challenges in the communities. "The thing that worries me is vaccine distrust and mistrust,” says vaccinology and immunology professor Teresa Lambe, who is the lead scientific investigator in the Oxford safety trials. “And even if we get vaccines that are fabulous, will they be used?”
She had been working on a hantavirus vaccine in May following the cruise ship outbreak when her phone lit up with a message from a former WHO employee about Ebola that made her swear out loud. She knew the instability in the DRC could make any Ebola outbreak escape control very rapidly, so she pivoted and kick-started her vaccine drive with philanthropic funding even before CEPI set up support.
"Covid was in some ways easier,” reflects Lambe, who says she hasn’t taken a day off since May. “We're not in a lockdown, we're not in a situation where people even know or care about what's going on in the DRC … You're not all pulling in the same direction because day-to-day life continues.”
Global responder organizations have been short of staff since the US withdrew from the World Health Organization and dismantled USAID at the start of President Donald Trump’s second term. His administration’s cuts to foreign aid have also left responders facing a shortage in basic medical equipment like masks, hand sanitizers, and testing gear.
The US State Department didn’t respond to a request for comment.
“CDC teams and partners are strengthening preparedness in the region by supporting surveillance, contact tracing, laboratory diagnostics, infection prevention and control, border health activities, community engagement, and other outbreak containment efforts in coordination with the governments of the DRC, Uganda, and other partners,” Emily Hillard, press secretary for the Department of Health and Human Services, writes in an email. She adds that in the US, the agency is helping provide “enhanced travel screening, clinical and public health guidance, laboratory readiness, and coordination with state and local health departments.”
While the US government committed $50 million to support CEPI’s work on countermeasures against the Bundibugyo outbreak in June, Lurie says that the group will run out of funds for its Ebola program by December unless it can raise more money. She adds that all governments need to play a role in supporting the work.
CEPI was set up in 2017 with funding from several governments and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation after the most widespread Ebola outbreak ever showed a need to stimulate and accelerate vaccine development for epidemics. By the time a vaccine had been developed and used to stem the 2014 to 2016 West Africa epidemic, more than 11,000 people had died. (This many months in, that outbreak had a little over 1,000 cases.)
Lurie was working in the Obama administration as assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the US Department of Health and Human Services during the West Africa Ebola epidemic. She recalls the “amazing amount of panic, and the phenomenal cost of what was required” to treat the 11 cases reported in the US. “I don’t think anybody really wants to go through that again.”

Water used to put out waste plant fire contaminated with PFAS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:43:07 UTC
18:43:07 KST

Water used to put out waste plant fire contaminated with PFAS
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Firefighters used water contaminated with PFAS chemicals to put out a blaze at a waste processing plant in Gelderland that was operating illegally.
Aalden municipal council said the water would have to be pumped out of the sewage network to prevent it polluting drinking water supplies, because the purification system is not able to filter it out.
The blaze in Dinxperlo, a village on the German border, burned for several hours on Monday night after a large pile of wood chippings caught fire, covering an area of 20m by 30m at its height.
Firefighters pumped water from Het Blauwe Meer, a nearby recreational lake that has been closed to swimmers since 2024 because of high levels of PFAS. Most of the water subsequently drained away into the sewage system.
The council said it was investigating the impact, but there was no reason to avoid drinking tap water. “At the moment there are no consequences for the use of the sewage network by residents,” a spokesman said.
Police are also investigating the fire. The waste processing plant was shut down in November 2025 on the orders of the council for “serious breaches of environmental regulations.”
No permits
The operators burned large quantities of waste that they did not have permits for and mixed different types of waste that should have been separated, the council found.
Recent studies found that high levels of PFAS are present in Dutch drinking water supplies, particularly in western areas where the water is taken from rivers that have been contaminated by agricultural use.
PFAS chemicals are widely used in pesticides, packaging and products ranging from waterproof clothing to non-stick cooking pans.
They are known as “forever chemicals” because of their high durability, but have also been linked to illnesses such as cancer, diseases of the immune system and complications in unborn babies.
The public health agency RIVM has called for a total ban on PFAS in pesticides by the EU, a move also supported in Germany and the Scandinavian nations.

Xinhua Commentary: A pivotal moment for stable China-U.S. relations
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:41:42 CST
18:41:42 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- China-U.S. relations are once again approaching a pivotal moment that has drawn keen global attention, as Chinese President Xi Jinping travels to the United States at the invitation of U.S. President Donald Trump.
Xi's state visit comes just months after Trump's China trip in May. The exchange of visits between the two heads of state within six months is of historic and milestone significance.
It would be unrealistic to expect a single meeting to resolve all the problems in China-U.S. relations, but the upcoming Xi-Trump summit itself is a key step forward, providing both sides with a crucial opportunity to make 2026 a historic year that opens a new chapter in China-U.S. relations.
During their last meeting in May, the two heads of state agreed to build a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability. The consensus charts a clear course for bilateral ties at a time when the two major countries in the world are seeking a right way for them to get along.
This time, the two sides can build on that vital mutual understanding and steer the giant ship of China-U.S. ties toward a steady course in the years ahead.
Despite Washington's protectionist trade policy against China in recent years, economic and trade cooperation remains a major pillar for the development of the relationship between the world's top two economies.
At present, more than 7,000 Chinese enterprises operate in the United States, and U.S. companies have established more than 84,000 enterprises in China. Two-way trade and investment have provided strong support for millions of jobs in the United States.
Even as some U.S. politicians clamor for "decoupling from China," a survey of its members conducted this year by the U.S.-China Business Council found that 95 percent of U.S. respondents described their China operations as "somewhat to very important" to maintaining global competitiveness. The presence of prominent business leaders in Trump's delegation on his May trip to China likewise spoke volumes about their eagerness to seize the opportunities created by China's development.
Differences and frictions are inevitable between two major economies, but they can be addressed through consultations on an equal footing. Since 2025, China and the United States have held multiple rounds of economic and trade talks. Through dialogue based on equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit, the two sides have made progress in stabilizing economic and trade relations.
The lesson is hard to ignore: both sides have far more to gain by looking at the bigger picture and keeping their long-term interests in view. Turning trade and economic ties into instruments of political or security maneuvering does not make either side safer or stronger; it merely fractures supply chains, distorts markets and ultimately drives up costs for businesses and consumers.
Moreover, keeping dialogue open and expanding practical cooperation, by contrast, can provide greater certainty for the two economies and the wider global community.
A more stable China-U.S. relationship does not mean the absence of competition. When competition does happen, it must be a healthy one where both sides learn from each other, pursue excellence together, and compete fairly in compliance with rules.
Apart from managing their competition, Washington needs to join Beijing in adhering to another fundamental principle to prevent the giant ship of China-U.S. relations from capsizing: respecting each other's core interests and major concerns, particularly the Taiwan question, the most important issue in China-U.S. relations.
Safeguarding peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait is the biggest common denominator between China and the United States. If the Taiwan question is handled properly, the bilateral relationship will enjoy overall stability. Otherwise, the two countries will have clashes and even conflicts, putting the entire relationship in great jeopardy.
Washington must match its stated commitment to the one-China policy with concrete actions, and respect Beijing's four red lines concerning the Taiwan question, democracy and human rights, China's path and system, and China's development right.
China, as it pursues national rejuvenation, will never seek hegemony, nor will it give up its legitimate rights and interests. No one should expect China to accept outcomes that come at the expense of its own interests.
A stable China-U.S. relationship also rests on strong ties between the two peoples. It underscores the need for stronger people-to-people exchanges between the two countries.
In 2023 in San Francisco, Xi proposed inviting 50,000 young Americans to China over five years for exchange and study. The target has been reached this year ahead of schedule.
The recent reunion in China of retired American teacher Ronald Sakolsky and his Chinese friend Yin Yuzhen rekindled their friendship and renewed a shared commitment to planting trees and combating desertification. This is just one of countless examples showing that friendship and cooperation between China and the United States remain the shared aspiration of the two peoples.
Looking back, the history of China-U.S. relations is replete with examples of the two countries working together in the face of common challenges.
From jointly fighting terrorism, responding to the global financial crisis, combating Ebola to addressing climate change, China and the United States have repeatedly shown that coordination and cooperation between the two countries can serve both their own interests and those of the wider world.
For China and the United States, keeping the world's most important bilateral relationship on a steady course is more about themselves: it is about whether the two major countries can work together to bring greater stability and hope to a turbulent world. ■

Economic Watch: Panda bond surge signals China's onshore market appeal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:41:37 CST
18:41:37 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Panda bond issuance in China has recorded rapid expansion so far this year, as lower financing costs and a steadily opening onshore market draw growing interest from global issuers.
As of Sept. 17, the issuance of the Chinese currency renminbi-denominated debt securities has surpassed 240 billion yuan (about 35.6 billion U.S. dollars) across 135 issues, up 81 percent and 65 percent, respectively, from a year earlier, according to Shanghai-based data provider Wind Information.
KEY PLAYERS DIVE IN
Such bonds are issued in China's onshore market by overseas entities such as sovereign governments, international financial institutions and multinational companies, with principal and interest paid in renminbi.
This year, a growing number of sovereign issuers have driven growth in panda bond issuance. Slovenia, Pakistan, Kazakhstan and Indonesia issued the bonds for the first time this year, while Brazil is expected to become the first Latin American sovereign issuer.
Foreign financial institutions have also joined the wave. Deutsche Bank has issued 9 billion yuan of panda bonds so far this year, while BNP Paribas issued twice this year, raising 11 billion yuan.
In August, UBS Group issued a 2-billion-yuan, five-year panda bond with a coupon rate of 1.78 percent, the first by a Swiss financial institution, drawing subscriptions tripling the offer size.
According to UBS, the transaction comes amid continued growth in China's panda bond market.
Accessing China's deep and increasingly sophisticated onshore bond market further diversified UBS's funding sources and enhanced the efficiency and flexibility of its overall funding profile, said Chris Chadie, UBS' head of issuance and funding strategy.
Other institutions, such as the New Development Bank, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and Asian Development Bank, have also used panda bonds for financing this year, regarding China's onshore bond market as stable and persistently attractive amid global market volatility.
LOWER COSTS, SOUND RETURNS, EASED POLICIES
Lower renminbi financing costs served as the main reason for the record-high panda bond issuance this year.
According to Zhang Jun, chief economist at China Galaxy Securities, major foreign banks issue panda bonds at rates of roughly 1.7 percent to 2.2 percent, while borrowing the same amount in the U.S. dollar market costs 4.5 percent to 5.5 percent.
Zhang noted that in recent years, China has continued to improve the registration and issuance mechanism for panda bonds, relaxed relevant rules on the management of proceeds, and clarified that proceeds can be remitted abroad for use.
"This makes fund use more flexible and strengthens overseas institutions' confidence in the steady development of the panda bond market," Zhang explained.
To date, cumulative panda bond issuance has exceeded 1.3 trillion yuan, with issuers spanning 26 countries and regions across the world. The People's Bank of China (PBOC), China's central bank, said it will support more eligible overseas entities in issuing such bonds.
The international institutions' panda bond issuance demonstrated their recognition of China's institutional environment, development prospects and the renminbi, said Zou Lan, PBOC's deputy governor.
Panda bonds, while helping expand global investors' channels for allocating renminbi assets, also foster a sustainable ecosystem for renminbi use, Zou noted.
Buyers have also shown strong interest in panda bonds because of their safety and stable returns, with subscriptions for some issues reaching more than five times their issuance size.
"Panda bonds have gained broad recognition among domestic investors, while overseas institutional investors, thanks to their better understanding of issuers, also regard panda bonds as a major investment and trading instrument," Zou said.
RMB INTERNATIONALIZATION
Analysts say the booming panda bond market is also creating a positive interplay with the yuan's internationalization.
Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank, noted that more companies are beginning to include the renminbi in global treasury management and use it for cross-border settlement, investment projects and other purposes.
This helps foster sustainable cross-border circulation of the renminbi and supports the long-term, steady progress in its internationalization, he said.
Zhang noted that with easier overseas participation in panda bond issuance and trading and steady renminbi internationalization, such bonds are expected to achieve new breakthroughs in scale, innovation, and investor breadth, injecting lasting momentum into China's high-level financial opening-up. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- China drew 0-0 with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in the final round of the men's football group stage at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Wednesday, finishing top of the group with five points to advance to the quarterfinals.
Going into the final round, China and Iran had four points apiece from one win and one draw, while DPRK and the UAE had one point each from one draw and one loss. All four teams are open for chances of advancing or being eliminated.
With a draw enough to secure qualification, China head coach Antonio Puche kept the same starting lineup and 5-3-2 formation used in the first two matches, with the team looking to launch counterattacks while maintaining a solid defense.
The first half was marked by intense physical contests and frequent stoppages for fouls, but neither side managed to create a clear scoring opportunity.
In the 51st minute, Zhang Yuning broke into the penalty area before shooting from a tight angle, with the ball narrowly missing the post. It was China's best chance of the whole match.
Two minutes later, players from both sides got involved in a heated confrontation. The referee showed yellow cards to Wang Yudong and Mansour Almenhali at the same time. As it was Wang's second yellow card of the tournament, he will miss the next match.
Needing a win to keep their qualification hopes alive, the UAE stepped up the pressure in the closing stages. In the 57th minute, it found the net on a quick counterattack, but the goal was ruled out for offside.
In the 78th minute, the UAE took a short corner, with Leonard Ameismeuku heading toward the far corner, only for goalkeeper Li Hao to make a superb save. The UAE failed to create any further clear chances, and the score remained 0-0 until the final whistle.
In the other group match played simultaneously, DPRK came from behind to beat Iran 4-1. China finished top with five points, while DPRK and Iran both had four points, with DPRK advancing in second place on head-to-head advantage. The UAE finished bottom with two points.
Puche said he had not paid attention to the result of the other match, instead focusing on his own team during the match.
"This group has been extremely difficult. Every match has been very tough, and today was not different. But our players were outstanding. They kept fighting. I don't know what words I can use to praise my players, but I am really proud, extremely proud," said the Spanish.
China will face the second-placed team from Group A, either Japan or Thailand, in the quarterfinals on Saturday.
"We will watch the match between Japan and Thailand. I won't be too concerned about who our opponent will be, but will focus more on our own situation. Whoever the opponent is, whoever comes, we will face them together," said Puche. ■

Asia's longest cave yields record 61 giant panda fossils
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:41:11 CST
18:41:11 KST

GUIYANG, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Fossilized remains of 61 individual giant pandas have been discovered in Shuanghe Cave, Asia's longest cave, in Suiyang County, southwest China's Guizhou Province, making it the site with the largest number of giant panda fossils in the world, according to findings released Wednesday at a press conference on the results of the 25th international cave scientific expedition.
The latest expedition added nine fossilized giant panda individuals to the total, with most specimens unearthed from newly discovered cave passage.
Two sites bearing giant panda claw marks were also discovered, said Wang Deyuan, an associate research fellow at the Guizhou Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Resources.
Wang said the pandas apparently entered the cave, moved more than ten meters inward and then fell into a vertical shaft. They did not die immediately after the fall and left claw marks as they tried to move. Eventually, they fell into a deeper shaft and became trapped, where they ultimately died.
The expedition also uncovered fossils of ancient animals including takin, rhinoceros and stegodon. Among them, fossils of a giant tapir and a clouded leopard were found in Shuanghe Cave for the first time, and the unearthed skeleton of a juvenile giant tapir is one of the most complete such remains preserved in China.
Zhou Wenlong, deputy director of the institute, said that since the late 1980s, 25 international joint scientific expeditions have been carried out at Shuanghe Cave. The explored length of the cave system now totals 481.5 kilometers, up 41.8 kilometers from the previous expedition, with a vertical depth of 912 meters and 124 connected entrances, making it the world's third longest and Asia's longest cave. ■

====================================================================================================

Alcohol labels often omit health risks: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:40:59 CST
18:40:59 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Alcohol companies are more than twice as likely to tell consumers to "drink responsibly" than to warn them about health risks, with current voluntary alcohol warnings largely hidden, uninformative and ineffective, an Australian study has found.
The study analyzed more than 6,000 alcohol labels across three major Australian retailers, examining the type and placement of voluntary health warnings and messages, according to a statement released Wednesday by the Public Health Association of Australia.
It found only 25 percent of products carried a voluntary health warning, with 99 percent of those advising specific groups, including minors, pregnant women and drivers, not to drink.
The findings, published in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Public Health, showed that 65 percent of products carried responsible consumption messages without providing information about health harms, such as alcohol's links to at least seven types of cancer and liver disease.
Health warnings or messages were almost always hidden from view on the back or bottom of packages, according to the study led by Australia's George Institute for Global Health.
Lead author Asad Yusoff from the George Institute said current lax alcohol labeling rules allowed alcohol companies to "feign corporate responsibility while keeping consumers in the dark about the real health harms of drinking."
The findings come after an Australian parliamentary committee last week recommended mandatory regulation of alcohol advertising and marketing. ■

China forum on international rule of law calls for fairer global governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:40:50 CST
18:40:50 KST

SHENZHEN, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The China Forum on International Legal Cooperation (2026) concluded in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Wednesday, with participants calling for practical and efficient international rule-of-law cooperation to help build a fairer and more equitable global governance system.
Hosted by the China Law Society (CLS), the forum brought together legal professionals from 38 countries and seven international organizations. Participants held high-level dialogues on global rule of law in the digital age, legal safeguards for high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, and legal education and legal talent cultivation.
Wang Hongxiang, Party secretary and executive vice president of the CLS, said that as major global changes accelerate, peace, development, security and governance deficits are intertwined.
He called for sustained efforts to deepen international rule-of-law exchanges and cooperation through mutual learning among legal civilizations, collaborative research on legal theory, and joint cultivation of legal talent, so as to promote a fairer and more equitable global governance system.
On digital rule of law, Luis de Arcos Pérez, head of the International Relations Service of the Spanish General Council for the Judiciary, said AI can serve as a tool for judges, but judges must not become subordinate to AI. Technology can improve efficiency and assist judicial work, but human beings must make decisions on facts, legal interpretation, and citizens' rights independently and responsibly, he said.
A white paper on Shenzhen's use of artificial intelligence in judicial applications was released on Wednesday, showcasing Shenzhen's exploration of AI-assisted adjudication.
On legal safeguards for high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, Samar Khamlichi, a professor at Morocco's Mohammed V University, said high-quality investment should be judged not only by the level of investor protection, but also by whether institutional and legal frameworks can incentivize investment to generate sustainable development benefits. These include quality job creation, improved worker skills, technology and knowledge transfer, support for local suppliers, participation of domestic enterprises, industrial upgrading and greater domestic value creation.
On legal education and talent cultivation, Kamalinne Pinitpuvadol, secretary-general of the Asian-African Legal Consultative Organization (AALCO), proposed five practical measures: establishing a regular training program for young international lawyers from Asia and Africa, building an international mentoring network, forming multinational young legal research teams, ensuring training programs produce practical outcomes, and setting up a China-AALCO alumni and professional network. ■

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:40:49 CST
18:40:49 KST

VIENTIANE, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Asian Development Bank (ADB) forecasts Laos' economy will grow by 4 percent in 2026, rising to 4.5 percent in 2027, as easing inflation and greater exchange-rate stability help restore confidence and support economic activity.
Despite projected economic growth, Laos remains vulnerable to external shocks, including higher global fuel and import costs, weaker external demand, limited fiscal and monetary policy space, and continued debt repayment pressures, according to the ADB's latest Asian Development Outlook (ADO), Socio-Economic News reported on Wednesday.
ADB Country Director for Laos Shanny Campbell said the country has made significant progress in restoring macroeconomic stability, with easing inflation and a more stable exchange rate supporting economic activity.
She said maintaining prudent macroeconomic policies, improving trade facilitation, diversifying exports, and integrating climate resilience into development planning will be important to sustaining an inclusive and resilient recovery.
The services sector remains a key driver of growth. International tourist arrivals reached 2.6 million in the first half of 2026, up 9.9 percent from the same period last year.
The industrial sector is also expected to support growth, driven by investment in renewable energy, construction and mining, as well as electricity exports. Meanwhile, the agricultural sector is projected to contribute less.
Both agriculture and industry, however, face growing climate-related risks, including floods, droughts and erratic rainfall. These could affect agricultural production and future hydropower generation.
ADB also forecasts average inflation to ease from 8 percent in 2026 to 6.5 percent in 2027. ■

Unknown Publisher

MANILA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Philippine Senate impeachment court on Wednesday voted to overturn its July ruling that required at least 16 senators' votes to convict Vice President Sara Duterte, a move seen as lowering the vote threshold for her impeachment conviction.
Under the newly adopted rule, the basis for conviction votes shall only cover senators who remain legally and factually capable of taking part in the impeachment proceedings at the time of voting. The Philippines has 24 senators, four of whom are currently unable to perform their duties due to detention, unknown whereabouts or medical leave abroad.
Under the Philippine Constitution, if two-thirds or more of the senators vote in favor of the impeachment, Sara will be convicted, removed from office, and barred from holding public office for life.
Thirteen senators voted in favor of the rule change and one voted against, with six senator-judges not participating. Sara's legal team on Wednesday said it is not discounting the possibility of bringing the issue of the conviction threshold before the Supreme Court.
The Philippine Senate in July commenced the impeachment trial against Sara. The articles of impeachment accused her of corruption, assassination plots and patterns of abuse, among others. Sara has denied these allegations. ■

Asian Games | China holds off Japan for third straight men's gymnastics team gold
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:40:48 CST
18:40:48 KST

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- China defended its men's team title in gymnastics at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Wednesday, claiming a third straight championship in the event.
The Chinese team of Zhang Boheng, Lan Xingyu, Zou Jingyuan, Sun Wei and Tian Hao won the title with 255.095 points, followed by Japan with 253.826 for silver and Chinese Taipei with 239.896 for bronze.
It was China's second gold medal here in gymnastics, following Zhang's men's all-around title on Monday.
The gap stayed tight in the opening floor exercise, where Japan's Tokyo Olympic all-around champion Daiki Hashimoto topped the field with 14.000, followed by China's Tian Hao with 13.966.
On pommel horse, Paris Olympic all-around champion Shinnosuke Oka, first up for Japan, fell off the apparatus and managed just 12.533. Hashimoto followed with a strong 14.466, but three solid routines from the Chinese trio kept China narrowly ahead on aggregate.
The crowd's excitement peaked during a scintillating rings battle between China and Japan, with neither side landing a dismount error as the two teams swept the top six spots. China's Lan Xingyu posted the event's top score of 15.200 - a 6.0 difficulty, 9.100 execution and 0.1 bonus - ahead of Japan's Kiichi Kaneta on 14.900.
On vault, Oka was the only gymnast among the competitors from the two teams to suffer a major error, while Hashimoto and Asian Games all-around champion Zhang both delivered strong routines, tying at 14.733 (Hashimoto later made a successful inquiry to add 0.1 points).
Zou Jingyuan, the Paris Olympic and four-time world champion on parallel bars, was in dominant form on the apparatus, scoring 15.400 on a 6.0 difficulty and 9.300 execution - a full 0.834 clear of second-placed Oka. China carried a 1.934-point cushion into the final rotation, high bar.
The horizontal bar competition swung back and forth: China's Sun, first up, suffered a fall, but Japan's Oka also faltered soon after. Hashimoto then delivered a near-flawless routine for 15.233.
Needing just 12.931 to seal the gold for China, Zhang - competing last - made sure there would be no repeat of his Paris Olympic heartbreak, scoring 14.200 to lift China to a final total of 255.095, 1.269 points clear of Japan.
Asked about Sun Wei's fall on the horizontal bar, China's team captain Zhang Boheng said the team's preparation had left them ready to absorb a setback without losing composure.
"We did extremely thorough, scientific preparation heading into the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. Even when a small mistake happens, we don't panic - we adjust immediately," Zhang said at the post-competition press conference.
"Across the whole competition we had 18 routines to get through, and with that kind of workload, one or two slips are within the range we can accept. Sun is a veteran who holds himself to a very high standard, so we told him not to worry - we still had it in hand," Zhang added.
Zhang said the team title meant even more to him than his individual all-around gold two days earlier.
"We put out every bit of difficulty we had. We'd trained this at home countless times, all building toward this gold medal today. So when I finished my final routine, it wasn't just me who was excited - everyone was," Zhang said. ■

====================================================================================================

Britain prepares for war in space as threats grow
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
10:40:43 BST
18:40:43 KST

Britain is developing capabilities for what it explicitly describes as “orbital warfare”, including systems able to disrupt, degrade and deny hostile activity in space as the Armed Forces prepare for conflict extending beyond the Earth’s atmosphere.
Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, Chief of the Air Staff and professional head of the Royal Air Force, set out the direction of travel at the UK Space Power Conference in London, warning that adversaries are not waiting for Britain to complete its preparations.
The conference is delivered by UK Space Command and led in partnership with the Freeman Air & Space Institute. Its programme brings together senior figures from Defence, government, the UK Space Agency and allied military organisations.
Smyth said: “Space has never been more important for our nation’s defence and security, for our prosperity and our daily lives, and our adversaries are not waiting until we’re ready for them.”
He added: “We must now get on with delivery of space capability and operational effect at pace.”
The most direct indication of how far that effort is moving came when Smyth described the development of capabilities specifically intended for operations against hostile activity in orbit.
He said: “To help our nation fulfil the control of space requirement, UK Defence is now developing capabilities for orbital warfare.”
Smyth defined this as “actions and effects conducted within space to achieve military objectives”, alongside electronic warfare, systems intended to counter anti-satellite weapons and other supporting operations.
He said: “These capabilities will help us to deter threats, defend our critical space infrastructure, and reduce an adversary’s freedom to operate against the UK and against our allies.”
The language marks a shift from treating space primarily as a supporting domain for communications, navigation and surveillance towards preparing to contest it directly if necessary.
Smyth said the objective was to secure freedom of action for Britain and NATO while denying an adversary the same advantage.
He said: “Through a whole-of-government approach, the UK will safeguard allied space interests. We will gain and maintain our freedom to operate in space, and we will deny our adversaries that same freedom.”
That effort is being backed by several large investment lines. Smyth said £2.3 billion is being committed to satellite communications between now and 2030, alongside £880 million for space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and space control, and £440 million for novel space technology.
Skynet remains central to the military communications architecture. Smyth described the satellite system as the backbone of Britain’s sovereign global communications capability and said an additional £50 million had been allocated to extend the life of the existing Skynet 5 satellites.
Skynet 6A is due to join them next year, while allied and commercial satellite communications are also expected to provide additional capacity and resilience.
Britain is also expanding its ability to detect and understand activity in orbit. Smyth pointed to RAF Fylingdales, the planned Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability being developed with Australia and the United States, and a growing network of optical and commercial sensors feeding the National Space Operations Centre.
He said the Borealis command, control and data-processing system had reached initial operating capability six months ahead of schedule under a five-year, £65 million programme, giving commanders a better picture of activity in space.
The UK is also examining newer sensor technologies, including neuromorphic systems intended to search large areas of space for unexpected activity around satellites while using considerably less power and communications bandwidth.
Those surveillance systems are intended to support the wider military effort rather than operate in isolation. Smyth described space as the “connective tissue” of the integrated force, linking communications, surveillance and targeting systems across land, sea and air.
Space-based intelligence is also expected to feed the Digital Targeting Web, a £1.8 billion programme intended to connect sensors, commanders and weapons and reduce the time between detecting a target and acting against it.
Alongside the new technology, Defence is expanding the military organisation responsible for operating it. No. 1 Space Operations Squadron already supports activity through the National Space Operations Centre, while No. 2 Space Warning Squadron carries out operations associated with RAF Fylingdales.
A new No. 3 Space Effects Squadron will provide personnel specifically for offensive and defensive space operations, with Smyth saying it will “disrupt, degrade, and deny hostile activity to defend UK space interests and gain operational advantage for the integrated force.”
Plans are also being developed for further numbered squadrons covering areas including tactics and training, the deep-space radar programme and space defence as part of a wider integrated air, space and missile defence structure.
Smyth was careful to frame the build-up as deterrence rather than an intention to initiate conflict.
He said: “No one wants a war in space. We are positioning to deter this. The UK will always operate responsibly in ways that promote stability and avoid escalation.”
But he also made clear that Defence is preparing for the possibility that deterrence fails.
He concluded that Britain must be able to “monitor space, make effective decisions, deter our adversaries, and, if necessary, prevail in this vital yet increasingly contested domain.”

‘Annihilate’ vs ‘crushing’ attacks: Why Iran, US up rhetoric amid talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:40:20 UTC
18:40:20 KST

‘Annihilate’ vs ‘crushing’ attacks: Why Iran, US up rhetoric amid talks
Trump threatens to ‘annihilate’ Iran and then boasts about diplomacy, provoking Tehran to warn of a ‘crushing’ response.
Speaking on the first day of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) on Tuesday, United States President Donald Trump threatened to “annihilate” Iran. Hours later, he told reporters that US officials held a “very good” meeting with Iranian leaders.
Iran’s military did not hold back. Dismissing Trump’s remarks, the Armed Forces General Staff – Iran’s highest military body – warned that it is ready to respond with “crushing” severer attacks than earlier in the war.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump: US-Iran meeting at UN was ‘very good’
- list 2 of 3US Republican calls for probe into Donald Trump Jr’s business dealings
- list 3 of 3Iran cancels Baghdad, Muscat flights as US aviation sanctions take effect
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, though not in direct response to Trump, used similarly combative imagery in a message marking the start of Iran’s academic year, describing knowledge combined with faith and morality as a “sharp sword” capable of cutting off the hands of aggressors.
Amid the rhetoric, the two sides held their first in-person meeting in months on the sidelines of the UNGA, reviving a diplomatic channel that had almost collapsed in the wake of repeated violations of the June memorandum of understanding (MoU), which subsequently lapsed last month, during nearly seven months of the US-Israel war on Iran.
The war has triggered a spike in fuel prices in the US – a major issue in the midterm elections due in November – while sanctions by Washington are squeezing Iran’s economy. While Tehran wants the economic measures as well as the US naval blockade on its ports lifted, Washington wants Iran to allow free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, and an end to its nuclear programme.
So, why are Washington and Tehran engaging in diplomacy aimed at finding a way out of the war while also issuing fiery and violent threats?
What were the US-Iran talks on at the UNGA?
Trump said his envoys – Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – met Iranian officials for about three hours on the sidelines of the UNGA. He described it as a “very good meeting”, while acknowledging the Iranian representatives were “not the highest level”.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi took part, with mediators shuttling between the US and Iranian teams.
Witkoff later said the discussions were completed and expressed hope they would prove “constructive and promising”.
The talks were believed to be the first in-person discussions between officials from the two countries since US Vice President JD Vance met senior Iranian officials in Switzerland in June.
Trump said another meeting was expected “in the very near future”, adding that he believed there was “a lot of momentum” towards an agreement.
What did Trump say?
Trump used his UN speech to offer Iran a choice: an opening for negotiations and simultaneously issued a threat of further destruction.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. He asked whether a deal would allow Iran to “rebuild and create a far greater country”, or “do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly”.
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival?” he added.
The Iranian delegation walked out shortly after Trump started to describe the nearly seven months of on-and-off military strikes against Iran, with only one person remaining seated.
What has Iran said?
In a statement carried by the Mehr news agency, Iran’s General Staff accused the US president of using the UN platform to justify “aggression”.
“Such words demonstrate America’s strategic dead end in its aggression against the Iranian nation,” it said, describing Trump’s repeated threats as “not a sign of power but a sign of their strategic desperation”.
The statement also warned Iran’s armed forces are ready to deliver strikes against the US and Israel that would be “more crushing and less predictable” than earlier in their war.
Khamenei also used combative language, although his remarks were not a direct response to Trump’s UN address.
In a message marking the start of the academic year, he described knowledge, faith and morality as weapons against the US and Israel.
“Power rooted in knowledge and coupled with piety and morality serves as an iron shield and a sharp sword that can cut off their aggressors’ hands from humanity,” Khamenei said, referring to what he called the “criminal US government” and Israel, Press TV reported.
Meanwhile, before departing Tehran on Tuesday, President Masoud Pezeshkian also struck a defiant tone, accusing the US of doing “everything they can to block every possible route” to force Iran and its people to surrender after failing to achieve that militarily.
Pezeshkian said Iran would use the UN gathering to highlight “the crimes that have been committed against” Iranians and the distrust created by the war.
Why the escalating rhetoric amid diplomacy?
The hostile rhetoric between Washington and Tehran should not necessarily be seen as contradicting ongoing diplomatic efforts, according to Andreas Krieg, associate professor at King’s College London.
Instead, Krieg argues, the public threats and tough language are part of a wider battle to shape how any eventual agreement is perceived at home and abroad.
“The violent rhetoric is not a contradiction to the diplomacy. It is part of the bargaining strategy,” Krieg told Al Jazeera.
For Trump, the objective is to demonstrate that Iran returned to negotiations because of the US pressure rather than any softening of Washington’s position.
Meanwhile, Iran’s leadership needs to construct almost the opposite narrative – that Tehran resisted US pressure, retained sufficient leverage and ultimately forced Washington to negotiate.
“This has become a major war over narratives as much as a war over material power,” Krieg said.
Both governments are therefore addressing several audiences simultaneously, including their domestic constituencies, each other, regional allies and the wider international community.
Moreover, Krieg said the rhetoric could, paradoxically, make an eventual compromise easier. “If both sides can convince their audiences that they negotiated from strength, they gain more political space to compromise privately without appearing to capitulate publicly,” he noted.
According to the academic, the real issue was “sequencing”.
“Iran wants movement on the blockade, sanctions and frozen assets before giving up leverage over Hormuz or accepting irreversible nuclear concessions. Washington wants tangible Iranian movement first, particularly on navigation and the nuclear file,” he said.
“Qatar’s role is crucial because Doha can turn those incompatible demands into reciprocal steps rather than forcing one side to move first. The danger is that rhetoric can still create its own momentum if there is a major attack, significant US casualties, an Israeli strike or escalation from Yemen.”

Britain says will revisit Chagos deal after latest Trump criticism
- Britain will revisit its 2025 deal with Mauritius to return the Chagos Islands due to strong opposition from US President Donald Trump, who called the agreement "an act of great stupidity".
- UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting expressed commitment to renegotiate the deal with US partners to protect the strategic military base on Diego Garcia.
- The Chagos Islands remain a sensitive security issue, with Britain facing legal and diplomatic challenges after the International Court of Justice advised returning the islands to Mauritius.
AI generated
LONDON - Britain will rework its deal to return the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, a minister confirmed on Sept 23, after US President Donald Trump branded the agreement “terrible” during his first meeting with British leader Andy Burnham.
London’s decision to hand back the Indian Ocean archipelago to its former colony and pay to lease a strategic US-British military base on Diego Garcia has been a bone of contention with Trump’s administration for months.
Britain confirmed in April it was pausing the plans agreed in 2025 between the Mauritian government and Britain’s then-prime minister Keir Starmer.
It faced vocal opposition from Trump, who had initially supported the pact, but then later branded it “an act of great stupidity”.
The unpredictable American leader railed against the deal again on Sept 22 in his first face-to-face meeting with Burnham, who replaced Keir Starmer in July.
Meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Trump said he believed Burnham would be reconsidering the “terrible” agreement, as the British leader sat beside him, nodded and said “yep”.
Burnham later told broadcasters Britain will “work hard” to find a resolution on the thorny issue and that he is “confident we can find it working with our US partners”.
Hours later, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting echoed the sentiment, saying Trump’s opposition was “not news to us” but that his latest comments “provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing”.
“So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where we can support it,” he told the BBC on Sept 23.
Streeting confirmed that annual payments worth at least £120 million (S$203.7 million) to lease back the military base from Mauritius would not be made “at this stage”.
Starmer struck the deal after insisting that international legal rulings have put Britain’s ownership of the Chagos in doubt and only a deal with Mauritius would guarantee that the base remains functional.
Britain kept control of the Chagos Islands after Mauritius gained independence in the 1960s.
It evicted thousands of Chagos islanders who have since mounted a series of legal claims for compensation in British courts.
In 2019, the International Court of Justice recommended that Britain hand the archipelago to Mauritius.
The deal would have given Britain a 99-year lease of the base, with the option to extend.
James Cartlidge, defence spokesman for the main opposition Conservative party, said the agreement “should be binned entirely”.
But Streeting told Times Radio: “The ostrich strategy of sticking our heads in the sand and hoping it (will) go away... is not a wise strategy when it concerns one of the most sensitive national security assets we have anywhere in the world.”
Jack Pannell, a senior researcher at the British Foreign Policy Group think-tank, said Burnham’s priorities with Trump would be on “the big international issues” like AI regulation, Ukraine and the Middle East.
“Success for Burnham means avoiding this issue becoming a millstone around his neck while he pursues his other foreign policy priorities and focuses on his domestic agenda,” Pannell told AFP.
“The chances of a breakthrough on this issue are slim, and that may suit the prime minister just fine.”
On Sept 22, Trump signed a security deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark that will allow the US to build two military bases in southern and eastern Greenland. AFP

Austrian property magnate Benko sentenced to prison
Austrian property tycoon René Benko has been sentenced to two-and-a-half years in prison after an Innsbruck court found he had caused losses to creditors.
The founder of the now-bankrupt Signa property group had paid an advance on rent of €360,000 (CHF338,000) for a property in Innsbruck, even though his business empire was already in a very precarious state, the court said on Tuesday when delivering its verdict.
Benko had already received a two-year jail sentence in October 2025 on these charges. He had, however, been acquitted on one count. The Supreme Court subsequently quashed this acquittal. This led to a retrial, during which the sentence had to be redetermined. The penalty range for the offence is one to ten years’ in jail.
Allegation of harming creditors
The charge centred on the allegation that Benko had made an advance payment of €360,000 towards the rent for a second residence even though he was on the verge of insolvency. He is alleged to have harmed his creditors as a result.
According to the APA news agency, Benko pleaded not guilty. He said that at the time he had been convinced that the restructuring of his Signa Group would be successful.
Benko said the house, in addition to his residence at the villa in Igls, had been rented at his wife’s request. The aim, he said, was to enable the children to lead a “normal life” and attend school as normal without the need for staff.

Benko, who denies all allegations, has been in pre-trial detention since January 2025. He had amassed a fortune worth billions through his property and retail empire, Signa. The Signa Group was also a co-owner of the Swiss department store group Globus, whose operational business has since been sold to its partner, the Thai Central Group. Iranian airlines cancel flights as US sanctions hit
TEHRAN – Iranian airlines were forced to cancel some international flights on Sept 23 after the US tightened sanctions on Iran’s aviation industry in a new effort to cripple its economy.
A travel agent in Tehran told AFP that flights to Baghdad, Muscat, Qatar, Georgia and Azerbaijan had all been suspended, but routes to multiple other destinations remained available, including China.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the new measures on Sept 21 as part of an earlier threat to impose “economic D-Day” on Iran, an attempt to force it into submission following their nearly seven-month war.
But Iran’s aviation sector has already been a target of sanctions for years, and it remains unclear what the full impact will be and whether other countries will comply.
Even after the new sanctions took effect on Sept 23, a flight from Tehran operated by Mahan Air, one of Iran’s biggest carriers, landed in Guangzhou in China, according to tracking data from FlightRadar24.
China on Sept 22 said it opposes the US sanctions and called them illegal. A flight to Shanghai was also due to depart on Sept 23, according to Tehran’s international airport.
Some flights to Istanbul were also scheduled, though others had been cancelled, the travel agent in Tehran told AFP.
“The situation is unstable and we are no longer selling tickets for the time being for fear of cancellations,” the the agent said, requesting anonymity.
A Mahan flight from Kabul was also expected to arrive in Tehran around midday. According to the website for Tehran’s international airport, other connections to Turkey and Armenia also remained possible using smaller Iranian airlines, including Varesh.
Flights to Najaf in Iraq and Dubai in the United Arab Emirates were also scheduled.
Bessent on Sept 21 vowed to “shut down” Iranian carriers and punish anyone doing business with them.
“If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” he warned other countries.
The restrictions will further complicate the ability of Iranians to travel abroad or return to their country.
Pilgrims
Iranian media also reported cancellations, with the Tasnim news agency on Sept 22 citing a civil aviation spokesman as saying that Baghdad and Muscat airports “will no longer accept” Iranian flights.
“Other international flights, including Istanbul, will operate as scheduled and as usual, and at present there are no problems with these flights,” Tasnim said.
According to Tasnim, Iran’s aviation authorities are in talks to reroute Baghdad flights to Najaf, a major destination for Iranian pilgrims.
On Sept 23, the agency said its correspondent in Najaf had reported Iranian flights to the city were running as normal.
It quoted a source at the airport as saying no order had been received from Iraqi authorities to halt flights.
While the Iraqi government has not publicly announced plans to enforce the ban, several sources including a senior government official told AFP that Baghdad would comply with the US measures.
The prospect of a suspension of flights between the two countries has sparked concerns from some Iraqi travel agents.
In Najaf, home to one of the most revered Shia Muslim shrines, agent Haidar Shamaa said “most travel companies in the city depend on booking flights” to Iranian airports.
Several travel agencies said panicked clients were calling for updates and were considering switching to land routes, which would mean much longer journeys. AFP

Grupa Recykl: A step towards the Scandinavian market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:38:10 UTC
18:38:10 KST

The signing of an agreement to supply a production line for SMAPOL, an additive for road asphalt, to Sweden is undoubtedly one of the company’s most important developments this year. Starting production of the additive on the other side of the Baltic Sea opens a new chapter for Grupa Recykl: licensing its own technology for converting textiles recovered from tyres into products for the road construction industry.
“This is the result of lengthy negotiations over recent months. We are entering a highly demanding and competitive Scandinavian market. It is a breakthrough for Grupa Recykl: SMAPOL is gaining not only new distributors, but also new producers and licensees outside Poland. I am confident that we will enter further markets. As before, however, we are developing our products and sales quietly, and we announce developments once they have happened.”
Another product that may reach foreign markets is Elitex, a filler for rubber compounds and thermoplastic polymers. It adjusts the mechanical properties of finished products while helping to reduce their carbon footprint and production costs. Discussions and assessments with international partners are ongoing, the company’s experts say.
Geopolitical uncertainty
The company is feeling the effects of geopolitical factors on its operations more strongly than at any time other than the pandemic. This is especially true in logistics and transport, where the conflict in the Middle East has driven up fuel and energy prices. Drought conditions in Poland have also put pressure on energy prices. Globally, these developments could add to inflationary pressure, creating risks for the recycling industry and the wider economy. At the same time, relatively strong economic growth is supporting demand for Grupa Recykl’s products and services.
“We expect the market trends observed since the beginning of this year to continue in the coming months, both in Poland and at our Lithuanian company, Recykl Litwa,” says Maciej Jasiewicz.
After Lithuania, Germany
Grupa Recykl is continuing the investments it began last year in the Lithuanian company APG, which now operates under the Recykl Litwa brand. The investments focus on expanding its vehicle and container fleet and developing its tyre collection network.
“We plan larger investments in that market in the coming years, eventually including the launch of SMAPOL additive production. Steady expansion from Lithuania into other Scandinavian markets will be important,” says Jasiewicz.
Alongside its investments in Poland and Lithuania, the group continues to work towards completing its acquisition of the German company HRV. “I want to stress that the aim is not simply to close the transaction, but also to integrate the acquired company successfully. We must be prepared for various costs, unforeseen developments and investments. That is a normal part of any M&A transaction,” says the Grupa Recykl president.
Recycling gains importance
Changes to national and European regulations are a key factor affecting Grupa Recykl’s current and planned operations. In early August, Poland’s Ministry of Climate and Environment published a draft amendment to the legislation governing businesses’ obligations in managing certain types of waste, product fees and waste management. The proposed changes are significant for the waste management industry and are intended to bring Polish rules into line with EU circular economy standards.
For pneumatic tyres, the draft proposes higher recovery and recycling targets. It would also bring solid tyres into the extended producer responsibility system.
“I am convinced that, if the legislative process is successful and the changes enter into force, they will make the industry more professional, reduce the scope for unregulated activity and strengthen professional operators, to the benefit of end customers. The changes would also support circular economy and environmental goals. In addition, they would bring our industry closer to Western markets, including in the level of mandatory recovery and recycling targets,” concludes Maciej Jasiewicz.

Following the resignation of Adalar Deputy Mayor Medine Pamuk due to health issues, an electiton was held to select a new deputy mayor. (DHA Photo)
Istanbul’s Adalar district municipality is now led by the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) after party candidate Kemal Türkyılmaz won a vote on Sept. 23 to become acting mayor.
Türkyılmaz won five votes in the third round, while the Republican People’s Party (CHP) candidate Aytül Ekşiyan received no votes after CHP and main opposition New Party council members declined to participate in the final round.
The vote followed the resignation of CHP’s acting mayor Medine Pamuk on Sept. 14, citing health problems. The Istanbul governor’s office had scheduled the initial vote for Sept. 21, but the election was postponed after CHP and New Party members did not participate, preventing the 12-member council from reaching a quorum.
Before the third round on Sept. 23, CHP and New Party members demanded that the vote be canceled, arguing that the procedure was irregular. A dispute broke out between the council members, after which the room where the vote was being held was cleared.
Under the rules governing acting mayor elections, a two-thirds majority is required in the first two rounds. If no candidate secures that threshold, a simple majority is required in the third round. If no candidate obtains a simple majority, a fourth round is held.
The AKP previously held only two of the 12 seats on the Adalar council, while the CHP held 10.
The balance shifted after several CHP council members became unable to participate in the vote following legal proceedings against the municipality’s leadership. Adalar Mayor Ali Ercan Akpolat and Deputy Mayor Fırat Durak were arrested on June 19 as part of an investigation into allegations including bribery, extortion, forgery of official documents, forming and managing a criminal organization and abuse of office.
CHP council member Mehmet Nuri Kaya is also in custody.
Council members Yavuz Çiftçioğlu and Nesimi Aday, who were subject to judicial-control measures, had been barred from participating in the vote after being suspended from their duties. Çiftçioğlu’s restriction was lifted before the final vote, allowing him to participate.
The CHP referred Çiftçioğlu, İsmail Onur Balbınar and Ahmet Tanay Garip to its disciplinary board seeking their expulsion after accusing them of voting for the AKP candidate.
Akpolat won the Adalar election in March 2024 with 55 percent of the vote. AKP candidate Uğur Sina Şen finished second with 22 percent.

Two SC Justices urge CJI to set up five-judge bench for deciding constitutional issues; why it matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:36:17 UTC
18:36:17 KST

A two-judge SC bench has requested the CJI to explore setting up a permanent 5-judge Constitutional Bench.
A two-judge Supreme Court bench, comprising Justice SC Sharma and Justice Datta, has requested the Chief Justice of India to explore the possibility of setting up a permanent five-judge Constitutional Bench to deal with questions involving interpretation of the Constitution.
Why this matters
Constitutional questions currently require bench formation: Under Article 145(3), cases involving a "substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution" must be heard by at least five judges.Such benches are constituted by the Chief Justice of India as required. Currently, there are 22 five-judge matters with 175 tagged matters pending in court.A permanent bench could make the process more predictable. Instead of repeatedly constituting a five-judge bench whenever a major constitutional question arises, a standing bench could hear such matters more continuously.It could also speed up constitutional litigation. Constitution Bench cases can remain pending for long periods because judges have multiple rosters and cases. A dedicated bench could potentially create greater continuity and reduce delays.
A permanent bench could also bring greater consistency as the same group of judges will be dealing regularly with constitutional questions, which could develop continuity in constitutional jurisprudence, rather than different combinations of judges being assembled for different cases.
It could also increase the importance of the CJI's roster decisions. The CJI is the master of the roster and decides which judges sit on particular benches. A permanent five-judge bench would therefore be a significant change in how the court allocates its most important constitutional cases.
Constitution Benches decide some of the country's most consequential questions, including the limits of Parliament's power, fundamental rights, federalism, separation of powers and challenges to constitutional amendments.The Supreme Court has used Constitution Benches extensively in recent years; for example, 16 Constitution Bench judgments were delivered during former CJI D.Y. Chandrachud's tenure.
Aashish Saxena is an Assistant News Editor at the Times of India. He has 14 years of editing and reporting experience in both print and digital media. He writes extensively on geopolitics, Indian politics, defence tech, and current affairs in South Asia and Middle East.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”. He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump”.
Trump himself declared last week that “major progress” was being made towards establishing the base, saying it was thanks to the “bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki”, who is a conservative ally of the US president.
Meanwhile, earlier this week, a Polish deputy defence minister, Stanisław Wziątek, also expressed confidence that the new base would soon be confirmed and said that it could see the number of US troops stationed in Poland rise to around 15,000.
President Karol Nawrocki said he hopes the US will finalize plans to establish a permanent military base in Poland and, if it does, the compound will be christened ‘Fort Trump' https://t.co/SB4DOy5Qp1 pic.twitter.com/aPmvl4JoFO
— Bloomberg TV (@BloombergTV) September 22, 2026
The US military presence in Poland has become a big issue this year following Washington’s unexpected last-minute decision in May to cancel the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 troops.
Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. In June, Poland formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory.
In a post on his social media platform, Truth Social, last week, Trump announced “major progress” in those plans and said that “if this happens, the location [of the base] will be announced very soon”. He called it a “historic step for our Great US/Polish Alliance”.
On Tuesday this week, speaking to Bloomberg during a visit to the US for the United Nations General Assembly, Nawrocki confirmed that plans for the base were at an advanced stage.
“The infrastructure is being chosen right now. Consultants from the US have already visited Poland,” he said. “I think that it’s hard for me to give specific dates, but I think that this matter is for sure confirmed because President Trump is famous for keeping his word.”
Nawrocki also expressed confidence that “President Trump will personally be able to participate in the inauguration of Fort Trump”. That name, Fort Trump, was first suggested in 2018 by Nawrocki’s predecessor, Andrzej Duda, when, during Trump’s first term, he sought a permanent US base in Poland.
Poland’s government, which regularly clashes with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and has also at times had tense relations with the Trump administration, has not commented on the idea of naming the new base after the US president.
However, the government is keen for the project to move ahead, and has been doing much of the legwork on making it happen. Although Poland’s president is commander-in-chief of the armed forces, his position is largely ceremonial, and it is the government that is responsible for implementing policy.
On Monday this week, deputy defence minister Stanisław Wziątek told broadcaster RMF that he was “convinced there is full agreement” on establishing the base, with the remaining question being the precise location.
Wziątek said that the announcement could be made before November’s midterm elections in the US, as Trump will be keen to encourage Polish Americans to vote Republican.

The deputy defence minister said that the base would be likely to host between 3,000 and 5,000 US troops, with 4,500 the “most realistic estimate, because that is the size of a brigade”.
In total, said Wziątek, Poland hoped to have “around 15,000” US soldiers in Poland, including the roughly 10,000 that have up until now been present on a rotational basis.
The minister admitted that the current rotational presence was lower, around 6,500-7,000, following the cancellation of May’s planned deployment. But he said that the figure should “soon” return to the previous higher level.
When asked about the cost to Poland of establishing the new permanent US base, Wziątek said it would “definitely be more than 15 billion zloty (€3.4 billion) but will depend on the level of involvement of the United States”.

The US has long been Poland’s most important security partner. In 2023, under President Joe Biden, it established its first permanent military garrison in Poland at Camp Kościuszko in the city of Poznań. The following year, a US missile defence base opened in Redzikowo on Poland’s northern Baltic coast.
This week, the mayor of Poznań, Jacek Jaśkowiak, told newspaper Fakt that his city was one of two locations being considered for the planned new US base. Recent Polish media reports have also identified the provinces of Lower Silesia and West Pomerania as potential locations.
While the Trump administration has chastised many NATO member states for failing to meet the alliance’s defence spending targets, it has hailed Poland, whose defence budget is one of NATO’s highest in relation to GDP, as a “model ally”.
Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery.
