Breadcrumb
Trump meets Arab, Muslim leaders at UNGA as Iran war rumbles on
President Donald Trump held a closed-door meeting with Arab and Muslim leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Tuesday amid continued uncertainty over the nearly seven-month Iran war.
The meeting comes as Gulf leaders warn about the impact of the continued disruption through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, which has sent global energy markets into a tailspin and piled economic pressure onto the region.
Attending the meeting were leaders of the Gulf Cooperation Council countries as well as leaders and representatives from several Arab and Muslim countries, including Egypt, Turkey, Lebanon, Syria, and Iraq.
The US has reportedly floated setting up a $10 billion investment fund with Arab states to repair the infrastructure damaged and destroyed during the conflict.
Three people familiar with the matter told the Financial Times that Trump officials were discussing the idea with regional partners ahead of the UN meeting.
In public remarks ahead of the meeting, Trump claimed to have achieved a "historic peace deal" in Gaza and talked up the US military campaign against Iran.
He occasionally deviated from the script, at one point pointing at Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and saying: "My friend right here from Turkey, he's a tough cookie, don't mess around with him … he's a fantastic guy."
Iran, US hold 'productive' talks
Trump talked up the prospects of a deal with Iran to end the war, describing an indirect meeting between the two sides in New York as "very productive".
Iranian state media earlier confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had participated in the discussions, which it said was requested by the Trump administration.
Trump envoy Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner represented the US during the three-hour talks, which were the first since the middle of June after the two sides agreed to an ill-fated truce.
"I think there's a lot of momentum for [the mediators] to make a deal," Trump said.
Iran's state broadcaster said the Iranian delegation stuck to "firm positions" during the talks, including its key demands to lift the US blockade, unfreeze its assets and permanently end the war across the region.
Trump's positive comments came after he threatened to "annihilate" Iran during his address to the General Assembly.
"I have a big decision to make - will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country?" he said in his speech, during which all but one member of the Iranian delegation walked out.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival?"
An Iranian official earlier in the day offered an olive branch, saying that Tehran could fully reopen the strait if the US lifts the blockade, according to Reuters.
'Why don’t you give New Jersey to Israelis?'
Syria's President Ahmed al-Sharaa said Tuesday that his government had reached the final stages of a security pact with Israel before Tel Aviv
"There were several sessions of negotiations with Israel, and we almost reached 90% of agreements," he said at an Atlantic Council event on the sidelines of the UN gathering.
It was at that point that the Israelis pulled out of talks, he said.
Following the downfall of the Assad regime, Israel invaded southern Syria and destroyed much of the country's military capabilities. In the months since, its occupying forces have staged frequent raids in southern towns, arresting locals and using military force.
"We are still engaging in this [diplomatic] track," Sharaa said, "but we need to protect the security and the rights of the Syrian Before that, we can't talk about peace".
Asked by an audience member about Trump's decision to recognise Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights, Sharaa recounted a remark he made to the US president during a visit to the White House.
"Why don't you give New Jersey to the Israelis? You don't own the Golan Heights to give it to them, but you own New Jersey," he said he told Trump.

Xi Jinping's visit to US to stabilize markets, geopolitical situation — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:35:18 UTC
18:35:18 KST

BEIJING, September 23. /TASS/. The upcoming visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping to the United States and his meeting with US President Donald Trump will have a positive impact on global markets and the geopolitical situation, Qian Feng, a researcher and director of the Research Department at Tsinghua University’s National Strategy Research Institute, told TASS.
"Following President Trump’s successful visit to China in May this year, President Xi Jinping’s trip to the United States will have a number of positive and far-reaching consequences for China-US relations," the expert said. "First, the visit will send a positive signal to the international community regarding the stabilization and improvement of China-US relations. It will help stabilize market expectations and the global geopolitical climate, while also setting a constructive tone for interaction between the two countries."
As Qian emphasized, Xi’s scheduled trip to the US will mark his second meeting with Trump in the past six months - an event of "immense strategic importance" for developing constructive relations and maintaining strategic stability.
"Through direct interaction between the two leaders, both sides will be able to more clearly define 'red lines' and key interests, as well as fine-tune crisis-management mechanisms," he said. "History shows that cooperation benefits both sides, while confrontation harms everyone. This visit will help create a 'safety barrier' around differences and prevent them from escalating into open confrontation."
The Chinese political analyst noted that the visit is expected to pave the way for a number of concrete bilateral cooperation agreements. Such engagement between Beijing and Washington, grounded in shared interests, could deepen the two countries’ economic interdependence and "undermine arguments for decoupling and the severing of supply chains."
Qian said Xi’s trip could help China and the US overcome short-term differences and "view the long-term development of bilateral relations from historical and philosophical perspectives."
"Through candid dialogue, the United States will gain a deeper understanding of the PRC’s development path and strategic intentions, while the Chinese side will be able to more accurately assess the direction of US policy. This will enable the shaping of a new, stable model of interaction between major powers," he said.
Aligning Positions on Key Areas
According to Qian, Xi and Trump are expected to coordinate their positions in several areas during the visit, particularly on global governance.
"As the world’s two largest economies, China and the United States bear a tremendous historical responsibility for addressing global issues," he said. "China hopes to strengthen policy coordination with the United States on global challenges such as public health and the regulation of artificial intelligence, and to jointly provide public goods for global peace and prosperity."
Qian noted that trade and economic cooperation between China and the US has "faced numerous new challenges" in recent years, particularly as a result of unilateral actions by Washington that "politicize trade and economic issues," impose additional tariffs on Chinese goods, erect barriers through stricter export controls and "hinder normal cooperation within industrial supply chains."
These measures, he said, undermine the stability of bilateral trade and the business environment, destabilize markets and dampen business confidence.
According to Qian, Beijing hopes that Xi’s visit will facilitate the resolution of structural issues in China-US trade, strengthen practical cooperation in new areas, reinforce the "stabilizing ballast" of bilateral ties, foster mutually beneficial cooperation and "deliver tangible benefits to the people of both countries."
Qian also pointed to what he described as "numerous real obstacles" facing cultural and people-to-people exchanges between China and the US. He said the US side "places excessive emphasis on security concerns regarding routine academic exchanges and scientific-technical cooperation," while tighter visa policies are creating a "chilling effect."
"This has led to a significant mutual reduction in the number of students studying in the two countries and a sharp decline in inter-university cooperation," Qian said. "Furthermore, long-standing biases against China within the American public exert constant pressure on the social atmosphere surrounding people-to-people exchanges, thereby eroding the foundation of cultural interaction."
China hopes Xi’s visit to the US will help restore and expand cultural exchanges and deepen mutual understanding between the peoples of the two countries, he added.
Qian recalled that, in its dealings with the United States, China "consistently adheres to the principles of mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, and mutually beneficial cooperation." Beijing seeks to foster bilateral ties, "build a constructive relationship of strategic stability," and promote "an expanded scope of cooperation and common ground in areas such as the economy, trade, and global governance," he said.
Qiang added that China seeks to resolve differences with the US through dialogue and consultation in order to prevent further escalation of bilateral tensions.
The Importance of High-Level Contacts
At the same time, Qian emphasized that while China firmly defends its sovereignty, security and legitimate development interests, it will also "resolutely push back unilateral acts of intimidation" and remain guided by its high-level diplomatic strategy.
China is "prepared to demonstrate goodwill toward the US and pave the way for steering the relationship between the two powers onto the right track," he said.
"In my view, at the political and diplomatic levels, China hopes that head-of-state diplomacy will play an indispensable, strategic and leading role," Qian said.
He believes that in-depth dialogue between Xi and Trump could enable Beijing and Washington to "reach a broader consensus, resolve differences, avoid strategic miscalculations, and reaffirm the principles of mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, and mutually beneficial cooperation."
In doing so, the leaders of the two countries would "infuse new substance into the constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability," Qian said, referring to a framework he said was agreed upon during the US president’s visit to China in May.
On Monday, China’s Foreign Ministry announced that Xi Jinping would visit the United States from September 23 to 25. During the visit, the Chinese leader will discuss "bilateral relations and important issues concerning global peace and development" with Trump.

Most Germans want Chancellor Merz to resign, poll says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:35:18 UTC
18:35:18 KST

Oliver Towfigh Nia
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
A majority of Germans want Chancellor Friedrich Merz to resign, according to a new survey released Wednesday, as his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party faced a series of dismal regional election results.
The poll, done for private broadcasters RTL and n-tv, found that 55% of respondents want Merz to step down, while 40% said he should remain chancellor.
In eastern Germany, support for his resignation rose to 68%, compared to 53 percent in the western part of the country.
Even among supporters of the CDU/CSU alliance, 21% said Merz should leave office.
 
Chancellor’s popularity hits all-time low
The chancellor is historically unpopular, as a Forsa trend barometer confirmed again this week. Only 11% are satisfied with Merz's performance in office, while 87% are not.
The people’s rejection of Merz may have played a role in the most recent state elections as well.
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU was ousted from the state parliament. In Saxony-Anhalt, its support plummeted to just over 17%. In Berlin, it suffered a clear defeat at the hands of The Left. Even in the latest poll, the CDU is now polling at only 20%.
 
Poll links election losses to decline in Merz’s voter support
The survey tried to get to the bottom of this decline in voter support. Some 66% of voters hold Merz personally responsible for the losses. However, there is another issue that respondents consider even more important: 81% say the CDU no longer cares about people’s everyday concerns.
The CDU leader is often described as out of touch, showing too little empathy for people's concerns, according to the poll.
Almost two-thirds of respondents (64%) pointed to another reason for the vote losses suffered by the CDU and CSU, notably the breaking of the election campaign promise not to incur new debt. Furthermore, 57% believe that government policy is not socially balanced.

Thousands live in Gaza's bombed-out houses despite risk of collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:33:00 UTC
18:33:00 KST

After Israel's genocidal war damaged or destroyed nearly 84% of the buildings in Gaza by October 2025 and hardly any reconstruction work since, thousands of Palestinians are forced to live in bombed out apartments at risk of collapse.
In her Gaza City apartment, Heba Arafat walks uphill across a living room slanted at a steep angle after Israeli airstrikes caused the building's foundations to collapse, leaving the entire structure tilted.
Like thousands of others, Arafat chose to risk living in an apartment building damaged during the nearly three-year war, with countless Israeli airstrikes on the Palestinian territory.
"We were forced to live here because we had nowhere else to go. All of our homes were destroyed, our land was razed and we have nothing left," said Arafat, 47.
According to the U.N., 84% of all structures in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed and Gaza's civil defense says 2,000 buildings across the territory are at risk of collapse.
Last week, 21 people, including 12 children, died in Gaza City after a six-story building that local authorities said had been hit repeatedly by Israeli airstrikes collapsed. Israel denied having struck the building.
Arafat lives with her six daughters and husband in their old apartment building in Gaza City's al-Shati Refugee Camp, which they left at the height of Israel's war that was triggered in October 2023 with the Hamas incursion.
The family returned after an October 2025 cease-fire, which has reduced but not ended Israeli strikes. They found that their four-story building, in which 30 people now live, had collapsed inward at the ground floor, the result, she said, of an Israeli ground operation in the area.
Like most buildings in Gaza City, the windows were blown away by blasts, with makeshift bed sheets spread across the frames providing little privacy.
As she spoke, Arafat illustrated her building's slant by leaving a water bottle sideways on the floor, only for it to quickly roll away to the other end of the room.
While no territory-wide estimate exists, Ramiz Alakbarov, the U.N. humanitarian coordinator for the Palestinian territories, said last week that people across Gaza were living in "hundreds of damaged and unsafe shelters."
"Where can we go? Even though this house is dangerous," Arafat said. "We have been terrified ever since we heard about houses collapsing. The danger has become even greater" than we thought.
Gaza City municipal staff patrol the streets to identify buildings at risk of collapse and mark them with stencils.
"These homes pose a genuine threat to the lives of the displaced persons sheltering inside them, as well as to residents in the vicinity and those in nearby displacement camps," said Hosni Muhanna, a Gaza City spokesman.
But Muhanna knows that people are likely to remain in these buildings for lack of better options.
"Thousands of displaced people are forced to seek shelter in these dilapidated buildings which are on the verge of collapse to escape the hardships of displacement camps that offer no protection against the summer heat or winter cold."
Most residents of Gaza were displaced at least once during the war, and many of them remain in enormous camps for the displaced, in tents provided by humanitarian organizations or in improvised shelters.
With diseases such as the skin infection impetigo rampaging through certain camps due to the lack of waste disposal and general overcrowding, many Gaza residents have found it safer to take the risks of moving into the damaged buildings.
And with Gaza's economy in tatters, many remain dependent on aid, which Israel has allowed into Gaza with restrictions since the declaration of the U.S.-brokered cease-fire in October 2025.
But Israel has kept carrying out airstrikes and has restricted the entry of a range of equipment that it says could also have military use, but which Gazans and international NGOs say are needed for the territory's vast reconstruction needs.
These can include large machinery needed to clear rubble from the site of destroyed buildings, or spare parts and lubricants needed to keep other tools running, U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric said in August.
With the cease-fire process stalled for months, reconstruction efforts planned under the cease-fire have yet to begin.
According to a joint assessment published by the United Nations, World Bank and European Union in April, Gaza will require $71.4 billion in recovery and reconstruction spending over the next decade.
"We're afraid a wall or the roof might fall on us, so we huddle together, afraid that one of us might get hurt," Arafat said.

Oil refineries, ports emerge as main customers for interceptor UAVs — expert

Unknown Publisher

SIMFEROPOL, September 23. /TASS/. Oil refineries and ports, including those not classified as critical infrastructure, are currently the main users of interceptor drones in Russia, Mikhail Filippov, founder and CEO of the all-Russian Archangel drone pilot training and unmanned technologies development project, told TASS.
"Orders for the development of protection systems using interceptor drones are currently coming primarily from oil sector enterprises, port operators, and warehouse owners--facilities that the enemy is actively targeting," he said.
According to him, the Ukrainian armed forces have also been targeting facilities that are not included in the list of critical infrastructure. This forces owners to bear additional costs to protect their facilities.
Filippov added that a number of warehouses are being included in the list, as the project facilitates this through cooperation with regional authorities. At the same time, most warehouses operate on a post-payment system--they store products from manufacturers, for which payment is received only upon delivery. Damage to warehouses leads to logistical disruptions and losses for manufacturers.
The Archangel project has been operated by a group of enthusiasts since 2022. The project has centers in various cities, with overall coordination handled from Moscow, Crimea, and the Zaporozhye Region.

The EU's top diplomat also pressed Tehran over a surge in executions, as part of a week of meetings in New York in which the bloc is pushing for respect for the UN Charter and freedom of navigation.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, where the two discussed diplomatic routes to ending the war between the United States and Iran and fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
In a post on X after the meeting, Kallas said ships should not have to pay to pass through the strait once the conflict ends. She noted that no tolls or fees were charged before the war, and said navigation must be "free and unimpeded" in both Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.
Kallas also said she had raised repression inside Iran with Araghchi, pointing to a sharp rise in executions and death sentences.
Kallas's meeting came as US and Iranian negotiators held indirect talks on the sidelines of the Assembly.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner took part on the American side, and Araghchi led for Iran. Witkoff said the sides had "successfully completed a round of discussions," and another is expected soon.
In his address to the General Assembly, US President Donald Trump said he faced a "big decision" over whether to strike a deal with Iran. But the gap remains wide.
Iran's parliament has approved rules to fine ships that cross the strait without authorisation, which runs against Kallas's call for toll-free passage.
Iranian-backed Houthi forces have also stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, opening a second front in the war that began in February.
Iran accuses Europe of 'double standards'
Araghchi has also met Dutch Foreign Minister Tom de Bruijn in New York, according to his Telegram channel.
During the meeting, Araghchi strongly criticised “the double standards of European countries” concerning regional developments, pointing specifically to their silence and appeasement regarding the “aggressive actions and crimes” committed by the US and Israel against Iran, the statement noted.
“The foreign minister [Araghchi] noted that European nations cannot, on the one hand, claim to uphold the rule of law and human rights while, on the other, remaining indifferent to – or even supporting – blatant military aggression by the US and Israel against Iran,” it added.
De Bruijn emphasised the importance of diplomacy and outlined his country’s perspectives on ongoing regional developments and interactions between Iran and Europe.
The European External Action Service says Kallas has come to New York with a clear and united message: international law and the UN Charter must be upheld, sovereignty and territorial integrity must be respected, and violations of international law must not go unpunished.
Kallas, European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen represented the bloc at the eighth trilateral meeting with the African Union and the United Nations on Sunday, and the three also held talks with UN Secretary-General António Guterres.
On Tuesday, the three EU leaders attended the opening of the General Debate. Kallas then co-hosted a high-level event on global food security and the Black Sea with Ukraine, France and Romania. On Wednesday, she co-hosts the annual meeting of EU and Latin American and Caribbean (CELAC) foreign ministers with Uruguay's foreign minister, as well as a ministerial event on maritime security.
This year's session is taking place under the theme "Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all".
Almost 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak during the General Debate, which runs until 28 September.

Also in the Donetsk region, near Volnovakha, a UAV depot belonging to the “Rubicon” unit was struck.
In addition, Ukrainian troops struck logistics facilities supporting Russian forces.
A fuel and lubricants depot was struck in the Kundryuchyi area of Luhansk region, and logistics depots were struck in the Hirnyk and Velyka Shyshivka areas of Donetsk region.
In the Krasnohorivka area of Donetsk region, a concentration of personnel from a UAV unit was struck.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 21, the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a facility used for the storage, preparation, and launch of attack UAVs near the village of Tsymbulova in the Oryol Oblast of the Russian Federation.

Grid radiator by Elisa Ossino for Tubes

====================================================================================================

Report: Iranian advisers helped direct Houthi blitz that seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:30:21 UTC
18:30:21 KST

Iranian Revolutionary Guard advisers were on the ground helping Houthi rebels direct their lightning offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, according to an Associated Press investigation that details Tehran’s most direct battlefield involvement with the group since Yemen’s civil war erupted in 2014.
The Houthis needed less than 48 hours to seize a 115-kilometer stretch of coastline from forces aligned with Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government, capturing the strategic port city of Mokha and nearby islands that give the group greater ability to threaten shipping in the Red Sea. Recent AP reporting has documented the Houthis’ capture of Mokha and expansion toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical maritime chokepoint.
The operation dealt a major blow to Saudi Arabia and other U.S.-aligned regional actors at a time when the Houthis have also renewed attacks on Saudi targets and the kingdom is facing pressure on its oil export routes. A separate drone attack recently disabled much of Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline for several weeks, further restricting oil flows toward the Red Sea.
The AP interviewed 10 officials and soldiers for its account, including a senior Houthi official, two regional officials, a senior Yemeni military commander and a member of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal decision-making.
Iranian advisers move closer to the front
Iran has supported the Houthis for years, but people familiar with the latest offensive told the AP that Revolutionary Guard advisers assumed a far more direct role than before.
A senior Houthi official said Iranian advisers had previously focused mainly on strategic planning, away from front-line operations. During the latest campaign, however, they were “present at all levels,” including tactical planning and work with battlefield commanders.
Two regional officials regularly briefed on developments in Yemen also told the AP that Iranian support contributed directly to the speed of the Houthi advance.
Security analyst Mzahem Alsaloum, who has tracked Iranian-backed groups for nearly a decade, said Iranian advisers also helped analyze intercepted communications and satellite intelligence, capabilities he said the Houthis previously lacked.
Iran’s mission to the United Nations did not respond to the AP’s request for comment.
The growing Iranian role followed months of expanded training and logistical assistance. Alsaloum said Tehran had increased support for more advanced missiles, drones and uncrewed attack boats during the past year.
In July, tensions escalated further after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of striking the airport in the rebel-held capital, Sanaa, apparently in an effort to prevent an Iranian flight from landing.
That flight later arrived carrying Revolutionary Guard advisers, according to Alsaloum and the senior Houthi official. They joined other Iranian and Hezbollah advisers already based in Yemen.
Rivalries weakened government defenses
The Houthis’ rapid advance was also made possible by deep divisions among the forces opposing them.
The National Resistance, which fields about 30,000 fighters, had been the strongest pro-government force along the coast but had not fought a major campaign there since 2017.
For about a month before Mokha fell, Houthi forces bombarded National Resistance positions with 130 ballistic missiles and 145 suicide drones, according to Maj. Gen. Sadiq Dwaid, a spokesman for the force.
He said government fighters were spread across a front roughly 170 kilometers long and were facing an estimated 75,000 Houthi fighters.
The Giants Brigade, another anti-Houthi force, moved in to support the National Resistance in early September and initially helped push the rebels back. But the deployment was poorly coordinated, according to a Yemeni government official, and revived longstanding rivalries between the two forces.
Those tensions reflected the broader competition between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates over Yemen’s anti-Houthi camp, a struggle that preceded the UAE’s withdrawal from Yemen in January.
“There was no unified command,” a senior Yemeni military official told the AP. “This was a priceless opportunity for the Houthis.”
Communications breach fuels collapse
On Sept. 9, Houthi forces pushed south through a narrow mountain valley toward Mokha while heavily bombarding government positions.
The Houthis had penetrated the National Resistance’s internal communications, one government official told the AP, allowing them to monitor troop movements and exploit confusion among commanders.
By that afternoon, the rebels had taken a mountain road and nearby military base, cutting supply lines to Mokha.
Lt. Gen. Tariq Saleh, head of the National Resistance, fled the area and later took refuge in Saudi Arabia.
At around 6 p.m., retreat orders were issued to National Resistance units. As thousands of fighters poured back toward Mokha, troops already stationed in the city mistakenly believed a major Houthi assault was about to begin and also started withdrawing, two fighters told the AP.
Resident Issa Gubwani said he watched military vehicles and pickup trucks stream out of the city.
“They left us to face our fate,” he said.
Tens of thousands of civilians joined the exodus. When Houthi forces entered Mokha early on Sept. 10, the senior Houthi official said, “the city was empty.”
The seizure of Mokha and nearby islands significantly expanded Houthi control along one of the world’s most important shipping corridors. The Houthis have since been building defensive positions in the newly captured territory, according to the official. The wider conflict has displaced large numbers of Yemenis and revived fears of a return to full-scale civil war.
Questions over Saudi response
Yemeni government forces were also surprised that Saudi aircraft did not strike the advancing Houthi columns, according to the senior military official.
The Saudi government media office did not respond to the AP’s request for comment.
The Houthis captured weapons and military equipment left behind by retreating forces, including armored vehicles, rockets, artillery shells and ammunition, two Yemeni officials said. Much of the equipment had originally been supplied by Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
The National Resistance said around 500 of its fighters were killed during the battles, a figure the AP could not independently verify. The Houthis have not disclosed their losses.
Government forces are now trying to regroup while rival anti-Houthi factions trade accusations over responsibility for the collapse.
“Losing the West Coast is not the end of the battle; rather, it marks the beginning of a fiercer battle,” Brig. Gen. Walid Ziyad, a senior National Resistance commander, wrote on social media.

Bill would end monthly counseling requirement for many unemployed Estonians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Bill would end monthly counseling requirement for many unemployed Estonians
Under a draft prepared at the Ministry of Economic Affairs, many people registered with the Unemployment Insurance Fund will no longer be required to attend counseling once a month, while young jobseekers and those with reduced work ability will face more frequent counseling.
The Riigikogu Social Affairs Committee decided to send to first reading an amendment to the Labour Market Measures Act that removes the obligation for registered jobseekers to attend monthly counseling sessions.
Committee chair Signe Riisalo told ERR that the main purpose of the amendment is to reduce time spent on unnecessary counseling for people who are already active jobseekers and find work quickly.
"The same time resource will be directed toward young people, whose risk of unemployment is high, and they will be offered intensive counseling four times a month," Riisalo said. "The Unemployment Insurance Fund also wants to extend four‑times‑a‑month counseling to people with reduced work ability."
According to Riisalo, the change will not result in savings, because resources will be redirected to groups that need more support.
"Some provisions in the draft will actually increase costs, as benefit payments will no longer be stopped and work‑ability payments will no longer be suspended after the first violation," Riisalo noted.
At the same time, costs for unemployment insurance benefits and work‑ability support will decrease, because after a third violation, a person's registration as unemployed will end, along with their benefit or support payments. This applies until they register again, or until the end of a 90‑day waiting period after a second termination.
As a result, combined costs will decrease in 2027–2028 by between €346,000 and €452,000.
The first reading of the bill is scheduled for 30 September, and the provisions in question are planned to take effect on 1 January 2027.

Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro Review: Premium but Paywalled
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Every bird enthusiast has probably heard of Birdfy and Birdbuddy smart bird feeders, but a handful of competitors have quietly been refining their models over multiple generations—to the point where they’re starting to outpace the OGs in engineering, features, and design. Kiwibit is one of them.
I tested Kiwibit’s first feeder, the Beako, in mid-2025 and was impressed by its robust plastic body, removable dual-sided seed reservoir, and three-minute video captures—there was nothing quite like it at the time, and almost all of its features were available sans subscription. However, the optional rooftop solar panel stopped working after six weeks, which kept it from being a pick in my guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders.
The Beako’s subsequent update, the Feeder 2, made the solar panel standard on all units, upped the panel’s output from 4.4 to 5 watts, and fixed the longevity issue—it’s currently my top pick for Best Design. The Feeder 2 Pro, meanwhile, has totally redone the camera to offer phase detection autofocus (PDAF) in 4K HDR—one of the most impressive smart feeder hardware offerings on the market. The companion app upgrade, however, still has some kinks to work out.
OK Computer
I tested the Feeder 2 Pro for a total of four weeks: one week at the non-subscription tier, and three weeks with Kiwibit Plus (also alternately referred to as “Family Premium” or “Premium Family), which at $90 a year offers AI ID, 60-day cloud recording (the feeder also supports microSD storage up to 512 GB), and new gallery views and roundup reports.
Without a subscription, camera quality is the same (some other feeder brands, like Birdbuddy, will paywall higher resolution), but here you’re limited to a bare-bones feed of video captures, and there’s no AI ID to sort or identify them—you’ll have to look at every image to make sure you didn’t miss anything interesting. This can be especially laborious if the same bird visits 15 times or more per day, especially since the camera placement means the thumbnails often show only the top of the bird’s head, if they show anything. This is atypical for a feeder with an MSRP of $290—most models at this price point include a lifetime subscription.
Thankfully, it is still easy to download and share 8-MP images and videos, and the camera records as long as the bird is there—up to three minutes—to ensure no movements are missed. The PDAF works to minimize blur and ensure all features are sharp. At various points during my test, I did notice the motion of the lens zooming in and out being clocked by multiple birds, who either immediately stopped eating to watch the camera warily or flew away. It didn’t happen often enough for me to wish the feature didn’t exist, but it is something to consider if your local birds are easily spooked.
The subscription gives you the same feed of video captures, but with labels of the bird species so you can skip past the ones that aren’t worth opening. There’s also a tile view under “Visits” that shows which birds have visited over the feeder’s lifetime and when they were last seen.
However, this is only so useful given that the AI ID is wrong a hefty percentage of the time—fish crows, Cape May warblers, mangrove warblers, red fox sparrows, and grackles are not found in western Washington state, where I live, but according to the Kiwibit app they are frequent visitors to my backyard. (I even had a “pileated woodpecker” visit the feeder, which would have been exceptionally rare, except the misidentified bird was a crow.) Also note that, unlike Birdfy feeders, the camera is not able to ID multiple birds on the feeder at a time.
Premium Pictures, Premium Fees
One area where Birdfy and Birdbuddy still beat their competitors is their intuitive, user-friendly apps. While Kiwibit’s non-subscription view has a simple interface, the subscription experience is a bit chaotic, as Kiwibit tries to cram a lot of information into too many places. There’s the tile view under “Birds,” the list of captures under “Feeds,” and a live view under “Live,” which you can click into to see a calendar of captures by day. Then, under “Me,” there’s a different calendar view with the number of bird visits per day, and a weekly Report tab that gives stats on that week’s visits. Even after four weeks of testing, I’m still not sure where I should first look when I simply want to see the birds that visited that day.

Literary sensation 'C'était ça ou mourir' faces AI authorship claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:29:51 UTC
18:29:51 KST

Quebecois writer of Haitian origin Thélyson Orélien, longlisted for several major literary prizes, rejects accusations from the "Balance ton Claude" account and says in a statement he has faced racist attacks since arriving in France.
Can an AI detector threaten the success of a literary bestseller that is in the running for one of the country's biggest literary prizes?
In France, the novel "C'était ça ou mourir" by Thélyson Orélien, hailed as one of the revelations of the autumn publishing season and already selling more than 35,000 copies, now stands accused of having been written by artificial intelligence.
The controversy was sparked by a message posted (source in French) on X on Monday 21 September by an anonymous account, "Balance ton Claude". "According to Pangram, this novel was written almost entirely by an artificial intelligence," it claims, saying it had tested several passages from the "manuscript" and almost always obtained "the same result: 100% AI".
According to the people behind the account, the US tool Pangram is "by far the most reliable AI detector", with a "false-positive rate of 0.0041%."
It is a particularly sensitive allegation for the 38-year-old author of Haitian origin, whose novel is being translated into more than 20 languages and has been included on the initial longlists for the Goncourt, Goncourt des lycéens, Femina, Médicis and Renaudot prizes.
The story follows Jonas, a young Haitian history and geography teacher forced to flee his country because of violence and insecurity, on his journey across the Americas. Before this debut novel, published last winter in Quebec and whose rights for French-speaking Europe have been acquired by Grasset, Thélyson Orélien had mainly published poetry.
From "rumours" to "racist attacks"?
Grasset initially insisted it was not paying attention to these "rumours".
"This is fake news. (...) These tools that are supposed to detect AI are themselves AIs that fantasise that the Bible was written artificially," the publisher told BFMTV (source in French) on Tuesday morning.
The publishing house with the yellow covers also said that dozens of AI-written novels are on offer on Amazon but that "none of them is successful" because "not one has any distinctiveness". "The exact opposite of Thélyson," Grasset, owned by the Vivendi group controlled by billionaire Vincent Bolloré, added.
By early Tuesday evening, the scale of the affair prompted Grasset to send a statement to several media outlets, including Euronews, giving the author the floor. In it, Thélyson Orélien explains that the "repetitions" he is accused of, presented as typical of AI-generated text, stem from "a Haitian and Caribbean literary tradition" with its own poetics.
He adds: "People can argue about my style, but turning its devices into proof of artificial intelligence has nothing to do with literary criticism."
The writer also took the opportunity to thank those readers who "make room in their lives" for his book: "In a world where some people always want to check where you come from before listening to what you say, this welcome moves me deeply."
In the same statement, the Grasset team say they are renewing "their absolute confidence" in the author, "against any machine or attempt to measure, standardise or silence writing that is forever free."
Contacted by Euronews, Thélyson Orélien declined to respond to our requests for comment. He did, however, tell Libération (source in French) that he has been the target of "numerous racist attacks" since arriving in France.
AI and a "creolised" language
Before the mainstream media picked it up, the controversy exploded on X. After the first post from "Balance ton Claude", many users relayed the anonymous account's accusations – including in English – as established fact, some even going so far as to mock (source in French) the literary world of criticism for having "fallen for it, hailing as wonderful a style not only written by AI but fundamentally mediocre and repetitive."
Others amused themselves by feeding Thélyson Orélien's reaction statement into Pangram, claiming (source in French) that it too was "100% AI."
The accusations also drew sceptical responses.
"I don't understand what would be problematic about using AI to write a book in 2026. Not using it would be the stupid thing," wrote (source in French) journalist Jérôme Colombain. "Ghostwriters have always existed. What matters, ultimately, is the author's responsibility," he added in the same post.
For his part, François Negroni (source in French), a writer who openly uses AI to produce books on aeronautics, explains that AI detectors analyse a text "by identifying statistical regularities: distribution of words, syntactic structure, sentence rhythm, lexical predictability." He goes on to say that Thélyson Orélien "doesn't fit into the boxes" of standard French on which the software is trained.
"He writes in a French that critics unanimously describe as 'creolised', mixed with Haitian Creole, Spanish and Portuguese, shot through with orality, aphorisms and rhythms from elsewhere," he argues, while stressing that he "doesn't know" whether the novel was written "wholly or partly with the help of an AI."
Writer Christophe Boutry (source in French) replies that it is "possible" that Pangram picked up on Thélyson Orélien's "creolised" style. "The studies that show bias against non-native speakers concern other detectors, other versions and, above all, English. That does not allow us to claim that Pangram 4 is confusing Haitian French with generated text here."
It should be noted that suspicions of AI use had already been voiced by readers on social media. One such case is that of Alphaleer, on Babelio (source in French). "It's a pity the entire book is written with... artificial intelligence. It gives the impression of being pretty, but it's hollow," this user wrote on 12 September. "The narrator is a sort of shadow, moving from step to step, from one border to another, without anything precise or in-depth," she goes on, pointing to the novel's "major inconsistencies".
On Facebook (source in French), writer Fabrice Colin highlights "stylistic tics that are, to say the least, off-putting," "end-of-chapter aphorisms" and "charming but distinctly questionable metaphors". While insisting he is not accusing the author of using AI and has no opinion on Pangram, he says he is pointing out "writing tics that harm the text", inviting everyone to make up their own mind.
"Balance ton Claude" calls for calm
On Tuesday, the previously obscure "Balance ton Claude" account enjoyed exceptional visibility, and now has more than 6,600 followers.
Late in the evening, the five people said by Radio France to be behind the name posted a final message calling on people to "go easy on the attacks against Thélyson Orélien," acknowledging that "there is a non-zero chance (...) that he is acting in good faith."
The collective then tried to explain its approach, saying it had "flagged this book" because it had "success", while admitting that the author had "a certain merit in managing to produce a coherent narrative that has satisfied many readers."
In their view, "the Paris intelligentsia probably still underestimates what AIs can do" and makes "little or no use of LLMs" – short for "large language models" – nor do they spend time on LinkedIn. This, they say, is why the literary press failed to recognise "the formulaic turns of phrase."
"What is the point for a creator in outsourcing their invention?"
Independent Lyon bookseller Gwilherm Perthuis says he is following the controversy from a distance and not taking sides.
"Obviously, I think it would be catastrophic to write a book by asking a generative AI," the manager of the bookshop L'œil cacodylate told Euronews, adding that this is "the polar opposite of my idea of literary creation, which is a singular, innovative working of language and form."
While, in his view, the machine "will create archetypes based on pre-existing average data," he asks: "In what way can AI help to invent? And what is the point for a creator in outsourcing their invention?"
The bookseller does, however, qualify his remarks, mentioning authors who "rely on AI to prepare their documentation and speed up their research before they start writing, when they need to access complex data."
"For me, that is AI's only real use, (...) its ability to produce almost instant results from among millions of data points that would take us years to sift through ourselves."
Will the "Balance ton Claude" affair derail "C'était ça ou mourir" in its race for the major literary prizes, or will it instead prompt readers who have not yet read it to make up their own minds?
The consequences for the novel's reputation, meanwhile, could quickly become apparent. The Goncourt and Renaudot prizes will be announced on Tuesday 3 November, the day after the Médicis prize. On Wednesday 4 November, it will be the turn of the Femina jury to reveal its winner. Finally, the Renaudot des lycéens and the Goncourt des lycéens will be awarded on Tuesday 17 and Thursday 26 November respectively.

US immigration agency who shot Venezuelan man in Texas didn't use body camera: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:29:51 UTC
18:29:51 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer who shot a Venezuelan man in the US state of Texas on Sunday was a recent recruit who had been issued a body camera but was not using it despite official mandates, The Washington Post reported Tuesday, citing two former US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials.
The officer, who previously worked for another federal law enforcement agency, joined ICE during last year's hiring drive.
Former officials have questioned whether some recruits were adequately vetted and trained. ICE has recently dismissed some new hires over performance issues or other concerns.
ICE Acting Director David Venturella said this summer that all officers would receive body cameras by the end of August. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said earlier this month that the rollout was still incomplete.
DHS has not explained why the officer was not recording, which the agency requires.
 
Shooting and medical care
The victim, Wilber Garces Perez, 28, who worked for food delivery service DoorDash, was shot after ICE officers attempted to stop him in the city of Austin in an unmarked SUV. Garces said he initially did not realize they were law enforcement.
His attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said an ICE vehicle sideswiped Garces' car and struck it again as he tried to make a U-turn. Bystander video shows an officer approaching the vehicle before shots were fired.
DHS called the incident a “dangerous attempt to evade arrest,” saying: “Resisting officers and evading arrest is dangerous for our officers, illegal aliens, and the public.”
Lincoln-Goldfinch questioned the lack of body-camera footage, saying: “You need to answer why your agents are not turning their body cams on.”
ICE later reminded officers that they “must activate” cameras during enforcement activities.
Garces was initially taken to a hospital but was transferred to ICE custody about four hours later with a bullet still lodged near his spine, according to his attorney. He was later taken to another hospital after reporting paralysis on his left side.
“We still do not have clarity about the cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said.
DHS disputed claims that Garces did not get adequate medical care, saying he was receiving pain medication “around the clock.”
 
Immigration case
Garces entered the US legally to seek asylum but later received a final removal order after missing an immigration hearing. His attorney said notice of the hearing was sent to an old address.
She has sued seeking his release and to block his potential deportation to Venezuela. US District Judge Orlando L. Garcia scheduled a hearing for Sept. 30 and ordered Garces to appear, according to court records.
The shooting comes amid increased scrutiny of ICE use of force and traffic stops.
ICE officers fatally shot Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and Colombian immigrant Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero in Maine in July. ICE briefly restricted traffic stop arrests after the Maine shooting but later lifted the measure.

"According to Pangram, this novel was written almost entirely by an artificial intelligence," it claims, saying it had tested several passages from the "manuscript" and almost always obtained "the same result: 100% AI".
According to the people behind the account, the US tool Pangram is "by far the most reliable AI detector", with a "false-positive rate of 0.0041%."
It is a particularly sensitive allegation for the 38-year-old author of Haitian origin, whose novel is being translated into more than 20 languages and has been included on the initial longlists for the Goncourt, Goncourt des lycéens, Femina, Médicis and Renaudot prizes.
The story follows Jonas, a young Haitian history and geography teacher forced to flee his country because of violence and insecurity, on his journey across the Americas. Before this debut novel, published last winter in Quebec and whose rights for French-speaking Europe have been acquired by Grasset, Thélyson Orélien had mainly published poetry.
From "rumours" to "racist attacks"?
Grasset initially insisted it was not paying attention to these "rumours".
"This is fake news. (...) These tools that are supposed to detect AI are themselves AIs that fantasise that the Bible was written artificially," the publisher told BFMTV (source in French) on Tuesday morning.
The publishing house with the yellow covers also said that dozens of AI-written novels are on offer on Amazon but that "none of them is successful" because "not one has any distinctiveness". "The exact opposite of Thélyson," Grasset, owned by the Vivendi group controlled by billionaire Vincent Bolloré, added.
By early Tuesday evening, the scale of the affair prompted Grasset to send a statement to several media outlets, including Euronews, giving the author the floor. In it, Thélyson Orélien explains that the "repetitions" he is accused of, presented as typical of AI-generated text, stem from "a Haitian and Caribbean literary tradition" with its own poetics.
He adds: "People can argue about my style, but turning its devices into proof of artificial intelligence has nothing to do with literary criticism."
The writer also took the opportunity to thank those readers who "make room in their lives" for his book: "In a world where some people always want to check where you come from before listening to what you say, this welcome moves me deeply."
In the same statement, the Grasset team say they are renewing "their absolute confidence" in the author, "against any machine or attempt to measure, standardise or silence writing that is forever free."
Contacted by Euronews, Thélyson Orélien declined to respond to our requests for comment. He did, however, tell Libération (source in French) that he has been the target of "numerous racist attacks" since arriving in France.
AI and a "creolised" language
Before the mainstream media picked it up, the controversy exploded on X. After the first post from "Balance ton Claude", many users relayed the anonymous account's accusations – including in English – as established fact, some even going so far as to mock (source in French) the literary world of criticism for having "fallen for it, hailing as wonderful a style not only written by AI but fundamentally mediocre and repetitive."
Others amused themselves by feeding Thélyson Orélien's reaction statement into Pangram, claiming (source in French) that it too was "100% AI."
The accusations also drew sceptical responses.
"I don't understand what would be problematic about using AI to write a book in 2026. Not using it would be the stupid thing," wrote (source in French) journalist Jérôme Colombain. "Ghostwriters have always existed. What matters, ultimately, is the author's responsibility," he added in the same post.
For his part, François Negroni (source in French), a writer who openly uses AI to produce books on aeronautics, explains that AI detectors analyse a text "by identifying statistical regularities: distribution of words, syntactic structure, sentence rhythm, lexical predictability." He goes on to say that Thélyson Orélien "doesn't fit into the boxes" of standard French on which the software is trained.
"He writes in a French that critics unanimously describe as 'creolised', mixed with Haitian Creole, Spanish and Portuguese, shot through with orality, aphorisms and rhythms from elsewhere," he argues, while stressing that he "doesn't know" whether the novel was written "wholly or partly with the help of an AI."
Writer Christophe Boutry (source in French) replies that it is "possible" that Pangram picked up on Thélyson Orélien's "creolised" style. "The studies that show bias against non-native speakers concern other detectors, other versions and, above all, English. That does not allow us to claim that Pangram 4 is confusing Haitian French with generated text here."
It should be noted that suspicions of AI use had already been voiced by readers on social media. One such case is that of Alphaleer, on Babelio (source in French). "It's a pity the entire book is written with... artificial intelligence. It gives the impression of being pretty, but it's hollow," this user wrote on 12 September. "The narrator is a sort of shadow, moving from step to step, from one border to another, without anything precise or in-depth," she goes on, pointing to the novel's "major inconsistencies".
On Facebook (source in French), writer Fabrice Colin highlights "stylistic tics that are, to say the least, off-putting," "end-of-chapter aphorisms" and "charming but distinctly questionable metaphors". While insisting he is not accusing the author of using AI and has no opinion on Pangram, he says he is pointing out "writing tics that harm the text", inviting everyone to make up their own mind.
"Balance ton Claude" calls for calm
On Tuesday, the previously obscure "Balance ton Claude" account enjoyed exceptional visibility, and now has more than 6,600 followers.
Late in the evening, the five people said by Radio France to be behind the name posted a final message calling on people to "go easy on the attacks against Thélyson Orélien," acknowledging that "there is a non-zero chance (...) that he is acting in good faith."
The collective then tried to explain its approach, saying it had "flagged this book" because it had "success", while admitting that the author had "a certain merit in managing to produce a coherent narrative that has satisfied many readers."
In their view, "the Paris intelligentsia probably still underestimates what AIs can do" and makes "little or no use of LLMs" – short for "large language models" – nor do they spend time on LinkedIn. This, they say, is why the literary press failed to recognise "the formulaic turns of phrase."
"What is the point for a creator in outsourcing their invention?"
Independent Lyon bookseller Gwilherm Perthuis says he is following the controversy from a distance and not taking sides.
"Obviously, I think it would be catastrophic to write a book by asking a generative AI," the manager of the bookshop L'œil cacodylate told Euronews, adding that this is "the polar opposite of my idea of literary creation, which is a singular, innovative working of language and form."
While, in his view, the machine "will create archetypes based on pre-existing average data," he asks: "In what way can AI help to invent? And what is the point for a creator in outsourcing their invention?"
The bookseller does, however, qualify his remarks, mentioning authors who "rely on AI to prepare their documentation and speed up their research before they start writing, when they need to access complex data."
"For me, that is AI's only real use, (...) its ability to produce almost instant results from among millions of data points that would take us years to sift through ourselves."
Will the "Balance ton Claude" affair derail "C'était ça ou mourir" in its race for the major literary prizes, or will it instead prompt readers who have not yet read it to make up their own minds?
The consequences for the novel's reputation, meanwhile, could quickly become apparent. The Goncourt and Renaudot prizes will be announced on Tuesday 3 November, the day after the Médicis prize. On Wednesday 4 November, it will be the turn of the Femina jury to reveal its winner. Finally, the Renaudot des lycéens and the Goncourt des lycéens will be awarded on Tuesday 17 and Thursday 26 November respectively.

Campus Project 2026: Georgia Takes Center Stage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:29:00 UTC
18:29:00 KST

Campus Project 2026: Georgia Takes Center Stage
September 23, 2026
Last June, a group of around 20 young German musicians — members of the Federal Youth Orchestra and Federal Youth Choir — arrived in Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia. They were immediately captivated by the Caucasus metropolis and its overwhelming atmosphere of relaxed freedom.
But that freedom can be deceptive. Everyone was aware of Georgia's tense political and social situation and had seen images of the pro-European protests in Tbilisi.
The next morning, the German musicians gathered in a simple room in central Tbilisi with an equally sized group of young Georgian musicians from the Tbilisi Youth Orchestra as well as singers from the independent music scene.
Finding a Shared Sound
The young musicians from Georgia and members of the Federal Youth Orchestra first met in June in Tbilisi to rehearse for the joint "Campus Concert" at the Beethovenfest in Bonn.
But before that, they had to find a shared sound and develop a program that would bring together two major musical traditions from the two countries.
"We Georgians are known as hot-blooded Southerners with a lot of raw emotion," says Mirian Kokhunaishvili, conductor and artistic director of the project. "Sometimes the intensity of our emotions is higher than in German music. But once you listen to German music, you understand that people are full of emotions there, too, but there's different approaches to how we express them. In music, I couldn't see any differences."
After final rehearsals in Bonn, joint concerts will take place on Sept. 23 and 24: first at the Beethovenfest in Bonn and the following day in Berlin. DW will broadcast the concert live on the DW Classical Music YouTube channel.
A Political Message Behind the Music
The Campus project is about more than an exciting musical experiment — and not just for the Georgian participants.
"One goal is to bring the classical repertoire of Georgian music closer to an international audience," says Mirian Kokhunaishvili. "And then we want to send a message. We couldn't simply play and sing without reflecting the reality around us."
For Kokhunaishvili, the music itself is the strongest message: "Our concert is about the geopolitical reality we live in. We want to express our hope for Europe — not just the hope of joining something somewhere, but that this is our shared home. We are fighting to belong there. The core message is that in Georgia, we share Western European values of human rights."
A highlight of the program is a new synthesis arranged by Georgian composer Mika Mdinaradze. The composition combines Beethoven's choral piece "Europa steht!" ("Europe Stands!") from the cantata "The Glorious Moment" with traditional Georgian songs.
"Beethoven naturally remains unmistakable, while the Georgian polyphonic structures preserve their own identity," Mdinaradze explains in an interview with DW. "Together, they create a sonic model of Europe — a dialogue instead of forced unity — a musical declaration of where Georgia belongs."
Making a Statement Through Campus
Since 2001, the Beethovenfest Bonn has organized the Campus project, a platform for exchange among young musicians, with a focus on countries experiencing historic transformation.
"Previous projects have included Ukraine, Afghanistan, Iran and now, for the second time, Georgia — after first participating in 2003," says Thomas Scheider, who leads the Campus project team at the Beethovenfest. "These are places where culture is not simply a side effect of history, but becomes a central field where history is understood, negotiated and questioned."
For the Federal Youth Orchestra (BJO), which has been a partner in shaping the Campus project for 10 years, the encounter also went far beyond music. "Although music is naturally at the center, the exchange showed so much more: personal connections, cultural richness, significant history, impressive nature and also the challenging current political situation," says Sönke Lentz, orchestra director of the BJO and one of the project organizers. "Pro-European artists and what is likely the vast majority of the population need our solidarity and support."
The Federal Youth Orchestra also incorporated the Campus project into this year's international tour, performing three concerts in Georgia under the direction of Mirian Khukhunaishvili and featuring soloist Giorgi Gigashvili. "Sold-out venues in Tbilisi and Kutaisi, with standing ovations, impressed us and showed us the importance of a project like this," says Sönke Lentz.
Tsotne Zedginidze: Georgian Prodigy and Campus Composer
"The new Mozart" — that is how none other than conductor Daniel Barenboim described Georgian pianist and composer Tsotne Zedginidze when he was just 16 years old.
Zedginidze has just turned 17, making him the project's youngest commissioned composer in the project's history. He composed "Chmebi: Georgian Fantasia" for piano and chamber orchestra. The Georgian word "chmebi" means "voices." The young composer himself will play piano at at the world premiere in Bonn and the subsequent performance in Berlin. "Beethoven would be completely shocked, but it would inspire him," Tsotne says with a smile about his work and the project as a whole.
In his score, Zedginidze draws on ancient, complex Georgian folk traditions for the first time, combining them with unconventional harmonies and fiery folk dance elements. "About my Georgian Fantasia, I tried not to be artificial. It resembles as much as possible Georgian music — all Genres and styles. But at the same time, it's my individual understanding, my own interpretation of Georgian music," he tells DW
Star violinist Lisa Batiashvili is eagerly awaiting the premiere of Tsotne's work. Through her foundation ((name of the foundation?)), the musician, who moved from Georgia to Germany at age 12, supports young artists in her home country. Tsotne is among the foundation's scholarship recipients.
"Over the past 20 years, I have been able to witness how the friendship between Germany and Georgia has grown and how openly and with such interest people here have approached my home country," says Batiashvili. "It is especially beautiful to see young musicians from both countries making music together, learning from each other and inspiring one another." And perhaps, Batiashvili says, something greater than music can emerge from this: a vision of a shared future.

UK charges doctor over Rwandan genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:28:19 UTC
18:28:19 KST

UK charges doctor over Rwandan genocide
A former Rwandan health official has been charged by British prosecutors over his alleged role in the 1994 genocide in his home country, bringing the first UK charges linked to the massacre.
Vincent Brown, formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, appeared in a London court on Tuesday. He faces one charge of conduct ancillary to genocide and six of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity. Prosecutors allege Brown, 65, led a group to a house in Kigali’s Rugenge district on April 8 and ordered three people shot. They say he subsequently ordered the killing of a woman and her infant son, and directed a group that stoned a taxi driver to death. Brown denies involvement.
“Dr. Brown… is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others,” chief crown prosecutor Frank Ferguson said.
More than 800,000 people, predominantly Tutsis and moderate Hutus, were killed in roughly 100 days after the genocide began on April 7, 1994. The UN tribunal established afterward indicted 93 people.
Brown, a physician, headed the family health department at Rwanda’s National Office of Population when the genocide began. He later moved to Britain as an asylum seeker and took the name Vincent Brown after gaining British citizenship in 2004. Rwanda sought his extradition, but UK courts refused over concerns that he would not receive a fair trial there. The British investigation began in 2019 following a request from Kigali. Brown, who denies involvement, is due back in court on October 9 after being released on £25,000 ($33,400) bail. His lawyer, Sam Blom-Cooper, described the killings as “appalling crimes” and said Brown welcomed the charges as an opportunity to clear his name, according to Reuters.
Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo welcomed the UK charges as a “long overdue” step toward accountability and urged Britain to speed up its remaining cases, local daily New Times reported. President Paul Kagame has previously accused the international community of failing to stop the killings, saying it failed Rwanda “whether from contempt or cowardice.”
The UK case follows prosecutions of suspects in other countries. In 2024, a French court upheld former Rwandan gendarme Philippe Hategekimana’s life sentence for organizing roadblocks and taking part in massacres around Nyanza. A Belgian court sentenced former militia leader Seraphin Twahirwa to life in 2023 for directing killings in Kigali and raping Tutsi women. Germany arrested another suspect, identified as Innocent S., in July on suspicion of complicity in genocide and involvement in 25 murders.
Rwandan businessman Felicien Kabuga, accused of financing militias and using his radio station to incite attacks on Tutsis, died in UN tribunal custody in May before his trial reached a verdict.

Three international bodies warn of risks of rising debt and soaring borrowing in major economies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
09:27:52 UTC
18:27:52 KST

Three heavyweight international bodies have issued stark warnings about the risks of rising debt levels and soaring borrowing costs across large economies.
The Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the International Institute of Finance (IIF), the voice of global banking, on Wednesday highlighted the dangers of soaring interest rates on $365tn (£275tn) in global borrowing.
In its quarterly debt monitor, the IIF predicted a “structurally debt-intensive future” as governments and companies scramble to invest in new technologies and bear the costs of ageing societies.
“The buildup in global debt is set to accelerate as governments and corporates compete to boost growth and secure their positions in an economy reshaped by structural changes,” it said.
It compared the current status of some of the world’s largest economies, including the UK, with crisis-hit emerging countries.
“The US, France, the UK, and Japan face persistently large deficits and rising interest expenses – challenges long associated with debt-distressed emerging market sovereigns.”
With many politicians facing elections in the coming months, and belt-tightening unlikely to be popular with voters, it said: “The risk is that already-unsustainable debt trajectories continue to deteriorate.”
While in New York this week for the UN general assembly, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, denied reports that he had been shocked by the parlous state of the public finances since he came to power in July.
“It’s not the case that we were surprised when we came in, not least because I was in access talks and understood very clearly the position,” he told reporters. “The truth of the matter is that because of the situation in the Middle East, the position changed, and has changed over the time I’ve been in. That’s just the reality of the situation that we’re in.”
The IIF’s warning came as the OECD highlighted the rising cost of servicing government debts as one key risk to the global economy in the coming months.
In its interim economic outlook the OECD said global growth had been more resilient than expected given the strains of the US-Israel war on Iran.
However, presenting the report, its secretary general, Mathias Cormann, warned: “Fiscal and financial risks have grown. Thirty-year government bond yields are at their highest in 15 years or more in six of the G7 economies. That means higher debt-servicing costs for governments whose budgets are already under strain, and it means higher borrowing costs for businesses and households.”
His words echoed a warning by the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, Kristalina Georgieva, who told the BBC the world’s advanced economies must take action to reduce their borrowing and bring down debt levels.
Georgieva said a succession of global economic shocks had been “pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven”, with governments taking “no action to contain that service cost. [It’s] time to take that action,” Georgieva said, adding that courage was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.
In its quarterly forecast update, the OECD highlighted the better-than-expected growth performance of the global economy this year but warned that the recent resurgence in oil and gas prices posed risks for the coming months.
“Global economic prospects remain heavily dependent on whether a durable resolution to the Middle East conflict is achieved,” it said.
It projected global economic growth of 2.9% this year – a modest 0.1 percentage point upgrade from the 2.8% it forecast in June. At the same time, it trimmed the outlook for next year slightly, from 3.1% to 3%.
It also identified the record-breaking El Niño weather system – expected to be the strongest in 1,000 years – as a “significant downside risk” to the global economy, warning that it could hit agricultural production and push up food prices.Looking at the UK, the OECD significantly cut its inflation forecast for this year, from 3.7% to 3.1%, after prices rose less dramatically than expected.
Economic growth for the UK is forecast at 1.1% for 2026, up from the 0.9% it had forecast in June and 0.7% in March, “with consumption expected to be supported by newly announced government support measures”.

SBI chairman C S Setty said at the SBI Banking and Economics Conclave in Mumbai on Wednesday.
MUMBAI: India’s financial system will need to evolve to finance the country’s next phase of economic expansion, with banks playing a larger role in supporting higher-value manufacturing, new technologies, the green transition and enterprises seeking to compete globally, SBI chairman C S Setty said at the SBI Banking and Economics Conclave in Mumbai on Wednesday.“The banking and financial system will need to evolve alongside it, providing the financial architecture that enables innovation, investment, and strength,” Setty said, referring to India’s transition towards becoming a leading economic force.Setty said India’s resilience through successive global and domestic headwinds had strengthened the financial system’s ability to participate in the next stage of economic expansion. India has the talent, entrepreneurial energy and technological capabilities to participate meaningfully in these sectors, he said.“The larger opportunity lies in translating these trends into businesses, technologies, manufacturing capabilities, and intellectual property that can command a global footprint,” Setty said.This transition will require the financial sector to support innovation and investment as the economy moves towards higher-value manufacturing and globally competitive enterprises. The banking sector, he said, would have a significant role in enhancing infrastructure, enterprise and innovation as part of the broader transformation of the productive economy.

Setty said the discussions should result not just in fresh perspectives but in ideas that could contribute to the country's next phase of development.
