Flags over Spitsbergen. What Arctic Biennale Expedition leaves on archipelago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:55:28 UTC
17:55:28 KST

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS Correspondents Konstantin Malykh, Maria Kartuz/. The Arctic Biennale art and scientific got to the Spitsbergen Archipelago onboard the Professor Molchanov scientific-research vessel. Despite the alarming situation around Norway's arrest of the ship, over a week on the archipelago, participants in the project, organized by Alexander Ponomarev's Free Elements Arts Center, were working on all the planned installations. This material by TASS is about what the artists left in Barentsburg and with what they were leaving the archipelago.
This story has no global analogues yet. Never before have artists, scientists, philosophers, and public figures embarked on a journey to explore the Arctic waters. The project's geography fascinates imagination with its high latitudes locations - Spitsbergen, Franz Josef Land, and the North Pole - these are just some points on the map that the biennale has planned.
"One of our mottos is "Mobile Within Mobile," because this is movement, process, action...," the expedition's leader, artist Alexander Ponomarev said.
Traveling to the Arctic
The traveling began early in the morning in Moscow, when the expedition participants got onto a big bus and departed for Murmansk. The trip was two days with an overnight accommodation in Petrozavodsk. The artists did not waste time and made quick sketches during short stops. Styles differ: while Katya Sergeeva was drawing with almost photographic precision, Karina Batrachenko used lines and geometric shapes.
The Professor Molchanov departed on the expedition from Murmansk at night. The voyage was due to be about three days long. The passengers quickly coped with the rolling (got "rolled up," as sailors say), and the expedition work continued. Oceanographers Sergey Pisarev and Alexey Sokov told everyone about the seas they are passing, explained why water in those sees did not freeze up, and shared curious and smart stories. Artists Marina Belova and Alexei Politov were particularly impressed by a story about the experiment to relocate penguins to the Far North. They call themselves "penguins of the world" and were taking to Spitsbergen a light installation dedicated to these symbols of the Antarctica. It was to be installed in the Barentsburg Museum (the center of Russia's presence in Spitsbergen), and, artists hoped, it would correct the unfair situation that their beloved pets were not represented in the Arctic.
The Prowling Art Group, having received the captain's permission, was installing a big dark figure on the forecastle (the front of the ship) - that was a visual part of their Pilot project, which was to be installed on the shore later on. According to Daria Dogaeva, their pilot could find ways when all regular landmarks cannot be seen. However, the Professor Molchanov's crew did not need help - after three and a half days of travel, the ship docked at Spitsbergen.
Arts shore
It took about three to four days to install most of the objects. The archipelago has many restrictions due to the fragile Arctic environment: whatever temporary objects further on must disappear without a trace, and whatever remaining installations must fit seamlessly the laconic architecture and strict regulations. One of such objects was the Arrow of Time by architect Totan Kuzembaev at Cape Heer. The object, which is based on a crane boom and coils from cables, is about time, memory, the Arctic's industrial development and present.
The Doomsday Light Storage Facility will remain in the Barentsburg coal mine. The installation by Vladimir Nasedkin and Tatiana Badanina consists of two parts: the first part is two four-meter-high snow-white figures on a mountain that "collect" light. The second part is five massive sarcophagi, where the collected light is "stored". The authors explained: it's not about just the lighting, it is about the light, love and warmth that are inside every person - if suddenly they disappear off the face of the Earth, their supply for new generations will remain available underground.
Marina Rin, the biennale curator, installed a "stone" whale on debris of the old whaling yard at Cape Finneset. According to her, this is a topo-myth - a legend predicting the Arctic Biennale: "The whale's shape is that of an ancient rock, on which all our projects are drawn in petroglyphs," Marina explained.
Giant flags are fluttering on that cape. This is Alexander Ponomarev's Telegraph of Momentary Joy. It is installed on the communications tower's remaining fragments. The colored flags resemble polar poppies, as they are turning the radio station debris into a live communication line between land and sea, into flashes of light in the coming polar night.
The Observatory is another "communication point" for the biennale term. This is a pavilion assembled on the shore from a huge old fuel barrel and road concrete slabs, where the roof is an openwork structure resembling the famous Shukhov Tower. Over the expedition, it was an exhibition space, and later on it will become an observation deck for Barentsburg's residents and visitors.
Artist Katerina Kovaleva found herself into a difficult situation. Her project - The Camp of Lost Expeditions - was planned for the abandoned village of Piramida. There is no road to there, and the only way to get to the village is by water from Barentsburg, while the arrested Professor Molchanov was still chained to the dock. However, Spitsbergen is a special territory. The locals say, wishes made here do come true. So, here is Katerina uploading the installation into a helicopter, heading for the old village. On the return flight, she brought photos and impressions.
"In an abandoned dining room in Piramida now there is a Camp of Lost Expeditions. I have fixed a parachute under the ceiling. On it there are three schooners of the Brusilov, Sedov and Rusanov expeditions. Their fate was tragic. Under the dome, I laid a table for 40 people: metal bowls, glasses covered with granite "bread". The table is ready, but no one will sit at it," the artist said.
Interestingly, it was thanks to Katerina that Otto Schmidt's personal belongings were brought to Spitsbergen for the first time. The artist has received them from the famous polar explorer's great-grandchildren. "Unfortunately," she said, "I couldn't bring many more, and some of the items will be presented during the Arctic Biennale's second stage."
During the biennale week, in small Barentsburg everything was literally filled with art. Even the word was visualized in an art object by artist Sergey Katran. There is no word for "art" in the Russian-Nenets dictionary. The artist asked native speakers to find new words for "art." They came up with neologisms like "valeybzo", "paskoyvava", "hale of the year". The artist recorded the new words' sound vibrations and depicted them as ice figures. The material, imitating ice, highlights the language vulnerability and the risk of its disappearance, the author said.
The expedition participants brought about 30 new art objects to Barentsburg. In addition to earlier mentioned objects, those were The Ear of God by Vladimir Chernyshev, The Rooks Have Arrived by Nikolay Polissky, The Extract of Joy by Evgeny Sautkin, The Art-Arctic by Sergey Serov, Is It Really Me? By Katya Sergeeva, The Wasteland by Karina Batrachenko, The Germination by Anna Lapshinova, The Room by Yulia Nemova, We Hear Through the Wind by the Prowling Art Group, The Imaginary Museum by Katerina Kovaleva, a capsule collection of Arctic Linen by Katerina Terekhova, and The Cover by Alexander Konstantinov.
The Arktikatarsis installation by Vladimir Kuzmin was the project's symbolic unifying line. The work created from mining helmets on the village's main observation deck was based on the most recognizable architectural proportion: the golden ratio. "The symbol of labor in Barentsburg becomes part of the artistic idea and designates differently this place in the Arctic landscape," the artist said.
Right on the last day of the artists' visit to the archipelago, they opened the most complex and big-scale object - The Drunken Ship by Alexander Ponomarev. The composition, about 20 m high, is a system of masts, yards and sails on a sloop mounted on a port crane boom. The structure is made of the so-called thrown timber. "These logs have traveled a long and mysterious route in salt water. They have become strong and durable, like art that has passed many challenges," the Arctic Biennale's leader Alexander Ponomarev said.
The first part of the Arctic Biennale in Spitsbergen finished on time, despite the Professor Molchanov's arrest. All participants in the expedition have returned home safely, and now they are preparing expositions for the next stage, which is scheduled for December in Nizhny Novgorod at the branch of the Pushkin State Fine Arts Museum (Arsenal).

Fox caught after second rescue call to Viru shopping center
Last Friday morning, the Emergency Response Center was once again notified that a fox was running around the third floor of the parking garage at the Viru shopping center in Tallinn.
According to the Northern Rescue Center's press office, security guards at Viru attempted to catch the animal themselves, but the fox hid between structural elements. Rescuers who arrived to help were also unable to catch it, either with snares or with a net. They decided not to break the wall and to return once the animal came out of its hiding place.
A little over an hour later, rescuers were called back to the shopping center, and this time they managed to catch the fox and release it into the forest.
A week earlier, on the morning of 11 September, a fox had also been spotted on the third floor of Viru. On that occasion, the shopping center's security guards managed to catch the animal before rescuers arrived. The rescuers placed the fox in a cage and took it to the forest.

China's new travel rules unsettle tech giants and talent
September 23, 2026
For decades, China has faced accusations from the United States and the European Union of stealing their technology.
From robotics and advanced semiconductors to precision engineering and automotive parts, Chinese firms have recruited top engineers, allegedly spied on Western rivals and been linked to cyberattacks aimed at gaining access to valuable trade secrets.
It is perhaps ironic, then, that China is now taking steps to prevent its own high-end technologies and talent from escaping abroad.
China's Great Wall around its top brains
Last week, new entry-exit rules took effect, giving Chinese authorities the power to stop engineers, founders and other specialists from leaving the country if their expertise in batteries, rare earths or artificial intelligence (AI) is judged a threat to "industrial and technological security."
Recently, China has also tightened outbound-investment rules, cracked down on Chinese nationals holding their wealth offshore and restricted the posting of technical staff overseas.
Henry Gao, a law professor at Singapore Management University (SMU), believes that, taken together, the curbs "offer a rare glimpse into the true state of China's economy."
"These measures suggest that Beijing is deeply concerned about economic weakness and substantial capital outflows," Gao told DW, adding that authorities are also determined to stop "entrepreneurs and skilled personnel from leaving the country."
The strain on China's economy is increasingly hard to hide. While demand for exports remains strong — especially for high-tech goods — the country's property crash has severely weakened domestic consumption.
Bank lending fell to a record low over the summer, and new car sales in August dropped nearly a quarter year-on-year.
Beijing blocks deals, founders seek exit
The same anxiety now extends to people and money leaving. The most prominent recent example is Manus, an AI startup created by two Chinese nationals in Beijing. Last year, the company moved its headquarters to Singapore, partly to avoid US investment curbs and expand into global markets.
When Facebook owner Meta tried to acquire Manus last December for $2 billion (€1.74 billion), Beijing blocked the move and barred the firm's two founders from leaving the country.
Just this month, Chinese social media has been awash with rumors that Huawei founder and CEO Ren Zhengfei and his daughter, CFO Meng Wanzhou, may have left the country.
The claims were picked up by Taiwanese and Indian media outlets. On Wednesday, however, Chinese-language media shared a photo of Ren in Shenzhen a day earlier, signing a cooperation deal with a Chinese automaker.
Wealthy Chinese struggle to get capital out
Bloomberg Intelligence estimated that some $1 trillion in Chinese wealth had exited the country last year — the largest amount of "hot money" leaving since 2006, when records began.
Beijing has not tightened its annual $50,000 foreign-exchange quota that households may take out of the country. What has tightened, says Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific at French investment bank Natixis, are the unofficial routes the wealthy used around that cap.
"They haven't changed the $50,000 quota. They are now squeezing the people and agents that money usually travels with," Garcia-Herrero told DW.
An entire industry has grown up, in China and abroad, to help people get themselves and their capital out. Emigration agents arrange visas and relocations, while offshore brokers and trusts help Chinese nationals to park wealth overseas.
Companies sometimes use a foreign subsidiary, a listing or a staff posting to take money and know-how out together.
New rules may spur workarounds
SMU's Gao believes the new curbs may prove counterproductive, as the more difficult it becomes to move capital or people abroad, the greater the incentive for those with the means to find other ways out.
"Over time, that could further erode confidence, accelerate capital flight and deepen the very economic problems the measures are intended to contain," Gao told DW.
Garcia-Herrero, meanwhile, thinks the block on talent will matter more than the squeeze on capital.
"You can still move money slowly, with approvals," she told DW. "You cannot easily replace a process engineer who cannot board a plane — or who will not take an overseas job because of an indefinite ban."
AI talent now needs permission to fly
The risk is already hitting China's AI firms, which are fast catching up with their US rivals in the race to produce the most advanced AI systems.
In May, Bloomberg reported that Chinese authorities now required top AI researchers, founders and executives at firms like Alibaba and DeepSeek to obtain approval before traveling abroad.
Last year, some DeepSeek staff were asked to hand in their passports, according to tech news site The Information. Beijing has neither confirmed nor denied the practice.
Bloomberg reported in January last year that other tech engineers face similar pressure, including those helping foreign firms cut their reliance on China by building factories in Vietnam and India.
Lawyers and officials tighten legal advice
For foreign nationals, both Chinese and foreign firms sometimes disguise a working visit to China to avoid scrutiny and visa delays. They may suggest a trip is for tourism, business meetings or a factory tour rather than actual work.
Ahead of the new curbs, international law firms like DLA Piper advised companies to keep visa filings "truthful" and "complete," warning that a mismatch between the paperwork and the actual work could now mean an entry ban of up to five years.
The new rules state that a visitor should, in principle, be told if they are banned. However, Chinese authorities may withhold notification if it "may affect national security or the investigation of criminal cases."
In an updated travel advisory earlier this month, the US State Department went further, warning Americans to "exercise increased caution in mainland China due to ... the use of exit bans without a fair and transparent process under the law, and the risk of unjust arrest or detention."

Editor's note: This article was first published on September 23, 2026 and was updated shortly after to reflect new reporting on the whereabouts of Huawei's founder.

Airbus seeks space collaboration with Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:53:55 UTC
17:53:55 KST

Airbus Defense and Space seeks to expand its collaboration with Türkiye to benefit from the country’s existing satellite expertise and to accelerate domestic technological capabilities.
Carlo Mirra, sales director of Airbus’ corporate business growth and development unit, told Anadolu that the company monitors Türkiye’s expanding focus and growing industrial capacity in the space sector.
Mirra said the aerospace ties between the firm and Türkiye could expand further via direct industrial collaboration or intergovernmental agreements involving Türkiye, the European Space Agency (ESA), the European Commission, or Airbus’ founding nations.
These discussions came to the fore as Türkiye prepares to host the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC 2026) in the southwestern city of Antalya under the coordination of the Industry and Technology Ministry and the Turkish Space Agency, with Anadolu serving as global communications partner.
Mirra expressed strong excitement about the event, noting that he has never visited Antalya before.
Mirra noted that he began working with the IAC and the International Astronautical Federation (IAF) in 1989 and currently chairs the federation’s industrial relations committee while managing ESA business relations at Airbus.
“I'm dealing primarily with European business, although I have a past in international business, especially in the US; nevertheless, we are observing here the rapid growth of the political attention and also industrial capacity in Türkiye, and as you know, our company in particular has been present in Türkiye for quite a while,” he said.
“The release of the National Space Program, the space plan, the flight of the astronauts, the ambition to have independent access to space are all important messages that the current political administration in Türkiye are giving in order to let the local industry develop and also emerge in the international environment,” he added.
Mirra stated that the IAC serves as a springboard to achieve this goal, with over 1,800 abstracts already submitted by Turkish institutions for the technical conference.
“This is providing a direct channel for Turkish researchers and industries also to present their technologies, the progress of their studies, to a truly international environment – from green propulsion to small satellite architectures, I think that this will be a very interesting confrontation for all of them,” he said.
He noted that both established firms and startups will meet international prime contractors and investors during the event.
He emphasized that establishing space diplomacy leadership is key, adding that hosting IAC 2026 demonstrates credibility in operating within a global environment.
“Türkiye is really committed to play a major role in this area, and this is proven also by the organization and investment into these events, and I think that this is providing, in terms of international cooperation, in terms of space sustainability and security, a very strong message in order to reinforce existing relationships and create new ones,” he said.
 
Türkiye has resources, manpower to develop capacity
 
Mirra highlighted that Türkiye boasts a population of 85 million people with an average age of 33, contrasting sharply with aging European demographics.
“This is a phenomenal potential to educate the space engineers and the scientists of the next decade – you have the resources (and) the manpower to develop this capacity,” he said.
“Europe is aging fast, we have ambitions in terms of programs, but the difficulty is in finding and educating qualified engineers,” he added.
Mirra noted that Türkiye’s capacity to cultivate motivated experts will fuel its long-term economic and technological objectives.
“And I'm sure that a conference like the IAC will have a very positive effect, especially with students and young generations,” he added.
Mirra stated that Airbus representatives in Ankara work at their permanent office to advance partnership-focused models.
He confirmed that negotiations with the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye (TUBITAK) remain underway.
“I observe three to four areas – there are some where the cooperation may be more direct and involved, certainly in lunar exploration,” he said, referring to ongoing talks between Airbus and TUBITAK on lunar exploration, human spaceflight, and satellite communications.
Mirra noted that Airbus played a key role in boosting capacity through the Turksat satellite program, where the aerospace giant aims to broaden its footprint.
“That is certainly an area where we would like to maintain the relationship and possibly also broaden that, either as a sort of industrial cooperation, but also under a government-to-government partnership – you know, if there is a Turkish government, for example, making a deal with the European Commission or with ESA or with some of the mother countries of Airbus, namely France, Germany, Spain, and UK, that is certainly something where we have an interest, so that is a development that we are observing with a lot of attention,” he added.

Von der Leyen says Hungary 'strengthened rule of law', unlocks €4.2bn in EU funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:53:52 UTC
17:53:52 KST

The European Commission has unlocked €4.2 billion in cohesion funds for Hungary and reopened Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe access, after PM Péter Magyar's government met EU rule-of-law conditions. Brussels froze the funds in 2022 over corruption and procurement concerns under the Orbán government.
The European Commission has unfrozen €4.2 billion in previously blocked cohesion funds for Hungary, judging that Budapest has addressed earlier rule-of-law breaches. The move also clears the way for Hungary to rejoin the Erasmus+ student exchange programme and the Horizon Europe research funding initiative.
In 2022, the EU suspended €6.3 billion in cohesion funding to Hungary under the conditionality mechanism, citing shortcomings in the country's anti-corruption framework, conflicts of interest, and systemic irregularities in public procurement.
Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who won a landslide election victory in April, had campaigned on a promise to unlock EU funds suspended during Viktor Orbán's 16-year rule.
"Hungary has taken important steps to strengthen the rule of law and protect the Union's financial interests," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
"Today, we are proposing to unlock €4.2 billion and reopen the doors of Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe to Hungarian students and researchers. I am glad that they will once again fully benefit from the opportunities our Union creates. This shows that reforms deliver results."
In May, Magyar and von der Leyen agreed to release €16.4 billion in EU funding on the condition that the country met key rule-of-law milestones. In total, Hungary was required to deliver on 27 so-called "super milestones" and more than 100 others.
In late August, Hungary announced it had met all of the conditions, including resolving the situation surrounding public interest trusts (KEKVA) — a legal structure the previous government had used to take control of public institutions such as universities.
Beyond the €4.2 billion released, Hungary is also seeking to withdraw €10 billion in recovery funds; the Commission's assessment of that request is ongoing.
A further €2 billion in cohesion funding remains blocked over concerns about the asylum system, child protection law, and academic freedom. Magyar has pledged to resolve these issues by the end of the year.

Three shooters killed at least 11 people including a woman who was believed to be pregnant in an attack at a house party in South Africa, police said on Wednesday.
Three others were wounded in the mass shooting late on Tuesday night in KwaMakhutha township around 30km (19 miles) south of the city of Durban on the east coast.
The people had gathered at the house for a party when the suspects entered the house and opened fire, police said. Ten people, including the pregnant woman, died at the scene and an 11th was declared dead at the hospital.
Authorities did not immediately give out details on the condition of the three people who were wounded.

Belgium faces worst drought in decades as water levels fall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:49:44 UTC
17:49:44 KST

Melike Pala
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Belgium is facing its driest period in decades, with prolonged rainfall shortages raising concerns over drinking water production, particularly in Brussels, according to the Royal Meteorological Institute (KMI).
The country is facing a significant precipitation deficit, with around 80% of its territory affected, KMI meteorologist Pascal Mormal told public broadcaster VRT on Wednesday.
The situation is particularly severe in southern Belgium, while some areas of West Flanders and Limburg have recorded closer-to-normal rainfall levels.
In Uccle, a Brussels municipality where the KMI maintains a long-term observation station, only around 21 to 22 millimeters of rain is expected this month, compared with a normal monthly average of about 65 millimeters.
Mormal said no substantial rainfall is expected in the short term, with significant precipitation potentially not arriving until November.
"For such a long, uninterrupted period of drought, we have to go all the way back to the 1970s," Mormal said, adding that the current situation is comparable to the drought of 2018 but could worsen if the dry conditions continue.
The prolonged drought is also affecting water production.
Vivaqua, the company responsible for supplying drinking water to Brussels and several municipalities in Wallonia and Flanders, may have to further reduce water extraction at its Profondeville facility along the Meuse River.
The facility accounts for around 30% of Vivaqua's water supply.
The drought is also affecting municipalities across the Wallonia Region.
Restrictions on drinking water consumption are currently in place in 17 municipalities, while tanker trucks have been deployed in Libramont, in the Luxembourg province, to help secure local water supplies.
In Flanders, authorities have so far maintained a code-yellow drought alert, calling for increased vigilance without introducing additional measures.
Meteorologists expect wetter conditions in November and December, but officials caution that prolonged, steady rainfall will be needed to replenish depleted water resources.
Heavy downpours alone may not be sufficient, as much of the water can run off rapidly rather than replenish groundwater and other reserves.

UK economic outlook brighter as new government measures will boost growth, says OECD
The outlook for the UK economy has brightened, according to the Paris-based OECD, with inflation lower than expected while new government support measures are likely to boost growth.
The think tank has significantly cut its inflation forecast for this year, from 3.7% to 3.1%, after prices rose less dramatically than expected.
Economic growth for the UK is forecast at 1.1% for 2026, up from the 0.9% it had forecast in June and 0.7% in March, “with consumption expected to be supported by newly announced government support measures”.
In response, the chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said:
Despite unprecedented pressures and conflict in both the Middle East and in Europe, the UK economy is showing strong resilience.
We will face these challenges together and we are already giving families space to breathe. We had the fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of the year and we are starting the big, long-term changes needed to create good jobs and growth in every postcode.
Andy Burnham, who became the UK prime minister on 20 July, announced a cut in VAT on electricity bills as one of his first policy measures on coming to power in July, and has suggested there may be more measures to give consumers “breathing space” in next month’s budget.
Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, have seen UK borrowing costs rise sharply amid turmoil in global bond markets as ongoing conflicts have disrupted the oil supplies, driving up inflation.
The world’s advanced economies have been warned they need to take action to reduce their borrowing and bring down debt levels, at a time of surging government borrowing costs, according to the head of the International Monetary Fund.
Kristalina Georgieva told the BBC that global economic shocks had been “pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven” despite governments taking “no action to contain that service cost. [It’s] time to take that action,” Georgieva said, adding that courage was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.

Chip-related companies saw their shares slide, with AMD down 2.1%, Nvidia losing 1.1% and Intel 3.2% lower.
Meta Platforms shares rose 1.3%, adding to its 10% plus jump this week as its new personal AI agent Muse has been a hit.

Business growth in the US has picked up to its fastest pace in more than five years and hiring also rose sharply in September, while price pressures also intensified.
The composite PMI output index from S&P Global, a closely-watched monthly survey, rose to 58.4 from 56 in August.
The services business activity rose to 58.7 from 56.5 while the manufacturing output index leapt to 56.7 from 53.1. Any reading above 50 indicates expansion.
Employment rose sharply, with jobs added at a pace not seen for over four years, as firms sought to meet rising demand. Backlogs of work continued to rise at an increased rate and supply chain delays intensified, pointing to a lack of operating capacity which fed through to higher prices.
Input costs surged on the back of the recent spike in energy prices, adding to a worsening inflation picture.
Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said:
US business continues to boom, with output growing at the fastest rate for over five years in September. Historical comparisons suggest that the latest survey data point to annualized growth of around 5% with a 4% gain now signalled for the third quarter as a whole.
To put the growth surge in context, barring the spike in demand following the opening up of the economy after the COVID-19 lockdowns, the latest improvement in business activity is the greatest recorded since early 2015. Business is clearly booming now in both manufacturing and services.
However, this growth is being accompanied by some of the most severe supply chain bottlenecks seen in the near-two-decade survey history if the pandemic is excluded, with companies also reporting increasing problems finding suitable staff.
Backlogs of work are consequently rising sharply. While this accumulation of uncompleted orders bodes well for the further expansion of output and capacity in the coming months, it also indicates that companies are developing more pricing power, and hence is a worry for the inflation outlook.
Firms’ input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher thanks to the rise in oil prices seen during the month, which will add further to the upward pressure on selling prices and inflation in the coming months.
Ryanair: Air fares in Europe will rise by up to 10%-20% next summer
Gwyn Topham
Air fares in Europe will rise “dramatically” next summer, by as much as 10%-20%, Ryanair has forecast, with airlines unable to absorb continued high oil prices.
Ryanair chief executive Michael O’Leary said a lack of refinery capacity meant jet fuel was likely to stay 40% higher than crude oil, and predicted several airlines could go bust this winter.
He said Ryanair itself would trim its capacity in the coming months, sending fares upwards, to avoid the high cost of unhedged fuel, around 20% of its fuel needs.
He added:
If I was planning a holiday I’d be booking [flights] today. There is only one way air fares in Europe are going next summer and that is dramatically upwards.
Speaking at a press conference in London, O’Leary repeated his calls for the sacking of Nats chief executive, Martin Rolfe, after the latest outages of air traffic control services in September.
He said Ryanair was calling for “urgent reform of failing UK Nats. What we mean by urgent reform: sack Martin Rolfe.”
The government has tasked the CAA to investigate Nats’ explanations for the major outage on 8 September, blaming a “millisecond’s software fault” for disruption to hundreds of thousands of passengers’ flights. The CAA is due to report next March.
O’Leary said:
We don’t need six months to learn lessons. The fundamental lesson to learn about Nats is it has an incompetent, overpaid CEO who needs to be dismissed.
He said Ryanair’s costs had run to 4-5million euros, and the airline was still seeking compensation in court for the 2023 Nats outage.
O’Leary meanwhile addressed his own recent €150m bonus deal, which was opposed by 40% of shareholders at Ryanair’s AGM this month. He said they would be consulting with shareholders to understand their concerns, but would not be changing the terms.
Asked if it was a pointless consultation, he agreed and said “Welcome to the world of ESG,” [environmental, social, and governance rules].

The Fed last week lifted its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75% to 4% – its first rate rise since 2023 – and signalled another increase could come before year-end.
Although gold is seen as a hedge against inflation, rising interest rates can reduce its attractiveness as investors pivot towards interest-bearing assets.

The meeting between Xi and Trump this week will be the second time that the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies have talked face to face this year. At the previous summit, held in Beijing in May, there was much talk of building a “strategic stability” between the two powers. But there was little by way of concrete outcomes: the countries remain at loggerheads over trade, export controls and geopolitics.
Despite the goodwill built in May, few anticipate any major breakthroughs this week when Xi makes his first state visit to the US since 2015. “Expectations are very low,” said Bonnie Glaser, a managing director at the US thinkthank the German Marshall Fund. “Nobody is using the term ‘deliverables’.”

JD sales fall with young people 'waiting for promotions to come'
Sarah Butler
Young people are now now “waiting for promotions to come” rather than looking out for trainer brands’ latest footwear launches, the boss of JD Sports has said, as the retailer’s core customers remaiun under pressure from rising unemployment and an increase in the cost of living.
Half-year sales at the group fell 0.8%, excluding exchange rate fluctuations, to £5.9bn, led by a 4% drop at established stores in North America where food prices have soared.
Sales were down 3.3% in Europe and 1.4% in the UK as JD’s chief executive Régis Schultz said retailers around the world were having to discount sports footwear to clear stock having not recognised that the market was maturing as shoppers reined in spending and the global shift from wearing leather shoes to trainers had worked its way through.
He said average selling prices were down in both the UK and Europe as shoppers were
waiting for promotions to come.
Three years ago customers were looking for a new launch, now they are looking for a new promotion and that’s having a negative impact on the industry.
He said UK sales had been better than elsewhere as young people were buying more performance sportswear as “running clubs are the new nightclubs” and he said JD was rapidly adapting by adding more clothing in the US, including own-label, and bringing in new brands such as On and Salomon in footwear as the bigger brands such as Nike face new competition.
Schultz called on the UK government to cut the cost of employing young people and to maintain flexibility on short-hours contracts as he said former chancellor Rachel Reeves’ increase on National Insurance contributions for employers and increase in the minimum wage for under 21s had been “really a wrong movement” and only pushed retailers to use more technology and hire fewer young people.
While he said JD did not use self checkouts, he added:
The more the cost of labour increases and the less flexibility [on working hours] the more retailers are inclined to invest in technology.

Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be looking to raise about $800m (£601m) from the IPO and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to 9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.

From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future.
We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.
Legal & General has confirmed that it is cutting 1,000 jobs, with a voluntary-first approach in the UK, and excluding asset management.
António Simões, the chief executive, said in an email to employees as he announced the voluntary redundancy programme:
Over the past two and a half years, we have made significant progress executing our strategy, simplifying L&G, establishing three core businesses, and creating a more focused business.
However, over the last decade, different structures, processes and ways of working have developed across L&G, making us more complex than we need to be. To deliver our strategy successfully, we now need to make sure the way we work reflects the business we are becoming. Across L&G, we need to change how we work today and, through this, become a leaner organisation. By the middle of next year, we expect to reduce the size of our organisation by around 1,000 roles.
An L&G spokesperson said:
Since 2024, L&G has become a simpler, more focused business. These changes represent the next stage of that transformation, ensuring that our organisation and ways of working reflect the business we are now building and the rapidly changing environment in which we operate.
They will also help us focus our resources and investment on the areas where we see the strongest opportunities for long-term growth. We recognise and take seriously the impact on colleagues and are committed to supporting our people throughout the process and consulting with our unions.
The British insurance and pensions firm Legal & General reportedly wants to cut 1,000 jobs by the middle of next year, amounting to a tenth of of its workforce.
António Simões, the chief executive, is wielding the axe as he tries to simplify the company’s operations.
The London-headquartered firm has kicked off a plan to eliminate about 1,000 roles by mid-2027, according to an email sent to employees on Wednesday seen by Bloomberg News.
The programme will initially be voluntary redundancies in the UK but L&G will consider mandatory cuts depending on take-up, Bloomberg said, citing a source. The investment management division, which oversees £1.2 trillion in assets, is excluded as it already has its own restructuring plan underway.

In UN farewell, Macron says Gaza a 'spectacle of shame'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:48:06 UTC
17:48:06 KST

Breadcrumb
In UN farewell, Macron denounces Trump's Gaza diplomacy as 'spectacle of shame'
France's President Emmanuel Macron on Tuesday dismissed US President Donald Trump's claims of having secured peace in Gaza, saying not a single humanitarian corridor had been reopened in the enclave despite the proclaimed peace.
In his final address to the United Nations before leaving office next year, Macron said the world was witnessing a spectacle that should shame everyone, rebuking Trump's portrayal of his Gaza peace plan as a diplomatic triumph.
He spoke at the United Nations General Assembly hours after Trump had from the same rostrum hailed his Gaza peace plan as a diplomatic triumph.
"A year ago, here in this very hall, about a dozen states had recognised Palestine. I hear the cynicism of some people: 'Recognition is just a piece of paper, look at the reality,'" Macron said, banging his fist on the podium in his last speech at the United Nations before stepping down next May.
"But what credibility do we have if we continue to remain inactive in the face of Gaza? Some boast of a supposed peace. But that peace has not reopened humanitarian access for a single second. Are we simply to stand by and watch this spectacle that should shame us all?"
In response to Macron's criticism, White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said: “President Trump ended the war between Israel and Hamas, freed all living hostages, returned the bodies of the deceased to their loved ones, and is now leading the implementation of the 20-Point Plan for Peace in Gaza. While others talk, this President took this complex problem head on. No one has done more for peace and stability in the region.”
Macron has faced criticism among some politicians and activists in France that he has done little since recognising a Palestinian state last September.
Despite the criticism, Paris has toughened its stance on Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, imposing some national sanctions and launching a process to ban products from Israeli settlements.
"Look at what is happening in the West Bank, where every day violations are committed. In whose name? Hamas has never operated in the West Bank," Macron said. "What is happening there is building, day by day, the impossibility of a project that should be based on respect for the legitimate right of the Palestinian people to exist."
France's ties with Israel have been particularly strained over the last year. Macron said those who believed that violating the sovereignty of all of Israel's neighbors would ensure its security were mistaken.
"They are weakening Israel's security, both today and in the future," he said.
Israel rebuked French President Emmanuel Macron too. "The grotesque absurdity of Emmanuel Macron's statement is staggering," said a statement by the office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is expected to deliver a defiant address to the world body on Thursday.
Seven months from France's next presidential election, Macron was making his last appearance after first taking to the rostrum in 2017.
Often showing a keen eye for the trappings of diplomacy—the grand settings, the symbolism, the personal connections—he has at the same time failed to translate this into lasting strategic gains, analysts say.
However, he has always been a staunch defender of the multilateral system and the United Nations.
Macron warned against a global "return to the law of the jungle", saying countries faced a choice between a world governed by power and coercion and a "civilised international society."
"Our duty, more than ever, is to stand alongside the United Nations. We cannot accept the new order of impunity that some would like to build," he said.
He ended his speech with "Long Live the United Nations!"

MSF expands response to Ebola disease with new treatment centres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:47:50 UTC
17:47:50 KST

In northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is expanding our response to the Ebola disease outbreak, as it spreads from the remote town of Nia Nia, in Ituri province, to Kisangani, the busy capital of neighbouring Tshopo province.
In Kisangani, MSF has been running the Ebola treatment centre (ETC) at Hôpital du Cinquantenaire, in collaboration with the Ministry of Health, since the end of June. In the first week of September, patients were transferred to a new 22-bed ETC, built and run by MSF, increasing treatment capacity in Kisangani.
In Nia Nia, MSF teams started working alongside the Ministry of Health at the ETC in the local hospital in early August. This week, MSF opened a new 50-bed ETC next to the hospital, further expanding access to Ebola care in the area.
The two locations are closely connected. Nia Nia is situated in an area with significant movement of people and goods between Ituri, Tshopo and Haut-Uele provinces. Since the first cases were reported there, people infected in or linked to Nia Nia have travelled to other areas, including Kisangani. Thirteen of the 14 positive cases recorded in Kisangani as of 1 September had an epidemiological link to Nia Nia.
Responding where the outbreak is spreading
Nia Nia has become a major focus of the outbreak in southern Ituri. The town recorded its first cases at the end of June, but the response has faced significant challenges, including limited access to healthcare, gaps in infection prevention and control, and fear and misinformation within the community.
MSF teams began working in Nia Nia in early August. As of 1 September, the Nia Nia ETC had admitted 85 people with symptoms matching Ebola. Of these, 59 were confirmed Ebola cases, including 15 patients who died. MSF opened a 50-bed ETC next to the existing facility, with 16 beds for suspected cases and 34 for confirmed cases, this week. The new centre is designed to provide safer and more effective care, with the protocols and bio-safety measures needed to treat patients with Ebola.
“In an Ebola treatment centre, what we can do is care for the individual patient, but epidemics are stopped in the community,” says Miriam Alia, MSF medical coordinator.
In an Ebola treatment centre, what we can do is care for the individual patient, but epidemics are stopped in the community.
When fear prevents people from seeking care
During the first weeks of the outbreak in Nia Nia, fewer patients were reaching the ETC than the number of confirmed deaths reported in the community. Many people remained at home rather than seeking care.
There are now signs of change. More people are reaching the treatment centre alive, giving them the opportunity to receive early, supportive treatment.
“Three weeks ago, we started receiving patients rather than only alerts about deaths in the community,” says Alia. “This is a major change because it means people are coming to the ETC earlier, when they develop symptoms.”
From the beginning, the response in Nia Nia has faced strong resistance, with rumours and misinformation fuelling fear. These have included claims that Ebola did not exist or that medical staff were bringing the disease into communities. Health workers were threatened, and an earlier treatment centre in the region was attacked and destroyed on 30 June.
“I didn’t believe that Ebola existed,” says Maurice, a recovered Ebola patient who was treated by MSF in Kisangani. “But when I was tested and found out that I had Ebola, that’s when I understood that it exists. But people still say that Ebola isn’t real. In my neighbourhood, in people’s homes, that’s what I used to hear.”
I didn’t believe that Ebola existed. But when I was tested and found out that I had Ebola, that’s when I understood that it exists.
MSF teams are working with community leaders, health workers and other local organisations to understand concerns, address misinformation, and build acceptance of the response.
“During Ebola outbreaks, we used to talk about two epidemics: the epidemic itself, and the epidemic of fear,” says Alia. “Now we have a third one: the epidemic of misinformation.”
From Nia-Nia to Kisangani
The link between Nia Nia and Kisangani shows why containing the outbreak in hard-to-reach areas is critical.
“In the past month, two other people were infected in Kisangani after coming into contact with a body that had arrived from Nia Nia,” says Amy Low, MSF project medical adviser in Kisangani.
Also in the past week, three patients with an epidemiological link to Nia Nia died at the MSF-supported ETC in Kisangani.
MSF is expanding our capacity in both locations. But treatment centres alone cannot stop Ebola. Surveillance, testing, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, early isolation, treatment and community engagement all need to work together to reduce transmission and ensure that communities, such as Nia Nia, are not left behind.

First-time Jewish voters could account for up to 12 Knesset seats in upcoming election - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:46:42 UTC
17:46:42 KST

Some 550,000 young Israelis are expected to be eligible to vote for the first time in the upcoming election, representing an estimated 10 to 12 Knesset seats, according to an N12 report published Wednesday.
Despite a strong ideological tilt toward the Right, support was divided among a wide range of parties rather than concentrated in a single political camp.
Seventy-four percent of respondents described their political views as right-wing or center-right, compared with 23% who identified with the Left or center-left. N12 said the corresponding figures among the wider adult population were 67% and 33%, respectively.
Asked which party they would support if elections were held now, 16% chose Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, while 14% selected Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud. Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad received 10%, United Torah Judaism received 9%, and Yair Golan's Democrats received 7%.
The results broadly reflect a fragmented national race in which Yashar and Likud have remained among the largest parties in several recent surveys. A series of polls published last week showed Yashar ahead of Likud in most surveys, although the balance between the broader political blocs remained unsettled.
Religious Zionism and Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu each received 6% among first-time voters in the N12 survey, followed by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit at 5%.
The joint list headed by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha received 4%, while Shas, led by Arye Deri, and Ofer Winter's People of Israel each received 3%. Other parties received around 1% each, while 10% of respondents remained undecided.
Surveys including adults present different figures, highlighting demographic differences
The figures differ in some respects from polling of the wider electorate. In a September 16-17 national survey, for example, Otzma Yehudit received eight projected Knesset seats, and Shas received seven. That poll surveyed Israeli adults, including Jewish and Arab respondents, limiting direct comparisons with the N12 first-time voter sample.
Among respondents in the N12 poll who identified as haredi (ultra-Orthodox), United Torah Judaism received 45%, while Shas received 20% and Otzma Yehudit received 13%. N12 assessed that some young haredi voters who might otherwise support Shas were moving toward Ben-Gvir's party.
Family voting patterns also appeared to remain influential. Fifty-nine percent said they planned to vote for the same party or political bloc as their parents, while 21% said they expected to vote differently.
Among those who said they would break with their parents' voting preference, 14% said they would support coalition parties. By comparison, 23% said their parents supported the Netanyahu bloc but that they intended to vote for what N12 termed the "change bloc."
The poll also asked respondents to compare potential prime minister candidates. In a matchup between Netanyahu and Bennett, 46% selected Netanyahu and 34% selected Bennett. Another 15% chose neither, while 5% said they did not know.
Against Eisenkot, Netanyahu received 47%, compared with 37% for the Yashar leader. Ten percent chose neither, and 6% said they did not know. These results differ from some recent surveys of the broader electorate, including polls in which Eisenkot has led Netanyahu when respondents were asked who was better suited to serve as prime minister.
Recent national surveys have otherwise shown considerable movement among the main parties and smaller lists as the election approaches, with parties near the electoral threshold potentially affecting the overall bloc arithmetic. Recent polling has shown a fragmented race and little separation between the two main blocs.
The Midgam survey, led by pollster Mano Geva, was conducted online from September 15 to 22 among a representative sample of Jewish Israelis ages 18 to 22 who are eligible to vote for the first time. A total of 301 people responded out of 1,521 invited to participate. The poll had a maximum sampling error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points and used stratified sampling followed by random sampling within the strata.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz attacked Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Liberman on Wednesday after the former defense minister proposed a Jordanian role in administering and providing security in parts of the West Bank.
Liberman told BeSheva that Jordan should exercise security control in Areas B and C of the West Bank, according to the outlet, a stance he has maintained in the past. The remarks prompted criticism from Netanyahu and his political allies.
"Liberman, I knew you were on the Left ever since you formed a government with Mansour Abbas. I know you are on the Left because you will form a government with Eisenkot, Yair Golan, Bennett, and the Arab parties. But I never believed that today you would propose that the Jordanian army control parts of the Land of Israel. Retract it immediately!" Netanyahu said.
"Liberman, who sees himself as a candidate for a rotating premiership, proposed until recently that Israel unilaterally withdraw from Gaza and hand Gaza and the Philadelphi Corridor smuggling route over to Egypt. Now, he is proposing to station a Jordanian army in Qalqilya, near Route 6, and hand Jordan security and administrative control over all Areas A and B in Judea and Samaria, even though Jordan’s declared policy is the establishment of a Palestinian state," Katz stated.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich also attacked Liberman over the proposal.
"Listen to Liberman. Someone who presents himself as a man of the Right is proposing that we give up our security responsibility in Judea and Samaria and transfer it to the Jordanians! To the Jordanians! Liberman wants to take Israel back to the days of the Jordanian Legion. We must not allow that to happen," Smotrich said.
Liberman stated his proposal would be for an 'Israeli-Jordanian confederation'
Minutes later, Liberman issued a clarification, saying his proposal concerned Jordanian administration of Areas A and B.
"The State of Israel must create territorial continuity between all of Area C and maintain absolute control there. At the same time, an alternative must be found for administrative and security control in Areas A and B," Liberman said.
He separately clarified his remarks by saying that Israel should "reach an agreement with Jordan on their administration of Areas A and B," describing the proposed framework as an "Israeli-Jordanian confederation."
The proposal is not the first time Liberman has advocated a Jordanian administrative role in Palestinian areas of the West Bank.
In a January 23, 2025 interview with Ynet, Liberman proposed an arrangement under which Jordan would administer Areas A and B while Israel would administer Area C.
The proposal built on an earlier plan he presented in 2024, under which Jordan would take responsibility for Area A and Egypt would assume responsibility for the Gaza Strip.
In the earlier proposal, Liberman argued that the Oslo framework had failed and called for a long-term Jordanian-Palestinian confederation in the West Bank.

Wife of US seismologist detained in China says Trump will ask Xi to free him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:46:19 UTC
17:46:19 KST

The wife of a US expert on North Korean nuclear tests who has been imprisoned in China since late 2024 said on Tuesday the White House has assured her that US President Donald Trump will ask Chinese leader Xi Jinping to free her husband when the pair meet this week.
Yufang Rong said she feared that Beijing planned to try her Chinese-born husband, Youlin Chen, on fabricated espionage charges even though his US-funded research was openly published, used publicly available data and was done in collaboration with Chinese scientists.
Trump will welcome Xi on Wednesday for their second meeting since May as the heads of the world's leading powers seek stability amid tensions ranging from trade to Iran and Taiwan.
Rong said she was assured during a Tuesday meeting at the White House with officials from the State Department and National Security Council that Trump would ask Xi to free her husband.
Chen, 54, is one of two Americans held by Beijing that the US has designated as "wrongfully detained," making their release a top priority. The other is Min Zin, a scholar arrested in June.
Rong said she was told that Trump also would press Xi to release Min Zin.
Trump raised Chen's case with Xi during a visit to Beijing in May, but it produced no action, Rong said.
"Resolving the wrongful detentions of US citizens is always a top priority for the president," a senior US official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said that the "relevant US person" is suspected of engaging in activities that endanger China's national security and violate Chinese law.
"China is a country with rule of law, and there is no such thing as wrongful detention," spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing, without elaborating and referring to Chen.
Chen's research funded by US Air Force, State Department
Chen, whose detention was revealed by Reuters in July, is a seismologist with a US government contractor. His work detecting shockwaves from North Korean underground nuclear tests has been openly funded by the State Department and the US Air Force Research Laboratory.
He became a US citizen in 2011 and settled in the Boston area.
He was arrested by Chinese state security officers on November 5, 2024, at Beijing International Airport as he prepared to fly home after visiting family and lecturing at two universities. Rong said her husband had been interrogated more than 100 times.
"I can't imagine how hard his life is there every day," she said.
She believes that China wants to use her husband's expertise to improve its ability to conceal nuclear tests using decoupling, a technique in which a device is detonated inside a large underground chamber to reduce the size of the shockwaves.
The US has accused China of using decoupling to try to mask a low-yield nuclear test blast on June 22, 2020. China, which, like the US, has signed but not ratified a 1996 international ban on nuclear tests, denies conducting the test.
US officials obly allowed to visit Chen once a month
US embassy officials had been allowed to visit Chen for about 30 minutes once a month, always in the presence of Chinese officials, Rong said. They read out letters she had written to him, and he dictated his replies.
"They record his appearance, his mental status, and just anything that they observe," she recounted, adding that Chen's Chinese lawyer was not allowed to discuss his visits with her.
Rong is concerned about the conditions of her husband's confinement, where she said he received substandard medical care and food. He suffered from high blood pressure and diabetes.
Asked what she would say to her husband if she could see him, Rong replied: "'Be strong. Be optimistic. There are a lot of people helping you. You will come back for sure.'"

Israel's diplomatic isolation prevents proper recognition for its military achievements - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:46:04 UTC
17:46:04 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to travel to the United States to address the UN General Assembly on Thursday, as Israel faces growing diplomatic isolation despite the strategic leverage it could offer allies across the Middle East and Europe.
Netanyahu is expected to appear before the UN General Assembly. Usually, attending the gathering brings with it a series of meetings with heads of state, defense officials, and military leaders.
The Middle East and the Arabian Gulf are currently in the midst of war and a process of reshaping. On the surface, the US appears to be seeking to reduce its military dominance in the region. At the same time, Europe understands that it is facing a new set of threats: Russia, the Iranian threat, and growing Islamist migration that is changing Europe's demographics.
Israel has a great deal to offer Europe in dealing with each of these threats. Israel is a key player in maintaining stability in the Middle East and the Arabian Gulf.
The fact is that some of the region's strongest countries, including Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and others, are facing economic and military difficulties amid aggression from Iran and the Houthis, as well as Turkey's interests in the Mediterranean, threats to the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, and pressure on other countries.
Netananyahu not meeting with Trump at UNGA, Israel facing diplomatic crisis
Under these circumstances, Netanyahu should have been among the most sought-after figures at the UN General Assembly. He should have been sitting at the Waldorf Astoria in Manhattan, with members of his staff handing out waiting numbers in the hotel lobby for meetings with him.
But the situation looks different. Even US President Donald Trump, one of Netanyahu's closest allies over the years, has indicated that he has no interest in meeting Netanyahu at this time. The absurdity is that he is, in principle, prepared to meet with Iranian officials who arrive for the UN General Assembly.
This is not a political matter. It is a genuine diplomatic crisis that directly affects the security situation. Israel's isolation could influence a series of military initiatives that were supposed to be developed.
Israel cannot rely on a cool relationship with the US superpower. It cannot build its strategy solely on a regional alliance with Cyprus and Greece in the face of the range of threats confronting it. Nor can it rely only on arms deals with Germany and other European countries.
Israel should be in a completely different position by now. The IDF's achievements over three years of war have been remarkable. But they should have been taken to the next level.
Israel's problem is that it does not truly have a functioning foreign minister, just as it does not have a full-time defense minister. Much of the Israeli government is made up of political operatives who lack diplomatic vision and strategic military thinking. It is doubtful whether many ministers have even taken courses in Middle Eastern studies.
If they had, the lobby of the Waldorf Astoria in Manhattan would likely be filled with leaders and defense officials waiting to meet Netanyahu.
Israeli submarine expected to strengthen alliance with Greece, Cyprus
On Thursday, the INS Drakon, the Israeli Navy's sixth submarine, is set to enter Israeli waters. It is the most expensive weapon system Israel has ever purchased. Its entry into service with the navy is expected to affect the balance of power, particularly against countries in the third and fourth circles surrounding Israel.
The submarine could strengthen Israel's alliance with Greece and Cyprus, and it could also provide much of what Egypt and Italy lack in confronting Turkish assertiveness over the division of economic waters in the Mediterranean and Ankara's moves with Libya to create a new regional reality.
For now, it remains unclear how two open arenas will be resolved: the confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, and the second arena between the US and Iran surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's nuclear program, and the continued survival of the ayatollah regime.
What is clear is that Israel needs a series of diplomatic moves to emerge from its isolation, and it must become a force shaping the region both diplomatically and in security terms. It must also play a dominant role in shaping European security thinking, based on the understanding that what is bad for Europe now is also bad for Israel.

Israeli security officials fear possible regional escalation amid Iran, Houthis, West Bank tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:45:57 UTC
17:45:57 KST

Despite a tense but relatively stable security period, the Middle East is approaching the risk of a broader escalation as multiple flashpoints converge across the region, Israeli security officials told Walla on Wednesday.
From the confrontation between the US and Iran and the activation of Iranian proxies, through Saudi Arabia's campaign against the Houthis and Hezbollah's military buildup, to the deadlock in Gaza and tensions in the West Bank, the Israeli defense establishment is monitoring the various arenas and preparing for the possibility that deterioration in one could affect the region as a whole.
US President Donald Trump is eager to bring the conflict with Iran to an end before the midterm elections. According to assessments by Israeli security officials, he is therefore heightening tensions in the Middle East with threats against Iran in an effort to demonstrate seriousness ahead of a possible return to the negotiating table.
According to Israeli sources, mediators between Tehran and Washington have so far failed to produce positive developments. Officials broadly assess that the Iranians recognize Trump's reluctance to return to active fighting and are therefore holding firm to their uncompromising position: refusing to abandon the nuclear project and refusing to open the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump is also continuing to tighten economic sanctions on Iran and threaten those cooperating with Tehran in an effort to revive its faltering economy.
The Iranian regime is operating on several fronts. The first is an attempt to maneuver between severe US economic sanctions and the possibility that regime opponents could take to the streets to protest the difficult conditions.
At the same time, the Iranian regime continues preparing for war in several arenas. It has begun producing surface-to-surface missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles and is also preparing for a possible ground invasion.
In addition, and perhaps most sensitively, the Iranian regime under Mojtaba Khamenei continues to pursue a hard-line and uncompromising approach toward the US and Israel while simultaneously strengthening its relationship with its "proxies": Hezbollah on Israel's border, the Houthis in Yemen against Saudi Arabia and possibly against Israel in the foreseeable future, and pro-Iranian Shi'ite militias in Iraq against the pro-Western Iraqi government and, in the foreseeable future, against American and Israeli interests.
More than anything else, this issue makes the region particularly volatile. The concern is that Iran could decide to escalate the region gradually and call on its "proxies," which receive funding, weapons, intelligence, and training from Tehran, to join the confrontation.
Saudi Arabia seeking support from US over Houthi attacks
Saudi Arabia received a lesson from the Americans over the past week. Senior Saudi officials were alarmed by the Houthis' broad attack on the capital Riyadh, Mecca, facilities belonging to Aramco, one of the world's largest energy companies, and by a ground incursion toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which threatened Red Sea shipping routes and the passage of oil tankers.
According to Israeli security officials, the Saudis called the Americans, demanding immediate assistance.
Trump held consultations and ultimately decided not to strike the Houthis, instead offering intelligence or assistance with weapons systems.
This raises several significant questions: Will Saudi Arabia succeed in assembling an anti-Houthi coalition? How involved will Israel be? Will it limit itself to intelligence sharing?
For now, the Saudis remain alone in the campaign. The entire arena is therefore fragile. If the Houthis feel backed into a corner, they could also attack Israel, where American interests, including bases, are located.
Hezbollah restrained, Hamas negotiations at dead end
Hezbollah remains restrained, but it is building its capabilities for a future war with Iranian support, with a particular focus on aircraft and fiber-optic drones. In other words, if Tehran orders Hezbollah to join a campaign, Israel could find itself under attack from the north.
In addition, air and ground strikes are carried out almost daily against Hezbollah targets in southern Lebanon. Some strikes target operatives and field commanders preparing attacks against Israel, while others are aimed at Hezbollah's military reconstruction efforts and terrorist infrastructure.
Negotiations by the Board of Peace with Hamas over disarming in the Gaza Strip and transferring control to a third party have reached a dead end.
Hamas has so far limited itself to hollow statements and a general agreement to hand weapons over to a third party, while Israel firmly opposes any arrangement under which Hamas remains a legitimate organization that retains weapons in the Gaza Strip.
Senior IDF officials are insisting on adopting the "Ali Taher Ridge" model in Gaza City. Under this approach, IDF troops would maneuver into the heart of the city and dismantle all major terrorist infrastructure above and below ground that Hamas has built over more than 20 years.
According to assessments in the defense establishment, a decision on this issue will be made after the Israeli elections and the US midterm elections.
At this stage, the concern is that Hamas or other terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip could attempt attacks. High alert is therefore being maintained along the Yellow Line.
West Bank nationalist crime causing concerns among security officials
The West Bank is the arena causing the greatest concern. The area and the Jordan Valley are known as particularly volatile arenas during the holiday period.
Recently, nationalist crime has added to tensions, alongside growing friction between the Israeli and Palestinian populations.
Central Command is concerned that any incident could ignite the area and lead to revenge attacks or terrorist attacks. The IDF Operations Directorate has therefore reinforced the West Bank with battalions and additional units taking part in protecting communities and major roads.
In the background is the "turning the guns" scenario, referring to the possibility that Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, also known as Abu Mazen, could die and succession struggles could move from rhetoric to violence, creating chaos and gunfire directed at Israeli civilians and IDF soldiers.
According to senior Central Command officials, there are no signs at this stage of "turning the guns." However, succession struggles have already begun, and there are senior disappointed and frustrated figures in the West Bank, the Gulf and the Gaza Strip who are pulling strings and trying, among other things, to turn the West Bank into an arena in which terrorism is mobilized.
The Syrian arena is considered relatively quiet and stable.
Division 210, commanded by Brig.-Gen. Yair Palai, is taking the initiative in the Syrian arena. When intelligence is received about arms dealers in the area or elements hostile to Israel, the division launches an operation.
In addition, Israel's borders with Jordan and Egypt continue to serve as focal points for weapons smuggling. The concern is that these routes could one day become infiltration routes for terrorists.
The maritime arena has also been upgraded since Maj.-Gen. Eyal Barel took command of the Israel Navy, with additional vessels and a more proactive operational approach across greater distances and broader areas of operation in preparation for any scenario intended to challenge the IDF, with particular emphasis on the missile boat flotilla and the submarine flotilla.

2026-09-23
08:45:16 UTC
17:45:16 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Health and Welfare will launch its health token program on Oct. 1.
It will allow people to earn points for health checkups, cancer screenings, vaccinations, and other health-related activities. Redemptions begin Dec. 1.
Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said Wednesday that the first wave of redemption options will cover five categories:
- Convenience stores and retailers
- Pharmacies
- Hospitals
- Sports venues
- Life insurance companies
Participating businesses will generally follow a rate of one health token for NT$1 (3 cents), although the program will primarily use small-value discounts rather than full-price redemptions, per a press release.
People must accumulate at least 1,000 health tokens before they can begin redeeming them. The government said the threshold is intended to encourage people to complete actual health-related activities rather than immediately spending the initial points earned through registration and questionnaires.
The National Health Insurance Express app will allow users to check their accumulated points, while the Health Promotion Administration's Health GO app will be used to redeem rewards. Shih said more details on eligible products and services will be announced at a news conference in November.
At convenience stores and retailers, the initial program includes 14 products: six sugar-free or healthy beverages, six fresh-food items, and two coffee products. The products are expected to be changed every two to three months.
The initial list of participating convenience stores includes 7-Eleven, FamilyMart and PX Mart. Shih said tea eggs will not be included in the first wave, despite earlier discussion of the popular convenience-store item as a potential health token reward.
The convenience-store rewards will generally be provided as small discounts rather than free products. For example, a beverage could receive a NT$5 discount. Shih said the approach is designed to encourage people to accumulate and use the points repeatedly rather than spend them all at once, per UDN.
Pharmacies are expected to offer about 30 to 50 products, including blood glucose meters, blood pressure monitors, special nutritional products, and health foods. Discounts are expected to range from about 10% to 20%, with some products intended for people with chronic conditions such as diabetes and kidney disease.
Sports venues will offer different types of discounts depending on the participating provider, including reductions on sports equipment, classes, and membership fees.
To earn health tokens, users can register through the National Health Insurance app and access the health ledger section. The Health Promotion Administration said adults aged 18 and older can participate.
Shih said the government plans to gradually expand the program by working with local governments and regional businesses and linking health token rewards with local health incentive programs.

08:45:08 UTC

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Institute for Information Industry said on Wednesday that it partnered with systems firm Yotoma to co-develop generative AI for the textile industry, per a press release.
The textile industry relies heavily on senior staff to interpret equipment status, with oversight often causing errors. Both firms trained an AI model using collected data to help enterprises with maintenance and upkeep.
The diagnostic AI allows staff to ask questions about equipment status. It is embedded in the factory's network so data does not need to go through a cloud service, protecting sensitive information.
The institute said the AI was asked 58 questions in Mandarin and 16 in English and answered them all correctly. It added that the AI can manage systems across different locations, improving overall efficiency.
The institute said the AI collects knitting machine data in real time to schedule upkeep. It can also assess component condition and identify equipment quirks, reducing parts waste while saving electricity.
The institute said the AI translates data into workable information. It said the AI can be flexibly deployed to other textile equipment such as dyeing and setting machines, with potential in precision manufacturing.

Escalating conflict, strong El Nino risk Asia-Pacific developing economies: ADB
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:44:44 CST
17:44:44 KST

MANILA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Escalating conflict and strong El Nino are two main risks for developing Asia and the Pacific economies, according to a report released by the Asian Development Bank (ADB) on Wednesday.
The Asian Development Outlook (ADO) September 2026 forecasts that growth in developing Asia and the Pacific will moderate from 5.5 percent in 2025 to 5 percent this year before edging up to 5.1 percent in 2027. The projection is 0.1 percentage points higher than the previous outlook in July.
According to ADB, the inflation forecast of Asia-Pacific developing economies for 2026 is trimmed to 4.2 percent from 4.3 percent in July, as price stabilization measures partly offset the impact of persistently high energy prices.
However, the inflation forecast for 2027 is revised up slightly to 3.5 percent, compared with 3.4 percent in July. The revised inflation projections for both years remain above the 3 percent recorded in 2025.
ADB said a broadening of the Middle East conflict and an intensification of the Russia-Ukraine conflict could keep global energy prices elevated and volatile, and spill over to other commodities.
The report also noted that a very strong El Nino is forecast to persist through the first quarter of 2027. The weather could be drier and cause smaller harvests and reduced hydropower, raising energy demand, lowering agricultural production, and pushing up fuel and food prices.
ADB President Masato Kanda said governments need to prepare and protect the people most exposed, against the backdrop of strengthening El Nino, prolonged energy crisis, and renewed risks in financial markets. ■
