Which countries are banning Iranian airlines over US sanctions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:08:33 UTC
17:08:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Which countries are banning Iranian airlines to avoid US sanctions?
Several countries have begun restricting Iranian airlines from operating at their airports as sweeping new US sanctions targeting Iran's aviation sector came into force on Wednesday.
The measures are beginning to disrupt international routes operated by Iranian carriers, with restrictions ranging from blanket bans to the suspension of individual airlines or destinations.
The restrictions come after the administration of US President Donald Trump placed Iran's entire aviation sector under sanctions earlier this month, threatening foreign airports and companies with penalties if they continue providing services to Iranian carriers.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned this week that Iranian airlines would struggle to operate internationally from 23 September as Washington targets foreign companies providing them with essential services.
"If they land, you can't fuel them, you can't provide landing services, you can't sell their tickets, or you're going to be kicked out of the dollar system," Bessent told CNBC.
Iran has 27 airlines, most of which operate domestic services. Flag carrier Iran Air and privately owned Mahan Air are among the country's main international operators, flying particularly to neighbouring countries as well as Russia and China.
Why are Iranian airlines being banned?
The restrictions stem from Washington's decision to target Iran's entire aviation sector.
Under the measures, foreign companies that provide services to Iranian airlines risk being hit with US secondary sanctions.
That potentially includes airports allowing Iranian aircraft to land, companies supplying them with fuel and businesses selling tickets for Iranian carriers.
The threat of losing access to the dollar-based financial system puts significant pressure on foreign airports and aviation companies to stop dealing with Iranian carriers, even where their governments have not directly banned Iranian flights.
The restrictions come as Iran's international aviation links remain severely disrupted by the US-Israel war on the country.
Iran closed its airspace entirely shortly after the war began in late February. Flights have gradually resumed as hostilities eased, but Iranian carriers remain the only airlines operating international services to and from the country.
The latest sanctions could therefore further reduce options for Iranians seeking to travel abroad or return home.
Which countries have restricted Iranian flights?
Georgia has banned all Iranian flights to and from the country since Monday.
Azerbaijan has also barred Iranian airlines, with Azerbaijan Airlines saying flights operated by Iranian carriers had been suspended from 22 September because of the new US sanctions on Iran's aviation sector.
"Due to the new package of sanctions imposed by the United States on Iran, particularly the sanctions imposed on the aviation sector, it has been decided to suspend Iranian airline flights from September 22, 2026," the airline said, according to Russia's Sputnik news agency.
Mahan Air halts flights to Turkey
Turkey has also been affected, although the measure reported so far is narrower. Iranian carrier Mahan Air said it had suspended its flights to Turkey at Ankara's request.
Iran's Civil Aviation Organisation said on Wednesday that other international services, including flights to Istanbul, were continuing according to schedule, suggesting the Turkish restrictions do not currently amount to a blanket ban on all Iranian carriers.
Iraq halts Iranian flights to Baghdad
In Iraq, authorities ordered the country's Civil Aviation Authority to suspend Iranian flights to Baghdad airport from Wednesday, two sources told Reuters.
The Iraqi government is discussing whether Iranian flights could instead be diverted to Najaf, a major destination for religious travellers.
Iraq is an important market for Iranian airlines, which carry Iranian pilgrims to Shia religious sites in the country and Iraqi travellers in the opposite direction.
Travel agencies are considering expanding overland transport between the two countries to compensate for the lost flights.
Tehran-Muscat flights cancelled
Flights between Tehran and Oman have also been cancelled from Wednesday, according to Iran's Civil Aviation Organisation.
An Iranian aviation spokesman said Iranian passengers were "currently not permitted to enter at the airport in Oman", adding that consultations were under way.
Oman's restrictions do not appear to amount to a blanket ban on all Iranian airlines, distinguishing the measures from the broader bans imposed by Georgia and Azerbaijan.

UK firm tests robot sailboats to track hidden submarines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:08:17 UTC
17:08:17 KST

- Oshen deployed six hydrophone-equipped C-Star sailboats at REPMUS26 in Portugal to test a distributed acoustic picket line against live targets.
- The company plans to bring eight C-Stars to the Maritime Big Play exercise in San Diego next month to test the concept in a U.S. setting.
Oshen, a UK maritime technology company based in Plymouth, is testing what it calls the first “acoustic picket line” built from small robotic sailboats at REPMUS26, a monthlong multinational maritime robotics exercise underway in Portugal. The company has deployed six of its C-Star sailboats, each about 1.2 meters (4 feet) long and fitted with a hydrophone, to form a distributed underwater listening network, and is testing the concept against live targets for the first time.
Passive sonar detection has traditionally relied on towed arrays, long cables carrying up to 100 hydrophones pulled behind surface ships. Those arrays give precise local detection and bearing data but cover a limited area and pick up noise from the towing vessel itself. Oshen’s approach spreads many small, low-cost sensors across a wide stretch of ocean instead, using a fleet of C-Stars to form what the company describes as an acoustic barrier that can be reshaped based on the threat picture. Because the boats are spread across a wide area rather than clustered on one vessel, the network can pinpoint a target’s location rather than just its bearing, and can help direct other sensors such as towed arrays toward it.
“A defensive network built from a host of individual hydrophone platforms behaves very differently to one built from a handful of expensive towed arrays,” said Gordon Jones, Defence and Oceanography Lead at Oshen. “It is wider, more resilient and harder for an adversary to characterise. REPMUS is the first real test of that model against live targets, and it points the way to how persistent undersea surveillance can be evolved.”
“REPMUS embodies what our technology is designed to do: take a capability that normally depends on a handful of expensive assets and turn it into something that can be deployed at scale, cheaply and continuously,” said Anahita Laverack, CEO of Oshen. “There are many potential applications, including an acoustic picket line to help protect the GIUK Gap.”
The GIUK Gap, the stretch of ocean between Greenland, Iceland, and the United Kingdom, has been a chokepoint for tracking submarines transiting between the North Atlantic and open ocean since the Cold War, when the U.S. Navy’s SOSUS seabed hydrophone network monitored the same waters.
Oshen says its C-Stars are built to survive extended missions in rough conditions, and the company has said one of its boats transmitted data from inside a Category 5 hurricane. Being small and low in the water, the boats are difficult to detect, and Oshen argues that even if individual units are spotted or lost, the wider network can keep functioning and makes it harder for an adversary to work out which vessels are carrying active sensors.
REPMUS is designed to test more than new hardware. The exercise brings together vessels ranging from Oshen’s 50-kg C-Stars to 3,000-tonne manned frigates, and organizers use it to check whether command and control systems can coordinate across that range of platforms in a congested environment. Oshen said its engineers worked with naval partners ahead of the exercise to integrate its software with NATO systems and make sure data from the C-Stars would not overwhelm communication channels.
Oshen currently runs three active projects with the Royal Navy, including one through the UK’s Defence and Security Accelerator program, and holds a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Navy covering single-beam sonar applications. The company plans to bring eight C-Stars to the Maritime Big Play exercise in San Diego next month to test the same acoustic picket line concept in a U.S. setting.

BAE’s self-funded armored vehicle passes U.S. Army field tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:04:28 UTC
17:04:28 KST

- BAE Systems self-funded two AMPV 30 prototypes with Kongsberg 30mm turrets, delivered to a U.S. Army Transformation in Contact unit in April.
- The Army has not committed to procuring the AMPV 30, though it expects two more prototypes in early 2027 for further testing.
BAE Systems said it has delivered two AMPV 30 prototypes armed with Kongsberg’s Medium Caliber Turret to a U.S. Army Transformation in Contact 2.0 unit, funding the six-month development effort itself with $17 million in internal research money.
The company disclosed the delivery in a Sept. 22 release, though the vehicles reached the Army’s 1st Cavalry Division at Fort Hood, Texas, in April.
The AMPV 30 pairs the Army’s existing Armored Multi-Purpose Vehicle chassis with a remotely operated Kongsberg turret carrying a 30mm Mk 44 Bushmaster II cannon. The same turret is already in production for the Marine Corps’ Amphibious Combat Vehicle. BAE Systems built the two prototypes without a government contract or an Army requirement behind them, a point the Army has confirmed publicly since the vehicles first arrived at Fort Hood.
“Our mission was speed and innovation, and we delivered beyond expectations,” said Bill Sheehy, vice president of BAE Systems’ Ground Maneuver futures. “With today’s battlefield evolving faster than ever, it’s paramount that Soldiers have the capabilities they need to win the fight. Throughout this effort, our team demonstrated how we can integrate new design solutions in a time-effective and more cost-efficient manner for the Army.”
Since the April delivery, the 2nd Battalion, 5th Cavalry Regiment has run the AMPV 30s through field evaluations, including live-fire testing, to compare the platform against what soldiers say they need on the battlefield. Beyond the cannon, the vehicles carry counter-drone detection systems, a cross-platform target handoff system that lets multiple vehicles share targeting data, and a 360-degree camera system that lets crews see their surroundings without exposing themselves outside the armor.
The AMPV’s open architecture lets BAE Systems swap in more than 30 different turret systems on the same common top plate, according to the company. These two vehicles bring the total number of turreted AMPV prototypes BAE Systems has self-funded to eight over the past two years. The Army has said it expects two more AMPV 30 prototypes in early 2027, with plans to run them through a rotation at the National Training Center at Fort Irwin, California.
Defense analyst Nicholas Drummond, assessing the vehicle on social media, wrote that the AMPV fitted with the latest Kongsberg MCT-30 turret and an Echodyne MESA radar amounts to “your XM30 right there,” referring to the Army’s long-running effort to find a Bradley Fighting Vehicle replacement. He called it “a nicely done evolutionary upgrade. Reduced risk, cost, and time to deliver. Big uplift in performance.” Kongsberg has separately announced integrating Echodyne’s MESA radar into its Protector remote weapon stations for counter-drone use, though BAE Systems has not confirmed that radar is fitted to these specific AMPV 30 prototypes.
The Army has not committed to buying the AMPV 30 or issued a formal requirement for it. BAE Systems and the Army have both described the current vehicles as company-funded prototypes under evaluation, not a program of record.

Roche obesity shot reduced body weight by 15.5% in trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:02:18 UTC
17:02:18 KST

Roche obesity shot reduced body weight by 15.5% in trial
Roche’s experimental obesity shot enicepatide cut both blood sugar and body weight in type-2 diabetes patients who were overweight or obese in a mid-stage trial.
Patients receiving the highest 24-milligram dose had a 2.65% reduction in HbA1c – a measure of blood sugar – and lost an average 15.5% of their body weight after 48 weeks with no plateau observed, Roche said.
The data “look competitive” against results for rival drugs in Phase 3 trials, Goldman Sachs analyst James Quigley and colleagues said. They cautioned, however, that they need to see detailed placebo-adjusted data and the results replicated in Phase 3 trials to confirm the benefit.
Roche shares fell 0.19% at the end of the trading day in Zurich.
The Swiss drugmaker is seeking to compete with Eli Lilly & Co and Novo Nordisk A/S with a once-weekly shot that works similarly to Lilly’s Zepbound — by simultaneously activating the GLP-1 and GIP hormones involved in regulating metabolism. The global market for weight-loss drugs is estimated to reach as much as $150 billion.
More
Can Swiss pharma giant Roche reshape the obesity market?
Roche’s discontinuation rates due to side effects were just 2% after 48 weeks. In a mid-stage trial of Lilly’s Mounjaro in patients with diabetes that was carried out over a shorter period, discontinuation rates varied from 5% to 24.5%.
The results of the trial have been very promising, Manu Chakravarthy, senior vice president and global head of cardiovascular, renal and metabolism product development at Roche, said in an interview.
“What it tells us and underscores for us is the incredible potency of this molecule,” he said. “You’re losing weight, you have no hypoglycemia, and you’re dropping your sugar in a very, very healthy range. And that to me as an endocrinologist is the greatest boon you can offer people with poorly controlled diabetes today, because they don’t really have such a solution.”
Late stage trials underway
About 62% of the people were brought within 48 weeks to the normal glycemic range, he said.
One of the strategies the company is embarking upon, especially with enicepatide, is to cover the broadest range, from obese or overweight people without any co-morbidities to very significant co-morbidities like cardiovascular disease, heart failure, type 1 diabetes and others, he said.
More
What will be the next obesity blockbuster?
Roche already has two late-stage obesity trials underway. In early 2027, it plans to expand testing to diabetes and cardiovascular outcomes.
The company also plans to test higher doses of enicepatide and is exploring combinations with other weight-loss drugs. At its half-year media conference in July, pharmaceuticals chief Teresa Graham said Roche was looking to develop the drug both on its own and in combination, particularly for patients who need “greater weight loss and/or better glycemic control.”
Enicepatide, formerly known as CT-388, was first developed by Carmot Therapeutics, which Roche acquired for $3.1 billion in 2023.
Enicepatide has a “competitive profile” in patients with type 2 diabetes and obesity, Vontobel analyst Stefan Schneider said, pointing to the combination of normalised glucose levels in a meaningful share of patients and sustained weight loss. Schneider expects the drug could launch as early as 2028 and reach peak sales of CHF2.5 billion ($3.05 billion).
Previous data suggested enicepatide is “as good as rivals on weight loss,” Bloomberg Intelligence analysts Michael Shah and Christos Nikoletopoulos wrote in June. The drug is expected to win approval by 2030, the analysts wrote, and could have peak sales of $4 billion.
(Updates with Roche SVP comments from seventh paragraph.)

Families of victims of Kenneth Law to address court as sentencing hearing begins in Canada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:02:13 UTC
17:02:13 KST

Law admitted targeting buyers on a suicide forum and shipping his products to 41 countries, and families angry that he escaped murder charges will now tell the court how their loved ones' deaths affected them.
Relatives of people who died after buying lethal substances from Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law are due to speak in court this week, as a judge begins deliberating how long the former chef should spend in prison.
Justice Michelle Fuerst has set aside four days at a court in Newmarket, just north of Toronto, to hear victim impact statements and further evidence. It is not yet clear when she will hand down her sentence.
Law pleaded guilty in May to aiding the suicides of 14 people in Canada. Prosecutors dropped murder charges after concluding they did not have enough evidence to secure a conviction over the online forums where he advised people on how to end their lives.
Under an agreed statement of facts signed by both sides, Law admitted seeking out buyers by posting on a suicide discussion forum under a false name and offering lethal products for sale. His packages reached customers in at least 41 countries, including China, France and Brazil, with 330 sent to the United Kingdom.
Several bereaved families have said they are angry Law will not stand trial for murder, arguing he bears direct responsibility for the deaths of mostly young and vulnerable people. Legal experts say prosecutors are likely to push for a heavy sentence, potentially up to 20 years.
UK deaths under scrutiny since 2023
Britain's role in the case came to light soon after Law's arrest. In August 2023, UK authorities were investigating 88 deaths linked to Law, with the National Crime Agency working to trace people in Britain who may have bought his products.
Police in Surrey had contacted Law in October 2022 over the death of 22-year-old Tom Parfett, who died in 2021 after apparently visiting one of Law's websites, and a later inquiry into his death raised questions about why the force had not investigated Law further.
'Not a diabolical madman'
Earlier this month, Canada's Globe and Mail reported details of interviews Law gave to a psychiatrist in prison after his guilty plea. According to court documents obtained by the paper, Law said he had been "trying to serve a need that I thought was humane," adding: "I'm not a diabolical madman."
The documents show that after his arrest in 2023, Law considered himself blameless, insisting he never made the final decision to end anyone's life and was simply selling a product, the Globe reported.
Law, now in his 60s, worked as a chef at a luxury hotel in downtown Toronto before setting up his online forums during the Covid-19 pandemic. He has admitted to shipping lethal substances within Canada and abroad, typically charging around $80 per package.
Among his victims was 18-year-old Jeshennia Bedoya-Lopez, who died in 2022. Speaking outside court in May, her father Leonardo Bedoya said he had found her dead in her bedroom. Describing his only daughter as the "light in my life", he called the prosecutors' decision to drop the murder charges "a disgrace."

‘Ghost patient’ policy wrongly removing at-risk people from GP lists, doctors say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:00:18 UTC
17:00:18 KST

An NHS policy to remove “ghost patients” from GP lists is inadvertently leaving some of the poorest people in England without vital healthcare, analysis has found.
Under previous NHS rules, inactive patients at risk of being removed from their GP practice were given six months to respond to outreach. But under NHS England’s accelerated list validation timeline, introduced last October, patients now have only three months to reply.
According to analysis by Healthtech-1, registered GP lists in English practices declined by 483,019 patients between October 2025 and July 2026, with the most deprived fifth of practices accounting for about 138,400 of the net decline – just under 30% of the national decline.
While GP lists need reviewing as people move away or die, GPs have said the accelerated timeline has inadvertently led to patients from deprived areas being incorrectly removed, creating barriers to receiving treatment.
Consequently, GPs and practice managers have reported having to re-register vulnerable and elderly patients, creating an additional administrative burden.
De-registering patients can also cause gaps in care and disruption to treatment. Since GP practices’ income also depend on the number of registered patients, a drop can leave practices struggling to pay for running costs.
A GP at a university practice in Southampton said the accelerated timeline was causing problems because patients were being incorrectly removed from their list and were struggling to access their prescriptions and treatment.
“If you give prescriptions out to people, they’re on repeat and once they get kicked off the lists they can no longer access any prescriptions,” he said. “The risk is that if you’re unable to access your repeat prescriptions, your treatment will be affected.”
He added: “If you’re narrowing the window from six to three months, more people are going to be kicked off and therefore more people will be put into the position where they cannot access treatment.”
The GP also warned that, besides reducing a practice’s income, the policy change was hitting patients from deprived and vulnerable backgrounds hardest.
“In our case, we had around 100 people who were taken off our list who didn’t leave at all. That worked out as around £10,000 in lost income for our practice,” he said.
“We were later contacted by these patients telling us that they couldn’t access their prescriptions and that they hadn’t gone anywhere.
“The money we’ve lost hasn’t been compensated, and I know of another practice locally that has lost £100,000 that they also won’t be compensated for.
“For those who have been erroneously taken off, we’re being penalised. We’re going to have to make cuts somehow to make up the shortfalls.”
Dr Clare Bannon, the chair of the British Medical Association’s GP committee, said GPs across England support the principle of keeping patient lists accurate but the current list-cleansing process is “seriously flawed”.
Bannon said: “We have called on NHS England to pause the exercise. The approach is overly aggressive, leading to practices losing tens of thousands of pounds in income and causing active patients, including vulnerable individuals, to be removed in error.
“It is essential that active patients are not deprived of access to a GP through no fault of their own.”
An NHS spokesperson said: “There are robust checks in place to ensure that vulnerable groups are not removed from GP lists – people are contacted through multiple different channels with the thorough processes lasting up to five months before any action is taken.
“This process ensures that patient contact details are correct so that they receive vital information about screening and vaccination appointments, while ensuring NHS funding resources are allocated fairly with money no longer spent on people who do not live in England.”

Apple unveils music venue within Battersea Power Station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:00:11 UTC
17:00:11 KST

Apple unveils music venue within Battersea Power Station
Tech brand Apple has revealed the 600-seat Apple Music Hall, its first live music venue, which sits alongside its offices within London's Battersea Power Station.
Set to open later this year, the venue overlooks the power station's Turbine A at the northern end of the huge brick building. It will be Apple's first permanent performance venue.
Designed by Apple's in-house team led by Apple Places vice president Kristina Raspe, the venue takes its industrial language directly from the Giles Gilbert Scott-designed power station.
The venue is flanked by brick walls, while the building's huge structural steel joists are exposed at the rear of the performance space.
As a nod to the art deco design of the original power station, a series of four illuminated, streamline-styled arches span the venue.
Bronze, art deco balconies were placed between the arches, as box-like areas overlooking the main venue space.
According to Apple, the flexible venue was designed to give artists an "unprecedented level of creative control".
The venue has an 11.5-metre-wide stage and can be arranged in multiple configurations as either an all-seated or all-standing venue, or a combination of the two.
Music will be played through a 48-speaker spatial sound system, while 16 hardwired cameras can capture performances to be broadcast.
"In short, an artist can perform an intimate live show for fans at Apple Music Hall and walk out with a finished Spatial Audio recording, a broadcast-ready mix, and multicamera video — all from a single show," said Apple.
Alongside the main venue space is what Apple describes as a "full production facility" that contains a pair of professional-standard recording and mix studios.
The venue also includes a dedicated space for Apple's radio station – Apple Music Radio, which will now broadcast from inside the building.
Apple Music Hall was built alongside Apple's Foster + Partners-designed European HQ, which occupies the centre of Battersea Power Station. One of London's best-known buildings, the power station was refurbished in 2022 by architecture studio WilkinsonEyre after being derelict for 40 years.
It now contains apartments on the upper floors, with restaurants and shops, including an Apple Store in the former turbine halls.
The photography is courtesy of Apple.

Voting opens in Alaska’s annual Fat Bear Week
- Voting has begun for Alaska’s Fat Bear Week, an online contest where people choose the fattest brown bear preparing for hibernation.
- The contest highlights bears’ weight gain as vital for surviving a five-month winter fast, with the 2025 winner named Chunk.
- Started in 2014, the event now attracts over a million voters annually to raise awareness of brown bears and their environmental threats.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – Polls opened on Sept 22 in the only American election that really matters: Fat Bear Week.
While the United States might be gearing up for midterm ballots that will decide who runs Washington, hundreds of thousands of people were readying to vote on animals gorging themselves in rural Alaska.
In a contest that has rapidly become one of the internet’s favorite moments, the brown bears of Katmai National Park unwittingly compete in a series of head-to-head contests to see which one of them has most impressively piled on the pounds ahead of hibernation.
Viewers can watch a livestream of the enormous animals as they scoop salmon from the Brooks River, or browse biographies of some of the top contenders, including before-and-after pictures showing how much weight the bears have gained over a summer of feasting.
“For each match-up, vote for the bear you believe best exemplifies fatness and success in brown bears,” said organisers.
“The bear with the most votes advances to the next round. Only one will be crowned Fat Bear Week champion.”
The 2025 winner, Chunk, beat out a stiff challenge from two-time winner Grazer.
Summer and early autumn are key fueling periods for the brown bears, which will not eat for five months of hibernation, relying on their store of fat to survive the punishing Alaskan winter.
The online contest began in 2014 with just a few thousand people voting, but has now turned into an eagerly awaited exercise in tongue-in-cheek democracy with more than a million people voting every year.
The aim is to raise awareness of brown bears and their habitat in Alaska, and the risks they face from human activity. AFP

Swiss Senate votes for 90% CET1 capital backing for UBS

Swiss Senate votes for 90% CET1 capital backing for UBS
The Swiss Senate has backed tough new capital rules for UBS, requiring the banking giant to finance 90% of its foreign holdings with core equity capital.
The new rules are intended to tighten the “too-big-to-fail” framework in Switzerland. The Senate reached its decision on Wednesday by 29 votes to 16. In doing so, it opted for an approach proposed by a significant minority.
In the days leading up to the decision, UBS and major trade associations had publicly opposed this motion. A 90% requirement for Common Equity Tier 1 capital was not a compromise on the Federal Council’s proposal, said UBS, adding that it would cause lasting damage to its competitiveness.
+ UBS global units must be backed by ‘hard capital’: SNB
UBS and several major business associations would have preferred the compromise drafted by the majority, which was ultimately rejected. Under this proposal, the bank would have had to underpin at least 50% of its foreign holdings with Common Equity Tier 1 capital. For the remainder up to 50%, AT1 (Additional Tier 1) bonds would have been permissible.
More
Why a monster UBS bank scares Switzerland
The Federal Council and a minority of senators had sought an even stricter requirement, calling for full underpinning of foreign holdings with hard equity capital. However, their motion was defeated on Wednesday.
The capital rules bill, part of measures drawn up following
the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse, will now move to the lower
house of parliament, with a final decision expected at the end
of this year at the earliest, and more likely in 2027.

Zelenskyy and von der Leyen’s meeting in New York took place amid Kyiv’s concerns about a possible escalation by Russia in winter and disputes over further EU support for Ukraine. Bloomberg reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to a person familiar with the negotiations, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen held a tense meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday at the UN headquarters in New York.
According to the source, the Ukrainian side expressed concern about the prospect of escalation by Russia in winter, amid limited air-defense capabilities to protect Ukrainian cities. The Ukrainians were also outraged by the EU’s decision to lift sanctions on two Russian oligarchs as part of an agreement to extend the sanctions.
"More defense support is already on its way. And as reforms advance in the Verkhovna Rada, there will also be more budget support," von der Leyen wrote in a post on X after the meeting, referring to the Ukrainian parliament. "We still have €37 billion available for this calendar year."
As the publication notes, after more than four years of full-scale war, differences have begun to emerge between Kyiv and its key allies as preparations are made for another difficult winter under Russian attacks. Ukraine is becoming increasingly frustrated by the unwillingness of some European allies to supply critically important interceptors that Kyiv can use against Russian missiles, while European countries are growing increasingly irritated by rising financial demands.
Ukraine asked its allies to help cover an unforeseen budget deficit of about €26 billion ($30 billion), and also called on the EU to expedite the allocation of a €90 billion loan. These funds were intended to provide financing for Ukraine through the end of next year.
The EU opposed some of Ukraine’s calculations and proposed that other partners, including Canada, Norway, and Japan, provide additional financing. Zelenskyy told journalists that their teams would meet again in seven to ten days for further negotiations on the issue, and expressed hope that a solution would be found.
According to him, the Europeans said for the first time that they saw "growing risks of aggressive actions by Russia against other European countries."

Macron says Hamas was ‘never active’ in West Bank. Nearly 40 years of terror campaign say otherwise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:54:10 UTC
16:54:10 KST

French President Emmanuel Macron’s speech Tuesday night at the UN General Assembly immediately sparked an uproar in Israel after he claimed that Hamas had never “caused trouble” in the West Bank, a statement contradicted by nearly four decades of the terrorist organization’s activity there.
Just two days earlier, hours before Yom Kippur began, Netanel Shukrun, a French citizen and father of six, was killed in a shooting attack at the Ein Re’iya spring. The attacker, Qadri Samara, was identified as a Hamas operative.
Hamas’ presence in the West Bank did not begin this week. In fact, its activity there dates back to the late 1980s, not long after the terrorist organization was founded in the Gaza Strip in December 1987, with the outbreak of the First Intifada.
The organization began participating in demonstrations and clashes with IDF forces while simultaneously building an independent infrastructure that competed with the PLO and Fatah, and established a leadership presence on the ground that continues to this day.
During the late 1980s and early 1990s, Hamas operated an underground network in the West Bank that also carried out attacks against Israelis. In April 1993, several months before the Oslo Accords, Hamas reached a turning point when it carried out its first suicide bombing, at Mehola Junction in the Jordan Valley.
The signing of the Oslo Accords in September of that year turned Hamas into a major opponent of the diplomatic process, particularly in its confrontation with more moderate Palestinian organizations in the West Bank. The group rejected mutual recognition between Israel and the PLO and the establishment of the Palestinian Authority, and continued violent activity aimed, among other things, at undermining the process.
During the wave of attacks in the 1990s, Hamas claimed responsibility for dozens of attacks in which Israelis were killed, including attacks carried out by terrorists who came from the West Bank.
In 1996, Hamas’ bombing campaign reached a peak when, over roughly two weeks, it claimed responsibility for four deadly attacks in Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Ashkelon in which 59 Israelis were killed. Hamas continued carrying out attacks afterward.
With the outbreak of the Second Intifada, Hamas became an even more significant force in the armed struggle against Israel, which had initially been led by Fatah. The organization’s infrastructure in the West Bank quickly became a central part of the deadly terrorist campaign, while Hamas also gained strength in Palestinian public opinion.
Over three and a half years of the Second Intifada, Hamas carried out hundreds of attacks. The terrorist organization was behind, among others, the Dolphinarium bombing, in which 21 people were killed and dozens more wounded, and the 2002 Passover bombing at the Park Hotel in Netanya, in which 30 people were killed and more than 150 wounded.
The Park Hotel bombing is considered a principal reason Israel launched Operation Defensive Shield, during which Israeli forces conducted a broad campaign against terrorist infrastructure in the West Bank.
Later, after Hamas seized control of the Gaza Strip, it continued building its presence in the West Bank. In 2014, Marwan Qawasmeh, a Hamas terrorist released in the deal to free Gilad Shalit, commanded the kidnapping of three Israeli teenagers in Gush Etzion: Naftali Fraenkel, Gilad Shaar and Eyal Yifrach.
Israeli security officials determined at the time that Hamas was the principal threat in the West Bank amid its efforts to rebuild a military infrastructure in the territory.
In the years since, and continuing to this day, Hamas has launched attacks from the West Bank and continued trying to harm Israelis through its operatives. Numerous Hamas cells and terrorist infrastructures have also been uncovered and dismantled in IDF operations and raids, including Operations Home and Garden, Break the Wave and Summer Camps.
IDF activity in the West Bank has become a daily occurrence since Oct. 7, 2023, while Hamas and other organizations have intensified efforts to expand their operations there.
In addition to the deadly attack in which Shukrun was killed in front of his son, Duvdevan troops arrested two Hamas-affiliated terrorists in Qabatiya in the northern West Bank during Yom Kippur. The two were suspected of planning to carry out an attack “in the immediate timeframe.”
The arrests followed a series of thwarted plots in recent weeks in which several terrorists and local cells suspected of planning imminent attacks were detained.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu quickly responded to Macron’s remarks through the Prime Minister’s Office.
“The grotesque absurdity of Emmanuel Macron’s statement is astounding,” Netanyahu said. “On Sunday, the eve of Yom Kippur, just two days ago, Netanel Shukrun, a French citizen and father of six, was murdered in his car by a Hamas terrorist in Judea and Samaria.”
“With his final breath, he told his son to run. Hamas terrorists carry out attacks against Jews almost every day. They have murdered countless Israeli civilians in Judea and Samaria. Ignorance is no excuse for erasing their blood.”

Catalonia’s political landscape shifts as far-right separatists surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:52:00 UTC
16:52:00 KST

Nearly a decade after Catalonia’s failed independence bid, voters are increasingly prioritizing immigration and crime over secession, fueling the rise of the far-right separatist party Aliança Catalana.
The party, which draws much of its support from working- and middle-class voters in rural areas outside Barcelona, has surged in the polls and now ranks second behind Spain’s ruling Socialists ahead of Catalonia’s next election in 2028.
Although Aliança says it would pursue unilateral independence from Spain if it won power in the wealthy northeastern region, its political message has focused increasingly on curbing immigration and tackling crime, reflecting a broader shift in the issues shaping Catalan politics.
Its growing influence is reshaping Catalan politics. Earlier this month, riot police prevented violent clashes between Aliança supporters and left-wing separatists in Barcelona, overshadowing Catalonia’s Sept. 11 national day celebrations, which have historically drawn large pro-independence crowds.
The episode highlighted divisions within the separatist movement, potentially complicating efforts to form a coalition to unseat the region’s ruling Socialist Party. Traditional pro-independence parties have ruled out governing agreements with Aliança.
As its support has grown, other separatist parties have adopted more conservative positions, including lobbying Madrid to let the region restrict migration.
The party’s appeal cuts across Catalonia’s traditional political divides. Much of its support comes from voters who previously backed the separatist center-right Junts or the far-right, staunchly anti-independence Vox, according to a Catalan government survey published in July.
Aliança’s rise has been driven largely by its outspoken leader, Silvia Orriols, 41, who studied to become a librarian and comes from a middle-class farming family.
Orriols told Reuters her party was tapping into frustration with established politicians and concerns that immigration was diluting Catalan identity.
“People have regained hope and drive to fight for the restoration of the Catalan state, to implement policies aimed at preserving our identity,” said Orriols, who frequently invokes Catalonia’s history in her speeches.
She said the far-right Alternative for Germany’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt state earlier this month showed that “Europe is awakening.”
“We Europeans are shielding ourselves in order to survive,” she said.
Aliança rose to prominence in 2023 after Orriols won a local election in Ripoll. Her anti-Muslim message gained traction in the mountainous town where most of the Moroccan-born perpetrators of the 2017 Barcelona terror attacks had lived.
The party entered Catalonia’s parliament a year later with two seats. Since then, it has grown from 3.8% to 16.7% of voter intentions for the next regional election, according to a poll published by El Mundo newspaper this month. It was 2.6 percentage points ahead of fellow separatist party ERC.
Eloi Radovan, whose family traditionally backed left-wing pro-independence parties such as ERC, is among those who have shifted their support to Aliança.
“I feel betrayed,” said Radovan, 19, referring to how parties such as ERC and Junts failed to follow through on the 2017 referendum in which Catalans voted in favor of independence. He also criticized their cooperation with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
He supports Aliança’s call for a total ban on migration because, he said, “Catalonia is increasingly becoming less Catalan.”
Junts is seeking to counter Aliança’s appeal by presenting itself as a more pragmatic centrist alternative while offering its own proposals on migration and security. Two senior Junts officials told Reuters they viewed Aliança’s plans as unrealistic and discriminatory.
The party’s gains have coincided with shifting priorities among Catalan voters.
Affordable housing, migration and crime topped the list of concerns in the July survey. Two years earlier, political dissatisfaction and Catalonia’s relationship with the rest of Spain ranked highest.
“The (2017) independence push was driven by economic anxiety, whereas Aliança responds to demographic anxiety,” said historian Joan Esculies.
Aliança’s rise is “an expression of frustration at the lack of a viable path toward independence and a cry born of fear as new waves of immigration pose a greater threat to (Catalan) language,” he said.
Yet support for independence has remained resilient despite divisions within the movement and the loss of the regional presidency in 2024 after a decade in power. The July survey showed 45% backing independence, down from a peak of 49% in 2017.
Critics say Aliança is exploiting those frustrations rather than offering solutions.
The party offers no real solutions and other separatists must combat its “xenophobic, racist discourse of exclusion,” said left-wing separatist Hug Lucchetti, 45, during this month’s protests.
“The independence movement is alive,” he said. “New ranks of activists continue to emerge.”

TPP legislator says labor minister oversteps role on minimum wage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:49:50 UTC
16:49:50 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TPP Legislator Chen Chao-tzu (陳昭姿) said that Labor Minister Hung Sun-han (洪申翰) should not have pre-empted the formal process for setting the minimum wage, UDN reported Wednesday.
Hung said that the minimum wage was likely to rise in 2027 and that the monthly rate could exceed NT$30,000 (US$955). He said the final amount would still be decided by the Minimum Wage Deliberation Committee, which includes representatives from labor, employers, government, and academia.
Chen said the minimum wage cannot be decided by the labor minister or the committee chair alone. She said the adjustment process is set by law and should not be presented as a benefit granted by an individual minister.
Under the Minimum Wage Act, the committee considers inflation, economic growth, wage levels, household income and spending, and other economic indicators when reviewing the rate. Chen said any adjustment should therefore be made through the statutory review process.
CNA reported that the Minimum Wage Deliberation Committee will meet Thursday to review the country’s minimum wage for 2027. Even if the legal minimum rises, workers may not receive the same increase in basic salary.
The labor ministry defines the monthly minimum wage as the lowest compensation a monthly paid worker must receive for normal working hours. It does not require an employer to set basic salary at the full minimum-wage level.
Under the Labor Standards Act, wages can include salaries, bonuses, allowances, and other payments made in return for work. Attendance bonuses, performance bonuses, and some allowances may therefore count toward the legal minimum.
Not every payment can be included. Whether a bonus or allowance counts as wages depends on its purpose and whether it is compensation for work, rather than what the employer calls it.
The monthly minimum wage is currently NT$29,500, while the hourly rate is NT$196. Because qualifying bonuses and allowances can be included, a worker’s basic salary can legally remain below NT$29,500 as long as total qualifying wages meet the threshold.
This means a higher minimum wage does not guarantee an equal increase in basic pay. If a worker’s existing basic salary and other qualifying payments already meet the new threshold, the employer may comply without raising basic salary by the full amount.

Taiwan drone industry output to exceed NT$50 billion by 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:49:45 UTC
16:49:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Economics Minister Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said drone industry output is expected to exceed NT$50 billion (US$1.59 billion) by 2030, CNA reported Wednesday.
Speaking in an interview with the Digital Transformation Institute, Kung said the industry is growing faster than expected and could reach its original 2030 target of NT$40 billion ahead of schedule. The government has therefore raised the target to more than NT$50 billion.
Kung said the Russia-Ukraine war has highlighted the growing role of drones in modern warfare. Many drones have short operational lives, increasing demand for rapid production, replacement parts, and reliable supply chains.
Taiwan has strong manufacturing capabilities and a well-developed industrial supply chain, he said. Growing international demand for drone systems that reduce reliance on China is also creating opportunities for companies.
The government is supporting the industry through government and defense orders, technology development, testing facilities, and regulatory measures. It has also formed an overseas business alliance involving more than 200 domestic drone companies to help them expand into international markets.
Kung said defense orders can provide more stable demand for the sector, which is made up largely of small- and medium-sized companies. Stable orders can help manufacturers invest in production lines and increase capacity, but companies must also develop overseas markets rather than depend only on government contracts.
Taipei still relies on foreign suppliers for some thermal imaging equipment, satellite positioning systems, communications chips, and other key components. The economics ministry plans to support research and industry projects to strengthen domestic production while promoting international cooperation.
The nation currently produces about 70% of the parts and technology needed for small drones domestically, compared with about 60% for medium-sized drones and 30% for large drones. The government aims to raise the domestic production rate for key technologies and components to 90% across all three categories by 2030.

Outgoing UN chief makes climate push at New York summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:49:35 UTC
16:49:35 KST

UN chief Antonio Guterres has made climate change a defining issue of his tenure that ends on December 31. (AFP Photo)
Fresh from accusing fossil fuel interests of treating the atmosphere like an "open sewer," outgoing U.N. chief Antonio Guterres is set to host his final climate summit on Sept. 23 at the world organization's New York headquarters.
The stakes are clearer than ever, as the impacts of climate change surge around the world — from heat waves and wildfires in Europe to catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet triggered by a glacier collapse.
Extreme weather impacts are set to worsen with an El Nino weather pattern that has tied for the most intense ever.
And the world is set to shoot past — at least temporarily — 1.5C of warming, beyond which scientists say it will see worse catastrophes from climate change.
The "High-level Event on Climate Action and the Just Transition" will have opening remarks by Guterres followed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
The two countries are co-hosting COP31 climate talks in Antalya in November in an unusual arrangement, with Australia running the talks but Türkiye hosting the event and rallying support for voluntary pledges.
Guterres, who made climate change a defining issue of his tenure that ends on December 31, set the tone on Sept. 22 when he called out "Big Oil" for treating the atmosphere like an "open sewer."
"Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, five major Western oil companies have pocketed nearly half a trillion dollars in profits," he continued.
He compared the amount with the just $34 billion in financing that has been mobilized to help developing countries adapt to a warming world.
"Guterres is an extraordinary climate champion," Rachel Cleetus of the nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists told AFP.
She praised the former Portuguese prime minister for using his position "to elevate the voices of the less powerful and highlight the need for climate justice."
Emissions cuts, financing, electrification
The meeting agenda calls on leaders to focus on areas like accelerating action to green their economies and mobilizing financing for developing countries to help them achieve their carbon goals and build resilience against a warming world.
Momentum is also gathering for electrification: switching combustion-based systems, like in heating and vehicles, to electricity.
Türkiye has advanced a "35x35" target to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035. However, it has not specified that the electricity should be generated by renewables, which is key to tackling climate change.
There are some glimmers of hope, as global renewable power capacity grew by a record amount last year. But as energy demand increases from AI data centers and air conditioning in a warming world, clean energy is not rising fast enough to displace fossil fuels.
Observers will be watching the level of ambition the two hosts — both fossil fuel-dependent economies — bring in the run-up to COP31.
"We need to come together to meet the problem head-on. There's no avoiding the scale of our responsibility or the cost of inaction," Albanese said at the start of the week, extolling his nation's rising share of renewables in its energy mix.
Yet his climate change and energy minister Chris Bowen is traveling to India and Saudi Arabia this week for talks on strengthening Australia's oil supplies.
Pledges for Nepal — where thousands remain missing — could also feature.
Nepalese Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal recently told Kantipur TV that financial support "is not a matter of charity; it is a matter of legal and moral liability" for his climate-vulnerable country, which produces negligible emissions.
Cleetus said the response for Nepal would be a credibility test for the Loss and Damage Fund, created to help the nations most vulnerable to the ravages of climate change, but so far vastly underfinanced.

The report said the commissioners had flagged issues relating to the addition and deletion of voters as well as the handling of voter data.Senior Congress leaders KC Venugopal and P Chidambaram also stepped up their attack on the poll panel following the report.Chidambaram said the opposition had already contended that several decisions concerning the SIR were wrong and questioned how Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's view could become the decision of the Commission if the two Election Commissioners had taken a contrary position.
"The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that if the decision-making process is flawed or wrong, the decision will also be flawed or wrong. The opposition has contended that many decisions concerning SIR were wrong. Now, it is revealed that the decision-making process was also wrong," Chidambaram said."If two ECs have taken a contrary view, how could the CEC make his view the 'decision' of the ECI? All decisions of the ECI in recent years should be reviewed by a Parliamentary Committee. Meanwhile, the SIR process should be suspended immediately all over the country," he added.Congress general secretary KC Venugopal also targeted CEC Gyanesh Kumar and demanded his removal."There is no doubt remaining. Mr Gyanesh Kumar has no right to remain in office. How the hell can one man, acting on His Master's orders, strike off names at whim? How can he sideline fellow Constitutional officers to only take blatantly illegal steps that put our democracy in danger?" Venugopal said."The right to vote is an essential Constitutional power given to every citizen, the fundamental bedrock of our democracy. If it is to be taken away, due process must be followed with utmost probity," he added.
EC rejects reports of differences
The Election Commission, however, rejected reports of differences within the poll panel over the SIR and said all decisions related to the exercise were taken unanimously.
Officials told news agency PTI that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi did raise concerns over some aspects of voter roll deletion and database handling, but these did not amount to disagreement with the final decisions taken by the Commission.
EC sources said all decisions of the Commission, including those relating to the SIR, had the approval of Sandhu, Joshi and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Officials also pointed out that the law governing the Election Commission, as well as a Supreme Court judgment, provides that decisions should, as far as possible, be taken unanimously. Where unanimity is not possible, the majority view prevails.

His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

Morocco votes for new parliament under shadow of Gen Z protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:48:36 UTC
16:48:36 KST

Breadcrumb
Morocco votes for a new parliament after Gen Z protests and migration surge to Ceuta
Moroccan voters are choosing a new parliament Wednesday in an election shaped by mounting frustration among young people, high unemployment despite a thriving economy, and demands for better schools, hospitals and housing.
Voting centers across the North African kingdom will open from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time, allowing nearly 16 million registered voters to cast ballots for the 395-seat House of Representatives.
The vote will determine the next prime minister and the makeup of the government, which will serve alongside a powerful monarchy that retains broad authority over strategic affairs. Results are expected Thursday.
The next government will oversee billions of dollars in investment as Morocco prepares to co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup, prompting some to describe it as the “World Cup government.” The new political leadership will also face pressure to address everyday concerns, including jobs, wages and the cost of living.
For many young Moroccans, the election comes as doubts grow that political participation can improve their daily lives. Some have turned to street protests, while others have considered leaving the country or staying away from the ballot box.
The Moroccan Constitution requires the king to appoint the head of government from the party that wins the most seats in legislative elections. Since no single party is expected to obtain an absolute majority, the winner will need to negotiate with others to form a governing coalition.
Voters will choose among 7,288 candidates from 27 political parties. The election is the first since deadly youth-led protests nearly a year ago and a mass attempt by migrants to cross Morocco’s northern border into the Spanish territory of Ceuta.
Some, including the far-left party, The Democratic Path, called to boycott the election saying that it “lacks the minimum conditions of democracy.” Banned but tolerated Islamist association Al-Adl Wal Ihsane issued similar claims.
The constitution recognises the right to vote for Moroccans living abroad, but there is no voting by mail or ballot boxes at Moroccan consulates. Instead, they must travel to Morocco to vote or authorize a registered family member or acquaintance to vote on their behalf.
The number of registered voters has declined by 9.7% since the 2021 election, even as Morocco’s population has grown, and analysts expect turnout to be low.

China Focus: China strengthens crackdown on fentanyl-related crimes with detailed rules
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:48:35 CST
16:48:35 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's judicial and law enforcement authorities have issued a set of guidelines on handling criminal cases involving fentanyl-related substances, stressing severe punishment for such crimes in accordance with the law.
The guidelines, jointly issued by China's Supreme People's Court, Supreme People's Procuratorate and the Ministry of Public Security (MPS), aim to ensure the accurate enforcement of the law, protect public health and maintain social stability.
The 18-article document sets out clear thresholds and standards for the conviction and sentencing in fentanyl-related cases, with different standards applying to cases involving pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical fentanyl-related substances.
It defines the scope of fentanyl-related substances covered by relevant laws and rules, and specifies requirements for evidence collection and the recovery of illicit proceeds in related cases.
The guidelines further clarify the respective responsibilities of judicial and law enforcement authorities in handling such offenses.
The top procuratorial and police authorities also jointly issued a set of rules on investigation and prosecution standards for related criminal cases.
The three authorities said in a statement that they would continue to strengthen law-based punishment and comprehensive prevention of crimes involving fentanyl-related substances, while advancing efforts to combat all drug-related crimes.
China has adopted a package of measures to ensure sound and effective governance of fentanyl issues, including adding more substances to the control list, strengthening routine supervision, intensifying anti-smuggling efforts, and advocating global joint governance. It is actively promoting international cooperation, assisting relevant countries in addressing the threats and challenges brought by fentanyl-related substances.
China has taken the global lead in implementing category-wide management of fentanyl-related substances, innovatively including all eligible substances in the scope of regulation by scientifically defining the core chemical structural characteristics of fentanyl.
It is also enforcing strict control over precursors of fentanyl-related substances.
In November 2025, China added 13 types of precursors for fentanyl-related substances to its export control list and applied country-specific measures to the United States, Mexico and Canada. In May 2026, three additional types of fentanyl-related precursors were added to the list applicable to those three countries.
Wednesday's new rules are part of China's latest efforts to fight against narcotics and related offenses.
The country's anti-narcotics authorities on Tuesday warned companies and individuals to strictly comply with earlier regulations while handling medetomidine and tartaric acid, to prevent the two chemicals from entering illegal channels and being diverted into narcotics production.
Authorities have also stepped up enforcement against the illegal trafficking of precursor chemicals and other sensitive substances. The MPS said in May that since 2025, Chinese police had cracked 29 criminal cases involving such materials, arrested 157 suspects, and seized 720 kg of drugs, 1.3 tonnes of new psychoactive substances, 0.9 kg of stimulants and 27.7 tonnes of non-scheduled precursor chemicals. ■

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia on Wednesday hosted the International Conference on Combating Online Scams, aimed at sharing best practices and strengthening global cooperation against this growing threat.
In his keynote address, Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet emphasized that online scams constitute a cross-border regional issue rather than a single-country problem.
"We gather here today to exchange perspectives and to reaffirm a decisive and collective commitment against one of the most complex threats of our digital age," he told the conference.
He noted that Cambodia cannot eradicate this transnational crime alone, adding that sustained international cooperation is essential to overcoming the challenge.

Over the course of the two-day event, officials and experts from more than 20 countries and international organizations will participate in sessions covering online scams as a global emergency, regional and global responses to cyber fraud, technology, prevention, cyber resilience, and individual countries' counter-scam efforts.
Cambodia has launched an unprecedented nationwide crackdown on cyber scam networks since mid-last year to ensure public safety and restore its international image.
According to government data, authorities shut down 663 online scam sites across the country, 86 of which were classified as large-scale scam compounds, between July 2025 and August 2026. ■

China's population with higher education reaches 270 million
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:48:20 CST
16:48:20 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- China now has 270 million people with a higher education background, Vice Minister of Education Wang Guangyan said at a press conference on Wednesday.
Wang also cited figures from earlier stages of the education system: the gross enrollment rate for preschool education reached 92.9 percent, and the retention rate for compulsory education stood at 96.1 percent.
The gross enrollment rate for senior secondary education, he added, reached 92 percent.
Universities under China's "Double First-Class Initiative" will expand undergraduate enrollment by 76,000 places between 2027 and 2030, said Guo Peng, head of the ministry's development planning department, at the press conference.
The initiative supports a select group of universities and academic disciplines with the goal of achieving world-class status.
Guo said the expansion would involve more than simply increasing enrollment, with efforts also made to improve the structure and quality of higher education.
Universities will adjust academic programs to better match national priorities, with greater support for emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, integrated circuits, biomedicine and new energy, he said.
China will also tap central government funding and ultra-long special treasury bonds to help "Double First-Class" universities build new campuses and upgrade basic facilities, such as dormitories, cafeterias, sports venues and laboratories, Guo said.
China's gross enrollment rate in higher education reached 61.3 percent in 2025, with total enrollment standing at 48.73 million, according to Guo. ■

TOKYO, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's Olympic rider Alex Hua Tian successfully defended his individual eventing title at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Wednesday, overcoming heavy rain to finish on 26.90 penalty points after a clear cross-country round.
The 36-year-old, riding Manjushri, also known as Bodhi (Miaojixiang), entered the final phase in first place after dressage and show jumping and maintained his lead without adding any penalties in the cross-country finale.
Hua, who posted the best score in dressage and a clear round in show jumping, completed the cross-country course without penalty to secure his second consecutive Asian Games individual title. He finished 3.20 points clear of Thailand's Woraphat Sittiju, while Japan's Yoshiaki Oiwa took bronze.
"I'm just very relieved, mainly," Hua said after the competition. "Obviously, there's some pressure coming into a championship when you're defending a gold medal, but also bringing such a good horse like Miaojixiang."
"The most important thing is that I didn't let the team down, so I'm very, very, very happy about that," he added.
In the team event, Thailand won gold with 109.90 penalty points, followed by Japan on 115.20 and South Korea on 143.50. Hong Kong, China finished fourth on 144.70.
China missed out on a team medal after being reduced to three combinations from its original four following the withdrawal of Sun Huadong and Cadorico. With no discard score available, China had no margin for error. Shu Yuying and Diabolo D'ems Aa were eliminated in the final phase, while Shao Han and Suez Air finished on 50.50 penalty points and Hua completed the cross-country phase clear. The elimination left China with 1,050.50 penalty points overall.
Hua's gold gave China back-to-back Asian Games titles in the individual eventing competition following his victory in Hangzhou in 2023. ■

Singapore core inflation rises to 2.2 pct in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:48:00 CST
16:48:00 KST

SINGAPORE, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's core inflation rose to 2.2 percent year on year in August from 2 percent in July, reflecting higher services, retail and other goods, and food prices, official data showed Wednesday.
On a month-on-month basis, core prices rose by 0.3 percent in August, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Ministry of Trade and Industry said in a joint statement.
Consumer Price Index (CPI)-all items inflation also increased to 2.3 percent from 2.2 percent, driven by higher core inflation, which more than offset lower private transport inflation.
On a month-on-month basis, CPI-all items inflation rose 0.6 percent in August.
Elevated global energy prices have pushed up electricity and gas tariffs as well as transportation fares, while adverse weather conditions are expected to reduce agricultural yields and raise imported food prices, according to the statement.
Higher input costs are also expected to feed through global supply chains, lifting prices of a wider range of imported goods and services in the coming quarters.
MAS core inflation and CPI-all items inflation are projected to average 1.5 percent to 2.5 percent in 2026.
Core inflation is expected to remain elevated into 2027 before moderating more noticeably from around mid-2027, alongside an expected easing in global energy prices. Risks to the outlook remain tilted to the upside.
"Renewed disruptions in global energy supplies or worse-than-expected weather conditions could raise Singapore's imported costs by more than anticipated," said the statement. ■

China Focus: Fighting typhoons, heat and floods, Chinese farmers weather extremes to safeguard grain harvests
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
15:47:50 CST
16:47:50 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Rice grower Lu Weijun is preparing for harvest in about two weeks, as the crop enters the final stage of ripening, with stalks standing firm across fields in Quanjiao County, east China's Anhui Province.
A month earlier, however, the crop faced a test. "The weather forecast showed a typhoon was coming over the weekend, so we used 10 irrigation machines to pump water into the fields in advance," Lu recalled.
The measure worked. The added layer of water helped support the rice plants against strong winds, making them less likely to bend or topple. After the typhoon passed, Lu quickly drained the excess water to prevent waterlogging.
As China marks the Chinese farmers' harvest festival on Wednesday, autumn crops across the country have entered a critical stage of yield formation after weathering repeated bouts of extreme weather throughout the growing season.
Typhoons, torrential rain, heatwaves and droughts are increasingly challenging China's grain production. As one of the countries most severely affected by natural disasters, China is strengthening agricultural resilience through better infrastructure, new technologies and stronger disaster-response capacity, while shifting the focus from post-disaster relief toward prevention.
FIELD MANAGEMENT
High-standard farmland serves as an important first line of defense against extreme weather, with improved irrigation and drainage systems helping crops withstand both drought and flooding.
For Chen Zhanchao in Changling County, northeast China's Jilin Province, that resilience is easy to see. The area was once known for suffering drought "nine years out of ten." In recent years, efforts to build high-standard farmland have accelerated in Chen's village, with drip irrigation systems installed to deliver water and fertilizer directly to crops.
"Once the valve is opened, water, sometimes mixed with fertilizer, flows through the drip lines directly into the fields," Chen said. "It saves water and fertilizer and is easy to use."
Across China, more than 1 billion mu (about 66.67 million hectares) of high-standard farmland has been built. This year, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs has sent more than 20 work teams to major production areas to help farmers raise yields through appropriate dense planting and integrated water and fertilizer management techniques.
NEW TECHNOLOGY
As China's agriculture becomes more digital, satellites, drones and smart machinery are giving farmers new ways to respond to extreme weather and limit crop losses.
For Cheng Long, who heads a grain and cotton cooperative in Huimin County, east China's Shandong Province, this autumn's challenge came after days of rain. Newly harvested corn had a moisture content of more than 30 percent, raising the risk of mold and sprouting within days.
Two large drying towers installed by the cooperative this year offered a solution. Cheng said the towers can bring moisture down to safe storage levels in less than half a day.
Technology is also speeding up damage assessment. Using radar satellites, drones and field monitoring stations, local authorities can quickly map different levels of corn lodging and complete a damage assessment across the township within 24 hours.
With that information, Cheng and other farmers can pinpoint damaged and waterlogged fields, drain excess water quickly and take targeted measures based on the severity of the damage.
FINANCIAL SUPPORT
Agricultural insurance has become a key policy tool for protecting farmers' enthusiasm for grain production, providing a safety net against disaster risks and helping stabilize expected returns from growing grain.
This year, the central government implemented 16 policy measures supporting agriculture, including subsidies for agricultural insurance premiums, with full-cost and planting income insurance for rice, wheat, corn and soybeans available nationwide.
For Ma Jianjun, a farmer in Wudi County, east China's Shandong Province, that protection proved crucial after low temperatures damaged his wheat in March. Ma had insured 906.1 mu of wheat for 2026.
After Ma filed a claim, the insurer used satellite imagery to gauge the extent of the damage before sending claims staff into the fields. Drones and measuring equipment then assessed the affected area and estimated losses.
In the end, 581.8 mu of Ma's wheat was found to have suffered varying degrees of yield loss, resulting in a payout of 203,600 yuan (30,400 U.S. dollars) that helped him resume production.
GRAIN SECURITY AMID GLOBAL CHALLENGES
Despite serious weather-related damage in some parts of China this year, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs' latest crop monitoring shows that autumn grain acreage has increased slightly and crops are growing well overall.
The challenge extends well beyond China. The World Meteorological Organization said earlier this month that El Niño is set to become very strong in the coming months, raising the risks of extreme weather into 2027.
Global food security is also under growing strain from geopolitical conflicts that have disrupted transport and raised fertilizer and production costs. A UN report released in July estimated that about 645 million people, or 7.8 percent of the global population, faced hunger in 2025.
Against this backdrop, China has continued to strengthen the foundations of its food security. Liu Huanxin, head of the National Food and Strategic Reserves Administration, said earlier this week that China's grain market has remained generally stable and the country's food security is well guaranteed.
China's annual grain output exceeded 700 million tonnes in both 2024 and 2025. A five-year agricultural and rural modernization plan targets comprehensive grain production capacity of around 725 million tonnes by 2030. ■

Trump, Venezuela’s Rodriguez hold 1st meeting since Maduro’s capture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:39:00 UTC
16:39:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump met Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez Tuesday on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, their first face-to-face encounter since U.S. forces captured then-President Nicolas Maduro in a January raid.
The informal meeting took place at a reception hosted by Trump in New York during Rodriguez’s first visit to the United States since taking office. She is scheduled to address the General Assembly Wednesday afternoon.
The encounter comes as Caracas seeks to strengthen ties with Washington and attract international investment. Rodriguez’s delegation includes the vice president for the economy, the oil minister and officials from state oil company PDVSA.
Two people close to the delegation told Reuters that the group is focused on presenting Venezuela as an attractive destination for investment.
Rodriguez described the meeting as a historic step toward strengthening relations with the United States, saying the two sides discussed cooperation in strategic areas including energy, mining and security.
“Venezuela and the United States share a historic relationship that, in this new phase, we are called upon to steer through dialogue,” Rodriguez said in a post on Telegram after the meeting.
She said her administration would continue pursuing diplomacy aimed at achieving “concrete results and collective benefits” for the Venezuelan people.
A White House official said the meeting with Rodriguez included Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, and Stephen Miller, assistant to the president and deputy chief of staff for policy.
Trump has built a working relationship with Rodriguez, who served as Maduro’s vice president.
But critics say Washington has sidelined the opposition led by Maria Corina Machado, dropping demands for free elections in favor of oil and investment deals with the interim government.
Machado, who has been in exile since late last year, made three unsuccessful attempts to return to Venezuela by sea and air in recent hours, her team and media said Tuesday.
A small group of Venezuelans protested in New York, calling for elections.
In his speech to the General Assembly, Trump called Maduro an “outlaw dictator,” said hundreds of political prisoners had been freed since his capture and held up the raid as proof the U.S. would protect its interests in the Western Hemisphere.
“To the victor belong the spoils,” he said, calling an oil deal his administration signed with Caracas last month “perhaps the biggest deal ever made.” Trump has said he wants $100 billion in investment to flow into Venezuela’s oil industry.
Rodriguez arrived in New York on Monday with the delegation, which has been holding talks on energy, mining and debt with U.S. officials, multilateral lenders and companies, sources said.
The head of the Inter-American Development Bank is working to secure approval for a $2.5 billion loan for Venezuela but has faced pushback from some members of the lender’s board.
More than 50 protesters waving Venezuelan flags and carrying signs reading “No Vote, No Oil” and “New Face, Same Regime” gathered outside the U.N. earlier Tuesday to protest Rodriguez’s presence.
Many said they wanted Trump to push for free elections in the country.
They sang the Venezuelan national anthem and chanted, “Delcy, I swear, you’re going to Brooklyn with Maduro,” referring to the federal jail in Brooklyn, just across the East River from the U.N., where her predecessor is being held pending trial on drug trafficking charges.
“On one hand, it’s outrageous to see part of the regime meeting with the authorities of this country’s current government, but there’s also no doubt that thanks to this government, today we are one step closer to freedom,” said Miguel Eduardo Martinez, a 34-year-old social media manager who moved from Caracas in 2017.
Cesar Coello, who carried a sign depicting Rodriguez in an orange jumpsuit, said, “Delcy Rodriguez wasn’t born on Jan. 3, 2026. Delcy Rodriguez has been with the Chavista dictatorship for more than 20 years. She has been complicit.”
The reference was to chavismo, the political movement founded by the late Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez.
Coello said he hoped Trump and Rodriguez would discuss holding elections soon.
