Moroccans vote in parliamentary elections after migrant rush to Ceuta
Moroccan voters choose new parliament Wednesday in elections dominated by economic concerns after a mass migration surge to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July highlighted rising youth unemployment and cost of living concerns. Nearly 16 million Moroccans have registered to elect 395 members of the House of Representatives.
Moroccans began voting for a new parliament on Wednesday with unemployment and inequality front of mind, even as some expressed a lack of trust in the parties in contention.
Nearly 16 million Moroccans have registered to elect 395 members of the House of Representatives. But turnout will be a key test given the widespread voter disillusionment, especially among young people.
Though only four percent of registered voters are aged 18 to 24, youth-focused issues have found a spotlight, especially after the recent mass rush of young Moroccans into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, as well as last year's Gen Z protest movement demanding better health and education.
Read moreIn Ceuta, migrants stranded at Europe’s gates await their fate
Rising unemployment, higher prices and inequality were also at the heart of much campaign messaging, as were efforts to drum up voter engagement.
As of noon, the national turnout rate stood at 11.3 percent, according to official figures, with polls due to close at 7:00pm.
On the campaign trail, parties focused on promises to improve quality of life in Morocco.
But many, even among the older generation, say they wouldn't vote.
"I'm not going to vote because I have lost all faith in the political class," Majda Bakatir told AFP in Rabat.
"We want our country to move forward, but politicians do not seem to care about our problems regarding healthcare, education, and purchasing power," added the 59-year-old woman.
Others, like 55-year-old Karim Ennaciri, did vote in the hopes that the election would bring about change.
"This will allow us to see if there's a renewal within the parties," he said.
Polls opened at 8:00am, and preliminary results are expected to be announced overnight.
Morocco's prime minister is appointed by the king from the party that wins the most seats. The premier then forms a government for a five-year term, but the monarch retains control of major policy decisions.
RNI vs. PAM
Opinion polls are banned under Morocco's electoral law, but observers put the National Rally of Independents (RNI) – currently heading the governing coalition – among the favourites.
Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch led his party's campaign, although he has stepped down as head of the RNI, which will exclude him from heading the next government if his party wins the most seats.
Akhannouch has defended his government's record – including expanding social security coverage – and promised the RNI will do more if re-elected.
"We have done quite important work within the government," he said at a recent rally.
"We carried out reforms in education and health, we increased salaries... we were there when (Moroccans) needed us."
The wealthy businessman has nevertheless faced repeated accusations of conflicts of interest involving his company Afriquia, Morocco's leading fuel distributor.
Akhannouch also faced widespread calls for his resignation during the youth-led Gen Z protests.
The RNI's main rival is the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM). The two centre-right parties are ideologically close and were founded by figures with ties to the royal palace.
'Added value'
The PAM has recruited a popular figure, Budget Minister Fouzi Lekjaa, better known for his role as head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation.
"We want to make young people a force capable of bringing added value rather than being left behind," Lekjaa recently said, pledging higher wages and better purchasing power.
Read moreMorocco’s GenZ 212 youth collective calls for ‘peaceful sit-ins’ to demand reforms
But the PAM has no clear leader, and its other prominent figure is Fatima Ezzahra Mansouri, currently the minister for territorial planning and mayor of Marrakesh, who could become the country's first woman premier.
The PAM has also been hit by a corruption scandal. In June, a court sentenced two of its senior figures to 10 and 12 years in prison respectively in a major drug-trafficking case involving a kingpin dubbed the "Escobar of the Sahara".
Also in contention is Istiqlal, a right-wing party led by equipment minister Nizar Baraka, with a campaign focused on social issues.
And the Islamist opposition's Justice and Development Party has centred its campaign on fighting corruption.
The conservative party, led by former prime minister Abdelilah Benkirane, has also campaigned against women's rights to equal inheritance and the decriminalisation of consensual extramarital sex.

Morocco votes for new parliament as economic concerns mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:13:53 UTC
16:13:53 KST

Moroccans went to the polls on Wednesday to elect a new parliament, with young voters’ frustration over jobs, wages and public services casting a shadow over an election that will shape the country’s next government.
Polling stations opened at 8 am and were scheduled to close at 7 pm local time, with nearly 15.8 million registered voters eligible to choose all 395 members of the House of Representatives.
Official figures show 7,288 candidates are competing, while 28 political formations are taking part in the election. Results are expected Thursday.
The vote comes nearly a year after youth-led protests highlighted grievances over employment, education, healthcare and living conditions.
Despite Morocco’s economic growth and major investment projects, many young people say they have yet to see sufficient improvements in their daily lives.
A test of confidence among young voters
Youth participation is a particular concern. Official figures show that only four percent of registered voters are aged 18 to 24, while analysts expect turnout to be relatively low amid widespread political scepticism.
Some young Moroccans have taken their frustration to the streets, while others have considered emigrating or staying away from the ballot box.
Recent protests and a mass attempt by migrants to cross Morocco’s northern border into the Spanish territory of Ceuta have added to the pressure on political parties.
The election is also unfolding against the backdrop of major infrastructure and investment plans linked to Morocco’s preparations to co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup.
The incoming government will oversee billions of dollars in projects while facing demands that economic gains translate into more jobs and better public services.
Coalition talks likely to shape next government
Morocco’s constitution requires the king to appoint the head of government from the party that wins the most seats in the parliamentary election.
With no single party expected to secure an outright majority, coalition negotiations are likely to determine the composition of the next government. The monarchy retains broad powers over strategic affairs, meaning the elected government will operate alongside a powerful royal institution.
Moroccans living abroad have the constitutional right to vote, but there is no postal voting system or ballot boxes at Moroccan consulates. Those wishing to participate generally must travel to Morocco or authorise an eligible person to vote on their behalf.
The number of registered voters has fallen since the 2021 election even as Morocco’s population has grown, underscoring the challenge facing political parties as they seek to rebuild confidence in electoral politics.

U.S. puts Ukraine-tested interceptor drones through border tests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:10:12 UTC
16:10:12 KST

- U.S. Northern Command tested Perennial Autonomy's Bumblebee interceptor drones during Falcon Peak 26.2 at Yuma Proving Ground, focused on Southern Border counter-drone challenges.
- Perennial Autonomy, founded by Eric Schmidt, holds a $500 million Pentagon contract for drones already credited with over 4,000 intercepts in Ukraine.
The U.S. Northern Command tested Bumblebee interceptor drones from Perennial Autonomy during Falcon Peak 26.2, a counter-drone experiment underway at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona, through Sept. 25.
The command said on Sept. 22 that the exercise is pulling lessons directly from Joint Task Force-Southern Border to sharpen how the military detects and stops unauthorized drones used for smuggling and surveillance along the U.S.-Mexico border.
Falcon Peak 26.2 is the fourth iteration of the recurring experiment and the first held at Yuma Proving Ground, run jointly by U.S. Northern Command and the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401. This round is focused specifically on the counter-drone challenges unique to the Southern Border, testing systems for detection, tracking, and low-collateral ways to bring drones down.
“Gaining and maintaining operational control of low-altitude airspace requires complete unity of effort across government partners,” U.S. Northern Command said. “At Falcon Peak 26.2, USNORTHCOM and JIATF-401 are integrating operational lessons directly from the Southern Border. By testing counter-drone systems alongside Joint Task Force-Southern Border and interagency partners, our teams are identifying the exact tools required to detect and interdict unauthorized drones used for illicit surveillance and smuggling. Developing shared tactics and integrated communications ensures our forces maintain decisive domain awareness along the nation’s borders.”
Bumblebee is a semi-autonomous quadcopter built to destroy small drones through direct collision, with a secondary role in reconnaissance and target tracking. Perennial Autonomy has said the system achieves a direct-hit rate above 70 percent using onboard artificial intelligence for terminal guidance, letting the drone stay locked on a target even if the target aircraft’s own operator loses control of it.
That AI-driven guidance is the common thread across Perennial Autonomy’s product line, not just the Bumblebee. Ukrainian forces have used different Bumblebee variants against Russian FPV drones and reconnaissance drones, while Merops has been credited with thousands of intercepts against Shahed-series one-way attack drones and Gerbera decoy and reconnaissance drones. Ukrainian officials and military bloggers have circulated numerous videos of Bumblebee interceptors downing Russian tactical strike drones and FPV drones. Ukrainian units have pointed to that autonomy-first design, more than any single platform, as the reason the company’s equipment has earned their trust.
Perennial Autonomy, founded by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, began under the names Project White Stork and Project Eagle before adopting its current name. The company built its flagship product, the AS-3 Merops interceptor, for Ukrainian forces fighting off Russian Shahed-series attack drones, and Ukrainian officials credit the system with more than 4,000 intercepts since mid-2024. The company’s Hornet strike drone has also seen use in Ukraine.
The Pentagon has moved to bring that combat record into U.S. service. Joint Interagency Task Force 401 awarded Perennial Autonomy a $5.2 million contract for the Bumblebee V2 system in January, followed by a three-year, $500 million ceiling contract in May covering the Merops, Bumblebee, and Hornet platforms across the joint force. U.S. forces in Central Command have used Merops interceptors against Iranian-designed Shahed drones, and the Marine Corps’ 2nd Marine Division trained on all three systems in August at the Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center in California.
Falcon Peak 26.2 runs through Sept. 25. U.S. Northern Command has not said which specific technologies from the exercise, including the Bumblebee, will move toward operational use along the Southern Border or on what timeline.

Argentina's Milei addresses UN as tensions rise over Falkland Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:06:33 UTC
16:06:33 KST

Argentina accuses UN of ignoring rising tensions over Falkland Islands
Sept 23 - Argentina's President Javier Milei on Wednesday criticized the United Nations for looking "the other way" amid escalating tensions with Britain over oil exploration around the Falkland Islands, a largely self-governing British overseas territory whose sovereignty Argentina has long disputed.
Speaking before world leaders at the UN General Assembly, Milei repeated Argentina's claim to the islands and said that the islanders do not have a right to self-determination. He reiterated his call for negotiations with the United Kingdom to find a peaceful solution to the conflict.
"We're choosing a pacific, practical and effective defense," he said.
Argentina earlier this month began sanctions proceedings against more than 60 companies and people linked to an offshore oil drilling project, a move that British officials have strongly pushed back on. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Tuesday told reporters that he would stand firm against Argentina's actions, saying "we will defend the right of the Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British."
On Thursday, Milei is due to meet with Israeli Prime Minister and close ally Benjamin Netanyahu. The Falklands oil drilling project has strong Israeli ties.
Argentina's claim of sovereignty over the islands located in the South Atlantic and which it calls the Malvinas remains central to its national identity. The country invaded the archipelago in 1982 and fought a 10-week war that ended with Argentina's surrender to Britain and is still commemorated in Buenos Aires in street murals for the fallen soldiers.
In a televised address this month, Milei said the drilling project violates a 1976 UN General Assembly resolution urging both countries to resolve the sovereignty dispute through dialogue and avoid unilateral decisions.
His speech came days after US President Donald Trump, a Milei ally, suggested Washington could reconsider its traditionally neutral position on the Falklands dispute.
'SHIFT THE AGENDA'
Milei's tougher stance marks a notable shift for a president who had been criticized by political opponents for showing little interest in the sovereignty dispute while pursuing closer ties with the US and Europe. Now Argentina's opposition is accusing Milei, who is expected to seek reelection in 2027, of using the dispute to bolster domestic support.
"It's simply something to look good in the eyes of society or to try to shift the agenda," said Guillermo Michel, a Peronist opposition congressman in the chamber of deputies.
However, a study by the Buenos Aires-based consultancy Inteligencia Analitica found that his televised address produced only a modest improvement in his public image.
"The Malvinas issue in Argentina transcends the president's speech," said Marcelo Escolar, the firm's director.
Last week, Milei presented a bill that aims to toughen sanctions on those deemed to unlawfully participate in activities utilizing natural resources in Argentina's maritime spaces and continental shelf.
The bill will first be referred to committee, as the government weighs its legislative priorities.
Milei lacks a majority in Congress but has managed to pass important economic reforms. Marcelo Seghini, a defense adviser in the lower house, said that while some parts of the sovereignty bill may have bipartisan support, other provisions unrelated to the Falklands dispute may spur opposition.
Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration, owners of the Sea Lion project offshore the Falklands, have indicated they do not expect Milei's actions to derail development. REUTERS

Europeans are exercising more. But who gets to take part?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:05:25 UTC
16:05:25 KST

More Europeans are playing sports and doing so more often than four years ago. However, disparities remain across countries, from how regularly people play sports to how well their cities support active living.
The European Commission's Eurobarometer survey on sport and physical activity shows that Europeans are, overall, doing more sport than they were in 2022. Yet significant differences remain between countries and socio-economic groups, even as many Europeans say physical activity benefits their physical and mental well-being.
“More Europeans are getting active, but the opportunity to take part still depends too much on income, age and education,” said Roxana Mînzatu, Executive Vice-President for Social Rights and Skills, Quality Jobs and Preparedness.
Nearly half of the 26,508 people surveyed, representing a range of social and demographic groups, said they exercise or play sport daily or several times a week. Meanwhile, 39% said they never exercise or play sport, down from 45% in 2022.
Finland and Denmark top the charts for daily exercise, with 21% and 20% of respondents respectively saying they exercise every day. In both countries, a further 59% said they exercise several times a week.
At the other end of the scale, 68% of respondents in Portugal said they never exercise or play sport, while Greece and Romania followed closely, both at 66%.
The reasons people give for exercising — whether for less than an hour a week or more than three hours — ranged from maintaining physical health to relaxing and improving mental well-being.
Nearly all respondents believe that being active contributes to improving mental health. Most also agree that it helps to build communities and improve the wellbeing of marginalised groups.
However, for those who don't exercise as much as they would like, time is the biggest barrier, cited by 37% of Europeans. Others named lack of motivation or interest 26% and health problems or injury 15%. Cost is also a factor for 12% of respondents.
Education and financial circumstances track closely with participation.
Some 59% of people who continued their education until at least age 20 exercise or play sport several times a week, compared with 23% of those who left education at 15 or younger. Those who have the most difficulty paying their bills are also twice as likely to say they never exercise as those who rarely or never struggle financially — 54% versus 26%.
“Everyone should have access to affordable sport and safe places to exercise, close to home," said Mînzatu. "This means opening doors to children whose families cannot afford club fees, older people and people with disabilities.”
The age divide is stark. Nearly three-quarters of 15- to 24-year-olds exercise or play sport at least several times a week, compared with just 25% of those aged 75 and over. Among the oldest respondents, health problems or injury is the most commonly cited barrier, while younger and middle-aged Europeans are much more likely to point to a lack of time.
The survey also looked at how often people engage in physical activity for other reasons, such as for commuting or gardening.
The share of people actively commuting increased the most across all surveyed categories, from 24% in 2022 to 37%. Walking for at least 10 minutes at a time is now reported by 72% of citizens, a significant increase compared to 16% in 2022.
However, not all Europeans feel that their neighbourhoods are well suited to walking or cycling, potentially limiting opportunities for active commuting.

However, not all Europeans feel that their neighbourhoods are well suited to walking or cycling, potentially limiting opportunities for active commuting.

Russia tried to interfere in the 2019 election, says UK
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:04:27 BST
16:04:27 KST

Britain has evidence that Russian agencies tried to interfere in the 2019 general election, the Prime Minister has told the United Nations General Assembly, as he tasked the country’s security chiefs with building a new National Centre for Information Defence.
Andy Burnham used his first address to the assembly, delivered in New York on Monday evening, to set out what he described as an industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in Britain and among its allies.
He said: “Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fears. They’ve used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles. Forged the branding of 28 British organisations, including universities and the BBC. They’ve amplified far right narratives. And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 General Election.”
He added that Russian agencies had also tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of what he called horrific events, saying the idea that anyone would use such things to their advantage is repulsive but is what they do.
Putting a figure on the effort, the Prime Minister said the Kremlin spends around £1.3 billion each year on manipulating information, describing “an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community, creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair. We have tiptoed around this for too long. Over the last decade we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality. Well, no more.”
He then announced a new body, to be built by the security services, with three functions attached to it. “Today I am tasking our security chiefs to begin work on a new National Centre for Information Defence, to detect, attribute and disrupt these kinds of hostile state information attacks. To support and defend our democracy,” he said.
Governments have generally been slower to name the source of an information operation than to acknowledge a cyber intrusion, partly because the evidence is circumstantial and partly because saying so publicly invites a demand to act on it.
Mr Burnham linked the threat directly to conditions at home, saying that someone struggling with the cost of living, or a young person not in employment, education or training, would be more vulnerable to that kind of influence, and that “faced with this information warfare, security starts in every home”.
Britain intends to share what it has learned with others facing the same problem, and the Prime Minister said the country had already supported Moldova in protecting its elections from Russian interference, and that with more elections approaching across Europe it stands ready to share its understanding of how these actors work and how they can be countered.
Cyber attacks on British companies and institutions were cited alongside the information campaign, with Mr Burnham warning that artificial intelligence will multiply the threat.
The commitment is part of a considerable body of work already under way across government, with ministers having committed to rewriting the War Books by the end of the year under an accelerated Home Defence Programme, and a national resilience public awareness campaign is due to launch later this year, while the Defence Secretary told the Commons this month that he would report back to Parliament with plans for a national conversation about the threats the country faces.

At least 11 killed in mass shooting in South African township
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:02:16 UTC
16:02:16 KST

Gunmen have killed 11 people and wounded three others in a late-night shooting at a home in South Africa’s eastern KwaZulu-Natal province.
The attack took place in KwaMakhutha township, south of Durban, shortly before 11 pm local time (2100 GMT) on Tuesday, South African broadcaster eNCA reported, saying a pregnant woman was among the victims.
The victims were gathered inside the home when unidentified attackers stormed the property and opened fire.
Ten victims died at the scene of the attack, while another individual succumbed to injuries while being transported to a hospital.
The attackers set fire to a vehicle belonging to the homeowner before fleeing.
The motive remains unknown, and authorities have not announced any arrests or identified the suspects.
One of the world’s highest murder rates
A local resident told eNCA that he had grown up with some of the victims.
"It's shocking and sad. These are guys I grew up with. I can't believe it. It's like a movie," he said. "I've been staying here all my life, and I've never seen anything like this."
South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, with about 60 people killed each day in a country of around 62 million.
Legal and illegal firearms are widespread, and shootings are common, often fuelled by gang rivalry and competition between informal businesses.
In March, soldiers were deployed to violence hotspots across the country to support police efforts to tackle rampant crime, which President Cyril Ramaphosa has described as one of the biggest threats facing South Africa.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – A US State Department spokesperson told Voice of America Tuesday in an interview that there has been “no change” in Washington’s Taiwan policy and the US will continue to support its meaningful participation in international organizations.
The US policy toward Taiwan has not changed in more than 45 years, Jakob Lengacher, the State Department’s Chinese-language spokesperson, said in Mandarin. “The US opposes any unilateral change to the status quo. Our focus is on peace and stability across the region.”
Lengacher was responding to questions on the sidelines of US President Donald Trump’s UN General Assembly speech in New York.
He said the US continues to support Taiwan’s meaningful participation in international organizations, including the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. “Like other APEC economies, Taiwan contributes to economic prosperity in the Asia-Pacific region,” Lengacher said.

Ahead of the high-level meeting, seven US senators urged Trump in a statement Tuesday to maintain Washington’s support for Taiwan.
“The Chinese military continues its pressure campaign against our vital democratic partner Taiwan as President Trump has retreated from longstanding security commitments,” the senators said.

Canada, India aim to wrap up trade talks by G20: Carney
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:01:47 UTC
16:01:47 KST

Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks during a media availability on the sidelines of the the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) at the UN headquarters on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. (The Canadian Press via AP)
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Sept. 22 that trade negotiations with India are making “good progress” and that the two countries are aiming to conclude talks by the G20 summit in mid-December.
Carney also said India had, to his understanding, confirmed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi would visit Canada around that time, though the precise date had not been finalized.
“We are making good progress in our trade negotiations with India,” Carney said at a news conference on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
Carney said he and Modi had committed to try to conclude negotiations by the G20. The summit is scheduled for Dec. 14-15 at Trump National Doral in Miami.
Carney wants to double Canada’s non-U.S. trade over the next decade and has made India part of a broader effort to reduce the country’s dependence on the United States as relations deteriorate under President Donald Trump.
Last week, Carney embraced the prospect of Canada becoming the European Union’s first associate member, saying deeper ties with Europe would help ensure no country could control Canada’s markets or undermine its sovereignty.
Carney also struck a deal with China earlier this year allowing a limited number of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at a sharply reduced tariff in exchange for China lowering tariffs on Canadian canola.
Canada and India formally launched negotiations on a comprehensive trade agreement in March, with both governments committing to conclude talks by the end of 2026.
The rapid economic rapprochement follows a deep diplomatic rupture over the 2023 killing of Canadian Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in British Columbia. Former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were credible allegations linking agents of the Indian government to Nijjar’s killing.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police later said it had evidence allegedly linking Indian government agents to homicides and other violent acts in Canada. Trudeau said Indian diplomats had collected information about Canadians that was passed to organized crime and resulted in violence. Canada expelled six Indian diplomats amid the allegations. India denied involvement and accused Canada of harboring Sikh separatists.
Carney has moved quickly to rebuild ties. His visit to India earlier this year was the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister since 2018.

Germany's saviour? How Klopp is looking to turn fortunes around
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
08:00:26 BST
16:00:26 KST

Germany's saviour? How Klopp is looking to turn fortunes around
- Published
It has been quite the ride since Jurgen Klopp was announced as Germany's head coach in July.
In his first news conference, Klopp admonished the media, urging them to treat him fairly and refrain from any attacks against his family.
Last Thursday, during another media conference, Klopp called for "positive patriotism" amid political turmoil in the country.
When asked whether he considers himself an ambassador for Germany in his new role, Klopp's answer was a serious one.
"From my perspective as a sportsman, I can say that I would very much like to reclaim the flag for myself, for all of us," said Klopp.
"I want it so that when someone waves it, no-one thinks: 'What is wrong with you?' Instead, I want people to understand: You are happy and realise how lucky you were to be born, grow up, or move to this wonderful country."
His statement was made in light of the success of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The anti-immigration party has since scored another win in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Klopp's remarks were widely and positively discussed in the media - the German national team represents a diverse Germany, as several players come from a migrant background.
KIopp also remarked about the recent success of Alexander Zverev at the US Open, the women's basketball team at the European Championship and German athletes at the European Athletics Championships, saying sport can ensure "a sense of community".
He added: "This is our mission: we need to create a good atmosphere."
Klopp knows, intentionally or not, how to make headlines.
However, the German Football Association (DFB) didn't hire the former Liverpool boss on an annual salary of £6m to become a commentator on the state of Germany - but to transform a floundering national team.
- Klopp wants to 'reclaim' flag amid German elections 
  - Published6 days ago
- Klopp starts Germany reign by threatening to quit 
  - Published24 July
Between the two news conferences, Klopp looked like the busiest national team boss on the planet, making countless visits to league games and training facilities.
One day fans could see Klopp sitting in the stands of Dortmund's Signal Iduna Park, his old stomping ground and, not long after, they may have caught a picture of him in the VIP lounge of Mainz's stadium or somewhere near Eintracht Frankfurt's training pitch talking to players.
Klopp has approached this new job with open eyes. Initially, the charismatic 59-year-old drew up a list of 57 players who could have been selected for this first international break.
"Players will receive chances who don't even expect it yet," Klopp said in July.
His first selection wasn't short of surprises. In the flavour of a trial-and-error principle, Klopp and his staff decided to select two almost completely different squads for the upcoming four games.
The first squad, including Joshua Kimmich, Kai Havertz and Jamal Musiala, will face arch-rivals the Netherlands at Johan Cruyff Arena on Thursday (19:45 BST) and host Greece on Sunday.
The second squad, with Florian Wirtz and Aleksandar Pavlovic, face Serbia at home and Greece on the road in the second half of this international break. The only player who was selected for both is back-up goalkeeper Finn Dahmen.
'It could be wild, but I accept that'
The selection process means we will not see Germany's best starting XI this time around. Instead, Klopp clearly intends to try out new players, some of whom played in Germany's second tier only a few months ago.
Take, for example, Felix Keidel, a 23-year-old full-back-midfielder hybrid from recently promoted SV Elversberg.
A year ago, Keidel was as far away from the national team as the Oktoberfest from Rio Carnival.
Now Keidel - just like Mika Baur, Bambase Conte, Max Rosenfelder, Philipp Treu, and Vitaly Janelt - has the chance to show he could be a valuable cog in the machine.
Klopp has never built his success merely on star names - he has always taken a liking to undervalued and overlooked players.
He once signed an little-known Polish winger by the name of Lukasz Piszczek and moulded him into one of the best right-backs in Europe who would go toe-to-toe with Cristiano Ronaldo in his prime. And he helped transform Andy Robertson into a force on Liverpool's left side.
Klopp's style helps to elevate all the members of his squad - not just the most talented.
Fitness and mental readiness are highly important, and some newcomers might just have that to impress the new manager.
But man-marking is prevalent in Germany's top flight, while Klopp prefers his teams to close down the player in possession to create superior numbers around the ball. So some of the Bundesliga players will have to adapt quickly.
"It is not important who plays but how someone plays," Klopp said last week. "I expect a lot from the beginning. It could be a bit wild, but I accept that. It just has to be lively."
Klopp has chosen younger squads compared to the ones we saw in the past couple of years. Manuel Neuer, Antonio Rudiger and Pascal Gross have retired from international football, and other 30-somethings might just not receive a chance to get into the team again.
"I think it is about time to wish the new generation best of luck," Gross said after Brighton's win over Arsenal on Saturday. "I still enjoy playing football here in the club, but there's a change in Germany and rightfully so."
Both squads for this international break have an average age between 24 and 25. Youth and energy seem to be preferred.
"I have the desire to work with guys who cannot wait to wear this jersey, who want to play the kind of football everybody enjoys and who perform even better wearing the national team jersey," Klopp said.
We can expect from him to simplify Germany's approach to ball possession. Predecessor Julian Nagelsmann bent over backwards to hide some of the flaws he detected in his squad and thus created highly complex tactical systems.
On the contrary, Klopp intends to put an emphasis on the wings and break defences there. We saw what he was able to achieve with the likes of Mohamed Salah, Trent Alexander-Arnold and Sadio Mane from wide areas.
While underwhelming at the past couple of international tournaments, Germany still possess a deep talent pool. Cologne's rising star Said El Mala and 18-year-old Bayern Munich talent Lennart Karl will get chances to show their skills on the wings.
Freiburg's Derry Scherhant and Barcelona's Karim Adeyemi provide plenty of speed, just like Brentford's Kevin Schade who has returned to the squad after being left out for the World Cup. There is potential for an exciting Germany side we have not seen in quite a while.
Finally, the emotional component plays a role in Klopp's entire approach. He works towards a fresh start for the national team and a new spirit in the country.
Last Thursday, he wore a cap that read "One of 83 million". It was a clear indication he wants to unite all 83 million Germans behind this team and they are all in it together.
Klopp has spent plenty of time thus far attempting to shape narratives off the field - but now the spotlight turns to his ability to get the best out of his group of players on the pitch.

  - Published28 August

Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson’s Disjointed But Endearing Brothers Coasts on Charm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:00:04 UTC
16:00:04 KST

As a nation still mourning Dolly Parton is all too aware, there aren’t many entertainers left who are embraced by Americans across demographics and ideologies. Among the few A-listers with bipartisan appeal are Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson, separately but especially as longtime best friends and occasional co-workers—two sons of Texas who, as you’ve probably heard, might also be sons of the same biological father. So it makes sense that Brothers, an Apple TV comedy that casts them as exaggerated versions of themselves, seems built to satisfy as broad a range of their fans as possible. Disjointed but breezy, it coasts on the chemistry between its leads.
Premiering with two episodes on Sept. 23, Brothers bills itself as being “based on a true rumor” whose plausibility Harrelson acknowledged in 2023: that McConaughey is the product of a tryst between his mom, Kay McConaughey, and Harrelson’s dad, the notorious contract killer Charles Voyde Harrelson, during her second divorce from James McConaughey. (Genetics aside, both families evidently have a flair for off-screen drama.) That’s certainly a big part of the show, supplying a central mystery and fueling tension between the stars after Kay, a.k.a. Ma Mac (Holland Taylor, playing delightfully against buttoned-up type as a hard-drinking, straight-talking, tanned-to-a-crisp matriarch), blurts out her secret to Woody. Can he bear to wound his bestie with the knowledge that Matthew might not share DNA with the late father he idolized?
But there are a lot of other things going on. Too many, really. When Woody, his wife Joy (Brittany Ishibashi), and their two daughters roll up to the McConaugheys’ Austin estate in a psychedelic bus, it’s because Joy refuses to let her husband abandon their eldest child, Olive (Highdee Kuan), as she heals from a broken engagement. Matthew has his own family and challenges, writing a speech for a public event honoring his dad while trying to nurture a bond with his kids, especially timid teenage son Wyatt (Nolan Almeida). Brothers is most generic in these double-family-sitcom storylines, with the two wild, larger-than-life leads constantly testing the patience of their more grounded, long-suffering, emotionally intelligent wives. A subplot for, perhaps, True Detective fans, in which two sickly old-timer crooks (Jeff Kober and Barry Corbin) try to extract from Woody a debt his dad owed them, feels like excerpts from a different show.
What actually works is, not surprisingly, the buddy-comedy stuff—the sillier, the better. Matthew and Woody squished into a rideshare with too many rowdy, young fans? A treat. Woody and Matthew donning ridiculous Sunset Strip rocker disguises, complete with facial prosthetics, to play an acoustic set at a coffee shop? Classic. Showrunner Lee Eisenberg (Stick, The Office), who created Brothers alongside McConaughey, Harrelson, and Schitt’s Creek alum David West Read, understands his leads’ personae, and they’re more than game to laugh at themselves. The series opens by showing us the versions that live in the public imagination; Woody enters smoking a joint and holding a surfboard, while Matthew roams the sun-dappled fields of Texas, sipping whisky in a cowboy hat as he recites an excerpt from his megahit memoir Greenlights in voiceover. He plays the charismatic, image-conscious, golden-boy straight man to Woody’s free-thinking hippie, a guy who doesn’t let fame stop him being as weird as he wants to be.
Then it pushes those archetypes without fully puncturing them. Woody’s discovery that they might literally be brothers from different mothers adds some useful pressure—though, truth be told, the storyline is less effective as a driver of plot than it is as a showcase for Taylor, who disappears into her role, making Ma Mac a spitfire but never a cartoon. Brothers gets more juice out of another ripped-from-the-headlines narrative: McConaughey’s political ambitions. While in real life he decided, after months of speculation, not to enter the 2022 Texas gubernatorial race, the show puts Matthew on the campaign trail. (What it carefully doesn’t do is align him with any party or cause. But boy does he love Texas!) It’s a fun reality check for a guy who’s great at kissing babies but can’t answer a simple question about housing policy. His jaded campaign manager, played to the hilt by Lisa Gilroy, gets the series’ most self-aware jokes (“Your Achilles’ heel is that you have been a celebrity for so, so long that your brain has turned into a big old sloppy pile of goo”). A cynical, Type A Armando Iannucci character in the land of alright, alright, alright, she’s deployed sparingly enough to add some edge without killing the laid-back vibe.
Really, though, the campaign could have been the whole show. It’s the perfect context for contrasting the stars’ personalities, pitting Matthew’s traditionalism and discretion against Woody’s unapologetic outlandishness. When the former announces he’s running, his old friend doesn’t mince words. “I’m a f-cking anarchist, and I think this is the stupidest, craziest f-cking idea you ever had,” Woody exclaims. But will he support Matthew on the trail anyway? Of course he will. Because, regardless of what any DNA test says, that is what makes a brother.

Text description provided by the architects. The project is based on a critical and conscious look at the act of building, understanding architecture not as an isolated object, but as a cultural, environmental, and social process deeply linked to the territory and the community that inhabits it. From this perspective, the intervention proposes the conservation and transformation of built heritage as an essential strategy to extend the life of buildings, recognizing the tangible and intangible value they contain. Reclaiming an existing structure does not imply freezing it in time; rather, it means reinterpreting it, allowing it to incorporate new layers of meaning and use, and ensuring it continues to be an active part of the place's evolution.

With a cloud of controversy hanging over former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko — who was dismissed last week after his office was raided by anti-corruption officers — information has now emerged about a mystery villa in Dubai.
Records show Kravchenko’s former mother in law was listed as the owner of the Dubai villa. But she denies making the purchase.
Alina Shkrobanets acquired villa for about $670,000 in 2023, according to leaked Dubai property data obtained by OCCRP and shared with Schemes, the investigative unit of RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service.
At the time, Kravchenko headed the Kyiv Regional Military Administration and was married to Alina Shkrobanets' daughter, Olena.
“I didn’t buy anything in the United Arab Emirates,” Alina Shkrobanets told Schemes, suggesting her identity details might have been used without her knowledge.
“I’m wondering if someone might have used my information against me,” she said in a phone interview.
Olena Shkrobanets, Kravchenko’s ex-wife, told Schemes she knew nothing about the villa in Dubai’s upscale Damac Lagoons development. Reporters did not receive responses to messages sent to Kravchenko over Facebook, where he has posted recently, or to his Ukrainian phone number.
At the time of recorded purchase, the Dubai villa was still under construction. By 2025, it had a new owner: Andriy Keibash, who confirmed purchasing the property in 2025, but declined to tell reporters who he bought it from.
Keibash manages La Veranda restaurant in Kyiv. Video posted on the restaurant’s Instagram account in 2022 showed Kravchenko dining there with Olena Shkrobanets, who he was married to at the time, along with her parents.
Kravchenko’s former father in law, Igor Shkrobanets, echoed his wife, telling reporters he knew nothing about the Dubai investment.
Igor Shkrobanets is a member of the Chernivtsi Regional Council in western Ukraine. As a public official, he is required by Ukrainian law to declare his family’s assets. The Dubai villa was not listed on his declaration for 2023 or 2024.
The property is not related in any way to the current investigation that led to the raid on the Prosecutor General's Office, which Kravchenko has led since June 2025.

Police close major highways into Islamabad as supporters of the jailed former prime minister plan to march into the capital.
Authorities in Pakistan have begun sealing off the main roads into the country’s capital, Islamabad, to block supporters of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan from reaching the city.
Police in Islamabad said on Wednesday that the Islamabad-Peshawar Motorway, the Islamabad-Dera Ismail Khan Motorway and the Grand Trunk Road would be closed at several points starting in the evening. They urged the public to plan travel accordingly.

Dawn, a leading Pakistani newspaper, reported that the closures were indefinite and aimed at preventing supporters of Khan’s party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), from marching to the capital on September 27.
The protesters are demanding the release of Khan, who has been jailed since August 2023 following a series of convictions that his party calls politically motivated. All but one have since been suspended or overturned on appeal.
Concerns about his health, in particular the condition of his right eye, which has required months of specialist treatment, have prompted the party’s campaign for his release.
The marches were expected to set out for Islamabad from Karachi, Pakistan’s largest city, about 1,150km (715 miles) to the southwest, and from Lahore, about 270km (170 miles) to the southeast.
The authorities have placed about 2,000 shipping containers around the capital and at Attock Bridge, a crossing from the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Dawn reported. Containers and sandbags have also been placed at Haroon Bridge, the other key crossing between Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Punjab, and nearly 30,000 security personnel have been deployed in the Attock district, it added.
Al Jazeera’s Kamal Hyder, reporting from Islamabad, said that the government had told “the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf to reconsider its plans”.
“But the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, on the other hand, says peaceful protest is their constitutional right; they want the release of their leader Imran Khan from jail, and they say they’re doing this in order to uphold the constitution.”
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had warned the PTI against the protest on Monday, saying “we have clearly told them that they can never achieve anything through such drama.” He added, “I will say again that there is still time; they should not go into this situation.”
On Sunday, the police arrested Khan’s sister Aleema Khan at her home in Lahore under a public order law. Two other sisters, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, were also arrested, along with several other relatives.
Separately, Jamaat-e-Islami, another opposition party, began its own march from Karachi to Islamabad on Sunday to protest high fuel prices. Before leaving by train, the party’s leader, Hafiz Naeem ur Rehman, warned that if the government did not scrap a levy on petroleum of more than 100 rupees ($0.36) per litre (0.26 gallons), the protest could become a campaign to topple it, Dawn reported.
But after reaching Multan in Punjab province on Monday night, Rehman said on Tuesday that the party would postpone its march, at the request of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, until the two could meet.

‘I had never heard of Eswatini’: Deported by the US to a country that rejects them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:56:42 UTC
15:56:42 KST

‘I had never heard of Eswatini’: Deported by the US to a country that rejects them
From our southern Africa correspondent – Migrants previously convicted by US courts have been imprisoned in Africa’s last absolute monarchy, Eswatini, over the past several months. Since being deported from the US, they have found themselves in a country about which they know nothing, and where local residents look on these “criminal” arrivals with suspicion. Their abrupt journey to the small southern African kingdom stems from a secret deal struck by Trump administration as part of his programme of mass deportations investigated by “The Deportation Project”, undertaken by Forbidden Stories and a network of 72 journalists across 15 countries.
Protests are rare in the small southern African kingdom of Eswatini, and largely repressed. But that didn’t stop more than a hundred women from gathering on July 18, 2025 in front of the US embassy in Manzini, the economic capital of the country still widely known by its former name of Swaziland.
“Come out, ambassador! Come out and talk with us!” they shouted.
What the women wanted to talk about was the secret arrival of foreign “criminals” who had just been transferred to Swazi prisons. Fearing for the safety of their children, the demonstrators were demanding that these prisoners be sent back to the US – where they had just been deported from.
Over the course of a year, four planes have discreetly touched down in Eswatini carrying 32 migrants deported by the administration of US President Donald Trump. Wedged between Mozambique and South Africa, this country is preparing to host 160 deportees in total.
Watch moreICE, Trump and Africa: Secret deals, broken lives
All of them will be held in the central prison of Matsapha, not far from Manzini. In a country where daily life is still largely shaped by tradition and where few dare to question the decisions of King Mswati III, the secret arrangement with Washington has nevertheless set off an outcry of rare force.
“If South African media hadn’t announced it, we never would have known,” said Sibusiso Nhlabatsi. Determined to meet these migrants face-to-face, the lawyer has been turned away from the prison five times. A well-known attorney and human rights specialist as well as a former colleague of Thulani Maseko, a human rights lawyer shot dead in 2023, Nhlabatsi is not taking no for an answer.
He took his case to the Supreme Court, which ruled in his favour in 2025. The government appealed the decision. In March 2026, the High Court of Mbabane finally authorised the detainees to see him.
“They had been transported like a bag of potatoes – and even with a bag of potatoes, if you transport it from one country to another, there are concerns that you have to go through, there are standards that must be met,” Nhlabatsi said. “They’ve been thrown in prison, despite the fact that they have never committed a crime in Eswatini.”
‘Whether we sign or not, we're still going to get left here’
Nhlabatsi has since travelled every week to the brand-new wing of the high security prison in Matsapha. The detainees’ cases can be hard to untangle, as the detainees come from as far afield as Vietnam, Laos, Yemen, Cuba, Ethiopia, the Democratic Republic of Congo or Jamaica.
The only thing they have in common is having been previously convicted by US courts – though Nhlabatsi stressed that they were not the monsters they were being made out to be.
“Most of them have been rehabilitated, most of them have rehabilitation certificates,” the lawyer said. “It’s not like they were taken straight from jail in the United States of America and then deported. They have been living in American society.”
The feeling of injustice is keenly felt behind the bars of Matsapha’s high-security prison. But not every detainee has the same strength left to fight for their return to their families in the US.
As part of a consortium of 26 media outlets coordinated by Forbidden Stories, RFI and FRANCE 24 spent six months investigating the secret deals struck between the administration of US President Donald Trump and several African countries. These “third countries” have agreed to host undocumented migrants detained by ICE and deported from the US.
From Ghana to Cameroon and Eswatini, our journalists spoke to the people deported to countries utterly unfamiliar to them.
Those who were the first to arrive are the most beaten-down by their fates.
“I had never heard of Eswatini,” said Vietnamese deportee Dung Nguyen in an exclusive interview with FRANCE 24 and Forbidden Stories. "They ... asked us to sign some papers, and I refused to sign the papers. And they said, whether we sign the papers or not, we're still going to get left here."
Nguyen was convicted of rape in 2011, and released in 2015. He has since married, bought a house and found work. Nguyen was living as a free man when he was arrested and bundled onto a military plane on July 16, 2025.
Despite his newfound detention, he said, he is not subject to the same strictures of Swazi inmates – he watches TV, eats better meals and has access to social media. Under the supervision of prison staff, he can even leave the prison to go to the nearest shopping mall.
The ‘Coca-Cola king’
Like Nguyen, most of the migrants held in this prison had never heard of King Mswati III, who has ruled the country since 1986. Over that time, he has earned another name for himself – the “Coca-Cola king”.
It’s not hard to see why. Not far from the prison, the largest Coca-Cola factory on the African continent stretches across more than 6,500 square metres. A wholly owned subsidiary of the Coca-Cola Company, Conco Ltd is the kingdom’s single largest source of foreign currency.
The royal family controls a 40 percent stake in Eswatini Coca Cola Beverages – the authorised bottler – through the Tibiyo Taka Ngwane sovereign wealth fund set up by king Sobhuza II in 1968.
Read moreInvestigation: In Cameroon, the victims of Trump’s deportations face uncertain fates
‘An evil deal’
The US and Eswatini have seemed to enjoy a good relationship for decades. But according to Siboniso Mkhabela, the national organising secretary of the opposition People’s United Democratic Movement (PUDEMO), that relationship has taken a turn since Trump came to power.
He described the agreement on migrant deportations struck between the US and Eswatini as “an evil deal".
"Before Trump came into the White House, we were this close to achieving a milestone in our struggle," the opposition activist said. "This resolution was simply saying those who were involved in the killing of a human rights lawyer and many others during the unrest in June 2021 must be held accountable."
But for many people, Washington has since kept its eyes firmly closed in the face of a regime that grows more repressive by the day in a monarchy that has never been so absolute as it is now.
Watch moreLawyers and activists in Eswatini challenge government for accepting US deportees
Mkhabela said that he can no longer wear a PUDEMO tee-shirt in public. Many opposition party supporters remain behind bars as a result of expansive counter-terrorism laws.
Critics of the agreement between Washington and Mbabane point out that the deal was negotiated during the period when the second Trump administration was dismantling its USAID programme, on which Eswatini heavily relied – more than half of the kingdom’s national budget for its AIDS programmes were financed by the US. Backed into a corner, the government may have had little choice but to make a deal.
While Swazi authorities have confirmed having received people deported from the US, the details of the deal have never been made public. But FRANCE 24 was able to obtain a copy of the document, signed on May 14 by Prime Minister Russell Dlamini. The agreement states that Eswatini will receive 160 migrants deported from the US, as well as the sum of $5.1 million “for reinforcing border and migrant migration capacity”.
Read moreFlight to Ghana: Expelled from the US to a country they’d never been to
‘How long are they going to stay?’
"The Nation is assured that these inmates pose no threat to the country or its citizens," government spokesperson Thabile Mdluli said, adding that the deportees were only “on transit” through the country. Justice Minister Prince Simelane insisted that the detainees would not be treated as prisoners, but as “guests of the king”.
These statements have done little to stem the rising anger in Eswatini’s population, with many people expressing shock that the detainees are allowed to walk around the Matsapha shopping centre.
“Why do they have better living conditions than other prisoners?” “How long are they going to stay in Eswatini?” “What’s going to happen if they have children with our women”? These are just a few of the questions that have been asked in Eswatini’s parliament in recent months.
Mzwandile Masuku, the son of opposition leader Mario Masuku, has another question to add: what’s happened to the $5 million?
“Our minister of finance is on record as having said that he had not seen the funds,” he said. “We cannot point to where the money was received and where those funds have ended up.”
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Questioned in parliament, ministers have given contradictory answers. Prime Minister Dlamini has stated publicly that there was no financial compensation, but that the agreement was intended to foster “better relations” between Eswatini and the US.
The finance minister later clarified to say that the funds had been deposited into an account belonging to the National Disaster Management Agency, to which he does not have access.
Government spokesperson Mdluli rejected repeated requests for an interview, saying that the information already shared with the public was sufficient.
Masuku, whose father has been imprisoned on multiple occasions, knows that he has to be careful. But he has been working tirelessly with his colleagues for months now to have the deal overturned before all 160 deportees arrive in Eswatini.
Whether he’s successful or not, the fact remains that Eswatini can’t keep these people behind bars indefinitely – and only five have returned to their home countries. Others hope to be granted permanent residency in the country they now find themselves in.
But they’ll first need to shake off the image of “criminals” that the US has imposed on them. In Matsapha, the detainees know that their future no longer depends on the US justice system, but on the goodwill of a kingdom they had never in their lives imagined setting foot in.

Britain forms squadron to strike threats in orbit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
07:54:49 BST
15:54:49 KST

The Royal Air Force is today forming No. III Space Effects Squadron, the first British unit dedicated to disrupting, degrading and denying hostile activity in space, the Ministry of Defence stated.
The squadron is being announced by the Chief of the Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Harv Smyth, at the first UK Space Power Conference today, and will bring together specialist personnel from across the armed forces to counter hostile activity in orbit and defend the satellites the country depends on.
Sir Harv will say: “Space no longer supports operations from the sidelines. It’s a domain of direct competition, where our military advantage can be won or lost. No. III Space Effects Squadron will safeguard the vital benefits that space gives to our integrated armed forces, and will be capable of denying those benefits to our adversaries.”
The new unit completes a trio of squadrons, since No. I Space Operations Squadron gives the Royal Air Force the ability to watch what is happening in orbit and No. II Space Warning Squadron provides warning of threats, while according to the department No. III will act against those threats using advanced technology including electronic warfare. It will support both offensive and defensive space operations and is expected to expand as new capabilities enter service.
The department describes the formation as contributing to developing British capabilities for space warfare, including electronic warfare and countermeasures against anti-satellite weapons, and delivering the Control of Space Requirement set out in the UK Space Strategy published earlier this month. That requirement covers maintaining freedom to operate in space while denying adversaries the same freedom.
Britain has formally ruled out destructive anti-satellite missile testing, the kind that generates long-lived debris fields, and the department says it continues to work through the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space to promote norms and principles of responsible behaviour in orbit. The government describes itself as committed to the peaceful and sustainable use of space while protecting critical infrastructure.
Alongside the announcement, the department restated an £880 million investment between 2026/27 and 2029/30 in space-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance and in space control activities.
The Strategic Defence Review stated that the ability to operate in, from and through space underpins British security, prosperity and daily life, and the Defence Investment Plan committed to the Deep Space Advanced Radar Capability, a trilateral programme with the United States and Australia whose British site is due to begin construction in April 2027 and which will provide continuous radar coverage of geostationary orbit.

Tech elite's new school aims to replace university
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
06:52:37 UTC
15:52:37 KST

Marc Andreessen (L) and Ben Horowitz (AP Photo)
The most powerful venture capital firm in Silicon Valley is starting a two-year private school for young people intended to replace college, as some U.S. tech elite question the benefits of a classical university education.
The Horowitz Andreessen Academy, or HAA, is backed by veteran investors Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, two towering figures of the U.S. tech industry and founders of venture capital giant Andreessen Horowitz.
The announcement said students would hear lectures from tech leaders including Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, Microsoft chief Satya Nadella, Uber founder Travis Kalanick and former OpenAI executive Mira Murati.
It framed San Francisco itself as central to the project, describing the city as unusually open to newcomers and a hub for innovation.
"We think this can be an elite institution that attracts top-tier talent — one that prepares students for the future rather than remaining stuck in the past," the academy's CEO, Gagan Biyani, said on X.
The venture has raised $42 million from investors, including Shopify chief executive Tobi Lutke, DoorDash chief executive Tony Xu, and former Instacart chief and OpenAI executive Fidji Simo.
"We live in an age of infinite knowledge, and we are entering an age of infinite doing," the academy said in its launch announcement.
Biyani said the program would replace lecture-heavy coursework with independent, business-oriented projects, describing the model as closer to Oxford's tutorial system or the Montessori method than a conventional university.
Some of the tech industry's most celebrated founders never finished college — Microsoft's Bill Gates and Facebook's Mark Zuckerberg both left Harvard, while Apple's Steve Jobs dropped out of Reed College.
This history is often invoked in Silicon Valley to argue that a degree is not a prerequisite for building a major company, and that young entrepreneurs should not waste time in the classroom.
The academy joins a growing list of venture-backed efforts to position elite young talent outside traditional four-year degree programs, often on the grounds that U.S. campuses are too liberal or anti-business.
The Thiel Fellowship, founded by right-wing billionaire investor Peter Thiel in 2011, pays selected young people to skip or leave college and build companies instead. Its current fellows receive $250,000 over two years.
Anthropic, Coinbase, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI, Palantir, Replit and Stripe are among more than 30 companies Biyani described as partners.
They will offer students work experience, advice and computing credits in exchange for early access to talent.
Applications are open for a tuition-free pilot year of 50 students starting in September 2027.
This will precede the eventual two-year, paid version of the program, which Biyani said would be similar in cost to an elite private university.
Annual tuition at Stanford University, in the heart of Silicon Valley, stands at $67,731 for the 2026-27 academic year, not including room and board.

S. Korea's August domestic migration hits 53-year low amid housing slowdown
China

14:52:20 CST
15:52:20 KST

SEOUL, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's August domestic migration hit a 53-year low amid a long-term population decline and a housing market slowdown, statistical ministry data showed Wednesday.
The number of those relocating to new homes shrank 4.5 percent from a year earlier to 471,000 in August, marking the lowest for August since 1973, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
The population mobility rate, or the number of movers per 100 people, sank 0.5 percentage points to 10.9 percent in August.
The sluggish migration was driven by structural demographic changes combined with a slowdown in both housing transactions and supply.
The number of housing transactions in June and July fell 4.4 percent year-on-year to 132,000, while the number of completed apartments, a key indicator of housing supply, plunged 29.1 percent to 43,000 in the two months.
Six provinces and cities recorded a net influx of residents, led by Gyeonggi province with 4,486, Incheon with 2,270 and North Chungcheong province with 562.
Ten municipalities saw a net outflow as Seoul posted the largest fall of 2,901, trailed by South Gyeongsang province with 1,230. ■

Feature: Seeing is understanding -- Hong Kong, Macao students explore country's development firsthand in Beijing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:52:04 CST
15:52:04 KST

Students from Hong Kong Special Administrative Region take selfies before watching the flag-raising ceremony at Tian'anmen Square in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 20, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Xiaoyu)
BEIJING, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- In the Chinese capital, groups of Cantonese-speaking students from Hong Kong and Macao made for a distinctive sight as they journeyed from iconic landmarks to cultural and technological venues.
The students, totaling around 1,000, are members of flag-raising teams from schools and universities across the Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions (SARs). They wrapped up their five-day visit to Beijing on Tuesday, with paying tribute to the national flag as its central theme.
The itinerary took them to the Great Hall of the People, the Palace Museum, the station of the Chinese People's Liberation Army guard of honor, as well as schools, companies, and science and technology sites -- offering them a firsthand look at the Chinese capital and a deeper understanding of their homeland.
Dyun Jeoi Ming, a student from Zheng Guanying Official School in Macao, gathered with his peers at Tian'anmen Square at dawn on Sunday for the national flag-raising ceremony. They stood in silence as the guards marched into view and joined in the national anthem as the five-starred red flag was slowly raised.
Though having watched the ceremony countless times on television and on the phone, Dyun said seeing it in person was an entirely different experience. "Standing here today, I am moved beyond words," he said.
For many of the students, raising the national flag is already a familiar part of school life in Hong Kong and Macao. Since their respective returns to China in the late 1990s, the two SARs have retained their capitalist systems and ways of life under the "one country, two systems" principle, but national flag-raising ceremonies and national security education have increasingly become an established part of school life.
In recent years, a wide range of initiatives have also helped young locals forge a better understanding of the country, from joining live "Tiangong Class" space lectures delivered by Chinese astronauts in orbit, to visiting Chinese naval vessels docking in Hong Kong, and taking part in study and exchange programs on the mainland.
As the students set off for Beijing this time, Kong Chi Meng, director of the Education and Youth Development Bureau of the Macao SAR government, said the trip was of "great significance," as it would help the participants strengthen their sense of national identity.
Over the past few days, the students visited historical sites including the ruins of the Old Summer Palace, or "Yuanmingyuan" in Chinese, and a tunnel warfare site, gaining a firsthand glimpse into China's painful wartime history and its resistance against foreign aggression.
Other experiences, from marveling at masterpieces of ancient Chinese bronze craftsmanship to exploring deep-sea laser spectroscopic probes and watching robotic arms swiftly operate along auto production lines, left the students in awe.
"Seeing firsthand what cannot be found in textbooks, I have come to better appreciate the wisdom behind the saying, 'One needs to not only read 10,000 books, but also travel 10,000 miles to know the world around us,'" said Cheung Wing-sam, from Cognitio College in Hong Kong.
Divided into groups, they also visited a dozen primary and secondary schools and universities in Beijing, where they talked and performed with their mainland counterparts.
Xu Xiangyue, deputy head of the Peking University flag guard team, said that students from Hong Kong and Macao come from different campuses and have different life experiences, but "when the national anthem plays and the national flag rises, our eyes naturally turn in the same direction."
For some, the trip may also open a window onto future possibilities, allowing them to align their personal aspirations with the country's broader development.
A senior student surnamed Chan at City University of Hong Kong said that an increasing number of university students in Hong Kong are considering pursuing career opportunities on the mainland after graduation.
"This event gives me a valuable opportunity to see for myself what the mainland is like," said Chan, who plans to share the experience with fellow students after returning to Hong Kong. ■
Members of flag-raising teams from schools and universities across the Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions visit the China National Arts and Crafts Museum in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 19, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Xiaoyu)

New Zealand introduces bill to strengthen border security
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
14:51:55 CST
15:51:55 KST

WELLINGTON, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- The New Zealand government introduced a bill to strengthen customs' ability to combat organized crime and growing border threats, a senior official said Wednesday.
The Customs and Excise (Border Security) Amendment Bill aims to update legislation to address changes in the border threat environment, including a "massive increase" in illicit drug seizures, Customs Minister Casey Costello said in a statement.
The volume of drug intercepts more than quadrupled from 1.5 tons in 2018 to 6.5 tons in 2024, while transnational, serious and organized crime groups are exploiting technology, legitimate trade and travel systems, and people with access to secure border areas such as baggage handlers, Costello said.
The bill would strengthen security requirements in customs-controlled areas and export storage facilities, increase penalties for serious offending, provide customs with additional operational powers, modernize information-sharing and digital border capabilities, and enhance officer safety, according to the statement.
Customs also needs improved powers to address the growing trade in child exploitation material, the minister said.
"When the original Customs and Excise Bill was passed in 1996, the main border issues involved individuals, offensive material in magazines and on videos and people trying to bring in extra cartons of duty-free cigarettes," she said, adding that customs is now dealing with criminal cartels involved in serious, high-value crimes backed by threats, intimidation and violence.
The bill recognizes customs' role in protecting national security and establishes a framework for information sharing with industry partners, Costello said. ■

Emerson and Marquette surveys also show a clear Democratic edge as control of Congress approaches a decisive test, Newsweek reported.
Candidates in competitive House and Senate races face a political climate shaped by dissatisfaction with the country’s direction and President Donald Trump’s low approval.
National generic-ballot polls measure which party voters prefer for Congress rather than testing named candidates.
They offer a broad view of the political environment, but local campaigns, district boundaries and turnout will determine who wins.
Quantus Insights’ survey of 1,389 likely voters, conducted September 15 to 18, found 50.3 percent supporting the Democratic candidate in their congressional district and 41.7 percent favoring the Republican.
Another 6.3 percent were undecided and 1.7 percent selected another candidate. The design-adjusted margin of error was plus or minus 2.9 percentage points.
Democrats retained an advantage among habitual voters.
Respondents who participated in the 2022 midterms favored the party 50 percent to 43.9 percent, while people who voted in all four general elections from 2018 through 2024 broke 50.3 percent to 43.9 percent.
Several demographic divides help explain the overall result.

World leaders want to strengthen oversight of AI, while Trump is betting on "superintelligence" - media
Kyiv • UNN
UN leaders call for stronger oversight of AI and the creation of global safeguards. Trump opposes regulation and supports the term "superintelligence".
Artificial intelligence has become one of the main topics of the UN General Assembly following cases in which the technology escaped human control, while warnings from industry representatives sparked global alarm and calls for stronger state oversight of the sector. Euronews reports, writes UNN.
Details
UN Secretary-General António Guterres opened the speeches by world leaders at the General Assembly with a call for stronger oversight of AI, issuing a vivid, though somewhat grim, warning about what could go wrong.
Let us agree that decisions on which life and death depend must never be delegated to machines. Killer robots must have no place in our future
He had also warned about AI in his first address to the General Assembly ten years ago.
Saying that the world needs to "create the conditions for the responsible development of AI and the additional safeguards needed to counter the risks," the UN will discuss at the Security Council on Wednesday how to establish a degree of control over the technology. Some of the industry's best-known representatives will take part in the meeting.
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump reaffirmed his firm opposition to AI regulation, saying that the word "artificial" diminishes the significance of the technology, and expressing hope that the rest of the world would adopt the new term.
"Super Intelligence" "sounds much better" and is "much more accurate," he said.
Trump wants to rename artificial intelligence as "superintelligence"22.09.26, 19:15 • 4640 views
He also compared warnings from AI safety advocates with warnings about climate change, whose anthropogenic nature is confirmed by the overwhelming majority of the scientific community.
Other countries call for safeguards
Ahead of the UN General Assembly, leaders of more than 20 predominantly European countries called for mandatory safety measures for advanced AI, warning that the development of the technology could outpace people's ability to control it.
China and the United States, the global leaders in AI, did not support the idea.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that during the UK's presidency of the G20 in 2027, the country would begin work on establishing global standards in the field of AI. He also announced a partnership with Washington in the defense sector aimed at detecting cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.
French President Emmanuel Macron proposed creating AI technology independent of the major powers.
I do not want anyone to become a vassal of one of the major powers. Our investment capabilities must be pooled to create an advanced open-source AI model that we can share. We must not depend on anyone else
The American tech giants themselves are increasingly calling for global coordination on AI safety issues. Sam Altman of OpenAI is expected to address the UN Security Council on Wednesday.
France, which holds the presidency of the Security Council this month, initiated the meeting, believing that the threat posed by AI to international peace and security has so far been insufficiently discussed at the UN.
